PLAYCRAFT: DESIGNING ENGAGING GAMES
FROM AGENT PLAY EXPERIENCE
Weihao Cheng
weihao.cheng@proton.me
ABSTRACT
Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily
engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires
extensive human play and tuning. We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework
that uses a vision-based agent to play games and draws on its detailed play experi-
ence to revise them for mastery. Starting from an initial game, PlayCraft alternates
between playing and crafting. In the playing stage, a player agent watches the game
screen, uses the controls, and pursues the game objective over repeated episodes
while retaining memory. After each episode, it reports its progress, outcomes,
decisions, and reflections. In the crafting stage, a crafter agent uses these reports
to revise the game. It estimates player abilities, predicts performance at different
proficiency levels, and compares those predictions with a target learning progres-
sion. It diagnoses the game and addresses the gaps by giving players meaningful
opportunities to improve through better decisions and execution. We evaluate
games in fresh runs with player agents across three intelligence settings, measuring
learning gain and learning slope. Compared with the initial games, PlayCraft yields
larger learning gains and steeper learning slopes in most games. It also outperforms
the baselines on the macro-average of each metric at every intelligence setting.
Website: https://xt4d.github.io/playcraft-web
Code: https://github.com/xt4d/PlayCraft
1
INTRODUCTION
Recent AI agents can generate playable games from human instructions (Huang et al., 2026), but
making these games engaging remains difficult. A central source of engagement is mastery, which is
the process of developing strategies and skills to overcome the challenges of a game (Koster, 2004).
A game supports mastery when players initially achieve limited success but reach substantially better
results as they become more proficient. This progression motivates repeated play, but designing for it
requires extensive human play and tuning. We therefore study how to automatically generate games
that support mastery.
Prior work generates games that reward stronger play by using play results from computational
players to guide designs (Togelius & Schmidhuber, 2008; Nasir et al., 2026). However, the strategies
these players find through search or game-specific training may differ from those people develop,
making their behavior less representative of human play. Other systems use feedback from repeated
playtests to revise generated games (Huang et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a). These
systems prioritize overall game quality, with limited explicit focus on player learning through practice.
Recent agents based on foundation models, such as GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026b), can play 2D and
3D games directly from rendered frames (Yu, 2026; Aggarwal & Welleck, 2026). They perceive only
what the game shows, act through the same controls as human players, and can learn from earlier
experience. They can also report their understanding of the game and the difficulties they encounter.
These capabilities make them suitable simulated players whose experience can shape challenges that
reward skillful play.
We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that starts from an initial playable game and alternates
between playing and crafting stages. In the playing stage, a foundation-model player agent observes

rendered frames and interacts with the game through the provided controls. It plays a series of
episodes, gaining experience with the mechanics and challenges it encounters. The game resets
between attempts, while the player agent retains its memory and the lessons it has learned. After each
episode, it writes a report covering its progress, outcomes, decisions, and reflections. In the crafting
stage, a crafter agent uses these reports to diagnose and revise the game to promote engagement
through mastery. It first estimates the baseline abilities that the player agent has before playing the
game. Using these abilities and the observed play, it estimates player performance in the current
game at beginner, intermediate, and expert levels. It then identifies gaps between these estimates and
a target progression, defined by performance anchors relative to the expected expert outcome. Lastly,
it addresses these gaps by revising the game to provide meaningful opportunities for better decisions
and execution, while preserving the objectives and core identity of the game.
We conduct experiments covering ten 2D and 3D games with varied execution and planning demands.
The games are evaluated at three agent intelligence settings using the visual play protocol from the
playing stage. We use gains in agent performance across episodes as a proxy for mastery, assuming
that the learning patterns of the player agent resemble those of human players. We compute learning
gain and learning slope (Li et al., 2026) for the initial games, games produced by PlayCraft, and
games revised through code analysis alone or playtesting with policy-based controllers. Compared
with the initial games, PlayCraft increases macro-average learning gain by 2.7, 14.0, and 21.9
percentage points at the Low, Medium, and High intelligence settings, respectively. Its macro-average
learning slope increases by 2.09 and 2.64 at Medium and High, respectively, and is nearly tied at
Low. PlayCraft also achieves higher macro-averages for both metrics than either baseline at every
intelligence setting.
2
RELATED WORK
Mastery and player experience. Game design theory has long tied engagement to learning. Koster
(2004) argues that games are fun because players learn their patterns and develop mastery, and self-
determination theory links enjoyment and continued play to perceived competence (Ryan et al., 2006).
Linehan et al. (2014) analyze how successful puzzle games pace their challenges as players learn.
Experience-driven procedural content generation (Yannakakis & Togelius, 2011) uses computational
models of player experience to guide the search for game content that elicits a desired experience.
PlayCraft takes mastery as its design goal and uses a surrogate based on gains in player performance
across repeated attempts.
Automatic game design with computational players. Automatic playtesting uses computational
players to simulate distinct play styles (Holmg˚ard et al., 2018), estimate difficulty for human players
(Gudmundsson et al., 2018), and predict player churn (Roohi et al., 2021). Agent performance
can also guide the selection of candidate designs or the tuning of game parameters. Togelius &
Schmidhuber (2008) evolve the rules of small grid games and score each game by how well neural
controllers learn to play it, treating learnability as a surrogate for fun. Later work uses self-play to
evaluate board-game quality (Browne & Maire, 2010) and exact game-theoretic values for restricted
play to assess competitive balance (Jaffe et al., 2012). Other systems use the win rate of a stronger
agent against a weaker one as a proxy for game depth (Liu et al., 2017; Todd et al., 2024). Mortar
(Nasir et al., 2026) applies this idea to game code, evolving game mechanics through LLM-driven
quality-diversity search and rewarding games in which fixed agents (MCTS with different budgets,
random, and no-op) rank in their expected order of skill. Fly, Fail, Fix (Zook et al., 2025) uses
a pretrained DQN to play Flappy Bird. It then uses GPT-4.1 (OpenAI, 2025) to adjust the pipe
parameters (gap size, spacing, and speed) based on the resulting play metrics and frame strips to
bring the score closer to a target. Computational players that rely on search or game-specific training
may behave differently from humans, require substantial computation to learn unfamiliar games, and
offer little insight into their decisions or difficulties. To better approximate human play, PlayCraft
uses a foundation-model agent that infers mechanics from visual cues, draws on prior knowledge to
begin playing, and reflects on earlier attempts to improve. The agent can also explain its decisions
and link difficulties to specific situations in the game.
LLM-based game generation and revision. LLM agents now generate playable games by decom-
posing prompts into hierarchical plans, coordinating specialized development and review agents,
and reusing skills and knowledge from earlier projects (Earle et al., 2024; Yin et al., 2026; Jiang
2
et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026). Benchmarks evaluate the resulting games through multimodal judging
and interaction-based tests (Zhang et al., 2025b; Luo et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b). Several
recent systems use playtest feedback to refine the games they generate. Play2Code (Huang et al.,
2026) alternates HTML game generation with playtesting by a rubric-blind GUI agent that returns
gameplay traces and actionable feedback. RSIGame (Wu et al., 2026) uses targeted playtests to
diagnose issues and verify edits, while a separate monitor compares builds and retains the one it
judges best. Recursive Game Creator (Chen et al., 2026a) organizes recursive refinement around
Designer, Builder, Player, and Reviewer roles. Its Player writes reusable policies that act through
programmatic interfaces, and its Reviewer uses the resulting trajectories to infer player preferences
and recommend changes. These systems aim to enhance overall game quality. PlayCraft focuses on
mastery, revising games so that players can improve their performance through practice.
Visual game-playing agents. Agents can play commercial video games through the same interface as
human players, choosing keyboard and mouse actions based on screen observations (Tan et al., 2024;
SIMA Team, 2024). Early benchmarks found that agents often struggled to use those observations to
make sustained progress toward game objectives (Paglieri et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a). More
recent benchmarks demonstrate the visual game-playing capabilities of GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026b).
On LOLPlay, it completed 9 of 36 League of Legends tasks using screenshots (Yu, 2026). In the
online track of GameHorizon-Bench, it completed 9 of 20 multi-step tasks in Minecraft (Wang et al.,
2026). On Gym-Anything-RT, it passed 9% of the minigames in real time and 75% with the games
paused between decisions (Aggarwal & Welleck, 2026). PlayCraft draws on these advances in visual
gameplay by using a foundation-model agent that observes rendered frames and acts through the
same controls available to human players.
Agent learning from experience. Agents can draw on earlier play when facing a new attempt or task.
Reflexion carries lessons from completed trials into later attempts (Shinn et al., 2023), and Voyager
stores acquired skills for reuse in new tasks (Wang et al., 2023). Learn2Play Bench measures agent
improvement over repeated attempts at text games with unfamiliar rules, using metrics such as the
learning gain between early and late episodes (Li et al., 2026). PlayCraft uses experience from the
player agent to guide game design and assesses support for mastery through performance gains across
episodes.
3
METHODOLOGY
3.1
FOUNDATION MODELS AS PLAYERS
Recent AI agents based on foundation models such as GPT-6 can play both 2D and 3D games like
human players. Given a brief game instruction, they infer the mechanics from screenshots, interact
through the provided controls, observe the outcomes, and improve their performance with continued
play. Three properties make them suitable as automatic players:
• They can draw on prior knowledge of game genres, controls, and conventions to begin
playing an arbitrary game.
• They can play from rendered frames and use the same controls as human players, so their
performance can reflect the visual cues and control demands that shape human play.
• They can learn across attempts by testing hypotheses about rules and strategies, then carrying
the lessons into later episodes. They can also report on their play experience, describing the
situations they encounter and sharing their perspective on the game.
Together, these capabilities let a foundation-model agent learn through repeated play and provide
valuable information for game design.
3.2
PLAYCRAFT
3.2.1
OVERVIEW
PlayCraft is an automated framework that designs games for mastery. It starts from an initial playable
game G0 and produces revised games G1, . . . , GK. Each play–craft iteration k = 0, . . . , K −1 has
two stages. In the playing stage, the player agent receives a brief game instruction and pursues the

a playing stage and a crafting stage. In the playing stage, the player agent receives a brief game

It then proposes and implements changes that address the gaps and give players room to improve
through better decisions and execution, producing Gk+1 for the next iteration. Figure 1 illustrates the
PlayCraft loop.
3.2.2
PLAYING STAGE
Setup. The player agent begins with a fresh context containing a brief game instruction that states
the objective, basic rules, and available controls. The player agent observes only rendered frames and
cannot inspect the game code or access the Internet. It generates every control action through model
inference rather than writing a program to control the game.
Interaction. A run consists of E episodes. Each episode ends when the game reaches a defined
endpoint or the active play budget T is exhausted. Game frames are captured at intervals of O,
and the player agent makes a decision at intervals of W. At each decision, it receives the frames
captured during the preceding decision interval and returns an action plan for the next interval of play.
The plan is a sequence of A control actions, each lasting for a duration W/A. A control action is
a combination of keys, mouse buttons, and mouse movements. While the plan executes, the game
advances and renders frames, which are included in the next decision request so that the player
observes the consequences of its previous plan. Game timers and animations pause while the model
generates the next action plan, so decision latency does not consume play time. With each plan,
the player also reports the visible result, such as the current score, and provides brief notes on its
observations and choices.
Learning across episodes. The player agent maintains a single conversation throughout a run. The
game resets between episodes, but the player retains its memory. After each episode, the player
reviews its play and writes a report covering (1) the starting conditions; (2) its progress, including
milestones and failures; (3) the final result; (4) its key decisions and the alternatives it considered;
(5) its perception of the game, including its understanding of the mechanics, points of confusion,
perceived difficulty, and discrepancies between expected and observed outcomes; and (6) the lessons
it learned. The player then updates a consolidated set of natural-language lessons, retaining supported
lessons, merging overlapping ones, and revising or removing contradicted ones. It begins the next
4
episode with its memory of earlier attempts and the updated lessons. The reports of all episodes form
the play record of the run, which is passed to the crafting stage.
3.2.3
CRAFTING STAGE
Design targets. The crafter agent revises the game toward two targets. The first is to ensure that
players at each proficiency level can meet the corresponding predefined performance target. The most
skilled players should be able to complete the objective within the active play budget T. In games
without an objective, they should be able to experience the core loop and major challenges within that
budget. Their expected result defines the 100% reference. Beginners and intermediate players should
achieve r0% and r1% of the expert reference, respectively, with r0 < r1. These results must come
from strategies that would remain advantageous without the time limit. The second is to give players
meaningful opportunities to improve through better decisions and execution. The game should make
the benefits, costs, and risks of different choices clear and allow expected performance to continue
rising as players gain skill.
Active play budget. We assume that players have a finite active play budget T, which can be set
arbitrarily large. Introducing T provides a reference range for player performance, allowing the
crafter agent to identify and address gaps between estimated performance and the anchors. Changing
T can affect the progression of the resulting game because the crafter uses play observed within that
budget as evidence for its design.
Diagnosis. The crafter agent reads the game instruction, the play records of all available runs, and
the archived history of earlier iterations. Because E episodes may not suffice for the player agent to
reach expert-level performance, the crafter agent cannot determine the 100% reference directly from
the records. It therefore first estimates the baseline abilities that the player agent has before playing
the game, including screen perception, control execution, and strategy discovery. A player without
prior experience of a game is not necessarily unskilled. From these abilities and the observed play,
it estimates the expected results of beginner, intermediate, and expert players in the current game
and compares them with the anchors. Where the estimates deviate from the anchors, it diagnoses
the causes, considering entry difficulty; demands on understanding, perception, and execution;
opportunities for strategic choice; reward structure; challenge progression; and performance ceiling.
If an earlier proposal exists, it also checks which expectations in that proposal the new records
support, contradict, or leave untested. It then chooses between building on the earlier direction and
exploring a new one.
Proposal. The crafter agent then writes a focused design proposal. It prioritizes distinctive changes or
additions that enable new strategies and meaningful choices while preserving the defining interactions

Figure 1 | O2LaF: One Prior, Two Dynamics — a self-supervised Latent Action learning Framework. Latent
actions from unlabeled videos share one unified space (center): e.g., the same 𝑧inferred from 1st- and
3rd-person videos drives turn right in both navigation and robot scenes (top). They also transfer zero-shot
across embodiments and domains (bottom).
Abstract. Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action
learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely
from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for both inverse and
forward dynamics. We introduce O2LaF, built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize
both models from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them to their distinct roles: a feed-forward
transition encoder with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics, and a causal, action-conditioned video
generator for forward dynamics. By controlling information access and optimizing both dynamics end-to-end
through a compact bottleneck, O2LaF learns transferable actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation
and robotic manipulation, O2LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing and enables stronger
zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments. Beyond generative video priors, we further
extend our framework to predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, achieving competitive performance.
Our findings suggest a broader paradigm for latent-action learning: repurposing pretrained video models to
discover transferable actions and predict their consequences.
1. Introduction
Videos provide abundant observations of how the world changes, but rarely reveal the actions that cause
those changes [1–3]. This missing supervision limits our ability to learn controllable world models [4–11] and
embodied agents [12–16] from internet-scale video.
Latent action learning [2, 17, 18] offers a way to recover such supervision directly from visual transitions. A
latent action model typically consists of an inverse dynamics model (IDM), which infers a latent action from
an observed transition, and a forward dynamics model (FDM), which predicts its consequence:

Figure 2 | Paradigms for self-supervised latent-action learning. Existing methods learn latent actions
(a) from scratch [3, 19, 20], (b) on frozen visual features [21, 22], (c) with a pretrained video generator as the
FDM only [23, 24], or (d) with an external video prior as auxiliary supervision [25]. Ours repurposes one
pretrained video DiT as both the IDM and the FDM.
A compact bottleneck limits what 𝑧𝑡can encode, encouraging it to retain important information to explain
visual changes. Learning useful latent actions therefore depends on both dynamics: the IDM must infer the
transition, while the FDM must depend on the inferred action to predict its consequence.
Existing methods differ in where pretrained priors enter this pipeline (Fig. 2), leaving a gap on each side.
On the inverse side, IDMs are learned from scratch, either on raw pixels [3, 19, 20] or on top of frozen
pretrained features [21, 22, 26]. They must learn to infer actions from transitions largely through the FDM’s
reconstruction supervision, and such specialized latent action models are outperformed by general visual
foundation models [26]. Olaf-World [25] aligns latent actions with an external video representation to improve
transferability, but its IDM is still learned from scratch. On the forward side, recent methods adopt a
pretrained video generator as the FDM [23, 24], whose initial-frame conditioning supplies appearance, reducing
its leakage into the latent actions. However, they keep the standard diffusion recipe, under which the generator
can learn to disregard the latent action [24], underusing its prior as a learning signal. Yet modern video
Diffusion Transformers (video DiTs) [27] are pretrained at scale to model how visual states evolve over
time [28–34]. Their representations encode rich temporal structure, while their generative dynamics learn to
predict complex visual changes. Much of the prior needed for latent action learning therefore already exists
inside a pretrained video generator. This raises a simple question: can a pretrained video DiT serve both
inverse and forward dynamics for latent action learning? Doing so is nontrivial: the two dynamics place
different demands on the same video prior, requiring careful control over what each can access.
We introduce O2LaF, a self-supervised latent-action framework built on a simple principle: one prior, two
dynamics. We initialize the IDM and FDM from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them independently
for their respective roles. For inverse dynamics, we repurpose the video DiT as a feed-forward transition
encoder, where action queries extract one compact latent action per visual transition under causal temporal
attention. For forward dynamics, we retain the generative role of the video DiT and introduce causal joint
prediction, which predicts the future state sequence jointly, conditioned on the inferred latent actions, while
preserving temporal causality. Unlike visual synthesis, where training often emphasizes intermediate-noise
timesteps [35, 36], the FDM here also provides the learning signal that shapes the latent-action space. At these
partially noisy timesteps, the noisy future still reveals much of the target, allowing the FDM to predict the
future with little reliance on the latent action. We therefore train at high noise, which suppresses this target
leakage and forces the FDM to depend on the inferred action. The two dynamics are optimized end-to-end
through a compact continuous latent-action space.
We further systematically study how the two dynamics shape the learned action space. For example, causal
joint prediction outperforms autoregressive prediction by removing clean-history shortcuts, while role-specific
noise levels reveal distinct information requirements for the two dynamics. Beyond generative video priors, we
also extend the repurposing principle to self-supervised predictive representation models [37] and language-
supervised video multimodal models [38] as alternative IDM backbones. Interestingly, stronger action probing
performance does not necessarily translate into better downstream generative control, highlighting the
importance of validating latent actions beyond probing through downstream applications.
We evaluate O2LaF across camera navigation and robotic manipulation. It sets a new state of the art in
few-shot action probing across both discrete and continuous action spaces, indicating stronger alignment with
ground-truth actions. Beyond probing, the learned actions also transfer without target adaptation, enabling
2
Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Self-Supervised Latent Action Learning
zero-shot control across first- and third-person navigation and human-to-robot transfer in manipulation. The
causal FDM readily serves as a video world model, while its learned action-conditioned dynamics provide a
strong initialization for higher-fidelity two-stage deployment. Our contributions are threefold:
• We introduce O2LaF, a self-supervised latent-action framework that repurposes a pretrained video DiT
into end-to-end trained inverse and forward dynamics models.
• Through a systematic study, we show that latent-action learning depends critically on how the two
dynamics are factorized and what information they receive.
• O2LaF achieves state-of-the-art few-shot action probing across camera navigation and robotic manipula-
tion, while demonstrating strong zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments and
reusable action-conditioned dynamics for world modeling.
2. Related Work
2.1. Latent Action Learning from Videos
Latent action learning turns large-scale action-unlabeled video into a reusable intermediate control rep-
resentation. The same representation can be consumed by a world model to control future visual evolu-
tion [3, 20, 22, 25, 39], or produced by a policy or planner as a surrogate for physical actions [2, 19, 21, 40–42].
Recent work further seeks to make this control space transferable across contexts and embodiments [25, 43–45].
Existing methods differ in where pretrained priors enter the inverse–forward dynamics pipeline (Fig. 2). Early
approaches learn both transition inference and prediction directly from the target videos [2, 3, 19, 20]. To
reduce shortcuts from raw-pixel reconstruction, later methods move the prediction target into pretrained
semantic feature spaces, emphasizing motion and task-relevant change over appearance details [21, 41, 46]. A
related direction strengthens the forward model with pretrained video priors, reducing appearance burden or
replacing the from-scratch FDM [23, 24, 47]. Pretrained video representations have also been used as external
temporal supervision to orient latent actions across visual contexts [25].
Orthogonal to where the prior enters, prior work also constrains the latent space through discrete or continuous
bottlenecks [22, 47, 48], semantic or cross-view objectives [49–52], motion and consistency supervision [53–56],
and physical or geometric grounding [40, 57]. These constraints are complementary to the structural question
of how the dynamics themselves are initialized. Motivated by the shared need for transition reasoning in both
inverse and forward dynamics, O2LaF repurposes the same pretrained video DiT for both.
2.2. Repurposing Pretrained Video Diffusion Transformers
Pretrained video generative models encode reusable spatiotemporal structure beyond synthesis. Prior work
exploits their internal representations for correspondence, tracking, and geometry [58–60], while more recent
methods repurpose the generative backbone itself for feed-forward perception and temporal reasoning [61–63].
Together, these works show that video generative pretraining provides reusable temporal computation, not
only a synthesis model.
This repurposing is increasingly extending to action learning. Recent robot-policy and world-action models use
pretrained video generators as predictive representations, policy backbones, or priors for action experts [64–69].
These methods transfer video priors into learning a physical action space grounded by robot supervision.
O2LaF instead uses the video prior to discover the action representation itself from action-free video.
3. Method
We introduce O2LaF, a self-supervised latent action learning framework. Our key premise is that large-scale
video pretraining already captures how visual states evolve, which both inverse and forward dynamics need.
We therefore initialize both from the same pretrained prior, but adapt each to its role by controlling what
information it can access.
3

3.1. Preliminaries and Motivation

VAE, a text encoder, and a video DiT. The VAE maps an RGB video V to 𝐾+1 spatiotemporal latent states
x = (𝑥0, . . . , 𝑥𝐾). Under rectified flow [35, 71], a clean video latent x is interpolated with Gaussian noise

clean video latents and 𝑡= 1 to pure Gaussian noise.
Action-aware video prior. Prior work [58–60, 63] has shown that pretrained video DiTs contain strong
temporal correspondence, enabling subjects or points to be tracked across video frames. We ask a different

SoK: Assessing the Evolution of LLM Capability in Software Vulnerability Research
Amine Lbath∗§, Manan Suri‡, Aurelien Delaitre∗, Vadim Okun∗, Massih-Reza Amini§ and Dinesh Manocha‡
∗National Institute of Standards and Technology
§Université Grenoble Alpes, CNRS
‡University of Maryland, College Park
Abstract—LLM-based agents are becoming increasingly capa-
ble at discovering, validating and patching vulnerabilities in
real software, and vendors and researchers report that this
is already changing how vulnerabilities are found and fixed.
These claims, however, are scattered across papers, vendor re-
ports and disclosures and are rarely comparable. We introduce
a framework that rates these capabilities on an autonomy scale
modeled on the levels of driving automation, and qualifies each
claim by its correctness, its availability and the strength of its
evidence. We use this framework to systematize the published
evidence on LLM capability in vulnerability research. We find
that agents discovered, validated, and patched vulnerabilities
in real-world software without human intervention before the
restricted frontier models of 2026, and that open-weight models
subsequently attained comparable autonomy for discovery and
validation. We then measure the consequences of evolving LLM
security capabilities in a decade of public vulnerability records,
advisories and exploitation data. In 2026 the number of dis-
closed vulnerabilities more than doubled, with an increasing
share rated critical or high, and severe bugs that had survived
a decade or more in widely used code were reported several
times more often than before. Yet the time between the stages
of a vulnerability’s life, from report to fix and from disclosure
to attack, has not shifted noticeably so far. We grade the
mitigations proposed in the literature with an explicit rubric
and draw guidance for each group of stakeholders from the
best-supported ones.
Index Terms—vulnerability research, LLM-based agents, au-
tonomy levels, vulnerability lifecycle, measurement, systemati-
zation of knowledge
1. Introduction
Software vulnerability research covers discovering vul-
nerabilities, proving that they are real and fixing them.
Automated tools such as fuzzers and static analyzers can
surface large numbers of candidate bugs, yet because many
of these candidates are false positives, triage, proof and
repair have remained the work of human experts. Recent
reports suggest that LLM-based systems are increasingly
Preprint. This work has not yet been peer reviewed.
capable of carrying out these steps autonomously on real
software. Google’s Big Sleep agent reported zero-day vul-
nerabilities in real-world code as early as 2024 [1]. By
2025, a growing number of systems, among them those
of DARPA’s AI Cyber Challenge (AIxCC), were finding
and patching vulnerabilities in open-source projects [2],
[3]. In April 2026, Anthropic reported that Claude Mythos
Preview had found thousands of high- and critical-severity
vulnerabilities, almost always without human intervention,
and restricted the model to selected partners [4], [5]. In
July 2026, agents under evaluation at OpenAI exploited a
previously unknown vulnerability to leave their environment
and attacked several systems, including those of Hugging
Face [6].
These reports have raised concern among practitioners,
who describe a “Vulnpocalypse”, a surge of findings that
maintainers may be unable to absorb [7], [8]. Labs warn
that exploits could follow fixes within hours [9], while others
expect the supply of bugs to run out once existing code has
been swept [10], [11]. Assessing these expectations requires
evidence on two questions, namely what these systems have
been shown to do, and what has changed so far in the
vulnerability lifecycle.
Neither question is easy to answer from the published
evidence. Capability reports describe tasks that range from
flagging suspicious code to delivering an accepted fix, and
they differ in how much a human contributed. Their correct-
ness also varies widely, from expert precision for the best
systems [12] to large numbers of invalid reports received by
maintainers [13]. Many reports come from the organizations
that build the systems, benchmarks tend to rely on curated
targets [14], and the most capable models are often reachable
only through interfaces that their developers control [15].
Statements about the consequences come from the same
parties and are rarely compared with public records.
In this SoK, we address both questions and treat them
as complementary. For the first, we introduce, to our knowl-
edge, the first framework that assesses the demonstrated
autonomy of LLM-based systems separately for each task of
vulnerability research, over time and across levels of access.
Following the Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) levels
of driving automation [16], we define each autonomy level
by the part of the task that remains with the human. A level
counts only when most of the results hold up, and every
arXiv:2611.26601v1  [cs.CR]  19 Nov 2026
claim also receives an access tier, from internal lab use to
open weights, and an evidence grade. To apply the frame-
work, we built an agentic workflow that collected more than
50,000 unique sources, including academic publications,
lab and vendor reports, maintainers’ accounts and incident
disclosures. Independent agents searched this indexed corpus
for the most relevant evidence on real software and scored
it, supporting each score with a quote checked against the
source. Two authors then reviewed the 128 dated steps
of the resulting map, and our conclusions draw only on
steps backed by direct evidence on real software. For the
second question, we collected the consequences commonly
expected of these capabilities from 503 verified statements
by labs, vendors, maintainers, government agencies and
researchers, and compared these expectations with a decade
of public records. These comprise more than 300,000 CVE
records [17] with their severity, the age of the vulnerable
code where it is known, the first public exploits and the
listings as exploited, as well as the timelines of about
1,400 coordinated disclosures and the records of disclosure
programs.
RQ1: What is the current capability of LLM-based
systems, in terms of autonomy and correctness, to
discover, validate and patch vulnerabilities in real-
world software? (Section 5.1)
RQ2: How has this capability evolved since 2024?
(Section 5.2)
RQ3: How rapidly do capabilities first demonstrated
by frontier-lab systems diffuse to publicly available
and open-weight models? (Section 5.3)
RQ4: What has changed so far in public vulnerabil-
ity records, and what has not? (Section 6)
RQ5: Which mitigations are supported by evidence,
and what guidance follows for each stakeholder?
(Section 7)
In addressing these questions, this paper makes four
contributions.
•
Assessment framework. To our knowledge, the first
framework that rates the demonstrated autonomy of
LLM-based systems for four tasks of vulnerability
research, together with the correctness of their re-
sults, their level of access and the strength of the
evidence (Section 3).
•
Capability map. A reproducible, dated map of
demonstrated capability since 2024 (Sections 4
and 5, Figure 1). Agents built it from a corpus of
more than 50,000 sources, and two authors reviewed
each of its steps. It shows that agents were able to
discover, validate and patch real vulnerabilities with-
out human intervention by October 2025, before the
restricted frontier models of 2026, that open-weight
models followed within months for discovery and
validation, and that remediation is the least measured
task.
•
Measurement of public records. A measurement
of the volume, severity and age of disclosed vul-
nerabilities, and of the time to fix and to attack,

in a decade of public records, compared with seven

closures more than doubled in 2026, with a growing
share rated Critical or High and several times more
old, severe bugs, whereas the time to fix and to attack
has not shifted noticeably so far.
•
Mitigations and research agenda. A rubric-based
grading of 15 proposed mitigations, followed by
guidance for each group of stakeholders and open
problems (Sections 7 and 8). The best-supported mit-
igations are established practices of secure design,
whereas those built on LLMs are the least measured.
2. Background and Related Work
Software vulnerability research.
Vulnerability re-
search begins with selecting a target and discovering a flaw,
which must then be validated, usually by a proof that it
can be triggered. Once the flaw is reported, the maintainer
triages it, develops and validates a patch, and releases it,
and operators finally deploy the fix. Under coordinated vul-
nerability disclosure, the finder gives the maintainer a fixed
period, commonly 90 days, to release a fix before the details
become public [18]. This practice presumes that discovery
is scarce, so that a reported vulnerability is unlikely to be
found by someone else before it is fixed. By one estimate,
only about 5.7% of privately held zero-day vulnerabilities
are rediscovered by others each year [19]. Deployment has
also consistently lagged behind the fix. In enterprises, a
patch for client software can take more than six months to
reach 90% of the machines [20].
Measuring the vulnerability lifecycle.
A long line
of empirical work has measured the lifecycle of vulner-
abilities. Zero-day attacks have been found to last 312
days on average before disclosure [21], and in one study
about 7% of 4,080 security fixes failed to fully remove
the vulnerability [22]. How often coordinated disclosure
achieves its intended order, with the fix available before the
details are public and before attacks begin, has also been
modeled and measured [23]. Whether finding vulnerabilities
eventually depletes them remains an open question. No clear
depletion was found in mature software [24], whereas a
decline was observed in OpenBSD after years of audits [25],
and vulnerabilities in open-source code can survive for years
before they are fixed [26]. These studies have described a
lifecycle driven by humans and fuzzers. Since 2024, LLM-
based systems have also been discovering and reporting vul-
nerabilities in real software. We therefore examine whether
this lifecycle has changed, and measure on public records
the time from the report to the fix and from disclosure to
the first exploit and attack (Section 6).
Levels of autonomy.
The SAE levels of driving au-
tomation define each level by the part of the task that
remains with the human driver [16]. Similar levels have been
proposed for general-purpose models and agents [27], [28].
These levels describe how a system is designed or deployed,
so the same model can be placed at several levels. We adopt
the structure of these scales, but we define each level by what
a system has been shown to do on real targets, separately for
each task. Frontier labs have also defined their own cyber
capability thresholds, which determine the safeguards that
a model requires before release [29]–[31]. These thresholds
are assessed mostly through evaluations within each lab. Our
map complements them with a comparison across labs, tiers
and time that is based on real-world evidence.
Surveys
and
measurement.
Existing surveys of
LLMs in software security have organized the techniques
and benchmarks for vulnerability detection [32]–[35], re-
pair [36]–[39] and penetration testing [40], [41], and have
reviewed security agents [42]. These surveys each focus on
one part of vulnerability research, and they largely report
results on benchmarks. Benchmarks evaluate models on
capture-the-flag tasks and on reproduced or injected vul-
nerabilities [14], [43]–[45], so their scores do not establish
what a system has achieved on real software or how much
of the work remained with a human. Three lines of work are
closer to ours. Security agents have been rated at each stage
of vulnerability research by the depth of their results [46],
recent work has argued that the bottleneck has moved from
discovery to remediation [47], and government evaluators
have used task suites to track frontier models and the pace
at which open-weight models follow [15], [48]–[50].
To our knowledge, no prior work has assessed all four
tasks on real software by both autonomy and correctness,
dated each result, graded the evidence behind it and recorded
who can access the system (Table 1). The absence of such
an assessment has made it difficult to compare the reports
of labs, vendors and maintainers with one another, and to
judge the expectations that are drawn from them. Our map
provides this assessment. We further compare it with public
vulnerability records and grade the proposed mitigations,
which connects the demonstrated capability to its observed
consequences and to the evidence for each response.

3. Assessment Framework
Capabilities. We assess the four tasks of vulnerability
research whose individual results can be checked (Table 2).
Choosing targets is captured by the highest level of the
autonomy scale, and we return to deployment and disclosure,
which have no comparable check, in Section 6. Three of
the four capabilities can serve attackers and defenders alike,
whereas patching is primarily defensive. Discovery and re-
mediation each consist of a step that produces a result and a
step that checks it. Discover means reporting weaknesses in
a codebase, binary, or running service that prove to be real
vulnerabilities, without being pointed to a candidate. Vali-
date vulnerability means confirming or rejecting a candidate
from any source and, when the candidate is real, producing
a proof of vulnerability (PoV) such as a working exploit. A
PoV is an input or procedure that shows that the flaw is real.
Patch means delivering a fix that removes the cause without
breaking the software, where passing the PoV and the tests is
necessary but not sufficient [52], [53]. Validate patch means
accepting correct fixes and rejecting wrong ones.
Scope.
We assess vulnerability research on software,
including source code, binaries, firmware, smart contracts
and running web services. Our assessment ends at the proof
that a vulnerability is real. This proof counts as validation
even when it is a working exploit, and we report it only as
an outcome. What an attacker does with the vulnerability
afterwards, such as intrusion into a system, is outside our
scope, as are social engineering and network configuration,
which have no comparable check of correctness. Results
on targets built or seeded for an evaluation, such as the
vulnerabilities that the organizers of AIxCC injected into
open-source projects, count as benchmark evidence.
Autonomy.
The autonomy scale has six levels, from
A0 to A5 (Table 3). Following the SAE levels of driving
automation [16], each level is defined by the work that
remains with the human. At A0, the system contributes
nothing to the task. At A1, it advises a human who performs
every action, and at A2 it carries out the very specific steps
that a human specifies. From A3 upward, the system plans
and runs the task itself, and we refer to it as an LLM-
based agent. At A3, a human still prepares each target or
steps in when the agent gets stuck, whereas at A4 the agent
completes the task on a given target without any human
intervention. A human who checks the results afterwards
does not lower the level, since this check is how correctness
is measured. At A5, the agent also chooses its own targets
and works across many of them over long periods.
Correctness. Correctness measures the capability of a
system as the share of the outcomes it delivers, whether
vulnerabilities, verdicts or patches, that are deemed correct
by the party receiving them, such as the maintainer, the
vendor or an independent reviewer (Table 3). This share
corresponds to the precision of the system. We chose it
because every delivered result can be checked, whereas the
vulnerabilities that a system misses in real software are
unknown. It can also serve as a good proxy for the amount
of human review that the results still require. Sources also
report task completion, the share of the given targets for
which a system delivers a result, and recall. We record
both with each result and keep them separate from the
category. Results are below the bar (C0) when most of
them do not hold up, capable (C1) when most of them
hold up, and expert (C2) when they hold up as often as
an expert’s. We anchor expert to the expert rate published
for the capability, or to about nine results in ten when none
is published. Expert in audited code (C3) denotes expert
precision on code that experts and fuzzers had examined
for years. A system reaches an autonomy level only from
C1 upward, so a level shown at C0 does not count. Where
no source publishes a rate for a level that a system has
demonstrated, the reviewing authors assign the category

Yang Meng, Zixin Ding, Robert L. Grossman, Yuxin Chen
University of Chicago
Abstract
Acquiring every feature of an instance is often costly: a mea-
surement can carry a monetary price, a time delay, or a pri-
vacy cost. Active Feature Acquisition (AFA) addresses this by
learning a policy that decides, per instance, which features to
acquire under a budget. Existing AFA methods train this pol-
icy by optimizing a self-constructed utility target rather than
distilling an explicit teacher. We construct this teacher ex-
plicitly. At training time the label and the unobserved feature
values are available, and together they determine the teacher in
closed form: an oracle that ranks every candidate by its effect
on the downstream predictor’s error. OracleImitator dis-
tills this ranking into a deployable policy by soft-target imita-
tion. Across multimodal medical diagnosis and the AFABench
benchmark, OracleImitator matches or outperforms exist-
ing AFA methods across the budget range, recovering 90%
of the attainable accuracy gain at under a quarter of the ac-
quisition cost. Because the teacher is an explicit algorithmic
object rather than an implicit optimization target, we can also
measure directly how much of its ranking is recoverable by a
policy restricted to what is visible at deployment.
1
Introduction
In many applications, obtaining the feature values of a data
instance is not free. A clinical diagnosis draws on tests
that differ widely in monetary cost, turnaround time, and
invasiveness (Ma et al. 2019); discovering a new material
or molecule requires costly wet-lab experiments or simula-
tions, each consuming reagents, compute, or instrument time
(Shahriari et al. 2016; Meng et al. 2026a; Ding et al. 2024,
2026); and a sensing or robotic platform must spend power,
time, or motion for each measurement (Krause, Singh, and
Guestrin 2008). Therefore, acquiring the full feature set for
every instance is often infeasible, and even when it is possible
the cost rarely justifies the marginal gain. Active Feature Ac-
quisition (AFA) (Ma et al. 2019) addresses this by learning
to select, for each instance, a small and informative subset
of features to acquire, maximizing predictive performance
under a fixed acquisition budget.
Progress in the field has come from increasingly sophis-
ticated ways of constructing an acquisition objective: an
information reward under a partial generative model (Ma
et al. 2019), conditional mutual information estimated by
a learned network (Covert et al. 2023; Gadgil, Covert, and
Lee 2024), a non-parametric acquisition oracle (Valancius,
Lennon, and Oliva 2024), or long-horizon return optimized
by reinforcement learning (Shim, Hwang, and Yang 2018;
Zannone et al. 2019). Despite the algorithmic diversity, all
of these methods share a structural property: the supervi-
sion signal is self-constructed – these methods both define
the acquisition objective and optimize toward it, and the ac-
quisition policy is never supervised by an external teacher.
This naturally raises a question. At training time we already
have access to information the deployed policy never sees:
the true label, and the actual values of the candidates that
have not been acquired, which are exactly the ingredients a
myopic acquisition oracle needs to rank candidates in closed
form. If that supervision is available for free, why spend the
algorithmic effort designing yet another surrogate?
We instead construct the acquisition teacher explicitly, as
a deterministic algorithm that scores each candidate by the
error the downstream predictor would incur were it acquired.
We then train a deployable student to reproduce the teacher’s
ranking. Distilling a teacher’s ranking into a student is a
known method, but prior work splits into two families that our
setting sits between. On the one hand, in capacity distillation
the teacher is a learned, larger model and the students exist to
cut inference cost as in ranking distillation for recommenda-
tion (Tang and Wang 2018; Reddi et al. 2021) and reranker
compression for large language models (Sun et al. 2023).
On the other hand, in privileged-information distillation the
teacher can see inputs the students cannot access at test time
and the student aims to close that information gap rather than
to save compute (Lopez-Paz et al. 2015). OracleImitator
belongs to the second family and sharpens it in two aspects
to tailor for AFA settings. First, our teacher is not a learned
model but a closed form oracle computed from the training
labels and the unacquired feature values, so there is no teacher
to train and thus no teacher approximation error. Second, the
distillation object is a budget-constrained acquisition rank-
ing, so the student is re-queried at each partial-observation
state and only its top candidate is acquired per step. The
resulting student, OracleImitator, is a mask-conditioned
network trained by soft-KL under a random-mask prior, and
it never sees the label or the unacquired feature values at test
time (Figure 1).
Across multimodal medical diagnosis and the AFABench
benchmarks (Schütz et al. 2025), six datasets in total, this ap-
proach matches or outperforms specialized utility-learning

a quarter of the acquisition cost. Making the teacher an ex-
plicit algorithmic object also makes it analyzable. Once the
teacher is a concrete mapping from observed state to ranked
action, we can ask questions the AFA literature could not pre-
viously address directly: how much of the teacher’s behavior
is recoverable by a student that sees only what is visible at
deployment, how student quality depends on the teacher it
distils, and which alternative explanations for the residual
oracle gap can be excluded by controlled ablations.
Contributions.
1. We reframe AFA as learning from an explicit privileged
acquisition teacher rather than from a self-constructed
utility surrogate (Section 2, formalized in Section 4).
2. We introduce OracleImitator, a deployable student pol-
icy trained by soft-target distillation from a myopic Brier
oracle under a random-mask prior (Section 4), and show it
matches or outperforms specialised utility learners across
six datasets (Section 5).
3. We use the explicit teacher as an instrument to study the
AFA problem itself, reporting a teacher-quality sweep
(Section 5.4), an empirical teacher-learnability diagnos-
tic, and controlled ablations that exclude architecture, pre-
dictor, cost scheme, and generalization as explanations for
the observed saturation (Section 6).
2
Related Work
Active feature acquisition (AFA).
AFA methods gener-
ate their acquisition supervision internally and differ mainly
in how. One line of work optimizes a self-constructed util-
ity (as stated in Section 1): EDDI (Ma et al. 2019) uses
an information-theoretic acquisition reward under a partial
VAE, Covert et al. (2023) amortize the greedy conditonal-
mutual-information policy, and DIME (Gadgil, Covert, and
Lee 2024) estimates the conditional mutual information it-
self. AACO (Valancius, Lennon, and Oliva 2024) applies
a nonparametric acquisition-conditioned oracle at inference,
whereas we distill an offline privileged oracle into a separate
deployable policy. A second line of work formulates acquisi-
tion as sequential decision-making problem and optimizes a
policy by RL (Shim, Hwang, and Yang 2018; Zannone et al.
2019; Kachuee et al. 2019; Jain et al. 2025). These methods
differ in what they optimize, utility versus return, but not
in where the signal comes from: the target is designed, not
distilled from a teacher. A recent benchmark further finds
that the RL-based methods often train unstably and do not
consistently outperform simpler greedy or oracle-based al-
ternatives (Schütz et al. 2025).
Learning from teachers.
A separate line of work learns
from an existing supervisor. Imitation learning and behavior
cloning (Pomerleau 1988; Ross, Gordon, and Bagnell 2011;
Osa et al. 2018) distil an expert’s demonstrations; learning us-
ing privileged information (Vapnik and Izmailov 2015; Vap-
nik and Vashist 2009) transfers a training-time-only signal
to the deployed model; and knowledge distillation (Hinton,
Vinyals, and Dean 2015; Bucilă, Caruana, and Niculescu-
Mizil 2006) matches a student to a pretrained teacher model.
In all cases, these works study how to transfer knowledge
from an existing teacher, rather than whether such a teacher
can be constructed in the first place.
Prediction under missing modalities.
Predicting from an
arbitrary observed subset is complementary to AFA: mask-
aware predictors trained under random feature masking pro-
duce a label from whatever has been acquired (Schütz et al.
2025; Gadgil, Covert, and Lee 2024; Covert et al. 2023). We
take such a predictor as given and study only which modali-
ties to acquire for it.
3
Problem Setup
3.1
Setting
Let x = (x(1), . . . , x(K)) ∈Rd be a feature vector parti-
tioned into K modalities, the units at which acquisition hap-
pens. In our motivating medical cohort a modality is a dis-
tinct diagnostic test (a clinical, transcriptomic, or histology
panel), each separately orderable; in the tabular benchmarks
a modality is an individual feature. Modality k carries an ac-
quisition cost ck ≥0, and we write c(S) = P

cost of a subset S ⊆[K]. A designated set FREE ⊆[K] is
available at no cost as ck = 0 for k ∈FREE. In the medical
setting these are the demographics recorded at intake. A sub-
set S ⊆{1, . . . , K} of already-observed modalities induces
a masked observation xS ∈Rd (values outside S are set to
zero) and a binary mask mS ∈{0, 1}K indicating S.
At each step t an acquisition policy π observes (xSt, mSt)

maps any observed subset to a class distribution, with pre-

the acquisition policy alone.
3.2
Learning objective
Call a policy deployable if it conditions only on the observed
(xS, mS), that is, never on the label y or on the values
of unacquired modalities. The subset a deployable policy π
acquires on input x under budget B is Sπ ≡Sπ(x, B). Our

in two ways. First, it is non-differentiable, as π enters only

4
Method: OracleImitator
The objective in Equation 1 is hard to optimize but easy to
evaluate offline: given a label and a full feature vector, the
effect of each candidate modality on the downstream error
can be measured directly, even though neither the label nor
the unacquired values is available at deployment.
Our method.
We treat the offline computation as a teacher
and learn a deployable student that imitates it. On training
data, we score every unacquired modality by the error the
shared predictor would incur if that modality were added, and
turn the scores into a ranking over candidates. We then train
a policy that sees only the observed subset and its mask to
reproduce that ranking. The teacher is discarded after training
and the student is deployable as-is.

The teacher
For a training pair (xi, yi) and observed subset S, the teacher
scores each candidate a /∈S by the Brier score (Brier 1950)

that the teacher ranks candidates by the quality of the full

and Raftery 2007). Boundedness also keeps a single catas-

terminology of Vapnik and Izmailov (2015), the teacher is
privileged in two ways, both of which disqualify at deploy-
ment: it reads the label yi, and it reads the value x(a) of a
modality it has not paid for.
Why a myopic teacher?
A natural alternative is a finite-
horizon oracle that plans several acquisitions ahead. We use
the one step version instead, for two reasons. First, it is well-
defined given nothing but the trained fθ, whereas a plan-
ning oracle introduces its own search hyperparameters and
its own approximation error. Second, on our datasets the
gains from non-myopic planning are limited, consistent with
the benchmark finding that this benefit is strongly dataset-
dependent (Schütz et al. 2025). We revisit this choice in
Appendix A.1.
Why this makes distillation easy.
Two properties of
teacher matter for downstream accuracy. First, it is an al-
gorithm rather than a fitted model: given (xi, yi, S) and fθ,
its scores are determined. There is no teacher to train on and
no teacher approximation error between the student and the
objective, in contrast to distilling a trained network (Hin-
ton, Vinyals, and Dean 2015; Vapnik and Izmailov 2015).
Second, the fθ inside the teacher is the same predictor the
student passes through at deployment, so the acquisition sig-
nal is measured on the model that will actually be scored. No
auxiliary per-mask classifier is trained.
4.2
The student
The student πϕ(a | xS, mS) conditions only on the ob-
served subset and its mask, which makes it deployable by
construction. It is a small mask-conditioned MLP mapping
[mS ⊙x, mS] through a shared trunk into an action head,
with one logit per candidate, and an auxiliary classifier head
used only during training as a multi-task regularizer (Caru-
ana 1997; Kendall, Gal, and Cipolla 2018; Ding et al. 2024).
At deployment we take argmax over the unobserved, afford-
able candidates from the action head and discard the out-
puts of classifier head. Training the action head is behavior
cloning of the teacher (Pomerleau 1988): we minimize cross-
entropy against the teacher’s selection on states drawn from
randomly masked subsets. Because random masking exposes
the student to a broad range of reachable partial-observation

PGX: Physically Grounded Execution for Long-Horizon Humanoid
Loco-Manipulation
Kai Lu1, Chenyang Ma2, Ioannis Havoutis1
Abstract— Robotic vision-language-action (VLA) models can
execute diverse individual manipulation skills, yet they still
struggle with long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks, where tem-
poral structure, skills, and precision are tightly coupled within a
monolithic model. We propose Physically Grounded Execution
(PGX), a framework that offloads temporal and precision con-
trol to two classical training-free components, allowing the VLA
to focus on stage-specific skill dynamics. PGX decomposes long-
horizon loco-manipulation into three layers: (i) a predicate-
based state machine governs task progression, using physical
predicates to gate phase transitions, trigger recovery, and
coordinate navigation and waiting. Shared predicate semantics
connect offline demonstration segmentation, online execution,
and stage-wise evaluation; (ii) VLA skills operate within active
manipulation phases, with flat or stage-trained models con-
centrating on task-relevant actions; and (iii) world-coordinate
locking (WCL) maintains spatial consistency through base
station keeping, object-relative positioning, and world-anchored
contact targets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PGX with
extensive experiments conducted on three simulated tasks and
one real-world task using a Unitree G1 humanoid robot for
long-horizon loco-manipulation, showing improvements in stage
progression and task success rates. Project page is available at
https://kl-research.github.io/pgx.
I. INTRODUCTION
Humanoid loco-manipulation for long-horizon tasks is
central to embodied intelligence and generalist robotics, with
applications in domestic assistance, healthcare, and industrial
logistics. Yet even seemingly routine tasks in these domains
demand complex, extended coordination between locomotion
and manipulation. For instance, fetching a coffee or clearing
a table interleaves walking, contact-rich manipulation, and
precise object-part interaction over long action sequences.
The challenge lies in jointly addressing three tightly coupled
aspects: temporal structure, skill dynamics, and precise con-
trol, all of which must be grounded in physical interaction
and integrated within a unified visuomotor control framework
(see Fig. 1).
Traditional methods for loco-manipulation separate these
concerns across modules: task and motion planning or be-
havior trees control timing [1]–[3], model-based whole-body
control owns precision, and manipulation is realized by hand-
designed motion primitives. These systems are transparent
and precise, but every skill must be engineered for a specific
object and scene, and contact-rich skills remain brittle.

Long-horizon Loco-manipulation Tasks
Fig. 1: Humanoid long-horizon loco-manipulation. This
work studies humanoid loco-manipulation tasks: with the
same VLA model, the flat policy fails before the machine,
whereas our method PGX completes the task by keeping
timing and world-frame precision outside the network, and
the VLA executes only the manipulation stages.
Learning-based methods offer a more generalizable al-
ternative: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) [4]–[9]
and learned whole-body controllers [10]–[12] acquire trans-
ferable manipulation skills and locomotion behaviors from
data, reducing the need for task- or object-specific pro-
gramming. However, learning and executing the entire long-
horizon loco-manipulation task with a single policy in-
troduces difficulties in maintaining task progress, coordi-
nating reference frames, and handling highly imbalanced
demonstrations. Without an explicit representation of task
progress, visually similar observations from different stages
can lead to incorrect skill execution [13]. Moreover, actions
represented relative to the moving pelvis frame make precise
manipulation difficult, since the action reference changes as
the humanoid moves. Long-horizon demonstrations are also
highly imbalanced: walking and low-motion segments dom-
inate the trajectory, which can bias imitation learning toward
conservative or near-static actions (e.g., standing still). Thus,
arXiv:2611.26596v1  [cs.RO]  19 Nov 2026
these challenges remain major obstacles to reliable end-to-
end long-horizon loco-manipulation, despite rapid progress
in humanoid whole-body control [11], [12], [14] and VLAs.
To this end, we aim to establish a physically grounded
framework bridging robot foundation models (i.e., VLAs)
and structured robot planning and control. Our insight is
that the aspects a flat VLA handles least reliably, deciding
when and where to act, can often be resolved directly from
physical quantities, whereas learning how to execute a skill
is precisely where VLAs are most effective. PGX therefore
uses physical structure to determine task progress, skill initi-
ation, and spatial grounding, while leaving the execution of
transferable manipulation skills to the VLA. By decoupling
timing and world-frame precision from the learned policy,
we hypothesize that the same foundation-model backbone
can execute long-horizon loco-manipulation more reliably.
Building on this insight, we introduce PGX (Physically
Grounded eXecution), a training-free execution framework
that separates deciding when and where to act from learning
how to act. Rather than modifying the VLA, introducing a
learned planner to infer sub-tasks from images [15]–[17], or
folding temporal structure into the policy itself [18], [19],
PGX assigns task progression and spatial precision to physi-
cally grounded components while preserving the VLA as the
manipulation skill executor. Specifically, PGX decomposes
long-horizon loco-manipulation into three layers. 1) Timing:
a predicate-gated finite state machine (FSM) maintains task
progress and memory, representing each stage as a tuple
of instruction, executor, guard predicate, timeout, and retry
policy. 2) Skills: the VLA operates only within manipulation
stages, while the execution layer re-establishes the start-
ing conditions under which each skill was trained; failed
guards trigger retries, and reverse transitions recover from
prematurely entered stages. 3) Precision: world-coordinate
locking (WCL) computes navigation goals from the current
object pose, holds the base at its manipulation-entry position,
and anchors precise contact targets in the world frame. In
this way, physical structure governs task progression and
spatial precision, allowing the VLA to focus on transferable
manipulation dynamics.
We evaluate PGX in Isaac Lab Arena on three tasks (box
transport, mug placement, and coffee fetching) and in a real-
world coffee task using a Unitree G1 Humanoid Robot. We
fine-tuned the state-of-the-art foundational VLA models π0.5
and GR00T N1.6 on collected human demonstrations. On
coffee fetching, PGX improves the task success rate of a fine-
tuned VLA from 35% to 80% with unchanged weights, and
improves stage progression and success on all three tasks for
both backbones. The real humanoid G1 experiment further
demonstrates the effectiveness of the execution structure.
In summary, the main contributions of our work are:
• We propose PGX, a physically grounded execution
framework that incorporates VLA models with a
predicate-gated state machine and a world-coordinate
locking layer, improving long-horizon capability.
• We develop predicate-gated stage sequencing with retry
and reverse transitions, together with WCL components,
and show that the decoupled layers supply structured
robot behaviors and generalize across VLA backbones.
• We evaluate the effectiveness of PGX on three simulated
loco-manipulation tasks and on a real humanoid, where
it turns near-failing flat policies into reliable long-
horizon execution.
II. RELATED WORK
A. Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
Recent progress on humanoids builds on learned whole-
body controllers that track retargeted human motion or tele-
operation commands [10], [14], [20]–[23], with decoupled
upper-body and locomotion interfaces that expose velocity
and joint targets to a higher-level policy [11], [12]. On
top of such controllers, generalist VLAs [4]–[7], [24] and
humanoid-specific policies [8], [9], [25] learn manipulation
and locomotion from demonstrations, while data-generation
pipelines synthesize demonstrations in simulation through
whole-body planning or procedural motion generation [26]–
[28]. These works primarily improve the controller, the data,
or the skill policy. Alternatively, our work takes a tuned VLA
and a whole-body control stack as given and studies how to
organize their skills into a long loco-manipulation task.
B. Long-Horizon Manipulation with VLAs
Many recent works tackle long-horizon tasks by decom-
posing them into sub-tasks, with the active sub-task inferred
by an LLM or VLM planner [15], [16], [29], [30], by the
VLA itself through embodied reasoning [6], [31], or by
a learned success or failure detector [32]. A second line
strengthens the temporal representation inside the policy,
through phase-aware input masking [18], explicit mem-
ory [19], or action chunking and flow-based decoders [5],
[33]. A third line chains separately learned skills, regulariz-
ing terminal states so that one skill starts where the previous
one ends [13], [34]–[37]. These methods leave task progress,
the switching decision, and the initial condition of each skill
to a network or a semantic model, whereas PGX chooses to
keep task progress in an external state machine and switch
skills on physical events rather than inferred semantics.
C. Structured Robotic Execution and Hybrid Control
Combining task structure with continuous control has been
studied for years, and recent work replaces parts of this
pipeline with learned or language-based components. Lan-
guage models now generate the task structure as programs
or plans and delegate execution to a library of learned
skills [29], [30], [38]. [17] tracks progress from images with
a foundation model and adjusts the stance with a VLM before
manipulation, while our approach gates stages on physical
predicates rather than image-based inference. Hybrid plan-
ners chain learned skills under feasibility checks [35], [37].
These build on the classical machinery of task and motion
planning [1], [3] and behavior trees [2], which make the
discrete structure explicit and hand execution to model-based
control. On humanoids, large learned whole-body controllers
now expose one command interface to teleoperation and

the standing position from which a skill starts is known to
dominate its success, motivating coupled base-arm imitation
policies [39], mostly on fixed or wheeled bases that do not
drift during manipulation. Our work targets a biped whose

III. PHYSICALLY GROUNDED EXECUTION
Our goal is to use a hierarchical execution structure
to address the key challenges of long-horizon humanoid
loco-manipulation, including task progress, spatial precision,
and highly imbalanced demonstrations. The overall frame-
work of PGX is shown in Fig. 2. A long-horizon loco-
manipulation task is executed by three layers: a predicate
state machine decides which stage is active and who executes
it, the VLA acts inside manipulation stages, and a world-
coordinate locking (WCL) layer keeps the base, the carried
object, and device targets consistent in the world frame.
The three layers are a division of responsibility rather than
three networks that every action must pass through. This
decomposition separates stages with distinct dynamics and
learning requirements, preventing long locomotion and low-
motion segments from dominating manipulation learning. We
state the problem in Sec. III-A, describe the three layers
in Secs. III-B–III-D, and show in Sec. III-C how the same
predicates segment demonstrations for training.
A. Problem Statement
We consider a long-horizon task given as a stage graph
G = (S, E), a trained VLA policy πθ, and a whole-body
control stack. The graph contains the nominal progression
path and the retry or reverse edges triggered by failure states.
The goal is to complete the task within a time budget.
We distinguish the policy observation ot, which contains
camera images and proprioception, from the executor state
zt, which additionally contains estimates of the base and
task-object poses, grasp evidence, and device states, provided
by the robot’s state estimation. The executor state is used
only for gating, navigation, and geometric control. Given ot
and the stage instruction ℓk, the VLA outputs an action chunk
of length H:
At = πθ(ot, ℓk),
At = (at, . . . , at+H−1),

which a model-specific interface maps to upper-body joint
targets, base velocity commands, and hand commands,
tracked by the whole-body controller. PGX does not change
the network or its parameters θ; at every control period it
selects, constrains, or replaces individual action channels
according to the stage and the physical state.
B. Predicate-Gated Stage Machine
Stage representation. Each stage is written as a tuple
sk = (ℓk, ck, gk, τk, ρk),
(2)
denoting its instruction, executor, completion guard, time
budget, and recovery policy. Walking stages are executed
by a navigation controller while the arms hold a ready
or carry posture; manipulation stages are executed by the
VLA while the executor manages the base; device waits are
handled by a state check or a timer, so the VLA never has
to generate a waiting behavior. In this work, the coffee task
has eight stages: approach, grasp, transport, place, press, re-
grasp, transport, and deliver, of which five are manipulation
stages, and the wait between press and re-grasp belongs to
the executor. Every stage exits on a physical outcome, never
on the end of an action chunk or a preset duration.
Predicate interface. Five predicates form the basic set:
grasped, placed, triggered, at-stance, and dropped. grasped
combines the hand state, the wrist–object distance, and a lift
above the object’s rest height,
grasped ⇔closed∧∥pW −pO∥< dg ∧zO −zrest > hg, (3)
so that closing an empty hand is not mistaken for a grasp.
placed requires the object to be inside the target region,
slower than vp, and released; for intermediate placements
it also requires the wrist to have retreated, leaving room
for the next interaction. triggered reads the device state, at-
stance compares the base pose with the stage’s reference
stance, and dropped fires when a held object leaves the hand
outside a placement region. Each predicate must hold for a
minimum duration, with hysteresis, so that one noisy frame
cannot advance the stage.
The key design choice is that one rule serves three
purposes. The same predicate determines skill boundaries in
demonstrations offline (Sec. III-C), gates transitions online,
and records task progress at evaluation. The training target,
the execution condition, and the metric are therefore tied
to one physical event; each use only sets thresholds and
hold times according to its sensor source, and nothing has
to redefine what “grasped” or “placed” means.
Recovery and reverse transitions. Each manipulation
stage receives a bounded number of attempts. When the
guard fails, the executor restores the stance and requests
a fresh action chunk, without releasing a held object and
without opening the hand close to the object. For stage
confusion the machine allows reverse transitions: if during
press the mug is grasped again while the device has not been
triggered, the executor returns to place and re-establishes the
pre-press condition, changing only the stage and the prompt.
An unrecoverable drop terminates the episode. Algorithm 1
summarizes the execution of one stage.
C. Skill Execution with Fine-Tuned VLAs
PGX treats the VLA as a policy that manipulates under
local conditions, not as the sole controller of the whole task.
Before a manipulation stage, the navigation controller brings
the robot to a stance relative to the target, the executor waits
for the stopping transient to decay and selects an arm posture
compatible with the coming skill: an empty-hand grasp starts
from the ready posture, a placement with an object starts
from the carry posture, and consecutive manipulations keep
a compatible end-effector state.
Two kinds of skill model are supported. A flat model is
trained on full demonstrations with one task-level instruction,
kept for every manipulation stage inside PGX. A stage model
is trained on manipulation segments cut from the same
demonstrations by the same predicates that gate execution: a
segment starts when effective hand motion begins after the

D. World-Coordinate Locking
WCL reduces the influence of base motion on skill inputs
and on interaction targets by maintaining task-relevant ref-

contact separately, rather than locking the end-effector for
