Realized versus Population Reliability:
Anytime-Valid Self-Consistency Certification under
Correlated Reasoning
Terence D. Agbeyegbe
Department of Economics
Hunter College and Graduate Center, CUNY
tagbeyeg@hunter.cuny.edu
Toneukarin G. Agbeyegbe
Department of Statistics
Rutgers University
tga17@scarletmail.rutgers.edu
November 2026
Abstract
Self-consistency certification treats repeated sampling from a language model as sequential
evidence accumulation and stops when an anytime-valid e-process crosses a threshold, guar-
anteeing finite-sample Type I error control by Ville’s inequality. Every construction in this line
assumes the sampled rollouts are conditionally independent. We show that this assumption is
not innocuous: realistic reasoning streams are positively correlated. Rollouts share a sampled
reasoning prefix, and aggregate certificates pool a population of prompts of heterogeneous dif-
ficulty, and correlation changes not merely the efficiency of a certificate but the hypothesis it
certifies.
We model the dependence through a latent state drawn once per certification unit (the
random-effects / intraclass-correlation structure from clustered data), inducing exchangeable,
equicorrelated increments with correlation ρ. Correlation splits the single null into two: a
realized null about the drawn belief and a population null about the model’s average behavior,
which coincide only when ρ = 0. Our results are: (i) the standard betting e-process remains
anytime-valid, but for the realized null, not the population null; (ii) read as a population-
null certificate, the asymptotic population-null crossing probability of a suitable mixture is
at least π = P(µ(Z) > 0) and need not respect the nominal ϵ; (iii) a design-effect saturation
result: for the within-unit mean, the variance-equivalent sample size tends to 1/ρ; additional
within-unit rollouts alone cannot restore population-null validity; and (iv) a prompt-level e-
process that restores population validity, with an allocation rule that, under a pure rollout
budget, is minimized at one rollout per prompt. We confirm the mechanism in simulation.
Measuring it on real rollouts (Claude Haiku 4.5), we find the gap is regime-dependent. On
GSM8K, ˆρ = 0.435 but the model is so self-consistent ( ˆθ = +0.96) that the gap is dormant.
On AIME the model scatters ( ˆρ = 0.480, ˆθ = −0.15 < 0), the estimated population margin is
negative, illustrating the mismatch: read as a population-null certificate, the single-unit rule
produces single-prompt crossings on 24% of prompts, whereas ϵ = 0.05 is a bound for tests of
a specified null, while the prompt-level procedure does not certify (empirical rate 0.00). The
contribution is a correctness result, not an efficiency one: it identifies which reliability claim
an anytime-valid self-consistency certificate is entitled to make under dependence.
1
Introduction
The deployment of large language models (LLMs) in reasoning tasks has revealed a fundamental
tension between reliability and computational cost. Test-time scaling—including sampling mul-
1
arXiv:2611.26592v1  [stat.ME]  19 Nov 2026
tiple responses, extending context windows, and running additional reasoning steps—improves
output quality but consumes resources. The question of when to stop is both statistical (is there suf-
ficient evidence for the conclusion?) and economic (is further computation worth the cost?). For
self-consistency [Wang et al., 2023], where an LLM is queried repeatedly at positive temperature
and the majority answer is selected, a recent line of work makes this rigorous: Cordero-Encinar
& Duncan [2025] formalize a Martingale Majority Certificate that, via test supermartingales and
Ville’s inequality [Ville, 1939], stops with exact, finite-sample, anytime-valid Type I error control.
This replaces the heuristic “sample a fixed number of times” with a principled certificate.
1.1
The gap: dependence
Every certificate in this line, and the broader anytime-valid toolkit it draws on [Howard et al.,
2021, Ramdas et al., 2023], assumes the rollouts are conditionally independent increments with a
single drift parameter. While essential for the underlying theory, this assumption fails to hold in
the two regimes of greatest practical interest.
Shared latent within a prompt.
Tree-of-thought branching, prefix-shared decoding, and batched
or speculative sampling produce rollouts that are independent only after conditioning on a rea-
soning prefix or plan that is itself sampled once. Marginally, the rollouts are correlated through
the shared prefix.
Across-prompt aggregation.
A deployment-level claim—“this model is reliable on this task”—pools
evidence across a population of prompts. Prompts differ in difficulty: a model is rock-solid on
easy items and scattered on hard ones, so the per-prompt margin is dispersed. That dispersion is
exactly between-unit variance, and it makes the pooled increments correlated.
In both regimes the increments are positively correlated, and correlation does something more
consequential than inflate variance. It splits the null hypothesis in two. The realized null concerns
whether, for this prompt’s drawn reasoning, the certified answer is favored; the population null
asks whether the answer is favored on average over the model’s randomness or the task distribu-
tion. When the increments are independent, these coincide. When they are correlated, they come
apart by exactly the correlation ρ, and a procedure that looks valid may be silently certifying the
wrong one.
1.2
Contributions
This is a correctness contribution, not an efficiency one. We do not propose a faster certificate; we
identify which reliability claim an anytime-valid certificate is entitled to make once rollouts are
correlated, and we repair it when the population claim is the target.
1. A dependent evidence model (Section 3). We transport the random-effects / intraclass cor-
relation model from clustered data to the reasoning stream: a latent state Z is drawn once
per certification unit, with rollouts conditionally i.i.d. given Z. This induces exchangeable,
equicorrelated increments with correlation ρ = σ2
B/(σ 2
B + σ 2
W ), where σ 2
B and σ2
W denote the
between- and within-unit variances. Consequently, the single null splits into a realized null
(µ(Z) ≤0, governing the unit’s conditional mean) and a population null (θ = E[µ(Z)] ≤0,
governing the overall mean).
2. Which null is controlled (Section 4). The standard betting e-process is not a supermartin-
gale under the population null because the data eventually reveal Z, so the marginal va-
lidity argument breaks whenever the fraction of units with positive realized drift satisfies
2
π = P(µ(Z) > 0) > 0. But it survives, exactly, for the realized null (Theorem 4.2). Read
as a population-null certificate, a suitable mixture has asymptotic population-null crossing
probability at least π, potentially exceeding the nominal error level ϵ (Proposition 4.5).
3. An impossibility (Section 5). For the within-unit sample mean, the variance-equivalent
effective sample size tends to 1/ρ (Theorem 5.1); the within-unit mean converges to the
realized belief µ(Z), and does not in general converge to the population drift θ. Without
additional structural information or independent units, a realized-null certificate does not
yield a population-null guarantee.
4. A remedy (Section 6). Genuine independence lives across units, so the e-process must too.
A prompt-level e-process on within-unit means restores exact population validity (Theo-
rem 6.2), and an allocation analysis shows that, under a pure rollout budget, the variance-
minimizing choice is one rollout per prompt; a per-prompt cost is required before extra roll-
outs help (Proposition 6.3).
5. Unknown ρ and beyond exchangeability (Section 7). Realized-null validity needs no knowl-
edge of ρ; population validity under unknown ρ uses variance-adaptive betting. Arbitrary
serial dependence within a unit is genuinely open and is where dependence-robust (HAC /
near-epoch-dependent) machinery is required.
6. Measurement (Section 8). Simulation confirms the mechanism and its repair. On real roll-
outs (Claude Haiku 4.5) we measure the across-prompt ρ on two benchmarks: GSM8K
( ˆρ = 0.435), where strong self-consistency ( ˆθ = +0.96) leaves the gap dormant, and AIME
( ˆρ = 0.480, ˆθ = −0.15 < 0), where the estimated population margin is negative and over-
certification occurs. Read as a population-null test, the single-unit rule produces single-
prompt crossings on 24% of prompts, versus a nominal ϵ = 0.05 population-test level, while
the prompt-level remedy declines.
Relation to prior certificates.
Our results do not contradict Cordero-Encinar & Duncan [2025]
or its successors. For a single prompt with independently sampled rollouts ρ = 0, the two nulls
coincide, and those certificates are exactly correct for the margin they target. The point is that un-
der the correlation present in shared-prefix decoding and in across-prompt aggregation, the same
construction controls the realized null while the application often wants the population null.
Dey & Bhandari [2023] study asymptotically optimal sequential multiple testing in an equicorre-
lated Gaussian model, the same correlation structure we adopt, but from a fixed-procedure opti-
mality viewpoint; we work in the anytime-valid e-process framework and isolate the hypothesis-
identification problem that dependence creates. Closest in setting is Ota et al. [2026], who give
anytime-valid certification of a target answer as the mode of the response distribution under
data-driven stopping and an unknown answer-category set, with minimax rates and experiments
on open models over hard benchmarks; that work operates under independence and addresses
the unknown category set, whereas we address dependence and the realized-versus-population
identification, which are complementary axes. Akter et al. [2025] similarly build self-normalized
empirical-Bernstein e-processes for LLM generation under unknown centering. Finally, Cordero-
Encinar & Duncan [2025] explicitly name applying anytime-valid certificates to correlated rollouts
as future work; the present paper takes up exactly that problem.
1.3
Outline
Section 2 recalls the anytime-valid toolkit as the ρ = 0 baseline. Section 3 develops the dependent
evidence model and the two nulls. Section 4 establishes which null the standard certificate con-
trols and the over-certification of the population null. Section 5 proves the information-saturation
3
impossibility. Section 6 gives the prompt-level remedy and allocation. Section 7 treats unknown
ρ and serial dependence. Section 8 reports simulations and the measured ρ. Section 9 discusses
scope and limitations.

We recall the anytime-valid machinery in the form we need, treating it throughout as the ρ = 0
special case of the dependent model of Section 3.

Probing the “Conscious” Mind1:
Selective Access and Global Workspace in Vision-Language Models
Jiahao Huang 1
Jun Wang 2†
1 Imperial College London, UK
2 University College London, UK
† Corresponding author.
Abstract
Vision-language models (VLMs) integrate visual and textual information to perform a range of multimodal
tasks, but their outputs do not reveal the models’ internal concept representations.
In brain science,
global workspace theory (GWT) proposes that information is selected from multiple parallel brain processes,
integrated in a shared workspace, and made available to different specialised processes. In this work, we
investigate multimodal concept processing in VLMs in relation to these global workspace functions. We
introduce the Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens), a multimodal Jacobian lens that combines vision
encoder and language decoder lenses. Both lenses map intermediate states into a shared semantic space
defined by the decoder’s output vocabulary, allowing us to compare concept accessibility across visual and
language processing. MC-Lens also supports internal concept interventions to examine the role of accessed
concepts in downstream computation. Our experiments address four related aspects. (i) Accessibility
and selective access.
Multimodal concept information is readable in intermediate states and can be
selectively accessed according to task demands. We extend the “readout carriers” from a single name token
to a set of tokens, to better capture and express concept information and support subsequent counterfactual
experiments.
(ii) Concepts in downstream computation.
Counterfactual experiments show that
the concept information we access is not only readable, but also participates in downstream computation
and reasoning.
(iii) Development of cross-modal alignment and selective access.
We develop
two J-space based metrics to track cross-modal concept alignment.
In controlled VLM training, these
metrics reflect its development more clearly than hidden state cosine.
The experiment also shows that
reliable selective access develops later in training than concept accessibility. (iv) Shared functions across
models. Across VLM families and sizes, we find shared patterns of concept accessibility, query-dependent
selectivity and cross-task intervention effects, despite differences in internal organisation. Together, these
findings provide an experimental basis for studying GWT in multimodal artificial systems, and open a way
to investigate how GWT can guide improvements in cross-modal alignment.

1
Introduction
Vision-language models (VLMs) can effectively integrate visual and textual information to per-
form a range of multimodal tasks (Alayrac et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Bai
et al., 2025). For example, we can ask a VLM to identify an object in an image or describe
its colour, and these questions require the model to extract different information from the same
image and integrate it with the textual query. However, although current VLMs can readily
answer these questions, their outputs do not reveal their internal concept representations. A
VLM can also answer a visual question incorrectly even when the visual information needed to
answer it remains readable from its intermediate states (Fu et al., 2025).
Existing interpretability methods aim to identify information in internal states and examine
its role in producing model outputs (Alain and Bengio, 2016; Neo et al., 2025; Kaduri et al.,
2025). Gurnee et al. (2026) proposed the Jacobian Lens (J-Lens), a Jacobian-based method that
provides vocabulary-based readouts of intermediate language-model states. Specifically, it maps
the model’s intermediate hidden states into the space of final-layer decoder states via averaged
Jacobian matrices, and provides concept directions for counterfactual intervention experiments.
Using J-Lens, Gurnee et al. (2026) identify functional and structural properties associated with
a global workspace in large language models (LLMs).
In brain science, global workspace theory (GWT) (Baars, 2005; Baars and Franklin, 2007; De-
haene et al., 1998) is an influential theory of consciousness that explains how information from
different sources is integrated to support flexible cognition. The core hypothesis of this theory
is that information is selected from the multiple parallel processes in the brain, integrated in a
shared workspace, and made available to different specialised processes. Building on the J-Lens
study, we extend this analysis to concept information expressed through different modalities,
and processed across the visual and language components of VLMs.
In this paper, we introduce the Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens), a multimodal Jacobian
lens that combines a vision encoder lens (V-Lens) and a language decoder lens (L-Lens). V-Lens
can access concept information from intermediate vision encoder states before visual information
is combined with the text input in the decoder. L-Lens can access concept information from
decoder states during the integration of visual and textual inputs, allowing us to examine select-
ive access under different text queries and during autoregressive generation. Both V-Lens and
L-Lens map intermediate states into a shared semantic space defined by the decoder’s output
vocabulary, so we can compare concept accessibility during multimodal information integra-
tion and processing. Figure 1 illustrates these readouts in a visual question answering (VQA)
example. We conduct counterfactual experiments using MC-Lens, where we intervene on inter-
mediate state components associated with the accessed concepts and observe the resulting model
outputs, to infer the role of these concepts in downstream computation. In addition, we also
investigate the functional properties and internal organisation of multimodal concept processing
in VLMs in relation to GWT. Specifically, our experiments address four related aspects.
(i) Accessibility and selective access.
Our experiments show that multimodal concept
information is readable in intermediate states and can be selectively accessed according to task
demands.
Spatial readouts further reveal object identity and attributes such as colour and
material at a fine spatial scale. In addition, we extend the “readout carriers” used to express a
concept, from a single name token to a set of tokens. This extension helps us better capture
and express concept information in intermediate states, and supports subsequent counterfactual
experiments on its role in downstream computation.
(ii) Concepts in downstream computation. The counterfactual experiments indicate that
the concept information we access is not merely shown on a “display board”, but also participates
in downstream computation and reasoning. In causal reasoning VQA tasks, we perform counter-
factual interventions on intermediate concept representations, and find that these interventions
2
can redirect answers to questions requiring multiple steps of reasoning, or influence multiple
aspects of downstream reasoning. And we find that these effects generally become stronger as
we expand the “readout carriers” using larger concept direction sets.
(iii) Development of cross-modal alignment and selective access. We develop two J-
space based metrics to track correspondence between visual states and language-defined concepts.
We also construct a controlled VLM training setting for vision-language alignment, and evaluate
these metrics across checkpoints at different stages of training. Our experiments show that our
proposed metrics reflect the development of cross-modal concept alignment more clearly than
the hidden state cosine baseline. Concept readouts from the same checkpoints further show
that concept accessibility improves early in alignment training, whereas reliable selective access
develops later.
(iv) Shared functions across models. We extend our experiments to VLMs of different sizes
from multiple model families (Bai et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2024; Gemma Team, 2025). Across
these models, we find shared patterns of concept accessibility, query-dependent selectivity and
cross-task intervention effects, despite differences in their internal workspace organisation.
Together, these findings provide an experimental basis for studying GWT in multimodal artificial
systems, and open a way to investigate how GWT can guide improvements in cross-modal
alignment.
2
MC-Lens: A Jacobian Lens for Multimodal Concepts
In general, a VLM’s output provides only a limited view of its internal processing. For example,
a VLM may correctly identify a bicycle in a photograph, but the answer itself does not tell us
where the concept of bicycle appears inside the model.
Therefore, we develop MC-Lens, a Jacobian-based method inspired by J-Lens (Gurnee et al.,
2026), to access concept information from intermediate states in the VLM and to investigate
the role of the accessed concepts in downstream computation and reasoning. In this section, we
focus on the mathematical formulation of MC-Lens.

Verify the Verifier: Specification-Grounded LLM
Cross-Checking for Bugs That Escape UVM Scoreboards
Ana E. Sanchez Villalobos, Michael D. Quinn, Aakash Tyagi, Minh D. Luu, David Kebo Houngninou
Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA
{anaeugenia.sv, m.d.quinn, tyagi, minh.luu, davidkebo}@tamu.edu
Abstract—A passing UVM regression shows the design agrees with
the reference model on what the scoreboard checks, not that it meets
the specification. Bugs that pass every test yet violate the specification,
termed scoreboard escapes, survive mature testbenches. We present
Verify the Verifier, to our knowledge the first framework whose LLM-
based Anomaly Cross-Checker examines a passing regression’s traces
against the specification. Of 564 bugs inserted into four OpenTitan IPs,
68 are candidate scoreboard escapes: non-equivalent, exercised by the
tests, yet passing. The framework confirmed 41 as scoreboard escapes
with assertions failing on the buggy design and proven on the original.
Index Terms—Functional verification, SystemVerilog assertions, large
language models, formal verification, simulation trace analysis.
I. INTRODUCTION
UVM is the industry-standard verification methodology for con-
structing and reusing testbench components in the functional veri-
fication of digital designs. Late in the verification cycle, once the
testbench is stable and the design has passed basic health checks,
teams run large regressions, and a fully passing regression is one of
the exit criteria the design must meet before it advances to the next
milestone, such as RTL freeze or tapeout. A bug that escapes this
regression is therefore carried into later stages of the design flow,
where it is more expensive to find and fix.
A passing regression, however, guarantees less than its role as an
exit criterion implies. A UVM scoreboard compares the transactions
observed at the design’s outputs with those a reference model predicts
for the stimulus each test applies, so a passing regression shows
only that the two agreed on the behavior the tests exercised and the
scoreboard compared. Functional coverage reports which behaviors
the test reached, but only among those someone chose to model:
a behavior without a covergroup is neither measured nor checked.
Neither certifies that the design complies with its specification.
We define a scoreboard escape as a bug that passes the full
regression yet still violates a specification requirement. Such bugs
exist even in mature, public environments. The scoreboard of the
OpenTitan PWM controller, for example, never measures the phase
delay, skips pulses with 0% and 100% duty cycles, and silently
discards any pulse whose period differs from the expected one, so
a bug that changes the period is never compared and the regression
still reports a PASS.
Recent LLM-based work on RTL debugging and repair starts from
a failure. Diagnosis methods such as VCDiag [1] analyze a failing
simulation, and repair frameworks such as MEIC [2] and UVLLM
[3] iterate until the tests pass, so a passing regression is treated as
the end point, not examined for undetected scoreboard escapes. LLMs
have also been used to generate stimulus [4] and assertions [5], but to
our knowledge none inspects the traces of the regression that already
passes. Finding scoreboard escapes therefore raises two challenges.
The first is observability: an escape is usually visible only in the
behavior of internal signals, which the scoreboard does not see. The
second is trust: a failing LLM-generated assertion is not, by itself,
a detection, because it may reveal either a bug in the design or an
error in the assertion itself, so it must be qualified independently
(Section III).
To address these two challenges, we propose Verify the Verifier, a
framework that treats a passing regression as evidence to be inspected
rather than a verdict to be trusted (Fig. 1). For observability, its
core component is the Anomaly Cross-Checker (ACC), an LLM that
receives the specification and a waveform trace of the simulation,
including internal signals, and flags behavior that may contradict
the specification even though the scoreboard reported a PASS. The
ACC never sees the RTL, so its findings come from what the design
did, not from how it was written. An Assertion Generator LLM (the
Generator) then turns these anomalies into SystemVerilog assertions,
using the specification and an excerpt of the RTL that drives the
flagged signals. For trust, deterministic guards discard malformed
assertions, and formal verification either proves each assertion or
falsifies it with a counterexample. For each counterexample, an Ad-
versarial Challenger LLM writes a directed test with the testbench’s
own UVM sequences, so that a finding becomes a reproducible test
that passes the scoreboard but fails the assertion.
To our knowledge, this is the first framework to use an LLM
to cross-check passing regression traces against the specification
and formally qualify each scoreboard escape. This work makes
the following contributions. First, we formulate the problem of
scoreboard escapes and define a criterion for qualified detection:
an assertion counts only if it fails with a counterexample on the
bug-inserted design and is proven, non-vacuously, on the reference
(Section III). Second, we present the Anomaly Cross-Checker, which
compares a signal digest against the specification without access
to the RTL, so that its findings come from the design’s behavior
rather than its implementation (Section IV-B). Third, we present an
assertion pipeline that combines an RTL excerpt around the flagged
signals, deterministic syntax guards, formal verification, and directed
UVM tests that target the counterexamples (Sections IV-C - IV-E).
Fourth, a benchmark of 68 non-equivalent scoreboard escapes in four
OpenTitan IPs, obtained by adapting BugGen [6] to keep the mutants
that pass the regression (Section V). Finally, we evaluate the frame-
work on four OpenTitan IPs with their native UVM environments
(Section VI). The ACC reported the effect of the injected bug for 55
of 68 candidate escapes, and for 41 of these, the framework produced
a qualified detection. On the designs without injected bugs, the ACC
reported only places where OpenTitan’s documentation contradicts its
own RTL, which is itself a finding about the reference documentation.
II. BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK
A UVM scoreboard compares observed DUT behavior against ex-
pected results derived from the reference model. However, its checks
are limited to the behaviors captured by the verification environment
and the properties explicitly implemented in the scoreboard. A test
passes when none of these comparisons fails, so its verdict is bounded
by what the reference model predicts and what the monitor captures.

Fig. 1.
Overview of Verify the Verifier. A regression that passes the scoreboard is inspected by the Anomaly Cross-Checker; the resulting assertions are
checked with formal verification, and each counterexample becomes a directed UVM test that passes the scoreboard but fails the assertion.
A behavior that does not follow the specification but still produces
an output the scoreboard accepts goes undetected.
LLM-based work on RTL debugging and repair starts from a
failure. VCDiag [1] triages failing simulations from their waveforms,
while repair frameworks such as MEIC [2] and UVLLM [3] iterate
between an LLM and the simulator until the tests pass. In all these
flows, a passing regression is an end point, even though UVLLM
reports that repairs which pass the given test cases can still overfit to
them [3]. We instead start from a regression in which every test passes
and use its simulation traces to look for behavior that contradicts the
specification, which later in the design flow can become a serious
bug.
AssertLLM [7] generates assertions from the specification doc-
ument and evaluates them by formal property verification against
a golden RTL, counting an assertion as correct if it holds on the
golden design and incorrect if it fails. We use the same kind of
check for a different purpose: to decide whether an assertion that fails
on a design is evidence of a bug or an error in the assertion. Our
assertions are not only derived from the specification, but also target
the anomalous behavior observed in the simulation trace. Finally,
BugGen [6] uses LLM agents to insert functional bugs into the RTL
and retains only the mutants that the regression detects. We invert its
acceptance rule to keep the mutants that pass the regression, which,
after deduplication, formal equivalence checking and an activation
check, yields a benchmark of candidate scoreboard escapes. BugGen
is not part of our framework; we use it only to build this benchmark.
Mutation-based testbench qualification, available commercially in
Certitude [8], has long inspected passing regressions by injecting
faults and checking whether any test detects them. It grades the test-
bench rather than repairing it, and it re-runs the regression for every
fault. LLMs have also been applied to other parts of the verification
flow: generating UVM testbenches [9] and test stimulus [4], writing
assertions from specifications before RTL exists [5] or within UVM
environments [10], and benchmarking these tasks end to end [11];
Bennett and Eder survey machine learning for design verification
more broadly [12]. None of these inspects the traces of a regression
that already passes.
III. PROBLEM FORMULATION
We define a scoreboard escape as a bug for which every test in the
regression passes, with no UVM ERROR or UVM FATAL reports,
while the design still violates a specification requirement that the
scoreboard does not check or checks incorrectly. Such escapes arise
because the scoreboard checks only the behavior its monitors capture,
and only under the conditions that the regression tests exercise.
A failing assertion is not, by itself, evidence of a bug. An assertion
can fail without a bug when it is incorrect, for example when it
bounds the timing of a requirement more tightly than the specification
does. Conversely, it can pass without checking anything when it
is vacuous, that is, when its precondition can never be reached.
For every assertion, JasperGold returns one of three results: proven,
counterexample (cex), or undetermined. A proof alone cannot reveal
vacuity, so for each assertion we also check a cover property on its
precondition; the proof counts as non-vacuous only if JasperGold
reaches this cover. We call an assertion qualified when three condi-
tions hold: it has a cex on the mutant, it is proven on the reference
RTL, and its precondition cover is reached on the reference RTL. An
assertion with a cex on the reference RTL is a false positive. Vacuous
and undetermined assertions are not qualified. Simulation on the
reference RTL is not enough evidence for this decision, because an
incorrect assertion can stay silent under the stimulus of the regression
tests. The reference RTL is used only because the bugs are injected,
as an evaluation instrument, not as a framework requirement.
Not every mutant is detectable by checking the design against
its specification; we distinguish the following types of mutants. An
equivalent mutant behaves the same as the reference for every input
sequence, so it is not a bug. A non-activated mutant is non-equivalent,
yet the regression stimulus never exercises the difference: every
output in its trace matches the reference on every cycle, leaving
nothing for a trace-based check to find. A mutant that changes only
behavior the specification does not state, or that makes the design
conform to it, violates no requirement. Only a mutant that violates a
stated requirement can be detected by such a check, including ours.
We discard any equivalent and non-activated mutants when building
the benchmark (Section V). Activating a non-activated mutant would
require new stimulus, which is outside the scope of this work: the
framework inspects the regression tests the team already runs. Its
reproduction step already writes directed tests (Section IV-E), so
extending it to activate such mutants is a natural next step.
IV. FRAMEWORK
A. Overview
The framework uses only artifacts a verification team already has
once its regression passes: the specification, the RTL, the UVM
environment, and the regression tests with their coverage results.
Fig. 1 shows how it processes them in five steps. Three of them
use an LLM (the Anomaly Cross-Checker, the Generator, and the
Adversarial Challenger); the other two are deterministic.
1) Observation. The regression tests selected by coverage criteria
(Section IV-B) are re-run with waveform dumping, and each
trace is converted into a signal digest: a compact text form
2
that keeps every value of every signal of the target module,
including internal ones.
2) Cross-checking. The Anomaly Cross-Checker reads the signal
digest and the specification and reports every behavior that may
contradict the specification (Section IV-B). The RTL is not used
for this step.
3) Assertion generation. From the anomaly report, the Generator
writes SystemVerilog assertions from the specification and
an excerpt of the RTL that drives the anomalous signals.
Deterministic guards remove or repair malformed assertions
(Section IV-C).
4) Formal check. The assertions are bound to the design, with-
out modifying it, and checked with JasperGold. Each one is
proven, refuted with a counterexample, or left undetermined
(Section IV-D).
5) Reproduction. For each counterexample, the Adversarial Chal-
lenger writes a directed test with the testbench’s own sequences.
The test runs in the native environment, to show the assertion
firing while the scoreboard still reports a pass (Section IV-E). If
the existing sequences cannot reproduce a counterexample, the
formal detection still stands; the test only adds a reproducible
case.
Two rules apply throughout the flow, one for checkers and one
for stimulus. First, the behavior an assertion requires always comes
from the specification, never from the implementation, so that the
bug is not written into an assertion as correct behavior. The RTL
enters only as an excerpt from which the Generator takes signal
names and conditions, and the RTL query tool returns declarations,
not logic. Second, stimulus may be derived from the design because a
counterexample decides only where the test drives the design, while
the verdict comes from an assertion grounded in the specification;
as long as the stimulus stays within what the testbench can legally
drive, a poor choice can miss a bug, but cannot create one.
B. Test Selection, Signal Digest Creation and Anomaly Cross-
Checker
The framework first uses per-test coverage from the regression
tests to select the tests that the ACC will observe. A test is selected
if it covers at least one coverage item that no other test covers, or
if it exercises a region of the design whose coverage still has holes.
Each selected test is then re-run at its original seed with waveform
dumping enabled for the target module, so that the ACC sees exactly
the behavior the passing regression produced. The resulting waveform
is converted into a signal digest, a compact text form of the trace
described below, and one digest per test is given to the ACC together
with the specification.
The signal digest covers every signal of the target module, in-
cluding internal ones, sampled at every rising clock edge. Instead of
writing the value of each signal at every cycle, it describes how the
signal behaves over a range of cycles: it stays constant, counts by a
fixed step, or repeats a short pattern. This makes the trace compact.
PWM’s smoke test alone includes 51,000 cycles of 389 signals, which
would take millions of tokens as one row per cycle. The encoding is
exact at cycle precision: before use, every signal digest is decoded
and compared, signal by signal and cycle by cycle, against the values
sampled from the simulation dump.
The signal digest, along with the specification, is given to the
ACC: it never sees the RTL or the reference design. The ACC
uses no retrieval (RAG) or external tools; the specification and the
signal digest are placed directly in the model’s context. Its task is
to point out any behavior that may contradict the specification. For
each anomaly it reports the signal, the test where it was found, the
specification requirement, the observed behavior and the discrepancy
between them. The prompt asks the ACC which behaviors in the
trace do not match the specification, rather than whether the observed
behavior is legal, because the latter starts from what the design did
and invites the LLM to construct a reading of the specification under
which that behavior is acceptable, so that an anomaly is explained
away rather than reported. A deterministic filter then discards entries
that the LLM itself marked as having no discrepancy. Because the
LLM’s output may vary from run to run, the ACC gets up to three
attempts and keeps the first non-empty result. The results of different
attempts are not merged, because their union would also merge the
false anomalies of each run.
C. Assertion Generation and Deterministic Guards
The Generator writes assertions from four inputs: the specification,
the anomaly report from the ACC, the RTL interface (names, widths,
and direction, without any logic), and an RTL excerpt. It never
receives any indication of which line was mutated. The RTL excerpt is
built deterministically, without an LLM or a human involved: it takes
the statements that drive each signal named in the anomaly report,
then the statements that drive the signals read by those statements,
up to two levels deep, crossing module boundaries only through port
connections. The same rule is applied to every design and every
mutant. All comments are removed before the excerpt reaches the
Generator.
What an assertion requires always comes from the specification.
The RTL excerpt given never supplies the required behavior; it
only provides exact signal names, their structural relations, and
enabling conditions. An enabling condition is an extra condition in
the antecedent that limits when a requirement applies. An enabling
condition is only used if it does not contradict the specification, and
every assertion records what it took from the excerpt and why it
does not contradict the specification. The Generator can also call
grep_rtl, a tool that returns the exact declaration of a signal
but never the logic behind it, so the LLM cannot read the design’s
behavior and turn it into the reference for its assertions.
Recurring LLM mistakes are caught by deterministic code rather
than left to the prompt, so they never reach formal verification. A
signal validator discards assertions that use identifiers that are not
RTL signals or locally declared names. A binder then wraps all
remaining assertions into a single checker module that is attached to
the DUT with a SystemVerilog bind, without modifying the RTL.
The same checker is used in formal verification and in simulation.
This binder also drops or fixes any construct that would break the
compilation, for example non-constant repetitions or local names that
can shadow DUT signals. Every guard acts only on the offending
assertion, so the remaining assertions are still compiled and checked.
D. Formal Verification

ProtoDiffusion: Token-per-Layer Generative Modeling of Multi-Layer Images
Adri`a Ciurana Lanau1
Harleen Hanspal1
Lusine Abrahamyan1
Emilio Tylson Baixauli1
Yu Cao2
Danai Triantafyllidou1
Stefano Zorzi1
Gustavo Zanoni Felipe3
Peter Griger1
Stefan Sietzen1
Petru-Daniel Tudosiu1
1Canva
2Queen Mary University of London
3Universidade Estadual de Maring´a
{adria,hhanspal,lusine,emilio,danai}@canva.com
{szorzi,gzanoni,petergriger,stefan,ptudosiu}@canva.com
Figure 1. ProtoDiffusion across its conditioning regimes. (a) Box-guided image-to-design: the input composite, with supplied element
boxes, is decomposed into editable RGBA layers. (b) Image-to-design: the same decomposition from the composite alone, without boxes.
(c) Text-to-design: generation of a layered design from a text prompt. Each group shows the composite at left and the recovered layers at
right.
Abstract
Graphic designs are ordered compositions of RGBA layers
whose separation enables selection, movement, and reuse.
Existing layered models represent each layer with a full-
canvas or region-sized spatial latent grid, so representa-
tion size grows with the cumulative spatial extent of the lay-
ers. We present ProtoDiffusion, a latent-diffusion framework
built on ProtoVAE, a multi-layer variational autoencoder
that encodes a design into one shared spatial prototype and
one candidate vector per layer. Each candidate conditions
a shared decoder to reconstruct its corresponding RGBA
layer. For N layers, the representation contains HW + N
tokens before backbone-specific packing, compared with
NHW for full-grid-per-layer representations. ProtoDiffu-
sion jointly denoises the prototype and a fixed set of candi-
date slots, conditioned on an image or text, with bounding
boxes as optional layout guidance. The model leaves un-
needed slots empty and determines the number of layers and,
in absence of boxes, their layout, requiring neither as input.
The same architecture supports both image-to-design and
text-to-design. ProtoVAE achieves high-fidelity reconstruc-
tion from its compact shared latent representation, reach-
ing 40.43 dB PSNR on layer crops. On the LayerD evalua-
tion split, image-to-design achieves RGB L1 scores of 0.040
with bounding boxes and 0.057 without, with box-guided al-
1
arXiv:2611.26586v1  [cs.AI]  19 Nov 2026
pha soft IoU (0.850) comparable to the strongest fine-tuned
baseline (0.871). On merged images, text-to-design reaches
66.41 FID versus 86.84 for FLUX.2 [klein], achieves a 0.860
text-accuracy score, and runs 19.1× faster than the same-
backbone generation-then-decomposition cascade.
1. Introduction
Graphic designs are ordered compositions of RGBA ele-
ments: text, shapes, cutouts, and photographs over a back-
ground. Blending these layers produces an alpha-composited
image. Keeping these elements separate enables selection,
movement, and reuse after generation. Standard text-to-
image diffusion [24] instead produces a flattened raster, in
which those editing units are entangled.
Layered models already generate coherent transparent
elements, but they share two constraints. First, every layer
has its own spatial latent: a full-canvas grid in Qwen-Image-
Layered (QIL) [34] and a region grid in MRT [27]. The
sequence processed by the denoiser, and with it compute
and memory, therefore grows with the number and extent of
layers (Section 4.5). Second, structure is decided before con-
tent: QIL takes a requested layer count, and MRT a layout
that is supplied or estimated beforehand, so the number of
layers, and in MRT their placement, is fixed before denoising
begins. The two are linked: deciding structure jointly with
content means denoising many candidate layers, which is
costly when each one is a spatial grid.
The use of a prior layout is analogous to two-stage in-
stance segmentation (e.g., Mask R-CNN [7]): propose re-
gions, then predict instances. As in that setting, the second
stage cannot revise what the first provides: a missing or
misplaced region is not corrected during layer generation,
and the layout must come from a separate model or the user.
Inspired by the shared prototype masks and per-instance co-
efficients in YOLACT [2], we instead factorize a design into
a shared spatial grid and layer-specific candidates, extending
the idea to joint generation and nonlinear decoding of RGBA
layers. We propose a token-per-layer representation. Proto-
VAE jointly encodes the layer stack into a shared spatial grid
(the prototype) and one candidate vector per layer, including
the background. Each candidate summarizes its layer in the
context of the full composition and conditions the decoder to
reconstruct the corresponding RGBA layer from the shared
grid (Figure 2).
ProtoDiffusion learns a diffusion model over this factor-
ization. A pretrained image-transformer stream processes the
shared grid, while a dedicated candidate stream exchanges
information with it through bidirectional cross-attention (Fig-
ure 3). The same model serves different tasks by changing
the conditioning: image-to-design conditions on the encoded
alpha-composited image, and text-to-design on a prompt.
Boxes guide candidates when available. The model denoises
a fixed set of candidate slots and leaves unneeded ones empty.
It thus determines the number of layers and, when no boxes
are given, their layout, requiring neither as input. Figure 1
illustrates image-to-design with and without boxes and text-
to-design generation. Specifically, our contributions are:
1. Compact latent representation. A token-per-layer fac-
torization, ProtoVAE, represents an RGBA design with
HW + N tokens before packing for N layers, versus
N ·HW for full-grid-per-layer representations. Each ad-
ditional layer costs one candidate vector rather than a
spatial grid. Section 3.3 derives the resulting denoiser
scaling separately from measured system-level speedups.
2. Joint denoising of design context and elements. A
two-stream diffusion architecture couples the shared pro-
totype grid and layer candidates through bidirectional
cross-attention, jointly modeling composition and layer
content.
3. Unified generation and decomposition. A single model
supports image-to-design with or without bounding boxes
and text-to-design generation through changes in condi-
tioning. Activity-based candidate selection recovers a
variable number of layers within a fixed capacity.
2. Related Work
Layered image generation and decomposition.
Layered
representations allow individual elements of an image to be
edited and reused. LayerDiffuse [35] introduces latent trans-
parency, enabling pretrained diffusion models to generate
transparent images and multiple interacting layers. Qwen-
Image-Layered [34] encodes each RGBA layer as a spa-
tial latent grid and models interactions across layers with
a variable-length diffusion transformer. Its decomposition
interface takes an image and a requested layer count, with-
out requiring bounding boxes. MRT [27] uses region-based
spatial latents and a masked diffusion formulation for text-to-
layer generation, image decomposition, and layer editing. Its
layer generator receives a layout specifying the regions and
their ordering. PSDiffusion [12] generates multiple layers
simultaneously, with global interactions that coordinate their
layout and appearance.
For image decomposition, LayerD [26] iteratively ex-
tracts unoccluded foreground layers through matting and
completes the remaining background through inpainting.
RevealLayer [28] focuses on natural-image decomposition,
including occluded content and layer separation, and in-
troduces RevealLayerBench. LayeringDiff [16] first gen-
erates a composite image and then uses generative priors
to disassemble it into foreground and background layers.
For iterative editing, SLEDGE [17] studies sequences of
instruction-guided layered edits, while Wu et al. [32] investi-
gate the effect of synthetic layered training data on design
decomposition.
ProtoVAE addresses the spatial cost of these representa-
2
tions by sharing one prototype across layers and adding only
one token per layer, instead of a full or regional grid.
Graphic design and layout generation. COLE [15]
uses hierarchical design planning and generation, while De-
sigen [30] predicts layouts conditioned on generated back-
grounds. LayoutDM [13] and LayoutGPT [6] generate lay-
outs through discrete diffusion and language models, respec-
tively. Our framework accepts optional boxes and otherwise
jointly models spatial structure and layer content from text
or image conditioning.
Latent generative representations. We build on latent
diffusion [24], transformer denoisers [23], and flow match-
ing [19] to jointly model the shared prototype and per-layer
candidates. The supplementary material discusses object-
centric representations and reconstruction objectives.
3. Method
We adopt a two-stage training procedure: ProtoVAE learns a
latent representation of layered designs, and ProtoDiffusion
is subsequently trained in this latent space. Figures 2 and 3
illustrate the representation and denoising architecture, re-
spectively. Throughout, H and W denote the latent spatial
dimensions, C the number of ProtoVAE latent channels, N
the number of design layers (including the background), and
M the number of diffusion slots.
3.1. ProtoVAE: Shared Spatial Context and Layer
Identity
Encoding.
Given an ordered design {xi}N
i=1 including its
background, the frozen QIL VAE encoder maps each RGBA
layer to a spatial latent, which is projected to hidden width
D. The projected layer maps are jointly processed by Layer-
Squasher, a layer-wise vision transformer that alternates spa-
tial self-attention within each layer (xy) with self-attention
across layers (z). This joint processing provides shared
spatial context for constructing the prototype and per-layer
candidates. A learned token zℓ∈RD is broadcast into an ad-
ditional spatial layer of size D×H×W and jointly processed
with the N projected layer maps. Its output aggregates infor-
mation from the entire design and parameterizes the shared
prototype posterior. The remaining N outputs are pooled to
parameterize candidate posteriors, each representing a layer
in the context of the full design.
Specifically, this pooling operation crops each contextual-
ized layer feature map to a region around its alpha-derived
bounding box and resizes it. A small CNN followed by
global average pooling summarizes the region into a vec-
tor. An attention-based distribution extractor refines this
vector using prototype context and box features. The boxes
are derived from observed layers during encoding; they are
not externally supplied generation-time layouts. The re-
sulting diagonal-Gaussian posteriors define the prototype
p ∈RC×H×W and candidates ci ∈RC, with C = 128.
Decoding. Each candidate conditions the shared proto-
type decoder through AdaLN-Zero [23], producing a spatial
latent for that layer; the QIL decoder converts it to RGBA
pixels. During ProtoVAE training, the QIL encoder remains
frozen, while LayerSquasher, the pooling operator, the pro-
totype decoder, and the QIL decoder are trained jointly. This
fine-tuning adapts the QIL decoder to design layers with
small elements, fine details, and large transparent regions;
the adapted decoder is retained for subsequent reconstruc-
tion and generation. All candidates therefore share spatial
context, but each selects its own reconstruction. The sup-
plementary material gives the encoder and decoder details,
including candidate refinement and training implementation.
Training objectives. We train ProtoVAE with pixel- and
latent-space reconstruction losses, KL regularization of the
prototype and candidate posteriors, prototype alignment, and
adversarial supervision. Reconstruction supervises complete
RGBA layers, including occluded content. Adversarial su-
pervision uses a discriminator on stacked layer latents and a
PatchGAN [14] on alpha-composited local crops. The sup-
plementary material provides further objective and training
details.
Prototype alignment. Inspired by DC-Gen [8], an align-
ment module encourages agreement between features of the
shared prototype and the frozen QIL encoding of the com-
posited image. This regularizes shared spatial context, while
per-layer reconstruction supervises hidden content; align-
ment does not require the prototype to equal the composite
latent.
Overlap and leakage weighting. We increase pixel-
and latent-space reconstruction weights in regions of inter-
layer overlap to emphasize occluded content. Just outside
each layer’s support, alpha-only weighting penalizes leakage
without constraining invisible RGB.
3.2. Joint Prototype and Candidate Diffusion
The transformer adapts FLUX.2-Klein-4B [1] to the Pro-
toVAE prototype–candidate latent space.
Prototype to-
kens use the backbone’s image self-attention and spatial
RoPE [25].
Candidates have a dedicated self-attention
stream with AdaLN-Zero timestep conditioning. Bidirec-
tional cross-attention synchronizes the streams every k = 4
blocks, allowing layer identities and spatial context to inter-
act during denoising.
Conditioning and occupancy. Training slots follow in-
creasing stacking level (z-layer), then top-to-bottom and left-
to-right box-center order within each level. Generated layers
are alpha-composited in retained slot order. For image-to-
design, the alpha-composited input image is encoded directly
by the frozen QIL encoder, without running the layered-input
ProtoVAE encoder. For text-to-design, the prototype and M
candidate slots are sampled jointly from noise under text
conditioning. Candidate conditioning and occupancy are
3
Figure 2. ProtoVAE: shared grid, one candidate per layer. (a) The frozen QIL encoder maps each RGBA layer to a spatial latent; a
layer-wise transformer jointly processes the projected layer maps with a learned layer token, whose output parameterizes the shared prototype
posterior, giving HW + N tokens per design before backbone-specific packing. (b) Candidate extraction maps each contextualized layer
map to a candidate posterior: a crop around the alpha-derived box, a CNN with average pooling, and a cross-attention distribution extractor.
(c) Each candidate modulates the shared prototype decoder through AdaLN-Zero, and the jointly trained QIL decoder reconstructs its RGBA
layer. Snowflakes mark frozen modules and flames mark trainable modules. Feature grids and outputs are schematic.
Figure 3. ProtoDiffusion: conditioning, noising, and joint denoising. Image and text conditioning remain clean while the shared prototype
and M candidate slots are jointly denoised through interacting streams. Training interpolates the clean state z0 and Gaussian noise z1
as zt = (1 −t)z0 + tz1; generation starts at z1. Optional bounding boxes provide spatial guidance. Activity-based selection retains

backbone-specific packing. Snowflakes and flames indicate frozen and trainable modules during diffusion training. Output thumbnails are
schematic.
handled as follows:
• With boxes (layout-guided): box-derived RoPE and
Fourier box embeddings provide spatial conditioning.
• Without boxes: candidate-ID RoPE identifies the slots,
and box embeddings are zeroed; no external layout is
supplied.
• Layer count: unused slots are trained toward an empty
state. For each denoised candidate vector ˜ci, we compute
ai = | mean(˜ci)|+std(˜ci) across channels and retain slots
with ai > θ. The highest-scoring slot is always retained,
yielding 1 ≤N ≤M.
We set the default candidate capacity to M
= 50.
Occupancy-based selection removes the need to request an
exact count, but retains a capacity setting and an occupancy
threshold. Even when boxes specify a count, the current
implementation still denoises M slots. Autoregressive can-
didate generation with a learned stopping criterion could
remove this fixed-slot constraint; we leave this extension to
4
future work. The supplementary material reports a threshold-
calibration study on 1,954 samples.
Diffusion training. We use flow matching with zt =
(1−t)z0 +tϵ, where ϵ ∼N(0, I), and velocity target ϵ−z0.
The training objective is
L = Lp + λcLc + λlayer
�LQIL-L1 + λsepLsep

.
Here, Lp and Lc are mean squared velocity errors, normal-
ized separately within the prototype and candidate streams.
Real and empty candidate slots are also reduced separately,
so candidate supervision does not scale with the number of
padding slots. For layered supervision, the predicted clean
prototype and candidates are decoded through the frozen
ProtoVAE decoder into per-layer QIL latents, retaining gra-
dients with respect to the predicted prototype and candidates.
The reconstruction term LQIL-L1 measures weighted L1 er-
ror against the target latents, emphasizing occluded regions
and excluding padding layers. Inspired by RevealLayer [28],
Lsep contrasts each predicted layer with its own target and
other layers. The comparison uses corresponding canvas
positions, without pooling or crop recentering. The supple-
mentary material provides the loss definitions, weighting
schemes, and reduction details.
3.3. Representation Cost
Before backbone-specific packing, a design’s latent repre-
sentation has
LProtoVAE = HW + N,
Ldiffusion = HW + M.
A full-grid-per-layer representation has NHW tokens; re-
gion grids instead incur an area-dependent cost. After pack-
ing, let S be the spatial token count per grid. At fixed depth,
hidden widths, and conditioning length, our two-stream at-
tention costs O(S2 + M 2 + SM), including cross-stream
exchange, versus O((NS)2) for joint dense attention over N
full grids. Token-wise projections and MLPs process S +M
rather than NS tokens. Thus increasing layer capacity adds
candidate tokens instead of spatial grids. With M fixed,
retaining more layers does not lengthen denoising; RGBA
decoding still scales with output count.
Figure 6 complements this analysis with system-level
latency and memory measurements, which also reflect dif-
ferences in backbone, conditioning, and execution. The
supplementary material provides the full complexity analy-
sis.
4. Experiments
We evaluate reconstruction fidelity, image-to-design decom-
position, text-to-design generation, and computational effi-
ciency.
4.1. Experimental Setup
Training datasets.
We train on layered graphic designs
and PrismLayersPro [4] compositions, augmented with syn-
thetic compositions built from COYO [3] images and graphic

GEOHunter: Mapping a Generative Engine
Optimization Network in the Wild
Sean Tang1, Peiran Wang1, Ying Li1, Esha Shivakumar1, Tao Meng2, Yuan Tian1
1University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)
2Georgia Institute of Technology
Abstract
Generative engines synthesize retrieved web pages into
answers, recommendations, and rankings. Generative en-
gine optimization (GEO) services sell visibility in these an-
swers by publishing promotional articles on user-generated-
content (UGC) platforms for paying clients. Such promotion
raises concerns in medical and financial domains, where
misleading advice can cause harm. To study the severity
of this problem, we measure one such paid-content opera-
tion across three major Chinese UGC platforms, uncover-
ing 1,985 accounts associated with the network compris-
ing 466,357 inferred promotional placements. We find that
the network promotes products across diverse categories
through a growing pool of accounts, conducting coordi-
nated campaigns spanning months across multiple plat-
forms while evolving its listicle content over time. Across
nine generative engines from both the US and China, we
find that 4.5% to 20% of retrievable cited pages are attribut-
able to the network, depending on how strictly attribution
is drawn. On eight of these engines, its clients are named in
52% of answers, against 68% for category leaders. Our work
demonstrates the effectiveness of UGC GEO placement at in-
fluencing generative engine outcomes, and reveals content-
level defenses as insufficient against coordinated UGC place-
ments, where account-level and platform-level signals are
necessary for proper defense.
CCS Concepts
• Information systems →Web mining; Web searching
and information discovery; • Security and privacy →Social
network security and privacy.
Keywords
Generative engine optimization, generative search, Web
measurement, paid content, coordinated behavior, content
platforms
1
Introduction
AI assistants with web search are now a common way to
get answers and recommendations. In China, more than 700
million people had used generative AI services by mid-2026,
and 76% of them say they use these services to answer ques-
tions.1 Unlike a search engine, which returns a list of links,
such an assistant retrieves web pages, passes them to a lan-
guage model, and returns a single answer that lists some
of the pages as references. What the answer says therefore
depends on which pages the assistant retrieves.
Generative engine optimization (GEO) services sell influ-
ence over those pages. A GEO vendor writes promotional
articles for paying clients, which we call placements, and
publishes them through accounts it controls on content plat-
forms that assistants retrieve (§2). Such services are adver-
tised openly, mostly for ordinary consumer brands but also
for dietary supplements, private hospitals, stock-tipping ser-
vices, consumer-loan apps and immigration consultancies,
where a misleading recommendation is costly. In March
2026, China’s national consumer-rights broadcast showed
a GEO service that made major assistants recommend a fic-
titious product as the best in its category within days (Ap-
pendix H, S1). The effect also appears in ordinary answers.
Asked to rank road-bike brands, Baidu’s Wenxin assistant
described, in two of three runs, a “one king and four queens”
hierarchy of makers that crowns one brand as king. That
brand is a client of the network we study, whose accounts
have published 1,185 placements naming it since June 2024
(§4.3). Wenxin’s answers draw on that campaign: 51 of the
98 references behind them carry the brand or the hierarchy
in their titles. On Bilibili alone, the phrase appears in the
titles of 254 articles from 107 accounts.
Existing research has examined the engines that cite web
content and the attacks that could manipulate them, but
not the operations that supply the content: audits of gen-
erative search measure which kinds of sources assistants
cite [2, 16, 31, 36], but cannot say who produced them. Lab-
oratory studies show that crafted text can raise a product’s
rank in a generated answer [1, 12, 22, 24], but do not observe
whether anyone does so at scale. Measurements of black-hat
search engine optimization map the supply side of manipu-
lation [6, 25–27, 29], but the operations they study build do-
mains and links for human readers who click. No study has
connected a production network observed in the wild to the
answers that assistants give, in part because such a network
is hard to see: each placement reads as an ordinary article,
1CNNIC report, via Xinhua, 29 Sep. 2026.

and the accounts that publish them do not signal that they
work together.
This paper measures one such operation, from the ac-
counts that publish its articles to the answers that cite them
(Figure 1), through two research questions:
RQ1 (supply, §4). Who publishes the placements, what
do they promote, and how is their publication coordinated
across accounts and platforms?
RQ2 (exposure, §5). Which AI assistants retrieve the net-
work’s articles, what share of their references do these arti-
cles make up, and what do the answers do with them?
To carry out the measurement, we build two tools, one for
each question. GEOHunteR finds the network’s accounts by
following client names (§3.1). Every placement must name
its client, and ordinary writers rarely post about the same
niche brand on several accounts on the same day. We there-
fore start from two accounts that published articles we or-
dered for a fictitious company (Appendix A), search the plat-
forms for the client names in their articles to find more ac-
counts, and accept an account into the network when its
posting pattern shows coordination. GEOPRobe then asks
nine assistants the buyer questions found to be targeted by
the network’s articles, each paired with a category leader as
control, and traces every cited page in the assistant answer
back to the network at three levels of strictness (§3.2).
Our measurement shows that the network promotes or-
dinary consumer products through coordinated accounts,
and that all nine assistants we probed cite its articles. For
RQ1 (§4), 96% of the network’s niche placements promote
ordinary consumer goods and services rather than the illicit
products common in search spam, and listicles, articles that
rank products in a category, grew from 16% to 57% of place-
ments on the network’s core Bilibili accounts between 2024
and 2025. The accounts present themselves as news outlets
or experts but have a median of 9 followers on Bilibili, and
for 98 of 175 niche clients, they post about the same client in
the same weeks more often than chance. For RQ2 (§5), 4.5%
to 20% of the pages that the assistants cite come from the
network, depending on how strictly we attribute them. An-
swers name the network’s clients in 52% of cases, compared
with 68% for the category leaders we used as controls, and
they repeat the network’s claims.
We make the following contributions.
• Tools and data. We build GEOHunteR, which maps
a network of 3,755 accounts on three platforms, and
GEOPRobe, which traces assistant citations back to
the network. We validate the membership rule, esti-
mate crawl coverage, and will release both tools with a
pseudonymized dataset (§3).
• Supply. We characterize the clients, formats, accounts
and campaigns of the operation from 1,985 accounts and
466,357 placements, and its response to exposure (§4).
• Exposure. We measure how its articles reach the refer-
ences and text of nine assistants, and derive recommen-
dations for providers, platforms and auditors (§5, §7).
2
Background
Generative engines and UGC The platforms an engine
retrieves from matter most when the engine’s operator
also runs them. We study this practice in China, where
the operators of the largest search engines and content
platforms also offer conversational assistants with web
search. Widely used assistants include Baidu’s Wenxin,
ByteDance’s Doubao, DeepSeek and Tencent’s Yuanbao,
together with the AI search engines Metaso and 360 AI
Search.2 Several of these operators run user-generated-
content (UGC) platforms whose articles their own engines
can retrieve, and audits of deployed engines find platform-
level biases that steer each engine’s retriever toward particu-
lar sites [16, 36]. Baidu operates Baijiahao, a self-publishing
platform whose pages are among the hosts most frequently
referenced in Baidu’s AI overviews [16], and Qihoo 360 op-
erates 360kuai alongside 360 AI Search.3 Bilibili, a video
platform that also hosts public image-and-text articles, is in-
dexed by the major search engines and is retrieved by some
of the assistants we probe (§5). Placements on these three
platforms are the subject of our measurement (§3.1).
Generative engine optimization Brands that want to ap-
pear in generated answers have taken up generative engine
optimization (GEO), the practice of optimizing web content
2文心, 豆包, DeepSeek, 腾讯元宝, 秘塔, 360 AI 搜索.
3百家号, 360快资讯, 哔哩哔哩.
2
GEOHunteR: Mapping a Generative Engine Optimization Network in the Wild
for ingestion and visibility by generative engines [1]. Labo-
ratory studies show that rewriting content can raise its vis-
ibility in generated answers [1, 12, 22, 24], that a few in-
jected documents can corrupt retrieval-augmented genera-
tion [37], and that web-scale data can be poisoned at low
cost [4]. In practice, GEO therefore has two parts: creating
content that engines favor, such as ranked recommendation
lists, and placing that content, persistently and in a coordi-
nated way, on the platforms that each target engine reads.
Most brands cannot sustain such placement themselves, so
agencies sell it as a service, advertising distribution to a
dozen content platforms as a way to be recommended by
AI assistants (Appendix H, S1, S2). Paid articles once took
editorial forms such as product reviews, buyer’s guides and
news items; they are increasingly written for the engine.
Regulation Chinese regulators treat undisclosed promo-
tion of this kind as a consumer-protection problem. The
Advertising Law requires advertising to be identifiable as
such, and a 2024 enforcement guide applies that require-
ment to online content that promotes goods or services
without an advertising label (Appendix H, S3, S4). Follow-
ing the March 2026 broadcast (S1), the Cyberspace Admin-
istration of China launched a campaign against the misuse
of AI applications, whose second-phase bulletin named ma-
licious marketing through GEO as a form of AI data poi-
soning (S5, S6). These actions target individual vendors and
articles; they do not describe the operations that produce
placements at scale, which is what we measure.
3
Methodology
Answering RQ1 requires observing the accounts that pub-
lish placements, and answering RQ2 requires observing
what the assistants cite and say. Neither view is enough
alone: the accounts show who publishes what, but not
whether assistants use it, and the answers show what as-
sistants cite, but not who wrote it. We therefore build two
tools, one for each side (Figure 2). GEOHunteR finds the
network’s accounts and collects their articles (§3.1). GEO-
PRobe asks the assistants the buyer questions that the net-
work’s articles answer, and traces each cited page back to
the network (§3.2).
Terms A client is an entity that placements promote, after
merging spelling variants of one brand; nationally known
brands with independent coverage are major brands and the
rest niche clients, the focus of our client-level analyses. An
account returned by our searches is a found account, and one
that the rule of §3.1 accepts is a network account. A place-
ment is an article by a network account that our labeling

stage classifies as paid promotion; padding is one it classi-
fies as not promotional, mostly reposted news and corpo-
rate announcements. An analyzed account is a network ac-
count whose article feed we collected, excluding genuine
news outlets, and a core account is an analyzed account out-
side the automotive segment, whose accounts mainly pub-
lish car makers’ press releases. An answer is an assistant’s
response to one question and a reference a page it cites.
3.1
GEOHunteR: Mapping the Network
No list of the network’s accounts exists, but every placement
names its client. We therefore search the platforms for client
names and follow them to new accounts; prior work used
keyword snowballing to map promotional content on search
engines [29, 32]. The crawl repeats five steps (Figure 2).
(1) Seed. Because every other membership is inferred, the
crawl starts from the only placements we know to be
paid: we ordered two articles promoting a fictitious com-
pany from a commercial GEO vendor, and the Bilibili
and 360kuai accounts that published them are the seeds
(Appendix A). Baijiahao was seeded with client names
first found on Bilibili.
(2) Mine. Given a seed or an accepted account, we collect its
available article history and ask an LLM judge to propose
client names from the titles.
(3) Vet. A proposed name is searched only if it is specific
(one entity, not a category), verbatim (printed as other
placements print it), promoted (what the article sells, not
what it mentions) and rare in organic writing, which ex-
cludes generic products and well-known brands.
(4) Search. For each vetted name, we query each platform’s
own search (Appendix D) and record every account with
an article whose title contains it verbatim.
(5) Judge. A found account is a network account if it pub-
lished its last article in 2025 or later and shows at least
one of three signals of coordinated publishing: several
clients, copied titles shared with another account for the
3
Anonymous et al.
same client, or same-day bursts, posting a client within
a day of at least two other accounts that post it (thresh-
olds in Appendix D). Accounts whose titles mostly adver-
tise fake after-sales hotlines belong to a different opera-
tion and are excluded, and 51 accepted accounts that are
genuine news outlets carrying sponsored content are set
aside from the analysis population. Accepted accounts
return to step 2 and are mined in turn, though the crawl
ended before all of them were mined.
Dataset Table 1 summarizes what the loop produced on
each platform: on Bilibili, 8,525 accounts were found and
2,397 accepted as network accounts, 3,755 across the three
platforms. We collected article feeds for 2,016 of the 3,755
network accounts; excluding 31 genuine news outlets leaves
1,985 analyzed accounts, and excluding a further 345 au-
tomotive accounts leaves 1,640 core accounts. Outside the
seed articles, promotional status and network membership
are inferred from the observed records, and because the
crawl reaches only accounts whose titles carry a searched
name, all counts are lower bounds on the size of the network.
Bilibili is the core of the study, where the crawl started and
complete account histories are available; Baijiahao serves
as a second platform throughout, and 360kuai adds a third
platform for the totals, for replications and for the cross-
platform analysis of §4.3.
Article labels Client names alone cannot identify place-
ments, because only 11% of the 466,357 placements name
an identified client in the title. The remainder are labeled
by format markers in the title (232,830), by a text classifier
trained on labels that an LLM judge assigned to clusters of
similar titles (159,973), and by the account’s history (20,100).
One annotator agreed with the resulting placement labels
on 89% of 153 Bilibili articles (𝜅= 0.52; Appendix D).
Crawl coverage We stop crawling a platform when its
searches stop finding new accounts: for each search that
returns at least five accounts, we compute the share of re-
turned accounts that are new network accounts, and we stop
once the mean of this share over the last five searches falls
below 15% (Appendix D gives the formula). Figure 3 shows
each platform reaching that floor. Because the stopping rule
bounds the marginal return of further searches rather than
the share of the network found, we estimate coverage sepa-
rately: treating each searched name as a capture occasion, a
Chao2 estimator places the crawl at about 66% of the Bilibili
accounts reachable by name search, 74% on Baijiahao and
90% on 360kuai (Appendix D); accounts that no searched
name reaches remain outside this estimate.
Account identification accuracy To test the membership
rule, an annotator labeled a stratified sample of Bilibili ac-
counts from their complete article lists, without seeing the
