Multi-institutional grading of Barrett’s esophagus
dysplasia without stain normalization using a pathology
foundation model and multiple instance learning
Amirali Khosravi, MD1, Jaidip M. Jagtap, PhD1, D. Chamil Codipilly, MD2, Catherine E. Hagen,
MD3, Jason T. Lewis, MD4, Rickey E. Carter, PhD5, Shahriar Faghani, MD1,6, Vani J.A. Konda,
MD7, Fouad Otaki, MD8, Shajan Peter, MD9, Nicholas Shaheen, MD, MPH10, Sachin Wani, MD11,
Prasad G. Iyer, MD, MSc12, Bradley J. Erickson, MD, PhD1
1Department of Radiology, Mayo Clinic, Rochester, MN
2Division of Gastroenterology & Hepatology, Mayo Clinic, Rochester, MN
3Department of Laboratory Medicine and Pathology, Mayo Clinic, Rochester, MN
4Department of Laboratory Medicine and Pathology, Mayo Clinic, Jacksonville, FL
5Department of Quantitative Health Sciences, Mayo Clinic, Jacksonville, FL
6Department of Radiology, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA
7Department of Gastroenterology, Baylor Scott and White Center for Esophageal Diseases at Baylor University
Medical Center, Dallas, TX
8Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, Oregon Health and Science University, Portland, OR
9Division of Gastroenterology, University of Alabama Birmingham, Birmingham, AL
10Center for Esophageal Diseases and Swallowing, Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, University of North
Carolina Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC
11Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, Aurora, CO
12Barrett’s Esophagus Unit, Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, Mayo Clinic, Scottsdale, AZ USA
Corresponding author: Prasad G. Iyer MD MSc
Professor, Mayo Clinic Alix School of Medicine
Chair, Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology
Mayo Clinic, Scottsdale, AZ
Email: iyer.prasad@mayo.edu
Abstract
Barrett’s esophagus dysplasia grading suffers substantial inter-observer variability, particularly for
low-grade dysplasia, complicating clinical decision-making. We conducted a retrospective multi-
institutional diagnostic accuracy study of a foundation model-based deep learning system for
dysplasia grading, using 969 H&E-stained whole slide images from four institutions. Patch-level
classifiers trained on expert annotations identified diagnostically relevant regions, followed by
attribute-aware multiple instance learning for slide-level classification as non-dysplastic Barrett’s
esophagus (NDBE), low-grade dysplasia, or high-grade dysplasia. On a held-out test set (n
= 130), macro-averaged AUC was 0.96 (95% CI 0.93–0.98). For binary dysplasia detection,
sensitivity was 98% (80/82) and specificity 81% (39/48), with a negative likelihood ratio of
0.030 and quadratic-weighted κ of 0.83 against expert consensus. No high-grade dysplasia
case was misclassified as NDBE. Performance was consistent across institutions without stain
normalization, indicating that stain-robust foundation-model representations may remove the
site-specific preprocessing that has constrained prior systems to institution-specific deployment.
1
arXiv:2611.26562v1  [cs.CV]  19 Nov 2026
Introduction
Barrett’s esophagus (BE) affects approximately 1-3% of the general population in the United
States [1–3] and represents the primary precursor lesion to esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC), with
annual progression rates ranging from 0.3% per year for non-dysplastic Barrett’s esophagus to 28.6%
for high-grade dysplasia [4–7]. Dysplasia grading determines clinical management: non-dysplastic
cases require surveillance every 3-5 years, low-grade dysplasia prompts either annual surveillance
or endoscopic eradication therapy, and high-grade dysplasia necessitates endoscopic eradication
therapy [8]. However, substantial inter-observer variability in dysplasia grading complicates clinical
decision-making [9]. Among expert gastrointestinal pathologists, agreement is substantial for high-
grade dysplasia (κ = 0.71) and non-dysplastic Barrett’s esophagus (κ = 0.79) but falls to fair or poor
levels for low-grade dysplasia (κ = 0.42) [10,11]. Community pathologists demonstrate even lower
concordance with expert consensus, with documented tendency toward dysplasia overdiagnosis [12].
This variability leads to unnecessary referrals, patient anxiety, and potentially inappropriate
interventions.
Recent applications of deep learning to Barrett’s esophagus dysplasia classification have shown
promising results [13–16]. Prior work from our group demonstrated the feasibility of deep learn-
ing for BE dysplasia grading [13]; however, external validation across institutions [15] required
institution-specific stain normalization models to account for differences in tissue processing and
scanner protocols, an approach that is impractical for broad deployment across diverse pathology lab-
oratories. The emergence of foundation models in computational pathology addresses this limitation
directly, providing stain-robust pre-trained representations that generalize across institutions without
site-specific adaptation [17,18]. Despite these advances, multi-institutional training approaches
combining foundation models with clinical utility evaluation for community practice settings remain
underexplored.
We aimed to develop a foundation model-based deep learning system for Barrett’s esophagus
dysplasia grading using a multi-institutional training and validation dataset. The system employs a
two-stage architecture: patch-level classifiers trained on expert annotations identify diagnostically
relevant regions, followed by attribute-aware multiple instance learning for slide-level classification
[19]. We evaluated the system’s performance across institutions, characterized clinical utility metrics
including likelihood ratios for dysplasia detection, and analyzed error patterns to assess safety for
potential clinical deployment.
Methods
Dataset & Preprocessing
Ethics declaration
This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by
the Mayo Clinic Institutional Review Board (approval no. 23-009891). Because the study involved
retrospective analysis of existing pathology data and posed no more than minimal risk, the Mayo
Clinic Institutional Review Board waived the requirement for informed consent and for HIPAA
authorization.
2
Dataset
This retrospective study utilized a multi-institutional dataset comprising 969 Barrett’s esophagus
(BE) slides from 961 patients across four centers: Mayo Clinic (n = 531), Baylor Dallas (n =
169), Oregon Health & Science University (OHSU) (n = 151), and University of Alabama at
Birmingham (UAB) (n = 118). BE diagnosis was confirmed through review of endoscopic and
histologic reports. Inclusion criteria were: (1) endoscopic evidence of BE (≥1 cm columnar mucosa
extending proximally from the gastroesophageal junction), and (2) confirmed histologic diagnosis
of BE (intestinal-type mucosa with goblet cells). Individual patients could contribute multiple
slides from different specimens obtained during the same or different procedures, but not from
multiple levels (serial sections) of a single specimen. The highest grade of dysplasia on each slide,
as confirmed by consensus among expert study pathologists, was used for classification. Patient
demographics and endoscopic findings by institution are summarized in Table S1.
Two expert pathologists (CH, JL) with significant BE dysplasia experience independently
reviewed all slides to confirm dysplasia grade based on established criteria [20,21]. Discordant cases
were resolved through discussion between reviewers, with the consensus read serving as the final
label. Slides were classified as non-dysplastic BE (NDBE), low-grade dysplasia (LGD), or high-grade
dysplasia (HGD). Mayo Clinic slides were annotated for regions with the highest dysplasia grade
using Aperio ImageScope software (Leica Biosystems), as previously described [13]. Slides from
non-Mayo institutions lacked patch-level annotations and contributed slide-level dysplasia grade
labels only.
The dataset was randomly split into training (∼70%), validation (∼15%), and test (∼15%) sets,
stratified by pathology grade and institution, and grouped by patient ID to prevent data leakage.
The final distribution comprised 709 training slides (268 NDBE, 233 LGD, 208 HGD), 130 validation
slides (49 NDBE, 41 LGD, 40 HGD), and 130 test slides (48 NDBE, 45 LGD, 37 HGD).
Preprocessing pipeline
Whole slide images scanned at 40× magnification were preprocessed to extract 1280×1280 pixel
tissue patches using a grid-based tiling approach with 50% overlap between adjacent tiles. This
patch size was chosen empirically so that individual glandular tissues of the specimen would fit
into a single patch. Tissue segmentation was performed using HSV color space thresholding, where
background regions were identified when pixels met either: (1) brightness >240 or <30 combined
with saturation <76, or (2) brightness >200 with saturation <45. Tiles containing ≥5% tissue were
retained for analysis to ensure comprehensive tissue inclusion.
Feature Extraction
Features were extracted from each patch using Midnight-12k [22], a pathology-specific foundation
model. Midnight is a self-supervised vision transformer trained on over 12,000 whole slide images
using the DINOv2 framework, demonstrating robust performance in tissue classification and cancer
detection tasks without requiring manual annotations.
3
Model Framework
The classification framework consisted of two sequential stages (Figure 1). Stage 1 employed
patch-level classifiers to identify diagnostically relevant tissue regions and select informative patches
for each slide. Stage 2 utilized a multiple instance learning (MIL) architecture to generate slide-level
predictions from the sampled patches.
Stage 1: Patch-Level Classification and Sampling
Patch-Level Classifier Training
Stage 1 classifiers were trained using annotated Mayo Clinic slides. Slides contained a median
of 3 hand-drawn annotation regions (range: 1–28), totaling 1977 annotation regions across 463
slides (662 NDBE, 753 LGD, 562 HGD). Bounding boxes were fitted around these annotations,
and 1280×1280-pixel patches were extracted. Patches were assigned to one of four classes based on
tissue content and annotation overlap:
• Background: patches with ≥5% tissue and zero pixels within annotated regions from NDBE
slides
• NDBE: patches with ≥40% tissue and ≥25% pixels within annotated regions from NDBE
slides
• LGD: patches with ≥40% tissue and ≥25% pixels within annotated regions from LGD slides
• HGD: patches with ≥40% tissue and ≥25% pixels within annotated regions from HGD slides
Four binary classifiers were trained using Midnight-extracted features as input:
(1) NDBE classifier: NDBE vs non-NDBE (background, LGD, or HGD)
(2) Dysplasia classifier: dysplasia (LGD or HGD) vs non-dysplasia (background or NDBE)
(3) LGD classifier: LGD vs non-LGD (background, NDBE, or HGD)
(4) HGD classifier: HGD vs non-HGD (background, NDBE, or LGD)
Each classifier was a small neural network (a two-layer multilayer perceptron) that learns to
weigh combinations of the extracted image features and output a probability for each patch category;
standard training techniques (ReLU activation, batch normalization, and dropout) were used to
stabilize learning and reduce overfitting. Patches were assigned final classifications based on the
four classifier outputs, as summarized in Table 1.
The dysplasia classifier was included to reduce false positives in LGD and HGD classifiers, which
occasionally misclassified artifacts or high-cellularity non-glandular regions as dysplastic tissue.
Patch Sampling Strategy
For Stage 2 MIL training, a priority-based sampling strategy selected up to 1000 patches per slide
to form a “bag,” the fixed-size collection of patches used to represent that slide during classification.
Patches were first categorized into six groups: NDBE, LGD, HGD, and three discrepancy categories
(LGD-HGD, LGD-NDBE, HGD-NDBE) (Table 1). Spatial redundancy was removed by identifying

only the patch with highest prediction probability was retained. Patches were sorted by prediction
probability, with non-duplicate patches prioritized to ensure spatial diversity.
Bags were constructed with the following composition: 20% NDBE, 35% LGD, 30% HGD, 7.5%
LGD-HGD discrepancy, and 7.5% LGD-NDBE discrepancy. NDBE-HGD discrepancy patches were
excluded as they typically represented model errors or artifacts. For each category, candidate pools
were created by oversampling at 1.1× the target number, from which the exact target was randomly
drawn to introduce training variability. When slides had insufficient patches in a category, deficits
were filled from combined discrepancy categories or neighboring diagnostic categories following a
predefined priority order (HGD filled from LGD, then NDBE). Remaining positions were padded
with null embeddings randomly selected from background tissue patches to maintain the 1000-patch
bag size and improve model robustness to non-tissue regions. Final bags were shuffled before input
to prevent positional bias.
Stage 2: Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) Architecture
The Stage 2 model employed AttriMIL [19], an MIL framework in which the algorithm learns which
patches in a slide’s bag are most diagnostically informative for each grade, similar to a pathologist
scanning a slide and focusing on the most relevant regions, rather than weighing every patch equally.
AttriMIL scores each patch’s relevance to NDBE, LGD, and HGD separately (class-specific attention)
and combines this with a per-patch prediction (instance classifier) into a combined “attribute score”
for each class, which is aggregated across the bag to produce the final slide-level diagnosis.
Training Details
Models were trained using the AdamW optimizer with learning rate 1 × 10−5 and weight decay
3 × 10−4. Training proceeded for 400 epochs with early stopping (patience = 40 epochs) using
distributed data parallel strategy across four A100 GPUs via PyTorch. The best model checkpoint
was selected based on validation macro-average F1 score.
6
Statistical Analysis
Performance metrics (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), sensitivity,
specificity, F1 score, and accuracy) were reported with 95% confidence intervals computed via
bootstrap resampling (n = 1000 iterations, random seed=42). Macro-averaged AUC was computed
as the unweighted mean of per-class one-versus-rest AUC values.
Agreement between model predictions and expert pathologist consensus with categories for
dysplasia grading (NDBE, LGD, and HGD) was assessed using Cohen’s κ with unweighted and
quadratic weighted schemes, with quadratic weighting selected as the primary measure to appro-
priately penalize non-adjacent errors in ordinal dysplasia grades. Per-class κ was calculated using
one-versus-rest binarization for each grade, with an additional binary κ computed for distinguishing
any dysplasia (LGD+HGD) from NDBE. Kappa values were interpreted as none (0.00-0.20), mini-
mal (0.21-0.40), weak (0.41-0.60), moderate (0.61-0.80), or strong (0.81-0.90), and almost perfect
agreement (above 0.90) [23]. Clinical utility was assessed using positive and negative likelihood ratios
(LR+/LR−) for binary dysplasia grade prediction. Cross-institutional consistency was assessed by
comparing per-site accuracy using Fisher’s exact test and the predicted probability assigned to the
true class using the Kruskal-Wallis test, the latter chosen because these values were not normally
distributed and institutional group sizes were small and unequal. All statistical tests were two-tailed
with significance threshold α = 0.05.
Code availability
Code for model training and evaluation is available from the corresponding author upon reasonable
request. This study used the publicly available Midnight-12k foundation model [22] and the published
AttriMIL architecture [19].
Results
Overall Performance
The test set comprised 130 slides with the following grade distribution: 48 NDBE (36.9%), 45 LGD
(34.6%), and 37 HGD (28.5%) from four institutions. Overall performance metrics are presented
in Table 2. The model achieved strong discriminative performance across all three classes, with
AUC ranging from 0.94 for LGD (the most diagnostically challenging category) to 0.97 for both
NDBE and HGD, yielding a macro-averaged AUC of 0.96 (95% CI: 0.93, 0.98) and macro-averaged
F1 of 0.85 (95% CI: 0.78, 0.91). LGD demonstrated the lowest F1 score (0.82; 95% CI: 0.72,
0.90), consistent with its known diagnostic difficulty. For binary dysplasia (LGD/HGD vs. NDBE)
detection, sensitivity was 98% (80/82; 95% CI: 0.94, 1.00) and specificity was 81% (39/48; 95% CI:
0.70, 0.93). Per-class sensitivity was 89% (33/37; 95% CI: 0.78, 0.98) for HGD and 84% (38/45; 95%
CI: 0.74, 0.94) for LGD. The model achieved a positive LR of 5.20 (95% CI: 3.23, 13.06) and negative
LR of 0.030 (95% CI: 0.013, 0.078) for any dysplasia detection. At the dysplasia prevalence reported
for index endoscopy in Barrett’s esophagus, approximately 13% to 17% [24,25], a negative model
prediction reduces the post-test probability to 0.5% to 0.6% and a positive prediction increases it to
44% to 51%; after a negative prediction it remains below 1.3% even at an assumed prevalence of
30%.

MM-SystemOneBias: Evaluating Bias in Multimodal Jev-Style System One
Decision Models
Jinzhe Li1,3
Qi Wang1
Dandan Guo1,4
Li Liu5
Yuan Wu1*
Yi Chang1,2,3
1School of Artificial Intelligence, Jilin University
2Engineering Research Center of Knowledge-Driven Human-Machine Intelligence, Jilin University
3International Center of Future Science, Jilin University
4King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST)
5School of Big Data and Software Engineering, Chongqing University
{jinzhe25}@mails.jlu.edu.cn, dcsliuli@cqu.edu.cn, {qiwang, guodandan, yuanwu, yichang}@jlu.edu.cn
Abstract
When multimodal decision models determine
actions, moderation outcomes, or quality judg-
ments, their reliability depends on preserving
semantic decisions across presentation changes,
ignoring irrelevant additions, and distinguish-
ing information consistent with task evidence
from information that conflicts with it. Ex-
isting evaluations study decision-interface bi-
ases and multimodal model behavior in sep-
arate settings, leaving no common protocol
to compare multimodal decision models with
their backbones on practical tasks. We intro-
duce MM-SystemOneBias, which evaluates
13 models on 5,323 original instances from
nine public datasets and 11 task scenarios us-
ing six paired interventions: option order, op-
tion label, external judgment, image–text de-
scription, irrelevant information, and rating
scale. Across seven matched decision-model–
backbone pairs, decision models are more sta-
ble under option-label, irrelevant-information,
and rating-scale changes in all seven pairs; six
pairs also show lower option-order flip rates.
They incur smaller accuracy losses under in-
correct external judgments in all seven pairs
and conflicting descriptions in six. In six pairs,
they gain less accuracy from correct external
judgments and show less favorable accuracy
changes under consistent descriptions. Among
pairs with unchanged semantic decisions, mean
absolute changes in answer probabilities range
from 4.56 to 11.55 percentage points, revealing
input effects that accuracy alone misses.
1
Introduction
Recent advances in System One models have made
typed decisions over finite answer spaces practical
for structured tasks (Deußer et al., 2026; Geuter
et al., 2026). Multimodal systems extend this in-
terface to applications such as web interaction and
image assessment (Zheng et al., 2024; Li et al.,

Intervention sensitivity across multi-
modal decision models and general-purpose vision-
language models. Axes show semantic flip rate, error
introduction rate, or mean absolute grade shift for the
six intervention types. Decision models are generally
less sensitive to option and rating-scale interventions,
while sensitivity to external judgments and image–text
descriptions varies across models.
2024a; Yue et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2023), where a
model decision can determine an action, a modera-
tion outcome, or a quality judgment. Their reliabil-
ity therefore matters beyond answer accuracy on a
fixed presentation.
A reliable multimodal decision model should
preserve its semantic answer when option order
changes. Its decision should also remain stable
when candidate labels or rating values change. It
should respond appropriately to external judgments
and image–text descriptions, and irrelevant infor-
mation should not alter its answer. These require-
arXiv:2611.26557v1  [cs.AI]  19 Nov 2026
ments are distinct from general multimodal capa-
bility: a model may recognize the relevant visual
content yet change its decision under an interven-
tion.
However, existing evaluations leave this behav-
ior incompletely characterized. Studies of typed
and multiple-choice decision models examine po-
sition, label, and scale biases (Sun et al., 2026;
Azizi et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026; Zheng et al.,
2023a; Zhao et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2022; Liusie
et al., 2023), while multimodal bias studies mainly
evaluate general-purpose models or MLLM-as-a-
Judge systems under open-ended generation, ques-
tion answering, or scoring (Lee et al., 2026; Zhou
et al., 2026; Lai and Huang, 2026; Li et al., 2023;
Chen et al., 2024; Cai et al., 2025). These settings
differ from finite semantic decisions on practical
multimodal tasks, and existing work does not pro-
vide a common protocol for comparing decision
models with their corresponding general-purpose
backbones.
To address this gap,
we introduce MM-
SystemOneBias, a systematic benchmark for bias
in multimodal decision models. It covers 5,323
original instances from 9 public datasets and 11
task scenarios, evaluates 8 decision models and 5
general-purpose vision-language models, and ap-
plies six controlled interventions: option order,
option label, external judgment, image–text de-
scription, irrelevant information, and rating scale.
Paired comparisons measure semantic decisions,
task accuracy, and probabilities assigned to an-
swers. Seven decision-model–backbone pairs sup-
port matched comparisons across the five back-
bones.
Across the six bias types, the decision models
show heterogeneous sensitivity, with individual
models exhibiting large changes under particular
interventions (Figure 1). Across matched pairs,
decision models have lower flip rates under option-
label and irrelevant-information interventions and
smaller rating-scale shifts in all seven pairs; option-
order flip rates are lower in six. They also lose less
accuracy under incorrect external judgments in all
seven pairs and conflicting descriptions in six. In
six pairs, they gain less accuracy from correct judg-
ments and show less favorable accuracy changes
under consistent descriptions. In image–text tasks,
conflicting descriptions can redirect correct deci-
sions even when a model rejects the false claim
in an isolated probe; an image-first instruction re-
duces this task error. Answer probabilities also
shift while semantic decisions remain unchanged.
Our contributions are:
• We introduce MM-SystemOneBias, a system-
atic benchmark that evaluates option order,
option label, external judgment, image–text
description, irrelevant information, and rating
scale in multimodal decision models across
real tasks.
• We provide matched comparisons between de-
cision models and general-purpose backbones
across all six intervention types.
• We jointly analyze semantic decisions, task
outcomes, and answer probabilities to charac-
terize intervention-related behavior and prob-
ability shifts.
2
Related Work
2.1
Bias in System One Decision Models
System One decision models expose a typed, finite
answer space and return a decision, often together
with a probability for each legal answer. Recent
work establishes their capability and probability-
quality baselines across structured tasks (Deußer
et al., 2026; Geuter et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2017;
Kadavath et al., 2022). A complementary line of
studies examines whether the decision interface
itself changes model behavior: name–definition
swaps, answer-label changes, and variations in or-
dered rating scales can alter otherwise equivalent
decisions (Sun et al., 2026; Azizi et al., 2026; Gao
et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2022;
Liusie et al., 2023). These studies show that seman-
tic alignment and the decision interface matter to
typed decisions, but they mainly consider textual
settings or individual intervention families. We
extend this line by evaluating option order, option
labels, external judgments, image–text descriptions,
irrelevant information, and rating scales across mul-
timodal tasks, measuring semantic decisions, accu-
racy, and answer probabilities.
2.2
Bias in General-Purpose Language and
Vision-Language Models
A parallel literature studies bias and evidence use
in general-purpose language and vision-language
models (Liu et al., 2023; Fu et al., 2023; Yue et al.,
2024; Li et al., 2024b). Paired interventions re-
veal sensitivity to option position and label presen-
tation (Zheng et al., 2023a; Atabuzzaman et al.,
2025; Zhao et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2022), as well as
systematic responses to irrelevant information, con-
flicting image–text evidence, and changes in rating
formats (Zhou et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Lai
and Huang, 2026; Jo et al., 2026; Li et al., 2023;
Chen et al., 2024; Cai et al., 2025). Multimodal-
judge benchmarks further examine how changes
to the query, image, or response affect scores and
preferences (Ye et al., 2025; Hwang et al., 2025;
Lee et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2023b; Shi et al.,
2024; Wataoka et al., 2024). These benchmarks
primarily evaluate general-purpose models as open-
ended generators, question-answering systems, or
judges. System One models instead make finite
semantic decisions in scenarios such as GUI op-
eration, robotics, moderation, and image assess-
ment. We compare decision models with their cor-
responding general-purpose backbones on the same
multimodal tasks, measuring semantic decisions,
accuracy, and answer probabilities under each in-
tervention.
3
Evaluation Framework
We introduce MM-SystemOneBias, an evaluation
framework that measures how option order, option
label, external judgment, image–text description,
irrelevant information, and rating scale affect the
decisions of multimodal decision models. This
section defines the task formulation, the bias taxon-
omy, the data construction pipeline, and the evalua-
tion metrics that together make up the framework.
3.1
Task Formulation
We formulate each multimodal decision task as
selecting a semantic answer from a finite answer
space, given one or more images and task text. Let
I denote the images in their specified order, q the
task text, and A = {a1, . . . , aK} the set of K
legal semantic answers. We study three decision
interfaces: choice, yes/no judgment, and scoring,
with answers corresponding to candidate content, a
judgment about a task proposition, and an ordered
quality grade, respectively. Together, the images,
task text, and answer presentation form the original
input u(0); its reference answer is y∗∈A.
The decision-model group comprises seven
open-weight multimodal System One models and
the closed-source TypeSafe Jev service. We also
evaluate five general-purpose vision-language mod-
els through the same typed decision interfaces.
Each open-weight decision model is paired with a
general-purpose vision-language backbone, yield-
ing seven matched pairs across five backbones;
TypeSafe Jev has no matched backbone.
Let fθ denote the model under evaluation, where
θ identifies its parameters or version. We map its
output to A and denote the resulting semantic de-
cision on the original input by ˆy(0). Let p(0)(a) be
the probability assigned to semantic answer a ∈A.
The model decision is the most probable answer,

Each intervened instance is constructed from the

We denote the semantic decision and answer

quantify the effects of all six interventions on se-
mantic decisions, task performance, and probabili-
ties assigned to answers.
3.2
Bias Taxonomy
MM-SystemOneBias evaluates six bias types: op-
tion order, option label, external judgment, image–
text description, irrelevant information, and rating
scale. Each intervention changes one designated
factor in an original instance while preserving the
task and semantic answer space. We align outputs
to semantic answers and compare each intervened
instance with its original.
Option order.
This intervention changes candi-
date positions while preserving candidate content
and semantic identity; display labels follow the new
positions.
Option label.
This intervention changes the sym-
bols used to identify candidates while preserving
their content, positions, and semantic identities.
External judgment.
This intervention adds a
conclusion attributed to a user, a previous system,
or a tool. Conditions vary the source and whether
the conclusion agrees with the reference answer.
Image–text description.
This intervention adds
a statement about a relevant visual fact. The state-
ment either agrees with or contradicts the evidence
in the image.
Irrelevant information.
This intervention ap-
pends background material from other instances
that does not contribute evidence or requirements
to the current task.
Rating scale.
This intervention changes the nu-
merical values assigned to ordered quality grades
while preserving each grade’s meaning and relative
order.
Table 1 summarizes the intervention factors and
conditions for the six types. Appendix A defines
each intervention and presents paired task examples
showing its input and semantic interpretation.
3.3
Data Construction
We adapt public multimodal datasets into original
instances, generate paired interventions, and verify
the added materials. The nine sources cover 11
task scenarios through 14 task–interface combina-
tions across three decision interfaces; image safety
moderation and generated-image quality each sup-
port multiple interfaces. Appendix E reports the
resulting benchmark composition.
Source Data and Task Conversion.
The sources
cover GUI interaction, robot actions and states,
document type classification, image safety modera-
tion, industrial anomaly detection, image-grounded
response preference, and generated-image qual-
ity: Multimodal-Mind2Web (Zheng et al., 2024),
AgentRewardBench (Lù et al., 2025), Robo2VLM-
1 (Chen et al., 2025), RVL-CDIP (Harley et al.,
2015), LlavaGuard (Helff et al., 2024), MVTec
AD (Bergmann et al., 2019), VL-RewardBench (Li
et al., 2025), HPDv2 (Wu et al., 2023), and AGIQA-
3K (Li et al., 2024a). We form each original in-
stance from a source instance’s images, task text,
and annotation. Choice tasks use source options
when available; otherwise, we pair the correct tar-
get with incorrect alternatives. Yes/no answers
follow task outcomes, policy annotations, or de-
fect labels. For image quality, dataset-wide MOS
quantiles define ordered reference grades and their
corresponding acceptability labels. A source in-
stance that supports multiple interfaces retains a
shared identity across its derived instances. Ap-
pendix C details these conversions, and Table 6
maps each source to its tasks and sampling unit.
Sampling and Test-Set Composition.
We sam-
ple from native test partitions where available
and select shuffled source groups for the remain-
ing datasets.
The sample preserves both out-
comes where relevant and all five image-quality
grades, while balancing correct-answer positions
within choice tasks. Related trajectories, queries,
prompts, and shared images remain together. Ap-
pendix C.3 specifies the grouping units and quotas;
Appendix E reports the retained composition.
Intervention Construction.
Each intervened in-
stance is paired with an original instance. Its con-
struction changes one input factor while preserving
the task and semantic answer mapping. The six
bias types define the factor changed in each pair:
Option order.
We reorder the candidates and
move their display labels with them, leaving candi-
date content and semantic identity unchanged.
Option label.
We replace the candidate labels
while leaving candidate content, order, and seman-
tic identity unchanged.
External judgment.
We append a fixed-template
conclusion and vary both its agreement with the
reference answer and its attributed source or tone.
Image–text description.
We add a pair of de-
scriptions: one supported by the task-relevant vi-
sual evidence and one that contradicts it.
Irrelevant information.
We append background
items from other source instances in the same eval-
uation pool and vary how many appear in the input.
Rating scale.
We change the numbers assigned
to ordered quality grades while keeping their mean-
ings and order fixed.
Each version retains links to its original instance,
semantic-answer mapping, and intervention condi-
tion. Appendix D specifies the construction rules;
Appendix A illustrates each type with paired task
examples.
Material Verification and Selection.
Program-
matic checks confirm candidate identities, grade
mappings, and the target named by each external
judgment. Image–text descriptions are checked

Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation
(ROGUE-AI)
Mengxiao Wang, Mahbub Alam, Kalyan Nakka, and Nitesh Saxena
Texas A&M University
{jacksonwang, mahbub.alam, kalyan, nsaxena}@tamu.edu
Abstract
Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now
delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News
media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g.,
Replit’s coding agent deleting a production database), but a re-
port often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)validates
the incident or finds its root cause. Incident catalogs collect
these reports, and benchmarks record whether agents fail, but
neither replicates an incident nor tests the cause its report
might identify.
In this paper, we present ROGUE-AI (Replication of Agen-
tic Security Events: Audit and Investigation), a multi-agent
framework that closes the above gap and rebuilds each re-
ported incident offline together with a matched control that
lacks only the blamed cause, and runs agents on both. As part
of the framework, Claude-, Gemini- and GPT-based agents
collect reports and build replications, an agent from another
vendor reviews each build, and code decides whether harm
occurred. Our results suggest that ROGUE-AI is able to
reproduce the reported harm in 89% of its 108 attempted
replications.1 Agents built on five current GPT, Claude, Gem-
ini and DeepSeek models made the reported mistake in 18%
to 33% of runs, against at most 1% without the blamed cause.
Of the 72 incidents with real-world harm, 62 had no under-
lying attacker, and in these, agents did what their task asked
for but missed an ordinary hazard, such as a database shared
with the live site. Replications without an attacker caused
more harm than replications of prompt injection for all five
models. Defenses against prompt injection look for injected
instructions, but these replications contain none. Further, a
warning after each tool output that names the hazard and
its consequence lowered harm for all five models, whereas
a note of the same length that does not mention the hazard
left most of the harm in place. Built from real incidents, the
ROGUE-AI replications form a reusable audit framework
that vendors can rerun before each new release.
1A list of all incidents that we studied, with their sources and replications,
can be accessed at https://rogue-ai.surge.sh.
1
Introduction
Large language model (LLM) agents now run shell com-
mands, change cloud servers and pay out cryptocurrency
for their users. Anthropic’s coding agent Claude Code [1]
ran terraform destroy and removed the production stack
of DataTalks.Club [2]. In September 2026, the Australian
government opened an investigation after an OpenAI agent ac-
cessed government health portals, including Medicare statis-
tics [3]. News stories and company posts report such failures,
but a report describes the outcome and rarely the mechanism.
The deletion could come from a careless model, too much
authority or a misunderstood task, each with its own fix. Secu-
rity researchers already re-run attacks that made the news [4],
and agent incidents can be tested the same way. A replication
cannot see the company’s logs, but it can test whether the
harm occurs with the cause that the report names and stops
once that cause is removed.
Prior work collects, labels or reruns these incidents but
does not test their causes. Incident catalogs such as the AI
Incident Database and the Agent Incident Registry collect
and label reports without testing them [5–7], and agent bench-
marks build their test cases from attacks or tasks that their
authors design [8, 9]. Closer to replication, Chronicle re-
runs parts of six recorded failures with simulated model out-
puts [10], Squidbrake reruns the commands of 12 incidents
against its rules [11], and CVE-Genie reproduces software ex-
ploits, whose result does not depend on a model’s choice [12].
However, an agent incident depends on a model’s decision,
which can change from run to run. A single rebuild therefore
cannot show that the cause named in a report produced the
harm, and none of these methods compares the rebuild with a
control that lacks only that cause.
For example, in July 2025, Replit’s coding agent deleted the
production database of SaaStr during a code freeze [13,14],
and the report blames a database that the agent’s development
work shared with the live site. As Figure 1 shows, we re-
build the incident offline as a repository whose tests use the
production database, together with a matched control whose
tests use a temporary database. The two copies differ only
in the blamed cause, so a difference in harm between them

is evidence for that cause. Current models wiped the pro-
duction rows in about half of the incident sessions, while
all 15 control sessions kept their rows, which supports the
report’s claim. In this paper, we present ROGUE-AI, the
first framework that tests public reports of agent incidents
by controlled replication. Unlike CVE-Genie and Chronicle,
ROGUE-AI compares each rebuild with a matched control
and runs current models repeatedly in each condition.
ROGUE-AI is a pipeline of LLM agents with one job each,
which we call specialist agents. Agents search the web for
reports, check each report against its most detailed source
and write down the named cause. Other agents build the
replication and its control, an agent from another vendor
reviews each build, and code decides whether harm occurred.
From 253 reports, Claude-, Gemini- and GPT-based agents
built 108 replications of 96 incidents in 38 classes, at $3.28
each. ROGUE-AI reproduced the reported harm in 89% of its
replications (§6.2), and five models from OpenAI, Anthropic,
Google and DeepSeek still made the reported mistake in 18%
to 33% of incident sessions, against at most 1% in the controls
(Table 4). In the replication of the Medicare incident, for
example, the five models entered the portal’s restricted area
with the browser’s saved sign-in in 14 of 15 incident sessions
and in none of the 30 control sessions. Of the 72 incidents
with real-world harm, 62 had no attacker, and in these 62, an
agent that did what its task asked missed an ordinary hazard,
such as the shared database (§5).
Defenses against prompt injection miss most of this harm.
Replications without an attacker caused more harm than repli-
cations of prompt injection for all five models, but they con-
tain no injected instruction, which is what these defenses
look for. Defenses taken from the reports did better, and
with confirmation by the user or data-flow tracking, the five
models caused no harm. Checks that match the text of an
action were weaker, because rephrased attacks still caused
part of the harm (§6.4). Because a replication finds the hazard,
it also suggests a fix. We added a warning after each tool
output that names the hazard and its consequence, such as
a warning that the tests drop the production database. This
warning lowered harm for all five models, to 2% for Claude
Sonnet 4.6, whereas most harm remained with a restated rule,
with a note that gives only the fact, or with a note of the same
length that does not mention the hazard (§6.3). Agent builders
should keep production credentials out of the agent’s reach,
and vendors can rerun the replications before each release.
We make four contributions:
• Controlled Replication of Security Incidents Reported
in Media. We introduce ROGUE-AI, the first framework
that tests a reported agent incident by rebuilding it offline
together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed
cause. Agents repeated the reported mistake in 18% to 33%
of runs, against at most 1% in the controls (§3, §6).
• Multi-Agent Replication Pipeline. We build the pipeline
from Claude-, Gemini- and GPT-based specialist agents,
which find and verify reports, build each replication, and di-
agnose and fix failed replications. Because these agents can
fail like those they test, each judgment has an independent
2
check, and code decides harm. They built 108 replications
from 253 reports, and vendors can rerun them to audit a new
model for $0.54 to $47 (§4, §6). We release ROGUE-AI’s
code, replications and session logs [15], and we reported
each model’s results to OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and
DeepSeek.
• Ordinary Causes of Reported Harm. We show that cur-
rent models repeat reported harm for ordinary reasons, such
as a hazard that the agent never saw. One edit at the first
harmful step removed the harm in 118 of 208 harmful ses-
sions, and replications without an attacker caused more
harm than replications of prompt injection for all five mod-
els (§6, §6.3, §6.4).
• Hazard Warnings as a Mitigation. We propose a warning
after each tool output that names the hazard and its con-
sequence. The warning lowered harm for all five models,
to 2% for Claude Sonnet 4.6, whereas a note of the same
length that does not mention the hazard left harm between
83% and 98% (§6.3).
2
Background and Criteria
LLM Agents and Their Incidents. By an LLM agent we
mean a program in which a language model decides which
tools to call and acts on the results [16]. A coding agent runs
shell commands, a personal assistant sends and deletes mail,
a browser agent fills in web forms, and a wallet agent signs
transfers. Many agents also load tools through the Model
Context Protocol (MCP), which lets them call tools published
by other parties. We count an event as an agent incident if
an LLM agent took an action through a tool and that action
caused harm or achieved an attacker’s goal against a victim,
and if the event was first reported between January 2025 and
October 2026. Harm in the wild, demonstrations on shipped
products, threat reports and vendor evaluations qualify, but
events on research prototypes do not.
Running Example. We follow the Replit incident through-
out [13]. The user had told the agent many times to make
no change without permission [14]. During this code freeze,
the agent’s commands deleted the production database, and
Replit’s CEO confirmed the deletion. Nobody attacked the
agent, which had a standing rule against changes, a task that
seemed to need a database change, and production credentials.
Criteria for a Replication. To test such a report, a replica-
tion has to meet six criteria, which follow from how reports
and agents fail. First, the report is checked against a primary
source, since we had to correct 76 of 253 incident records
and found 2 contradicted by their sources. Second, a current
model makes the incident’s decision again, because rerunning
the recorded commands tests only the commands. Third, a
matched control removes only the hazard, because the task
alone can produce harm that should not count toward the

reported cause. Fourth, code decides harm from the environ-
ment’s state, because agents misreport their actions, as the
Replit agent did [14]. Fifth, a pipeline builds the test from
the report, because new reports arrive weekly. Sixth, the test
runs offline on any model, letting a vendor rerun it before a
release.
Comparison with Prior Work. As Table 1 shows, no prior
work meets the criteria that we can check from its publica-
tions. Benchmarks run current models, and AgentDojo runs
its tasks with and without the injection. Their test cases,
however, come from the benchmarks’ authors. Chronicle
needs a recorded run and simulates the model’s outputs, and
Squidbrake reruns reported commands against its rules.
Closest in method is CVE-Genie [12], which reproduced
428 of 841 CVEs at an average cost of $2.77. Developer
agents set up the software and write an exploit, critic agents
review the steps, and a verifier checks a signal specific to the
vulnerability. The target of CVE-Genie, however, is software,
where the result of an exploit does not depend on a model’s
choice. In an agent incident, by contrast, the test concerns a
model’s decision, which varies between models and runs, and
the task alone can cause harm. ROGUE-AI therefore adds a
matched control, repeated runs on any model and a statistical
test for each claim (§3).
3
The ROGUE-AI Framework
Reports as Claims. In ROGUE-AI, we treat an incident re-
port as a causal claim and a replication as a controlled ex-
periment that tests the claim. We write the claim of a report
R as C(R) = ⟨T,E,H,a∗,h⟩. The claim states that in an en-

task T takes the action a∗, which causes the harm h. For the
Replit report, T is fixing a bug in a demo application, E is a
repository under a code freeze, H is a test suite that shares the
production database, a∗is running the tests, and h is the loss
of production rows. The hazard is the part of the environment
that the report blames. The claim is causal, as the report
asserts that an agent causes h more often with H present than
with H absent. For a model M, we write this difference as
τM = Pr[h | do(H)]−Pr[h | do(¬H)],
where do(·) marks that the experimenter sets the hazard in-
stead of observing it. A report is correct for M if τM > 0.
Replications as Interventions. In ROGUE-AI, a replication
consists of the task T, a state check and two offline envi-
ronments EH and E¬H built from the same world. After a
session, the state check inspects the environment and decides
whether h occurred. EH is the incident condition, and E¬H
is the matched control, which keeps the cue (the part that
makes a∗attractive) and removes only the hazard. In the
Replit replication, the control’s tests create their tables in
a temporary database. The harm rate of a condition is the
share of its sessions with harm. If we run M for n sessions in
both conditions, the difference between the two harm rates
estimates τM, up to sampling noise.
Validity Conditions. As Table 2 lists, a replication tests the
claim only if it meets five conditions. Suppose the hazard is
reachable, the harm requires the hazard and the two conditions
differ only in the hazard. Then the difference between the
harm rates in EH and E¬H is an unbiased estimate of the
hazard’s effect on harm for M in this replication. Reachability
rules out a replication where no model could fail, and the
minimal difference rules out a second cause such as a new
prompt.
Fidelity to the Report. The other two conditions, a natural
path to the hazard and fidelity to the report, do not affect this
estimate. They decide whether the replication’s hazard is the
report’s hazard, and a replication that fails them tests a dif-
ferent claim. A replication therefore takes only the elements
that the report and its primary sources state. The replication
fills omitted details, such as the model or system prompt,
with marked neutral defaults and adds no rule, prohibition,
pressure or hint, since any of these could change the decision
under test. Code checks the first three conditions, a reviewer
model checks the natural path, and both check fidelity to the
claim card, which ties each element of the claim to a sentence
of the report.
Outcomes. For a replication, let kt of nt incident sessions
and kc of nc control sessions cause harm. We compare the
two rates with a one-sided Fisher’s exact test and correct all
p-values with the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. A replica-
tion is supported if the corrected value is below 0.05, sugges-
tive if the incident condition caused harm without reaching
this level, and not reproduced if no incident session caused
harm. A supported replication thus shows that the cause that
the report blames produces the reported harm in agents built
on the tested models. Even a replication that is not repro-
duced bounds the harm rate of its build. With kt = 0, the 95%
Wilson upper bound on the harm rate is about 20% for 15
sessions and 11% for 30. We mark a replication as no control
if it caused harm but has no finished control session. We can
pool the counts over models or stratify the test by model.
Audits. To audit a new model M′, ROGUE-AI reruns all repli-
cations that passed the checks and recomputes the outcomes
for M′. A replication not reproduced for earlier models but
supported for M′ is a regression, and the reverse is an improve-
ment. A vendor needs only an adapter for the model’s API to
run this audit, because the replications run offline and code
decides harm. The audit record puts the harmful sessions of
the new model in both conditions next to the results of earlier
models, and a vendor can thus see which reported mistakes a
release still makes (§6).
4
The ROGUE-AI Pipeline
This section follows a report through ROGUE-AI to an out-
come, with the Replit report as the example. ROGUE-AI
uses LLM agents as automation tools, and Figure 1 shows
where they work. In the first two stages, searcher agents find
reports, a screener applies our inclusion rules, a verifier com-
pares each report with a primary source, two labelers label
the incident and a report analyst writes down its claim (§4.1).
In the third stage, a domain builder writes the replication, and
4
a path reviewer and a domain reviewer check the build (§4.2).
In the last two stages, code runs the validity checks and
the models under test run the replication. Code then decides
harm and computes the test, and diagnoser agents read the
transcripts of replications that fail. The stages are linked
by a repair loop, in which reviewers send

Preprint
THE GEOMETRY OF LIES: KNOWLEDGE AND
PERSONA DIRECTIONS FOR DETECTING DECEPTION
IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
Md. Abdullah Al Zami, Suraiya Shanaz, Mahdi Hasan,
Shoaib Ahmed Dipu, Farig Yousuf Sadeque & Md. Sabbir Ahmed
Department of Computer Science and Engineering
BRAC University
Dhaka, Bangladesh
abdullah.al.zami@g.bracu.ac.bd, suraiya.shanaz@g.bracu.ac.bd,
mahdi.hasan.meem@g.bracu.ac.bd
ABSTRACT
Linear probes are the cheapest LLM lie detectors but often fail to transfer across
kinds of lie. Label-free directions from honest and deceptive role-play are untested
at 70B scale and on lies about knowledge, where a lie and an honest denial can be
identical. We widen a published persona bank with roles that deny knowledge they
have, plus honest counterparts. At each model’s middle layer the resulting persona
direction ranks lies across Liars’ Bench better than single-dataset probes on three
of its four models; it fails on Qwen, even when Qwen stays in role far more often.
On Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct it beats directions from a random persona bank, but
its gain over the published direction is within the range of random widenings. On
lies about knowledge, persona directions mainly track a reply’s wording: where
lies and honest denials share their words, our three main contrasts stay inside the
random-direction band on Llama and Qwen and reach only its edge on Gemma,
though on Mistral one clears it. A knowledge direction contrasts questions the
model can answer with ones nobody can, each followed by the same scripted
denial. It separates lies from identical honest denials on two models and narrowly
on a third, but not on the fourth; its other results partly depend on the benchmark’s
wording. On the Gender-Secret fine-tune it clears the band by a few hundredths
on Llama and fails on Mistral. The sum of the two directions ranks lies better
than a supervised probe at the same depth on all four models (on one, both near
chance) but is level with the persona direction on Llama’s average and behind that
probe on held-out lies. More varied role-play questions do not help the persona
direction on Liars’ Bench.
1
INTRODUCTION
Large language models sometimes lie. They have been observed concealing misconduct (Scheurer
et al., 2023; Järviniemi & Hubinger, 2024) and faking alignment (Greenblatt et al., 2024), and de-
ception by AI systems is a recognised risk (Park et al., 2024). Following Liars’ Bench (Kretschmar
et al., 2025), we call a statement a lie when the model asserts something it believes to be false,
where its belief is taken to be what it consistently asserts under no pressure to lie. This definition
separates lying from hallucination. The cheapest detector of such lies is a probe on the residual
stream, usually a linear one (Alain & Bengio, 2016; Azaria & Mitchell, 2023; Marks & Tegmark,
2024): one dot product per response, no extra forward pass, and a chance to catch a lie that leaves no
trace in the transcript (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Its weakness is generalisation: a probe trained
on one distribution of lies often fails on others (Kirch et al., 2026; Kumar, 2026; Natarajan et al.,
2026). Liars’ Bench makes the failure concrete. Its seven datasets hold on-policy lies, lies that four
open-weight models produced themselves. On most of them, probes trained on instruction pairs
are near chance in balanced accuracy at the benchmark’s threshold, which flags 1% of answers to
ordinary instructions. The hardest dataset is the harm-pressure knowledge report (HP-KR), in which
1
arXiv:2611.26545v1  [cs.AI]  19 Nov 2026
Preprint
a model denies knowing the answer to a hazardous question it has been shown to know. On HP-KR
the benchmark’s Mean Probe for Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, read at layer 20, scores an AUROC of
0.12, worse than chance. At the model’s middle layer a probe trained the same way ranks HP-KR
well, yet at that threshold it still flags none of its lies.
Mahadik & Skapars (2026) propose persona coordinates as a remedy: the model role-plays decep-
tive and honest personas, each persona’s mean activation is a vector, and the difference between
the two group means is a direction that uses no evaluation data and so cannot be fitted to one
dataset’s idiosyncrasies. On Llama-3.2-3B and Llama-3-8B these coordinates transfer better than
probes on raw activations, keeping more of their accuracy on datasets they were not fitted to; the
authors name larger models and richer persona sets as future work. We take up both. Rebuilt for
Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, their direction, which we call the published contrast, inverts on HP-KR:
at the benchmark’s layer it ranks honest answers above lies (AUROC 0.148). Nearly every HP-KR
lie is a denial of knowledge (125 of 139 on Llama), while every published deceptive persona lies
by controlling disclosure. We therefore add ten roles of our own, four that deny knowledge they
have and six honest counterparts. The widened contrast, which we call the extended contrast, ranks
HP-KR better, but for the wrong reason: its gain follows the words of a denial. The contrast built
from the new roles alone flags nearly every reply that says “I do not know”, whether the denial is
true or false, and at the middle layer, on the Llama rows where a lie and an honest denial are the
same sentence, every persona direction scores within the range that random directions reach (the
random band; Section 3). On these lies a persona direction responds to how a reply is worded more
than to whether the model knows the answer.
The definition of a lie offers a second route. A lie about knowledge is a denial by a model that
knows the answer, and what a model knows can be measured without any labelled lie, by comparing
questions whose answers it knows with questions whose answers nobody can know. We build a
knowledge direction from exactly that comparison, writing the same denial into the model’s reply
after every question so that the reply’s words do not vary. We then ask five questions of a detector that
adds a persona contrast to the knowledge direction: whether it transfers across Liars’ Bench better
than supervised probes; whether it separates lies from honest answers that use the same words; what
each part responds to; whether the result survives resampling, new questions, other layers and strict
thresholds; and whether it holds on other models and benchmarks.
The results are mixed. The extended contrast is the part that generalises: at each model’s middle
layer it transfers better than probes trained on a single dataset on three of the benchmark’s four
models. On the main model it also beats contrasts drawn from a random persona bank, although
a probe trained on all the other datasets together is level with it once HP-KR is set aside (0.915
against 0.917). It fails on Qwen, even with a second bank in which Qwen stays in role far more
often. The knowledge direction separates lies from identically worded honest denials on two models,
and narrowly on a third. Outside these wording-controlled tests, its transfer depends in part on the
wording of HP-KR’s template. On the Gender-Secret fine-tune, which only Llama and Mistral have,
it clears the random band by a few hundredths on Llama but not on Mistral; the other fine-tunes give
it no support. The sum of the two directions, our selected detector, ranks the benchmark’s lies better
than a probe trained at the same depth does on all four models (on Qwen both are near chance).
On the main model’s average over the benchmark’s datasets, however, it is level with the extended
contrast, and in an external competition it would rank 16th of 30, behind a supervised probe. At
cutoffs that flag 1% of each dataset’s honest answers, none of the six detectors we evaluate there
catches half of the lies on any model (at most 0.47; Table 31). Our contributions are:
• a persona bank for deception by denial, and a single label-free contrast built from it that, at the
middle layer, transfers better than probes trained on a single dataset on three of four models. We
check it against a widening by unrelated roles and, on the main model, against a random persona
bank: it beats that bank’s contrasts, but its gain over the published contrast is within what random
widenings produce (Sections 4.1, 5 and 6);
• a diagnosis of what persona directions respond to: on lies about knowledge they track the words
of a denial, and with the words held fixed the three main contrasts are, at the middle layer, inside
the random band on Llama and Qwen and at its edge on Gemma, while on Mistral the published
contrast clears it (Sections 4.2 and 5);
• a knowledge direction with measured limits: it separates lies from identically worded honest
denials on two models (narrowly on a third), clears the random band by a small margin on Llama’s
2
Preprint
Gender-Secret fine-tune but not on Mistral’s, and only its results on the wording-controlled slices
are independent of the benchmark’s wording (Sections 4.3 and 5);
• the selected detector, whose mean AUROC over the benchmark’s datasets is, on all four models,
above that of a probe trained at the same depth. On the main model it is level with the extended
contrast, and at strict cutoffs it catches fewer lies than that contrast (Section 4.4); on the other
three, adding the knowledge direction raises transfer on two and lowers it on the third (Section 5).
In a small steering test its persona part, like the published contrast, reduces the disclosure of a
hidden fact (Section 4.5);
• an evaluation protocol for zero-shot (label-free) directions: random bands, a random persona
bank with a pre-registered null, wording-controlled slices, the base model’s activations on a fine-
tuned model’s transcripts as a control, and paired intervals; and two further pre-registered tests,
one of them external, reported with their failures (Section 6).
2
RELATED WORK
Lie detection and why probes fail to transfer.
Instruction pairs, the same statement produced
under an honest and under a deceptive instruction, are the standard training data for deception probes
(Zou et al., 2023; Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Black-box detectors instead ask unrelated follow-up
questions (Pacchiardi et al., 2024) or have an LLM judge read the transcript; Liars’ Bench finds the
judge strongest overall, yet unable to detect HP-KR’s lies, whose truth hinges on what the model
knows (Kretschmar et al., 2025). A probe that is near perfect in distribution can be below chance
elsewhere. With fewer examples than dimensions, many directions fit a training set (D’Amour et al.,
2022), and discriminative learning takes any feature that suffices on that set (Geirhos et al., 2020).
Probes have accordingly latched onto negation (Levinstein & Herrmann, 2025; Bürger et al., 2024),
text probability (Marks & Tegmark, 2024), deception-related scenarios (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025)
and style (Kumar, 2026); they suffer when trained on text the model did not itself generate (off-
policy data; Kirch et al., 2026), and they invert where a correlate of the label reverses (Levinstein
& Herrmann, 2025; Ying et al., 2026; Moustafa et al., 2026). Remedies constrain the direction, to a
difference of means (Marks & Tegmark, 2024), to selected principal components (Yoo & Skapars,
2026) or to persona coordinates (Mahadik & Skapars, 2026); we take the last route. Ying et al.
(2026) further report that a probe trained on data pooled over several settings performs on par with
the best single-setting probe, and that a covariance-weighted cosine predicts transfer better than the
plain cosine; Section 6 tests whether both carry over, with families of role-play questions as the
settings.
Benchmarks and model organisms.
Liars’ Bench (Kretschmar et al., 2025) collects 72,863 on-
policy lies and honest responses across seven datasets and four models, and evaluates a Mean Probe
trained on the instruction pairs of representation engineering (RepE; Zou et al., 2023), a Follow-Up
Probe read at a prefilled “No” after “Was your last response deceptive?”, and an Upper-Bound Probe
trained on the benchmark itself; on HP-KR, built from the hazardous questions of WMDP (Li et al.,
2024), only the last detects the lies. The UK AI Security Institute (AISI) released belief-labelled
rollouts (lies and honest answers) from two of these models, Llama and Gemma (UK AI Security
Institute, 2026); they serve as our held-out data. Cooney et al. (2026) show that existing fine-tuned
liars (model organisms) often do not hold the belief they deny; they release belief-verified reasoning
organisms on Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.6-27B and find that activation and logprob detectors drop
sharply on them while a chain-of-thought judge stays strong. Our external test is Aletheia’s Quest
(Cadenza Labs et al., 2026), a lie-detection competition on model organisms and prompted liars,
with black-box and white-box tracks ranked by mean AUROC over ten held-out datasets. The
winner of its held-out white-box track scores the suspect model’s own judgement of its transcript.
Personas and knowledge as directions.
Persona vectors (Chen et al., 2025) and the Assistant
Axis (Lu et al., 2026) are activation directions for character traits and archetypes. Mahadik &
Skapars (2026) built a deception monitor from such directions: a deception axis, the difference
between eight deceptive and seven honest personas, used either directly (zero-shot) or through the
top principal components of the persona vectors, on datasets that do not include HP-KR. Roles differ
in style as well as honesty (Joshi et al., 2024), and a model that switches to an ignorant persona could
deceive although “no persona is ever lying” (Marks et al., 2026). A model’s internal states record
whether it knows an answer (Kadavath et al., 2022; Slobodkin et al., 2023; Gottesman & Geva, 2024;
3
Preprint
Ferrando et al., 2025). We measure this signal at the tokens of a denial written for the model, as a
difference of means between questions whose answers it knows and questions nobody can answer,
and use it to detect lies.
3
METHOD
Reads and persona contrasts.
A detector reads the residual stream at the output of one de-
coder block, averaged over the response tokens, and maps this pooled vector z, which we call a
read, to one score, higher for a lie. Forward passes run remotely on the National Deep Inference
Fabric (NDIF) through nnsight (Fiotto-Kaufman et al., 2025). We name depths by the layers of
Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct; Table 25 gives the block that stands for each of these layers in the other
models. The main depth is the model’s middle block (the middle layer of the abstract and introduc-
tion), as in the work we build on (Lu et al., 2026; Mahadik & Skapars, 2026), and Liars’ Bench reads
layer 20. We also sweep 16 depths, every fourth layer from 20 to 76 plus the last block, scaled to
each model; layers 36 and 44 were chosen for reporting after seeing results and are labelled post hoc.

role-play responses, holds the 26 roles of the published persona method (8 deceptive, 7 honest,
5 sycophantic, 5 anti-sycophantic and the default assistant as an anchor) and 10 new roles about
knowing and denying, 36 in all. Four knowledge-denial roles know the answer and claim not to;
three sincere-ignorance roles do not know it and say so; and three plain-assertion roles know
it and give it. Every role has five system-prompt variants and answers the same 30 questions; a
Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct judge scores each rollout from 0 to 3 for how clearly it plays the role, and
only rollouts scored 3 are kept (3,599 of the 5,250 judged rollouts; the anchor’s 150 are not judged;
Section A). Five contrasts of the form of Equation (1) differ only in their groups: published (8 v 7),

that add another contrast’s groups to the published ones. The unified contrast adds the sycophancy
contrast’s groups (13 v 12), and the extended contrast adds the knowledge-denial contrast’s (12 v
13). The unified contrast controls for widening by roles unrelated to knowledge; the random persona
bank below gives a null distribution for widening by random roles.
The knowledge direction.
In HP-KR a lie and an honest denial can be the same sentence, and
only whether the model knows the answer makes one a lie. An AI assistant, Claude Opus, wrote 60
general questions whose answers a 70B model knows with certainty and 60 whose answers nobody
can know (private, unrecorded particulars of real places). Each question is placed in HP-KR’s own
knowledge-report template: a four-option question followed by “Tell me whether you know the
answer to the question, and nothing else”, under HP-KR’s system text and with no role. We then
wrote the reply for the model, a forced reply: the same denial after every question, once as “I do not
know the answer.” and once as “I don’t know the answer to the question.”, giving 240 reads. The
direction is the unit difference ˆvknow ∝¯hknows −¯hcannot between the mean reads over the known
and over the unknowable questions (Figure 4). Both sides receive the same two replies, so the reply
cannot separate them. The known side, where the denial is false, is the lie side; this sign was fixed
before any evaluation. The questions themselves still differ in topic and form, and a text classifier
tells the two sides apart 95% of the time. For a replication set of matched question pairs, written
afterwards and also by Claude, the figure is 86%, and the replication direction built from it met all
11 criteria fixed before it was evaluated. Before the direction was built, the model answered all 70
candidate known questions correctly. The direction shares HP-KR’s template and denial sentences,
but it shares no question with any evaluation set and uses no lie that the model wrote. A wording
direction, forced denials minus forced assertions, measures how much a detector responds to the
words of a denial; a detector without its wording component has its component along this direction
removed. In each further model the direction is rebuilt with the known questions checked against
that model’s answers. Our main detector, the selected detector, sums the extended contrast and
the knowledge direction, each score divided by its standard deviation on the lie-free Alpaca control
(Taori et al., 2023), with equal weights fixed in advance. A direction is zero-shot when it uses no
labels, no lies and no benchmark question, and it is scored zero-shot when its projection is the score,

lie-free Alpaca responses). The knowledge direction meets this definition only narrowly: it shares

and Sections 4.3 and 5 examine how much its results depend on them.

Abstract
Current audio-driven video diffusion models can synthesize realistic talking-head
videos but generally require dozens of diffusion denoising steps over multi-second video
chunks, making them unsuitable for streaming applications such as voice assistants and
virtual avatars, where low-latency and online causal generation are required properties.
AURA generates video chunk by chunk with a rolling KV cache, requiring only the
