COHEN ET AL.: AURA: AUDIO-DRIVEN STREAMING AVATAR
audio of the current chunk to start generating, rather than a multi-second audio look-
ahead like bidirectional models. It comes in two sizes: AURA 1.3B streams 576p video
in real time on a single GPU (20.7 fps for a 16 Hz playback rate), making it suited to
interactive avatar applications, and AURA 5B streams 720p video at 9.7 fps. Our two-
stage distillation pipeline first aligns the causal student with the teacher, by training it
to match the teacher’s trajectories with fewer diffusion steps and a chunk-wise sliding
window causal attention mask, then applies Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD)
with backward simulation to close the remaining quality gap. On standard talking-head
benchmarks, AURA 1.3B runs 23× faster than its own bidirectional teacher and reaches
a quality comparable to TalkVerse at a lower resolution, and AURA 5B matches its Talk-
Verse teacher at 720p while running 17× faster. To support reproducibility and further
research on streaming avatar generation, we release the weights of both models along
with a dataset of 30K synthetic videos and their precomputed teacher trajectories.
1
Introduction
Recent speech-to-speech models [12, 41] are able to model full-duplex voice interaction in
real-time, paving the way for voice assistants that hold natural and smooth conversations.
However, these models only generate audio signal. In contrast, human spoken communi-
cation relies on visual cues and facial expressions, via an interplay of the audio and visual
modalities. For instance, lip motion alters perceived phonemes [36], visual cues sharpen
comprehension in noise [47], and an embodied talking face enhances the sense of social pres-
ence over voice alone [6]. To model such behaviors, audio-driven video generation models
can synthesize talking-head videos from a reference image and an input speech audio, en-
abling applications such as virtual avatars, synthetic presenters, and non-player characters
in games. All these applications, however, share a common constraint: the avatar must be
generated on-the-fly, as the audio arrives, from a stream of audio of unbounded duration.
State-of-the-art talking-head models such as TalkVerse [52] and Wan-S2V [17] produce
high-quality audio-driven videos but are ill-suited to the streaming setting. Because they rely
on bidirectional attention, they must generate entire video chunks of several seconds at once,
running dozens of denoising steps over the full chunk before producing any frame, which on
a single GPU takes minutes per chunk. Recently, CausVid [59] and Self-Forcing [23] have
explored distilling such bidirectional video diffusion teachers into few-step causal students
that generate video chunk by chunk in an autoregressive manner. However, these methods
target only the text-to-video and image-to-video settings. Extending this approach to the
audio-driven setting, where the model must additionally track a dense time-aligned speech
signal, has so far been demonstrated only on much larger models (14–18B parameters) [24,
33, 42], which remain too large for real-time inference on a single GPU (only 2 fps). A
second obstacle is the scarcity of suitable training data: existing public talking-head datasets
such as Hallo3 [9] and CelebV [63] consist of clips too short to cover the chunk length of
modern teachers like TalkVerse, ruling them out for distillation (see Section 3.6).
We introduce AURA, a family of causal few-step speech-to-video (S2V) models that
generate streaming talking-head videos from live audio. In particular, AURA 1.3B runs in
real time, generating 576p video at 20.7 frames per second for a 16 Hz playback rate on a
single GPU, which makes it directly usable for the interactive applications above, such as
a talking face for a voice assistant. AURA 5B targets higher resolution: it streams 720p
video at 9.7 fps, a 17× speedup over its TalkVerse teacher. For training, we generate and
release a new talking-head dataset comprising 30K videos (38.7 hours) produced with Talk-
COHEN ET AL.: AURA: AUDIO-DRIVEN STREAMING AVATAR
3
Verse, conditioned on reference images and text descriptions from the Hallo3 dataset [9] and
synthetic speech audio. To train our model, we use a two-stage distillation pipeline, simi-
lar to CausVid: Stage 1 first trains the causal student to match the bidirectional TalkVerse
teacher’s Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) trajectories in order to reduce the gap be-
tween the bidirectional teacher and the causal student architecture. Then, Stage 2 closes the
few-step gap with Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) and backward simulation: by
training the student on intermediate states from its own denoising rollouts, the Stage 2 loss
reflects accumulating errors the student may actually produce at inference. To further im-
prove efficiency, we train the model to support chunk-wise causal sliding window attention,
allowing us to use a rolling KV cache with bounded memory at inference. We also use a
single KV cache for all diffusion denoising timesteps, further reducing memory footprint.
With this approach, on standard talking-avatar benchmarks, AURA 5B matches or im-
proves on its bidirectional teacher on visual quality (FVD [50] and JEDi [34] metrics) and
audio-visual alignment, while running 17× faster with only four denoising steps per chunk,
and AURA 1.3B reaches a comparable quality at a lower resolution and in real time (23×
faster than its own teacher). Both models are faster than all baselines we compare against in
the same single-GPU setting. Figure 1 shows an excerpt of qualitative samples generated by
both models, as well as their speed–quality tradeoff against prior work.
In summary, we introduce AURA, which makes the following contributions:
• A two-stage distillation method (ODE-trajectory initialization followed by Distribution
Matching Distillation with backward simulation) paired with a streaming inference scheme
based on a rolling KV cache of past chunks, shared by both models;
• AURA 5B, a causal few-step S2V model that matches or improves on its bidirectional
teacher on FVD and JEDi metrics, with a 17× speedup. Our inference pipeline streams
720p video at 9.7 fps on a single GPU, the highest throughput among audio-driven base-
lines we compare against;
• AURA 1.3B, a smaller model trained with the same pipeline, which streams 576p video in
real time on a single GPU (20.7 fps generated for a 16 Hz playback rate), a 23× speedup
over its own bidirectional teacher;
• A public dataset of 30K talking-head videos generated by TalkVerse from synthetic speech,
released both as decoded videos and as the latent ODE trajectories of the teacher, to sup-
port future research on streaming S2V distillation, together with the weights of our 1.3B
teacher and its own 30K ODE trajectories;
• A live demo coupling AURA 1.3B with Unmute, a cascaded voice assistant built on Kyu-
tai’s streaming speech-to-text and text-to-speech models [60] and a text LLM, in which
users hold a natural spoken conversation with a synthetic avatar in real time on a single
H100 GPU, available at kyutai.org/aura.
2
Related Work
Diffusion and Flow Matching.
Image Generative models have evolved through several
paradigms: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) [4, 18, 25] are efficient as they gener-
ate images in a single forward pass but suffer from known limitations around mode coverage
and training stability. More recently, diffusion models [15, 20, 26, 40, 44, 45] and flow
matching [30, 32] have become the dominant paradigm for image generation. Indeed, both
4
COHEN ET AL.: AURA: AUDIO-DRIVEN STREAMING AVATAR
frameworks are closely related and model data through an iterative multi-step refinement
process, yielding stable training with high sample diversity but at the cost of slow sampling.
Most modern large-scale video generators, including our teacher TalkVerse [52], are trained
under the flow matching framework, and our work also builds on this formulation.
Video Diffusion Models.
Recent work has further scaled diffusion for video generation.
Early efforts such as Imagen Video [21], Make-A-Video [43], Align Your Latents [3], and
Stable Video Diffusion [2] extended image diffusion to short clips, typically by inflating 2D
architectures with temporal layers. More recent open-source and industrial models, Sora [5],
Movie Gen [38], Open-Sora [62], CogVideoX [56], HunyuanVideo [27], and Wan [51]—
adopt diffusion transformer (DiT) architectures and operate in a compressed latent space,
scaling to 720p–1080p resolutions and minute-long clips. These models are typically non-
causal: they generate the entire video sequence jointly over 50 or more denoising steps,
and are thus not well adapted to the latency requirements of streaming applications. Cur-
rent SotA talking-head models are based on such architectures. For instance, Hallo3 [9]
adapts CogVideoX [56] for portrait animation with a DiT-adapted identity reference net-
work, while closed-source systems such as OmniHuman [29] extend DiT-based audio-driven
generation to full-body animation. In this work, we distill two such non-causal teachers built
on Wan, TalkVerse [52] (from Wan2.2-5B) for AURA 5B and a 1.3B teacher that we train
from Wan2.1-1.3B for AURA 1.3B, into causal, few-step streaming students.
Distillation of Diffusion Models.
The slow inference of diffusion models has motivated
extensive work on distillation, training a faster few-step student to reproduce a slow teacher’s
output distribution. One particularly successful line is Distribution Matching Distillation
(DMD) [58], which trains a one-step student to minimize the reverse KL to the teacher via
a learned critic; DMD2 [57] extends it to a few-step generator and introduces backward
simulation, computing the loss on the student’s own rollouts rather than forward-diffused
data. CausVid [59] applies DMD to distill a non-causal video teacher into a causal few-step
student for streaming text-to-video. A challenge specific to causal video distillation is the
train/test gap: the student is trained on teacher-provided past frames but must condition on its
own previously generated frames at inference. Self-Forcing [23] and its variants [10, 31, 54,
64] address this temporal gap by rolling the student out autoregressively through a training-
time KV cache with stop-gradient. We instead build on DMD2’s backward simulation [57],
which exposes the student to its own denoising trajectory, and adapt it to streaming video
(Sec. 3.4) so that the student also conditions on its own past generations, without maintaining
a training-time cache.
Streaming Talking Heads.
A handful of recent works tackle audio-driven talking-head
generation in a streaming and few-step setting. Talking Machines [33] is, to our knowledge,
the first to address this regime, distilling a 18B model with DMD and sparse causal attention;
weights are not released. Live Avatar [24] distills the 14B Wan-S2V model [17] into a 14B
few-step student that runs at 16 fps and 480p on a 5-GPU setup. SoulX-FlashTalk [42] adopts
a similar few-step distillation strategy from a 14B teacher into a 14B student and requires 4
GPUs to reach real-time throughput. In contrast, AURA streams on a single GPU: AURA 5B
distills a 5B teacher into a same-size causal 4-step student that delivers 720p video at 9.7 fps,
and AURA 1.3B, trained with the same pipeline from our own 1.3B teacher, reaches real time
at 576p (20.7 fps for a 16 Hz playback rate). Closest to our work is Avatar Forcing [11] whose
pre-print was concurrently published: It uses a similar DMD-based distillation process but
requires a look-ahead window of future audio to generate each frame by design, leading to a
small yet incompressible streaming delay.
COHEN ET AL.: AURA: AUDIO-DRIVEN STREAMING AVATAR
5
3
Method
In this section, we present AURA, our two-stage pipeline that distills a non-causal audio-
driven video diffusion teacher (TalkVerse) into a 4-step causal student. We first recall Dis-
tribution Matching Distillation (Sec. 3.1) and the TalkVerse teacher (Sec. 3.1) to introduce
necessary notations and context. Section 3.2 then introduces the causal student and the per-
chunk mixed-timestep design that enables a compact KV cache. Section 3.3 and Section 3.4
cover the two training stages, and Section 3.5 finally describes streaming inference.
3.1
Preliminaries
Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD).
DMD [58] trains a few-step student gener-
ator Gθ to match a multi-step teacher diffusion model at the distribution level, rather than
along individual sampling trajectories. Concretely, DMD minimizes, in expectation over the
diffusion timestep t ∼U(0,1), the reverse KL divergence between the student distribution
pgen and the data distribution pdata, both diffused to noise level t. We adopt t ∈[0,1] through-
out this paper, with t = 0 corresponding to clean latents and t = 1 to pure noise. While the
densities pgen and pdata are intractable, the gradient of the KL with respect to θ admits a
closed-form expression as a difference of two score functions evaluated on student samples:

produces a sample at noise level t, sdata is the frozen teacher score, and sgen,η is an online

Backward simulation.
Directly applying DMD to multi-step students yields a training-
inference mismatch: at training time, the student is fed forward-diffused real samples xt =
Ψ(x0,t), whereas at inference time, intermediate inputs come from previous denoising steps
of the student itself. To close this gap, DMD2 [57] introduces backward simulation. At
each training iteration, the student is unrolled for a few denoising steps to produce a syn-

to the DMD objective. Because Gθ is itself a few-step generator, this unrolling is cheap.
The DMD gradient and the score-matching update for sgen,η are then computed at ˆxt rather
than at Ψ(x0,t), aligning the input distribution seen during training with the one produced
at inference. DMD2 also adds a GAN loss on real data. We adopt backward simulation,
together with the two time-scale update rule of DMD2, in the second stage of our pipeline
(Sec. 3.4), but not the GAN loss: it requires real videos and makes training less stable. The
DMD objective alone already brings our student close to its teacher (Sec. 4.3).
TalkVerse Architecture.
We use TalkVerse [52] as our teacher model, a 5B-parameter
audio-driven video diffusion model built on the Wan2.2-5B [51] DiT backbone. Its video
VAE uses compression factors (t,h,w) = (4,16,16), enabling efficient 720p generation.
The model is conditioned on a reference identity image, a speech audio track encoded with
Wav2Vec2 [1] and injected via cross-attention to temporally aligned visual tokens, and a text

noised window. Inference uses 50 denoising steps with a flow-matching solver and classifier-
free guidance. We provide a more detailed description in the supplementary material A.1.
TalkVerse is directly the teacher of AURA 5B; for AURA 1.3B, we train a 1.3B teacher with

LLM GerryMandering: Separating Interactions from Additive Effects in LLM
Audits
GEORGE RAHUL, International Institute of Information Technology Hyderabad, India
RONIT JAHILAL, International Institute of Information Technology Hyderabad, India
BHASKARA HANUMA VEDULA, International Institute of Information Technology Hyderabad, India
PONNURANGAM KUMARAGURU, International Institute of Information Technology Hyderabad, India
PUSHKAR SHUKLA, Cloudphysician.ai, USA
Intersectional bias arises when a model treats people who hold several marginalised identities at once differently from what their
separate identities would predict. Auditing such intersectional subgroups remains a challenge: their number grows quadratically,
and there is no agreed baseline for what independent attributes would predict. Without such a baseline, many existing audits flag a
subgroup when it exceeds each attribute alone, a condition that attributes acting independently already satisfy. We test this standard
criterion on 150 synthetic datasets built with no interaction. With the shuffle null, it flags 66.1 false subgroups per dataset on average,
and at least one in every dataset. When we plant interactions of known size into these datasets, a repaired null lets the criterion
recover only 32% of them.
We introduce Addis (Additive Intersectional Screen), which fits an additive model over all attributes, scores each subgroup by its
Additive Residual Distance (Ard) from that model’s prediction, and tests it against a Freedman–Lane null. On our synthetic benchmark,
Addis flags 0.09 false subgroups per dataset and recovers 84% of the same planted interactions. We then build IndiPersona, 10,000
synthetic Indian personas with six identity attributes, and audit 13 open language models. The standard criterion flags 7.1% of the 738
tested subgroups on average; Addis flags 3.0%. Gender identity crossed with sexual orientation is the largest pairing in every model,
and counterfactual personas confirm it and additionally reveal a caste × class interaction in all but one model that the observational
test lacked the data to detect. Much of what audits report as intersectional bias can thus arise from independent single-attribute effects
alone, yet a small core of interactions survives.
CCS Concepts: • Computing methodologies →Natural language processing; • Social and professional topics →User
characteristics; • Mathematics of computing →Hypothesis testing and confidence interval computation.
Additional Key Words and Phrases: Intersectionality, Disparate Treatment, Algorithmic Auditing, Large Language Models, India, Caste
1
Introduction
Language models are increasingly deployed in systems that judge people, from ranking job applicants to answering
a patient’s medical questions [3, 61]. Audits report that responses depend on identity, and that some combinations
are treated differently from either identity alone [1, 22, 48, 61]. Most audits nevertheless examine one identity at a
time. Intersectionality theory makes a specific claim about people who hold several identities at once: the harm they
face is not reducible to the harms attached to each identity on its own, or even to their sum. Crenshaw writes that the
intersectional experience is “greater than the sum of racism and sexism” [9, p. 140], so the quantity to be exceeded is
the sum of the parts. We operationalize this claim by asking whether a model’s response to a combination of identities
departs from what its separate identities predict.

Fig. 1. The single-attribute criterion cannot tell addition from interaction. Relative to a Hindu man, woman adds 3 points of attributed
anxiety and Muslim 4 of depression. Points beyond the dashed arc are flagged, and red marks Ard 𝛿from their sum (open circle). (a)
Without interaction, the Muslim woman is still flagged. (b, c) The same interaction raises the excess more along the sum than at a
right angle. (d) If Muslim lowers anxiety instead, the shifts nearly cancel and a real interaction stays inside the arc.
Consider a model that attributes anxiety and depression to personas, and rates a woman three points higher on
anxiety and a Muslim four points higher on depression. A Muslim woman then lies five points from the reference,
farther than under either identity alone (Figure 1a). Yet, it is exactly where the two effects add, so no interaction is
involved. Only a departure from this sum, such as the 1.5 points in Figure 1b, indicates an interaction, so exceeding
each part is not equivalent to exceeding the sum of the parts.
Detecting such interactions at scale is challenging, because candidate subgroups multiply quadratically with the
number of identity attributes while the observations available for each decrease [25, 29]. Testing hundreds of subgroups
simultaneously also inflates false discoveries unless the error rate is controlled across all of them. Automated subgroup
discovery makes this search systematic [29, 70], and the baseline against which it ranks subgroups determines which
ones can be found. A common baseline in intersectional audits of language models, which we term the single-attribute
criterion, reports a combination when it fares worse than each of its attributes alone [22, 48, 61]. As the example shows,
merely additive effects satisfy this criterion. Conversely, it can miss real interactions when the two effects point in
opposite directions, or when the interaction is perpendicular to their sum.
We address this problem with Addis (Additive Intersectional Screen), which screens every pair of identity attributes
for interactions in how language models treat people. We replace the single-attribute baseline with an additive prediction.
We fit a linear regression over the whole dataset, giving every level of every attribute its own coefficient. It has no
interaction terms. A subgroup’s prediction is the sum of the coefficients of the attributes it carries. We define the additive
residual distance (Ard) 𝛿as the distance between a subgroup’s observed mean response profile and this prediction. It is
equal for interactions of equal magnitude in any direction. Figure 1 contrasts the two baselines on our example. We test
each subgroup against a null that keeps every attribute’s effect and removes only the interaction effect, so the test asks
whether two identities interact, not whether identity matters at all. We control the family-wise error rate at 5% across
the search (§3.3).
In a natural sample of data, the attributes are correlated, so a pair’s effect cannot be separated from its parts’, and some
subgroups are too small to study. So, we generate the personas we test, and sample their attributes independently of one
another. The exception to this is caste, which is paired only with religions it actually occurs in. The dataset, IndiPersona,
is ten thousand Indian personas crossing six attributes: gender identity, age, sexual orientation, socioeconomic status,
caste and religion, each described in one of 50 everyday scenes. Fourteen models answer the same 82 questionnaire
Manuscript submitted to ACM
LLM GerryMandering: Separating Interactions from Additive Effects in LLM Audits
3
items about every persona. We test all 738 pairs of identity values with at least 50 personas, and use within-persona
counterfactuals for combinations the main sample cannot estimate.
We test both baselines on data we build ourselves. It contains no interaction, so every subgroup a method flags
in it is a false positive. We build it from the real design and the models’ own answers, keeping each attribute’s own
effect and destroying only intersectional effects. Across 150 such datasets, each with 738 subgroups, Addis flags 0.09
false subgroups per dataset on continuous answers. The single-attribute baseline flags 66.1, and fires on every dataset.
We also synthetically add real intersectional effects into the dataset, of sizes we choose. Addis recovers 84% of them,
against 32% for the single-attribute baseline given the same null. On answers rounded to the Likert scale, rounding
itself creates interactions and raises every method’s error rate. We ran every other published method through the same
test: per-item interaction regressions [31], MAIHDA [14] and PERMANOVA [2]. Each raises a false flag in at least 73%
of datasets, compared to our 20%. With interactions planted, the precision of Addis is 0.72, compared to 0.02–0.28 for
the alternatives.
After running Addis on the 13 open models, an average of only 3.0% of subgroups are found to be intersectional on
scale scores. By contrast, given the same statistical treatment, the single-attribute baseline flags 7.1% (52 subgroups
per model), of which only about nine coincide with ours. Gender identity crossed with sexual orientation is the single
largest pairing, in every model we audit. Within-persona counterfactuals reproduce that effect in all 13 open models,
and find a caste × class interaction in 12 of them, a result the observational test could not find due to lack of data. The
location of these interactions holds up when we reword the prompt, draw a fresh sample of personas, or adjust for the
template, though their direction depends on the wording. Ard measures interaction in what models attribute to people,
not harm, and our data come from one country, so we read the flagged combinations as candidates for closer scrutiny,
not as estimates of how much discrimination exists in the world. Our contributions are as follows.
(1) A metric for intersectional subgroup discovery. We compare each subgroup against the sum of its attributes’
separate effects, and test the difference against a null built for it.
(2) A benchmark for intersectional metrics. We build synthetic data with controllable interactions between
the subgroups, so that the ground truth is known. On questionnaire-style answers, rounding weakens the error
control of every method, but every published alternative we tried makes false positives far more often than ours.
(3) A factorial persona dataset and an audit of fourteen models. Ten thousand Indian personas whose identity
attributes vary nearly independently, an audit of thirteen open models and one closed model, and the finding
that only a small minority of subgroups survive a calibrated test, concentrated on a single pairing of attributes.
2
Related Work
Intersectional bias in language models. Bias in language models is often strongest where identities meet, in
embeddings, generated text, question answering and hiring decisions [1, 21, 31, 34, 38, 46, 68]. Fairness for each
group does not imply fairness for their combinations [8, 29]. Most of this work uses Western categories such as race
and gender [21, 46], while social hierarchies and the biases attached to them differ across countries, languages and
regions [6, 26, 42, 51, 55].
Bias evaluation in India. Work on India began with word embeddings, which encode caste, religious and gender
associations in Hindi and other Indian languages [4, 32, 40]. Studies of Hindi then found that detecting gender bias
needs community input [23] and that models are more biased when generating Hindi than English [27]. Stereotype
benchmarks for language models followed, covering Indian axes of disparity [5], caste and religion [30, 65], several

Benchmarks of this kind test whether a model repeats known associations, so they depend on curated inventories
whose validity is often unclear [7], and they miss harms outside them. Later work therefore studied open-ended
generation [11, 18, 50, 56] and decisions. Decision audits hold a task fixed and change only the identity, in hiring [52],
economic guidance [44], matchmaking [43] and education [22]. Because only the identity changes, they measure how a
model treats a person rather than which words it associates, and our audit follows the same design.
How intersections are tested. Few of these audits test intersections systematically. Stereotype benchmarks include
a few predefined pairs, mostly with gender [54, 62], and decision audits change one attribute at a time [44] or a few
within one task [22, 43], as do audits outside India with race, gender and age [1, 3, 24, 59]. When an audit compares a
combination with its parts, it usually asks whether the combination fares worse than each part alone [22, 34, 48, 60, 61],
the single-attribute baseline that §3.2 shows addition alone can satisfy. Other audits fit an interaction term for one
outcome at a time [3, 31]. Recent work widens the set of combinations, by pairing multi-attribute instances with their
single-attribute sources [71] or by flagging failures that appear only when two identity words are swapped together [57],
but it fits no additive baseline across all attributes and does not control false positives across cells. Two studies come
closest to our critique. Kanubala and Valera [28] show that intersectional fairness metrics for classifiers respond more
to additive bias than to interaction, and Rennard and Xypolopoulos [53] compare simulated personas with an additive
prediction and find that models represent intersectional identities in only one or two dimensions. Searching over many
subgroups is also established for classifiers, through subgroup fairness audits [29] and scan statistics [70]. Table 1
compares these methods with ours. Unlike this work, we test every pairwise cell of a multivariate answer profile against
an additive baseline fitted over all six attributes, control the family-wise error rate across cells, and confirm the main
cells with counterfactuals.

Abstract
Large Web platforms operate large fleets of ranking models, each se-
lecting features from a shared pool of tens of thousands. We present
an end-to-end agentic system that optimizes features across the
fleet under resource constraints shared across models and those set
per model, such as feature pipeline cost and serving throughput
(QPS), respectively. In this system, LLM agents propose hypotheses,
and deterministic tools execute experiments and verify them. For
each model, an LLM generates and shortlists cross features from a
combinatorial candidate space, and all features are then ranked by
several importance methods. Feature blending mixes these rank-
ings into a single selection, using Pareto fronts across tasks for
multi-task models. An LLM Researcher agent then tunes the feature
selection in 10–25 asynchronous trials under resource caps, and a
trimming step keeps the pipeline cost within budget. Across pro-
duction models, the system improves normalized entropy by 0.31%
on average within each model’s budget, and the trimming step
cuts pipeline cost by 2.3% with no regression beyond measurement
noise. The optimized models were launched, and in online A/B tests
they improved a primary online metric by 0.20%.
CCS Concepts
• Information systems →Computational advertising; Rec-
ommender systems; • Computing methodologies →Feature
selection; Intelligent agents.
Keywords
Feature selection, LLM agents, Ads ranking, Recommender systems,
Cost-aware optimization
1
Introduction
Online platforms often run large numbers of ranking models cater-
ing to different surfaces and intents, while each model selects from
an ever-growing pool of features.
As every feature performs differently across models and has its
own serving and infrastructure cost, feature selection is an inte-
gral component of model performance and prediction relevancy.
Due to these constraints, feature selection is a cost-sensitive trade
between prediction accuracy and test-time feature cost [12] that
so far required manual reasoning and actions by ML practition-
ers. Recently, LLMs have been used to select [6, 14] and engineer
features [5], while LLM agents have shown increasing capabilities
of running ML experimentation end to end [2, 11]. These works
study a single model in isolation. We design a scalable agentic
system that generates, optimizes and selects features for every
model without per-model engineering, under two kinds of budgets:
per-model serving-cost caps (throughput, latency, memory) and
feature pipeline budgets (processing, data, logging) shared across
models. Two fleet-level mechanisms set it apart from per-model
tools: a single retrieval LLM fine-tuned on feature outcomes from
many models, so feature creation improves as more models are op-
timized; and fleet-aware pipeline-cost trimming, which optimizes
each model’s features against the rest of the fleet: a feature another
model under the same budget already uses adds no pipeline cost.
We make three contributions. (1) LLM-driven Agentic Feature
Creation that uses raw signals of features to reason and generate
transformed feature candidates, with one generator fine-tuned on
outcomes across the fleet (Section 2). (2) A novel feature-importance
(FI) blending algorithm that combines rankings across tasks by
Pareto optimality and across FI estimators, including ones scored
on high-value traffic slices, by a tunable mixture (Sections 3 and 4).
(3) An agentic feature selection system that re-selects features at
every refresh without manual additions or removals, balancing
model quality against serving cost and the pipeline cost models
share (Section 5). Fig. 1a illustrates the complete system.
2
Agentic Feature Creation
Feature categories. The model input layer is built from four fea-
ture categories. Dense features are real-valued scalars fed to multi-
layer perceptron (MLP) and are the cheapest per slot. Sparse features

are lists of IDs, each mapped to a learned vector in an embedding
table inside the model; these tables dominate model memory. Em-
bedding features are fixed-length vectors produced upstream; they
need no table, but their large vectors are costly to log and store.
Sparse features add table-lookup cost and embedding features add
matrix-multiplication cost (a per-feature MLP projection), so which
costs more serving throughput depends on the setting, such as GPU
or CPU serving. Transform features (such as the cross features) are
derived inside the model from features it already receives. Feature
categories differ in diminishing returns as well as cost, so improving
a model usually means rebalancing volume across feature categories
rather than scaling every category up.
Cross-feature creation. Cross features (or n-gram features), the
cross product of two or more ID features such as user_country
× ad_category, often improve key metrics [4], but they are hand-
crafted, and exhaustive search is quadratic in the pool size. Au-
tomated crossing [9] evaluates candidates by repeated training,
which does not scale to production. We generalize crosses to fea-
ture transforms 𝑡= (𝑜,𝑈), which apply an operator 𝑜∈O (n-gram,
ID matching, bucketization, etc.) to a feature subset 𝑈⊂F and are
computed inside the model. Let T be the set of candidate transforms
over the input feature pool F ; for bigrams alone, |T | = 𝑂(|O| |F |2),
which reaches tens of millions. Feature Ranking (Section 3), a de-
terministic FI stage, is accurate but runs out of memory well before
millions of candidates, so we use two stages. (1) LLM retrieval
(recall). For each feature we store static signals (name, lineage,
aggregation window, coverage, an LLM-written semantic descrip-
tion) and model-specific signals (importance, interaction scores) in
a fleet-wide Signal database. An LLM scores each candidate in a sin-
gle forward pass, and the top 𝑁𝑟≪|T | are kept. (2) FI re-ranking
(precision). After the shortlist of candidate features is generated,
we use Feature Ranking to rank and select the final set under a
budget. (3) Continual fine-tuning. The FI scores that Feature
Ranking assigns to the shortlisted cross features of many models
serve as labels to continuously fine-tune a single retrieval LLM
shared across the fleet, so feature creation improves as more mod-
els are optimized. Cross features further enlarge the pool beyond
what any model can use, so Agentic Feature Selection (Section 5)
picks the highest-ROI subset under constraints.
3
Feature Ranking
Feature Ranking scores every candidate deterministically from a sin-
gle model trained once on the full candidate pool, i.e., every feature
eligible under data-governance and privacy constraints, including
generated cross features (Section 2). Scores are normalized to sum
to one, per task and in aggregate, using one of several estimators: (i)
permutation importance [7] scores a feature by how much the loss
increases when its values are shuffled across an evaluation batch. It
underrates correlated features, motivating two Shapley estimators:
(ii) Shapley value sampling [1], the average loss reduction from
adding a feature to those preceding it in randomly sampled order-
ings, and (iii) Kernel SHAP [8], which estimates Shapley values as
the coefficients of a weighted linear model over sampled feature
coalitions. (iv) A segment-aware variant of any above estimator
trains and scores only on a small but valuable slice of traffic, such
as high-value users in the top revenue buckets, to surface features
that global importance can bury.
4
Feature Blending
A growing number of production ads ranking models are multi-task,
predicting several outcomes (e.g., clicks and conversions) [3]. These
models make it hard to rank features globally as per-task FI scores
come from losses of different magnitudes, and often different units
(e.g., classification vs. regression heads). So a weighted sum of per-
task scores depends on hand-tuned task weights that are subjective
and hard to maintain across model refreshes. We therefore select
features by Pareto optimality (PO), which compares features without
merging their scores.
Let a model have 𝐽tasks. Feature 𝑖is described by its importance
vector f𝑖= (𝑓𝑖1, . . . , 𝑓𝑖𝐽), where 𝑓𝑖𝑗is its importance for task 𝑗.

strict inequality for at least one task. The features that no other

and repeating gives successive fronts P2, . . . , P𝐿, stopping at the

5
Agentic Feature Selection with Constraints
In production ads ranking, a feature’s value is weighed against two
kinds of cost: serving cost and feature pipeline cost (pipeline cost).
Serving cost spans throughput, latency and memory. Throughput,
the queries per second (QPS) the hardware can serve, is tracked
through its common proxy, inference compute in floating-point op-
erations (FLOPs) per example. Latency includes feature fetching and
extraction, which takes a large share of CPU in some serving stages
and slows ad delivery. Memory is dominated by the embedding
tables of sparse features: each added sparse feature brings a table
that must fit in accelerator and host memory. Pipeline cost is paid
upstream for every feature a model consumes [10]: processing (the
queries that generate it), data (storage of its source data) and logging
(storage and ingestion of its logged training values). These costs are
multi-dimensional, type-dependent (a variable-length sparse fea-
ture can cost far more than a dense scalar) and set-dependent rather
than additive, so selecting the top features by importance up to a
count cap is suboptimal under these constraints. Our agentic selec-
tion system therefore combines feature creation (Section 2), ranking
(Section 3) and blending (Section 4) to balance model quality against
them, replacing today’s practice of inheriting the incumbent’s fea-
tures with manual additions and removals.

Backtracking Agent Applications Security Incidents
Yicheng Cai
Pennsylvania State University
University Park, PA, USA
yccai@psu.edu
Taegyu Kim
Pennsylvania State University
University Park, PA, USA
tgkim@psu.edu
Peng Liu∗
Pennsylvania State University
University Park, PA, USA
pxl20@psu.edu
Abstract
Agent applications are increasingly deployed, yet agent-
specific attacks pose real threats to them. Upon a security
incident, organizations backtrack to identify the CEP (com-
promise entry point), remediate the damage, and prevent
its recurrence. The main artifacts available for backtracking
are trajectory logs, which record agent functionalities, and
source code; app(lication)-specific function call logs are of-
ten fairly limited. However, trajectory logs are at the agent
functionality abstraction layer, while the CEP candidates
are function calls at the app code execution layer. Due to
this semantic gap, the analyst needs to manually inspect
the relevant code for each CEP candidate to infer its cor-
responding agent functionality. In this work, we present
Origin, a backtracking tool for the analyst to submit a small
number of queries to identify CEPs that existing tools can-
not provide. Our approach poses two challenges: (1) define
the intermediate abstraction that captures the mapping re-
lationships between the two semantic layers; (2) determine
the region-to-variable mapping for constructing the cross-
layer graph defined in the intermediate abstraction. Each
region is a specific group of agent functionalities. Origin
addresses the challenges by (1) the cross-layer dependency
graph (CLDG) that connects region-inferred functions at the
semantic level to the variables in the low-level taint propa-
gation subgraph, plus the associated query language, and (2)
the region inference algorithm. Case studies on five popular
agent applications across eight attack incidents show that
an analyst using Origin correctly identifies all the CEPs.
CCS Concepts: • Security and privacy →Software and
application security.
Keywords: Backtracking, Agent application, Intermediate
abstraction, Indirect prompt injection, Memory poisoning
1
Introduction
Agent applications powered by large language models (LLMs)
have been widely deployed. For example, an open-source
agent application, GPT-Researcher, accumulated over 24,000
GitHub stars after release [6]. Moreover, enterprise agent
applications may increase from under 5% in 2025 to about
40% by the end of 2026, according to a recent Gartner fore-
cast [32].
∗Corresponding author.
Meanwhile, such agent applications are under threat from
emerging agent-specific attacks, among which indirect prompt
injection (IPI) [29, 36, 48, 76] and memory & context poison-
ing (MC-Poison) [23, 63, 82] are the most prevalent two of
the OWASP Top 10 threats for agent applications [54]. For
instance, a number of IPI CVEs [1, 5, 9, 58] and MC-Poison-
based red-teaming [34, 49, 57] have been reported across
multiple commercial agent applications.
When a security incident occurs in deployed agent ap-
plications, organizations backtrack the incident in order to
identify the CEP (compromise entry point), remediate the
damage, and prevent its recurrence. The main artifacts avail-
able for backtracking are: (1) trajectory logs, which record
a sequence of agent observations and actions [81] mapping
to agent functionalities, such as planning, acting by invok-
ing tools, and recalling information from memory [46]; (2)
source code of the compromised applications. It is worth
noting that application-specific function call logs are often
fairly limited: developers may not anticipate which calls are
diagnostically relevant to emerging agent-specific attacks
and consequently omit the corresponding log printing state-
ments [74], or complete logging is disabled due to overhead
thresholds and privacy considerations [75, 80].
Motivating example. Consider an MC-Poison security
incident on GPT-Researcher, where an analyst received an
incident report from a user/victim of the application (Sec-
tion 3.1). There are three stakeholders: the analyst, the rem-
edy administrator (usually the user), and the developers. The
analyst aimed to backtrack the incident to identify the CEP,
i.e., the function call that first introduced the malicious con-
tent to the application (Section 4.3). When the corresponding
input arguments of the CEP function call are already logged,
the analyst can (1) provide the remedy admin with a concrete,
actionable remedy, e.g., the exact poisoned file to remove
from a knowledge base that may contain hundreds of docu-
ments in various formats; when the corresponding function
call log entry is missing, the analyst can (2) deliver to the
developers the log printing statement placement around the
CEP function call, enabling more efficient logging that makes
the application diagnosable for future incidents.
Identifying the CEPs requires significant manual
effort from the analyst. The analyst first triaged and ex-
amined the trajectory log and narrowed down the suspect
cause to a particular agent functionality (i.e., knowledge-base
retrieval). However, it remains difficult to identify the CEPs
1
arXiv:2611.26525v1  [cs.CR]  19 Nov 2026
based only on the agent functionality since one agent func-
tionality typically corresponds to many function calls, and
no trajectory log records concrete function calls (Listing 1).
Fundamentally speaking, trajectory logs are at the agent
functionality abstraction layer, while function calls are at a
lower layer (i.e., the app code execution layer). Static anal-
ysis on the source code of the application can complement
trajectory-log-based agent-functionality-level diagnosis by
pinpointing the CEPs through variable-level taint analysis.
However, the analysis is hindered by a large set of CEP can-
didates: only a small subset is associated with the suspected
initial compromise. After log-based pruning, there are still
1,518 candidates left in GPT-Researcher source code; to infer
if a candidate belongs to the suspected initial compromise,
the analyst spent hours on manual code inspection, detailed
in Section 3.1. The main reason is that the code around the
candidates carries little agent functionality semantics, and
the analyst needs to gather enough evidence along the cor-
responding code paths before making a deduction.
None of the existing approaches can provide stake-
holders with the two “can provide” benefits mentioned
in the motivating example, since trajectory-log-based
failure diagnosis [52, 78, 81], detection-based failure attri-
bution [24, 44, 79], and preventive information flow con-
trol [28] do not provide the analyst with the CEPs but
faulty agent execution state [52, 79, 81], faulty agent [78] or
agent-owner [24], and LLM tool calls (not function calls at
the source code level) [28, 44] instead.
Our approach can provide stakeholders with the two
benefits because it backtracks the security incident.
As mentioned in the motivating example, narrowing the
CEPs during backtracking requires significant manual ef-
fort since the analyst needs to do code inspection to recover
the agent functionality semantics from the program source
code. Our insight is to introduce a new intermediate
abstraction (Section 4.4) that enables the analyst to write a
few queries at the agent-functionality-level, and the query
processing outputs can exclude irrelevant CEP candidates
directly. However, identifying which CEP candidates seman-
tically correspond to specific agent functionalities is hard
since program structures and implementations vary, making
it difficult to generalize how to identify the mapping rela-
tionships. Fortunately, we observe that agent functionalities
can be grouped into a small number of regions depending on
the type of information source (Section 2) with which they
interact. Each region is a set of program variables that imple-
ment agent functionalities of the same group. The variables
that receive the return values of the CEP candidates are also
included. Based on this insight, we build a tool named
Origin that realizes this abstraction as a graph across
two layers. Origin takes as input the source code of an
agent application and a small set of developer-provided la-
bels, and produces the cross-layer graph that can be queried
by analysts using a query language during security incident
investigations: (i) narrow down candidates at the region lev-
el/layer, (ii) identify the CEPs at the variable level.
Challenges. Our approach poses two challenges. First, de-
fine the intermediate abstraction that captures the mapping
relationships between two semantic layers: the agent func-
tionality layer vs. the application code execution layer. Since
the implementation of the same agent functionality by dif-
ferent agent applications varies (e.g., the functions/variables
naming, the used agent frameworks), we believe such an in-
termediate abstraction can provide an analyst with the same
interface when backtracking security incidents of different
applications. Second, constructing the cross-layer graph (de-
fined in the intermediate abstraction) requires determining
which region each variable belongs to. This is because a vari-
able’s region is determined by which information source its
data came from or flows into, but a variable’s name, type, or
enclosing function does not carry these semantics.
Solutions. For the first challenge, we design the Cross-
Layer Dependency Graph (CLDG) (Section 5) that connects
region-inferred functions to the underlying variables in the
taint graph through cross-plane edges. We also design the as-
sociated query language. As in BackTracker [45], the essence
of backtracking is dependence analysis. Since the agent ap-
plication CEPs are specific function calls, static taint analysis
is suitable to identify the two types of dependencies a back-
tracking tool can rely on: variable-level data dependencies
and function-level data dependencies. For the second chal-
lenge, we design region inference (Section 6.3) that mimics
the analyst’s code inspection process by rules, which requires
only a small set of developer-provided labels and automati-
cally infers the regions for the variables.
Contributions. We make the following contributions.
• We design the CLDG plus the associated query lan-
guage, a new intermediate abstraction that bridges the
semantic gap between agent-functionality-level reasoning
and program-variable-level application code execution.
• We design region inference, a technique that maps pro-
gram variables into the relevant regions by rule-guided
propagation of label information to the relevant functions
along tainted program paths.
• We build and evaluate Origin on five real-world agent
applications across eight attack incidents. Origin correctly
identifies every CEP with a single candidate per incident,
reducing the analyst’s inspection scope by 64–94% com-
pared to the full taint graph and replacing exhaustive
source code inspection with region-guided diagnosis.
To foster research on this topic, we will release the source
code of Origin to GitHub.
2
Background
Agent Applications. An LLM-powered agent application
interacts with diverse information sources for implementing
2
various agent functionalities (e.g., perceiving the user instruc-
tions, planning, acting by invoking tools, and recalling infor-
mation from memory) [46]. Such applications produce tra-
jectory logs to record the invocations of agent functionalities
during a concrete execution [52, 81]. Two types of information
sources are: (1) external information sources outside the appli-
cations, including but not limited to user inputs, interactions
with humans or agents, sensor readings, network-accessible
content (e.g., web pages and emails), and LLM-generated con-
tent; (2) internal information sources within the applications
such as knowledge bases and memory. The memory stores
multi-round interactions between the user and the agent,
persisted on disk in either original or summarized form, so
that the agent can recall prior context across sessions [46].
Attacks on Agent Applications. Agent-specific attacks
such as IPI [36, 48, 76] and MC-Poison [23, 54, 82] compro-
mise the agent applications by injecting manipulated content
into legitimate information sources of the applications. MC-
Poison attacks usually involve two phases that occur in sep-
arate executions: a poisoning phase, in which malicious data
is written to an internal information source, and an exploita-
tion phase, in which the stored data is retrieved and causes
harm. In some incidents, poisoning occurs outside the appli-
cation (e.g., an attacker directly modifies a knowledge base
document), and only the exploitation phase is observable.
Static Taint Analyzers. Existing taint-analysis frameworks
such as Joern [7], Pysa [17], and CodeQL [4] can already com-
pute propagation paths over program variables and expres-
sions. These capabilities can be repurposed for backtracking
agent application security incidents. However, they expose
only program code-level semantics and do not provide ab-
stractions aligned with agent functionalities.
3
Motivation
3.1
Motivating Example
Security Incident. Consider GPT-Researcher, an agent ap-
plication that conducts research for users and generates syn-
thesized content [6]. A security analyst receives an incident
report from a user of the application. The report states that
the application produced a research synthesis containing
incorrect information for one particular research task, while
other tasks were completed correctly. The report includes:
a description of how the application is used, a PDF of the
research synthesis, a trajectory log [81] of the application
(Listing 1), and the application’s source code. According to
the user description, the application used both a knowledge
base and web data for this failed task. The analyst listed
three likely accident causes: the LLM was hallucinating, the
scraped webpages were manipulated, or the knowledge base
was poisoned, where the latter two are security-oriented.
Three Stakeholders. There are three stakeholders in the
incident: the analyst, the remedy administrator (usually the
user), and the developers. The remedy admin needs a con-
crete, actionable remedy for the damage, e.g., removing the
exact poisoned file from the knowledge base with hundreds
of documents; the developers need the log printing statement
placement suggestion that makes the application more diag-
nosable for future incidents, e.g., log the parameter values of
the function call corresponding to the initial compromise im-
mediately before that call (Listing 2, Line 83). To provide the
two stakeholders with the two benefits, the analyst aimed to
identify the CEP, i.e., the function call that first introduced
the malicious content to the application (Section 4.3).
Log Triage. To identify the CEP of the incident, the analyst
first triaged the trajectory log (Listing 1), which records the
user task, the application’s research plan, links to scraped
webpages, and HTTP requests to an LLM provider. These
coarse-grained traces were sufficient to rule out LLM halluci-
nation and manipulated webpages, leaving knowledge-base
poisoning as the remaining suspect cause. However, the log
could not help identify which function call is responsible
for the initial compromise (i.e., retrieving poisoned content
from the knowledge base), because the trajectory log did not
record concrete function calls. Fundamentally speaking, tra-
jectory logs are at the agent functionality abstraction layer,
while function calls are at the app code execution layer.

Static Taint Analysis. To identify the CEP, the analyst
complemented the trajectory-log-based agent-functionality-
level diagnosis by variable-level static taint analysis on the
application’s source code. The analysis extracted 1,895 API
calls as taint source candidates, i.e., function calls that could
potentially introduce untrusted content. Using distinctive
log patterns (e.g., “Starting research for ...” colored red in
Listing 1), the analyst located the corresponding log printing
statements in the source code, identified their callers, and
pruned program paths that cannot reach the callers, filtering
out candidates on irrelevant paths. This log-guided pruning
reduced the candidates from 1,895 to 1,518, but the analyst
still needs to determine which of these candidates are related
to knowledge-base retrieval functionality.

Manual Code Inspection Burden. Without tool support
to filter candidates by their functionality, the analyst’s only
option is to inspect each candidate manually. Yet even de-
termining whether a candidate is related to knowledge-base
retrieval requires multi-step code inspection. For instance,
to determine that the candidate loader.load() in Listing 2
retrieves facts from a knowledge base, the analyst had to
(a) trace the variable loader back to its definition, (b) ex-
amine each class in loader_dict and its load function,
and (c) combine these observations with the caller name
_load_document to infer the developer’s intent. Repeating
this process across 1,518 candidates would take hours.
3.2
Limitations of Existing Approaches
Existing approaches for analyzing and defending agent appli-
cations cannot provide stakeholders with the two benefits
illustrated above. The main reason is that trajectory-log-
based failure diagnosis [52, 78, 81], detection-based failure
attribution [24, 44, 79], and preventive information flow con-
trol [28] do not provide the analyst with the CEPs. They
instead provide the analyst with the faulty agent execution
state [52, 79, 81] (e.g., an agent forming an incorrect plan),
faulty agent [78] or agent-owner [24], and LLM tool calls
(not function calls at the source code level) [28, 44].
4
Approach Overview
4.1
Scope
Existing agent applications can be classified into two cate-
gories: predefined workflow (C1), where application source
code rather than LLM decides control flow among agent
functionalities; OpenClaw-like agents [2, 13, 15] (C2), where
the LLM decides at runtime which agent functionality to
invoke next. The C2 agents have recently emerged; however,
most existing applications belong to C1. Our approach is
directly motivated by C1, not by C2. Hence, the scope of this
work is C1; C2 and agent library frameworks [8, 11, 65] are
out of scope and remain an area for future research.
4.2
Threat Model
We assume that adversaries can launch two categories of
agent-specific attacks by methods proposed in existing works:
IPI [36] and MC-Poison [23, 30]. The two attack classes are
the most prevalent among the OWASP Top 10 threats for
agent applications and can cover all the risk categories in
the report that target agent functionalities of the applica-
tions [54]. The remaining categories are either risks inherited
from traditional software security (i.e., remote code execu-
tion, privilege escalation, and supply chain i

GLiDE: A Fast, Calibrated Decision Model Distilled from
Reasoning Teachers
Sahibzada Allahyar
Julia White
Dhruv Atreja
George Hurn-Maloney
Urchade Zaratiana
Fastino Labs
{sahibzada,jwhite,dhruv,g,uz}@fastino.ai
Abstract
Decision models enable fast, confidence-aware
decisions by scoring candidate answers in a
single forward pass, without generating text or
intermediate reasoning. Yet reasoning can sub-
stantially improve decision quality, raising the
question of whether its benefits can be retained
without the cost of generating it. We investigate
this question with GLiDE, a family of decision
models spanning 0.4B to 27B parameters.
Building on Qwen hybrid language models,
GLiDE enables bidirectional interactions be-
tween the context, question, and candidate an-
swers by removing causal masking from full-
attention layers. To transfer reasoning capa-
bilities into single-pass inference, we combine
soft-target distillation from multiple teachers,
including a reasoning model, with progressive
post-training on diverse decision tasks. We fur-
ther explore parameter-free recurrent depth to
increase inference-time computation without
generating tokens.
Across five model sizes, GLiDE lies on the
performance–parameter Pareto frontier of the
Hugging Face Decision Index, with each model
outperforming evaluated alternatives of equal
or smaller size. GLiDE V1.2 (27B) ranks first
on the Hugging Face Decision Index (edition
0.4.1, 22 October 2026) with a hidden-set score
of 71.52, an expected calibration error of 2.0%
and a median latency of 92.9 ms on a single
GPU. It also shares first place on all three
versions of the Artificial Analysis Decision
Index (5, 8 and 15 November 2026). Both
leaderboards are run by their maintainers, who
evaluate every model themselves on test sets
that model developers cannot see: fully hid-
den on Hugging Face, partly private on Ar-
tificial Analysis. Further checkpoint averag-
ing and parameter-free recurrent depth yield
GLiDE 27B, which reaches 73.37 with an ex-
pected calibration error of 2.1%.

highest score across three versions of the Artificial Anal-
ysis Decision Index. The model was not retrained between
versions. Numbers are the scores the leaderboard showed on
the date above each panel, in whole points. In unrounded
scores GLiDE V1.2 is 0.2, 0.6 and 0.1 points below the high-

of its test data is private.
1
Introduction
Decision models and the reasoning gap.
Large
language models are increasingly used not only to
generate text, but also to make decisions: select-
ing tools, routing requests, classifying inputs, and
choosing among predefined actions. In these set-
tings, generating an answer token by token is often
unnecessary. Decision models instead score candi-
date answers in a single forward pass, producing a
probability distribution over the available choices.
This approach has evolved from compact, schema-
conditioned encoders such as GLiNER2 (Zaratiana
et al., 2025) to larger systems including Jev (Type-
Safe AI, 2026), Decider (Perplexity AI, 2026), and
Mammoth (Kirkby et al., 2026). Yet a central ten-
sion remains: multi-step reasoning can substan-
tially improve decision quality, while generating
that reasoning introduces precisely the sequential
computation that decision models seek to avoid.
The challenge is therefore to capture the benefits
of reasoning while retaining the speed of direct
prediction, without sacrificing calibration or gen-
eralization (Tian et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2024;
1
arXiv:2611.26509v1  [cs.AI]  19 Nov 2026
Recht et al., 2019).
Our approach.
We introduce GLiDE, a family
of single-pass decision models spanning 0.4B to
27B parameters. Starting from Qwen hybrid lan-
guage models, we remove causal masking from
their full-attention layers, allowing the context,
question, and candidate answers to interact bidirec-
tionally while retaining causal Gated DeltaNet lay-
ers (Figure 2). A dedicated readout then produces
probabilities over the offered options. To trans-
fer reasoning-informed supervision into this archi-
tecture, we combine soft-target distillation from
multiple teachers, including a model evaluated af-
ter reasoning, with progressive post-training on
diverse decision tasks. In this way, GLiDE learns
from the distributions produced by reasoning with-
out generating intermediate reasoning at inference
time.
Decision performance and calibration.
We first
evaluate GLiDE on the Hugging Face Decision In-
dex (Passos, 2026a), which ranks models using in-
dependently administered hidden test sets. On edi-
tion 0.4.1 (22 October 2026), GLiDE V1.2 (27B)
achieves a score of 71.52, ranking first among 225
models and outperforming the runner-up by 1.77
points (Figure 4). It also leads on both hidden
components, covering unseen questions from estab-
lished skills and decisions in new domains. This
performance is accompanied by an expected cal-
ibration error of 2.0% and a median latency of
92.9 ms on a single RTX PRO 6000 GPU, demon-
strating that strong decision accuracy can coexist
with reliable confidence estimates and efficient in-
ference.
Hidden-set evaluation.
The Hugging Face De-
cision Index evaluates submitted models using pri-
vate test sets administered by the benchmark main-
tainers. As of November 15, 2026, GLiDE mod-
els achieved competitive performance across mul-
tiple leaderboard revisions, with GLiDE 27B scor-
ing 73.37 on the hidden evaluation sets. All five
model sizes also lie on the reported performance–
parameter Pareto frontier.
Scaling and recurrent depth.
Finally, we inves-
tigate how the approach extends across model sizes
and inference-time computation budgets. We de-
velop four smaller GLiDE models through progres-
sive training and distillation from the 27B model.
All five models lie on the performance–parameter
Pareto frontier of the Hugging Face Decision In-
dex, each outperforming every evaluated alterna-
tive of equal or smaller size. We also investigate
parameter-free recurrent depth, which increases
computation by reapplying selected middle layers
without introducing new weights or generating to-
kens. Combined with further checkpoint averaging,
this produces GLiDE 27B, which reaches 73.37 on
the Hugging Face Decision Index with an expected
calibration error of 2.1%. Together, these results
establish GLiDE as a family of fast, calibrated deci-
sion models that benefit from reasoning-informed
training without requiring explicit reasoning gener-
ation at inference time.
Taken together, these findings show that strong,
calibrated decision performance can be achieved
across model scales without generating explicit rea-
soning at inference time. More broadly, GLiDE
demonstrates how reasoning-informed supervision
and additional computation within the model can
improve decision quality while preserving the effi-
ciency of direct candidate scoring.
2
Decision Model Architecture
Readers new to decision models may prefer to start
with Appendix A, which builds the model from the
base language model step by step.
2.1

3
Training
We train GLiDE V1.2 through progressive post-
training, transferring reasoning capabilities into
3
single-pass inference and refining them with di-
verse decision data and multi-teacher supervision.
Figure 9 illustrates the evolution of the model
across stages.
3.1
Progressive Training and Distillation
We train GLiDE through four successive stages,
each building on the checkpoint produced by the
preceding stage. The procedure first develops a
reasoning-capable teacher, then converts it into a
single-pass decision model before progressively
refining its predictions.
Stage 1: Reasoning teacher.
We first adapt
Qwen3.8-27B using LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) in
two steps.
We begin by generating reasoning
traces for training questions and retaining approxi-
mately 6,400 examples whose reasoning leads to
the correct answer. Rank-64 LoRA adapters are
trained on these examples with the base weights
frozen, using next-token prediction on the reason-
ing traces and cross-entropy on the final answers.
Next, the adapted model reasons over approxi-
mately 135K additional questions, and we collect
its post-thinking probability distributions over the
candidate answers. A second LoRA round trains
the model to predict these distributions directly,
without producing written reasoning. The result-
ing teacher can operate with or without explicit
reasoning, providing both direct and post-thinking
predictions for subsequent distillation. This is the
only stage that uses LoRA.
Stage 2: Single-pass conversion.
Starting from
the reasoning teacher, we remove causal masking
from the full-attention layers and introduce the ded-
icated option readout. We then distill soft probabil-
ity distributions from multiple teachers, including
the reasoning model’s post-thinking predictions, to
train the architecture for direct decision scoring in
a single forward pass.
Stage 3: Short training rounds.
We then con-
tinue training through five short rounds. After each
round, the updated checkpoint is averaged equally
with its parent, yielding GLiDE V1.1. This re-
cursive averaging gives the latest update half of
the final weight, the preceding update one quarter,
and progressively smaller contributions to earlier
rounds, helping retain previously learned capabili-
ties while incorporating new refinements.
Stage 4: Final post-training.
Finally, we con-
tinue training GLiDE V1.1 on a rebuilt mixture of
diverse decision tasks, using task-specific multi-
teacher distributions as supervision. This stage
consolidates the preceding improvements and pro-
duces GLiDE V1.2, our final decision model.

3.4
Optimization Details
The final stage uses full-parameter fine-tuning with
AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019), a learn-
ing rate of 10−6, batch size 128, and 2,928 steps
over one epoch. Candidate options are shuffled
during training to reduce position bias. Each seed
requires approximately six hours on eight B200
GPUs. The released model averages the weights of
two independently trained seeds (Wortsman et al.,
2022).
4
Experimental Setup
We evaluate GLiDE V1.2 on decision-making
benchmarks covering accuracy, generalization, cal-
ibration, and inference efficiency. Our primary
evaluation is the Hugging Face Decision Index,
complemented by externally administered bench-
marks and held-out internal evaluation sets.
4.1
Benchmarks
Decision Index.
The Decision Index (Passos,
2026a) evaluates decision models across 37 public
benchmarks spanning five task categories. Since
October 20, 2026, its official ranking has relied
exclusively on two hidden evaluation sets adminis-
tered by the benchmark maintainers: (i) same-skill,
measuring generalization to unseen questions from
known task families, and (ii) new-domain, evalu-
ating decisions in domains absent from the public
benchmarks. Let S and O denote the normalized
scores on the two hidden sets. The overall ranking
score is Full = 0.6S + 0.4O. Models must com-
plete inference without intermediate reasoning and
satisfy a one-second latency limit on a single RTX
PRO 6000

FLUID: Flexible, Evidence-Grounded Situated Task Guidance
Yunqi Zhao*
Run Peng*
Ze Dong
Ryan Lu
Yinpei Dai
Joyce Chai
University of Michigan
{rickzhao, roihn, chaijy}@umich.edu
Abstract
Real-time task guidance is inherently flexible:
when an agent guides a user through a task,
multiple responses and timings can be appropri-
ate, and sometimes the best action is to remain
silent. Existing benchmarks often miss this
flexibility by treating synthesized dialogues as
fixed targets for what to say and when to say
it. We introduce FLUID (Flexible, Evidence-
Grounded Situated Task Guidance), a unified
framework for modeling, evaluating, and en-
abling flexible interaction in multimodal task
guidance. Using naturally occurring human-
human guidance from WTaG and HoloAssist,
FLUID grounds interventions in their support-
ing evidence, necessity, and timing flexibil-
ity, and uses this representation both to eval-
uate flexible guidance and to build a real-time
agent for task guidance. Our agent achieves the
strongest overall balance of response correct-
ness, intervention precision, timely guidance,
and response latency among evaluated systems,
while still leaving room for improvement in
avoiding speech overlap. Together, FLUID
moves situated task guidance beyond rigid
reference matching toward more natural and
adaptive human-AI interaction. Project page:
https://fluid-guidance.github.io.
1
Introduction
With the growing adoption of smart glasses and
other wearable devices, multimodal AI assistants
are becoming increasingly accessible for providing
real-time, situated assistance in everyday activi-
ties (Cui et al., 2026; OpenAI, 2026; Google Deep-
Mind, 2026). An important emerging application is
perceptual task guidance, where an AI assistant ob-
serves the user’s environment and ongoing actions
through an egocentric camera and provides context-
aware guidance through natural language as shown
in Figure 1. This kind of situated perceptual task
guidance requires continuous coordination between
visual perception, task understanding, and commu-
nication. The AI assistant must interpret the user’s
