Figure 1: Illustration of perceptual task guidance.
actions and task progress, respond to questions,
provide step-by-step instructions, detect mistakes,
and proactively offer assistance when appropriate.
To evaluate these capabilities, existing work
commonly relies on human-human interaction data
or synthetically generated dialogues as references
for expected guidance behaviors, measuring how
closely the AI instructor’s responses align with the
reference responses in both semantic content and
temporal placement (Bhattacharyya et al., 2025;
Zhang et al., 2025a; Shi et al., 2026). Although
a good starting point, these approaches treat refer-
ence interactions as fixed targets, overlooking the
inherent flexibility of situated guidance. In prac-
tice, human-human guidance is fluid and adaptive.
Certain situations, such as incorrect actions or im-
minent safety risks, require immediate intervention,
while others allow a wider range of appropriate tim-
ing for proactive assistance. Similarly, backchan-
nels and acknowledgments help maintain shared
understanding, but their timing and frequency can
vary considerably. This creates a fundamental mis-
match between rigid reference-based evaluation
and the flexible nature of real-world task guidance,
calling for evaluation criteria that can take into
account both the correctness of guidance and the
flexibility of communication.
Addressing this challenge requires a principled
framework for characterizing the flexibility of sit-
uated guidance. Importantly, flexibility does not
imply unconstrained behavior. Effective guidance
1
arXiv:2611.26491v1  [cs.AI]  19 Nov 2026
must remain grounded in perceptual and interaction
evidence, with different communicative behaviors
subject to different requirements. When AI as-
sistants decide to intervene or provide guidance,
some interventions (e.g., correcting a user mistake
or giving a warning about a potential hazard) are
necessary within narrow temporal windows, while
others (e.g., backchannel) are optional and allow
greater flexibility in content and timing. Human
references remain valuable for identifying effective
guidance behaviors, but should not prescribe a sin-
gle correct response at a fixed moment. Instead, the
key is to characterize the underlying evidence that
warrants communication and the conditions under
which different responses are appropriate. This
evidence-grounded perspective provides a founda-
tion for both evaluating and generating flexible
guidance behaviors.
In this paper, we introduce FLUID (Flexible,
Evidence-Grounded Situated Task Guidance), a
unified framework for characterizing, evaluat-
ing, and enabling flexible interaction dynamics
in multimodal task guidance. First, we develop
an evidence-grounded representation that char-
acterizes communicative behaviors in terms of
their necessity, supporting evidence, and tem-
poral flexibility (FLUID-Modeling).
Second,
we introduce an evaluation framework that lever-
ages human references while moving beyond
strict response matching to assess the appropri-
ateness of guidance content and timing (FLUID-
Evaluation). Third, we propose an agent architec-
ture that explicitly models and adapts to evolving
interaction dynamics, enabling flexible, evidence-
grounded decisions about when and how to com-
municate, including reactive responses, proac-
tive guidance, and appropriate silence (FLUID-
Agent).
Together, these contributions provide
a systematic approach to understanding, evaluat-
ing, and generating flexible, evidence-grounded
guidance, advancing multimodal AI assistants
toward more natural and adaptive human–AI
interaction.
2
Related Work
Real-Time Interaction.
Recent advances in mul-
timodal systems have rapidly expanded real-time
human-AI interaction, from streaming audio-visual
perception (OpenAI, 2026; Qwen Team, 2026a)
to low-latency, full-duplex spoken interaction (Cui
et al., 2026; Thinking Machines Lab, 2026; Group,
2026; ByteDance Seed, 2026; Google DeepMind,
2026). Scaling such interactive capabilities has
increasingly relied on synthetic or automatically
constructed interaction data, often by repurposing
existing egocentric videos (Grauman et al., 2022;
Peddi et al., 2024; Damen et al., 2018; Huang
et al., 2024) and generating intervention traces
at scale (Shi et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025a;
Kundu et al., 2026).
In contrast, naturally oc-
curring human-human interactions in which one
person continuously observes and guides another
through a physical task remain scarce. Existing
efforts include WTaG (Bao et al., 2023), Holo-
Assist (Wang et al., 2023), EgoInstruct (Sakai
et al., 2025), Ego-EXTRA (Ragusa et al., 2026),
and Ego-MC-Bench (Bhattacharyya et al., 2026),
but some of them remain limited in released
modalities. In this work, we primarily build on
WTaG and HoloAssist, both of which provide
audio alongside egocentric video, to study how
interactions naturally unfold during human guid-
ance.
Proactive Agent Modeling.
Existing proactive
video agents span query-conditioned event re-
sponse, continuous commentary, and situated pro-
cedural guidance (Wang et al., 2025; Lu et al.,
2026; Chen et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2025; Qian et al.,
2025; Wang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2025; Zhang
et al., 2025a). Representative systems typically pro-
duce textual responses or discrete decisions about
whether to intervene, with timing supervision de-
rived from annotated event boundaries, task tran-
sitions, mistakes, or synthesized utterances (Pan-
chal et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023, 2025b; Bhat-
tacharyya et al., 2025; Kundu et al., 2026). Recent
methods move beyond purely event-triggered poli-
cies: Pro²Assist additionally annotates assistance
need, while Vinci2 generates visually grounded
service opportunities and reasons about whether in-
tervention is warranted (Xu et al., 2026; Gong et al.,
2026). They provide increasingly rich supervision;
however, their assistance targets are constructed
from task states or annotated events rather than nat-
urally occurring intervention decisions. In contrast,
we study human-human guidance. This preserves
a broader range of communicative behaviors and
enables intervention-specific annotations of neces-
sity and valid timing, characterizing not only when
assistance may occur but how much flexibility each
interaction permits.
2
3
FLUID-Modeling: Grounded Evidence
in Task Guidance
3.1
Problem Definition
In real-time task guidance, an agent continuously
observes a user performing a task and must decide
how to respond appropriately as the task and inter-
action evolve. We characterize each intervention
decision along four dimensions. WHY: what ev-
idence warrants the intervention, namely the user
utterance, action, or state that the guide reacts to;
we refer to it as the grounded evidence of the
intervention. WHETHER: whether the interven-
tion is necessary, optional, or not needed. WHEN:
the period during which the intervention is use-
ful. WHAT: the interaction act of the intervention
and its content. Interventions triggered by a user
utterance are reactive; all others are proactive.
3.2
Source Data
We study WTaG (Bao et al., 2023) and Holo-
Assist (Wang et al., 2023), two egocentric datasets
of naturally occurring human-human task guid-
ance in which a remote instructor observes the
user’s view and provides verbal guidance. The
two datasets exhibit complementary interaction
regimes.
WTaG is relatively self-paced: users
receive a high-level task recipe in advance and
can often proceed independently, which produces
mixed-initiative interaction.
HoloAssist has a
stronger knowledge asymmetry and is predomi-
nantly instructor-led, with users relying on ongoing
guidance for each step. In total, we select 43 WTaG
sessions and 72 HoloAssist sessions with substan-
tive interactions between users and instructors.
3.3
Multi-Layer Annotation
To reveal the interaction semantics underlying nat-
urally occurring human interventions, we augment
WTaG and HoloAssist with four linked annotation
layers, which together cover the four dimensions
of Section 3.1 (see Figure 2 for an example).
Layer 1:
Utterance Taxonomy.
We catego-
rize every user and instructor utterance using an
utterance-level taxonomy with 11 user categories
and 13 instructor categories.
Layer 2: Action and State.
We annotate user ac-
tions and states that are closely related to instructor
interventions, including hand actions, visual loss,
stalling, and searching. Each action is further la-
beled by whether it is valid or deviating and by its
effect on task execution, such as task progress, step
completion, or recovery.
Layer 3: Trigger Link.
Using the annotated ut-
terances and actions, we link each instructor inter-
vention to the preceding utterance, action, or state
that triggered it, forming a grounded evidence
link that explains why the human instructor de-
cided to intervene. Each link receives a trigger
type derived from the linked events, such as Step
Done, Error, or User Query. We further catego-
rize each intervention as necessary if, without it,
the user would make a mistake, get stuck, or lack
needed information; optional if the user would pro-
ceed correctly on their own, so that speaking and
remaining silent are both acceptable; and excluded
if it is irrelevant to the task, such as self-repairs, or
relies on knowledge that cannot be obtained from
the shared egocentric view, the dialogue, or the task
knowledge.
Layer 4: Evidence Onset and Intervention Win-
dow.
We annotate temporal anchor points for in-
terventions, which define the time window within
which an intervention should be initiated. For reac-
tive interventions, we annotate (1) the time at which
the user finishes their most recent utterance, tusr,
and (2) the latest time at which the intervention
remains useful, tlatest. For proactive interventions,
there is no corresponding tusr; instead, we annotate
(1) the earliest time at which initial signs suggest
that an intervention may be necessary, tearly, and
(2) the time at which enough evidence becomes
available to determine that the intervention is nec-
essary, tevid, together with tlatest. Together, these
anchors define an evidence-derived window for
evaluating intervention timing.
Annotation Workflow.
For WTaG, we first use
majority voting across multiple language-model
annotators to produce initial annotations, followed
by careful manual review of all instances. Based
on the errors and practical observations identified
during this process, we refine the machine annota-
tion pipeline and apply it to the selected HoloAssist
sessions, and manually review about 10% of the
generated annotations to ensure the synthetic data
quality.
3.4
Interventions Are Context-Dependent
Our annotations show that natural human guidance
does not follow a fixed trigger-to-intervention map-
ping: whether an intervention is needed, and what

form it should take, depends on the surrounding
interaction context.
Similar situations may or may not require in-
tervention.
Among step completions on the self-
paced WTaG, only 12.9% are followed by a nec-
essary intervention (e.g., providing the next-step
instruction), while 17.5% are optional (e.g., “Nice”
or “uh-huh”) and 69.6% receive no intervention
(n = 418). In the more instructor-led HoloAssist
setting, the corresponding proportions are 65.9%,
12.2%, and 21.9% (n = 649). Thus, whether a step
completion warrants guidance depends strongly
on the surrounding interaction regime and context,
rather than on the event type alone. In contrast,
existing approaches often use a more rigid event-to-
response mapping, such as triggering a next-step
instruction whenever a step is completed.
These observations motivate evaluating guidance
against the grounded evidence that warrants an in-
tervention, whether intervention is necessary, and
when it remains useful.
4
FLUID-Evaluation on Task Guidance
Existing reference-based evaluations assess guid-
ance primarily through content similarity and tem-
poral proximity to human reference utterances, of-
ten using a fixed timing window (Zhang et al.,
2025a; Bhattacharyya et al., 2025, 2026). Such cri-
teria overlook the flexibility of natural interaction,
where appropriate guidance depends on task evi-
dence and may vary in necessity and timing. We in-
troduce an evidence-derived evaluation framework
that leverages our annotations to evaluate interven-
tion appropriateness based on supporting evidence,
necessity, and valid timing windows. Appendix C
specifies the protocol and metrics in full.
4.1
Intervention Matching
Real-time interaction does not follow fixed turn
boundaries: within any time interval, a system may
produce zero, one, or multiple utterances, whereas
evaluation requires a one-to-one correspondence
between system utterances and annotated human
interventions. We therefore first match them based
on content and supporting evidence. For each nec-
essary or optional intervention, we consider candi-
date system utterances within a matching window
that covers its annotated evidence window and the
surrounding intervals of adjacent reference utter-
ances. An LLM judge then assesses content equiv-
alence based on the dialogue history and triggering
evidence. Since a system may generate multiple
equivalent utterances within the same time interval,
we select the earliest qualifying utterance as the
match.
4.2
Timing Appropriateness
Evaluating the timing of matched interventions is
essential, yet common approaches (Zhang et al.,
2025a; Bhattacharyya et al., 2025, 2026) have two
limitations: (1) fixed timing windows ignore when
an intervention becomes possible and when it stops
being useful, admitting invalid onsets and exclud-
ing valid ones; and (2) binary in-window scoring
treats all onsets within a window as equally appro-
priate, although their usefulness varies with timing.
4
For the first limitation , we derive intervention-
specific valid windows from the temporal anchors
annotated in Section 3.3: [tusr, tlatest) for reactive
guidance and [tearly, tlatest) for proactive guidance.
Unlike a fixed timing window around the reference
utterance, each window opens after the user’s turn
ends or at the first sign of need, and closes when
the intervention is no longer useful. An onset is
valid if it falls anywhere within the window of the
corresponding intervention.
We validate these windows with a human study
that isolates timing from content.
For each of
79 WTaG instructor utterances, we keep the utter-
ance fixed and sample six candidate onsets around
its annotated anchors, spanning early, in-window,
and late times and including the instructor’s ac-
tual onset. Three researchers rate how appropriate
it would be to deliver the same utterance at each
onset on a 0-10 scale (See Appendix G for more
details). We treat an onset as acceptable when its
mean human rating is at least 6, and compare this
label with whether the onset falls within the pro-
posed intervention window. We report Macro-F1 to
measure how well the window classification agrees
with human judgments across acceptable and un-
acceptable timings. Overall, our evidence-derived
windows outperform the fixed [−6, +3]s window
around reference utterance onsets adopted from
ProAssist (Zhang et al., 2025a) (Macro-F1: 0.788
vs. 0.713). The improvement is more pronounced
for reactive guidance, where our windows exclude
inappropriate onsets that would interrupt the user,
while for proactive guidance, our windows achieve
comparable performance while admitting earlier
evidence-supported onsets missed by the fixed win-
dow.
For the second limitation, we introduce a contin-
uous timing score that captures varying degrees of
timing appropriateness. The score peaks at a pre-
ferred response time tpref and decreases for earlier
or later onsets. For reactive guidance, tpref = tusr,
since responding immediately after the user fin-
ishes speaking is preferred; for proactive guidance,
tpref = tevid, when sufficient evidence becomes
available. An earlier utterance lacks supporting
evidence, and a later one becomes less useful as
the task progresses.
Next, we test whether a continuous timing score
better reflects human preferences than binary in-
window scoring. We start with

A NEW ALGORITHMIC APPROACH FOR FINDING FLAT MINIMA:
CRITICALLY DAMPED POLYAK STEPSIZES
FRANCESCO CAPORALI, JASON M. ALTSCHULER, AND BORIS HANIN
Abstract. We present a new adaptive stepsize rule that biases gradient descent toward flatter
minima in both theory and practice, and establish the first uniform-in-time guarantees for both
sharpness and loss reduction for a broad class of locally quadratic objectives. Our critically damped
Polyak (CDP) stepsizes multiply the classical Polyak rule by 4 and a mild damping factor. The
factor 4 is critical in that it produces equioscillations around the manifold of minimizers M to
leading order; damping provably drives convergence to M.
CDP thus operates at the edge of
stability by adapting its stepsizes to local curvature. Once the loss is small, its projected iterates
follow gradient descent on log λ1(∇2L) along M to leading order, paralleling the flatness bias of
normalized gradient descent [ALP22]. Unlike normalized gradient descent, CDP step lengths shrink
with the distance to M, enabling convergence to an interpolating solution that locally minimizes
sharpness at finite learning rate. We establish our theory for a broad class of non-negative losses with
locally quadratic Morse–Bott structure near M, capturing regular interpolation regimes in smooth
overparameterized neural networks. Empirically, CDP stepsizes produce a flattening effect similar
to that of Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) [For+21], reducing sharpness even in settings
beyond our theory, including nonlinear teacher-student networks and fine-tuning of pre-trained
LLMs.
1. Introduction
Modern machine learning is predicated on efficient optimization in high dimensions. A prototypical
example is learning the parameters θ of a model such as a neural network by minimizing an empirical
risk L(θ) using a first-order method such as gradient descent (GD)

eterized models, the set of global loss minima can form large, continuously varying families, and
empirical studies find low-loss paths connecting trained solutions [Coo18; Gar+18].

Monte Carlo Pass Search for Setpieces 
Simulating every delivery and set-up a team could have used, and how all 22 players 
respond 
Andrew Kang 
Abstract 
Set pieces produce about a third of non-penalty expected goals (xG), yet they are usually evaluated 
by what happened next. We present Monte Carlo Pass Search (MCPS) for set pieces, which treats 
a corner or a lofted free kick as a distribution over plausible executions and plausible futures 
instead of a single realised event. From the pre-kick state, MCPS proposes counterfactual 
deliveries and counterfactual set-ups (where the attackers stand at the kick), plays each out many 
times in a world model (3D ball physics, a generative model of all 22 players, the keeper's come-or-
stay decision and a Player-to-Touch model) and scores every future with a value model. On 249 
deliveries from 30 Serie A 2025/26 matches, with every model applied only to matches it never saw, 
the best available delivery is worth 0.0085 xG more than the one kicked (+28 %), mainly because it 
reaches an attacker before the keeper. Searching where the attackers stand as well adds +0.0027 
xG with the observed ball and +0.0033 on top of the best ball; designing their runs too adds +0.0007 
more. We show how to keep such a search honest, and estimate how much more data each 
component needs before a club could rely on it. 
1  Motivation 
Set pieces decide matches. In our 30 matches, possessions that start from a corner or a free kick 
produce 33 % of non-penalty xG and 29 % of non-penalty goals. They are also the most designable 
phase of play: the ball is dead, players walk into chosen positions, and one player chooses where to 
aim. Both choices, the delivery and the set-up, are decisions, and a decision should be judged 
against the alternatives that were available at the time. 
Sports analytics is dominated by simpler methods that score the realised event: counts and rates 
(shots per corner, first-contact win rates), delivery-zone maps, and value models such as xG, 
expected threat (xT), VAEP and possession value (PV) [3, 4, 14]. They are cheap, transparent and 
useful, but they are point estimates of what happened, which limits them for set-piece decisions 
in three ways. 
•	 Outcome bias. A team takes about 160 lofted set-piece deliveries a season. One header in or out 
flips a zone's record, and a good delivery that a defender happens to clear is scored as a bad 
one. 
•	 No counterfactuals. Counts describe what was kicked, not what could have been. A zone 
nobody aims at, or a set-up nobody uses, has no data. 
•	 Interaction. A delivery's value depends on how all 22 players respond: the attacker who times 
his run, the defender who follows him, the keeper who comes or stays. "What if the ball had gone 
3 m further and lower?" cannot be read off past plays in which the players did something else. 
1
MCPS takes a different view, adapted from open-play passing [7] (Figure 1). A delivery is a 
distribution over plausible kicks and plausible short-term futures. We borrow the search-and-
evaluate idea of Monte Carlo Tree Search [12] with three parts: a policy that proposes 
counterfactual deliveries and set-ups, a world model that plays each one forward until the first 
touch, and a value model that scores the result. Averaging over futures gives each option's 
expected value; comparing options gives the best available choice and how much it beats the one 
that was made. 
 
Figure 1: From point estimates to distributions. Right: outcome-based evaluation scores the one future that happened 
(here the keeper reaches a Napoli corner first and the shot that follows is worth 0.021 xG). Left: MCPS plays the same pre-
kick state forward many times with a world model, values every future, and compares the observed delivery's value 
distribution with that of the best alternative. 
Contributions.  
•	 A set-piece world model built from standard event and tracking data, including 3D ball flights 
reconstructed from tracking that never measures the ball's height. Each component is a 
separate model, validated on held-out matches, so it can be checked, replaced or retrained on 
its own. 
•	 Local, global and set-up search. Local search samples execution variants of the observed 
delivery (how sensitive was it to the kick?); global search samples alternative deliveries (was a 
better ball available?); set-up search samples where the attackers stand at the kick, with the 
defending team's set-up responding through a learned model. 
•	 An evaluation protocol for decisions made with learned simulators: fresh futures, an 
independent value model as the judge, and a realism constraint on recommendations. It 
changes the answer more than any modelling choice. 
•	 An evaluation of every set piece, team and player on all three decisions (ball, set-up, runs), 
with player rankings built from the same counterfactuals. 
•	 A data-needs study for professional use: which components still improve with more seasons, 
and roughly how many seasons each needs. 
2
2  How MCPS works 
 
Figure 2: Workflow for each simulated set piece. Every labelled step is a separate model; the policy chooses the kick 
(and, in set-up search, where the attackers stand), the world model plays it out to the first touch, and the value model 
scores it. 
Each future follows the steps in Figure 2. 
•	 Kick parameters. A delivery is a 3D launch velocity plus spin. For the observed delivery we infer 
them by fitting ball physics to the event and tracking data. Alternatives are a target point in the 
box (8 depths × 13 lateral positions) at one of three heights (apex 3, 4.5 or 7 m): about 180 
feasible options per set piece. A delivery is a shot, not a cross, and is never considered if its 
intended flight would enter the goal untouched or drop onto the goal line (within 1 m of it, 
between the posts and under the bar), or if at least 1 in 10 of its executions would go in (95 % of 
real corners stay below that rate); a real delivery that is a shot is kept as the baseline but never 
recommended. The taker never hits a target exactly, so every kick receives execution noise (5 % 
speed, 2.5° direction, 2° elevation, spin). 
•	 In-flight physics. Gravity, drag, spin and bounce fly the ball. The key output is where and when it 
comes down through head height (2.3 m), the drop point L. 
•	 Set-up. Where every player stands at the kick: the observed positions, or a searched set-up for 
the attackers with the defending team's response drawn from a learned set-up model (Section 
3). 
•	 Intent. A destination model draws, for every player, where he is heading when the ball arrives, 
from the scene at the kick and L [19]. 
•	 Generative player trajectories. A motion-token transformer in the style of SMART [18] (256 
tokens of 0.4 s, 6.7 M parameters) moves each player towards his destination with realistic path 
spread and body spacing. 
•	 Keeper. A come-or-stay model decides whether the keeper attacks the ball; if he comes, he 
runs to it after a reaction delay. 
•	 Player-to-Touch. A survival model gives, every 0.08 s, the probability that each player makes 
the first touch; the ball may also go untouched. 
3
•	 Value model. The first touch is worth the probability that the attacking team shoots within 3 s, 
times that shot's xG. Defenders' and keepers' touches keep a small value (second balls). 
Intent, then execution. A generator that only predicts each player's next 0.4 s from his recent 
motion is accurate step by step, but loses the purpose of a run within about a second. On held-out 
set pieces, real players near the drop point close in on it by 0.61 m in the first 1.6 s; such a generator 
closes in by 0.02 m, because every random step reads as a change of plan. Drawing a destination 
once per player and executing it keeps the purpose: with the true destinations the generator 
reproduces the real 0.56 m. 
Calibrated to cause. Because the destination model sees L, it could simply follow the ball and make 
simulated players react to every candidate delivery more than real ones do. We measured how far 
real players move per metre that L moves, holding the pre-kick scene fixed (double machine 
learning [2] on the part of L the scene does not predict): attackers 0.048, defenders 0.076, keepers 
0.058 m per m by the time the ball arrives. One weight per role on the destination model [6] 
reproduces these responses (0.055 / 0.072 / 0.058). 
3  Searching deliveries and set-ups 
Two measures. We keep the terms of the original MCPS [7]. The surplus of one option over another 
is the difference of their values (xG per set piece), each the mean over its simulated futures. The 
mean surplus of what happened is its value minus the mean value of its simulated futures: positive 
when it turned out better than a typical future of the same choice. 
Local search: execution sensitivity. Execution variants of the observed delivery show how much 
its value depended on the kick. The mean surplus of what happened over the observed delivery's 
futures separates a good decision that went wrong (negative) from a poor decision that got lucky 
(positive). 
Global search: the best alternative. Every alternative delivery is screened with 8 futures; the best 
ten and the best realistic ones are re-tested with 48. We report the surplus of the best alternative 
over the observed delivery, both in the same scene. 
Set-up search: where attackers stand. The same machinery can move the attackers before the 
kick. A set-up model predicts where each player stands at the kick given the players already 
placed, one player at a time. Each player is either placed relative to an already-placed player 
(marking, stacking, screening the keeper) or in a zone relative to the goal; the defending team is 
placed after the attackers, so its markers follow the attackers wherever they are moved. Trained on 
26 k open-play situations and the set pieces of the training matches, its sampled defences mark as 
tightly as real ones (on held-out matches a box attacker has a defender within 1 m 24.2 % of the 
time, 24.0 % in tracking). For every set piece we sample 19 alternative attacker set-ups from the 
model (half move every attacker in the box, half move one to three of them), draw a fresh defending 
set-up for every future, let every player choose a destination from his new starting point, and 
search set-up and delivery together. 
Keeping the search honest. Picking the maximum of noisy estimates flatters the winner, and with 
learned models in more than one way [15]. Three rules keep the reported gain honest. 
4
•	 Fresh futures. Chosen options are re-valued on new futures, never on those used to choose 
them. 
•	 An independent judge. The search also favours options whose value its own value model 
happens to overestimate, and fresh futures do not remove that. We search with one 5-seed 
ensemble [8] and judge with a separately trained one (or with models trained on disjoint halves 
of the matches). For set-up search the defenders' set-up model is also swapped for an 
independently trained one. 
•	 Realistic recommendations. We also report the best delivery that resembles real ones (its 
distance to the five nearest real deliveries of other matches within the 75th percentile of real 
deliveries' own). 
4  Results 
Data. Serie A 2025/26 event data (StatsBomb) and 25 Hz tracking for the 30 matches among six 
clubs; 249 lofted deliveries (170 corners, 79 free kicks into the box). Five match-grouped folds: 
every number comes from models that never saw that play's match. Everything runs on one GPU 
(about 9 s per set piece for the delivery search, 20 s with the set-up search). 
Table 1: Surplus of global search's best delivery over the observed one (249 set pieces; ± s.e. over plays). 
What the better ball looks like. Averaged over set pieces, the best realistic delivery raises the 
attackers' share of first touches from 0.28 to 0.38 and cuts the keeper's from 0.13 to 0.06; balls 
nobody touches fall from 0.14 to 0.09. It is flatter (apex 4.3 vs 5.0 m; the 4.5 m profile in 114 plays, 3 
m in 97, 7 m in 38), slightly more central (3.9 vs 4.1 m from the middle of the goal) and at about the 
same depth (6.3 m from the goal line). Per team-season, 0.0085 xG per delivery is about 1.4 xG. 
One set piece in depth. Figure 3 takes one Napoli corner apart. The keeper reached the real 
delivery first and the attack's follow-up shot was worth 0.021 xG (a). Global search finds a lower, 
faster ball (apex 4.5 m, 31 m/s) that drops 7.5 m from the goal line instead of 4.1 m: the real 7 m lob 
gives the keeper time to come. Over 256 futures each (b), the observed delivery is worth 0.019 xG 
and the searched one 0.045, a surplus of +0.026; what actually happened has a mean surplus of 
+0.002 over the observed delivery's futures, so the taker executed his choice about as well as usual 
and the loss came from the choice. Most executions of the observed delivery come down where the 
keeper arrives first (keeper first in 49% of futures); the searched ball moves the first touch from 
the keeper to the attackers (c: attackers 0.16 → 0.42, keeper 0.49 → 0.01). The set-up search (d)

0.024 xG, the best set-up 0.020, the best ball 0.048 and both together 0.046. Here the ball is the

Searching the set-up. Table 2 compares the set-up search with the delivery search, all with the

the set-up adds +0.0033 (corners +0.0037, free kicks +0.0026), more than designing the runs 
(+0.0012, below). Designing the attackers' runs as well, for the best three set-up and delivery 
combinations, adds +0.0007 on top of the best set-up and delivery, and searching all three together 
gains +0.0124 over the observed play (Table 2). The better set-ups mostly bring one more attacker 
into the box at corners (6.5 → 7.6, 1.1 fewer waiting outside it) and more into the six-yard box (2.2 → 
2.9); set-ups sampled at random from the model have 7.4 and 2.3, so the search selects rather than 
copying the model's habits. The search's own models, the independent ones and a differently 
trained destination model agree (Appendix E). One caveat matters for coaches: the value model 
counts only the attacking team's shots within 3 s, so the counter-attack risk of pulling the edge-of-
box player forward is not priced. 
6
Table 2: Set-up search (independent set-up model and value ensemble as judge; ± s.e. over plays). Every row uses 
sampled defenders. The last two rows also design the attackers' runs (2.8 m destination zones) for the best three set-up 
and delivery combinations and are judged on separate fresh futures. 
Robustness. The best delivery's surplus survives every alternative we tried (Appendix D): five 
independently trained pipelines (the best delivery is better for a majority of them in 70 % of plays), 
players reacting to the ball at the observational upper bound (−0.0001), a fixed keeper rule 
(+0.0004), four times more ball spin (−0.0006), defenders that respond to the attackers' 
destinations (−0.0016) and soft collision handling (+0.0002). Individual recommendations are less 
stable: independently trained pipelines scatter the best target by a median 2.7 m, so they should be 
read as zones, not points. 
Designing the runs. Searching the attackers' run destinations (a 2.8 m zone per attacker) together 
with the ball adds only 0.0012 xG over the best ball (free kicks 0.0015, corners 0.0010), and a fixed 
routine, the three nearest attackers attacking the drop zone, adds 0.0023. With the set-up 
searched as well, designed runs add +0.0007 on top of the best set-up and delivery. Runs are worth 
little because there is little time: between the kick and the ball's descent real attackers move a 
median 2.2 m (90 % less than 5.5 m), so where an attacker stands at the kick decides most of where 
he meets the ball, which is why the set-up matters more. Designed runs do take effect, and 
simulated runners gain as much separation from defenders as real ones (0.18 vs 0.13 m per metre 
run). 
Every set piece, every team, every player. The same machinery evaluates each of the 249 
observed set pieces on all three decisions (Figure 4, top). Per set piece, the surplus of a better ball 
is +0.0085 xG, of a better set-up +0.0027 and of designed runs +0.0011. The observed set-up has a 
mean surplus of +0.0013 over the set-ups the model proposes for the same players, and is worth 
less than their mean in 37 % of set pieces. The exact kick has a mean surplus of +0.0024 over noisy 
executions of the same delivery, and what happened one of +0.0019 ± 0.0015 over its simulated 
futures, close to zero as it should be if the futures are calibrated. Teams differ mostly in the ball: 
Juventus and Napoli left 0.0116–0.0125 xG per set piece with it, Inter 0.0066. Real players move 
better than the model's typical players on both sides (attackers' runs +0.011 xG per set piece, 
defending 0.009), so the two largely cancel; making simulated players less passive is the clearest 
use for more data. Ranking players by the same quantities (Figure 4, bottom), Baturina, Dybala, 
Dimarco leave the least on the table per delivery (0.0057–0.0059 xG) and Yildiz the most (0.0144);

A CPU Inside an LLM: Zero-Gradient Compilation of
Exact Circuits into Pretrained Weights
Tanmay Sah 1
Abstract
Pretrained language models (LMs) remain un-
reliable on exact multi-digit arithmetic without
gradient fine-tuning or external tool interpreters.
We introduce closed-form, zero-gradient circuit-
grafting primitives that compile deterministic
computation directly into pretrained LM weights
using zero training examples and zero runtime
hooks, while bounding per-layer normalization
drift and preserving natural-language (NL) com-
petence. Our construction combines three ana-
lytical mechanisms: (1) two-layer Mellin-GLU
quadrature over bias-free SwiGLU/GeGLU lay-
ers, turning unknown per-token RMSNorm scal-
ing into translation along a log-spaced gate grid
(> 250× dynamic range) with IEEE 754 er-
ror bounds; (2) cross-token scale cancellation
via signed Chebyshev Indefinite-RoPE self-sink
attention and memoryless SiLU-antisymmetric
GatedDeltaNet shifts; and (3) axis-aligned
width extension (d →d + K) with
p
d/(d + K)
norm compensation, Base-1000 canonical BPE
emission, and differential (+254, −256) tied un-
embeddings. An automated 5-stage compiler syn-
thesizes 4–8 digit signed {+, −, ×} circuits in
constant TC0 depth alongside 3-literal Boolean
(100%, N=1,728; plus 42-layer Gemma 4 E4B
audits) and 5-bit Majority/Parity (100%) circuits.
On 6-digit arithmetic (N=1,200, BF16), IBM
Granite 4.2 3B (1.07M–1.33M active non-zeros,
≤0.036%) and Alibaba Qwen 3.5 4B (2.25M–
2.39M non-zeros, ≤

and 100.00% ALU-prefix accuracy (100% with
an FP32 sidecar) and 98%–100% mid-sentence
resumption—outperforming 12.8K-sample LoRA
(42.2% / 61.7%, 0% inline continuation). A fac-
torized block-sparse sidecar holds A100 mem-
ory at 7.89 / 10.65 GiB (4.60 / 8.14 GiB under
INT8/INT4 + FP32 sidecar) while passing all

1. Introduction
Autoregressive LMs interleave natural-language reasoning
with deterministic sub-computations, yet next-token pre-
diction remains brittle on exact multi-digit arithmetic (Liu
& Low, 2023; McLeish et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024).
Deployed systems route around this via host tool wrap-
pers (Schick et al., 2023) that pause decoding to invoke
external interpreters. Conversely, RASP (Weiss et al., 2021)
and Tracr (Lindner et al., 2023) compile high-level pro-
grams into scratch-built toy Transformers without normal-
ization invariants, and weight-space virtual machines such
as Percepta’s CALM WASM VM (Tzamos & Percepta Re-
search, 2026) execute multi-thousand-token traces inside
dedicated VMs. Embedding exact digital logic directly into
general-purpose pretrained LMs without gradient optimiza-
tion or host routing—while maintaining noninferior accu-
racy on evaluated language benchmarks and mid-sentence
continuation—poses distinct theoretical, numerical, sys-
tems, and tokenization challenges.
Scope and Contributions. Building a 5-stage declarative
compiler atop reusable analytical primitives, we contribute:
1. Scale- and Architecture-Invariant Primitives (Sec-
tion 3, Appendix A): Single-layer impossibility for bias-
free GLU steps plus payload-linear truncation and kernel-
explicit IEEE 754 / TF32 bounds for Mellin-GLU
quadrature (Theorem 3.2), Indefinite-RoPE GQA and
memoryless GatedDeltaNet shifts (Theorem 3.3),
and axis-aligned width extension with arbitrary-tree tied-
GEMM bounds (Theorem 3.4).
2. Automated Multi-Digit ALU, TC0 DAGs, & Sparse
Sidecar (Section 4):
Automated 4–8 digit BPE
{+, −, ×} (1.07M–2.25M nnz) and reference 6-digit
patches in granite-4.2-3b and Qwen3.5-4B
(0/8 Attn), a factorized block-sparse sidecar (cutting
A100 VRAM 42%–44% and pairing INT8/INT4 WNL
with an FP32 sidecar; Table 3), declarative Boolean
(100%, N=1,728) & 5-bit Majority/Parity, triad BPE
alignment, and 42L Gemma 4 E4B audits.

2. Related Work
Compiled Circuits, CoNNs, and Subspace Injection.
RASP (Weiss et al., 2021) and Tracr (Lindner et al., 2023)
compile declarative programs into scratch Transformers as-
suming MLP biases, absolute positions, and unnormalized
wires—violated by RMSNorm (Zhang & Sennrich, 2019),
bias-free SwiGLU/GeGLU (Shazeer, 2020), RoPE (Su
et al., 2024), and GatedDeltaNet (Yang et al., 2025).
CoNNs (Weng et al., 2024) fuse external rule modules
via gradient-trained adapters, and Tracr-Injection (Vergara-
Browne & Soto, 2025) pairs subspace projection (P⊥=
Id −UU ⊤) with gradient distillation; we benchmark zero-
gradient P⊥and matched-(d + K) controls in Section 5
(Table 1). Sparse Weight Decomposition (Yan et al., 2026)
factorizes weights to extract existing circuits (including on
Qwen 3.5), complementing our forward < 0.06%-nonzero
synthesis.
Weight-Space VMs, Tokenization, and Tool Routers.
Looped Transformers (Giannou et al., 2023) and Percepta’s
CALM VM (Tzamos & Percepta Research, 2026) execute
traces in dedicated VMs rather than general pretrained LMs,
while concurrent Weight-Space Programming (Takehi et al.,
2026; Hu et al., 2026) heuristically perturbs ∼103 scalars.
Unlike gradient fine-tuning (Liu & Low, 2023; McLeish
et al., 2024) or host Python routers such as PAL (Gao
et al., 2023) and Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023), we com-
pile closed-form gates aligned with numeric BPE chunk-
ing (Singh & Strouse, 2024).

their composition in robotic manipulation. Mind tasks test history-based reasoning, Act tasks test precise and timely physical
execution, and Mind2Act tasks test their closed-loop composition, where action outcomes guide subsequent decisions. The

diagnosis loop then attributes the failed episodes of a system to Mind, Act or their composition and summarizes them in a
model profile card that points to its next improvement. Top: the three views of Mind2Act World. Middle: the application
domains, capability categories, tasks and diagnosis loop. Bottom: the open-source ecosystem, the evaluated models and the
continuously updated leaderboards.

A BST R ACT
Embodied intelligence aims to enable robots to perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability
and reliability, which requires three complementary capabilities: history-based cognitive reasoning, precise
and timely physical execution, and the composition of reasoning and execution through environmental
feedback. Yet existing benchmarks often evaluate reasoning and execution within the same tasks, or evaluate
them in separate assessments without examining their composition, thus providing limited insight into
whether failures arise from reasoning, physical execution, or their composition. To fill this gap, we introduce
Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark comprising 30 simulated manipulation tasks across five real-world
application domains. Each task features three difficulty levels and two scene settings (Clean and Random),
yielding 180 configurations. These tasks are organized into three views: Mind emphasizes decisions based
on historical observation, Act assesses precise and timely execution, and Mind2Act integrates reasoning and
physical execution in closed-loop tasks, where action outcomes guide subsequent decisions. By contrasting
performance across the three views, Mind2Act World reveals whether a system lacks a capability or fails to
compose the capabilities it already has. Furthermore, we develop a diagnosis harness that attributes the failed
episodes of three representative systems to Mind, Act, or their composition and summarizes each system in a
per-model report called a profile card. Our evaluation of multimodal agents, vision-language-action models
(VLAs), and world-action models (WAMs) shows that competence in a single view does not carry over to
Mind2Act tasks. Even the strongest agent succeeds in 52.7% of Mind and 39.0% of Act episodes but in only
12.0% of Mind2Act episodes. The strongest agent retains task state but struggles with sustained contact,
whereas end-to-end policies execute practiced motions but retain little task state. These findings point to the
composition of reasoning and execution through environmental feedback as the main open problem.
1 Introduction
“Knowledge is the beginning of action and action is the completion of knowledge.”
— Wang Yangming
The central ambition of embodied intelligence is to enable robots to perform complex physical tasks with
human-like adaptability and reliability. Studies of human sensorimotor control indicate that adaptive
and reliable manipulation involves reasoning over task-relevant information, executing physical actions
precisely, and adapting behavior through environmental feedback [1–3]. In the cooking task of Fig. 1,
a robot must remember which ingredient to add next, coordinate both arms to add the ingredient, and
switch the stove from heating to keep-warm mode based on temperature feedback. These requirements
motivate three capabilities. Mind decides what to do from earlier observations. Act produces the required
physical effect in time. Mind-Action Composition closes the loop, so that remembered information
guides each action and each physical outcome updates the next decision.
Recent embodied systems spanning multimodal agents [32], vision-language-action models (VLAs) [19,
20], world-action models (WAMs) [23, 26], and hybrid architectures [27, 28] have substantially advanced
robotic manipulation. However, their capabilities in Mind, Act, and Mind-Action Composition remain
poorly understood, which makes it difficult to identify capability bottlenecks and guide further development.
Two limitations of existing embodied benchmarks [4, 6–8, 12] explain why. First, conventional benchmarks
often assess cognitive reasoning and physical execution within the same tasks and report only whether a task
succeeds [4–6], so a failure cannot be traced to Mind or Act. Second, although recent benchmarks have
introduced finer-grained diagnostics and separate assessments of reasoning and physical execution [8, 11–
13], they rarely evaluate Mind-Action Composition, particularly whether physical outcomes can effectively
inform subsequent decisions. Closing this gap requires tasks that stress one capability while keeping the
others present but easy, a judgment of composition based on verified physical outcomes, and a comparison
of systems with different action interfaces and inference speeds on equal terms.
To this end, we introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark for Mind, Act, and Mind-Action
Composition in robotic manipulation (Fig. 1). Its 30 tasks come from five real-world application domains
and are organized into three views of ten tasks each, covering 12 capability categories. Each view
emphasizes one demand by design. Mind tasks keep physical operations simple, Act tasks state the
Research preprint
3
mmlab@SIGS
required operation explicitly, and Mind2Act tasks chain dependent operations so that each physical
outcome decides what comes next. Success is judged from physical predicates on the environment, and the
evaluator records stages and events within each episode. Each task has three difficulty levels that raise its
demands while keeping the objective fixed. Each level runs in a Clean and a Random scene, which share
the same instance but differ in clutter, materials and lighting (180 configurations in total). Agents and
end-to-end policies share the same tasks, information contract and evaluator, and 4,500 demonstrations
(75.8 hours) are provided for fine-tuning end-to-end policies. A diagnosis harness combines rule-based
analysis of the evaluator’s stage and event records with an LLM judge to attribute each failed episode of
three representative systems to Mind, Act, or their composition. It summarizes each of these systems
in a per-model report called a model profile card (Fig. 6; Appendix E.4).
Our evaluation on Mind2Act World reveals a clear pattern. Existing architectures are uneven across
Mind and Act, yet all struggle with Mind-Action Composition. The strongest agent retains task state
well but struggles to sustain contact, and its timed successes are measured with a simulator that pauses
during inference. End-to-end policies respond within a fraction of a second and execute practiced motions,
but retain little task state, and the memory of the VLAs largely disappears under scene randomization.
Notably, on Mind2Act, the strongest system succeeds in only 12.0% of episodes, far below its 52.7%
on Mind and 39.0% on Act, and no end-to-end policy exceeds 3.6%. Competence in either capability
therefore does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks.
The contributions of this work are summarized as follows:
• We introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark comprising 30 manipulation tasks grounded
in real-world requirements. Organized into three views, it systematically evaluates Mind, Act, and
Mind-Action Composition.
• We develop a diagnosis harness that combines rule-based analysis with an LLM judge to identify
the stage at which each failed episode first breaks down and to attribute the failure to Mind, Act,
or Mind-Action Composition. The harness also summarizes three representative models in model
profile cards of their failure patterns and behavioral tendencies.
• We evaluate representative multimodal agents, VLAs, and WAMs on shared tasks and scoring, with
separate leaderboards for agents and end-to-end policies. Our results show that systems differ in which
of Mind and Act is weaker, and that all of them struggle with Mind-Action Composition.
2 Related Work
2.1 Embodied Policies and Agents
Robot manipulation policies have evolved from imitation learning [15–17] to large-scale generalist policies.
Vision-language-action models such as OpenVLA [19], 𝜋0.5 [20], RDT2 [21] and G0.5 [22] improve
instruction following and cross-task transfer, while world-action models such as LDA-1B [24], Motus [25]
and DreamZero [26] couple predictive modeling with control. Agent-based systems take a different route,
turning language-model reasoning into executable programs [32] and feeding success detection back into
planning [67, 68]. Recent work also addresses memory-augmented manipulation [29, 30, 55], dynamic
manipulation [61, 62], and force- or tactile-aware control [65, 66].
Despite this progress, each line is usually evaluated where only its own demand is hard: memory methods
on tasks with simple execution, dynamic and contact-aware controllers on tasks whose target is given,
and agents on tasks where perceiving the outcome is assumed. In practice, a failure may come from
holding the wrong task state, missing the intended physical effect, or continuing without checking that
the effect occurred. Mind2Act World therefore makes all three demands hard within the same tasks
and evaluates agents, VLAs and WAMs on them.

Abstract
Frontier text-to-image (T2I) foundation models predominantly rely on multi-billion parameter
Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) pretrained across massive compute clusters, creating an accessibility
barrier for academic laboratories. When training DiTs from scratch on single consumer GPUs
(e.g., an NVIDIA RTX 4090 with 24 GB VRAM), practitioners encounter three primary bottlenecks:
quadratic attention sequence costs, Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation graph breaks induced by variable
aspect-ratio bucketing, and an autoencoder throughput wall where frozen Variational Autoencoder
(VAE) operations dominate step latency. In this work, we introduce Asuka-FM, an end-to-end system
and architectural framework demonstrating that competitive dual-stream DiTs (∼206M parameters)
can be pretrained from scratch on a single consumer GPU in ∼160 GPU hours for under $55.
Asuka-FM integrates four core designs: (i) an AdaLN-free dual-stream DiT backbone reducing
parameter count; (ii) structured sequence sparsification via Sparse-Dense Residual Fusion (SPRINT)
to cut attention FLOPs by over 50%; (iii) continuous aspect-normalized Rotary Position Embeddings
(RoPE) coupled with shifted square crop training, guaranteeing static tensor shapes while unlocking
zero-shot virtual camera control; and (iv) a pixel adaptation phase utilizing a lightweight (10M
parameter) Patch Detailer Head operating under velocity regression (v-prediction). Evaluated on
open-domain benchmarks without benchmark-specific fine-tuning, Asuka-FM achieves GenEval
0.588 / DPG 78.96 scores at 256px and GenEval 0.609 / DPG 78.51 scores at 512px, setting a new
Pareto-optimal efficiency standard for democratic foundation modeling.
1
arXiv:2611.26437v1  [cs.CV]  19 Nov 2026
Figure 2: High-fidelity zero-shot visual synthesis from scratch on a single consumer GPU. Curated open-
domain samples synthesized by Asuka-FM (206M backbone) following two-stage pretraining (2562 →5122) on a
single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU in 149.0 hours ($49.17).
2
1
Introduction
The emergence of Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) [34] trained via flow matching [27] has established a
new state of the art in high-fidelity text-to-image (T2I) synthesis. However, state-of-the-art models, such
as FLUX.1 (12B) [3], SD3 (8B) [16], and Qwen-Image (20B) [45], have scaled parameter counts and
training datasets to regimes that require industrial-scale data centers. This trajectory has widened the
accessibility gap, preventing independent researchers and academic groups with limited resources from
training generative models from scratch.
When attempting to pretrain generative diffusion models under compute-constrained environments
(e.g., a single workstation with an NVIDIA RTX 4090 with 24 GB GDDR6X), the standard pretraining
paradigm encounters three fundamental systems bottlenecks:
• (i) Quadratic Attention Sequence Redundancy: Standard homogeneous DiTs allocate identical
full-token sequence lengths across every transformer block. However, recent representational
analyses [33] reveal that early layers primarily capture local high-frequency textures, whereas deep
middle blocks model global macro-semantics. Processing full-length sequences across deep layers
wastes limited floating-point operations (FLOPs) on redundant spatial details, slowing convergence.
• (ii) Just-In-Time (JIT) Compilation Graph Breaks vs. Aspect-Ratio Bucketing: Real-world
images feature diverse aspect ratios. Conventional pipelines handle this via dynamic aspect-ratio
bucketing, grouping images of varying shapes into specialized mini-batches. Under modern
tracing and JIT compiler runtimes (e.g., torch.compile with TorchInductor), changing spatial
dimensions dynamically triggers continuous kernel recompilations, invalidates static CUDA graphs,
and severely degrades actual Model FLOPs Utilization (MFUact).
• (iii) The Autoencoder Throughput Wall: In conventional Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) [36],
an autoencoder (such as the FLUX.2 VAE [4]) compresses images into a regularized latent space.
At high resolutions (1024 × 1024), storing pre-computed 32-channel float16 latents for hundreds
of thousands of images requires multiple terabytes of high-speed storage, exceeding consumer
NVMe capacities. Consequently, latents must be computed on-the-fly. On consumer silicon during
the training stage, the frozen VAE forward pass consumes ≈60% of total wall-time, whereas
a compiled 200M DiT forward-backward pass requires only ≈35% (Figure 7 in Appendix A).
Furthermore, at inference, VAE decoding accounts for over 70% of wall-clock latency under
few-step regimes, creating a computational bottleneck for downstream reinforcement learning (e.g.,
Flow-GRPO [28]) and distillation.
To address these challenges, we introduce Asuka-FM, an end-to-end system and architectural co-
design framework proving that a competitive ∼206M-parameter Dual-Stream DiT can be pretrained
from scratch on a single desktop GPU in ∼160 GPU hours for under $551. As showcased in Figure 2,
our open-domain model achieves sharp textural coherence, rich lighting, and diverse multi-concept
synthesis (additional domain-specialized anime samples are shown in Figure 19 in Appendix H). To
achieve this efficiency, we propose a multi-stage training roadmap (Figure 3) coupling structured sequence
sparsification, canvas scaling, and latent-to-pixel adaptation. Our primary contributions are:
• System-Architectural Pretraining Recipe: We establish an engineering pipeline integrating
in-RAM latent caching for low-resolution stages, network streaming for intermediate scales, and
FlashAttention-2 kernel fusion within a fully static torch.compile execution graph. This setup
sustains an average 75.6% physical MFUact on a single consumer RTX 4090 GPU.
• High-Efficiency Dual-Stream Architecture: We couple an AdaLN-free Dual-Stream DiT back-
bone with three synergistic mechanisms: (i) SPRINT sequence sparsification [33], routing 75%-
sparse token sequences through 9 heavy middle blocks to slash attention FLOPs by over 50%;

Figure 3: Comprehensive multi-stage training roadmap of Asuka-FM. Pretraining advances through
two latent resolution tiers (2562 →5122) coupling 75% SPRINT sequence sparsification with full-
token dense refinement and Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD). Stage 3 transitions the converged 512px
foundation prior to pixel space using a 10M convolutional Patch Detailer Head (PDH) trained under
native v-prediction across synthetic and real datasets, permanently removing the VAE decode barrier
during few-step inference.
(ii) Continuous Aspect-Normalized RoPE and shifted square cropping [44, 47], supported by
a mathematical derivation proving that uncalibrated continuous RoPE undergoes spatial phase
collapse, and a full-spectrum frequency calibration that ensures isotropic decay while conferring
zero-shot virtual camera control; and (iii) Decoupled Latent-to-Pixel Adaptation, which attaches a
lightweight (10M parameter) convolutional Patch Detailer Head (PDH) [10] under native velocity
regression (v-prediction) to eliminate the online VAE wall.
• Empirical Ablations and Profiling with Systems Analysis: We discover an Amortization Asym-
metry: while pixel adaptation eliminates the online VAE encoding wall during pretraining, its
recurrent convolutional evaluation makes standard multi-step sampling (N ≥13) slower than latent
ODE integration, delivering superior efficiency exclusively in few-step regimes (N ≤8, yielding
up to 3.34× speedups at N = 1 step).
• Open-Domain Validation: Trained on a balanced 625K multi-source open corpus without
benchmark-specific fine-tuning (avoiding BLIP3o-60K overfitting), Asuka-FM achieves a GenEval
score of 0.588 and DPG-Bench score of 78.96 at 256px (68h), converging to 0.609 GenEval and
78.51 DPG-Bench at 512px (81h).
2
Related Work
Diffusion Transformers and Conditioning Paradigms. The transition from U-Nets to Diffusion
Transformers (DiTs) [34] established transformers as the standard generative backbone. Multi-Modal
DiTs (MMDiT) in SD3 [16], FLUX.1 [3] utilize separate weights per modality with shared self-attention,
while single-stream models (Lumina-T2X [18], Z-Image [40]) concatenate modalities directly. To
eliminate parameter overhead from per-block Adaptive Layer Normalization (AdaLN-Zero), DiT-Air [6]
shared AdaLN parameters globally. While Peebles & Xie [34] initially explored concatenating class
tokens in single-stream models, i1 [49] showed that explicit modulation can be entirely omitted when
stabilized by Sandwich RMSNorm [15] and SwiGLU activations [38]. Asuka-FM adopts this principle
4
by replacing AdaLN with in-context temporal conditioning, prepending a continuous sinusoidal timestep
token directly to the multimodal sequence.
Sequence Sparsification and Token Dropping. Because self-attention complexity scales as O(N2)
with sequence length N, token dropping provides significant acceleration. MaskDiT [50] and MDTv2 [19]
introduced masked autoencoding objectives, while TREAD [25] bypassed subsets of tokens through inner
layers. SPRINT [33] demonstrated that structural specialization—combining a dense shallow encoder
(fθ), a 75%-sparse middle path (gθ), and a dense decoder (hθ) fused via linear skips—permits aggressive
token dropping without fidelity loss. We extend SPRINT to open-domain multimodal conditioning and
evaluate its scaling limits.
Looped Transformers: Parameter-Efficient Depth Scaling. Looped transformers [12, 14, 20]
achieve parameter efficiency by repeatedly executing a shared group of middle transformer blocks. In
Looped-DiT [12], cycling through shared blocks keeps weights resident in on-chip SRAM and L2
cache, mitigating memory bandwidth bottlenecks. While looped models compress parameter count
across recurrent depth, Asuka-FM focuses on sequence-length compression via SPRINT, providing
complementary architectural paths toward efficient pretraining.
Micro-Budget Foundation Modeling and Pixel Diffusion. Micro-budget training has gained
significant attention. Stretching Each Dollar [37] demonstrated T2I pretraining from scratch for $1,890
on 8× H100s using mixture-of-experts and deferred masking. Concurrently, HDM [47] trained a 343M
model for $535–620 on 4× RTX 5090 GPUs using shifted square cropping and aspect-normalized
RoPE with learnable frequency parameters. In pixel-space diffusion, early works suffered from slow
convergence [8, 22]. JiT [26] and Jiang et al. [24] advocated clean data prediction (x0-prediction), but
Iris-3B [5] showed that velocity regression (v-prediction) provides equal stability. DiP [10] introduced
the Patch Detailer Head (PDH) to bridge latent efficiency with pixel generation. Asuka-FM synthesizes
these insights into an integrated low-cost training pipeline.
3
Preliminaries
3.1
Continuous Normalizing Flows and Flow Matching
We formulate image generation through Continuous Normalizing Flows (CNF) and Conditional Flow
Matching (CFM) [27, 29]. Let x0 ∼p0(x) denote an empirical sample from data distribution p0(x) on
a low-dimensional manifold M ⊂Rddata of ambient dimension ddata, and let x1 ∼p1(x) = N(0, I)
denote noise from a standard Gaussian prior with zero mean 0 and identity covariance I. Under the
optimal-transport linear probability path across continuous time t ∈[0, 1], intermediate noisy states xt
are constructed via:
xt = (1 −t)x0 + tx1,
t ∈[0, 1].
(1)
Differentiating Eq. (1) yields the conditional velocity field ut(xt | x0, x1) = x1 −x0. A neural vector
field regressor vθ(xt, t, c), conditioned on prompt context c, is trained via the simulation-free objective:
LCFM(θ) = Et,x0,x1

2

(2)
At inference, novel samples are generated by drawing x1 ∼N(0, I) and integrating the probability flow
ODE: dxt = vθ(xt, t, c) dt from t = 1 to t = 0.
3.2
Latent Diffusion and Dual-Stream Tokenization
Following the Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) framework [36], an autoencoder compresses raw pixel
images of target training resolution H0 × W0 (e.g., H0 = W0 = 256) into a latent space Z = RC×H×W
with C channels and spatial dimensions H × W via spatial downsampling factor f = H0/H = W0/W
(e.g., f = 8, C = 32 for the FLUX.2 VAE). Following Diffusion Transformers (DiT) [34], noisy latent
tensors zt ∈RC×H×W at timestep t are divided into non-overlapping spatial patches of size p × p (giving
5
effective pixel patch size P = f · p = 16), producing a flattened sequence of image tokens zimg ∈RN×D,
where N = (H/p)(W/p) is the image token count and D = 768 is the transformer hidden dimension.
In Dual-Stream DiTs [16], image tokens zimg and text tokens ctext ∈RLtext×D (of text sequence
length Ltext) are mapped through dedicated linear projections into image and context queries, keys, and
values (Qimg, Kimg, Vimg and Qctx, Kctx, Vctx) while sharing joint attention blocks. These projections are
concatenated along the token sequence dimension (∥) to form the joint matrices Q, K, V :
Q = [Qimg ∥Qctx], K = [Kimg ∥Kctx], V = [Vimg ∥Vctx].
(3)
Spatial layout is anchored via 2D axial Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) [39], which apply a block-
diagonal rotation matrix Rp parameterized by continuous coordinates p = (y, x) to yield rotated image
queries and keys ˜Qimg = RpQimg and ˜Kimg = RpKimg. Here, (y, x) denotes the vertical and horizontal
center coordinates of each patch in matrix row-major convention.
3.3
Timestep Sampling and Time-SNR Shifting
To counteract signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) compression when scaling image resolution, we introduce
a resolution-dependent shift factor sshift ∈{1.0, 2.0} and sample an unconstrained log-odds variable
s ∼N(µ, σ2
s) from a normal distribution with mean µ = −ln(sshift) and standard deviation σs, mapping
it to t = sigmoid(s) [16]. We then compute the shifted timestep tshifted = (t · sshift)/[1 + (sshift −1)t] for
Eq. (1), biasing sampling toward the noise-dominant regime (t →1).
4
Asuka-FM Framework
Asuka-FM establishes an end-to-end system and architectural framework designed to train high-capacity
Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) from scratch within limited consumer-compute budgets. Our work extends
the Micro-Budget Foundation Modeling research to an even more accessible boundary: pretraining a
206M Dual-Stream DiT on a single consumer workstation equipped with an RTX 4090 GPU in 161.2
hours. Furthermore, the random square crops training [44] and the multi-captioning strategy of i1 [49]
demonstrate that a capable foundation model can be trained from scratch on fewer than one million
images.
Rather than relying on massive parameter scaling or distributed multi-node infrastructure, the frame-
work co-designs the model architecture, memory hierarchy, and training curriculum around four comple-
mentary pillars:
1. Minimalist Dual-Stream Backbone (Section 4.1): Completely eliminates per-block modulation
overhead reducing compute and parameters.
2. Structured Sequence Sparsification via SPRINT (Section 4.2): Reduces attention FLOPs by
over 50% while providing strong regularization.
3. Continuous Aspect-Normalized RoPE & Shifted Cropping (Section 4.3): Prevents rotary phase
collapse, enforces static tensor shapes to eliminate JIT compilation breaks, and provides zero-shot
virtual camera controls (pan and zoom).
4. Decoupled Latent-to-Pixel Adaptation (Section 4.5): Transfers converged latent priors directly
into raw pixel space, permanently bypassing the autoencoder decoding latency wall during down-
stream inference and reinforcement learning rollouts.
4.1
Minimalist Conditioning and Dual-Stream Backbone
Asuka-FM employs a 206M-parameter Dual-Stream DiT backbone optimized for single-GPU execution
(Table 1). Standard AdaLN-Zero requires projecting conditioning embeddings into six independent

Seer: Guiding Small Deep-Research Agents with Shared Decision Models
Yuhao Zhou1, Yang Zhou1, Yuanxi Li2, Jindi Lv1, Dan Si3, Qing Ye1, Jiancheng Lv1*
1Sichuan University
2University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign
3Lenovo Group Limited
Abstract
Deep-research agents repeatedly decide what to search, read,
and verify, often using large cloud-hosted language models
for action proposal. However, privacy and local control moti-
vate running agents on users’ devices, where limited memory
and compute favor smaller models and complicate on-device
training. Yet inference-time guidance faces three obstacles:
exploring alternatives through real execution adds tool calls,
prompted self-evaluation is bounded by the agent’s judgment,
and model-specific guidance risks repeated adaptation costs.
We introduce Seer, an inference-time framework providing
local guidance that separates the agent’s action proposal
from learned consequence prediction and value estimation.
From a shared corpus of real research trajectories, we train
two models: a tool-response simulator on observed call–
response pairs and a value estimator on histories labeled
with discounted terminal correctness. The simulator and es-
timator are trained offline and reused across agents without
further training. Moreover, Seer executes only the selected
action and adds only real tool responses to the commit-
ted history, avoiding tool calls on discarded candidates at
additional inference cost. Across multiple deep-research
benchmarks, Seer substantially improves agent performance
for different language models. For instance, GAIA accu-
racy rises from 13.6% to 41.7% for Qwen3.5-4B and from
22.3% to 50.5% for Qwen3.5-9B. Furthermore, our analy-
ses suggest that broader candidate coverage can compen-
sate for imperfect simulation, while prediction and scoring
errors limit the benefits of wider imagined search. These
findings highlight the potential of reusable models for pre-
diction and evaluation to strengthen small research agents
through extra local computation without the real execution
of the discarded candidates.
1. Introduction
Deep-research agents use language models to decide what to
search, read, and verify, integrating evidence across sources
to answer complex questions [64]. In practice, OpenAI
Deep Research [43] and Gemini Deep Research [11] offer
*Corresponding author: Jiancheng Lv.
multi-step web investigation and source-linked reports, while
open efforts such as DeepResearcher [65] and Tongyi Deep-
Research [53] advance research on sustained information
seeking. Meanwhile, benchmarks from GAIA’s real-world
reasoning and tool-use questions [39] to BrowseComp’s chal-
lenging web information-seeking tasks [58] evaluate agents’
ability to gather and integrate evidence.
For users applying these capabilities to sensitive tasks,
keeping an agent’s reasoning and decision-making on-device
offers greater local control, a motivation reflected in privacy-
oriented personal assistants [2]. However, deploying these
agents on users’ devices requires managing both local com-
putational resources and external tool-use costs. Memory
and compute constraints favor smaller language models [4],
while tool-call fees make repeated searches and page re-
trievals an additional deployment expense [34].
Under these constraints, training small models specifi-
cally for research is a natural way to improve agent perfor-
mance. However, collecting training data and optimizing
each model require additional resources, making repeated
adaptation costly for resource-constrained deployments. In-
stead, inference-time methods offer an alternative by improv-
ing agent decisions without updating the deployed model.
Specifically, output-level refinement [56, 57, 63] selects
or revises completed answers but cannot redirect actions
already executed. Decision-level evaluation [28, 59, 60, 66]
guides intermediate choices through search or learned critics,
but evaluating branches through real execution incurs tool
costs even for discarded candidates. Model-based looka-
head [5, 21, 24] reduces this overhead by evaluating pre-
dicted consequences before execution. To avoid shifting
adaptation costs to supporting components, such guidance
should transfer across agent models without retraining. Yet
approaches relying on the agent’s model for prompted pre-
diction and scoring remain bounded by its capabilities [55].
Figure 1 summarizes these limitations. The challenge is
therefore to provide reusable guidance that strengthens small
agents without model-specific retraining or the real execu-
tion of discarded candidates.
We introduce Seer, an inference-time framework provid-
ing local guidance in deep research. Our key idea is to decou-
ple action proposal from tool-response prediction and value

contributions are threefold.

and history-level value estimation across agents. This de-

discarded candidates.
2. We develop a shared training pipeline that collects real
trajectories across agents and tasks through Monte Carlo

training corpus provides complementary supervision: ob-

the value estimator.
3. Experiments with different models across extensive

agents, with benefits extending to larger-model settings.
Ablations and analyses reveal the trade-off between can-

2. Related Work
Research agents and tool use.
Research agents cou-
ple a language model’s parametric knowledge with infor-
mation acquired through tools: WebGPT [41] combines
browser-assisted question answering with human feedback,
ReAct [62] interleaves reasoning with actions, and Tool-
former [48] learns when to invoke APIs from self-supervised
examples. Within this setting, the task determines which
observations matter: an agent must judge which query or
goal-conditioned page visit is likely to reveal useful evi-
dence, which creates two deployment costs—the local com-
pute to run the model and the external tool calls to gather
evidence. Quantization [32], context management [55], and
tool budgeting [34] address deployment costs, while compact
research agents [6, 30, 54] target research capability. Distil-
lation [1, 20] and reinforcement learning [27, 65] strengthen
the agent’s model but require optimization for each adapted
model. Seer instead trains reusable decision models, com-
plementing these efficiency-oriented approaches without up-
dating or retraining the deployed agent.
Inference-time guidance. Guidance can act on com-
pleted outputs or intervene at intermediate decisions, and the
distinction matters because producing a candidate answer
may already consume substantial tool calls. Output-level
methods select or revise solutions: self-consistency [57]
aggregates independently sampled reasoning paths, Self-
Refine [38] alternates generation with feedback, and learned
verifiers [12] score candidates, with asymmetric verifica-
tion [63] allocating a modest verification budget to select
2
among expensive search trajectories. These methods cannot
recover tool calls already spent on discarded trajectories,
as our BoN@4 and AV@4 baselines illustrate. Decision-
level methods intervene earlier: Tree of Thoughts [61] ex-
plores intermediate reasoning states with self-evaluation,
Reflexion [50] uses verbal feedback from earlier attempts,
LATS [66] and web-agent tree search [28] combine search
with environmental feedback, and AgentRM [59] learns
a transferable reward model. Process-supervision evalua-
tors [9, 31, 36, 60] further supply learned ranking signals,
but branches explored through real interaction still incur tool
calls even when discarded, and prompted self-evaluation
depends on the agent’s judgment.
Model-based lookahead. A learned or prompted world
model can instead predict aspects of a candidate’s outcome
before execution. Dyna [52] integrates real experience with
model-based planning, MuZero [49] learns latent dynamics
together with planning-relevant predictions, and Dreamer-
style agents [23, 26] train behavior from imagined rollouts;
for language agents, DreamGym [8] and DynaWeb [14] use
predicted experience to train the agent itself. At inference
time, RAP [24] repurposes an LLM as a world model within
tree search, while WMA [5] and WebDreamer [21] learn
transition predictions for web navigation; SiRA [13] plans
with natural-language belief states, and MCP-Cosmos [18]
