LLM COT FOR Q-MATRIX
2
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) can generate Q-matrices for diagnostic classification models that
approximate expert specifications, but evaluations have focused on the final matrices, leaving
the basis of individual item–attribute assignments unexamined. This opacity limits the respon-
sible use of AI in measurement. We propose Reasoning-Trace Analysis (RTA), a framework
in which an LLM generates attribute-labeled reasoning steps through chain-of-thought (CoT)
prompting and these steps are analyzed to reconstruct, compare, and inspect each assignment.
RTA is intended to supplement expert review and empirical validation. In a simulation study
with perturbed fraction subtraction items, four LLMs recovered the required attributes and with-
held attributes the items did not require. In an empirical study with 11 fraction subtraction items,
responses from 536 examinees, four LLMs, up to three temperatures, and 100 replications per
condition, CoT-derived Q-matrices overlapped substantially with the reference Q-matrix (mean
overlap .809) but less than directly generated Q-matrices (.877), and they varied more across
replications. Inspection of the traces linked disagreements to item-type coding, labeling rules,
and how operations were expressed as steps. Q-matrices with similar overlap differed in fit to
examinee responses. RTA provides inspectable evidence that matrix-level agreement and fit do
not.
Keywords: Q-matrix, LLM, Chain-of-Thought, Cognitive Diagnosis, Psychometrics
LLM COT FOR Q-MATRIX
3
Reasoning-Trace Analysis Using Large Language Models for Interpretable Q-Matrix
Construction
Diagnostic classification models (DCMs), also called cognitive diagnostic models
(CDMs), are confirmatory latent class models that classify examinees into discrete mastery
profiles over predefined attributes. The validity and reliability of their classifications depend on a
well-specified Q-matrix that links each item to the attributes it is intended to measure. Q-matrices
are typically specified through expert judgment, which is effortful and largely subjective, and
then verified and revised with examinee responses and other evidence. Large language models
(LLMs) offer a potential way to construct Q-matrices more efficiently, and recent studies suggest
that LLMs acting as experts can generate Q-matrices that approximate human expert references
and, under some conditions, achieve competitive model fit (Aşiret & Ömür Sünbül, 2025; Xue &
Appleton, 2026; Zhang & Rao, 2026). Whether a Q-matrix is specified by experts or generated by
an LLM, evaluating its validity requires access to the reasoning behind individual item–attribute
assignments. Yet expert reasoning is rarely documented in an inspectable form, and evaluations
of LLM-generated Q-matrices mostly focus on the final matrices and their empirical performance.
Where a rationale is requested, it accompanies the Q-vector rather than producing it (Zhang &
Rao, 2026). In both cases, potential misspecifications remain difficult to detect, replicate, or
contest. For LLM-generated Q-matrices, this opacity poses a threat to the responsible use of
AI in measurement, which calls for AI-supported decisions to be transparent, explainable, and
accountable (Johnson, 2025).
Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting can elicit intermediate reasoning steps before a final
answer (Wei et al., 2022). In Q-matrix construction, these traces provide observable material
for examining how a model connects an item’s solution process to proposed cognitive attributes.
A related precedent is the application of Schoenfeld’s Episode Theory, originally developed for
human mathematical problem-solving, to the analysis of reasoning traces from large reasoning
models (M. Li, Zhang, et al., 2025). However, stated reasoning may not reflect the factors driving
a model’s predictions (Lanham et al., 2023; Turpin et al., 2023). Thus, whether elicited traces can
LLM COT FOR Q-MATRIX
4
provide a sound basis for evaluating the reasoning underlying individual item–attribute assign-
ments remains an open question.
To address this question, we propose Reasoning-Trace Analysis (RTA), a framework that
treats an elicited trace as a claim to be examined against external criteria rather than as direct evi-
dence of the model’s reasoning. Here, we apply RTA to Q-matrix construction. In RTA, an LLM
first generates reasoning steps labeled with the attributes they exercise through CoT prompting,
and these labeled steps are then analyzed to reconstruct and examine each item–attribute assign-
ment. This extends Q-matrix evaluation beyond the final matrix to the support for individual
item–attribute assignments. RTA is intended to supplement existing Q-matrix specification by
providing an initial Q-matrix with an inspectable basis for each assignment that remains subject
to expert review and empirical validation (Johnson, 2025). We evaluate the performance and use-
fulness of RTA through a simulation study and an empirical study. The following sections review
the relevant background, describe RTA, and state the research questions before reporting the two
studies.
Background
Q-Matrix Construction by Human Experts and LLMs
DCMs support fine-grained skill profiling in domains ranging from mathematics (Chen et
al., 2017) and reading (H. Li & Suen, 2013) to clinical and affective constructs (Iza et al., 2014;
Rupp et al., 2010). Q-matrix construction in DCMs requires analysts to define the relevant at-
tributes, justify item–attribute links, and evaluate the proposed matrix against substantive and
empirical evidence (Buck et al., 1998; Tatsuoka, 1983). Existing procedures often rely on think-
aloud protocols, expert ratings, committee deliberation, and response-data validation (H. Li &
Suen, 2013). These procedures remain labor-intensive, time-consuming, and costly, and misspec-
ified entries can distort item parameter estimates and examinee classification (Rupp & Templin,
2008).
When response data are available, empirical validation methods can identify item–
LLM COT FOR Q-MATRIX
5
attribute assignments whose modification may improve fit. Two such methods are the proportion
of variance accounted for (PVAF) method (de la Torre & Chiu, 2016) and the Hull method
(Nájera et al., 2021). Both de la Torre and Chiu (2016) and Culpepper (2019) illustrated their
methods with the fraction subtraction data from which the present items are drawn. These
methods require response data, and their suggestions still call for expert review before adoption
(Nájera et al., 2021).
LLM applications in assessment include scoring open-ended responses (Lee et al., 2024;
Mendonça et al., 2025), generating items (Chan et al., 2025), modeling item difficulty (M. Li,
Jiao, et al., 2025), and producing synthetic respondents for item calibration (Liu et al., 2025). Re-
cent LLM-based Q-matrix studies suggest that LLMs can approximate matrices built by human
experts at the overall matrix level. Aşiret and Ömür Sünbül (2025) showed that ChatGPT-4o can
draft Q-matrices directly that match human expert references on most entries. They evaluated the
generated Q-matrices using attribute-level and attribute-vector overlap rates, empirical Q-matrix
validation, Q-matrix recovery rates, and CDM model-fit indices. The study by Xue and Apple-
ton (2026) showed that AI-generated Q-matrices can approximate human expert baselines with
competitive model fit. Their evaluation used chatbot–human matching accuracy, Q-matrix den-
sity, classification discrepancies, and model-fit statistics across model and prompting conditions.
Fan et al. (2026) compared Q-matrices generated by several general-purpose LLMs for a reading
comprehension test with the validated Q-matrix of H. Li and Suen (2013) and found substantial
variation in agreement across models, with lower agreement for newer model versions. Zhang
and Rao (2026) combined an LLM-proposed Q-matrix with response-based refinement under the
deterministic inputs, noisy “and” gate (DINA) model and asked the LLM for a brief rationale for
each Q-vector, which experts then rated.
The metrics used in these studies show whether the final generated Q-matrix resembles a
human expert matrix or yields acceptable model-data fit. However, they do not show how each
item–attribute assignment is inferred or whether a disagreement reflects model error, prompt
sensitivity, or an alternative problem-solving path. From a measurement perspective, validity
LLM COT FOR Q-MATRIX
6
evidence based on the response processes behind these matrices is therefore missing, which limits
the responsible use of AI in measurement. Moreover, the expert reference is itself a specification
rather than a ground truth, so fit to examinee responses must be examined alongside agreement
with it. In addition, repeated sampling of the same prompt yields different traces and sometimes
different answers, so aggregation across generations has become a common way to summarize
what a model produces (Wang et al., 2023). For Q-matrix construction, Kim (2026) found that re-
generating a Q-matrix with the same model at the same temperature changed the mastery profiles
assigned to many examinees, and that majority voting across runs did not remove this instability.
Responsible AI in Assessment
Johnson (2025) described responsible AI for measurement as the use of AI to improve
how human capabilities are measured while protecting individual rights. Among its principles
are transparency, explainability, and accountability, together with the requirement that infer-
ences made by AI be valid for their intended use. The same report places final authority over
AI-supported judgments with human educators, an approach described as human-in-the-loop.
Bulut et al. (2024) similarly identified validity, reliability, transparency, and fairness among the
central ethical concerns raised by AI in educational measurement. In Q-matrix construction, an
LLM acting as an expert makes decisions that determine what a diagnostic assessment measures.
If the basis of these decisions cannot be inspected, the validity of the resulting Q-matrix cannot
be fully examined, and human reviewers have little on which to base their judgment.
Reasoning Traces From LLMs
One directly observable form of evidence for LLM reasoning is CoT output. CoT pro-
duces observable intermediate reasoning steps, either by supplying worked examples (Wei et al.,
2022) or by instructing the model to reason step by step without examples (Kojima et al., 2022).
Compared with direct prompting, CoT often provides modest average gains in accuracy and can
produce less stable answers in some settings (Meincke et al., 2025).
LLM COT FOR Q-MATRIX
7
LLM-generated reasoning can be conceptualized as a sequence of problem-solving
episodes rather than as a single final output. Drawing on Schoenfeld’s Episode Theory, which
was originally developed to characterize human mathematical problem solving, M. Li, Zhang, et
al. (2025) analyzed the output of reasoning models using six episode types: Read, Analyze, Plan,
Implement, Explore, and Verify. Their analysis indicated that elicited reasoning traces can exhibit
episode-level structures that resemble categories used to describe human problem solving. This
correspondence does not establish that LLMs reason like humans, but it provides a conceptual
basis for examining how generated steps align with human-defined cognitive skills.
Beyond classifying the forms of reasoning expressed in model output, prior work has
examined the mechanisms by which transformer models solve mathematical problems. Hu et
al. (2024) distinguished case-based reasoning from rule-based reasoning. In their framework,
case-based reasoning solves a new problem by retrieving or matching similar cases encountered
during training, whereas rule-based reasoning applies an abstract rule to new problems. Across
intervention experiments on five mathematical tasks, the authors found that the tested transformer
models relied primarily on case-based reasoning, even when scratchpads were used. This finding
indicates that a correct answer may be reached without applying the intended rule.
Consequently, an elicited reasoning trace is not, by itself, evidence that the stated rea-
soning is correct, faithful, or aligned with the intended cognitive attributes. The extent to which
a final answer depends on the stated steps varies across tasks and model sizes (Lanham et al.,
2023), and some apparent reasoning is decorative rather than load-bearing (Zhao et al., 2025).
It therefore remains unclear whether elicited traces recover the attributes an item requires, even
when those attributes are known in advance.
Verbal Reports and Response-Process Evidence
RTA draws its logic from the analysis of human verbal reports. Protocol analysis treats
concurrent verbal reports as data on the cognitive processes used in a task and specifies condi-
tions under which such reports are valid and complete (Ericsson & Simon, 1993). In achievement
LLM COT FOR Q-MATRIX
8
testing, what an examinee says while solving an item is coded against external criteria rather
than accepted as a transparent record of cognition (Leighton, 2004), and Leighton (2017) dis-
tinguished think-aloud interviews for problem solving from cognitive laboratory interviews for
comprehension. The Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (American Educa-
tional Research Association et al., 2014) list response processes as a source of validity evidence,
and Padilla and Benítez (2014) reviewed the methods available for obtaining it. These works
concern human examinees. RTA applies the same logic to the reasoning steps of an LLM.
Overview of Reasoning-Trace Analysis
This section describes the proposed RTA framework, which will be evaluated in the sim-
ulation and empirical studies. RTA consists of two components: trace generation (Step 0), in
which an LLM produces attribute-labeled reasoning traces through CoT prompting, and a four-
step analysis of these traces against external criteria (see Figure 1). The external criteria are a
set of expert-defined attributes and a reference Q-matrix that specifies the attributes each item is
expected to require.
LLM COT FOR Q-MATRIX
9
Figure 1
Reasoning-Trace Analysis Framework
Note. Expert-defined examples are optional. Expert review and empirical validation (dashed box)
lie outside RTA.
Trace Generation
Trace generation is inspired by the rule-following principle of Rule-Following Fine-
Tuning (RFFT), proposed by Hu et al. (2024). RFFT trains transformer models to recite and
apply explicit rules step by step and improved length generalization in their addition experiments.
RTA adapts this principle at inference time without fine-tuning the model. Given an item, the
expert-defined attributes, and optionally expert-defined examples, the LLM is instructed to solve
the item step by step and label each step with the attribute it exercises, using the format Step
N [SKILL]: description. Procedural steps are labeled [Other], and the response ends with
Answer: <value>. The expert-defined examples can be worked examples of the labeled format
(Wei et al., 2022), or they can be omitted and the model instructed to reason step by step (Kojima
et al., 2022).
LLM COT FOR Q-MATRIX
10
Trace Analysis
The labeled reasoning steps are then analyzed in four steps. First, in trace inspection and
coding, the stepwise outputs are inspected against the expert-defined attributes to identify at-
tributes that are used, omitted, merely mentioned, or introduced despite not being required by the
item’s solution. Second, in Q-vector reconstruction, the Q-vector of each item is reconstructed
from the model-generated skill labels. An attribute is marked present if at least one reasoning
step is labeled with it, and the resulting matrix is referred to as the CoT-derived Q-matrix. Third,
in reference comparison, the CoT-derived Q-matrix is compared with the reference Q-matrix to
identify item–attribute disagreements. Finally, in discrepancy inspection, these disagreements are
traced to the corresponding reasoning steps to examine whether they involve omitted or misclassi-
fied attributes or potentially legitimate alternative solution paths. Consistent with the supplemen-
tary role of RTA described in the Introduction, the resulting CoT-derived Q-matrix serves as an
initial specification for expert review and empirical validation.
Current Study
The current study evaluates RTA for Q-matrix construction using fraction subtraction as
an example, a domain with an established expert reference Q-matrix used in cognitive diagno-
sis research (Tatsuoka, 1990). The evaluation is guided by three open issues that remain to be
addressed, which are stated below as research questions. Both studies used four expert-defined
attributes. A1 (basic fraction subtraction) involves subtracting numerators after equalizing de-
nominators. A2 (simplifying/reducing) involves reducing fractions to lowest terms or eliminating
zero components. A3 (separating whole number from fraction) involves decomposing mixed
numbers or converting improper fractions. A4 (borrowing from whole number) involves con-
verting one whole unit into a fraction when the minuend fraction is smaller than the subtrahend
fraction.

Two workflows were compared (see Figure 2). The CoT tracing workflow (hereafter, the
CoT workflow) implements RTA as described in the Overview. The empirical study used CoT

- A1: basic fraction subtraction
- A2: simplifying/reducing
- A3: separating whole number
- A4: borrowing from whole number
Format each step as: Step N [SKILL]: description
End with Answer: <value>.
Rules:
- Label a skill only if the step actually performs that operation.
- If a step only checks, states, or mentions an operation without
performing it, label it [Other].
- If a result is already in simplest form, label that step [Other] rather
than [A2].
- Use multiple skill labels separated by & when a single step performs
more than one operation.
- Use [Other] for procedural steps such as writing the final answer.
Solve step by step.

The direct Q-matrix workflow (hereafter, the direct workflow) corresponds to the direct

50,000 hours of egocentric stereo video with synchronized whole-body motion (left). We pretrain Awaken-HI
on human motion and retargeted robot actions, then fine-tune it on robot demonstrations (center). The right
panels summarize scaling and generalization results alongside the full model’s 93.75% mean success rate
across eight individual tasks.
Abstract
A central goal of humanoid robotics is for robots to perform the everyday work people do in homes
and workplaces. Existing egocentric video datasets cover many of these activities but provide little
synchronized whole-body motion data for learning loco-manipulation at scale. We build Awaken-Human,
which pairs approximately 50,000 hours of egocentric stereo video with synchronized whole-body human
motion and covers more than 100 skills. Building on this, we also introduce Awaken-HI (Humanoid
Intelligence), a vision-language-action model for humanoid loco-manipulation that jointly predicts
original human motion and retargeted robot actions through a shared action expert. We show that
loco-manipulation skills transfer more effectively from people to humanoids when human trajectories
directly supervise the shared action expert. Increasing human pretraining data reduces held-out robot
action prediction error according to an empirical scaling law and raises the mean success rate on
downstream real-robot tasks. After full-corpus pretraining and T800 adaptation, Awaken-HI achieves a
mean success rate of 93.75% across eight individual tasks and outperforms GR00T N1.7 and 𝜋0.5 in both
individual and long-horizon evaluations. The same policy generalizes to objects unseen during robot
post-training and to new pairings of familiar objects and destinations.

Awaken-HI: Scaling Humanoid Intelligence with Whole-Body Human Experience
1. Introduction
Humanoid robots could help people with a wide range of tasks in homes and workplaces. Many require whole-
body loco-manipulation, in which the robot coordinates its steps and posture with its hand movements [17, 24].
Vision-language-action (VLA) models [5, 16, 31] and world action models [22, 47, 48] have shown that robots
can learn diverse manipulation skills from demonstrations. For humanoids, however, the cost of whole-body
teleoperation limits the range of tasks and environments represented in robot demonstrations [13, 49].
Human experience of everyday activity offers a more scalable alternative to robot teleoperation. Recent
work draws on the variety of activities and environments in these videos [43, 46] to pretrain manipulation
policies [23, 41, 52]. Despite this diversity, visual observations alone provide no explicit targets for whole-body
motion. Prior work therefore retargets recorded human motion to obtain robot action targets [7, 21]. However,
differences in body proportions and joint structure can cause the resulting postures and hand trajectories to
deviate from those in the human demonstration [2]. These deviations motivate retaining the original human
motion as a training signal alongside the retargeted robot actions. Using that signal at scale requires egocentric
video paired with synchronized whole-body motion across diverse tasks and environments. Yet many large
egocentric datasets provide video alone or primarily track the head and hands [11, 15], while datasets such as
Nymeria [28] offer only a few hundred hours of paired recordings.
We address this data gap with Awaken-Human, a dataset for humanoid pretraining that pairs approximately
50,000 hours of egocentric stereo video with synchronized whole-body human motion. Collected under a
common protocol using lightweight wearable sensors, the demonstrations cover more than 100 skills across
homes, workplaces, retail spaces, and storage areas. We reconstruct 3D hand motion from the video and
annotate the demonstrations with subtask descriptions and frame-level depth maps. For each demonstration,
we retain the original human trajectory alongside the corresponding retargeted robot actions.
Building on Awaken-Human, we introduce Awaken-HI, a VLA model for humanoid loco-manipulation. By
predicting human motion alongside retargeted robot actions, its shared action expert receives direct supervision
from the original human trajectories. During pretraining, the expert also predicts camera-frame wrist poses,
while separate heads estimate current and future depth and describe the current subtask. We then post-train
the policy on approximately 150 hours of T800 teleoperation data using the same robot action interface.
We observe that Awaken-HI’s robot action prediction error on held-out data follows an empirical scaling law,
decreasing as the pretraining set grows from 5,000 to 50,000 hours of human demonstrations. With the same
T800 demonstrations for post-training, more human pretraining data also raises the policy’s mean success rate
on three household tasks. Controlled ablations show that adding human motion supervision reduces action
prediction error and improves real-robot task success compared with pretraining on retargeted actions alone.
After full-corpus pretraining, we post-train Awaken-HI on the same T800 demonstrations used for GR00T
N1.7 [31] and 𝜋0.5 [16]. Awaken-HI outperforms both baselines on all eight individual loco-manipulation
tasks, averaging 93.75% success. It retains this advantage on long-horizon industrial and household tasks. The
policy also follows instructions that pair familiar objects and destinations in new ways and applies a learned
manipulation skill to objects unseen during robot post-training.
Our main contributions are as follows:
• We introduce Awaken-HI, a VLA model for humanoid loco-manipulation that jointly predicts original
human motion and robot actions through a shared action expert.
• We build Awaken-Human, a dataset pairing 50,000 hours of egocentric stereo video with synchronized
whole-body human motion across diverse tasks and environments.
• We find that as human pretraining data grows, action prediction error decreases according to an empirical
scaling law and real-robot success rates rise. Awaken-HI also generalizes to new pairings of familiar
objects and destinations and to objects unseen during robot post-training.

2. Related Work
2.1. Foundation Models for Robot Control
Generalist robot policies map observations and instructions to actions across a wide range of manipulation
tasks [5, 6, 16, 20, 31, 39, 44]. For a humanoid, loco-manipulation additionally requires moving and staying
balanced while adjusting posture to reach objects at different heights and distances. One line of work separates
the control interfaces for the upper and lower body. WholeBodyVLA [17] and Ψ0 [41] predict upper-body
actions and coarse base commands, which a locomotion controller converts into lower-body motion. More recent
approaches predict whole-body motion, enabling the policy to learn coordination between locomotion and
manipulation [21, 24, 51]. Our Awaken-HI follows this approach and learns motion priors through large-scale
human pretraining.
2.2. Egocentric Data and Motion Alignment
Egocentric datasets have grown rapidly in scale, but largely at the cost of recorded whole-body motion or
a consistent protocol. Nymeria [28] uses an inertial motion-capture suit, and HumanVerse in 𝜆0 [21] uses
a headset with body-worn trackers, yet each covers only a few hundred hours. Larger datasets such as
Ego4D [11], EgoVerse [33], and EgoDex [15] provide video with at most head, hand, or upper-body poses,
while Ego-Exo4D [12] derives body pose from exocentric cameras. Pretraining corpora such as EgoScale [52]
and Ego4WAM [38] exceed 10,000 hours by aggregating many sources, which differ in sensors and annotation
pipelines. We build Awaken-Human to fill this gap with 50,000 hours of egocentric video and whole-body
motion recorded by wearable trackers, all captured under the same protocol. Table 1 compares Awaken-Human
with other egocentric datasets in terms of scale, capture setup, and annotation coverage.
To construct robot-action supervision, human motion is mapped to robot embodiments through direct joint
mappings [10] or geometric retargeting, as in GMR [2]. Differences in body proportions and joint structure
can alter the resulting postures and end-effector trajectories [2, 14]. Controller dynamics introduce further
discrepancies between references and execution [7, 18]. Controller-aware refinement [7, 50] and causal state
reconstruction, as in EgoAlign [18], improve the consistency of human-derived supervision with robot behavior.
Our annotation pipeline replaces noisy hand annotations with 3D hand poses reconstructed from egocentric
video and uses them to refine end-effector alignment, reducing end-effector errors relative to GMR.

2.3. Learning from Egocentric Demonstrations
Human demonstrations are typically used in embodied learning to supervise perception, world modeling, and
action learning. R3M [30] pretrains a visual encoder on egocentric human video so that manipulation policies
can be learned from fewer robot demonstrations. World-action models instead use future frames as prediction
targets, learning how scenes change as people interact with objects even without action labels [38, 51]. When
hand or body trajectories are available, human demonstrations can also supervise action learning [34, 41, 45].
EgoMimic [19] aligns human hand trajectories with robot end-effector trajectories in a common coordinate
frame to train a shared manipulation policy. EgoScale [52] and 𝜆0 [21] retarget human motion into robot
hand or whole-body actions and train on these labels. However, constrained by morphological differences,
retargeting inevitably introduces global errors and distorted postures [2, 7]. We therefore train Awaken-HI on
the original human motion together with the retargeted robot actions, learning motion priors directly from the
demonstrations.
3. Awaken-Human
3.1. Large-Scale Egocentric Corpus
We build Awaken-Human to study how the scale of human demonstrations affects humanoid pretraining. The
corpus pairs 50,000 hours of egocentric video with synchronized whole-body human motion recorded by
wearable sensors, making it the largest such dataset to our knowledge. It comprises approximately 17.02
million episodes, 5.41 billion pose frames, and 11.18 million valid language instructions.
Our setup consists of a PICO headset and five body-worn trackers, synchronously recording stereo RGB video
and skeletal sequences from PICO’s body-tracking system [7, 18]. Collectors follow task goals and adapt
their walking paths, stance, and grasping strategies to the scene, preserving natural repositioning and motion
transitions within continuous interactions. The corresponding task instructions are retained alongside raw
video, motion trajectories, and camera and device parameters for subsequent annotation and alignment.
The demonstrations cover more than 100 skills across homes, workplaces, retail spaces, and storage areas.

3.2. Egocentric Data Annotation
We develop an annotation pipeline for whole-body egocentric demonstrations that first undistorts raw stereo

Semantic annotation. We fine-tuned a vision-language model (VLM) for egocentric demonstration annotation.
The model produces initial annotations comprising temporal segment boundaries, segment-level language
descriptions, and atomic action labels selected from a predefined library. Human reviewers verify and correct
these initial annotations to produce segment-level semantic labels for training and data selection.

jitter that affect supervision of fine-grained hand motion. To address these issues, we use our in-house 3D

We use these quality labels to exclude low-quality segments and replace the original PICO hand annotations

ZeroVLN: Learning to Navigate without
Supervised Fine-Tuning of the VLM Brain
Zixuan Huang1,2,†, Yang Zhou2,3,†, Guli Zhang2, Sunzhu Li2, Hongyan Xie1, Zehao Chen1, Fuzhen
Zhuang1, Kaixuan Wang2, Xiaozhi Chen2, Yikun Ban1,∗, Deqing Wang1,∗
1Beihang University, 2Zhuoyu Technology, Shenzhen, China, 3Zhejiang University
†Equal contribution, ∗Corresponding author
Representative vision-language navigation (VLN) methods typically couple a vision-language model
(VLM) brain with a learnable action head and fine-tune the VLM brain on navigation-domain data
to predict geometric goals.
However, such adaptation can substantially alter base VLM weights
and degrade general visual capabilities. We introduce ZeroVLN, a slow–fast navigation framework
that achieves effective navigation with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain. Rather than
teaching the brain to predict geometric goals, we equip it with a semantic tool-calling interface for
conveying movement decisions to an action expert in natural language. We first adapt the action ex-
pert to carry out these movement requests, then jointly improve the brain’s movement decisions and
the action expert’s continuous execution through closed-loop reinforcement learning (RL). Trained
on the same navigation episodes, ZeroVLN substantially outperforms representative SFT-based hier-
archical VLN methods on standard VLN-CE (continuous environments) benchmarks, while inducing
only minor changes to the brain’s weights and largely preserving its general capabilities. To our
knowledge, ZeroVLN is the first slow–fast VLN framework with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM
brain, and the first to jointly optimize its slow and fast policies through closed-loop agentic RL in VLN-CE.
Date: 2026.11.17
Correspondence: huang_zx@buaa.edu.cn
Code: https://github.com/hzx122/ZeroVLN
Model: https://huggingface.co/hzxllll/ZeroVLN
1
Introduction
VLN requires an embodied agent to connect movement decisions with precise movement [4, 13, 27, 28, 36, 47].
Representative methods adapt a general-purpose VLM through navigation-domain supervision to predict
geometric goals for an action expert [20, 49] or generate numerical movement commands in a predefined for-
mat [13]. However, we observe substantial displacement of the base VLM’s weights and degraded performance
of general visual capability following this adaptation, as shown in Figure 1.
Inspired by DeepSeek-R1-Zero [21], which demonstrates that reasoning capabilities can emerge through RL
directly from a base language model without prior SFT, we introduce ZeroVLN, the first slow–fast navigation
framework that learns navigation through environment interaction with zero navigation-domain SFT of the
VLM brain. Rather than adapting the brain to predict geometric goals, we introduce a semantic tool interface
that connects it to a trainable flow-matching action expert [54]. Through natural-language tool calls, the
brain conveys movement decisions to the action expert, which translates them into continuous motion.
Within this framework, we first construct reference trajectories from the brain’s own movement requests, col-
lected through online rollouts with the brain frozen. To ground these requests in executable motion, we design
a privileged trajectory planner that leverages a semantic map derived from the scene mesh [35]. The resulting
reference trajectories are paired with their originating requests to provide semantically aligned supervision
for the action expert.
We then jointly optimize the brain’s movement decisions and the action expert’s continuous execution through
multi-round agentic RL [18, 61]. To address sparse success signals in challenging long-horizon navigation
1
arXiv:2611.26414v1  [cs.AI]  19 Nov 2026
tasks, we design complementary process and outcome rewards that distinguish useful progress even when task
completion fails.
Beyond conventional slow–fast frameworks, our design provides two key benefits: (1) the semantic interface
leverages the brain’s native capabilities for flexible tool use and feedback-driven recovery [29, 56]; (2) Rather
than specializing the model for navigation through SFT, ZeroVLN builds upon its existing language and navi-
gation decision-making capabilities, using RL to enhance navigation performance while largely preserving its
general-purpose abilities.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:
• We introduce ZeroVLN, the first slow–fast VLN framework that connects a VLM brain with an action
expert policy through a semantic tool interface, achieving zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain.
• We develop a two-stage training paradigm that first aligns continuous execution with the brain’s seman-
tic requests through request-grounded supervision and execution-prefix learning, then jointly optimizes
the slow and fast policies through closed-loop agentic RL.
• Across mainstream VLN-CE benchmarks, ZeroVLN substantially outperforms representative SFT-based
baselines trained on the same navigation episodes, with only 0.01497% VLM weight displacement while
largely preserving general visual capabilities.

Flow Matching from Non-Gaussian Sources:
A Theory of Efficient Sampling
Yuchen Zhou∗
Lili Zheng∗
Yuxin Chen†
Gen Li‡
November 20, 2026
Abstract
Flow matching is a versatile framework for generative modeling that transports a source distribution
to a target data distribution.
A key advantage is its flexibility in the choice of source distribution,
such as heavy-tailed and multimodal sources.
Yet finite-step sampling guarantees for non-Gaussian
sources remain limited. We establish a nonasymptotic convergence theory for Euler discretization of flow
matching with linear interpolation. Suppose the source distribution on Rd has an everywhere positive,
continuously differentiable density, finite total variance TotVarbase, and an L-Lipschitz score. Using the
population velocity field and a suitable time grid, this sampler achieves total variation error at most ε in
eO
LdTotVarbase
ε

iterations, provided the target distribution satisfies a mild second-moment condition. These assumptions
cover, among many examples, source distributions such as multivariate Student’s t distributions with
more than two degrees of freedom and finite Gaussian mixtures with shared covariance, while accommo-
dating target distributions with neither a smooth density nor bounded support.
Keywords: flow matching, rectified flow, Euler discretization, nonasymptotic convergence, non-Gaussian
sources
1
Introduction
Flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023; Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2023; Liu et al., 2023) has established itself
as a powerful and versatile framework for generative modeling, achieving compelling performance in image
generation (Esser et al., 2024), speech synthesis (Le et al., 2023), and even molecule generation (Song et al.,
2023) and protein structure generation (Bose et al., 2024). In a nutshell, flow matching seeks to transport a
source distribution toward a target data distribution by means of an ordinary differential equation (ODE):
d
dtXt = vt(Xt),
t ∈[0, 1),
X0 ∼Pbase,
(1)
where Pbase represents a source distribution on Rd that is easy to sample from, and vt : Rd →Rd stands for a
time-dependent vector field (often referred to as the velocity field). Ideally, the distribution of Xt converges
to the target data distribution — denoted by Pdata — as t approaches 1. Flow matching is typically composed
of two stages: during training, the population vector field vt(·) is learned by regression using samples drawn
from the source and target distributions; during sampling, one draws X0 ∼Pbase and numerically solves
the ODE (1) from this initialization X0, using a standard approach such as Euler’s method, to obtain an
approximate sample from Pdata.

The popularity of flow matching stems in part from its simulation-free training, empirical effectiveness,
conceptual simplicity, and flexibility in choosing the source distribution and, in some formulations, the source-
target coupling (Liu et al., 2023; Tong et al., 2024; Pooladian et al., 2023). Given the widespread adoption
of flow matching in generative modeling, an important practical consideration is its sampling efficiency. As
with ODE-based samplers for diffusion models, generating a sample with flow matching requires numerically
solving an ODE driven by a learned velocity field, typically by discretizing time into a grid and evaluating
the field at each step. A finer time grid can reduce discretization error and improve sampling accuracy, but
it also requires more evaluations of the velocity field, each typically involving a forward pass through a large
neural network. To understand this tradeoff and guide the choice of time grid in practice, the present paper
seeks to characterize the iteration complexity of the flow matching sampler, namely, the number of steps
needed to achieve a prescribed sampling accuracy.
Notably, while substantial work has been devoted to establishing convergence theory for diffusion models
— whose probability flow ODEs can be formulated as flow matching with Gaussian sources (Albergo et al.,
2025) — the analyses and insights therein do not directly carry over to flow matching with non-Gaussian
sources. This theoretical gap matters in practice because non-Gaussian sources can be highly versatile: they
support sampling from heavy-tailed or multimodal distributions, data-to-data transport, and the generation
of non-Euclidean data. This motivates a closer examination of the role of non-Gaussian sources and the
theoretical support for them.
1.1
Non-Gaussian sources in flow matching
Conventionally, Gaussian sources are the standard choice in diffusion models: the forward process of a
diffusion model gradually adds Gaussian noise until the data distribution approaches a Gaussian source,
while preserving tractable forward transition distributions (Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021, 2020). However,
Gaussian sources may be less well suited to target distributions with heavy tails or to data with discrete
or geometric structure. Alternative source distributions have therefore been explored, with tractability as
a key consideration; examples include Gamma and α-stable noise with suitable closure properties under
addition (Nachmani et al., 2021; Yoon et al., 2023; Popov et al., 2025; Shariatian et al., 2025), and discrete
corruption schemes that allow multi-step transition probabilities to be computed tractably (Austin et al.,
2021).
By contrast, flow matching offers greater flexibility in the choice of source distribution. Given samples
from any source and target distributions, the velocity field can be learned through regression. For heavy-
tailed targets, prior work explored multivariate t distributions as sources, reporting improved performance
over Gaussian-source baselines, while other work proposed to learn quantile-based source distributions that
adapt to heavy-tailed data (Pandey et al., 2025; Guan et al., 2026a; Chemseddine et al., 2026). Gaussian
mixture sources have also been used effectively to generate multimodal targets (Luo et al., 2026; Wang et al.,
2026a). Other work employed non-Euclidean source distributions to generate discrete data or data lying on a
manifold, such as DNA sequences, proteins, crystals, and geographic locations (Stark et al., 2024; Chen and
Lipman, 2024; Miller et al., 2024; Bose et al., 2024; Sriram et al., 2024). In addition, flow matching has been
used for data-to-data transport, such as translating images between domains, where the source is itself a
non-Gaussian data distribution (Liu et al., 2023; Tong et al., 2024). Despite these promising applications of
non-Gaussian sources, the effects of source choice on training and sampling remain under debate (Cherkaoui
et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2025). It is largely unclear to what extent existing convergence results for standard
Gaussian sources carry over to more general sources.
A few recent studies began to analyze the convergence behavior of flow matching and its variants with non-
Gaussian sources. Some assumed the learned velocity field is bounded (Guan et al., 2026b), an assumption
that may be restrictive for source distributions with unbounded support. Others imposed tail conditions on
the target data distribution (Guan et al., 2026a) or introduced Gaussian smoothing along the flow trajectory
through stochastic interpolants (Liu et al., 2025, 2026; Silveri et al., 2026). This motivates the following
question:
For commonly used non-Gaussian sources, can we establish nonasymptotic convergence guaran-
tees without introducing Gaussian smoothing or imposing stronger assumptions on the target?
2
1.2
This paper
Main contributions.
In this paper, we address the above question by analyzing the Euler sampler for
flow matching when the true velocity field is available. Our results hold under the following conditions on
the source and target distributions, which are satisfied by a broad class of commonly used distributions:
• The source distribution Pbase has an everywhere positive and continuously differentiable density on Rd,
finite total variance, and an L-Lipschitz score function.
• The target distribution Pdata has a finite second moment that is not overly large relative to the source’s
second moment.
Under these conditions, we prove that the Euler sampler for flow matching achieves a total-variation-based
error of at most ε using at most

Our convergence theory is established under substantially milder assumptions on the source and target
distributions than those imposed in prior work. For the source distribution, the assumptions of a Lipschitz
score and a finite second moment are satisfied, for example, by multivariate Gaussian distributions with
positive definite covariance matrices, multivariate Student’s t distributions with more than two degrees of
freedom, and finite Gaussian mixtures whose components share a positive definite covariance matrix; note
that both Student’s t distributions and Gaussian mixtures have been used as non-Gaussian sources in flow
matching applications (Pandey et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2026). For the target distribution, we require only a
finite second moment that is not too large relative to that of the source, with no additional tail assumptions.
These results demonstrate that flow matching samplers can efficiently transport a broad class of non-Gaussian
source distributions, including heavy-tailed distributions, to fairly general target distributions.
From a technical standpoint, our analysis rests on carefully characterizing the nonlinear score of the source
distribution and establishing a restricted injectivity property for the Euler map. Both of these technical steps
are more involved than in the Gaussian case, the latter of which features an affine source score and a globally
injective Euler map.
Organization.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 formally introduces the
flow matching sampler. Section 3 presents our main convergence theory and its consequences, followed by
additional related work in Section 4. Section 5 outlines the proof strategy and highlights the key steps for
handling non-Gaussian source distributions. Section 6 proves the main theorem, with proofs of auxiliary
results deferred to the appendix. Section 7 concludes the paper by discussing directions for future work.

In this section, we formalize the flow-matching setup and the Euler sampler studied in this paper.
Flow matching setup.
Recall that Pbase and Pdata denote the source and target distributions on Rd,
respectively. Flow matching models the transport from a source distribution Pbase to Pdata through an ODE
driven by a time-dependent velocity field:

Democratizing Cross-Project Knowledge for 
Transforming Water Governance and Climate 
Resilience: an Agentic AI Ecosystem 
Oriol Alàs1*[0009-0001-6875-922X], Ian Palacín1*[0009-0000-0148-7437], Iván Cester1[0009-0005-6326-
0146] and Edgar Rubión1[0000-0003-3886-3170] 
1Eurecat, Centre Tecnològic de Catalunya, Barcelona, Spain 
edgar.rubion@eurecat.org 
Abstract. EU-funded projects produce extensive evidence in the form of de-
liverables, reports, and case studies. However, this knowledge is typically scat-
tered across projects and document structures, making it difficult to locate rele-
vant, contextual information when making decisions. This paper introduces an 
Agentic AI Ecosystem that consolidates heterogeneous project documentation 
into a domain-aware knowledge base and provides adaptive access through an 
agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline. Documents from three EU-
funded projects (IMPETUS, NATALIE, and InnWater) are reconstructed into hi-
erarchical section trees and indexed with structured metadata. Retrieval is sup-
ported by two domain-specific embedding models fine-tuned on domain data 
(water and climate). On top of this knowledge base, a ReAct-style controller it-
eratively orchestrates retrieval actions by allocating retrieval budget across do-
main collections and accumulating evidence until a stopping criterion is met. In 
a retrieval benchmark over the corpus, the proposed approach improves Mean 
Reciprocal Rank by 26.7% (relative) compared to a single-domain embedding 
baseline, indicating more consistent retrieval of relevant evidence to support 
cross-project knowledge synthesis and climate-resilient decision-making. 
Keywords: Agentic AI, Knowledge Democratization, Embedding Fine-Tuning, 
Water Governance. 
1 
Introduction 
Horizon Europe and related EU programmes have generated substantial technical evi-
dence for climate adaptation and water governance in the form of technical deliverables 
and reports. In practice, these outputs are distributed across projects and embedded in 
long documents with heterogeneous structures, which makes it costly for local author-
ities, NGOs, and policymakers to identify the specific, contextual fragments needed for 
planning and decision-making. As recognized by the EU Climate Adaptation Strategy1  
 
*  Both authors contributed equally to this paper.  
1  European Commission, (2021), EU Strategy on Adaptation to Climate Change. 
2 
and the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report2, knowledge emerging from climate and envi-
ronmental research must be not only scientifically robust but also accessible, contextu-
alized, and inclusive to empower informed decision-making at all levels. 
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides a natural paradigm for querying 
such corpora by grounding model outputs in external sources [1]. However, standard 
one-shot RAG pipelines remain brittle in cross-project settings. Relevant evidence may 
be spread across multiple documents and projects, section-level context is often re-
quired for correct interpretation, and user queries frequently span multiple domains 
(e.g., climate adaptation and water governance). Under these conditions, a single re-
trieval call may either miss key context or surface partially relevant fragments without 
mechanisms to iteratively refine the search or consolidate evidence across sources [2]. 
Recent work has addressed adjacent limitations in two directions. First, hierarchical and 
tree-based retrieval methods build multi-level representations to retrieve both local de-
tail and global context from long documents, mitigating the shortcomings of flat chunk-
ing [3]. Second, agentic and adaptive RAG variants interleave reasoning with retrieval 
actions, deciding when to retrieve, refining queries or tool parameters, and accumulat-
ing evidence before answering, rather than committing to a fixed evidence set from a 
single call [4]. Despite this progress, cross-project decision-support scenarios impose 
an additional constraint: retrieval must be both domain-aware and provenance-preserv-
ing, with explicit control over how retrieval effort is allocated across heterogeneous 
project collections. 
Generic embedding models often underperform on specialized project corpora where 
key distinctions depend on domain terminology; synthetic query-passage generation 
can provide supervision for retriever adaptation when labeled data are scarce [5].  To 
train the models efficiently under practical compute constraints, parameter-efficient 
fine-tuning methods such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) offer a common strategy 
to update a small number of trainable parameters while keeping the base model largely 
frozen [6]. 
To address these limitations, we propose an Agentic AI Ecosystem for cross-project 
knowledge access, demonstrated on documentation from three EU-funded projects: 
IMPETUS3, NATALIE4, and InnWater5. The ecosystem combines (i) a domain-aware 
knowledge base that reconstructs project documentation into hierarchical section trees 
and indexes fragments with structural and provenance metadata, and (ii) an agentic or-
chestration layer that performs adaptive, multi-step retrieval over domain-specific col-
lections. 
The main contributions of this work are: (1) a cross-project, domain-aware 
knowledge base that preserves document hierarchy and provenance metadata; (2) two 
domain-specific embedding spaces trained with evidence-grounded synthetic supervi-
sion, improving the discoverability of policy-relevant knowledge expressed in project-
 
2  AR6 Synthesis Report (SYR), (2023) 
3  IMPETUS, Grant No. 101037084, https://climate-impetus.eu 
4  NATALIE, Grant No. 101112859, https://www.natalieproject.eu 
5  InnWater, Grant No. 101086512, https://www.innwater.eu 
3 
specific and technical language; (3) an iterative retrieval controller that allocates re-
trieval budget across domain collections via tool parameterization and evidence accu-
mulation, supporting cross-sectoral and multi-project knowledge synthesis; and (4) an 
empirical evaluation over the projects corpus showing  a 26.7% relative improvement 
in Mean Reciprocal Rank compared to a single-domain embedding baseline, indicating 
more reliable access to relevant evidence for decision-support scenarios. 
2 
System Architecture 
The proposed Agentic AI Ecosystem is designed to enable contextual, cross-project 
knowledge access across heterogeneous climate and water governance documentation. 
The architecture comprises two tightly coupled components: (i) a domain-aware 
knowledge database, responsible for ingesting, structuring, and indexing project docu-
mentation and (ii) a ReAct-style agent orchestration layer, which dynamically coordi-
nates retrieval actions across domain-specific collections. 
2.1 
Domain-aware Knowledge Database 
The ingestion pipeline turns unstructured and heterogeneous project documentation 
into a structured, section-aware knowledge base that preserves the original logical or-
ganization of each document. Our approach explicitly reconstructs the document’s hi-
erarchical structure and uses this structure as the backbone for downstream retrieval. 
The content is then indexed in a vector database using two domain-specific embedding 
models fine-tuned using project materials. 
Multimodal structure detection and traditional content extraction.  
Document ingestion employs a dual-parsing approach that combines AI-driven 
structural analysis with robust content extraction. A multimodal large language model 
(Google Gemini) is used to infer document structure through multimodal analysis, iden-
tifying section hierarchies, heading levels and organizational patterns. This approach 
improves robustness when processing documents with inconsistent formatting, visual 
noise, or irregular layouts, where rule-based parsers typically fail. In parallel, 
OpenParse, an open-source library designed for document parsing, is used to extract 
raw textual content, tables, and visual elements while preserving layout information. 
This enables filtering of non-content artefacts such as headers or page numbers and 
ensures accurate content recovery. Outputs from both parsers are aligned and merged 
into a unified representation by matching structurally inferred sections with their cor-
responding extracted content. 
Hierarchical Content Representation and Summarization 
The merged output is organized into a content-tree, where each node corresponds to 
a document section or subsection, and contains both raw content and associated 
4 
metadata (project, document identifier and section path). To support retrieval at multi-
ple levels of abstraction, the system generates hierarchical summaries using a depth-
first search (DFS) post-order traversal.  Leaf nodes are summarized directly from their 
raw text, while parent nodes recursively aggregate their own content with the summar-
ies of their children. 
Domain Specific Embedding 
Generic pre-trained embedding models often fail to capture domain-specific termi-
nology and relationships crucial for specialized retrieval tasks [7]. To address this lim-
itation, we fine-tune two domain-specific embedding models (one for water governance 
and one for climate adaptation) that better align with the semantic spaces. 
Silver Dataset Construction 
To obtain supervision without manual labeling, a synthetic data generation pipeline 
was implemented to create high-quality question-answer-passage (QAP) triplets auto-
matically. This pipeline utilizes Google Gemini to ingest raw project documentation 
and generate QAP samples only when they can be validated by verbatim evidence pre-
sent in the text. Each generated entry consists of a) a concise question, b) a direct answer 
derived exclusively from the document content and c) extracted passage, consisting of 
exact quotes from the source text that serve as ground truth. Few-shot technique was 
applied to improve quality and style of the responses of the model. This process yielded 
1064 high-quality triplets for the water domain and 846 for the climate domain. 
Fine-tuning 
To adapt the vector space to specific semantics of the water and climate domains, 
the multilingual BGE-M3 embedding model was fine-tuned (per domain) due to its 
multilingual coverage. Fine-tuning relied on a contrastive learning objective designed 
to improve semantic alignment for relevant query–passage pairs (positives) while de-
creasing similarity with non-relevant passages (negatives). For each query 𝑖, negatives 
were selected from a candidate set 𝒩(𝑖). Let 𝑞! denote the embedding of query 𝑖, 𝑝! 
the embedding of its positive passage, and 𝒩(𝑖) the set of negative passages considered 
for query 𝑖. The contrastive loss is defined as:

5 
Two-Stage Retrieval 
Retrieval exploits hierarchical document structure through a two-stage procedure. 
Let 𝑄 denote the user query and let each document be represented as a section tree, 
where each node has a summarized version of their children’s sections and its own 
content. 
Document-level scoping 
The search space is reduced by computing semantic similarity between 𝑄 and the 
root embedding of each document. Only documents whose scores exceeds a threshold 
𝜃-./ are retained. 
Node-level scoping 
For each shortlisted document, candidate nodes are scored using two complementary 
representations: (i) the embedding of the node’s raw content and (ii) the node’s gener-

threshold 𝜃0.-1, subject to a retrieval budget 𝑘. The output of retrieval is a set of evi-

2.2 
Agent orchestration layer 
The agent policy follows an iterative control loop that decides which retrieval action to 
execute, accumulates evidence across iterations, and stops to produce the final answer. 
Let 𝐷 denote the set of available domain collections. Given a query 𝑄, the loop main-
tains an evidence set 𝐸4 (initially empty). At each iteration 𝑡< 𝑛, the controller selects

6 
3 
Experimental Evaluation 
This section evaluates the impact of domain-specific embedding fine-tuning by com-
paring a generic embedding model within an information retrieval setup. The evalua-
tion focuses on the distinction of the embedding space topology and their effect on 
downstream retrieval performance. 
 
Fig. 1. Cosine Similarity Matrices for Question-Answer pairs from the water-domain validation 
set. Each row 𝑖 represents a synthetic question, and each column 𝑗 represents a corresponding 
answer fragment. 
 
Fig. 2. Kernel density of cosine similarity for correct and incorrect question–answer pairings 
using the base (generic) and fine-tuned water-domain embedding models. 
 
7 
To evaluate the impact of fine-tuning, we conducted a controlled similarity analysis 
using a held-out validation set consisting of QAP triplets. Figure 1 illustrates the result-
ing cosine similarity matrices, where each row represents a specific query and each 
column corresponds to a potential answer fragment. The diagonal elements (𝑖= 𝑗) de-
note correct pairs, while off-diagonal elements (𝑖 ≠𝑗) represent incorrect matches. In 
this visualization, a perfect retrieval model would concentrate all similarity on the di-
agonal and zero similarity elsewhere. The matrix for the generic model shows a diffu-
sion distribution with low contrast and significant noise; the similarity values for cor-
rect pairs (the diagonal) are often indistinguishable from those of incorrect pairs (the 
off-diagonal noise). Following domain-specific fine-tuning, the embedding space un-
dergoes a clearer separation: the diagonal becomes more prominent and the off-diago-
nal "background noise" is globally suppressed. This indicates that the fine-tuned model 
has learned to better distinguish relevant from irrelevant evidence, effectively increas-
ing the "margin" between correct and incorrect retrievals. The structural shift is further 
quantified in Figure 2.  In the generic model, the similarity distributions for correct and 
incorrect pairs show a high degree of overlap, which leads to retrieval ambiguity. In 
contrast, fine-tuning effectively decouples these distributions: it maintains high simi-
larity for correct matches while shifting the “noise” distribution toward lower values. 
This dual evidence demonstrates that the model has successfully learned to isolate rel-
evant evidence from irrelevant information. 
Finally, Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) [8] was used to quantify retrieval effective-
ness. For each query, the reciprocal rank is defined as the inverse of the rank position 
at which the first correct answer appears in the retrieved list. Formally, for a set of 𝑁 
queries, MRR is computed as (4):

places greater emphasis on retrieving the correct answer at higher ranks, assigning the 
maximum score when the correct item appears at the top position and lower score as 
the rank increases. The fine-tuned embedding model achieves a 26.7% relative im-
provement compared with the baseline RAG system. This improvement reflects both 
an increased frequency of correct answers appearing in top-ranked positions and a re-
duction in average rank across the evaluation set. In practical terms, relevant contextual 
fragments are retrieved earlier, providing information retrieval tools with more domain-
aligned evidence. 
4 
Conclusion 
By transforming static project documentation into a living knowledge ecosystem that 
evolves as new projects emerge, this work helps address the urgent need identified in 
EU policy frameworks to make research outputs accessible and actionable for local 
decision-makers, ultimately supporting the transition toward climate-resilient societies. 
Experimental results demonstrate a 26.7% relative improvement in MRR over a single-
8 
domain baseline, confirming that domain alignment and hierarchical scoping materially 
enhance early retrieval precision and discriminative separation in the embedding space. 
Building upon these findings, future research will focus on expanding the ecosystem’s 
capabilities through three primary avenues. First, the system will be extended with 
multi-modal retrieval capabilities to support richer evidence grounding and multimodal 
retrieval. Second, the ecosystem will be extended to additional EU-funded projects and 
adjacent policy domains to assess scalability, cross-domain generalization and embed-
ding transferability. Finally, human-in-the-loop evaluations are planned to assess the 
faithfulness and reasoning quality of the agentic responses in the real-word policy-mak-
ing scenarios.

World Models Favor Learned Priors over Visual Evidence
Han Xiao1
Zhiyong Bao2
Xiaotong Liu3
Yanhao Chen1
Qingqiang Wu1
1 Xiamen University
2 Northeastern University
3 Tongji University
cyhao@stu.xmu.edu.cn, wuqq@xmu.edu.cn
Abstract
World models are increasingly used to simulate physical
interactions, but training a separate model for each envi-
ronment limits scalability. Cross-environment prediction re-
quires identifying the current physical rule, which appear-
ance alone may not reveal. We therefore study visual cal-
ibration: using object motion and interactions in a short
video as direct evidence to infer the current rule and predict
motion under that rule from a different initial state. How-
ever, differences in data availability across physical con-
ditions can yield a long-tailed training distribution, bias-
ing models toward common rules even when evidence sup-
ports rare ones. To study this challenge, we introduce Tail-
World, which evaluates the transfer of demonstrated rules
across initial states while independently controlling train-
ing imbalance and calibration informativeness. The bench-
mark compares predictions with two reference futures from
the same prediction initial state, one following the demon-
strated rule and the other a common rule, to measure pre-
diction bias toward common dynamics. We further propose
Rule Inference for Transfer (RIFT), which learns how dif-
ferent rules affect object motion, infers the current rule from
calibration interactions, and applies it to prediction from a
new initial state. RIFT explicitly controls the influence of
training frequency on rule inference, allowing sufficiently
informative observational evidence to support rare rules.
Experiments on TailWorld show that RIFT improves pre-
diction accuracy and physical consistency across varying
training imbalances and distribution shifts, with gains in
predicting rare dynamics.
1. Introduction
World models are increasingly used to simulate how phys-
ical environments evolve [7, 15, 49]. Training a separate
model for each environment is costly and difficult to scale,
motivating world models that can predict across environ-
ments.
A key challenge is identifying the physical rule
governing the current environment. Visually similar objects
Figure 1. RIFT transfers calibrated physical rules across states to
predict rare dynamics.
may behave differently because their physical properties or
surrounding conditions differ, so appearance alone may be
insufficient [4, 46]. These properties and conditions shape
motion and interactions [5, 36, 41], allowing the dynamics
captured in a video to provide evidence for identifying the
current rule [6, 39]. We study visual calibration, where a
model infers the current rule from a short demonstration and
predicts motion under that rule from a different initial state
[4]. Changing the initial state makes replaying the demon-
strated trajectory insufficient, testing whether the model can
understand and transfer the underlying rule.
Recent methods primarily adapt models to different dy-
namics by updating environment-specific parameters from
limited observations [22, 25, 35] or conditioning predictions
on representations of observed trajectories [4, 11]. How-
ever, real-world objects, materials, and environments dif-
fer in prevalence and ease of data collection, leading to un-
even coverage of physical conditions and potentially a long-
tailed data distribution. Models trained on such data may
predict according to common rules even when calibration
evidence supports rare ones. The key challenge is whether
a model can base its predictions on sufficiently informative
observations when they conflict with preferences induced
by training frequency.
1
arXiv:2611.26366v1  [cs.AI]  19 Nov 2026
To study this challenge under controlled conditions, we
introduce TailWorld, a benchmark for visual calibration
under long-tailed dynamics. Each task requires prediction
from a different initial state under the rule demonstrated in
a calibration video. TailWorld independently controls rule
frequencies during training and calibration informativeness
to examine how training imbalance and observational ev-
idence jointly affect prediction. It also provides two ref-
erence futures from the same prediction initial state: one
follows the demonstrated rule, and the other follows a com-
mon rule. Comparing predictions with both quantifies their
deviation from the true future and any shift toward the com-
mon alternative, directly assessing the model’s preference
for common dynamics.
To enable models to infer rules from current evidence
and apply them to new trajectories, we propose Rule In-
ference for Transfer (RIFT). RIFT first learns how dif-
ferent physical rules affect object motion, then uses these
relationships to infer the current rule from interactions ob-
served in a calibration video. It applies the inferred rule to
prediction from a different initial state and keeps it fixed
throughout prediction. Crucially, RIFT explicitly controls
the influence of training frequency on rule inference, allow-
ing sufficiently informative observations to support rules
rarely seen during training. The model can thus draw on
knowledge learned across environments to predict motion
under the current rule from a new initial state. Experiments
on TailWorld show that RIFT improves prediction accuracy
and physical consistency across varying training imbalances
and distribution shifts, with gains extending to rare dynam-
ics. Our contributions are threefold:
1. We study visual calibration under long-tailed dynamics,
examining whether models can follow rare rules sup-
ported by observational evidence when predicting mo-
tion from different initial states.
2. We introduce TailWorld, which independently controls
training imbalance and calibration informativeness and
measures prediction bias toward common dynamics us-
ing reference futures under the demonstrated and com-
mon rules.
3. We propose RIFT, which infers the current rule from ob-
served interactions, explicitly controls the influence of
training frequency on inference, and applies the inferred
rule to prediction from different initial states.
2. Related Work
World models and dynamics adaptation.
World mod-
els predict environment evolution to support planning and
adaptation [1, 7, 15–17, 32, 49].
For physical systems,
interaction-based models capture object interactions and
their effects on motion [5, 9, 27, 36, 41]. Adaptation meth-
ods update model parameters or condition predictions on
limited observations [12, 14, 22, 25, 35, 40], while recent
work extracts physical information from trajectories and in-
teraction videos [11, 30]. Under imbalanced training fre-
quencies, however, predictions may favor a common rule
even when calibration evidence supports a rare one.
Visual physical inference and evaluation.
Visual phys-
ical inference recovers hidden properties and interactions
from observed motion [24, 28, 44–46].
Counterfactual
prediction tests whether inferred dynamics transfer across
initial conditions [4, 19].
Benchmarks evaluate physi-
cal plausibility, outcome prediction, and causal reasoning
[2, 6, 37, 39, 48], with further work probing hidden proper-
ties and challenging interactions [3, 21, 26, 33, 42]. Predic-
tion error alone, however, does not distinguish ambiguous
evidence from a preference for common dynamics. Tail-
World independently varies training imbalance and calibra-
tion informativeness, then compares predictions from a new
initial state with futures under the demonstrated and com-
mon rules. This reveals whether predictions favor common
dynamics despite evidence identifying a rare rule.
Long-tailed learning and prior correction.
Long-tailed
learning addresses target imbalance through reweighting,
margin adjustments, and decoupled training [8, 10, 20].
Prior-aware methods account for label frequencies and dis-
tribution shifts [18, 29, 31, 38], with extensions to continu-
ous targets [47]. These approaches motivate frequency cor-
rection, but physical prediction requires inferring a latent
rule from interactions and transferring it to a new initial
state. RIFT addresses this coupled problem by learning how
rules shape motion, inferring the governing rule from cali-
bration video while controlling training-frequency effects,
and using that rule to predict future dynamics.
3. TailWorld Benchmark
To examine how calibration evidence and training fre-
quency influence prediction, TailWorld separates observa-
tions that establish the query motion state from interactions
that reveal the governing rule. Each task pairs a calibration
video with a query trajectory under the same rule but dif-
ferent initial positions and velocities. The model observes
a collision-free query segment and predicts subsequent mo-
tion, using calibration interactions to distinguish rules that
the query history alone cannot identify.
We achieve this separation through collision scenes,
where restitution and mass ratio affect collision outcomes
but leave contact-free motion unchanged. The 2D scenes
contain a disc and a movable circular pillar (Fig. 2); the 3D
scenes contain a sphere and a movable finite cylinder, ob-
served by three calibrated cameras (Fig. 3). We vary resti-
tution, mass ratio, or both while keeping appearance and
scene geometry fixed. This construction makes calibration
2
Figure 2. Examples of 2D scenes in TailWorld.
informative about the governing rule and subsequent colli-
sions informative about which rule the prediction follows.
3.1. Two Futures from the Same Initial State
For each synthetic scene, we generate two future trajecto-
ries from exactly the same initial state: one follows the
rule demonstrated in the calibration video, and the other
follows a reference rule common in training. The model
observes the first 0.5 s of query motion and predicts both
objects over the next 5 s, corresponding to 15 observed and
150 predicted frames at 30 Hz. The observed segment must
be collision-free and identical under both rules. It there-
fore reveals object positions and velocities without distin-
guishing the rules, making calibration evidence necessary
for rule identification. For samples assessing bias toward
common rules, we further require the two futures to differ
clearly after subsequent collisions, ensuring that the govern-
ing rule materially affects prediction. Both complete tra-
jectories are withheld at inference and serve as references
for assessing whether predictions more closely follow the
calibration-supported or common rule.
3.2. Varying Training Frequency and Available Ev-
idence
We adjust sampling proportions within a fixed training
pool to progressively increase common-rule frequency
while keeping rare-rule sampling probability unchanged.
Rare cases retain 5% of the sampling probability, with
a common-to-rare sampling ratio of r : 1, where r ∈
{1, 4, 16}; other training cases receive the remaining prob-
ability. Under a fixed training budget, this preserves the ex-
pected number of rare-rule exposures, allowing us to exam-
ine the effect of increasing common-rule prevalence. Sep-
arately, we provide shorter or longer segments of the same
calibration video to test whether additional motion and in-
teraction evidence aids rule identification. The shorter seg-
ment ends 0.6 s after the first collision; the longer contains
the full 6 s trajectory. For each training distribution, we use
Figure 3. Examples of 3D scenes in TailWorld.
both calibration lengths on the same prediction tasks to ex-
amine the respective effects of training distribution and cur-
rent video evidence on prediction.
3.3. Testing Rule Transfer
Beyond assessing prediction under rules infrequent in train-
ing, we test whether rules transfer to initial states not paired
with them during training. All test tasks combine rules and
initial states that have each appeared in training, but whose
pairings are excluded from training.
To assess transfer across initial states in real observa-
tions, we use pendulum recordings from IRIS [23] and
Delfys75 [13]. We pair separate recordings under the same
physical setting as calibration and query videos, holding out
selected settings for testing. These tasks use 0.5 s of query
history and a 3 s prediction horizon.
3.4. Demonstration Robustness and Control Cases
We complement the transfer tests with two checks on how
calibration affects prediction. First, we provide two dis-
tinct calibration trajectories per rule, each used separately
as input, to test whether predictions remain consistent
across demonstrations of the same rule. Second, we retain
cases where the demonstrated and common rules produce
nearly identical futures, checking for unnecessary predic-
tion changes when rule differences have little effect on the
target motion. Full parameters and construction details ap-
pear in Appendix B.
4. Methodology
4.1. Problem Formulation and Overview
We study cross-state physical prediction under long-tailed
training distributions.
Each sample pairs a calibration
demonstration C with a query sequence Q governed by the
same physical rule but initialized independently. The goal
is to infer this rule from observations in C and predict the
query’s future trajectory from its initial observations Qobs.
3
Figure 4. Overview of RIFT. RIFT infers physical rules from calibration interactions, explicitly controls the influence of training frequency
on rule selection, and transfers the inferred rule to trajectory prediction from different initial states.
Rule Inference for Transfer (RIFT) infers a rule from ob-
served motion and applies it to prediction from a new ini-
tial state. A learned rule vector represents the environmen-
tal rule, shared across trajectories in the same environment.
The motion model maps the current state to a base correc-
tion and a response matrix, making next-step position pre-
dictions linear in this vector. Calibration observations thus
yield linear constraints for recovering it. During query pre-
diction, the vector remains fixed while the state-dependent
motion response evolves with the query motion.
To let calibration evidence support rare rules, RIFT se-
lects candidates using separate explanatory cost and train-
ing frequency terms. Reference rule vectors fitted to train-
ing trajectories form a Rule Atlas.
For each reference,
RIFT balances calibration fit against deviation from that
reference, yielding an updated candidate and its explana-
tory cost. Selection combines this cost with an indepen-
dently adjustable frequency term. A rare candidate can be
selected when its explanatory cost advantage outweighs the
frequency preference for common candidates.
4.2. Learning Motion Relationships for Rule Iden-
tification
This module learns how rules affect motion while keeping
predictions linear in the rule vector, enabling its recovery
from calibration and reuse for prediction from different ini-
