How Much Should an Agent Remember?
Deployment Lessons from Self-Distilled Memory for LLM Agents
K. R. Jayaram, Vatche Isahagian, Aswath Vaithinathan Aravindan, Vinod Muthusamy,
Punleuk Oum, Gaodan Fang, Michal Ulewicz, Gegi Thomas, and Evelyn Duesterwald
IBM
Abstract
LLM agents on long-horizon tasks fail in recurring, procedu-
ral ways. They mis-paginate an API, resolve the wrong entity,
or answer when no answer was asked. We built a pipeline that
lets an agent learn from its own history. It first mines short
lessons from the agent’s own trajectories, one to three per
episode. It then consolidates those lessons into a smaller set
of guidelines, where each guideline records how many lessons
it merged. At inference the agent receives either all guidelines
or a selected subset. The pipeline ships in the open-source
altk-evolve library and is deployed in IBM’s CUGA agent and
watsonx Orchestrate platform. We report what we learned
building, measuring, and productizing it. Our primary instru-
ment is the AppWorld benchmark, across models spanning
40–92% baseline task completion. The central finding is that
the right amount of memory is a property of the model, not the
memory. A strong model keeps improving as guidelines are
added. DeepSeek-V3.2 gains +9.5 points of task completion
and +16.1 points of scenario completion with its full 191-
guideline set. A weak model gains less from the same full set
than from a small selected subset. gpt-oss-120b starts at 39.9%
task completion. It reaches 51.2% with all 199 of its guidelines
but 55.4% (mean of two runs) with a selected subset of about
29. Around that result we report what went wrong: a high-
support guideline that backfired, provenance silently dropped
during consolidation, a swallowed API error that failed every
task while producing a plausible log, and a baseline confound
that nearly produced a misleading comparison with a prior
method. We distill these into recommendations for teams de-
ploying agent memory.
Introduction
Agents built on large language models fail on realistic multi-
step tasks in a distinctive way. We read hundreds of trajecto-
ries of IBM’s CUGA agent and of the AppWorld reference
agent. The failures are rarely knowledge gaps. The model
knows the API, yet it mis-paginates it. It knows the user has
contacts, yet it resolves the wrong one. It knows how to return
an answer, yet it returns one when nothing was asked. These
are procedural lapses, and they recur. That makes them look
learnable from the agent’s own history.
That observation is now widely shared. Recent systems let
an agent write notes about its experience and read them back
Copyright © 2027, Association for the Advancement of Artificial
Intelligence (www.aaai.org). All rights reserved.
later. Examples include ExpeL (Zhao et al. 2024), Agentic
Context Engineering (ACE) (Zhang et al. 2026), and re-
flective memory in generative agents (Park et al. 2023). In
products, Anthropic’s “dreaming” consolidates memory for
managed agents (Anthropic 2026). What remains scarce is
an account of what happens when such a system is built,
measured carefully, and shipped.
This paper is that account. Our pipeline has three stages. It
first extracts lessons from the agent’s own trajectories: short,
imperative notes about what to do differently, one to three per
episode. It then consolidates those lessons into guidelines,
a smaller set in which each guideline records how many
lessons support it. Finally, it delivers guidelines to the agent at
inference, either all of them or a selected subset. The pipeline
is part of the open-source altk-evolve library (AgentToolkit
2026). It is deployed in IBM products, including the CUGA
agent and the watsonx Orchestrate platform. To measure it
we used AppWorld (Trivedi et al. 2024). AppWorld offers
three things a deployment needs and a production log rarely
provides: an authoritative pass/fail verdict per task, graded
difficulty, and a clean train/dev/test separation.
The method is not the contribution of this paper. Several
of its pieces have precedents, which we credit below. The
contribution is what we learned deploying it across models
from 40% to 92% baseline task completion. In the spirit of
this track, we focus on what went wrong:
• The right amount of memory is a property of the model.
A strong model keeps improving as guidelines are added.
A weak model gains more from a small, selected subset
than from the same full set (Insight 1).
• Compressing memory to a tidy checklist discards most of
its value. The value lives in one-off, situational lessons
(Insight 2).
• Selection is only possible if provenance survives consol-
idation. During productization it silently did not, twice
(Insight 3).
• A frequently derived guideline can still be wrong. Support
measures recurrence, not correctness (Insight 4).
• Run-to-run noise on a fixed configuration is large enough
to fabricate a “win” (Insight 5).
• Comparing memory systems across different agent scaf-
folds nearly produced a misleading headline (Insight 6).
arXiv:2611.26361v1  [cs.AI]  19 Nov 2026
• Silent failures cost more calendar time than any model-
ing problem: a swallowed HTTP error, an idle-dropped
connection, and a write hook that never fired (Insight 7).
We close with the practices we now apply and with a sec-
tion on deployment in IBM’s products. That section reports
CUGA benchmark results re-collected after the write-path
bug described in Insight 7, with GPT-4.1 and GLM-5.3-
Flash, and a qualitative example from watsonx Orchestrate.
The System: altk-evolve
The library.
altk-evolve is an open-source library for
agents that learn from their own runs (AgentToolkit 2026).
Its guideline generation builds on our group’s earlier work
on trajectory-informed memory (Fang et al. 2026). It cap-
tures trajectories in three ways. It can instrument common
client libraries directly (OpenAI, LiteLLM, smolagents, and
the OpenAI Agents SDK). It can sync traces from an observ-
ability store such as Arize Phoenix. Or an agent can hand
over a trajectory through an MCP tool at the end of a task.
From each trajectory an LLM extracts short lessons, option-
ally after segmenting the trajectory into subtasks. Lessons,
and the guidelines consolidated from them, are stored as
entities with metadata (category, rationale, trigger, source
task, and support) in a pluggable backend: a filesystem store
for development, or Milvus or Postgres with pgvector for
semantic search. Consolidation clusters related lessons on
their source-task embeddings and merges within each clus-
ter with an LLM. It is support-conserving: every guideline
records how many lessons it merged, and delivery can select
by that count. Both are described below. Agents consume
memory through an MCP server that exposes tools such
as get_guidelines, get_relevant_guidelines,
and save_trajectory. A Python client, a CLI, and a
web UI serve developers and reviewers. CUGA connects to
the library over MCP. The rest of this section describes each
stage as we ran it for this study.
Extraction.
We run the agent on the benchmark’s train and
dev splits and keep every trajectory, successes and failures
alike. For each trajectory, the extraction stage prompts an
LLM to write one to three short imperative lessons about
what to do differently next time. Whether a lesson counts
as success- or failure-evidence comes from the task’s actual
outcome, as judged by the evaluator. It never comes from
the LLM’s self-report. For DeepSeek-V3.2, 147 train/dev
trajectories yield 290 raw lessons. Of these, 62 come from
failures and 228 from successes.
Why consolidation is forced.
Raw episodic memory does
not stay small. Most of what accumulates is near-duplicate.
Five different tasks discover pagination the hard way, and all
five write it down. Left alone, this breaks the natural delivery
mechanism, retrieval. The top-k slots fill with copies of the
same lesson. Genuinely different guidance is crowded out.
Irrelevant one-offs arrive as dead context. Consolidation is
therefore not a cost optimization. It is what makes memory
retrievable at all.
Support-conserving
consolidation.
The
consolidation
stage embeds the lessons and clusters near-duplicates. It then
prompts an LLM to merge only within a cluster, and only
when following one lesson is equivalent to following the
other. Each surviving guideline carries a support count: how
many independent lessons collapsed into it. It also carries a
merged evidence polarity (success, failure, or both). One in-
variant is enforced: the sum of support over the output equals
the number of raw lessons. Anything the LLM fails to cover
is carried through unchanged. For DeepSeek this turns 290
lessons into 191 guidelines, of which 144 have support one.
Delivery.
A guideline set can be injected statically, or
delivered by retrieval. In retrieval, a core of high-support
guidelines (support ≥3) is always included. The top-k fur-
ther guidelines are then added, chosen by how similar their
source task is to the current task. Candidates already cov-
ered by the core, or duplicating one another, are dropped.
Thresholding by support (“sup2”, “sup3”) happens at selec-
tion time and never deletes anything from the store. In altk-
evolve these are configuration: consolidation_mode,
min_support, core_support, retrieval_top_k,
and injection_mode.
Deployment constraint.
altk-evolve generally uses the
same model that the agent uses. In this study, the model
that ran the agent is also the model that extracted its lessons
and consolidated them. There is no separate teacher model
and no human labeling. This mirrors the deployment we care
about, an agent that improves from its own logs. It also makes
the capability-dependence in Insight 1 an unavoidable design
question rather than a curiosity.
Measurement Setting
AppWorld simulates nine applications (email, payments,
music, shopping, and others) behind 457 APIs and about
a hundred simulated people (Trivedi et al. 2024). Its 750
tasks require writing and executing Python against those
APIs. We use test_normal (168 tasks) throughout and
test_challenge (417 tasks) where noted. The agent is
the reference ReAct code agent. Each step is one model call
that writes Python, and the environment returns the output.
We report two metrics. TGC is the fraction of tasks that pass
all of their evaluation checks. SGC is the stricter fraction of
scenarios in which every task variant passes. Eight models
were baselined and six were run with memory. All memory is
mined from train/dev only. Because dev is consumed by min-
ing, no held-out split was left for choosing a configuration.
We compared configurations directly on test_normal:
five for DeepSeek-V3.2, four for gpt-oss-120b, two each for
GPT-5.5, GLM-5, and Gemma-4-31B, and one for Claude
Opus 4.6. Table 2 therefore reports, next to each model’s best
configuration, a fixed rule decided before any test run: inject
all guidelines. Results are single runs, the benchmark’s con-
vention, except where noted. Insight 5 quantifies what that
hides.
Insights
Insight 1: The right dose is a property of the model
What we expected. That memory would help every model
roughly in proportion to its headroom.

What happened. Table 2 and Figure 1. Three regimes ap-
peared. A strong model with headroom keeps improving as
memory grows. DeepSeek-V3.2 climbs 79.8 →82.7 →83.9
→85.7 →89.3 TGC as the injected set grows from 0 to
12 to 19 to 47 to all 191 guidelines. Each step is two to
four tasks and within noise on its own. The trend is not:
the endpoints are 16 tasks apart. SGC rises from 64.3 to
80.4. The gain holds on the hard split (60.4 →72.9 TGC,
41.7 →58.3 SGC). GPT-5.5, already at 92.3, still gains with
all 207 of its own guidelines (95.2/89.3). The TGC gain is
about five tasks, at the noise floor. The SGC gain is larger.
A weak model shows a different curve. gpt-oss-120b starts
at 39.9. With all 199 guidelines it scores 51.2. That is no
better than the 53.6 it scores with a 24-guideline core, a gap
of four tasks. Its best result comes from about 29 selected
guidelines: 55.4 TGC, the mean of two runs (56.0 and 54.8).
That is seven tasks above the full set, at essentially baseline
token cost (116K vs. 110K per task). The fixed all-guidelines
rule in Table 2 leaves every model at or above its baseline
and keeps both large gains: +9.5 for DeepSeek and +11.3
for gpt-oss. Two further regimes bracket the range. GLM-5
is saturated: it scores 87.5 with or without its 72 guidelines.
Gemma-4-31B is too weak to apply memory: a wash overall,
and hurt by an over-tight core.
What we changed. The first implementation had one deliv-
ery mode. The shipped one exposes dose as configuration. It
defaults conservatively to retrieval with a high-support core,
because the failure mode of too much memory on a weak
model is silent. The agent does not error. It just does worse.
We also stopped saying “memory helps.” The honest state-
ment is that the optimal amount is a function of capability. A
memory system that cannot vary it will be wrong for some
of its users.
Where the gains land.

Insight 2: Do not compress. The value is in the long

What we expected. Our first consolidation prompt asked the
LLM for a small set of highly relevant rules, which is what a
person would ask for. It produced twelve, and they read well.
What happened. Those twelve gave DeepSeek +2.9 TGC.
The full set of 191 gave +9.5 and more than doubled the
SGC gain. The two differ by eleven tasks, well above noise.
Every intermediate dose fell between them. The difference
is the 144 guidelines with support one. These are situational
lessons that a summarizer discards as unimportant, precisely
because each occurred once. This corroborates, from outside,

What we changed. Lossless became the default consol-
idation mode, and compression became an explicit opt-in.
Insight 1 is the necessary qualifier. On a weak model the full
long tail is exactly what drowns it. “Keep everything” is only
right when delivery can select.
Insight 3: Selection needs provenance, and
provenance is easy to lose
What we expected. That consolidation and selection were
independent stages.
What happened. They are not. Selection by support re-
quires that support survive consolidation. Retrieval by source
task requires that the source task survive it. When we pro-
ductized into altk-evolve we found two independent ways
this had already broken. An earlier version of the consoli-
dation stage rebuilt each merged guideline’s metadata from
a fixed field list. It silently dropped any provenance not on
the list, including the support count and a generation-method
tag another team was relying on. Separately, the first version
of support attribution double-counted a member whenever
the LLM repeated an index inside one merge. An automated
code reviewer caught it before a person did.
What we changed. Conservation is now an enforced invari-
ant with a regression test, not a convention. Consolidation
reports total support before and after. Any lesson the LLM
fails to cover is carried through verbatim. The lesson gen-
eralizes to any memory pipeline. If a later stage, such as
selection, filters or ranks on a field, then every earlier stage,
such as extraction and consolidation, must preserve that field
as an invariant.
Insight 4: Support is recurrence, not correctness
What we expected. That a lesson derived independently by
many episodes was safe to trust.
What happened. A high-support pagination guideline read
“loop until fewer than the page limit are returned.” The rule
is correct only if the agent knows the page limit, and it did
not. It assumed a limit of 20, while the API’s default page
size was 5. The first page therefore held 5 items. Since 5
is fewer than 20, the agent concluded that it had seen the
last page and stopped. It missed every later page. That was
a regression on a task the baseline had passed. We fixed it
by hand. The reworded guideline says “pass an explicit page
limit and loop until a page comes back empty,” which no
longer depends on guessing the default. The task recovered,
and hard-tier TGC rose from 66.7 to 73.0.
What we changed. Nothing automatic, and that is the in-
sight. Support counts how often a lesson was derived. That is
evidence of generality, not of correctness. A popular wrong
lesson scores high. Our pipeline has no notion of a guide-
line being contradicted, stale, or harmful. Systems designed
as ongoing maintenance loops do. Anthropic’s dreaming re-
solves contradictions in favor of the most recent value and
prunes stale entries (Anthropic 2026). ExpeL lets the model
down-vote an insight to deletion (Zhao et al. 2024). Genera-
tive agents weight retrieval by recency (Park et al. 2023). We
now regard a correctness or recency signal as the most im-
portant missing component. We would not run an unattended
memory loop without one.
Insight 5: Measure the noise floor before believing
a delta
What we expected. That temperature zero and a fixed seed
made runs comparable.
What happened. Two runs of an identical gpt-oss-120b

Beam Model Technical Report, Reflection Team et al.
Abstract
Beam is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 501.3B total parameters and 23.4B
active parameters, specifically built and optimized for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads.
Beam delivers frontier level reasoning, while requiring 3-4x less inference compute than many
models of its class. Pretrained on 23.8T diverse, curated, high-quality tokens, Beam features
a 1M-token context window achieved through a novel two-stage midtraining phase, built on
verifiable, correctness-anchored data. Post-training leveraged a large-scale, fully asynchronous
reinforcement learning (RL) campaign across 10.5K GB300 GPUs, generating over 100M rollouts
over 4 weeks of training. We believe this is one of the largest scale RL runs conducted by any open
lab to date. Across our evaluation suite, capabilities continued to improve as we increased RL
compute, with no sign of a plateau. Supported by deep hardware-model co-design, FP8/NVFP4
quantization, and a 1.93B-parameter speculative decoding drafter (DFlash 2), Beam maximizes
serving throughput with efficient, flexible deployment. Averaged across conversation turns and
harm categories, Beam refuses or pivots on 88.9% of harmful requests while complying with
81.5% of harmless requests, achieving the highest refusal/pivot rate on harmful requests among
open-weight models on the Pareto frontier.
1
Introduction
We are introducing Beam, Reflection’s first open-weight model. Beam is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model
with 501.3B total parameters and 23.4B active parameters across 52 layers, 256 experts, and a 152K vocabulary
size, specifically built and optimized for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads.
Beam’s capabilities stem from major investments across pretraining, midtraining, post-training, and infrastructure.
Beam advances the Western open-weight frontier and achieves competitive performance with larger models like
GLM-5.2 while approaching Qwen 3.8-Max on LongBench-v2, while delivering frontier-level reasoning, while
requiring 3-4x less inference compute than many models of its class.
The foundation of Beam’s efficiency and numerical stability lies in rigorous data curation and controlled scaling.
Pretrained on 23.8T diverse, curated, high-quality tokens—including high-value STEM, math, and code tokens
preserved via novel domain-specific curation pipelines and internet-scale OCR—Beam’s scaling held predictably
across four orders of magnitude in pretraining compute, training models from 300M to 23.4B active parameters.
Beam’s base architecture employs auxiliary-loss-free load balancing with cosine decay, sequence-level balancing,
and depth-based residual scaling to achieve near-uniform expert utilization and bounded residual norms. It was
pretrained end-to-end in under four weeks on 6,144 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs with a 92.3% goodput toward the end
and 21% MFU during steady-state training, after accounting for restarts.
To bridge foundational knowledge and agentic execution, a novel two-stage midtraining pipeline expanded Beam’s
effective context length to 1M tokens on correctness-anchored data without degrading general capabilities. Post-
training was centered around a high-compute reinforcement learning (RL) campaign, where our high-compute
RL run generated over 100M rollouts on 10.5K NVIDIA GB300 GPUs over four weeks of training. We believe
this is one of the largest scale RL runs conducted by any open lab to date, enabled by a fully asynchronous
platform with 110K concurrent rollouts, fast 12-second weight updates, and 99.99% dynamic batch packing, Beam
organically developed tool-use, web browsing, and problem-decomposition capabilities. Across our evaluation
suite, capabilities continued to improve as we increased RL compute, with no sign of a plateau. For serving, Beam
leverages hardware-model co-design, FP8/NVFP4 quantization, and DFlash 2 (a 1.93B-parameter speculative
decoding drafter) to reduce memory footprint and maximize throughput.
Safety and alignment were prioritized across the entire model development cycle. Pretraining filtered harmful
content and PII, while post-training combined deliberative alignment SFT with context-aware RL across multi-
turn, jailbreak, and agentic tasks. Dedicated safety and RL teacher capabilities were merged using multi-teacher
on-policy distillation (MOPD). Under Reflection’s Open Safety Framework (OSF), we assessed Beam as Limited
across all four systemic-risk categories: Biological Weapons, Chemical Weapons, Loss of Control, and Cyber

Context as a Resource
Xufei Tian 1 Han Hu 1 Wenli Du 1
§ Code: https://github.com/Viacol0916/ClonAct
 Blog: https://viacol.pages.dev/blog/context-as-a-resource/
Abstract
Managing concurrent tasks across separate agent
sessions quickly exhausts human attention, mo-
tivating always-on personal agents behind a sin-
gle continuous interface. Yet when every context
shares identical frozen backbone weights, fun-
neling interleaved dialogues and external events
into one linear session induces cross-topic con-
straint bleed and head-of-line stalling. Conversely,
router–ticket hierarchies incur lossy prose hand-
offs, heavy routing overhead, and blind merges—
collapsing true-conflict repository merges to
a 33.3% three-run mean despite high isolated
branch passes. Rather than scheduling anthropo-
morphic roles, we introduce CLONACT, a router-
less architecture that virtualizes context blocks
directly through a pluggable single-pass non-
generative Context MMU, in-place Context Cells,
a footprint-aware Synaptic Bus with an isolated
trial merge gate, and a wave-flushed Shared Trunk.
Across three programmatic multi-stream bench-
marks and three model families, our portable trial
merge gate lifts true-conflict merges to 63.3%,
while CLONACT’s routerless virtualization attains
this ceiling with 45.9% fewer prompt tokens and
prevents compact-model router collapse. Under
continuous surge streams, CLONACT matches top
completion (95.0%) with the lowest median wait
and zero timed-out status checks.
1. Introduction
Modern tool-using language model agents can complete a
range of coding and workflow tasks end-to-end within an
isolated session (Yao et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024; Wang
et al., 2025). In daily work, however, tasks rarely run one at
a time: users advance multiple tasks in parallel while asyn-
chronous requests and notifications continue arriving from

external channels (Froger et al., 2026). Today, users typi-
cally isolate concurrent work by manually opening separate
sessions and workspaces, yet monitoring progress, switch-
ing focus, and ferrying intermediate findings across many
live sessions quickly exhausts human attention (Qiao, 2026;
DeepSeek Harness Team, 2026). Building an always-on per-
sonal agent therefore requires hiding session management
inside the runtime so that users interact through a single con-
tinuous interface (Packer et al., 2023; DeepSeek Harness
Team, 2026)—raising a central architectural question: how
should an agent system coordinate concurrent tasks behind
one unified window when every underlying instance shares
the same model weights?
Long-context studies document sensitivity to input length
and evidence position (Liu et al., 2024; Levy et al., 2024).
In our interleaved-task diagnosis (Section 2), a single lin-
ear context (DSH-Mono, Figure 1a) also exhibits cross-task
constraint bleed—a read-only lookup caveat can suppress
an in-flight code change—while long tool turns stall status
queries by 3.9× (Figure 2a). Moreover, as cumulative-
request experiments by Qiao (2026) demonstrate, subagent
delegation in a monolithic session is prompt-dependent and
1

Context as a Resource
not guaranteed, motivating structural separation behind one
entry point via multi-role teams (DSH-AgentTeam; Hong
et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2024) or a res-
ident top-level router that summarizes dialogues into iso-
lated worker mandates (DSH-SuperAgent, Figure 1b; Qiao,
2026; DeepSeek Harness Team, 2026). Yet unlike human
organizations whose heterogeneous expertise requires role
division and verbal handoffs, agent instances sharing iden-
tical System-2 weights (θ1 = θ2 = θ) can be scheduled
to continue the same supplied context without a new prose
handoff. Under a locked execution kernel (Section 2), when
workloads move from independent tasks to interactive clarifi-
cation and shared-repository edits, interposing role or router
layers incurs three measurable costs: handoff serialization
loss as static tickets drop alignment nuances (Section 4.6), a
last-mile merge cliff where concurrent workers pass 90.0%
of true-conflict pairs inside isolated branches yet drop to
a 33.3% three-run mean (10.0% in Run 1) upon merging,
and up to 2.6× prompt token volume over single-session
execution from repeated router decoding.
Motivated by effective single-agent loops in existing de-
ployments (Sarkis, 2026), we decouple cross-task multi-
plexing from top-down task decomposition and propose
CLONACT (Figure 1c; Section 3, Figure 3), which schedules
context blocks, rather than anthropomorphic roles, directly
as virtualized resources. All System-2 execution and dia-
logue Context Cells share identical frozen weights πθ with
zero generative router layer, while a pluggable single-pass
non-generative Context MMU—instantiated either with a
lightweight probability-scoring classifier or same-weight
single-token log-probability probing of πθ—routes user
turns and external events directly to independent Context
Cells. Each cell clarifies requirements with the user in
a zero-directory read-only state and, upon confirmation,
promotes in-place to lazy-mounted Git worktree execu-
tion along its exact alignment token spine—avoiding ticket
rewriting while retaining stable prefixes compatible with
provider-side caching. Across concurrent cells, a footprint-
aware Synaptic Bus blocks raw tool noise while synchro-
nizing shared AST and resource footprints ahead of a three-
stage isolated trial merge gate, atop a byte-locked Shared
Trunk that grounds workspace conventions across cells.
To complement task-based coding and app benchmarks
(Jimenez et al., 2024; Trivedi et al., 2024) with inter-
leaved intake and shared-workspace concurrency, we con-
struct three zero-overlap programmatic suites (Section 4.1):
Synaptic-Bench-150, pairing live repository, database, and
office sandboxes with deterministic tool-count Step-Hooks;
AppWorld-Micro-30, an uncoupled everyday-errand con-
trol; and Synaptic-Stream-60, feeding continuous 240-event
omnichannel streams under moderate and 2.5× surge ar-
rival rates. Across 1,800 episodic rollouts, 170 diagnostic
controls, and 36 continuous streams over three model fami-
lies, our controls separate two complementary effects: the
portable trial merge gate lifts true-conflict merges from
33.3% to 63.3% across three runs (10.0% →80.0% in
Run 1), while CLONACT’s routerless virtualization attains
this ceiling with 45.9% fewer prompt tokens than DSH-
SuperAgent, 100.0% orchestration safety, and zero penalty
on uncoupled errands. Under conflict-free surge streams,
CLONACT matches top completion (95.0%) with the lowest
median wait and zero timed-out status checks, while dual-
tier billing exposes explicit load-dependent cost trade-offs.
Pre-registered ablations validate target-slice causal disso-
ciation and same-weight log-probability gating, and cross-
backbone runs improve pooled resolution by +11.5 pp over
DSH-SuperAgent while preventing compact-model router
collapse.
Our contributions are threefold:
• We propose CLONACT, a routerless architecture that
schedules homogeneous System-2 Context Cells as vir-
tualized resources via a pluggable single-pass Context
MMU, in-place align-to-execute promotion, footprint-
aware synaptic reconciliation, and a wave-flushed Shared
Trunk (Section 3).
• We introduce Synaptic-Bench-150, AppWorld-Micro-
30, and Synaptic-Stream-60, zero-overlap multi-stream
benchmarks combining un-partitioned intake, determin-
istic Step-Hooks, live repository conflicts, and dual-rate
continuous arrival streams under deterministic state ora-
cles (Section 4.1).
• We isolate the causal roles of trial-merge settlement and
routerless virtualization across three model families, re-
solving bleed and merge cliffs while exposing explicit
dual-tier cost and backbone-floor trade-offs (Section 4).
2. Problem Formulation and Mechanism
Diagnosis
Before introducing our architecture, we formalize concur-
rent agent orchestration over homogeneous model weights,
recover existing paradigms as structural special cases, and
empirically isolate why each breaks down under interleaved
and state-coupled workloads.
2.1. Two-Operator Formulation of Concurrent Agents
Consider an always-on personal agent backed by a
frozen black-box language model policy πθ acting over
a mutable shared workspace Wt (code repositories, rela-
tional databases, filesystems, and personal applications).
Rather than receiving one isolated prompt, the system ob-
serves an arrival-ordered omnichannel event stream E =
{(et, τt, st)}T
t=1 (τ1 ≤· · · ≤τT ), interleaving foreground
user dialogue (st = chat: multi-turn clarifications, mid-

Trivial Base Case and Paradigm Specializations. When

(4) Resident router–ticket–worker (DSH-SuperAgent; Qiao,

Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2027
DEEPQUEST: FROM KNOWLEDGE GAPS TO SCIEN-
TIFIC DISCOVERY IN ALZHEIMER’S DISEASE
Chunbo Jiang1,*, Yifei Chen2,*, Beining Wu1, Fuyou Mao3, Weihong Chen1,
Enyu Bao1, Mingxuan Liu2, Feiwei Qin1,†, Qiyuan Tian2,†
1Hangzhou Dianzi University
2Tsinghua University
3Central South University
ABSTRACT
Automating experiments does not necessarily advance scientific understanding.
Research agents must identify meaningful knowledge gaps, determine what avail-
able data can resolve, and assess whether their findings advance existing knowl-
edge. We introduce DeepQuest, a knowledge-gap-driven AI scientist framework
for Alzheimer’s disease research. DeepQuest transforms unresolved questions
from domain reviews into traceable, testable hypotheses and prioritizes them
through data feasibility screening and groupwise Elo ranking. It couples itera-
tive experimentation with two-level auditing that separates experimental reliability
from knowledge contribution relative to two frozen literature corpora. On OASIS-
3, DeepQuest produces 42 feasible hypotheses and outperforms the strongest base-
lines in 14 of 15 evaluator–dimension comparisons across three language-model
reviewers. The full framework achieves an audit-assessed scientific finding rate
of 95.24%, outperforming both general-purpose executors and domain-specific
research agents. This scientific finding rate remains stable across literature cor-
pora and evaluator model families. Representative findings concern neuropsy-
chiatric symptoms and dementia risk, longitudinal amyloid spatial stability, and
neocortical tau-associated clinical impairment, with key associations supported in
independent ADNI and AIBL cohorts. These results show how aligning knowl-
edge gaps, data feasibility, and evidence auditing can turn automated research into
traceable, evidence-supported scientific discovery. Our source code is available at
https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DeepQuest-3066/.
1
INTRODUCTION
A central challenge in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) research is to translate the growing body of hetero-
geneous evidence into testable scientific questions that advance understanding of the disease. The
complex pathology of AD spans multiple biological levels (Jack Jr et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025;
Shwab et al., 2025). Large scale cohorts and data sharing initiatives have assembled multimodal data
encompassing clinical assessments, cognitive measures, genetic information, biofluid biomarkers,
magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and positron emission tomography (PET), providing a founda-
tion for investigating disease states, progression, and pathological associations (Travaglia & Hoff-
mann, 2024; Toga et al., 2024; Veitch et al., 2026; Weiner et al., 2025). DiaMond learns cross-modal
disease representations from MRI and PET (Li et al., 2025b). CARE-AD extracts information on
disease evolution from longitudinal clinical records (Li et al., 2025a). The multitask model proposed
by Wang et al. (2025) jointly analyzes brain age, cognition, and amyloid pathology. These advances
strengthen data analysis while placing greater demands on evidence organization, research question
formulation, and the evaluation of existing disease understanding.
Research agents have extended automation across multiple stages of the scientific work-
flow, yet completing the workflow does not by itself ensure scientifically valuable discov-
eries.
General-purpose AI Scientist systems such as DeepScientist can generate candi-
date hypotheses, plan experiments, and iteratively refine their exploration based on feedback

integrates knowledge-gap-driven hypothesis formulation, data-constrained task selection, iterative
experimentation, and literature-based knowledge contribution assessment.
(Weng et al., 2026; Yamada et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2025). Domain-specific systems, such as Med-
ical AI Scientist, AMID and SPARK, further integrate domain knowledge, specialized tools, and
quality control mechanisms to support complex analytical workflows in medicine and neuroscience
(Wu et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Han et al., 2026; Trost et al., 2026). However, generating hypothe-
ses and executing experiments for a predefined objective still requires assessing whether they address
important knowledge gaps, are testable with available data, and advance existing understanding.
Autonomous scientific discovery in AD requires three interdependent decisions: problem formula-
tion, task selection, and knowledge contribution assessment. First, limitations identified in the liter-
ature must be translated into experimentally testable hypotheses with explicit evidential provenance,
thereby establishing a traceable link between existing knowledge and newly formulated research
questions. Second, scientifically meaningful questions are not necessarily answerable with available
medical data. Task selection must therefore balance scientific value against execution cost under
constraints imposed by data feasibility and experimental resources. Third, experimental reliability
and scientific contribution should be assessed separately. Improvements in predictive performance
or statistical significance may support specific experimental conclusions, but neither alone estab-
lishes that a study has produced new understanding of the disease. Integrating these stages enables
research agents to pursue questions according to their potential knowledge gain.
To this end, we propose DeepQuest, an AI scientist framework for AD research designed to advance
existing knowledge by integrating knowledge gap identification, data-constrained task selection, ex-
perimental validation, and knowledge contribution assessment as shown in Fig. 1. DeepQuest first
extracts structured research limitations from domain reviews and transforms them into testable hy-
potheses. It then applies multi-stage screening and relative priority ranking under data feasibility
constraints to select research tasks that are both scientifically valuable and feasible to execute. Dur-
ing experimentation, DeepQuest combines iterative execution with a two-level audit of workflow
reliability and the contribution of conclusions beyond existing knowledge. This integrates problem
formulation, task selection, and conclusion assessment into a unified research process.
Experimental results support the effectiveness of DeepQuest at three levels: hypothesis quality,
knowledge contribution assessment, and validation on independent cohorts. Across all three eval-
uator models, mean evaluation scores for the 42 executable hypotheses generated by DeepQuest
were better than those for five strong generative-model baselines. The evidence audit classified the
resulting experimental claims from 40 of 42 hypotheses (95.24%) as Candidate New Discovery or
Extension. All ten top-ranked hypotheses were identified as having the potential to advance existing
2
Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2027
knowledge. Three representative case studies on amyloid spatial topology, neuropsychiatric symp-
toms and dementia risk, and the relationship between tau pathology and clinical impairment further
demonstrate DeepQuest’s ability to carry research from problem formulation through evidence val-
idation. The corresponding findings were broadly supported in independent external cohorts.
Overall, our contributions are as follows:
• We introduce a review-driven approach to formulating scientific questions in AD research.
The method transforms research limitations identified in AD domain reviews into structured
representations and testable hypotheses, establishing a traceable mapping from literature
evidence and knowledge gaps to research questions.
• We introduce a data-constrained task selection and optimization approach. It formulates
task selection as an optimization problem over the intersection between the literature-
derived research space and the data feasibility region. Through multi-stage screening and
priority ranking, it balances scientific value with execution feasibility.
• We develop a two-level auditing mechanism that separates experimental reliability from
knowledge contribution. DeepQuest independently examines whether experiments are re-
liable and conclusions extend beyond existing knowledge, providing traceable evidence for
assessing candidate scientific discoveries and their contributions.
2
RELATED WORK
General Autonomous Scientific Research Systems. General-purpose AI research systems auto-
mate multiple research stages by connecting hypothesis generation, experimental search, and feed-
back (Lu et al., 2024; Schmidgall et al., 2025; Mitchener et al., 2025). AI Scientist-v2 (Yamada
et al., 2025) organizes experimental exploration through agent-based tree search and performs result
analysis and manuscript generation. AI-Researcher (Tang et al., 2025) integrates literature inves-
tigation, hypothesis formulation, and algorithm implementation through multiagent collaboration.
DeepScientist (Weng et al., 2026) formulates scientific discovery as a Bayesian optimization prob-
lem and combines discovery memory with hierarchical validation to iteratively select and explore
promising candidate directions. Collectively, these systems demonstrate the capacity for open-ended
scientific ideation and autonomous research direction selection, with representative evaluations con-
ducted primarily on machine learning tasks. Applying these mechanisms to AD cohort studies
requires aligning hypotheses with target populations, observable variables, follow-up windows, and
confounding-control requirements, so empirical evidence constrains question selection.
Biomedical Research Agents. Biomedical research agents advance hypothesis exploration for med-
ical problems by incorporating domain knowledge and specialized validation procedures (Huang
et al., 2026). Co-Scientist (Gottweis et al., 2026) iteratively refines research directions through
hypothesis generation, critique, and ranking, and conducts experimental validation in biomedical
settings. Robin (Ghareeb et al., 2026) combines literature-based reasoning, candidate selection, and
experimental feedback to support the discovery of therapeutic candidates. Medical AI Scientist (Wu
et al., 2026) provides three modes for paper-based reproduction, literature-inspired innovation, and
task-driven exploration, using coordinated medical and engineering reasoning to identify research
gaps, formulate hypotheses, and execute experiments. These systems integrate literature-grounded
reasoning and question exploration into scientific workflows, providing important points of refer-
ence for developing autonomous biomedical research.
Research agents for medical imaging and clinical cohort studies further incorporate data adaptation,
analytical reliability, and hypothesis validation into the scientific workflow. AMID (Liu et al., 2026)
plans candidate methods according to the characteristics and constraints of available data and inte-
grates experimental auditing into model optimization. NEXUS (Han et al., 2026) uses quality feed-
back to revise neuroimaging analysis pipelines. NeuroAgent (Zhong et al., 2026) connects multi-
modal preprocessing, predictive modeling, and interactive analysis within a unified workflow. More
closely related to our setting, the Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias (ADRD) hypothesis-
testing system proposed by Saichandran et al. (2025) maps literature-derived hypotheses to available
variables in the NACC cohort and uses iterative analysis and methodological review to assess testa-
bility and conduct statistical tests. Its evaluation focuses primarily on replicating previously reported
associations. Our work extends the focus to the formulation, selection, and contribution assessment
3

of candidate research questions in AD. DeepQuest constructs structured domain-specific knowledge
gaps from domain reviews, prioritizes research tasks under data constraints, and separately audits
experimental reliability and the incremental contribution of conclusions beyond existing knowledge.

driven hypothesis formulation, (b) data-constrained task selection, (c) iterative experimentation with
execution auditing, and (d) literature-based knowledge contribution assessment.
3
METHOD
3.1
PROBLEM FORMULATION AND FRAMEWORK OVERVIEW
We formulate automated AD research as a knowledge-gap-driven process of task selection under
data constraints and evidence assessment. Given a collection of domain reviews R and medical data
D, DeepQuest constructs candidate research directions ui = (li, Hi), where li denotes a structured
research limitation and Hi denotes the corresponding set of hypotheses. It then proceeds through
knowledge gap extraction, data feasibility assessment, research priority ranking, iterative experi-
mentation, and knowledge contribution assessment, as illustrated in Fig. 2.
3.2
REVIEW-DRIVEN KNOWLEDGE GAP AND HYPOTHESIS CONSTRUCTION
Knowledge gap extraction organizes established knowledge and key unknowns from domain reviews
into traceable research limitations. DeepQuest extracts findings and unresolved relationships con-
cerning AD pathology, biomarkers, imaging, and clinical research. Each limitation records known
facts, unresolved phenomena, and supporting source evidence. Semantically equivalent unknowns
across reviews are consolidated into a unified limitation li.
Hypothesis construction transforms research limitations into scientific propositions testable against
observable outcomes. For each li, DeepQuest generates a hypothesis set Hi = {hij}ni
j=1 and spec-
ifies empirical predictions that distinguish competing explanations. Each knowledge gap and its
hypothesis set constitute a candidate research direction. This organization separates unresolved
questions from explanations while preserving traceability to the original problem.
3.3
DATA FEASIBILITY ASSESSMENT AND RESEARCH ASSET PREPARATION
The data summary provides an initial assessment of whether candidate research questions can be
examined with the available data. A data analysis agent examines the available variables, subject
structure, imaging records, and multimodal longitudinal follow-up relationships, and constructs the
following comprehensive structured representation:

DeepQuest applies soft gating to remove research directions that are clearly unsupported by the

Hypothesis-level assessment determines whether available data meet the requirements for empirical
validation. A data preparation agent examines each hypothesis alongside the structured summary
and raw data, checking correspondence among variables, samples, temporal information, and imag-
ing modalities. The feasible hypothesis set for each knowledge gap is denoted by Hfeas

retained individual hypotheses form UD. This stage establishes testability and specific analytical

Research asset preparation organizes the validated data into reusable inputs for downstream experi-
ments. DeepQuest registers verified assets according to data granularity, variable type, and scope of
applicability, and prioritizes retrieval and reuse of existing results. For data that have not yet been
curated, the system extracts and integrates the required information according to the variables and
observation levels specified by each hypothesis. Imaging preprocessing is performed in a modality-
specific manner. Structured data and preprocessed images are available for later experiments.
3.4
GROUPWISE COMPARATIVE RESEARCH PRIORITIZATION
Research ranking compares the value of exploring different knowledge gaps among data feasible
candidates under the available cohort and modality constraints. DeepQuest further filters hypotheses
that address core unresolved questions in AD, offer potential knowledge gain, and admit empirically
discriminative predictions, yielding the candidate set UC ⊆UD.

Training LLMs to Follow Reasoning Instructions
with Minimal Edits
Alexandra Yakovleva
Aalto University
alexandra.yakovleva@aalto.fi
Luat Gia Khoi Nguyen
System 2 AI
Juho Kannala
Aalto University
University of Oulu
Harri Valpola
System 2 AI
Alexander Ilin
System 2 AI
Abstract
Large language models increasingly rely on extended reasoning traces, yet the train-
ing signals used to shape this behavior remain coarse. Supervised fine-tuning on
full trajectories forces the model to imitate an entire demonstration, overconstrain-
ing its output distribution, while trajectory-level reinforcement learning provides
only weak credit assignment, rewarding or penalizing whole completions without
identifying where they succeed or fail. We propose edit-based training, a gen-
eral framework for learning from a model’s own trajectories via localized textual
corrections. Given a sampled completion, an editor identifies the first point of
failure under a specified criterion and proposes a minimal replacement span. The
model is then supervised only on these edited spans. By design, this concentrates
supervision where the model’s reasoning first breaks down and aims to preserve
its existing reasoning patterns elsewhere. The method applies both offline and
online, with the latter continually adapting supervision to the model’s evolving
failure modes. We instantiate this approach on reasoning instruction following with
Qwen3-32B on the ReasonIF benchmark. Compared to full-trajectory imitation and
trajectory-level reinforcement learning baselines, edit-based training substantially
improves compliance with the reasoning instruction while largely preserving the
model’s skills on untargeted tasks. These results suggest that localized correction
is an effective complement to these approaches for shaping how LLMs reason.
1
Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly trained to solve problems through extended reasoning.
In many recent systems, reasoning traces are not directly supervised step by step; instead, they emerge
from optimization procedures that reward successful final behavior. This indirect supervision is partly
a practical necessity. Specifying high-quality reasoning traces is difficult: good reasoning is often
task-dependent, may admit many valid forms, and is hard to supervise at scale. Moreover, effective
reasoning must remain compatible with the knowledge, linguistic patterns, and latent capabilities
already present in the pretrained model.
At the same time, control over the reasoning process is increasingly important. Reasoning is not
merely a means of producing an answer; it is also where a model interprets the task, forms a
plan, applies constraints, checks assumptions, and determines which intermediate conclusions to
trust. Better control over these steps could improve reliability, alignment, and robustness. Concrete
needs include articulating intermediate steps the model would otherwise compress, blocking known
shortcuts, requesting verification before the answer, or constraining style for downstream auditing.
40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: Transitioning from Pre-training to
Post-training.
arXiv:2611.26342v1  [cs.AI]  19 Nov 2026
Reliable reasoning instruction following is a prerequisite for using such constraints to make models
more controllable and transparent while reducing shortcuts, hallucinations, and reward hacking inside
reasoning traces [1]. In practice, however, current reasoning-capable LLMs often fail to follow such
instructions; they omit required steps, ignore constraints, or deviate from a prescribed strategy even
when the requirements are stated explicitly [1, 2], and open reasoning models comply on fewer than
25% of ReasonIF traces. This motivates the central goal of our work: to make language models more
reliably follow instructions about their reasoning process, not only instructions about the final answer.
A second motivation arises from how reasoning models are commonly trained. Reinforcement-
learning methods for reasoning, including Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)-style ap-
proaches [3], typically assign rewards or advantages to entire sampled trajectories. A reasoning
trace is therefore encouraged or discouraged as a whole, often based on its final outcome. Such
trajectory-level feedback can be inefficient. An incorrect trajectory may contain mostly sound reason-
ing, with failure caused by a single local mistake, such as a missed constraint, an invalid inference,
or an arithmetic error. Penalizing the entire trajectory risks discouraging useful reasoning behavior
together with the specific step that should be corrected. Conversely, a trajectory that reaches the
correct answer may still contain unnecessary, brittle, or logically flawed intermediate steps; rewarding
the full trajectory can reinforce these undesirable patterns simply because the final answer is correct.
These observations suggest that improving reasoning requires more targeted interventions. Instead of
treating a reasoning trace as an indivisible object, we seek to identify the critical point at which the
model first goes wrong and provide supervision only at that point. Our approach begins by sampling a
reasoning trace from the model. We then evaluate the trace to locate the first violation of the reasoning
instruction. Once this point is identified, we employ an editing model, or editor, to revise only the
local span that contains the error.
The edited span becomes the training target. Rather than training the model to imitate an entire
corrected trajectory, we apply the edit loss only to the small number of tokens needed to repair the
mistake. This design is based on the observation that small local corrections can redirect the model’s
subsequent reasoning. When a trace is repaired with just enough correct text at the critical point, the
corrected tokens can steer the model away from an erroneous path and toward a better continuation.
As a result, the method applies minimal supervision and is designed to preserve much of the model’s
original reasoning behavior. It intervenes only where the model’s reasoning first breaks down,
allowing the remaining trajectory to be generated according to the model’s existing capabilities and
priors. In this sense, our approach lies between reinforcement learning and conventional SFT. Like
reinforcement learning, it provides sparse guidance rather than full demonstration trajectories. Unlike
trajectory-level reinforcement learning, however, the guidance is textual and localized: it specifies
what should have been produced at the precise point where the reasoning fails. We argue that this
form of localized correction offers a practical route toward more controllable training while limiting
changes unrelated to the specified failure.
Our contributions are threefold. First, we introduce edit-based training, a framework that converts
model-generated reasoning failures into localized textual supervision at the first point of violation.
Second, we instantiate the framework in offline and online variants for reasoning instruction following,
with editors that can be scripted verifiers, LLM editors, or hybrids of the two. Third, we compare
edit-based training against full-trajectory SFT and trajectory-level GRPO, and show that it improves
reasoning instruction following while largely preserving the base model’s skills on the untargeted
tasks we measure.
2
Edit-based training for reasoning instruction following
2.1
Problem setting
We study the problem of training language models to better follow instructions about their reasoning
process. Our focus is not primarily on improving final task accuracy. Instead, we consider settings in
which the user specifies constraints on how reasoning should proceed, and the model must satisfy
those constraints while generating its solution. Examples of such reasoning-process instructions
include requirements to use a prescribed format, follow a specified sequence of steps, check particular
assumptions, avoid certain intermediate shortcuts, explicitly apply given constraints, reason in a
particular language or style, or separate planning, computation, and final answering. We treat final
2
performance improvement as a natural downstream application, but the central objective of this work
is reasoning control: making the model’s intermediate reasoning more compliant with the requested
procedure.
A natural approach is to construct full reasoning traces that satisfy the desired constraints and train
the model using supervised fine-tuning (SFT). One option is to prompt a stronger model to generate
complete compliant reasoning traces. However, this can introduce a distribution mismatch. The
stronger model may have different linguistic habits, may use reasoning patterns unavailable to the
target model, may solve the problem using different priors or latent capabilities, or may produce
demonstrations that are formally correct but unnatural for the target model to imitate. Another option
is to ask a stronger model to rewrite full traces produced by the target model so that they satisfy the
instructions. This reduces the mismatch, but it still imposes complete corrected trajectories on the
target model.
Full-trajectory SFT has a more fundamental limitation: it treats one complete reasoning trace as the
desired behavior, even though many valid continuations may exist. As a result, it can unnecessarily
reduce the entropy of the model’s reasoning distribution. The model is trained not only to avoid the
mistake, but also to imitate many incidental choices in the demonstration. This problem is especially
severe when the training set is small. With limited demonstrations, full-trajectory SFT can overfit to
narrow reasoning styles or solution paths. In contrast, our goal is to fix the model’s behavior while
avoiding this entropy-collapse problem [4, 5].
Another natural approach is to use reinforcement learning, such as GRPO-style training, with rewards
based on whether the generated reasoning satisfies the specified constraints. This approach avoids
full demonstrations and can optimize directly for instruction satisfaction. However, trajectory-level
rewards provide coarse feedback. If a long reasoning trace violates an instruction because of one
local mistake, the reward penalizes the entire trajectory. The central difficulty is credit assignment:
terminal rewards indicate whether a completion succeeded, but not where it first failed or what local
change would have repaired it. Our method addresses this limitation by replacing trajectory-level
feedback with localized textual corrections at the first point of failure.
2.2
Edit-based training procedure
Given a prompt with an instruction about the desired reasoning process, we first sample a response
from the current model (see Figure 1). We then inspect the generated reasoning trace to find the
first point at which it fails to follow the instruction. At that point, an editor proposes a minimal
replacement span. The replacement is designed to be surgical: it changes only the local text needed to
repair the failure. Such an edit may consist of only a few tokens, for example replacing an incorrect
transition, inserting a missing constraint, correcting a computation, or changing a step that violates
the required format. We intentionally avoid rewriting the entire reasoning trace.
After applying the edit, we continue sampling from the model conditioned on the corrected prefix.
The corrected tokens may redirect the subsequent reasoning, allowing the model to recover and
continue in a compliant way. We then evaluate the new continuation again, locate the first failure
in the new continuation if one exists, and propose another local edit. This process can be repeated
until the resulting trajectory satisfies the reasoning instruction or a stopping criterion is reached. The
final output of the procedure is a single model-generated trajectory containing several short corrected
spans. During training, the edit loss targets only the corrected spans. Thus, corrective supervision
focuses on the counterfactual local actions that would have prevented the reasoning failure.
The editor is a module that receives a prompt, a generated trace, and the reasoning instruction. Its role
is to identify the earliest span where the trace violates the instruction and to propose a replacement
span. The editor may be implemented in different ways depending on the task: as a scripted verifier
for formal or easily checkable constraints, as an LLM editor for more semantic reasoning instructions,
or as a hybrid system combining rule-based checks with model-based editing. In all cases, the editor
is instructed to make minimal edits rather than full rewrites. The proposed replacement is mapped to
the model’s tokens, and the first token that differs from the generated trace becomes the corrected
span. If, after this token, the model’s next generated token is the same as in the original trace, the
span is extended token by token until the next generated token differs from the original trace. On
average, a corrected span is shorter than two tokens.

Here, Dπ
fail denotes the distribution of failure prefixes induced by the current policy π. The important
distinction from standard supervised fine-tuning is that supervision is applied only at the edited span,
not over the full trajectory. If multiple edits are found in one trajectory, the cross-entropy is averaged
over the tokens of all edited spans. On the generated continuations between edits, we additionally
apply a KL regularizer toward the base model (Appendix B.7).
We consider two ways of applying the edit-based training procedure. In the offline setting, we first
generate a fixed dataset of model completions. We run the editor on these completions to produce
corrected spans, and then train the model on this fixed edit dataset. In the online setting, we repeatedly
generate completions using the current model. We then identify the current model’s failures, produce
edits, and train on those edits. As the model improves, the distribution of failures changes. Online
editing therefore focuses supervision on the mistakes that the current model actually makes. This
makes the online variant near-on-policy: training data is drawn from the model’s evolving failure
distribution.
Choice of loss function.
We use cross-entropy on the edit span, as in (1). Treating the edit as a
preference pair and optimizing the policy with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) [6] is a natural
alternative (formulated in Appendix C); we leave a systematic comparison to future work.
Relation to standard SFT.
The key distinction from full-trajectory SFT is where supervision is
concentrated. Our SFT baseline uses the same trajectories as Offline, treating both the model’s own
generated continuations and the edited spans as targets. Offline applies supervision only to localized
edits. This comparison tests the benefit of accurate credit assignment with the training data held fixed.
Online additionally adapts the training data to the model’s evolving failure distribution.
Relation to online imitation learning.
Because edits can be generated from the current policy’s
failed completions, the online version resembles DAgger-style imitation learning [7]. The editor does
not provide a full expert trajectory from the initial state. Instead, the editor labels the states actually
4
reached by the learner. In our setting, these states are failure prefixes in generated reasoning traces.
This distinction is important because reasoning failures are often policy-dependent. A model may fail
in ways that are specific to its own style, knowledge, and decoding behavior. Online edit training
targets precisely these failures. The online version is therefore a form of online corrective imitation:
the learner is trained on the errors it actually induces, rather than on idealized demonstrations sampled
from a fixed expert distribution.
Relation to trajectory-level RL.
Similarly to reinforcement learning, our method does not require
full expert demonstrations. The key difference is the form of feedback. Trajectory-level RL typically
assigns a binary or scalar reward (or an advantage derived from such rewards) to an entire sampled
completion. This indicates whether the completion succeeded but not what local change would have
repaired it. Edit feedback provides this missing credit assignment. This localization is especially
useful for long reasoning traces. A trajectory-level advantage may affect many tokens unrelated to
the actual failure. Edit supervision instead concentrates the update at the editor-identified failure
location, leaving the rest of the trajectory unsupervised. This can reduce credit diffusion and provide
a lower-variance corrective signal. Edit supervision may be especially useful early in training, when
fully successful trajectories are rare. In that regime, reward-based methods may observe little useful
variation, since many completions receive the same failing reward. Edits, by contrast, are available
precisely on failed samples, making supervision abundant when the model most needs corrective
feedback. More broadly, edits and trajectory-level RL are complementary rather than substitutes. Edit
supervision provides a localized textual specification of the corrected continuation that trajectory-level
RL lacks at this granularity, while RL provides an outcome-grounded signal that edit supervision
does not. Combining the two is a natural extension: edits to bootstrap the policy where successful
trajectories are rare, RL to optimize for downstream task correctness once instruction compliance
becomes routine.
3
Related work
Reasoning instruction following.
ReasonIF [1] introduces a benchmark for evaluating whether
reasoning LLMs follow user-specified instructions throughout their reasoning traces (multilingual
reasoning, formatting, length control), and shows that compliance degrades as task difficulty in-
creases. MathIF [2] similarly finds that instruction following degrades as reasoning ability scales in
mathematical reason

Sirius-Tiamat: How Small Can a One-Pass Decision
Encoder Get Before Its Decisions Change?
Precision, layer deletion, weight rounding, early exit, distillation and vocabulary trimming of a 421-
million-parameter typed-decision model, measured by flipped decisions on in-family, unseen-schema
and out-of-family items, calibration drift and machine-independent cost
Mohammed Nayeem Khan
mohammed.nayeem.khan@intel.com
mnknayeem@gmail.com
Vrishank Tiwari
vrishank.tiwari@intel.com
Intel Corporation
v1 · 19 November 2026 · arXiv cs.AI (cross-list cs.CL, cs.LG)
Abstract
A one-pass decision encoder reads a text, a question and several named options, and returns a probability
for each option in a single forward pass. We ask how far Laya, a 421M-parameter encoder of this kind, can
be compressed before its decisions change. We count decisions that differ from Laya's own full-precision
(fp32) answer, and track calibration (how well confidence matches accuracy, measured by expected
calibration error, ECE), on 1,221 synthetic items with the training schemas, 273 with an unseen schema, and
800 out-of-family questions from ARC, MMLU and HellaSwag. Layer pruning of a related model family is
known; we add flips, calibration, held-out data and retraining. bf16 changes 0.2% of in-family decisions but
2.2% out of family; 6-bit grouped rounding 1.3% and 5.9%; deleting 6 layers 0.9% and 9.1%, while ECE rises
from 5.9% to 39.2%. One fitted temperature, needing no labels, restores it to 3.6%. One scale per tensor fails
below six bits, and CPU dynamic int8 changes 30% of decisions, nearly all through one layer. Total variation
tracks flips for rounding but not for deletion, and an early exit saves layers over a static cut only if its
confidence gate is first recalibrated. Distilling a 16-layer student cuts its in-family flips from 44% to 9% (45%
out of family). At equal stored size, rounding flips fewer decisions than deletion. Data are synthetic and LLM-
labelled, for one architecture.
Keywords: model compression; quantisation; layer pruning; decision flips; calibration; distillation; early exit; typed
decision models; encoder inference.
Key findings (every number recomputed at build time)
1. In-family numbers understate flips. On 800 public-benchmark questions the same recipes change several
times more decisions than on the 1,221 in-family items: bf16 0.2% against 2.2%, 4-bit grouped rounding
4.3% against 21.4% (Section 12).
2. Half precision is nearly free on the nine synthetic sets: the worst of bf16/fp16 changes 14 of 1,494
decisions on either checkpoint. The scale granularity of weight rounding matters more than the bit width:
per-tensor 4-bit changes 76% of decisions, per-channel 9.6% and groups of 32 5.5%.
3. PyTorch dynamic int8 changes 30% of decisions; keeping the feed-forward output projection in fp32
brings it to 2.9% (Section 5). Community int8 exports should be checked the same way.
4. Layers can be deleted from the top without retraining (top 6 within 1% flips, top 9 within 5% in family),
but the probabilities move first: ECE 5.9% to 39.2% at six layers. One temperature fitted without labels
brings it to 3.6%, with labels 2.8% (Section 16); on the unseen schema it stays at 7.1% without labels and
14.8% with them.
5. Total variation tracks flips for weight rounding (median flips per unit of TV 0.92) and not for layer
deletion; margins shift by an offset and not by shrinkage; the fp32 margin ranks flipped items with
AUROC 0.91 for 4-bit grouped rounding (Section 14).
6. A confidence-gated early exit saves layers over static deletion only with a recalibrated gate: 20.4 layers at
1% in-family flips against 22 for the static cut, and 22.8 with the raw top probability (Section 15).
7. A second backbone (mmBERT-base, 22 layers) behaves like the main one under rounding (4-bit grouped
11.0% against 13.2% of decisions) but not under layer deletion (six layers: 3.7% against 21.4%), so the
deletable depth has to be measured per model (Section 13).
8. A two-epoch distillation of the 12-layer student cuts in-family flips from 44% to 9% and out-of-family
flips from 62% to 45% (Section 18).
9. At 600 MiB the best rounding configuration changes 1.5% of decisions and the best layer deletion 11.9%;
the smallest tier-A recipe is 8-bit channel (bf16 weights) at 453 MiB (Section 19).
10. A per-task TF-IDF classifier scores 89.9% against 84.2% for fine-tuned Laya on six shared tasks (two out of
distribution for Laya), at about 2.3 MiB and 1.2 ms per item.
11. Not done: GPU timings, idle-machine CPU timings, quantisation-aware training and layer dropout, and
any real (non-synthetic) deployment data. All labels are LLM-made and all synthetic items come from one
generator.

1  Summary
A decision encoder that answers in one pass is attractive because it is cheap. This study asks how much
cheaper it can be made by changing the model alone (fewer bits, fewer layers, narrower layers, fewer
vocabulary rows, a short retraining) before the decisions it returns differ from the uncompressed model’s.
The model is Laya, a 421-million-parameter encoder that reads a text, a question and named options and
returns a probability for each option. We count decision flips against the model’s own fp32 answer rather
than only accuracy against labels, on 1,494 synthetic items in nine sets (eight from the training family of the
fine-tuned checkpoint, one with an unseen schema) and on 800 public-benchmark questions that are out of
family (Section 12).
What is and is not new. Training-free, decision-guided layer pruning of a decision model has been reported
for Jev models [17], flips as a metric for compressed language models come from Dutta et al. [19], and the
Hugging Face hub already lists at least nine community int8 builds of Laya without an evaluation (Section 2).
We do not claim to be first to compress a decision model. FastJEV measures task-score retention of a
multimodal model without retraining. We measure which decisions change on a text encoder, on items from
inside and outside its training family, and we add early exit, temperature repair, distillation and a noise floor
(Section 2 lists what each cited paper did and did not measure).
The headline is a shape, and the in-family numbers understate it. Some knobs are close to free in family (half
precision, per-channel 8-bit weights), some cost a predictable amount per step (bits below six, layers beyond
6), and some are traps (per-tensor scales below six bits, dynamic int8 on the feed-forward output projection,
deleting low layers, slicing feed-forward units or heads). On the public-benchmark questions every recipe
changes at least as large a share of decisions: bf16 changes 0.2% in family and 2.2% out of family, 6-bit
grouped rounding 1.3% and 5.9%, deleting six layers 0.9% and 9.1% (Section 12). Deleting top layers is the
surprising case because decisions survive while the reported probabilities do not, and a single temperature
repairs the probabilities without labels (Section 16). A two-epoch distillation of a 16-layer student cuts its in-
family flips from 44% to 9% but leaves 45% of out-of-family decisions changed (Section 18). At the same
stored size, weight rounding flips fewer decisions than deleting layers (Section  19). Against a classical
baseline, TF-IDF with logistic regression is within noise of the compressed model on several tasks at a tiny
fraction of the cost (Section 20).
