All labels are written by language models, the synthetic data come from one generator, the public-
benchmark questions are a stress test for an encoder trained on other schemas and not a benchmark of its
skill, all conclusions are about a handful of checkpoints of one architecture, and the machine was shared:
machine-independent cost (parameters, bytes, FLOPs) is the main cost axis and CPU timings are noisy
context. Section 21 says what that does and does not license.
2  Related work and what is new
Each of the 30 works cited here was looked up on 10 and 18 November 2026 at its Hugging Face paper page
or arXiv abstract page to confirm that title, authors and identifier match. For four of them (FastJEV, Dutta
et al., Almeida Felicio, and Blagojevich and Sunderland) we also read the introduction and the description of
the experiments in the downloaded text. For the others we read the abstract and, for the encoder paper, the
architecture description, so what we say about those is limited to what their abstracts claim. The reference
list is at the end of the report.
2.1  Typed decision models and their cost
Typed decision models answer a bounded question from one forward pass and are pitched as a cheap
replacement for calling a language model. Li et al. [6] report 22.7 to 64.5% lower median decision latency
than the fastest of three hosted LLMs for a Jev decision model on an edge admission path, and Cheng et al.
[7] describe a 2-billion-parameter typed decision model that answers in about 31  ms on a laptop GPU.
TypedBench [8] argues that such models must be judged jointly on policy adherence, wording robustness,
probability quality and induced decisions. We adopt its emphasis on probability quality (Section 11) but use
plain equal-width ECE without a noise floor, so our calibration numbers are not comparable with theirs. Rafe
and Das [16] compare eight decision-model checkpoints with trained classifiers and generative models on
accuracy; size reduction is outside their abstract. These papers treat the model as a fixed artefact. We vary
the artefact itself.
2.2  The closest prior work: compression of decision models
Two papers sit nearest to this one, and a third kind of evidence is not a paper at all. FastJEV [17] targets Jev
decision models that score candidate decisions for multimodal inputs. Besides reusing recurrent states and
sharing candidate prefixes, it prunes depth with a training-free rule that looks at relative score changes on a
small unlabelled set. By its abstract, the complete method cuts candidate depth by 43.75 to 45.83% across
three OmniJev sizes and keeps 93.66 to 97.52% of the original task score on average over six evaluation sets.
In the paper’s experiments the layer ranking comes from 32 OK-VQA inputs, the same mask is reused on
every task, the shared prefix still runs every block, and the outcome is accuracy retention against the original
model on public multimodal benchmarks and a reconstructed robotics question set. That is the same idea as
our greedy layer deletion (Section 7), applied to a different model family, a different input modality and a
different outcome (task score, not the share of changed decisions). It has no retraining, no calibration
measurement and no evaluation on a schema or a domain outside the benchmarks. We do not claim layer
deletion for a decision model as new. We keep the part that is ours and that FastJEV does not touch: which
decisions change (not only how much accuracy is kept), how the reported probabilities drift, what happens
on items from outside the training family, how layer deletion compares with rounding, slicing, early exit and
distillation at the same size, and whether a short retraining recovers the loss (Section 18). We report our
retained-score numbers next to theirs wherever the quantities are comparable (Section 7), and we say where
they are not.
Stekel [18] asks how small an encoder for closed-set decisions can be, comparing joint and per-option
reading at 17 million to 1 billion parameters, and reports that the smallest released joint encoder answers a
median request in 14 ms on 16 processor threads. Its route to a small model is to pick a smaller trained
model, with accuracy and latency as the outcomes. Ours is to shrink one trained model after the fact and to
ask which decisions change. The two are complementary: that paper gives the accuracy-versus-size curve
across independently trained models, this one gives the curve inside a single model and adds flips and
calibration drift. It also reports that reordering options changes 12 to 23% of the answers of joint models, a
reminder that one-pass decision encoders have a flip problem even before any compression.
Community builds. On 10 November 2026 a search of the Hugging Face hub for Laya-related repositories
returned nine whose names contain ‘int8’ (ONNX, OpenVINO and MNN exports, English and multilingual),
more than thirty ONNX conversions, and single fp16 and int4 variants. We read repository names and
creation dates only, not the model cards, and found no accompanying paper or evaluation of changed
decisions. Quantised Laya is therefore already in use; what we add is a measurement of what quantising it,
and the other compression knobs, does to its decisions.
2.3  Compression of transformer encoders
The tools we use are standard. Dettmers et al. [2] showed that int8 matrix multiplication of large language
models needs special handling of a few outlier feature dimensions once models pass several billion
parameters; our encoder is a thousand times smaller than that regime, so we test rather than assume where
plain rounding breaks. Sajjad et al. [3] dropped layers from BERT, RoBERTa and XLNet and kept up to 98% of
GLUE performance at 40% fewer layers, with the lower layers the most critical, a pattern we also see; Fan
et al. [4] train with structured layer dropout so that shallower sub-networks can be selected at inference time
without fine-tuning, and DistilBERT [5] obtains a smaller, faster student by distillation. Q8BERT [9] trains BERT
with quantisation-aware fine-tuning for a 4x size reduction at little accuracy cost; we only round after
training. D K et al. [15] prune the last layers of large language models used as text encoders before a short
supervised run and report that up to 30% of layers go with negligible loss, which parallels our top-layer
deletion (they retrain briefly, we do not). Vocabulary trimming [10] deletes embedding rows to shrink
multilingual models; we do the same on an English-heavy decision encoder and add a test of what happens
to the decisions when a test token falls outside the kept list.
2.4  Flips, divergence and noise
Dutta et  al. [19] introduced ‘flips’ for compressed language models, the share of answers that change
although accuracy does not, and measured them on benchmarks including MMLU, HellaSwag and ARC; we
use their metric and, in Section 12, the same benchmarks, converted to one-pass decisions. Almeida Felicio
[20] reports that the flip rate is close to the mean total variation between the dense and compressed
distributions for 19 language models, which we test on an encoder in Section 14; Wu et al. [21] propose that
quantization shrinks decision margins roughly linearly, which we test in the same section. Blagojevich and
Sunderland [22] state each quantization effect as the excess over the flips that engine, restart and batch
changes produce on two decision models; Section 13 measures the corresponding floor for Laya. None of
these measures layer deletion, slicing or retraining on a typed decision encoder, and none of them reports
out-of-family items for the decision model itself. Rababah et al. (2607.08734, abstract only) report a related
‘correctness agreement’ metric for quantised language models; we did not use it. Azizi et al. [29] (abstract
only) report that deleting every option definition leaves the accuracy of an open typed decision model, laya-
td among them, almost unchanged, so the option labels carry much of the decision; on our public-
benchmark rows the labels are bare letters and only the descriptions carry the answer, which may be part of
why the model is near chance there.
2.5  Healing, early exit and the choice between pruning and quantization
Healing a pruned model with a short training run is standard for language models: Gromov et al. [24] remove
deep layers and heal with low-rank adapters, and ShortGPT [25] scores layers by how little they change the
hidden state; Kim et al. [30] report that the calibration data matter more than the search algorithm for which
layers are removed. Patient distillation [26] trains a shallow student on a deep teacher’s intermediate layers.
Early exit and cascades spend fewer layers on easy inputs [27] [28]. Kuzmin et al. [23] compare pruning with
quantization on accuracy and find quantization better in most settings. We run each of these on one decision
encoder and score them with the same outcome, decisions changed, on in-family, unseen-schema and out-
of-family items (Section 15, Section 18, Section 19).
2.6  Who loses when a model is compressed
Aggregate accuracy hides changes in individual predictions. Hooker et  al. [11] show that compressed
networks diverge on a narrow subset of examples even when top-line accuracy matches, which is the
motivation for counting decision flips against the full-precision model, as we do. Proskurina et al. [12] find
that 4-bit GPTQ quantisation lowers confidence in true labels for language models and that it
disproportionately affects samples on which the full model was already unsure, which is the pattern Figure 11
shows for flips here, and Guo et al. [14] supply the calibration vocabulary (ECE, reliability) that we use for the
drift measurements. Jiang et al. [13] call the flip rate between a deployed and a new model ‘churn’ and treat
it as a cost in itself; a compressed model replacing a full one in a software branch has the same exposure.

One Framework to Diagnose Them All:
A Stratified Benchmark for Bengali LLM Hallucination
Asif Shahriyar Sushmit1∗, Shefayat E Shams Adib2∗, Abdullah Al Jubaer Gem2∗,
Ahmed Shafin Ruhan2∗, MD. Nazmuddoha Ansary3∗, Biplab Kumar Sarkar4∗,
Syed Rifat Raiyan2∗†, Ajwad Abrar2, Abdullah Bin Hasan5, Adib Sakhawat2, M. Sakeef Hossain2,
Ahmed Alfey Sani2, Arefin Mizan6, Sourab Chakma7, Quazi Adibur Rahman Adib8,
Wassie Haque5, Sanjay Kumar Sen5, Saad Tahmid5, Mohammad Mamun Or Rashid9

Alikbachan/Alikbachan
 alikbachan.github.io
Abstract
Hallucination research in low-resource lan-
guages fragments easily: each newly named
failure mode prompts its own dataset, spend-
ing scarce annotators on incomparable re-
sources. We argue for consolidation and test it
at community scale. Alikbachan is a Bengali
hallucination-detection benchmark stratified
along three crossed axes: a human-validated
cultural-distance band, six task types, and a
five-family, 32-mode hallucination taxonomy.
It comprises a harvested 2,516-item test set
(Phase 1) and a quota-constructed, gold-labeled
5,000-item set (Phase 2). The stratification is
diagnostic. Four zero-shot LLM judges vary
by over 30 macro-F1 points across strata, and
the item-level predictions of 99 Phase-1 and
32 Phase-2 competition systems reproduce the
profile: discourse-level omission defeats judges
and most teams alike, whereas only a minority
over-flag negative controls. The judges’ ver-
dict probabilities rank items well (ROC-AUC
0.74–0.95) but are overconfident (ECE 0.04–
0.29). An open competition on Alikbachan
drew 222 teams and 3,566 submissions, and
a single-prompt 32B judge reaches the 57th
percentile. Of the 25 teams in both phases, 24
regress on Phase 2 (mean −17.6 points) while
every zero-shot judge improves, and Phase-1
rank barely predicts Phase-2 rank (Spearman
ρ = 0.35), so a Phase-1 leaderboard alone
would have crowned a different winner.
1
Introduction
In a low-resource language, a fluent answer is both
the hardest kind to doubt and the most expensive
kind to check. A model that writes grammatical,
register-appropriate Bengali gives no sign when
it misattributes a poem or misdates a war, and

whose tacit premise is that such experts are plen-

(Joshi et al., 2020). Spent one dataset at a time, a
small pool of experts yields isolated resources with
incompatible schemas, labels and protocols, and
claims about overall progress grow harder to trust
(Dehghani et al., 2021; Raji et al., 2021).

Figure 2: The Alikbachan framework. Two independently sourced phases (1, 2) feed an open competition (3) and a
public release (4). An independent audit (5) reviewed a sample of the released items, and this paper (6) analyzes
zero-shot judges, the teams’ item-level predictions and the audit (§4–§6).
Hallucination makes the cost palpable.1 It is a
family of failures rather than one, and the family
keeps growing (Ji et al., 2023): detection bench-
marks now target parametric error, contextual in-
fidelity, adversarial manipulation and calibration
separately. Under annotation scarcity, enumerating
them one dataset at a time is a queue that never
clears. The failures also interact with language
and culture in ways an English-first taxonomy does
not anticipate. Factuality evaluation itself grows
less reliable as a language’s resources shrink (Kim
et al., 2024). Asked in Bengali who wrote the poem
Bidrohi, a model may name Rabindranath Tagore,
the Bengali poet best known abroad, instead of
its author, Kazi Nazrul Islam (Figure 1). Such an
answer is grammatical and culturally legible, so
nothing on its surface betrays it.
We argue for consolidation over enumeration.
If one resource is stratified along dimensions that
cut across failure modes, a newly identified phe-
nomenon enters as another cell rather than another
dataset. Benchmark and diagnostic then dovetail:
because every item carries its category metadata,
one evaluation run reports where a system fails as
well as how well it scores. The axes themselves
are not specific to Bengali. Cultural distance from
a model’s dominant pretraining distribution, task
type and an explicit hallucination taxonomy could
serve wherever annotators are scarce, although the
bands and corpora must be instantiated locally.
Bengali is a germane test case:
spoken by
over 280 million people, it is resourced far be-
low what that population would predict.
Alik-
bachan (অলীকবচন, ‘mirage of language’) crosses
three axes: a human-validated, three-level cultural-
1The word entered English in the 1640s from the Latin
hallucinationem, ‘to wander in the mind’; computer vision
once used it approvingly for algorithms that envision missing
pixels, before LLMs gave it the sense of fluent but fabricated
text (Maleki et al., 2024).
distance band, six task types and a five-family, 32-
mode hallucination taxonomy. Its items span gen-
eral knowledge, mathematics, Bengali grammar
and lexicon, history, literature, law and current af-
fairs, in two independently sourced phases (Fig-
ure 2): a harvested Phase-1 test set of 2,516 items
and a quota-constructed, gold-labeled Phase-2 set
of 5,000 items, of which 1,500 are public.
A resource’s authors cannot settle the consolida-
tion argument with their own evaluations, so we
test it externally. Alikbachan is the foundation of
an open research competition on Kaggle, with a
public leaderboard phase followed by an in-person
final for the top teams. Its complete submission
history is a litmus test for the argument: it shows
whether one stratified resource concentrates effort
that would otherwise fragment, and whether a sec-
ond stratified phase catches what a leaderboard
alone cannot. We make four contributions.
(1) We design a stratification for annotator-
constrained languages that crosses cultural dis-
tance, task type and hallucination family, and
we document how both phases were built, la-
beled and independently audited (§4).
(2) We show that the stratification is diagnostic. A
judge’s macro-F1 varies by more than 30 points
across strata, and the item-level predictions of
99 Phase-1 and 32 Phase-2 competition sys-
tems reproduce the profile, including a blind
spot for discourse-level omission that judges
and most teams share (§6).
(3) We analyze the complete submission history
of a 222-team competition and, through the
25 teams that entered both phases, expose a
generalization gap that neither phase reveals
alone (§6.3).
(4) We distill an independent audit into curation
lessons for low-resource benchmarks (§5).
2
2
Related Work
Hallucination detection. Detectors fall into three
broad families: consistency-based methods that
sample several generations and flag disagreement
(Manakul et al., 2023); evidence-grounded meth-
ods that check a response against a reference
through entailment or question answering (Fabbri
et al., 2022; Min et al., 2023); and supervised clas-
sifiers trained on labeled faithful and hallucinated
pairs (Li et al., 2023). LLMs also serve directly
as judges (Zheng et al., 2023), as our baselines do;
we additionally measure how well calibrated their
verdicts are, a property long studied for neural clas-
sifiers (Guo et al., 2017). Alikbachan serves all
these families (§6.1).
Multilingual and low-resource factuality.
Be-
yond the English-first benchmarks, Bengali now
has a multi-task hallucination evaluation (Adib
et al., 2026) and a culturally grounded study of
idiom understanding (Sakhawat et al., 2026), but
no stratified framework that diagnoses many hallu-
cination types at once. Hu et al. (2020) showed that
one unified multilingual benchmark can replace
disjoint monolingual ones; we apply the same prin-
ciple within a single low-resource language.
Benchmark proliferation. Dehghani et al. and
Raji et al. argue that a sprawling, poorly coor-
dinated set of benchmarks makes claims about
progress hard to trust, and that effort is better spent
on fewer, carefully designed evaluations, an ar-
gument §3 applies to low-resource hallucination
detection. We know of no prior work that tests this
argument against a full open research competition
rather than an internal set of baselines.
Bengali resources and models. Bengali bench-
marks cover sentiment analysis (Kabir et al., 2023),
medical named-entity recognition (Khan et al.,
2023), social bias and cultural reasoning (Tasnim
et al., 2026) and text detoxification (Mohsin et al.,
2025). Encoders such as BanglaBERT (Bhattachar-
jee et al., 2022) and multilingual ones (Devlin et al.,
2019; Conneau et al., 2020) could anchor super-
vised detectors. Bengali-adapted LLMs include
TigerLLM (Raihan and Zampieri, 2025), TituLLM
(Nahin et al., 2025) and BanglaLlama (Zehady
et al., 2026); we test all three as zero-shot judges.
3
The Case Against Fragmentation
A newly identified failure, such as a model sub-
stituting a Western officeholder for a Bangladeshi
one, usually prompts a targeted dataset. In Ben-
gali this is costly. A small pool of experts must
verify every item against government documents,
statutes, curricula and literary or historical sources,
and single-purpose benchmarks drawn from it du-
plicate effort and yield hard-to-compare results. We
propose to spend the same effort on one framework
instead and state the desiderata it must meet.
(i) Axes that cut across failure modes, so that a
new failure enters as a new combination of
labels rather than a new dataset. Alikbachan
uses cultural distance, task type and a hallu-
cination taxonomy (§4.3 and §4.4).
(ii) Item-level metadata, so that one evaluation
run reports where a system fails as well as
how well it scores (§6.2).
(iii) A second, independently constructed phase,
so that overfitting to a public leaderboard
becomes visible (§6.3).
(iv) An independent audit that separates construc-
tion defects from model errors (§5).
Internal evaluation alone cannot show that such a
framework works at scale. If one well-stratified re-
source can absorb broad participation without frag-
menting into task-specific benchmarks, its value
should persist across independently built systems,
and the open competition in §6.3 tests exactly that.
4
The Alikbachan Framework
4.1
Task Definition
Each item is a triple (c, p, r) of an optional con-
text c (a passage, or the token [NULL]), a Bengali
prompt p and a candidate response r. The task is to
predict y ∈{0, 1}, where y = 1 marks a faithful
response and y = 0 a hallucinated one, i.e. one
with fabricated, unsupported or factually incorrect
content. With a null context the response is judged
against world knowledge; otherwise it is judged
against the context, even where the context deliber-
ately departs from reality. Both phases share this
formulation and differ only in how their items were
built and in the metadata that accompany them.
Every term used below is defined in §A.
4.2
Two Phases, One Schema
Alikbachan was built along two independently
sourced tracks (Figure 2). Phase 1 harvests short-
answer questions from four vetted Bengali sources
(two examination and quiz paper collections, a
newspaper corpus and an encyclopedia) and pairs
them with responses written by LLMs or people,
so it follows a real question distribution rather than
a synthetic one. Of its 2,516 test items, 1,361 carry
3
a supporting context and 1,155 are closed-book; a
further 299 labeled items form a sample set.
Phase 2 is constructed under explicit quotas over
six task types, three cultural bands and the 32 fail-
ure modes of five families (§4.3 and §4.4). Its
items draw on seven Bengali corpora: Wikipedia
and Banglapedia (1,100 items), government pub-
lications (900), newspapers, National Curriculum
and Textbook Board texts and Bangladeshi statutes
(700 each), e-Bangla Library texts (550) and Com-
mon Crawl (350). Of its 5,000 items, 3,250 are
theory-authored around a target failure mode and
1,750 are theory-confirmed, built from real source
content. Every quota was met exactly (§B gives the
specification and the joint counts).
Release. During the competition the Phase-1 test
labels sat behind the leaderboard; they are now
public, as is the sample set. Phase 2 is split 30/70
into a public set of 1,500 items, sampled so that
every failure mode keeps its share to within four
items, and 3,500 items held out as a contamination-
resistant test set. A further 500-item hard split was
used only in the competition. All analyses below
use the full 5,000 Phase-2 items. The data are
released under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, together with
the judge scripts and a scorer that reports macro-F1,
error rates, ROC-AUC and ECE per stratum.
4.3
Cultural-Distance Bands
The central organizing axis is a three-level cultural-
distance band. C0 (globally stable) covers culture-
independent facts in science, geography or math-
ematics, such as the boiling point of water, and
serves as the control band. C1 (culturally situated)
covers answers that are specific to Bangladesh or
differ from a globally dominant default, such as
Bengali literary authorship, Liberation War dates,
national monuments and regional administration; it
hosts the headline phenomenon of fluent but locally
wrong output. C2 (contested or time-sensitive)
covers current officeholders and revised statistics,
where a hallucination must be told apart from out-
dated knowledge. Phase 2 fixes the band sizes at
750, 3,500 and 750 items. In Phase 1 the bands
were assigned after harvesting through a human-
validated protocol (2,014, 483 and 19 items; §C).
4.4
Task Types and Hallucination Families
Phase 2 spans six task types: short- and long-form
open-book QA (short-ob-qa, long-ob-qa), both
context-grounded; short-form closed-book QA
(short-cb-qa); summarization; Bengali–English
translation; and adversarial probes built on false
premises, prompt injections, counterfactual con-
texts or instruction constraints (adversarial).
Phase 1 distinguishes only closed-book from
context-grounded QA, and with no separate transla-
tion or long-form clusters it is best read as a short-
answer QA benchmark.
Every Phase-2 item also belongs to one of five
hallucination families, the diagnostic axis of §6:
(A) content or parametric errors in dates, enti-
ties or attributions, independent of any context;
(B) context or intrinsic errors that contradict or em-
bellish the given context; (C) linguistic or cultural
errors of Bengali script, register, lexicon or transla-
tion; (D) adversarial or robustness failures, from
prompt injection to miscalibration; and (E) meta or
pipeline artifacts, such as ambiguous gold labels,
imperfect sources and encoding variants, that a ro-
bust judge should see through. The families divide
into 32 failure modes of 50–400 items each.
4.5
Annotation and Audit
Two separate teams of five undergraduate volun-
teers built and checked Alikbachan. The annota-
tion team labeled every Phase-1 item and wrote
Phase 2: theory-authored items are labeled by
construction and theory-confirmed items by re-
view against their source. A 30-item spot-check
of theory-authored items during construction cor-
rected one label (3.3%).
The audit team, fluent Bengali speakers, none
of whom helped build either phase, reviewed the
data after both phases were complete. They were
first trained on a four-way evidential protocol (§5)
and given few-shot examples of the three bands.
They then reviewed a random sample of 500 items,
200 from the Phase-1 sample set and 300 from
Phase 2. Three auditors labeled a shared 100-item
subset independently (Fleiss’ κ = 0.74) and split
the remaining 400 (about 133 each); disagreements,
mostly between REFUTED and NOT ENTAILED,
were settled in a consensus discussion led by a se-
nior researcher. The audit found 310 SUPPORTED,
65 REFUTED, 100 NOT ENTAILED and 25 MAL-
FORMED items and overturned 24 of the 500 ev-
idential labels (4.8%). A separate review of 250
items’ band and domain assignments made 11 band
and 8 domain changes.
A worked example. The first panel of Figure 1
shows a theory-authored Phase-2 item from the
Wikipedia and Banglapedia track.
Asked who
wrote the poem বিদ্রোহী(Bidrohi, ‘The Rebel’), the

widely known Bengali poet, instead of its author,

(short-cb-qa), and the error swaps a local fact for
a global default (Family A, cultural-default substi-

ClosureBench:
A Benchmark for Reasoning under Closure Assumptions
Francesco Belardinelli
francesco.belardinelli@imperial.ac.uk
Imperial College London
Flavio Corradini
flavio.corradini@unicam.it
Matteo Leonesi∗
matteo.leonesi@unicam.it
University of Camerino
Editors: Alessandra Mileo, Andrea Passerini and Cogan Shimizu
Abstract
AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) often answer questions from incomplete
records. Missing information might be interpreted as unknown or false, depending on the
completeness of the source. Current evaluations fail to distinguish these two aspects, as
they are usually interwoven with other reasoning demands. We present ClosureBench, a
benchmark that tests whether LLMs follow the stated rules for dealing with missing in-
formation. Every base scenario is tested under OWA, CWA, and LCWA, and only the
treatment of missing information changes between variants. ClosureBench provides a veri-
fied base benchmark as well as agent extensions for action choice, source scope, and updates.
A model is considered correct on a base scenario only if it provides correct answers in all
of its closure variants. Across 960 instances, overall accuracy can mask substantial closure
mistakes. Models achieve overall accuracy from 71.18% to 99.86% across replicated runs,
but their core switch accuracy, measured on the scenarios whose gold label actually changes
with the contract, varies between 18.23% and 99.31%. Large discrepancies emerge under
LCWA. For example, some agents choose unknown despite the prompt indicating that miss-
ing information should be treated as false. Our findings demonstrate that evaluations of
AI agents should not only measure whether agents can reason over existing facts but also
whether they use the appropriate assumption when information is absent.
1. Introduction
AI agents often look up incomplete external sources before acting (Xu et al., 2025; Mis-
erendino et al., 2025; Barres et al., 2025; Qi et al., 2025b; Vijayvargiya et al., 2026). Missing
information can be read either as unknown or as false. Consider a deployment request where
the record says that a service passed unit tests, but says nothing about whether the service
has deployment approval. If the record is incomplete, the approval status remains unknown.
If the approval predicate is complete, the missing approval counts as false, even though the
visible facts are unchanged. Only the rule for reading the missing atom changes. We call
this rule the closure contract. It specifies how to interpret missing atoms under the Open
World Assumption (OWA), the Closed World Assumption (CWA), or the Local Closed
World Assumption (LCWA). Closure assumptions have long been studied in the symbolic
AI tradition, especially in knowledge representation and database theory (Reiter, 1978;
Horrocks et al., 2003; Darari et al., 2014; Razniewski et al., 2024; Oudshoorn et al., 2026).
∗Corresponding author.
© 2026 F. Belardinelli, F. Corradini & M. Leonesi.
arXiv:2611.26335v1  [cs.AI]  19 Nov 2026
Belardinelli Corradini Leonesi
The same issue becomes practical for LLM-based agents that operate over partial records,
where symbolic closure assumptions determine whether the absence of a fact should re-
main unresolved, support a negative answer, or justify an action. Under OWA, an atom
that is not stated or derivable remains unknown. Under CWA, such an atom is taken to
be false. Under LCWA, this negative inference is allowed only for predicates declared
complete. Prior work characterizes when a knowledge base is complete enough to license
these negative conclusions (Darari et al., 2014; Razniewski et al., 2024), and recent work
on ontology validation shows that the gap between OWA reasoning and CWA validation
remains important in data systems (Oudshoorn et al., 2026). Existing reasoning and agent
benchmarks often combine this issue with other abilities (Zhu et al., 2025; Kirichenko et al.,
2025; Dou et al., 2026; Hasan, 2026). As a result, it is difficult to tell whether a model fails
because it cannot apply the rules or because it does not respect the intended closure policy
for unstated and underivable atoms.
Contribution.
We introduce ClosureBench, a benchmark for testing whether models fol-
low explicit closure contracts. Each instance defines a small rule base centered on a target
atom, together with the predicate vocabulary and the predicates listed as complete. The
prompt states the active closure contract, so the model does not need to infer which predi-
cates are complete. For each base scenario, we generate OWA, CWA, and LCWA variants.
The symbolic case stays fixed, and only the interpretation of unstated and underivable
atoms changes.
• We introduce ClosureBench, a benchmark for testing OWA, CWA, and LCWA rea-
soning. Each label is verified from the symbolic specification and closure contract.
The benchmark also includes three agent extensions. Ask/Act turns truth labels into
actions, SourceScope moves the task to a multi-agent source setting, and ClosureShift
moves it to a multi-turn update setting. These settings matter because agents rarely
answer truth queries in isolation. The extensions test whether a closure error carries
over into the decisions an agent makes.
• We introduce closure switch accuracy, which counts a scenario as correct only when
the model answers all of its variants correctly. Grouping instances this way follows
behavioral testing (Ribeiro et al., 2020) and shows that high accuracy can still hide
closure errors.
• We use ClosureBench to characterize when closure reasoning fails. The results show
that LCWA is the hardest setting because the model must close only the predicates
declared complete.
In the agent extensions, the same errors affect decisions.
In
Ask/Act, models ask for more information when they should deny. In SourceScope,
they sometimes ignore that the complete source already supports a false answer, or
treat absence from an incomplete source as false. In ClosureShift, they fail to keep
valid local closure after updates.
Code and data are available on GitHub.
2
ClosureBench
2. Related work
Open world, closed world, and locally closed world assumptions.
Recent knowl-
edge representation (KR) work studies how open and closed predicates affect validation and
query answering under incomplete data (Oudshoorn et al., 2026; Ahmetaj et al., 2024; Mar-
coni and Rosati, 2025). ClosureBench uses this distinction as an explicit closure contract
in the prompt. The facts stay the same, while the closure contract changes.
Logic and rule reasoning benchmarks.
Recent logic benchmarks evaluate controlled
logic and rule reasoning tasks (Han et al., 2024; Patel et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024a,b; Zhou
et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Qi et al., 2025a; Dou et al., 2026; Hasan,
2026; Rabern et al., 2026). Most of these works test reasoning under one fixed semantics.
ClosureBench keeps the symbolic case fixed and tests whether the model changes its answer
only when the closure contract changes.
Abstention, ambiguity, and uncertainty.
Abstention and clarification work studies
cases where the available evidence is not enough for a direct answer (Liu et al., 2024a; Zhang
et al., 2024; Zhang and Choi, 2025; Luo et al., 2025; Su and Cardie, 2026; Liu et al., 2025;
Kirichenko et al., 2025). ClosureBench treats unknown more strictly. It is a label implied
by the stated closure contract, not a general uncertainty score.
Agent benchmarks and source scope.
Recent agent benchmarks test broad agent
capabilities in operational settings (Yao et al., 2025; Barres et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025;
Debenedetti et al., 2024; Diao et al., 2025; Qi et al., 2025b; Xu et al., 2025; Miserendino
et al., 2025; Vijayvargiya et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024b; Zhou et al., 2024).
ClosureBench complements these suites by isolating source scope. Absence from a complete
source can support denial, while absence from an incomplete source should stay unknown.
Table 1 compares the closest benchmarks along the features that separate ClosureBench
from them and shows that ClosureBench is the only suite that keeps the symbolic case fixed
while changing only the closure contract, then carries that distinction into LCWA scope
and the agent extensions.
3. The ClosureBench Method
We first define the closure semantics that fix the gold labels (Section 3.1), then describe the
dataset (Section 3.2), and finally present three agent extensions (Section 3.3).
3.1. Closure Semantics
We use instance for a single prompt with its gold label and base scenario for the shared
symbolic case. Each base scenario has three instances, one per contract. Each instance
contains positive ground atoms F +, explicit negative atoms F −, and a set of rules R.
A ground atom is a predicate applied to named entities, with no variables, for example
has deployment approval(Service F). It also has a query atom q = P(e), where P is the
predicate being asked about and e is the entity. We write the predicate vocabulary as V.
Under LCWA, the instance also gives a set C ⊆V of complete predicates. The verifier first
applies the rules in the positive direction. Starting from F +, it repeatedly adds every rule

2. Else, if q ∈F −, the label is false.
3. Else, q is missing. Missing queries are labeled according to the active closure contract:
• under OWA, the label is unknown;
• under CWA, the label is false;
• under LCWA, the label is false if P ∈C, and unknown otherwise.
This procedure follows the semantics of definite logic programs. Rule bodies contain no
negation, so ClR(F +) is the least fixpoint of forward chaining, and the CWA label for a
missing atom is the usual negation-as-failure reading on the minimal model (Reiter, 1978).
The one departure is F −, which the verifier checks before any closure applies.
Exam-
ple 1 shows this procedure on a concrete instance. We exclude target atoms that are both
derivable and explicitly negated, since they would mix closure reasoning with the separate
problem of resolving a conflict between a rule and an explicit fact, which is out of scope.
The verifier does not reason backwards. If a rule condition is missing, the rule does not
fire, and any false label for a missing query comes from the active closure contract, not a
failed rule.
3.2. Benchmark Design
ClosureBench has 960 English instances built from 320 base scenarios. Each scenario ap-
pears under all three closure contracts. All three variants use the same facts, rules, explicit
negatives, and target atom. The scenarios use eight domains, with 120 instances in each
4
ClosureBench
one. These domains are cloud deployment, finance controls, hospital access, library services,
university registration, procurement review, manufacturing quality, and robotics operations.
The instances mix missing direct facts and missing rule antecedents with distractors and
controls where the target is entailed or explicitly negated. The base dataset has a core
contrastive set and two control groups: of the 320 base scenarios, 192 are core contrastive
scenarios, where changing the closure contract can change the gold label, and 128 are con-
trol scenarios whose gold label is stable across all three contracts (64 with a target that
is entailed and 64 with a target that is explicitly negated). Each instance stores a gold
answer and a reason type, so the answer can be traced to a fact derived by a rule, an
explicit negative, or a missing target read using the active closure contract. We built the
dataset from domain templates. For each domain, templates define the ontology and the
case families used to generate the scenarios. A fixed script expanded these templates into
base scenarios and created the three semantic variants for each scenario. We reviewed the
generated blocks and ran a validation script that checks structural consistency, semantic
labels, predicate completeness, and prompt contract agreement. When grouped by scenario,
control labels stay the same under all three contracts, while core contrastive labels change
only because the closure contract changes. The symbolic case stays fixed, but the active
closure contract changes how the missing target is read. The extensions keep this base
structure while moving the closure contrast into three agent formats. An example instance
is discussed in Example 1 and reproduced in full in Appendix D.
3.3. Agent Extensions
The base benchmark asks for a truth value. We add three agent extensions where the same
closure contract decides something else. In Ask/Act it decides an action, in SourceScope
a choice between sources of different completeness, and in ClosureShift an answer revised
across turns. The labels still come from the same symbolic truth labels and closure contracts
used in the base dataset.
Ask/Act.
The ClosureBench Ask/Act extension keeps the base instance and adds a de-
cision. True targets become approve decisions, false targets become deny decisions, and
unknown targets become requests for information. The symbolic case and truth label stay
fixed. For request information instances, the dataset records whether the model should
ask about the target itself or the first missing rule condition. The model also returns the
missing field when needed, a question, and a rationale.
SourceScope.
The ClosureBench SourceScope extension splits evidence between two sources.
Source A is complete only for the listed predicates. Source B is partial, so a missing fact from
Source B does not support a false answer by itself. The coordinator must answer the query
and justify both source choice and absence treatment. This extension has 360 instances
from 120 base scenarios, and each selected scenario keeps the same OWA/CWA/LCWA
triple.
ClosureShift.
The ClosureBench ClosureShift extension tests whether the model updates
its answer when completeness changes. Each dialogue has three turns. The facts, rules,
glossary, and target stay fixed, while the complete predicates change. Turn 1 leaves every
predicate open, so missing facts stay unknown. Turn 2 makes the full vocabulary complete,
5
Belardinelli Corradini Leonesi
so missing facts count as false. Turn 3 replaces that full set with a smaller local set. In
half of the dialogues, the local set still covers the target, so the answer should stay false.
In the other half, the local set no longer covers the target, so the answer should return to
unknown. The model returns the current answer, whether it changed, the update type, and
a rationale.
Example 1 For example, one dataset instance says that Service F passed unit tests. It also
says that a service may deploy to production when it passed unit tests and has deployment
approval. The target asks whether Service F may deploy to production. The antecedent
has deployment approval and the target may deploy are different predicates. The instance
never says whether Service F has deployment approval, so the rule cannot fire and the target
is not derived. The three variants keep the same fact, rule, and target, and only the closure
contract changes.
The same base instance drives the three extensions.
In Ask/Act the
OWA variant becomes an ask while CWA and LCWA become a deny. In ClosureShift the
answer shifts from unknown to false and back as the complete set changes across turns. In
SourceScope absence counts against a complete source but not an open one.
4. Empirical Evaluation
This section presents the experimental setup and the results on the benchmark and its agent
extensions.
4.1. Experimental Setup
We evaluate six model configurations, namely DeepSeek V4 Flash and DeepSeek V4 Pro
(DeepSeek-AI, 2026), Mistral Small 2603 (Mistral AI, 2026b), Mistral Medium 3.5 (Mistral
AI, 2026a), Llama 4 Scout (Meta, 2025b), and Llama 4 Maverick (Meta, 2025a)1. The run-
ners call OpenAI compatible chat completion APIs at temperature 0. The system prompt
restricts the model to the symbolic specification and closure contract and requires a single
JSON object with an answer field and a rationale. The answer must be true, false, or
unknown. We read the answer field and score any unparseable instance as incorrect. All
results are mean ± sample standard deviation over three full runs. Hosted APIs are not
fully deterministic even at temperature 0, because of effects such as nondeterministic ker-
nels and server side batching. The three runs therefore measure how stable a model is from
one run to the next, not decoding noise, and the deviations are small. We also rerun the
base benchmark at temperature 1 as a robustness probe. All reported base and Ask/Act
runs score their full 960 instance datasets. ClosureShift runs score all 100 dialogues and 300
turns. The 100 dialogues are sampled, with a fixed seed, from the core contrastive base sce-
narios, balanced evenly between dialogues that persist after narrowing and dialogues that
reopen. SourceScope runs score all 360 extension instances, built from 120 base scenarios.
The base dataset also stores train, development, and test splits by base scenario for future
model development. The comparisons here use the full suite, and Section 4.4 explains why
we report these numbers rather than results on the held out test split.

Online Temporal Rotations for 2 Bit KV-Cache Quantization
in Video Diffusion Transformers
Ryan Lucas
Petros Prastakos
Rahul Mazumder
Operations Research Center, Massachusetts Institute of Technology
{ryanlu,pprastak,rahulmaz}@mit.edu
Abstract
Video diffusion transformers reuse key–value (KV) caches
across denoising steps, which quickly becomes a bottleneck
for long video generation. We find that quantizing temporally
distant cache vectors leads to a large range and high quanti-
zation error, but that nearby video tokens in the KV-cache
share a persistent pattern per channel. These patterns also
vary across videos, motivating rotations that are adapted
to each video’s unique cache. We propose Temporal Rota-
tion Quantization (TRQ), a method that rotates frames in the
cache that are adjacent in time before quantization. For each
block of temporally adjacent cache vectors, TRQ fits an or-
thogonal transform that maps the block’s per-channel means
to a vector that is close to a constant across channels. To
keep the quantization format lightweight, we parameterize
this rotation as a tree of 2 × 2 planar rotations, each stored
with only two bits, followed by a fixed Hadamard transform
shared across all blocks. The rotations are fit without gradi-
ents or changes to model weights, and we prove that a simple
greedy fit is globally optimal for our ’mean-flattening’ objec-
tive. The transforms are fit online for each new video, and we
release fused Triton kernels to make this process efficient at
inference. At 2-bit precision and matched compression, TRQ
improves VBench subject consistency over the state-of-the-
art method QVG from 90.38 to 92.02 on LongCat-Video-13B
and from 86.33 to 87.61 on HY-WorldPlay-8B, as well as
improving other metrics.
1. Introduction
Diffusion transformers (DiTs) [19] have become the domi-
nant architecture for video generation. They underpin pro-
prietary systems such as Sora [3] and Movie Gen [20], as
well as open models including CogVideoX [27], Hunyuan-
Video [11], and Wan [24], which synthesize high-fidelity
videos from text or image prompts. To go beyond a few
seconds of footage, toward minute-scale or interactive gen-
eration, recent work produces video autoregressively or by
continuation, denoising one chunk at a time conditioned on
previously generated content [4, 5, 10, 17, 21, 28]. Like au-
toregressive language models, these systems store the keys
and values of past frames in a KV-cache, so the history need
not be recomputed at every denoising step.
However, this computational saving from the KV-cache
brings with it substantial memory requirements. Each frame
contributes thousands of tokens, and the cache holds a key
and a value vector per token, head, and layer. It therefore
grows linearly with the generated history and can reach tens
of gigabytes, more than commodity GPUs can hold [26].
Capping the cache, for example with a sliding window,
shrinks the context the model can attend to and erodes long-
range consistency of subjects, scene layout, and motion [26].
KV-cache quantization is mature for large language mod-
els [2, 8, 14], but these methods were designed for the unique
structure of LLM KV-caches and lose substantial accuracy
when applied directly to video DiTs [26].
Rotation transforms have proved remarkably effective
for low-bit LLM quantization [2, 15, 16, 22]. A central
motivation for rotations in KV-cache quantization of LLMs
is the empirically well-documented outlier structure along
the channel dimension of the activations and KV-cache of
LLMs. A small set of channels contain consistently large
values across all tokens, forcing low-bit quantization to cover
a wide range at the expense of resolution for smaller values.
One intuition for why rotations are so effective in LLMs
is that they take linear combinations of channels, ‘mixing’
the outlier channels with more benign channels and thus
leading to much flatter distributions that are more friendly to
quantization [2].
We identify two unique properties of video diffusion KV-
caches that motivate online temporal rotations (Figure 1).
(i) Temporal structure within a video. For a given
video and channel of the cache, keys and values are highly
correlated across nearby frames, with only localized changes
as the scene evolves. We illustrate this structure in the first
five panels of Figure 1. This similarity, however, decays over
time. Frames that are distant in time, such as frames 20 and
64 of the first video, can have substantially different values.

frame. We observe that (i) Within a video, nearby frames share persistent spatial patterns and (ii) the final two panels show that these patterns
differ across videos, even at the same frame index and channel. Together, these observations motivate fitting rotations online to each video’s
cache and sharing them within local temporal blocks. For other channels, see Section 7 of the appendix.
(ii) Heterogeneous structure across videos. Although
the cache is stable over adjacent frames within a video, the

two panels of Figure 1 show frame 64 of two different videos

A generic channel rotation, such as the fixed random ro-
tations used by QuaRot [2], does not explicitly exploit either
of these properties. A fixed rotation must simultaneously
accommodate temporal and cross-channel variation with a
single rotation. Moreover, because this temporal structure
differs across videos, a rotation chosen before generation
cannot adapt to the cache of the video actually being gen-
erated. Instead of applying a single rotation shared across
all tokens, TRQ allows adjacent frames within one video to
share a rotation adapted to the content they have in common.
Specifically, we divide the cache at each patch into blocks of
nB consecutive latent frames and fit one orthogonal rotation
RB per block, which is applied to every frame in the block
(Fig. 2). Fitting the rotation separately for each video and
block allows it to track the scene as it evolves, while sharing
the rotation within a block amortizes its storage cost over
nB cache vectors.

What should this shared rotation accomplish? An asym-
metric quantizer stores a separate offset for each vector,
allowing any component that is constant across channels to
be represented without introducing additional quantization
error. However, the temporal mean shared by nearby frames
generally varies across channels, widening the range that
must be quantized even when frame-specific deviations are
small. We therefore seek a rotation RB that transforms the
block’s mean over time into a vector that is nearly constant
across channels. This lets the quantizer’s offset to capture
the shared component, leaving its limited quantization lev-
els to represent the smaller frame-specific deviations more
accurately (we make this more concrete in Section 4).
A general d × d rotation per block would be prohibitively
expensive for a KV-cache quantized to two bits per scalar.
To reduce this overhead, we construct each rotation as a
balanced tree of 2 × 2 planar rotations followed by a fixed
Hadamard transform shared across all blocks. Each planar
rotation mixes two channels, with its angle chosen from
{0, π/4, π/2, 3π/4}. It is therefore stored with two bits
and applied using only additions, subtractions, and a shared
scaling. The tree uses d −1 such rotations to progressively
concentrate the energy of the block’s temporal mean into a
single coordinate (Fig. 3), which the Hadamard transform
then spreads evenly across all d channels. For d = 128, the
adaptive rotation parameters require only 254 bits per block.
We fit the angles greedily, level by level in the tree, with-
out gradients or changes to model weights. For a fixed tree
(which refers to the chosen pairings of channels for the pla-
nar rotations), this procedure is globally optimal for our
mean-flattening objective (Theorem 1). We also provide a
custom Triton implementation of our scheme, which means
that these rotations can be optimized online with almost no
run-time overhead (Sec. 4.6). In experiments on LongCat-
Video-13B, Self-Forcing-Wan-1.3B, and HY-WorldPlay-8B,
TRQ outperforms the state-of-the-art video KV-cache quan-
tization method QVG [26] at matched compression on all
seven evaluated video fidelity and quality metrics for Long-
Cat and Self-Forcing, and on six of seven for HY-WorldPlay
(Sec. 5).
2. Related Work
Diffusion and flow-based generation.
Diffusion trans-
formers replace convolutional denoisers with transformer
2
backbones in latent generative models [19]. LongCat-Video
combines a diffusion-transformer architecture with video-
continuation training and long-video inference [17]. HY-
WorldPlay-8B is a streaming video diffusion world model
that generates long-horizon video autoregressively in chunks,
conditioned on user actions such as camera motion, and dy-
namically reconstitutes context from past frames to maintain
long-term geometric consistency [23]. Our method targets
the conditioning KV-cache used during such long-horizon
generation. It does not alter the training objective, sampling
schedule, or model parameters.
Quantization of diffusion models.
Q-Diffusion addresses
post-training quantization of denoising networks through
timestep-aware calibration and split shortcut quantiza-
tion [12]. Those mechanisms concern quantizing the de-
noiser activations and network weights. The goal of this
work is to instead quantize the KV-cache which is reused
over a continuation’s denoising steps. The closest work is
QVG [26], which groups similar cache tokens, subtracts each
group’s centroid and quantizes the remaining residuals in sev-
eral stages. QVG explicitly represents cache patterns using
centroids. Our method instead represents a local temporal
mean implicitly through an adaptive orthogonal transform,
motivated by the success of orthogonal transforms for the
quantization of LLMs [2, 15, 16].
Rotations and KV-cache quantization in LLMs.
Early
methods for KV-cache quantization in LLMs mainly exploit
the distinct structure of keys and values. KIVI quantizes
keys per channel and values per token [14], and KVQuant
finds that pre-RoPE keys are more friendly for quantiza-
tion [8]. A second line of work rotates the cache before
quantization so that outlier channels are spread across many
coordinates. QuaRot uses orthogonal rotations to redistribute
activation outliers while folding the inverse transform into
the weights [2], SpinQuant learns rotations using Cayley
SGD [15], and RotateKV applies them before RoPE and
across grouped heads [22]. PolarQuant and TurboQuant use
random rotations to make the coordinate distribution pre-
dictable enough for simple scalar or polar quantizers [7, 29].
In all of these methods, the rotation is either fixed or cali-
brated once and shared across tokens, and it targets outliers
within each vector. Our transform instead adapts to each
temporal block and targets the mean shared by neighboring
frames. Because these transforms vary across blocks, they
cannot be absorbed into one global rotation, so we parame-
terize them in a much more light-weight fashion (Sec. 4.2).
3. Preliminaries
3.1. Video continuation and conditioning caches
Video diffusion transformers generate in the compressed
latent space of a video VAE, where each latent time index
summarizes several RGB frames and each spatial position
corresponds to an image patch. Long videos are produced by
continuation: rather than generating the whole video at once,
the model generates it chunk by chunk, each chunk a short se-
quence of latent frames conditioned on everything generated
so far. Let x1, . . . , xc denote the chunks generated (or pro-
vided by the user) so far. The next chunk x∗= xc+1 is gen-
erated conditioned on the clean prefix xctx

Rigel-Ladon: An Option-Count Law for a One-Pass
Decision Encoder, Tested on Held-Out Option Counts and
Held-Out Schemas
Nested option sets, independence from irrelevant alternatives, position and rival effects, fixes that fail to
transfer, and the twenty threshold tests of the first version
Mohammed Nayeem Khan
mohammed.nayeem.khan@intel.com
mnknayeem@gmail.com
Vrishank Tiwari
vrishank.tiwari@intel.com
Navin Kumar R
navin.kumar.r@intel.com
Intel Corporation
v1 · 19 November 2026 · arXiv cs.AI (cross-list cs.CL, cs.LG)
Abstract
Laya is a small neural network that reads a text, a question and K written options, and returns one probability
per option in a single pass. We ask how its accuracy falls as K grows from 2 to 35 and whether that can be
predicted. We score nested option sets (every K-option question contains the smaller ones) on four question
pools, for the released model (Base) and our fine-tune (FT), and score every item against each single rival. FT
trained on one 12-option topic question (in-family); a 12-option HR (department-routing) question is out-of-
family. Logit accuracy (the log of correct over incorrect answers) is linear in log(K-1) with slope 0.68 to 0.88.
Fitted on K up to 6, the law predicts K=7 to 12 within 0.6 points and K up to 24 within 1.2 (a log-linear rule: 1.6
and 6.7). Taking the slope from the topic question and measuring only two-option accuracy on HR predicts its
other K within 0.3 points (FT) and 0.7 (Base). On a 35-label pool of five schemas the law fails (5 to 11 points).
Independence of irrelevant alternatives is rejected: the gold-versus-rival log-odds shifts by +0.24 to +2.07 nats
per doubling of K, yet pairwise answers reproduce K-way accuracy within 4.7 points. Order averaging (averaging
over several orderings of the options), shortlists, a temperature law and calibrated prediction sets did not
transfer (FT's 90% sets cover 84% on HR). 2 of 10 predictions made in advance held. Caveats: one model family
and LLM-labelled synthetic text.
Keywords: option-count scaling; independence of irrelevant alternatives; typed-decision encoder; many-option
questions; held-out evaluation; order averaging; conformal prediction; token budget.
Key results (all values recomputed at build time)
1. Logit accuracy is linear in log(K-1): slope c = 0.68 to 0.88 in all eight cells (intervals in Table 6 of Section 5).
Fitted on K up to 6, it predicts K=7 to 12 within 0.6 points (log-linear rule 1.6, IIA with c=1 3.1) and K=16 to 24
on Pool-24 within 1.2 (6.7 for the log-linear rule).
2. With the slope borrowed from the topic schema and only two-option accuracy measured, the law predicts
all other K on HR-12, a schema FT never saw, within 0.3 points (FT) and 0.7 (Base); a borrowed log-linear
slope is off by 3.0 and 6.2. On Mega-35, fitted on two points, it fails by 5 to 11 points at K above 12.
3. IIA is rejected: the raw gap between the gold option and a fixed rival rises by +0.24 to +2.07 nats per
doubling of K, with every interval excluding zero; composing the K-1 pairwise answers still reproduces K-way
accuracy within 4.7 points and misses the probability by 9 to 23.
4. The strongest pairwise rival predicts K-way errors with AUROC 0.83 to 0.96, against 0.75 to 0.84 for the
count of rivals that win; a rival from another schema is no easier than one from the same schema.
5. Position: the pre-stated spread test passes in 1 of 6 cells; an exploratory trend test shows earlier slots more
accurate on HR-12 and Pool-24 by 6 to 8 points from first to last slot.
6. Fixes tested on held-out schemas: ten-order averaging gains at most 2.2 points with every interval including
zero; shortlist-then-compare and a temperature law fitted on the topic schema do not help reliably; a 90%
conformal set calibrated on topics covers 84% on HR-12 (FT) and 99% (Base, sets of 5.9 options).
7. 2 of 10 pre-stated predictions held (Section 10); the others are reported as refuted or half-confirmed.
8. Part II, the twenty threshold tests of the first version: released 5 pass / 8 fail / 1 inconclusive; fine-tuned 13 /
4 / 3. Every threshold is a convention, stated with its rationale next to the test.
9. The stored 11+ temperature (0.1006) is applied as 0.5; confidence at K=12 is 95% at 74% accuracy (T-02 fail);
the in-sample ECE-optimal total temperature is about 2.2.
10. Short 24-option questions are insensitive to head_max_len (0 of 468 items change; head 185 tokens); long
ones are at 5% (Base) to 4% (FT) at 192 and 38% for FT at 768, and the collapsed-options flag fires on 0% of
the questions that lose every informative token.
11. The K=12 fine-tune gains +1.5 points on an unseen schema (p=0.541), short of the 5-point bar (T-14 fail); 443
in-schema rows give +6.6 (p=0.002); a TF-IDF baseline is within 0.7 points on HR.

1  Introduction
Accuracy on a multiple-choice question depends on how many options are listed, and the dependence is not the
same for every model. Laya is a small encoder that reads a text together with a question and the written options
in one forward pass and returns one probability for every option. The caller decides how many options to list,
and the model card gives a temperature table for the option counts it was tuned on, up to 12. What an
application needs to know before it lists 16 or 24 options is how much accuracy it will lose and whether the
confidence can be trusted. The first version of this report answered with twenty pass-or-fail tests, each with a
threshold that we had chosen, and the thresholds were the weakest part: a verdict of fail at 90% retention says
little about how accuracy behaves at 13 options or at 35.
We keep those tests as a second part (Sections 11 to 21) and build the first part around quantities that can be
predicted and checked. The experiments use nested option sets, so that a K-option question contains every
smaller question of the same item (Section 4). We measured accuracy and the probability of every option from
K=2 up to 35 on four pools of questions, two models and up to 10 draws per item, and we scored every item
against every single rival.
We report five results.
1. Accuracy follows a law with one free exponent. Logit accuracy falls linearly in log(K-1), and the fitted slope is
0.68 to 0.88 in every pool and model. Fitted on K up to 6, the law predicts accuracy at K from 7 to 12 within
0.6 points on average, against 1.6 for a log-linear rule, and on Pool-24, the only pool of the four that goes past
K=12 and stops at 24, within 1.2 points at K above 12, against 6.7. On the 35-label pool built from five schemas
the law fails, by 5 to 11 points at K above 12 when it is fitted on two points of that pool (Section 5).
2. The exponent transfers. Taking it from the topic schema and measuring only two-option accuracy on a
different schema (HR) predicts every other K there within 0.3 points for the fine-tune and 0.7 for the
released checkpoint, where a borrowed log-linear slope is off by 3.0 and 6.2.
3. IIA fails in both models. The gap between the gold option and a fixed rival changes by +0.24 to +2.07 nats per
doubling of K, with every interval excluding zero. The gap grows with K, so added options help the gold
option against that rival, and the probability of one option has to be read together with the list around it
(Section 6).
4. Position matters little by the test we pre-stated. The spread of accuracy over the slot of the gold option
exceeds a permutation null in 1 of 6 cells. A trend test that we added afterwards finds that early slots are
more accurate on HR-12 and Pool-24, by 6 to 8 points from the first to the last slot (Section 7).
5. The fixes behave differently on held-out schemas (Section 8). Several of our pre-stated predictions failed,
and Section 10 lists which.
The question of what is in-family matters for every headline. The fine-tuned model (FT) trained on the topic
schema, and Topic-12 is therefore its in-family test. HR-12 is out-of-family for FT, and Pool-24 and Mega-35
contain both kinds of item. The released checkpoint (Base) has no training data we can inspect. Whenever a
number below comes from an in-family condition the text says so.
2  Related work and positioning
Searches covered Hugging Face Papers and arXiv at title and abstract level on 10 and 18 November 2026. Every
paper cited below was opened, and what is said about it goes no further than its abstract, except for the five
papers on option-set dependence, order dependence, per-option scoring, conformal sets and pairwise ranking,
whose method and evaluation sections we also read. The search is not exhaustive.
2.1  Typed-decision models and their evaluations
A typed decision maps evidence, a question and caller-defined options to one probability per option in a single
forward pass. Jev introduced the interface and Laya is an open encoder that implements it. Sharma et al. [2026]
built TypedBench to score such models on accuracy across paraphrases, calibration against the noise floor of a
perfectly calibrated predictor, and cost, and report that decoder baselines degrade as options are added. We
borrow the noise-floor idea for the T-04 threshold. Rafe and Das [2026] find a fine-tuned DeBERTa-v3-large
most accurate on almost every labelled benchmark they test; T-18 runs the same kind of check at twelve labels
with a TF-IDF classifier.
2.2  Option order, position and option count
Selection bias and order sensitivity are established for decoder language models on multiple-choice questions
[Zheng et al. 2023; Pezeshkpour and Hruschka 2023], and Ok et al. [2026] split an option-bias score into a flip
rate and a positional skew. For typed decisions, Zhang et al. [2026] (AnyJev) report on two 20-option tasks that a
readout from a pretrained language model favours some labels and some list positions. They correct both
without training, by dividing out a label prior and averaging log-probabilities over the K cyclic rotations of the
option list; the flip rate falls from 0.33 to 0.14 and 0.18, at the price of K prefills. Teke [2026] scores each option
blind to the others, and a sequential head trained with shuffled options still changed 2.3 to 2.8% of answers
when only the order changed. Li and Wang [2026] (Jeva) require permutation invariance and candidate sets that
scale to thousands of options.
T-11 and T-12 measure the same two defects on the sequential head of Laya at K=12. The released checkpoint flips
31% of items over 24 random orderings, a shuffle-trained fine-tune 11%, and the parallel layout 0%. The released
checkpoint’s share is close in size to the 0.33 that AnyJev reports for unmodified readouts, but the models, the
tasks and the flip statistic differ, so the numbers are not comparable. Section 8 runs prior division and averaging
over random orderings on the nested draws. A majority vote over the 24 orderings of T-11, a rough analogue of
rotation averaging, moves accuracy by +1.4 points for Base and -0.1 for FT (Table 24).
The effect of the option count itself is less settled. MMLU-Pro [Wang et al. 2024] raised the choice set from four
to ten options together with harder questions, and accuracy fell by 16 to 33%, so the two changes are
confounded; Song et al. [2025] report that the number of options influences accuracy in a study of five language
models; Gao et al. [2026] refine ordinal scales from K=2 to 14 with items and source scores held fixed and find
that scale utilisation falls for every model they test. The K-curves in Section 14 also hold the item fixed and
change only the sampled distractors, for a nominal question and an encoder, from K=2 to 12 and (with a second
schema) to 24, and they report chance-adjusted skill.
2.3  Labels, descriptions and the token budget
Azizi et al. [2026] show that the probability in Jev-style typed-decision models follows the option labels more
than their written definitions, and they trace the effect in Laya to the rendering of each option as a label
followed by its definition. T-07 builds the converse case: the names carry no information, so the description is
the only evidence, and the head budget cuts the description. The controls in Table 26 (names only against
descriptions only) point the same way for the released checkpoints. The backbone, ModernBERT, was trained
with a native sequence length of 8192 [Warner et al. 2024], so the default 192-token head and 512-token sequence
are runtime settings. Liu et al. [2023] show that decoder models use long contexts less well as they grow, which is
a possible but untested reading of our loss at a 1536-token head. Milios et al. [2023] handle a large label space in
an in-context classifier by showing only a retrieved part of it, the same idea as the shortlist helper that the Laya
runtime ships; Section 8 tests a shortlist built from the encoder’s own scores.
2.4  Calibration
Temperature scaling is the standard post-hoc fix for over-confident networks [Guo et al. 2017]; Kull et al. [2019]
propose a natively multiclass alternative to a single scalar, and Desai and Durrett [2020] analyse the calibration
of pre-trained transformers in and out of domain. Teke [2026] finds that temperature scaling lowers calibration
error on a development set but raises it on held-out questions. T-04 fits its multiplier on the same 270 items that
it scores, so the optimum is optimistic. It is used only to show the direction and size of the error of the shipped
scale. Errors in test labels can reorder systems [Northcutt et al. 2021], the reason for T-19.
2.5  Independence of irrelevant alternatives, shortlists and conformal sets
Rajput et al. [2026] test independence from irrelevant alternatives (IIA) on a hosted Jev model with 299,463 calls
on intent and topic classification, and find that every added option moves the log-odds between the gold label
and its strongest wrong rival, with a distortion that grows with the logarithm of the number of options and
reaches about 1 nat at 255 options. Huang et al. [2026] show that the order dependence of System One models
grows with the number of options and that cyclic averaging reduces it without removing it; their Runoff method
scores every option alone to build a shortlist and compares the shortlisted options in listings where each takes
every position. Stekel [2026] compares joint and per-option scoring in compact encoders and reports that joint
encoders change 12 to 23% of their answers when the options are reordered. Qin et al. [2023] use pairwise
comparisons to rank candidates with decoder models, which is the decomposition that our composition test
applies to a choice question. Kumar et al. [2023] apply conformal prediction to multiple-choice questions and
examine out-of-subject questions, where exchangeability can fail.
Section 6 repeats the IIA test on an open encoder with a nested design and adds a composition test that turns
pairwise results into a K-way prediction. Section 5 fits a law of accuracy against K and tests it on K and schemas
held out of the fit. Section 8 runs the order averaging, shortlist and conformal procedures of this literature on
the same questions.
2.6  Position of this report
The IIA question and the order dependence are earlier findings; our contribution is to test them on an open
model with a design that holds the question fixed while K changes, and to turn the K-dependence into a fitted
and checked law. Within the searches above we found no earlier work on the token budget that cuts the option
block of a typed-decision encoder, on the stored and applied option-count temperature of Laya, or on schema
transfer of a Laya fine-tune; those measurements, the fitted exponent and its transfer, and the held-out tests of
the fixes are what we add. The measurements are one encoder family on synthetic, LLM-labelled data, so the
exponent is a result about Laya on these schemas and not a constant of the field.
3  System under test, data and conventions
3.1  Component under test
Laya reads a question and a piece of text together. The question is rendered as [CLS] choice question:
<instruction> [SEP] [MASK] name: description [MASK] name: description … [SEP] <text> [SEP]. A ModernBERT-
large encoder (28 layers) processes the whole sequence once. The hidden state at each [MASK] marker is the state
of that option; a two-layer transformer head lets the option states attend to one another and a scorer emits one
logit per option. Logits are divided by a temperature that depends on the question type and on how many
options the question has (buckets 2, 3-5, 6-10, 11+), then soft-maxed; the top probability is reported as
answer_confidence. Because every option is read from a position inside one bounded sequence, two budgets
matter once K grows: how many tokens the option block may occupy and how many the whole sequence may.
Figure 1. Test rig: the path of a K-option question through the runtime, left to right, and the test cases (red) that probe each
stage. T-03 and T-10 read configuration and call the runtime’s own functions without a model; all other tests replay frozen

The test material has two parts. The topic schema is a 12-way support-ticket question whose option descriptions
are the labels themselves, so options are 3-5 tokens long; the HR schema is a 12-way question with keyword

A Control-Theoretic Approximation to
Predictive Coding Dynamics
Ryan Fayyazi∗
New York University
ryan.fayyazi@nyu.edu
Kyle Daruwalla∗
Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory
daruwal@cshl.edu
Mitra Javadzadeh
Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory
javadzadeh@cshl.edu
Abstract
Backpropagation remains the dominant method for training deep neural networks,
but its reliance on non-local computations has motivated the search for biologically
plausible alternatives. Two prominent frameworks, predictive coding (PC) and
deep feedback control (DFC), offer distinct approaches to local learning, yet their
relationship remains unclear. Here, we show that DFC arises as a local approxi-
mation to predictive coding dynamics near fixed points, with exact equivalence in
shallow linear networks and systematic deviations arising with depth, nonlinearity,
and distance from equilibrium. We characterize how this approximation, which we
call Approx PC, deviates from PC in its activity dynamics, and show that these de-
viations can be mitigated by relinearizing the feedback controller and approaching
the output target through a sequence of intermediate nudges. In networks trained
on MNIST and FashionMNIST, Approx PC reaches task performance comparable
to PC trained with the same nudges, and weights learned with it transfer directly to
PC inference. Our results unify energy-based and control-theoretic perspectives on
learning and open the door to applying tools from control theory to the training of
predictive coding networks.
1
Introduction
Backpropagation has become the dominant algorithm for training deep neural networks, yet it relies
on computational primitives that are difficult to reconcile with biological neural circuits, including
weight transport across layers [1], global error signals [17, 22], and phased learning stages [7].
The brain, on the other hand, relies on synaptic plasticity, which is widely believed to depend on
local information available at each synapse, such as pre- and post-synaptic activity and modulatory
feedback, and does not require distinct forward and backward passes [18]. This contrast has motivated
a large body of work seeking biologically plausible alternatives for credit assignment in deep neural
networks [2, 3, 10, 23, 20, 4, 6, 11, 9, 12]. Among these, two influential approaches have emerged
from distinct perspectives: (1) predictive coding (PC) networks [21, 5, 24, 16], inspired by sensory
processing in cortical circuits and typically formulated as energy-based models that minimize a
global objective by reducing local mismatch between bottom-up and top-down signals, and (2) deep
feedback control (DFC) [13], motivated by principles of motor control and rooted in control-theoretic
frameworks, where credit assignment is achieved via dynamical error correction through a feedback
controller.
While both frameworks implement local learning rules, their underlying neural dynamics appear
markedly different. Although both rely on error signals, their origin and role differ: in PC, errors are
computed locally at each layer, whereas in DFC they arise from a global target and are distributed
through the network via the controller (see Figure 1). This apparent difference raises the question
∗Equal contribution.
40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026).
arXiv:2611.26319v1  [cs.LG]  19 Nov 2026
of whether these two classes of models implement fundamentally distinct mechanisms for credit
assignment, or whether they can be understood within a common framework.
Figure 1: Illustrations of error signal sources in predictive coding (left) and deep feedback control
(right). PC errors are distributed while DFC is centralized. Pathways involved in calculating errors
are denoted by solid lines, while general information pathways are denoted by dashed lines.
From a biological perspective, the connectivity motifs required by both frameworks are present in the
cortex: hierarchical organization with local feedforward–feedback loops supports predictive coding,
while long-range feedback from higher-order to early sensory areas enables global control signals.
This suggests that the brain may support both local error correction mechanisms and more global
control-driven dynamics, raising the possibility that the two frameworks reflect different regimes of a
shared underlying computation.
Here, we show that DFC can be interpreted as a local approximation to PC dynamics in the vicinity
of fixed points. This equivalence is exact for shallow linear networks and progressively breaks down
with increasing network depth, with the introduction of nonlinearities, and as the system moves
further from equilibrium. Building on this connection, we propose a practical scheme to approximate
PC using DFC by decomposing the trajectory toward a target into a sequence of intermediate
subgoals. Within each subgoal, DFC dynamics drive the network toward a local equilibrium before
transitioning to the next stage. This perspective suggests that distributed, layer-wise error signals can
be effectively replaced by a centralized feedback controller that sequentially guides the network
through intermediate targets. Our contributions are organized in three parts:
Theory:
We establish a formal connection between predictive coding and deep feedback
control by showing that PC activity dynamics can be written as a distributed feedback controller,
which reduces near fixed points to a DFC-style controller driven by the output error. We call the
resulting approximate dynamics Approx PC. In linear networks, we show that the two are exactly
equivalent with a single hidden layer, and that with two hidden layers they share the same fixed point
and differ only by an additional damping term in PC.
Characterizing the approximation:
Through controlled probes of activity dynamics on sin-
gle inputs, we show how Approx PC deviates from PC as perturbation size, depth, and nonlinearity
increase. We demonstrate that these deviations are mitigated by relinearizing the feedback controller
or by approaching the output target through a sequence of intermediate nudges.
Validation under learning:
We test whether the approximation error compounds during
training and find that it does not substantially affect what the network learns. On MNIST [8] and
FashionMNIST [25], networks trained with Approx PC reach task performance comparable to that of
PC trained with the same nudges, their learned weights transfer directly to PC inference, and their
hyperparameter sensitivity is similar to that of PC.1
2
Related work
Although not the focus of this work, many alternative biologically plausible learning rules use local
signals and objectives to learn [23, 20, 4] or various centralized feedback pathways to drive learning
[2, 3, 10, 20, 4, 6]. Many of these have theoretical relationships to both PC and DFC, but our
objective is to understand PC through a specific family of control-based rules. In particular, while
recent hierarchical variants of PC incorporate long-range feedback pathways, here we focus on the
standard PC formulation. The work most closely related to ours is [15], where the authors briefly note
that PC can be understood as a solution to a least-control problem. Yet the controller they propose is
distributed rather than a DFC-style feedback controller driven by the final layer’s error. We discuss
these distinctions in more detail in Section 4.
1Code is available at https://github.com/darsnack/pc-dfc.
