C-LiTE: A Lightweight Foundation Model for Cellular
feature learning in Histopathology
Esha Sadia Nasira,∗, Jiaqi Lva, Gozde N. Guneslia, Shan E Ahmed Razaa
aVISION Lab, Department of Computer Science, University of Warwick, Coventry, UK
Abstract
Characterising individual cells is fundamental to computational pathology,
as cellular morphology informs tasks such as tumour grading, mitotic assess-
ment and immune profiling. However, most pathology foundation models are
trained on tissue patches and capture cellular features only implicitly, while
existing cell-level models are either restricted to specific cell populations or
rely on computationally expensive architectures with hundreds of millions of
parameters. Applying vision transformers (ViTs) directly to small cellular
crops also presents an architectural challenge: upsampling increases compu-
tational cost without adding morphological information and may introduce
interpolation artefacts, whereas conventional patch embeddings applied at
native resolution yield insufficient spatial tokens for effective self-attention.
To address these limitations, we introduce C-LiTE, a lightweight founda-
tion model for cellular representation learning in H&E-stained histopathol-
ogy, with only 22 million parameters. C-LiTE employs a native-resolution
tokenisation strategy tailored to cellular inputs, processing 64 × 64 px cell-
centred crops using a 4 × 4 patch embedding to produce a 16 × 16 token grid
without image upsampling. To transfer visual knowledge from large-scale
pre-training, we adapt the patch embedding weights of a pre-trained ViT-
5-S using a Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse-based transformation, enabling
weight initialisation at the finer patch resolution. We further assemble a pre-
training dataset of 60 million cell-centred crops from The Cancer Genome
Atlas (TCGA), balanced across 19 cancer types and 16 tissue types.
To
our knowledge, this represents the largest publicly available dataset for self-
supervised pre-training on H&E images at the cellular level.
∗Corresponding author
Email address: esha.nasir@warwick.ac.uk (Esha Sadia Nasir)
arXiv:2611.26316v1  [cs.CV]  19 Nov 2026
We evaluate C-LiTE on seven public datasets spanning mitotic figure
recognition, nucleus and cell-type classification, and immune cell phenotyp-
ing.
Under frozen-feature evaluation, C-LiTE achieves a mean macro-F1
of 0.670, approaching CytoFormer (0.682) with approximately 30× fewer
parameters, while outperforming tissue-level foundation models, including
Virchow2 and UNI2. These results highlight the potential of compact, cell-
centric architectures for learning transferable cellular representations.
Keywords:
foundation model, self-supervised learning, computational
pathology, cell morphology, digital pathology, cell classification
1. Introduction
Haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining forms the basis of histopatholog-
ical diagnosis, providing information about tissue architecture and cellular
composition. A single H&E-stained WSI contains hundreds of thousands of
nuclei belonging to different cell types. Analysis of these WSIs involves iden-
tifying the cell types (inferred from nuclei) present, quantifying their relative
abundance, and characterising their spatial organisation (Yao et al., 2026).
These cellular features, such as immune infiltration, provide important infor-
mation for diagnostic, prognostic, and treatment decisions (Virchow, 1863;
Zhang et al., 2025) in clinical practice. However, extracting such information
accurately at scale remains challenging. In current computational workflows,
this often requires manual annotation of cells or nuclei by pathologists, fol-
lowed by the development of supervised models specific to individual datasets
(Hörst et al., 2023; Lv et al., 2026; Nasir et al., 2023). Such models typi-
cally require fine-tuning or retraining when applied to new datasets, limiting
their generalisability and increasing the reliance on task-specific and dataset-
specific annotations.
Recent advances in self-supervised foundation models offer a promising
alternative, enabling the learning of transferable features from large-scale
histopathology data that can be adapted to a wide range of downstream
tasks. Models such as UNI (Chen et al., 2024b), Virchow2 (Zimmermann
et al., 2024), CONCH (Lu et al., 2023), CTransPath (Wang et al., 2022),
Phikon (Filiot et al., 2024), Prov-GigaPath (Xu et al., 2024), and TITAN
(Ding et al., 2025) have established a powerful paradigm for learning general-
isable features from WSIs. These models are trained on either image patches
containing hundreds of cells or whole-slide images (WSIs) containing thou-
2
sands of cells, allowing them to capture a combination of cellular morphology,
stromal composition, tissue architecture, and spatial context. However, these
models are primarily developed for whole-slide or patch-level feature extrac-
tion and cannot adequately capture the fine-grained morphological features
required to distinguish individual cell types. Moreover, the substantial com-
putational and memory requirements of these models present a significant
challenge for cell-level analysis.
Applying these models independently to
thousands of nuclei within a single WSI would be computationally expen-
sive and difficult to scale, limiting their practical utility for high-throughput
cellular characterisation.
Recognising these limitations, recent work has shifted towards cell-centric
feature learning in histopathology (Chadoutaud et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026).
By focusing explicitly on individual cells, these approaches aim to learn fea-
tures that better capture intrinsic cellular morphology and state. However,
this shift towards cell-level modelling does not fully resolve the computational
challenge. For example, CytoFormer (Yao et al., 2026), a recent cell-centric
foundation model, comprises approximately 681 million parameters, retain-
ing substantial computational and memory requirements comparable to those
of existing pathology foundation models. This presents practical challenges
for inference and limits the efficiency of cell-centric foundation models in
large-scale cellular analysis. These limitations highlight the need for an effi-
cient and lightweight foundation model for H&E-stained cells. Such a model
should learn rich and generalisable cellular representations while reducing
computational requirements. This need is further reinforced by growing con-
cerns about the computational and environmental costs of modern AI. The
Green AI framework advocates treating computational efficiency as an ob-
jective alongside predictive performance, highlighting the financial and envi-
ronmental costs of deep learning and the contribution of inference to overall
AI deployment costs (Schwartz et al., 2020; Strubell et al., 2019; Luccioni
et al., 2024). To address this need, we introduce C-LiTE, a compact self-
supervised model for generalisable cellular feature learning at single-cell reso-
lution. C-LiTE is pre-trained on approximately 60M cell-centric image crops
spanning 19 cancer types, 16 tissue types, and multiple staining protocols.
This diverse training corpus captures a broad spectrum of cellular morpholo-
gies. We adapt the ViT-5 backbone within a teacher–student self-supervised
framework using DINO and iBOT objectives. The resulting model learns
transferable cellular representations that generalise across datasets and down-
stream tasks while preserving continuous morphological variation without
3
being constrained by predefined cell categories. C-LiTE supports a diverse
range of applications, including label-free cellular phenotyping, cell classifica-
tion, mitosis classification, and morphology-based feature extraction. Across
extensive evaluations, it achieves competitive performance against substan-
tially larger cell-centric foundation models and tile-level pathology founda-
tion models evaluated on cell crops. These results demonstrate the ability
of C-LiTE to deliver high-quality cellular representations at substantially
lower computational cost. The overall architecture of the proposed C-LiTE
framework is presented in Fig. 1. The main contributions of our work are as
follows:
• We develop C-LiTE, comprising:
– a compact 22M-parameter model for cellular feature learning,
adapting the ViT-5 backbone to process 64 × 64 px cell crops at
native resolution within a self-supervised teacher–student frame-
work.
– a large and diverse cell-centric pre-training corpus comprising over
60M cell-centric image crops, spanning 19 cancer types and
16 tissue types, and covering diverse tissue contexts.
– the Pseudoinverse-Initialised Patch Embedding formulation
(PI-PatchEmbed), which transfers pre-trained ViT-5-S weights
from 16 × 16 to 4 × 4 patch projections using a Moore–Penrose
pseudoinverse-based spatial transfer operator.
• We demonstrate that C-LiTE learns transferable cellular representa-
tions that generalise across datasets and downstream tasks, achieving
performance comparable to CytoFormer (Yao et al., 2026) despite hav-
ing approximately 30× fewer parameters.
• We demonstrate the versatility of C-LiTE across diverse tasks, includ-
ing immune cell phenotyping, cell-type classification, pan-cancer nu-
cleus classification, hierarchical cell classification, and mitosis classifi-
cation.
• We provide open access to the C-LiTE models, pre-training dataset,
source code, and training configurations to facilitate reproducibility
and encourage the research community to build upon our work.

2. Related Work
2.1. Pathology Foundation Models
The emergence of pathology foundation models has reshaped computa-
tional pathology, with self-supervised pre-training becoming a widely adopted
approach for learning transferable features from large-scale histopathology
5
data (Hua et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2026). Early transformer-based meth-
ods, such as CTransPath (Wang et al., 2022), demonstrated that features
learned from a large collection of unlabelled tissue patches could transfer
effectively across a range of downstream tasks.
HIPT (Hierarchical Im-
age Pyramid Transformer) (Chen et al., 2022) subsequently extended this
paradigm through hierarchical pre-training at multiple magnification levels,
enabling the modelling of information across cellular and tissue scales.
Subsequent work has increasingly focused on scaling training data and
model capacity, together with advances in pre-training strategies. For ex-
ample, UNI (Chen et al., 2024b) adapted the DINOv2 framework and pre-
trained a ViT-Large model on more than 100M image patches extracted
from over 100K diagnostic slides spanning 20 tissue types. Building on this
approach, UNI2 employs a ViT-Giant architecture and was trained on ap-
proximately 200M image tiles sampled from more than 350K diverse H&E
and IHC-stained slides.
Virchow and Virchow2 (Zimmermann et al., 2024) further increased both
model and dataset scale, employing a ViT-Huge architecture and training on
approximately 3.1M WSIs.
Their training framework uses a similar self-
supervised teacher–student paradigm with global and local crops, together
with extended-context translation (ECT) augmentation to preserve cellu-
lar morphology. In addition, the standard KoLeo regulariser was replaced
with a kernel density estimation (KDE)-based regulariser to improve the
learned feature distribution. Phikon further increased the scale and diver-
sity of training data, using approximately 460M pathology tiles spanning
more than 30 cancer sites. It also adopts a DINOv2-based self-supervised
framework (Filiot et al., 2024).
Alongside these image-based approaches,
alternative pre-training paradigms have emerged that extend beyond image-
only representation learning. CONCH (CONtrastive learning from Captions
for Histopathology) (Lu et al., 2023) introduced contrastive vision–language
learning using diverse histopathology images and biomedical text, including
more than 1.17M image–caption pairs within a task-agnostic pre-training
framework. Prov-GigaPath (Xu et al., 2024) shifted the focus towards slide-
level representation learning for WSIs understanding. It was pre-trained on
1.3B 256 × 256 px image tiles extracted from 171K WSIs spanning 31 tissue
types. A key component of its training strategy was the incorporation of
an adapted LongNet architecture to enable efficient modelling of whole-slide
sequences. Extending the development of pathology foundation models to-
wards multimodal learning, TITAN (Ding et al., 2025) was trained on 335K
6
WSIs using self-supervised learning and vision–language alignment. Collec-
tively, these studies have established tissue patches and WSIs as the predom-
inant training units for pathology foundation models, while demonstrating
the value of increasing data scale, model capacity, and pre-training diversity
for learning generalisable pathology features (Rajendran et al., 2027).
2.2. Supervised Cell Classification Models
At the cellular level, computational pathology has traditionally relied
on supervised methods for cell detection, segmentation, and classification.
Approaches such as HoVer-Net (Graham et al., 2019), StarDist (Schmidt
et al., 2018), and CellViT (Hörst et al., 2023) have achieved strong per-
formance through training on densely annotated datasets with predefined
cell taxonomies. However, these methods are typically designed for specific
downstream tasks, with their learned representations closely tied to the anno-
tations and cell categories available during training. Developing such models
often requires extensive manual annotation by experts, which limits scalabil-
ity and can restrict generalisability across datasets. These limitations have
motivated a shift towards learning transferable cellular features directly from
large-scale, unlabelled histopathology data.
2.3. Pathology Cell Foundation Models
Building on this motivation, recent foundation models have explored self-
supervised learning to capture generalisable features across diverse cellular
morphologies and tissue contexts. VOLTA (Nakhli et al., 2024) introduced
environment-aware contrastive learning to jointly model individual cells and
their surrounding micro-environment. It was trained on approximately 700K
cells from 4 cancer types and demonstrated that meaningful cellular pheno-
types can be learnt without manual annotation. DinoBloom (Koch et al.,
2024) further extended self-supervised pre-training to approximately 380K
white blood cells (WBCs) from blood and bone marrow tissue across 13
publicly available datasets, producing features that transfer across a range
of haematological tasks. More recently, LEMON (Chadoutaud et al., 2026)
adopted a MoCo v3-based self-supervised framework and was trained on
approximately 10M individual nuclei from 10 tissue types. Using 40 × 40
px nuclear crops, LEMON demonstrated that nuclear morphology contains
rich biological information that can be captured without explicit cell-type
labels. Similarly, CytoFormer (Yao et al., 2026) further advanced cell-centric
7
foundation modelling in histopathology by leveraging paired H&E and spa-
tial transcriptomics data to derive molecularly informed cell-type supervision
across 16 tissue types. Together, these studies demonstrate the feasibility of
learning transferable cellular representations at scale, but differ substantially
in their cellular coverage, supervision, and model design.
Limitations of Existing Methods
Existing supervised approaches remain focused on specific cellular datasets,
while self-supervised cell foundation models require substantially larger ar-
chitectures and, in some cases, additional molecular supervision. These ap-
proaches also face challenges in preserving fine-grained cellular information.
For example, resizing cell crops from 56×56 µm to 224×224 µm changes the
native spatial scale of the input and may lead to the loss of fine morpholog-
ical detail. In contrast, LEMON operates on smaller 40 × 40 crops with an
8 × 8 patch size, producing only 25 patch tokens. This is substantially fewer
than the 256 patch tokens produced by a standard DINOv2 configuration
using a 224 × 224 px input with a 14 × 14 patch size. The limited number of
patch tokens may therefore restrict the spatial information available to the
transformer for modelling fine-grained cellular morphology.
These limitations raise many open questions.
• How effectively can pre-trained models transfer to cell crops smaller
than their standard input resolution?
• What patch size is most appropriate for self-supervised learning at
cellular resolution?
• More broadly, can a compact model trained directly on a large and
diverse collection of histopathological cells learn transferable feature
representations of cellular morphology without relying on increasingly
large architectures or explicit molecular supervision?
Building on these questions, C-LiTE extends cell-centric foundation mod-
elling to a substantially larger and more diverse histopathology corpus while
maintaining a compact architecture.
3. Pre-training Data
A key contribution of C-LiTE is the construction of, to the best of our
knowledge, one of the largest and most diverse cell-centric histopathology
8
pre-training corpora reported to date. The corpus comprises approximately
60M cell-centred image crops derived from TCGA WSIs across 19 cancer
types. This heterogeneous collection provides a large-scale pre-training re-
source designed to capture diverse cellular morphologies and support the
learning of robust and transferable cellular representations. The resulting
model is subsequently evaluated across a diverse set of downstream tasks,
including immune cell phenotyping, nucleus classification, cell-type classifi-
cation, and mitosis classification.
3.1. TCGA Cell Dataset
The primary source of pre-training data in this study is The Cancer
Genome Atlas (TCGA). The dataset covers 19 cancer types, including breast
carcinoma (BRCA), lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), lung squamous cell car-
cinoma (LUSC), ovarian serous cystadenocarcinoma (OV), colon adenocarci-
noma (COAD), rectal adenocarcinoma (READ), cervical squamous cell carci-
noma and endocervical adenocarcinoma (CESC), kidney renal clear cell car-
cinoma (KIRC), kidney renal papillary cell carcinoma (KIRP), pancreatic
adenocarcinoma (PAAD), liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC), prostate
adenocarcinoma (PRAD), uterine corpus endometrial carcinoma (UCEC),
uterine carcinosarcoma (UCS), thyroid carcinoma (THCA), stomach adeno-
carcinoma (STAD), head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC), bladder
urothelial carcinoma (BLCA), and adrenoco

Actor-Predictor Architecture for Reinforcement Learning with Formal
Specification Objectives
Josef Brozovich
University of Michigan, Ann Arbor
broz@umich.edu
Qining Zhang
University of Michigan, Ann Arbor
qiningz@umich.edu
Lei Ying
University of Michigan, Ann Arbor
leiying@umich.edu
Abstract
One fundamental challenge in reinforcement learning (RL) is enforcing temporal safety constraints, such
as satisfying formal specifications. Existing methods often transform logic formulas into automata for state
augmentation and reward shaping. However, this approach assumes that automaton construction is both feasible
and tractable, which limits its applicability to small specifications and linear temporal logic (LTL). This paper
proposes Actor-Predictor, a framework that learns a surrogate representation of logic progress without explicitly
constructing an automaton. The predictor continuously estimates whether a partial trajectory will satisfy the
formal specification in a later step, and its learned features are provided as auxiliary inputs to the actor, which
is then optimized using GRPO and RWR. We show theoretically that, under sufficient predictive accuracy, the
learned representation is equivalent to the automaton state. Experiments on grid world and robotic tasks in
Isaac Lab demonstrate that Actor-Predictor outperforms automaton-based baselines on LTL-constrained tasks.
It also performs well on non-regular formal specifications, such as panbnq, for which finite-automaton-based
approaches are not applicable.
1
Introduction
Formal specification is a framework for describing complex, time-dependent behaviors, such as safety constraints.
Reinforcement learning (RL) with formal specifications is a data-driven approach to train an agent to learn policies
that optimize objectives described by temporal logic formulas or non-regular specifications, which faces two
fundamental challenges. First, formal specifications introduce long-range temporal dependencies, meaning that the
optimal policy is generally non-Markovian, which may depend on the history of observations and actions rather
than solely on the current environment state. Second, formal specification objectives yield binary, trajectory-level
feedback, causing extreme reward sparsity that results in challenging cold-starts.
The standard approach to overcome this challenge is through automata theory and reward shaping (Shah et al.,
2024; Manganaris et al., 2025), which converts a temporal logic (TL) formula into a finite-state automaton and then
optimizes the TL objective over the product state space including both the automaton state and the environment
state. It often further modifies the reward function to provide dense feedback throughout the trajectory. However,
it has been shown that translating an LTL formula into a limit-deterministic Büchi automaton (LDBA) can be
computationally infeasible, where in the worst case, the complexity is double-exponential in the number of Atomic
Propositions (APs) (Sickert et al., 2016). Furthermore, any language requiring an arbitrary counter is non-regular
and, therefore, cannot be represented by a finite automaton.
1
arXiv:2611.26313v1  [cs.AI]  19 Nov 2026
This paper takes a different approach. Our algorithm learns a surrogate representation of the automaton state
using the features from a predictor that predicts the future satisfaction probability of a given partial trajectory. The
intuition behind this approach is that an agent’s progress through an automaton uniquely maps to a probability of
reaching a future accepting state. The predictor network can be trained from a set of collected trajectories with
binary satisfactory labels. The feature of the predictor, when given a partial trajectory, can represent the automaton
state, thus avoiding the construction of a finite-state automaton. This leads to our proposed Actor-Predictor
approach.
1.1
Main contributions
The key contributions of this paper include:
• Theoretical Guarantees: For deterministic automata with accepting states, we prove that: (i) a well-trained
predictor’s hidden representation sufficiently captures the automaton state (Lemma 1); and (ii) policy
optimization over the surrogate product state yields an optimal policy for the formal specification objective
(Theorem 1).
• Algorithm & Evaluation: We implement Actor-Predictor using a Mamba predictor (Gu and Dao, 2024)
and a GRPO-optimized actor (Guo et al., 2025) with exponential reward weighting. Across quadruped
navigation (LTL) and grid-world (non-regular) tasks, experiments show: (1) Actor-Predictor outperforms
baselines like CyclER (Shah et al., 2024), (2) Mamba predictors outperform Transformer and LSTM
baselines (Vaswani et al., 2017; Graves, 2012); (3) learned representations exhibit transferability and
subformula compositionality; and (4) predictor features empirically suffice to reconstruct the automaton
state.
2
Related Work
Combining formal specification with reinforcement learning to provide a formal framework for safety and task
satisfaction is an active topic in RL (Li et al., 2017; Bozkurt et al., 2020; Hasanbeig et al., 2020, 2019; Li et al.,
2018; Cai et al., 2021; Chou et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021). Temporal logic enables specifications over trajectories
as a time-ordered sequence of steps. The standard approach to address RL in formal specification is to convert the
Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) formula into a limit-deterministic Büchi automaton (LDBA). A product Markov
decision process (PMDP) is then constructed by combining the system’s state space and the Büchi Automaton,
yielding the product state space Sϕ “ S ˆ B. This transformation renders the task Markovian, enabling stationary
policies over the augmented state space.
Using the LDBA, methods such as Automaton Constrained Q-Learning (ACQL), Cycle Experience Replay
(CyclER), and LTL-guided Counterfactual Experience Replay (LCER) leverage progress within the automaton
to automatically densify the reward signal (Shah et al., 2024; Manganaris et al., 2025; Voloshin et al., 2023).
Although these methods improve learning efficiency, they fundamentally rely on access to the explicit structure and
observability of the automaton. This restricts the expressivity of formal logic to regular languages. Consequently,
tasks requiring arbitrary counting form non-regular languages and cannot be solved using these approaches.
Our approach is inspired by predictive state representations (PSRs) for POMDPs (Littman and Sutton, 2001).
In PSR, the latent state is represented by predictions of a collection of future tests, where each test corresponds to
a sequence of future observations. While PSRs require carefully handcrafted tests, our predictor directly estimates
the eventual satisfaction of the given specification.

3.1
RL Problem
This paper considers an RL problem defined by a tuple M “ pS, A, P, K, rLq, where S is the state space, A

a linear TL (LTL) φ or a non-regular formal specification. For example, the reward rLpτq could be a simple

specification has been repeatedly satisfied, or the counter n of the L “ tanbnu task. Different from classic RL,
our formal specification reward rL is usually a function of the whole trajectory and cannot be decomposed into

Client Exits - A Way to Increase LLM
Transparency on the Client Side
Marc Jansen
Computer Science Institute
University of Applied Sciences Ruhr West
Bottrop
Germany
marc.jansen@hs-ruhrwest.de
Abstract. Textual recommendations generated by large language mod-
els (LLMs) can be difficult to inspect. This paper introduces Client Exits,
a lightweight mechanism for enriching LLM responses while separating
semantic intent from client-specific presentation. The model inserts pre-
defined, machine-interpretable markers into its output, and the receiving
client decides whether and how to realize the corresponding enrichments.
This allows supplementary information to be presented as graphics, text,
speech, or other modalities without prescribing a concrete interface. We
implement a prototype combining a finetuned Qwen model with a modified
LibreChat client. Using the Question–Option–Criteria (QOC) approach
including three XML-based client exits. We evaluate two QOC-oriented
model variants trained on essentially the same examples, with client-
exit annotations added for one variant. Across 100 test questions, the
client-exit model includes all three markers in every response. An LLM
judge, informed about the mechanism without being instructed to favor
it, prefers this model’s answers in 66% of the comparisons. These results
demonstrate successful marker generation on the evaluated test set and
support the feasibility of client-controlled enrichment.
Keywords: Large Language Model (LLM) · User Interface · Extensibility
1
Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) can formulate recommendations and explain them
in natural language. For questions involving multiple alternatives and competing
criteria, however, a textual answer alone may make it difficult to inspect how
the alternatives compare, which criteria distinguish them, or whether other
options are similarly suitable. Graphical overviews and statistical summaries offer
complementary ways of presenting this information. The challenge addressed in
this paper is how an LLM can indicate where such enrichments would be useful
without prescribing how a particular client must present them.
This challenge concerns the boundary between answer generation and client-
side presentation. Software engineering provides a useful precedent in predefined
arXiv:2611.26309v1  [cs.AI]  19 Nov 2026
2
Marc Jansen
extension points, such as User Exits, which allow application-specific functionality
to be introduced without modifying a standard implementation [1]. At the
presentation boundary of an LLM system, a corresponding mechanism should
allow the producer to indicate an opportunity for enrichment while leaving its
realization to the receiving client. In particular, the intended information should
remain separate from its graphical, textual, or spoken representation.
We propose Client Exits as a lightweight mechanism for this separation. An
LLM inserts predefined, machine-interpretable markers at selected positions
within its response. Before displaying the answer, the client identifies these
markers and decides whether and how to integrate supplementary information.
A marker may indicate an overview, an analysis, or an explanation, but does
not specify a concrete interface layout. The same response can therefore support
different presentations depending on the client’s capabilities and purpose. The
underlying research question is whether an LLM can learn to generate these
semantic extension points reliably and whether responses from a model trained
to include them are preferred over those from a comparable model without them.
This paper contributes the client-exit architecture, an end-to-end prototype,
and an initial comparative evaluation. The prototype combines a finetuned Qwen
model with a modified LibreChat client and uses the Question–Option–Criteria
(QOC) approach to structure decision-oriented answers [5, 4]. Three XML-based
client exits support a graph of the question, options, and criteria; a ranking of
criteria by their discriminating influence; and a comparison of alternatives with
scores close to the winning score. These enrichments make the generated analysis
available for inspection alongside the recommendation, rather than claiming to
expose the model’s internal computations.
For the evaluation, we finetuned two QOC-oriented model variants using
essentially the same training examples, with client-exit markers added for one
variant. Across 100 test questions, the client-exit model included all three mark-
ers in every response. An LLM judge, given a theoretical explanation of the
mechanism without instructions to favor it, preferred this model’s answer in
66% of the comparisons. These findings demonstrate successful marker genera-
tion on the evaluated test set and a majority preference for the corresponding
answers. They do not, however, establish improvements in factual accuracy or
human understanding. The approach thus provides an implemented basis for
client-controlled enrichment, with its practical transparency benefits remaining a
subject for further evaluation.
2
State of the Art
Extensibility is a long-established principle in software engineering. Rather than
modifying a standard implementation whenever application-specific functionality
is required, software systems can expose predefined extension points at which
additional functionality may be introduced. A prominent example is the concept
of User Exits in enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems. Brehm et al. [1]
identify User Exits as a distinct ERP-tailoring mechanism in which additional
Client Exits - A Way to Increase LLM Transparency on the Client Side
3
software code is introduced through predefined interfaces instead of modifying
the underlying package. Similarly, Ng [6] discusses SAP R/3 Customer Exits
as a mechanism for adding customer-specific functionality while preserving the
maintainability and upgradeability of the standard system.
Thus, the provider determines where extension is permitted and specifies the
corresponding interface, whereas the consumer determines whether and how the
extension is realized.
A structurally related development can be observed in contemporary LLM sys-
tems. Increasingly, LLMs are embedded into larger systems in which functionality
is distributed among models, external tools, data sources, and autonomous agents.
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes access from LLM applications
to external tools, resources, and contextual information [3]. Agent2Agent (A2A),
in contrast, addresses interoperability among autonomous agents and supports
capability discovery, task delegation, message exchange, and the communication
of resulting artifacts [2]. Recent taxonomies consequently distinguish agent-to-
context communication, exemplified by MCP, from agent-to-agent communication,
exemplified by A2A [8].
MCP and A2A are not User Exits in the strict technical sense. Nevertheless,
they serve the same broader architectural objective: functionality is composed
through explicitly defined interfaces rather than being incorporated into a mono-
lithic implementation.
These mechanisms primarily extend what an LLM-based system can access,
execute, or delegate. They do not directly address another relevant boundary:
the transition from the semantic result generated by an LLM to its presentation
by the receiving client.
The in this paper proposed Client Exit transfers the extension-point princi-
ple to this boundary. The LLM may insert a predefined, machine-interpretable
marker into or alongside its response to indicate that an additional presentation
or information artifact could be useful. The model determines the location and
semantic purpose of the exit, while the receiving client retains authority over
whether the marker is interpreted and how the corresponding enrichment is
realized.
This constitutes an inversion of the classical User Exit. Whereas a User Exit
allows externally provided code to participate in the execution of the standard
system, a Client Exit does not execute client-supplied functionality. Instead, the
producer exposes a semantic extension point and leaves its realization entirely to
the consumer. Consequently, Client Exits are distinct from tool calls: a tool call
requests an operation or capability, whereas a Client Exit specifies an optional
enrichment of the presentation of a result.
A central characteristic of this approach is the separation of semantic con-
tent and representation. An enrichment may, for example, request an overview,
statistical analysis, additional explanation, or evidence summary. Such semantic
intents do not determine whether the information must be represented as text,
graphics, speech, or another modality. Different clients may therefore realize the
same Client Exit differently according to their capabilities, interaction modality,
4
Marc Jansen
or local policy. An overview may be rendered graphically by a desktop client,
textually by a terminal, or acoustically by a voice-oriented interface. In this re-
spect, Client Exits implement a presentation-intent layer rather than prescribing
a concrete View.
Recent work on generative and agent-driven user interfaces provides the closest
related approaches. A2UI allows agents to communicate declarative interface
descriptions that are rendered using client-controlled components [10]. MCP
Apps similarly enables MCP tools to provide interactive user-interface resources
to supporting hosts [7]. Both approaches demonstrate the increasing importance
of standardized interaction between agent-generated information and client-
side presentation. Their abstraction level, however, differs from that proposed
here. MCP Apps primarily provides an interactive UI artifact, while A2UI
communicates declarative UI structures and components. Client Exits instead
operate at the level of semantic presentation intent: they specify what additional
information or presentation function would be useful without prescribing the
concrete interface structure used to realize it.
The resulting research gap concerns a lightweight mechanism that combines
predefined semantic extension points in LLM output with strict separation
between enrichment semantics and representation, while leaving interpretation
and realization under client control. Client Exits address this gap by transferring
the established software-engineering principle of predefined extension points from
application execution to the presentation boundary of LLM systems. The resulting
architecture separates generation of the semantic result from its client-specific
enrichment and representation.
3
Architecture
The proposed architecture, as shown in Fig. 1 separates the generation of an
answer from the presentation of supplementary information within that answer.
A Large Language Model, optionally finetuned for this purpose, inserts special
markers into its textual output. These markers act as client exits: designated
points at which the receiving client can enrich the answer with additional content.
The LLM determines where to place these markers, whereas the client determines
whether and how to interpret and present them. Consequently, the generated
response need not prescribe a particular user interface or output modality.
The interaction begins when a user enters a prompt into an LLM client. The
client forwards the prompt to the LLM, which generates a response containing
ordinary text and, where the model considers them appropriate, special markers.
Markers can occur at different positions throughout the response, allowing
supplementary information to be associated with the relevant parts of the answer
rather than being confined to a separate, fixed interface element.
Upon receiving the response, the client processes it before displaying it to
the user. It identifies the markers, interprets their meaning, and determines how
to handle each occurrence. For a supported marker, the client can obtain or
compute supplementary content and integrate its presentation at the indicated
Client Exits - A Way to Increase LLM Transparency on the Client Side
5
Fig. 1. Client-exit architecture: the LLM inserts markers into its response, and the
client interprets these markers to integrate supplementary information and adapt the
presentation of the response.
position. The user therefore receives an enriched answer rather than the raw
marker annotated output. This processing stage establishes a clear division of
responsibility: the LLM proposes points for enrichment, while the client retains
control over the resulting user experience.
The supplementary content may include visualizations, statistical analyses,
explanations, or other information that the client considers useful in context.
The marker provides an integration point; the corresponding client-side handler
determines the concrete enrichment. To support this interaction, the model and
the client need a shared marker convention that makes markers distinguishable
from ordinary text and defines their intended meaning. Any information needed
by a handler must be available through the marker, the surrounding response, or
the client’s context. The concrete marker syntax and handler implementation are
separate from this architectural separation of responsibilities.
Presentation depends on the client’s purpose and capabilities. A graphical
client might render a chart or an expandable explanation, whereas a voice-based
client might provide a spoken summary or an additional verbal explanation at
the corresponding point in the answer. An audio-oriented client could instead use
sound to convey supplementary information. Thus, the same marker-annotated
6
Marc Jansen
response can support different presentations without requiring the LLM to
generate a separate answer for each modality. The client can also choose not to
render an enrichment when it is unsupported or inappropriate for the current
interaction.
This separation is conceptually comparable to the Model–View–Controller
(MVC) design pattern. In this analogy, the generated text, its markers, and the
associated information constitute the data to be presented; client-side marker
interpretation and handler selection perform a controller-like role; and the graph-
ical, spoken, or other output constitutes the view. Here, the MVC notion of a
model refers to the underlying data rather than to the LLM itself. The central
similarity is that a common representation can give rise to differentviews through
client-side decisions. The architecture adopts this separation without requiring
every client to implement a strict MVC structure.
4
Implementation
To demonstrate the architecture described in Section 3, we implemented a
prototype combining a finetuned LLM with a modified LLM client. We first
finetuned a Qwen3.8-27B model to follow the Question–Option–Criteria (QOC)
thinking strategy [5, 4] and to insert client exits into its responses. The finetuning
thus addressed both the strategy used to structure the answer and the inclusion
of markers that enable client-side enrichment.
In the prototype, client exits were represented as self-closing XML tags with
an exit attribute identifying the requested client exit. The general form was:
<client exit="<name>" />
Here, <name> denotes a placeholder for the client-exit identifier, not a literal part
of the emitted attribute value. Identifiers can include a namespace prefix, allowing
client exits to be grouped by thinking strategy. This naming convention enables
a client to distinguish strategy-specific handlers and interpret exits differently
for different strategies. The namespace is encoded in the attribute value rather
than through an XML namespace declaration.
For the QOC strategy, we implemented the following three client exits:
<client exit="qoc.GraphOverview" />
<client exit="qoc.CriteriaInfluence" />
<client exit="qoc.SimilarGoodOptions" />
The shared qoc prefix associates these exits with the QOC strategy, while the
suffix distinguishes the individual exit. The tags identify the client-side enrichment
to invoke without specifying its visual representation, thereby preserving the
separation between marker generation and presentation.
On the client side, we modified a version of the open-source LLM client
LibreChat1 to recognize and handle these three client exits. The modified client
1 LibreChat repository: https://github.com/danny-avila/LibreChat.
Client Exits - A Way to Increase LLM Transparency on the Client Side
7
interprets the markers embedded in a response and integrates the corresponding
supplementary information into the displayed answer, rather than presenting
the markers as ordinary text. The client remains responsible for the concrete
presentation of each enrichment.
After connecting the modified LibreChat instance to the fine-tuned model,
the prototype successfully integrated additional, non-textual information into
the LLM’s displayed answers. This demonstrates the end-to-end operation of the
client-exit mechanism: the model supplies markers within its response, and the
client turns those markers into enrichments within the answer.
Figure 2 shows the graphical representation generated by the qoc.Graph-
Overview client exit for the example question, “Where should we spend our next
summer holiday?” Following the QOC paradigm, the graph connects the question
to the available destination options and relates each option to the criteria used
in the analysis, such as beach quality, flight duration, and overall cost. The
criterion nodes display their importance, while the edges between options and
criteria indicate how strongly each option supports the corresponding criterion.
Each option is annotated with an aggregate score, calculated as the sum of its
criterion support values weighted by the respective criterion importance. The
preferred option, Croatia (Hvar, Split), is visually highlighted. By embedding
this graph within the textual response, the client makes the relationships be-
tween the question, options, and criteria transparent for inspection alongside the
recommendation.
Fig. 2. Graph overview integrated into the LibreChat response through the
qoc.GraphOverview client exit.
8
Marc Jansen
Figure 3 shows the criteria influence view generated by the qoc.Criteria-
Influence client exit. The criteria are ranked in descending order of their impact
values, calculated by multiplying each criterion’s support spread by its importance.
The spread is the difference between the maximum and minimum support values
across the available options. This measure therefore captures how strongly a
criterion differentiates the options after accounting for its assigned importance,
rather than reflecting importance alone. The table displays the underlying values
alongside horizontal bars that visualize the resulting impact scores. In the holiday
example, flight duration and proximity to mid-Europe have the highest impact
value, followed by teen appeal and overall cost. This representation allows users
to inspect the relative discriminating influence of the criteria underlying the
recommendation; it does not, by itself, establish which criterion determines the
winning option.
Fig. 3. Criteria influence displayed through the qoc.CriteriaInfluence client exit,
ranking criteria by their support spread multiplied by their importance.
Figure 4 shows the statistical comparison generated by the qoc.Similar-
GoodOptions client exit. The visualization compares the aggregate scores of all
evaluated options and highlights alternatives considered similarly well suited to
the winning option. In this prototype, an alternative qualifies if its score lies
within one standard deviation of the highest score, where the standard deviation
is calculated across the aggregate scores of all evaluated options. Since no option
exceeds the winning score, the effective cutoff is the highest score minus this

A Tensor-Algebraic No-Go Theorem
for High-Dimensional Photonic Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger States
Discovered with AlphaProof Nexus
Mario Krenn,1 Moritz Firsching,2 George Tsoukalas,3 Rishikesh Gajjala,4 Xuemei Gu,5 and Swarat Chaudhuri3
1Department of Computer Science, Faculty of Science, University of T¨ubingen, T¨ubingen, Germany
2Google DeepMind, Z¨urich, CH
3Google DeepMind, London, UK
4Center for Quantum and Topological Systems, NYU Abu Dhabi, Abu Dhabi, UAE
5Institut f¨ur Festk¨orpertheorie und Optik, Friedrich-Schiller-Universit¨at Jena, Jena, Germany
Photonic GHZ states generated with probabilistic pair sources can be described by edge-coloured,
complex-weighted graphs. In this representation, conditioning on an event with one photon in every
detector turns the output amplitudes into coherent sums over perfect matchings, and generating
an N-photon D-dimensional GHZ state is equivalent to constructing a monochromatic quantum
graph. Here, we prove that no complex-weighted monochromatic quantum graph exists for any even
N ≥4 when D ≥N. The proof, discovered through AI-assisted formal proof search in Lean using
AlphaProof Nexus, constructs a weighted sum F of amplitudes whose coefficients factor vertex by
vertex.
Summing over the colours at one fixed vertex reduces the problem to an (N −1) × N
matrix of effective edge weights. For the graph amplitudes ω and GHZ target ∆, the row–column
imbalance yields F(ω) = 0 but F(∆)̸ = 0, contradicting the required equality ω = ∆. Finally, we
give a physical interpretation of the AI-discovered mathematical proof.
INTRODUCTION
High-dimensional multipartite entanglement is an in-
creasingly important resource in quantum information
science [1, 2]. Compared with the qubit case, increasing
the local dimension enlarges the joint state space rapidly
with both the number of particles and the local dimen-
sion, yielding a richer structure of quantum correlations
and new capabilities across a range of applications. These
include high-dimensional quantum communication [3, 4],
high-dimensional quantum teleportation [5, 6], and quan-
tum computation [7–10].
High-dimensional entangle-
ment also raises fundamental questions about quantum
correlations that have no direct analogue in bipartite or
qubit settings, including the existence and classification
of absolutely maximally entangled states [11, 12] and all-
versus-nothing violations of local realism [13, 14].
Photons are natural carriers of high-dimensional quan-
tum information, since their orbital angular momen-
tum, path, time-bin, frequency, and other internal de-
grees of freedom provide multi-level encodings within a
single particle.
Entangling such encodings across pho-
tons gives access to high-dimensional multipartite states.
Multi-photon high-dimensional entanglement was first
demonstrated using orbital angular momentum [15] and
path [16], followed by high-dimensional Greenberger–
Horne–Zeilinger states realised with orbital angular mo-
mentum [17] and path encoding [18, 19]. These experi-
ments generated three-dimensional (D = 3) GHZ states
of three and four particles (N = 3 and N = 4), respec-
tively. These experiments demonstrate that small-scale
high-dimensional multipartite entanglement can be gen-
erated in photonic systems and motivate a general ques-
tion:
Which high-dimensional multipartite entangled states
can be generated systematically with standard photonic
resources?
This question can be formulated precisely using a link
between quantum optics and graph theory [20–22]: it
asks whether a system of DN polynomial equations over
C in D2N(N−1)/2 complex variables has a solution. The
system has solutions for D = 2 and arbitrary even N, be-
cause photonic qubit GHZ states can be constructed [23–
26]; for four photons, qutrit GHZ states can also be cre-
ated [17–19]. Despite extensive numerical searches, no
solutions beyond these constructions are known. Theo-
retical work has shown that no other GHZ states can be
generated under restricted-resource assumptions, such as
the absence of multipartite interference [27] or restricted
correlations [28].
However, no proof has established
the existence or nonexistence of higher-dimensional GHZ
states when the full capabilities of linear quantum op-
tics [29] and probabilistic pair generation from nonlinear
sources [30] are available.
Here, we give the first unconditional proof that no
monochromatic quantum graph exists when D ≥N,
for every even N ≥4.
The proof was discovered by
AlphaProof Nexus [31], an agentic AI system which au-
tonomously searches for formalised proofs in Lean [32].
We first review the connection between photonic ex-
periments and graph theory, then present the proof, and
finally discuss its physical interpretation.

To construct a proof, we use

In this representation, the vertices of the graph corre-

at which photons may be detected.
An edge between
two vertices represents the creation of a correlated pho-

The colours

frontier language models with feedback from the Lean
compiler [31].
In this framework, the input is a Lean
file containing definitions and a target theorem whose
proof is missing; the agent iteratively edits the proof,
receives compiler feedback, introduces auxiliary lemmas,
and searches for a proof that compiles without unresolved
goals. In the present case, the formal proof led to the
tensor-algebraic argument developed in the next section.
The monochromatic quantum graph conjecture was
formalised in Lean as part of the Formal Conjec-
tures project [41]. The formalisation encodes both the
complex-weighted graphs and the coherent sums over
their perfect matchings. In Lean, the vertices are repre-
sented by Fin N, while EdgeN N D specifies two vertices
together with their endpoint colours. The edge-weight
function is defined as
/-- Weights on edges. -/
abbrev WeightsN (N D : Nat) (α : Type) :=
EdgeN N D →α
The sum over perfect matchings is computed recur-
sively. The function pmSumListAux selects the first re-
maining vertex, pairs it with each possible partner, mul-
tiplies the corresponding edge weight by the contribution
from the remaining vertices, and sums over all choices.
This implements the coherent addition of the amplitudes
of all perfect matchings:
def pmSumListAux {α : Type} [Semiring α] {N D : Nat}
(W : WeightsN N D α) (ι : V N →Fin D) :
Nat →List (V N) →α
| 0, _ => 1
| 1, _ => 0
| _ + 2, [] => 1
| _ + 2, [_] => 0
| n + 2, v :: vs =>
(vs.map (fun u =>
W (mkEdge v u (ι v) (ι u)) *
pmSumListAux W ι n (vs.erase u)
)).sum
Two further definitions apply this recursion to a vertex
list and ultimately to the full graph, using the canonical
ordering of its N vertices:
5
/-- Perfect-matching sum on a list. -/
def pmSumList {α : Type} [Semiring α] {N D : Nat}
(W : WeightsN N D α)
(ι : V N →Fin D) (L : List (V N)) : α :=
pmSumListAux W ι L.length L
/-- Perfect-matching sum for K_N. -/
def pmSumN {α : Type} [Semiring α] (N D : Nat)
(W : WeightsN N D α) (ι : V N →Fin D) : α :=
pmSumList W ι (vertices N)
The central predicate EqSystemN then defines the con-
ditions for a monochromatic quantum graph. For every
assignment of colours ι : VN →CD, the sum over perfect
matchings must equal 1 if all vertices inherit the same
colour, and 0 otherwise. In Lean, these conditions read
def EqSystemN {α : Type} [Semiring α]
(N D : Nat) (W : WeightsN N D α) : Prop :=
∀ι : V N →Fin D,
pmSumN N D W ι =
(if allEqual ι then (1 : α) else (0 : α))
Here, allEqual tests whether the inherited vertex
colouring is monochromatic.
The conjecture for even
N ≥6 and D ≥3 can therefore be expressed compactly
as follows (with the proof body omitted):
theorem eqSystem_no_solution_ge6_ge3 :
∀N D : Nat, N ≥6 →Even N →D ≥3 →
¬ ∃W : WeightsN N D C, EqSystemN N D W
The AI-discovered formal proof establishes a general
non-existence result for all even N ≥4 in the case D =
N, without restrictions on the complex edge weights.
The corresponding Lean theorem states
theorem
eqSystem_no_solution_even_ge4_d_eq_n_explicit :
∀N : Nat, N ≥4 →Even N →
¬ ∃W : WeightsN N N C, EqSystemN N N W
The symbols ∀, ∃, and ¬ denote universal quantifi-
cation, existence, and negation, respectively. Thus, the
theorem establishes that no assignment of complex edge
weights can satisfy the monochromatic quantum graph
equations when D = N. The complete machine-checked
proof is available online. As we show below, this result
extends to D > N by restricting the colour set.

MONOCHROMATIC GRAPHS WITH D ≥N
We prove the following theorem. The nontrivial case is
even N, since perfect matchings cover vertices in pairs.
Theorem. Let N ≥4 be even. There is no complex-

and D ≥N colours.
We first introduce effective edge weights and a

restricting to N colours.

Twice-Told Critiques: Claim-Level Homogenization of Peer Review in the
LLM Era
Ilya Gusev
Keenable / Amsterdam
phoenixilya@gmail.com
Abstract
Peer review relies on several readers finding dif-
ferent problems. We measure critique overlap
in conference and journal reviews. At ICLR,
measured overlap rose from 12.0% in 2026 to
21.3% in 2027, in reviews from the same stage
of the review process, with year-on-year rises
at NeurIPS, ICML and the F1000 and PLOS
journals. A third ICLR review of a paper added
5.46 new problems to the other two in 2027,
against 6.12 in 2026. We apply MELD, a de-
tector of LLM-generated text, to all reviews.
Within a paper, two reviews that MELD flags
overlap more than two unflagged reviews: by
3.0 points at ICLR in 2024–2025, by 4.5 points
in 2026–2027, and by 5.4 points across five
journal sources. These results provide evidence
that LLM-flagged reviews of one paper are
less distinct from each other than unflagged re-
views, and suggest that the diversity of critiques
among reviews of a single paper is falling.
1
Introduction
Peer review needs readers who find different prob-
lems. In one study, two reviewers usually shared
no critical point (Fiske and Fogg, 1990). In another
study about Nature-family reviews, 25.8% of one
reviewer’s criticisms match another’s (Kim et al.,
2026a). Our central question is: with widespread
LLM-generated text in ML reviews (Liang et al.,
2024a; Russo et al., 2025; Emi, 2025), do reviewers
still provide distinct critiques?
We measure shared problems by extracting and
matching critiques across reviews of one paper.
Whole-review similarity mixes wording and con-
tent (Liang et al., 2024a; Baumann et al., 2026) and
cannot establish that two reviews raise the same
problem. Prior studies find that synthetic LLM-
generated reviews are more similar to each other
than human reviews (Hou et al., 2026) and share
more criticisms (Kim et al., 2026a), a gap used

tique extraction (Liang et al., 2024b; Kim et al.,
2026a) to reviews that venues received, comparing
problems within papers and over time.
Our findings are:
• Critique overlap rose at ICLR from 12.0% in
2026 to 21.3% in 2027, at ICML in 2026 and
at NeurIPS in 2025 (Section 4, Figure 1).
• Within a paper, two LLM-flagged reviews
overlap more than two unflagged reviews at
ICLR, by 3.0 points in 2024–2025 and 4.5
points in 2026–2027 (Section 4, Figure 2).
• Pooled over five journal sources, the same
within-paper gap is 5.4 points (Section 4, Fig-
ure 4).
1

2
Related Work
LLM use in peer review.
ICLR and NeurIPS
reviews grew longer after ChatGPT, while LLM-
assisted ICLR reviews mention originality less (Wu
et al., 2026). LLM reviewers draw more than half
of their weaknesses from the appendix. In sam-
pled ICLR reviews, the share of such weaknesses
rose from 11.3% in 2026 to 27.6% in 2027 (Ghosh
et al., 2026). LLM-generated reviews at one man-
agement journal cover a narrower range of topics
(Gartenberg et al., 2026). At ICML 2026, a ran-
domized trial assigned papers and reviewers to a
policy that prohibited LLM use or to one that al-
lowed limited use. The second policy made reviews
5.5–7% longer and left scores and decisions almost
unchanged (Kim et al., 2026b). We compare shared
problems, not single-review topics.
Homogenization.
LLM assistance makes the
texts and ideas of different users more alike (Pad-
makumar and He, 2024; Anderson et al., 2024;
Doshi and Hauser, 2024). Model outputs are nar-
rower than training data (Wu et al., 2025). Sourati
et al. (2026) review this evidence. We extend the
question from creative tasks to expert critiques,
where independent readings are the goal.
3
Methodology
3.1
Data
Table 1 lists the samples. ICLR and NeurIPS come
from OpenReview (ulab-ai, 2025; Xu et al., 2025;
Heineman, 2025). ICML includes accepted pa-
pers from 2025–2026. ICLR 2027 reviews come
from the OpenReview API eight days after they
became public. Conference papers need at least
three reviews. Journal papers need at least two
first-round reviews: SciPost, F1000Research and
sister platforms (F1000), PLOS, BMC Medicine
(JerMa88, 2025), and Copernicus/EGU, covering
physics, medicine, biology and geoscience.
A
panel is the set of reviews of one paper.
3.2
Claim extraction
A critique claim identifies one problem that needs
one fix. We exclude praise and neutral text. In
pass 1, GPT-6 Luna (Luna) reads one review in full
and lists its claims. Each claim has a quote copied
from the review, a one-sentence paraphrase and a
category such as clarity or experiment scope.
We check pass 1 against human labels and
against other LLMs. For the human check, we use

against 80.5% between two members.
3.3
Claim grouping
In pass 2, a separate Luna call groups the claims
of one panel into problems. The call sees the claim
lists, not the review texts. Two claims join one
group only when they state the same problem in
the same paper element.
To check pass 2, each council member groups
Luna’s claim lists with the same prompt. Against
the majority vote of the three members on each
claim pair, Luna’s grouping has 83.6% precision
and 78.4% recall across 507 panels. With a coun-
cil member or the majority as grouper, the within-
paper flagged-pair gap of RQ2 is 7.0 to 7.3 points,
against 7.4 with Luna (Table 2). Each council mem-
ber also runs both passes on its own claims, and
all four pipelines give every contrast the same sign
(Table 3).

MELD (Li et al., 2026) scores reviews for LLM-

4
Results
RQ1: Do reviewers of one paper repeat more of
each other’s critiques?

These two years are directly comparable: both hold

ICML also rose in their latest cycles (Figure 1).

content, if two reviews in one LLM style are easier
to match. To test this style effect, Luna changes

5
Conclusion
Our results suggest that the reviews of one paper
have lost part of their independence, in content and
not only in wording. Reviews that the detector flags
are one part of this change and do not explain all of
it, because overlap also rose between reviews that
the detector does not flag. Two questions stay open:
how much of that rise comes from LLM use that
leaves no trace in the text, and whether the 2027
level holds after the discussion phase.
4
Limitations
LLM measurement. An LLM extracts and groups
claims. The council reference uses LLMs, not hu-
mans, and does not rule out shared model errors.
The human check covers pass 1 only. Extraction
and grouping errors can affect measured levels and
changes over time. The overlap level depends on
the grouper: council members give 10.9 to 14.8%
against Luna’s 11.1%. Luna misses more links
in papers with no flagged review. LLM groupers
agree that this error changes comparisons between
papers but not within-paper gaps.
Review snapshots. ICLR samples hold final
reviews before 2026 and reviews during the discus-
sion phase from 2026 on, so the ICLR series com-
pares reviews of one stage only from 2026 to 2027.
For the same reason, we report ICLR flagged-pair
gaps for 2024–2025 and 2026–2027 apart.
Detector labels. MELD trained on peer reviews
from sources it does not name. If these include
our pre-2023 reviews, the threshold is too low and
later flag rates too high. GigaCheck flags fewer
recent reviews than MELD, so flag rates depend on
the detector. MELD flags 39.5% of our polished
reviews, so a flag does not separate polishing from
generation. Other tools and prompts can polish dif-
ferently, and detectors label part of LLM-polished
reviews as AI-generated (Saha et al., 2026). A flag
does not tell which model wrote a review. Cri-
tique content differs between model versions and
families (Guo, 2026), so the flagged-pair gap can
change with the mix of models that reviewers use.
The rewrite control uses two models, two prompts
and pre-2023 reviews. Within-paper comparisons
remove paper-level differences, not reviewer-level
ones, and do not assign a causal effect to LLM use.
An unflagged review is not thereby human-written.
Detectors can err across language backgrounds,
fields and templates. Their labels must not support
action against an individual reviewer.
Selection and scope. NeurIPS and most jour-
nals publish accepted-paper reviews only, and our
ICML sample has accepted papers only. The jour-
nal gap rests on 2,228 papers with three or more
reviews and mixed flags, and its regression as-
sumes that each pair type shifts overlap by the same
amount in every paper. All texts are in English, and
most come from ML.
Use of LLM Assistants
The authors created the idea and the outlines of the
experiments, and acted as supervisors and editors.
Claude Fable 5.2 inside Claude Code and GPT-6
Astra inside Pi wrote all code and all text of this
paper. The authors take full responsibility for the
content.
