What If Chain-of-Thought Is Not Enough?
Marc Jansen
Computer Science Institute
University of Applied Sciences Ruhr West
Bottrop, Germany
marc.jansen@hs-ruhrwest.de
Abstract. Reasoning capabilities in large language models have evolved
from prompting-based methods to internalized model behaviors. In this
paper, we investigate whether the internal thinking model of an LLM can
be deliberately changed and whether such a change is beneficial. Instead
of relying on Chain-of-Thought, we train models to follow Question–
Option–Criteria (QOC), a structured decision process that decomposes
a task into explicit questions, competing options, and evaluation criteria.
We present a three-generation development pipeline that ranges from
a basic QOC decision core to richer answer synthesis and statistically
enriched QOC reasoning. We then evaluate the resulting models with
respect to both internal consistency and output quality. Across the re-
ported experiments, QOC-based fine-tuning improves answer quality rel-
ative to non-fine-tuned base models and yields particularly strong gains
once models are large enough to execute the underlying QOC computa-
tions reliably. The results suggest that the internal thinking model of an
LLM is trainable and that structured alternatives to Chain-of-Thought
can provide a promising path toward more reliable, interpretable, and
task-adapted decision support.
1
Introduction
This paper investigates a practical next step in the evolution of reasoning-
oriented large language models (LLMs): not only eliciting reasoning, but de-
liberately changing the internal thinking model that a model is trained to fol-
low. Early progress in reasoning quality was largely driven by prompting tech-
niques, most notably Chain-of-Thought (CoT), that encouraged non-thinking
base models to externalize intermediate reasoning steps [9, 5]. Over time, these
externally elicited traces became training signals, enabling models to internal-
ize structured reasoning behavior through rationale-based training and distilla-
tion pipelines [11, 4]. Our work follows this same development logic, but replaces
CoT with a different and more explicitly decision-oriented framework: Question–
Option–Criteria (QOC) [6].
The core hypothesis is that QOC offers a better scaffold for decision sup-
port tasks because it enforces separation between (i) the decision question, (ii)
competing options, and (iii) explicit evaluation criteria. This structure is par-
ticularly useful when explainability matters: rather than producing only a final
arXiv:2611.26282v1  [cs.CL]  19 Nov 2026
2
Marc Jansen
recommendation, the model can expose why certain options dominate and where
trade-offs occur, aligning with broader explainability goals in AI decision sup-
port [7, 3]. We therefore aim to improve both decision quality and interpretability
by training models to reason in QOC form and then communicate outcomes in
user-appropriate detail.
To operationalize this idea, we developed and trained three model genera-
tions, each extending the previous one.
In the first generation, the model was trained to produce a QOC thinking
structure and to return only the best-performing option to the user. The re-
sponse layer was intentionally minimal: no extended justification, no narrative
explanation, and no additional contextualization beyond the top-ranked option.
This generation served as a baseline for testing whether QOC alone can improve
internal decision consistency and option ranking quality.
In the second generation, we reused the same QOC thinking structure but
changed the response mechanism. Instead of returning only the winning option,
we fed the generated QOC structure back into an LLM—specifically, the same
model family that produced the structure—and prompted it to interpret the
result and provide a more detailed answer. This introduced a two-stage behavior:
structured decision formation followed by explanatory rendering. For training,
both artifacts were retained: the intermediate QOC reasoning representation and
the richer textual response used to communicate the decision.
In the third generation, we further expanded the reasoning structure by incor-
porating lightweight statistical analysis into the QOC stage. Beyond identifying
the best option, the model also computed comparative indicators for near-best
options, including dispersion-oriented measures such as standard deviation to re-
flect stability and sensitivity across criteria. As in generation two, the complete
enriched thinking structure was then passed back to the LLM for interpretation
into a rich, user-facing answer. Again, both components—the structured reason-
ing trace and the interpreted response—were included in fine-tuning data for the
corresponding model version.
Across these three generations, the development trajectory moves from pure
structured selection to structured-and-explained decision support, and finally
to statistically informed structured-and-explained decision support. This pro-
gression enables a direct evaluation of how much additional explanatory and
analytical layers contribute to internal consistency, output quality, and prac-
tical interpretability for end users. At the same time, it makes it possible to
study a broader question that emerged as central over the course of this paper:
whether deeper internal thinking structures are equally useful across model sizes,
or whether smaller and larger models benefit from different depths of structured
reasoning.
2
State-of-the-Art
Recent progress in LLM reasoning started with prompting methods that elicit
intermediate steps. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting established the core
What If Chain-of-Thought Is Not Enough?
3
paradigm for improving multi-step reasoning quality in sufficiently large mod-
els [9]. Closely related work showed that even simple zero-shot trigger phrases
can induce strong reasoning gains without handcrafted exemplars [5]. Beyond
greedy decoding, self-consistency improved CoT by sampling diverse reasoning
paths and selecting stable answers [8].
The transition from prompting to model-internal reasoning behavior has also
been supported by iterative rationale-based training methods such as STaR,
which bootstraps reasoning ability via self-generated and filtered rationales [11].
In parallel, ReAct demonstrated that combining explicit reasoning traces with
environment actions can improve both task performance and interpretability [10].
Distillation-based approaches further showed that stepwise reasoning traces can
be transferred into smaller models while retaining strong reasoning performance
[4]. Taken together, these lines of work suggest that reasoning quality does not
only depend on scale or prompting, but also on the form of the internal reasoning
structure that a model is encouraged or trained to follow.
For the QOC perspective adopted in this paper, the conceptual foundation is
design-space analysis with explicit Questions, Options, and Criteria [6]. In con-
trast to CoT-style reasoning, which typically unfolds as a free-form sequential
rationale, QOC imposes an explicitly decision-oriented structure by separating
the decision question, the available alternatives, and the evaluative criteria used
to compare them. This makes QOC especially relevant for settings in which
explainability, trade-off transparency, and auditable decision support are impor-
tant. The present work builds on this perspective by treating QOC not merely
as an output format, but as an internal thinking model that can be trained into
an LLM and evaluated with respect to both internal consistency and output
quality.
3
The QOC (Question-Option-Criteria) Thinking Model
In this paper, Question–Option–Criteria (QOC) is used as a structured decision-
making process that replaces unconstrained free-form reasoning with an explicit
sequence of analytical steps. Instead of asking the model to directly generate an
answer, we require it to first represent the problem in terms of a decision ques-
tion, a set of alternative options, and a set of criteria according to which these
options should be evaluated. This makes the reasoning process more transparent
and more suitable for supervision, because the intermediate decision structure
can be inspected, validated, and reused during fine-tuning.
The QOC process begins with an input task consisting of a question and
a supporting context. From this input, the model first formulates the concrete
decision question that has to be answered. It then identifies the relevant answer
options, that is, the competing alternatives between which the decision will be
made. In a next step, the model extracts or formulates the criteria that are rele-
vant for judging these options. These criteria provide the evaluative dimensions
of the decision and define what counts as a strong or weak option in the given
context.
4
Marc Jansen
Once the criteria have been identified, the QOC process assigns an impor-
tance weight to each criterion. These weights represent how strongly each cri-
terion should influence the final decision, or in other words, how relevant each
criterion is for identifying the final solution or best option. After that, every
option is assessed with respect to every criterion. In the formulation used in
this paper, this assessment is represented numerically as a score that indicates
how well a given option satisfies a given criterion. The central calculation step
of QOC then combines structure and quantification: for each option–criterion
pair, the criterion weight is multiplied by the corresponding option score. The
resulting weighted values are then summed across all criteria to obtain a final
overall score for each option.
The best option is the one with the highest total weighted score. In other
words, the QOC process turns qualitative judgment into a structured ranking
procedure in which the preferred answer is not chosen implicitly, but derived
from explicit intermediate calculations. This is important for our work because
it allows us to evaluate internal consistency: we can check whether the model
identifies reasonable criteria, whether the weighting and scoring steps are per-
formed correctly, whether the option-level products and final sums are correct,
and whether the option with the highest final score is in fact selected as the
recommendation.
This QOC representation serves different roles across the three model gen-
erations studied in the paper. In generation 1, the QOC process is used as the
complete decision core: the model produces the QOC structure and returns only
the best option as the answer. In generation 2, the same QOC structure is first
produced and then passed into a second interpretation step, in which the model
translates the structured decision result into a richer natural-language response
for the user. In generation 3, the QOC process is further extended with statistical
enrichment, so that the final interpretation can draw not only on the weighted
QOC scores but also on additional comparative indicators. Across all genera-
tions, however, the core QOC procedure remains the same: identify question,
options, and criteria; weight criteria; score options; compute weighted totals;
and select the best-supported option.
Within the training pipeline, this structured process is not only used at
inference time, but also to generate supervision data. Synthetic decision tasks
are created, processed through the QOC routine, and transformed into examples
for supervised fine-tuning. As a result, the fine-tuned models are encouraged to
internalize QOC as their thinking process rather than merely imitate isolated
outputs. The purpose of this design is to make decision support more reliable,
auditable, and interpretable than in a purely free-form reasoning setup.
4
Architecture
This section describes the end-to-end architecture of our QOC-based training
approach. Across all three generations, the core system is built around synthetic
data generation, structured QOC analysis, and supervised fine-tuning.
What If Chain-of-Thought Is Not Enough?
5
The shared pipeline is as follows. First, we generate synthetic decision tasks
consisting of a question and a context that are suitable for QOC-style decom-
position. Second, each task is processed by a prompt-based QOC agent that
executes a fixed analysis routine: identify options and criteria, assign criterion
weights, and score how strongly each option satisfies each criterion. Third, the
agent derives the best option from the weighted assessment. Finally, generated
artifacts are converted into training examples and used to fine-tune the target
LLM. This shared architecture is the backbone of all generations; each generation
differs only in what additional artifacts are produced and used during answer
synthesis.
4.1
Generation 1 Architecture: QOC-Only Decision Core
Generation 1 uses only the shared core pipeline, as illustrated in Figure 1. For
each synthetic task, the QOC agent produces the reasoning block and selects
the best option. The output artifact for training and inference is minimal: the
selected best option is returned as the final answer, without an additional inter-
pretation stage for rich natural-language explanation.
Fig. 1. Generation 1 pipeline creates synthetic decision tasks, applies structured QOC
analysis to identify the best option, and outputs this best option directly.
4.2
Generation 2 Architecture: QOC + Interpretation Layer
Generation 2 adds a dedicated interpretation component after best-option selec-
tion, as shown in Figure 2. The QOC thinking block together with the identified
best option is passed back to the LLM in a second step. This component gen-
erates a richer, user-facing response that explains the recommendation while
grounding the explanation in the structured QOC result. Relative to generation
1, the architectural extension is therefore a post-QOC answer-synthesis stage.
6
Marc Jansen
Fig. 2. Generation 2 architecture integrates a second-stage interpretation module syn-
thesizes a richer natural-language response grounded.
4.3
Generation 3 Architecture: QOC + Statistical Enrichment +
Interpretation
Generation 3 extends generation 2 with an additional statistical enrichment com-
ponent between QOC analysis and final answer synthesis, as illustrated in Fig-
ure 3. Besides the QOC block and best option, the system computes simple
statistical indicators over option performance (e.g., dispersion measures such as
standard deviation across criterion-level scores). These statistics are then pro-
vided to the LLM together with the QOC result and best option, enabling the
final rich response to incorporate both structured decision logic and quantitative
comparative evidence.
Fig. 3. Generation 3 pipeline extends the QOC decision core by incorporating statis-
tical enrichment.
5
Implementation
This section describes the implementation pipeline that operationalizes the QOC-
based training approach introduced in this paper. Figure 4 summarizes the end-
What If Chain-of-Thought Is Not Enough?
7
to-end implementation workflow, from task construction and QOC processing
to training data preparation and model fine-tuning. For the generation of the
synthetic data, we deliberately rely on the strongest open-weights model avail-
able in the respective setup in order to maximize the quality of the generated
reasoning traces and supervision signals. In the evaluation setting presented in
this paper, this role is fulfilled by Qwen3.5-27B. The pipeline is organized into
multiple layers, each of which contributes a distinct function in turning decision
tasks into supervised examples for QOC-based model development.
Fig. 4. Implementation pipeline of the QOC-based training workflow.
5.1
Task Generation Layer
The first layer of the implementation pipeline is responsible for constructing the
synthetic decision tasks used throughout the project. A corresponding Python
script ensures that these example tasks are drawn from different domains rather
than from a single narrow application area. Each task consists not only of a
question that should be answered by means of the QOC approach, but also
of a synthetic context that provides the background information required for
structured decomposition under the QOC framework. This layer therefore defines
the raw problem instances on which the remaining parts of the pipeline operate.
5.2
QOC Processing Layer
The second layer applies the QOC thinking procedure to each generated task. At
this stage, the system uses the relevant decision question, enumerates the avail-
able options, derives the criteria for evaluating these options, assigns criterion
weights, and scores how well each option satisfies each criterion. The weighted
criterion–option values are then aggregated so that the best-supported option
can be determined from the resulting totals.
8
Marc Jansen
5.3
Artifact Construction Layer
Once the QOC analysis has been completed, the implementation pipeline con-
verts the intermediate reasoning outputs into structured artifacts that serve as
the data input for the generation of the synthetic training data in the next
step. At this stage, the depth of the constructed QOC process depends on the
model generation. For generation 1, the constructed representation contains the
identified options, the criteria, the criterion weights, and the evaluation of how
strongly each option supports the different criteria. The weighted products be-
tween option-support values and criterion weights, together with the final sums
for each option, are also calculated so that the best option can be identified and
reported to the user in the simplest possible form, namely as the final selected
option. For generation 2, this process depth is extended by generating a more
detailed answer in a second pass through the LLM. This answer is grounded
in the QOC analysis and can reflect not only the best option, but also the rel-
ative standing of alternative options. In generation 3, the constructed process
is extended further with additional statistical measures, for example to identify
particularly important criteria or other relevant comparative properties of the
option structure. This layer therefore bridges raw reasoning traces and reusable
supervision signals for the subsequent generation of synthetic fine-tuning data.
5.4
Fine-Tuning Data Preparation Layer
The next layer transforms the generated artifacts into concrete supervised train-
ing examples. Based on the QOC data generated in the previous step, the model
is additionally asked to analyze the results of the QOC analysis and to produce
a final answer derived from this structured evaluation. For generation 1, this
simply means adding one sentence that recommends the option with the high-
est score. For generations 2 and 3, an additional run through the base LLM is
performed in order to obtain richer answers and increase transparency. The re-
sulting data is then organized so that the QOC analysis itself is injected into the
thinking block of the response, while the generated answer based on this QOC
analysis is injected as the final answer of the model. In this way, prompts, inter-
mediate QOC representations, preferred options, and, where applicable, richer
natural-language responses are assembled into a format suitable for fine-tuning.
The purpose of this layer is to ensure that the target model is not trained only on
final answers, but on outputs that reflect the intended QOC reasoning structure.
5.5
Model Fine-Tuning Layer
After the training examples have been prepared, they are used to fine-tune the
target LLMs. In the context of this paper, this layer corresponds to adapting
the different Qwen3.5 base models so that they internalize not only the QOC
procedure as part of their reasoning behavior, but also the generation of corre-
sponding final answers derived from this structured analysis. Fine-tuning thus
shifts the models from general-purpose base beha

Digitization of Analogue Gauges using Computer
Vision
1st Erico Kayumba Mutonkole
dept. of Computer Science
University of the Western Cape
Cape Town, South Africa
3805086@myuwc.ac.za
2nd Olasupo Ajayi
dept. of Computer Science
University of the Western Cape
Cape Town, South Africa
ooajayi@uwc.ac.za
3rd Omowunmi Isafiade
dept. of Computer Science
University of the Western Cape
Cape Town, South Africa
oisafiade@uwc.ac.za
Abstract—Analogue gauges remain prevalent in manufacturing
industries for measuring physical quantities, yet manual mon-
itoring by operators introduces human error and operational
inefficiency. This research developed and evaluated an automated
gauge reading system using computer vision and deep learning
techniques. Three hybrid approaches were implemented and
compared: OpenCV with Scikit-Image (traditional computer
vision), OpenCV with ResNet18, and OpenCV with VGG19
(deep learning approaches). A comprehensive dataset of 1,848
pressure gauge images (0-10 BAR range) was curated through
web scraping, synthetic generation, and augmentation techniques.
The experimental results demonstrate that ResNet18 significantly
outperforms the alternatives, achieving an accuracy of 97. 3%,
compared to VGG19’s 64.4% and Scikit-Image’s 63. 8%. The
study validates the effectiveness of residual learning architectures
for industrial gauge digitization, providing a robust foundation
for Industry 5.0 automation applications.
Index Terms—Analogue Gauge, Computer Vision, Image Pro-
cessing, OpenCV, Pytorch, ResNET18, Scikit-Image, VGG19.
I. INTRODUCTION
Analogue gauges are scientific instruments designed to
measure physical quantities. These include temperature, mass
and voltage to name a few. Despite being an older technology,
analogue gauges are still widely used in many industries
today to take measurement readings for various equipment
[4]. However, it is easier for users to read digital numbers
compared to reading from an analogue gauge thereby, reducing
guesses of what value the meter pointer is pointing to [2].
Manual gauge reading in industrial environments presents
significant operational challenges and costs. Studies indicate
that manual readings can have error rates of up to 5%, often
due to fatigue, distraction, or misinterpretations [2], [12], while
broader research on manual data entry shows typical error rates
of about 1%, with some studies reporting rates as high as
4% for data entered without verification layers [13], [14]. In
large industrial plants such as oil and gas refineries, manual
reading tasks are very error-prone, time-consuming and often
dangerous due to exposed positions of the gauges [5]. These
errors translate into production inefficiencies, unnecessary pro-
cess adjustments, and potential safety risks in critical industrial
operations.
When we take cost into consideration, especially in indus-
trial settings, rather than installing new digital meters, it might
be cheaper to attach tiny cameras attached to cheap single
board computers, such as Raspberry PI or ESP32, to capture
images that will be processed by image recognition models,
to obtain numeric readings [2]. Despite their practicality,
a comprehensive comparison between traditional computer
vision approaches and modern deep learning architectures for
gauge digitization on low resource devices remains limited in
existing literature.
This work aims at developing a system that converts
analogue readings to their digital equivalent using computer
vision. The research also addresses the gap in literature by
systematically comparing three distinct approaches: traditional
computer vision (OpenCV with Scikit-Image), modern resid-
ual learning (OpenCV with ResNet18), and deep sequential
learning (OpenCV with VGG19). The primary research objec-
tive is to determine whether architectural innovations in deep
learning, particularly residual connections, provide significant
performance advantages over traditional methods for analogue
gauge classification tasks. The OpenCV library will be used
to preprocess images of analogue gauges, which will then be
used to train the deep learning model. The trained model will
accurately determine the numerical or digital equivalent value
of the gauge’s reading.
II. LITERATURE REVIEW
A recent review on deep learning approaches for digital
image processing [1] examined a wide range of techniques tai-
lored for various application areas. The study provided a thor-
ough investigation into several image processing tasks, includ-
ing noise reduction, image enhancement, segmentation, feature
detection, and classification. To evaluate the performance and
effectiveness of these methods, several metrics were employed,
such as mean squared error (MSE), peak signal-to-noise ratio
(PSNR), structural similarity index (SSIM), mean structural
similarity index (MSSIM), mean absolute error (MAE), and
naturalness image quality evaluator (NIQE), among others.
The review highlighted the strong noise reduction capabilities
of methods like Self2Self neural networks, DnCNNs, and
DFT-Net. In terms of classification, architectures ranging from
Residual Networks to combinations like CNN-LSTM were
recognized for their promising accuracy [1].
In a study focused on water meter reading recognition using
deep learning techniques [2], three models namely Faster R-
arXiv:2611.26262v1  [cs.CV]  19 Nov 2026
CNN, SSD, and YOLOv3 were evaluated to identify which
offered superior performance. Among the models assessed,
YOLOv3 achieved the highest recognition accuracy, recording
a success rate of 90.61%.
A proposed automated system combined deep learning,
machine learning, and image processing to detect readings
from analogue gauges [3]. The researchers utilized image
processing techniques to generate supervised data from gauge
images, addressing the challenges of working with unsuper-
vised data and aiming to improve recognition accuracy. Three
models—DenseNet 169, InceptionNet V3, and VGG19—were
trained on 1,011 labeled images categorized into 9 classes with
labels from 0 to 8. VGG19 showed a high training accuracy of
97% but a lower testing accuracy of 75%, indicating possible
overfitting. In contrast, InceptionNet V3 showed consistent
performance across both datasets, while DenseNet 169 deliv-
ered the highest accuracy and strongest generalization ability
among the models [3].
In an effort to automate analogue gauge reading across
various industries, including healthcare and automotive, re-
searchers in [4] developed an algorithm called the Analogue
Gauge Reader (AGR) using artificial intelligence methods. The
algorithm was implemented with open-source tools such as
OpenCV, NumPy, and PIL. Experimental results demonstrated
a notable reduction in error rates following the application
of image preprocessing techniques. Moreover, the algorithm
proved adaptable to a range of analogue gauge types captured
under varying lighting conditions. In testing, the approach
achieved high accuracy and precision, ranging from 99% to
100% [4].
Analogue meters located in areas that were hard-to-access
or hazardous locations proved to be challenging as mea-
surements for various equipment in the manufacturing plant
were needed. A solution was proposed in [5] to remotely
monitor these analogue gauges in areas that are difficult to
reach or hazardous using a combination of a microcontroller
device and a camera. The process involved using the camera
to capture gauge images, which were then processed on a
local computer using a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)
with the CenterNet HourGlass104 model, segmentation of the
pointer was done with the Hough Transform, while polar
transformation was used to calculate the pointer angle. The
value indicated by the gauge was determined based on the
pointer’s angle, and displayed on a web-accessible dashboard.
The approach achieved an average relative error of 0.95%,
demonstrating good accuracy and robustness for industrial
environments [5].
A real-time mobile solution for reading circular single-
pointer analogue gauges using a lightweight CNN-based sys-
tem was presented in [6]. They used a synthetic dataset of
10,000 images with ground truth annotations to train the CNN
model they implemented. The focus of the research was to
implement an efficient method for processing both high- and
low-resolution gauge images on mobile phones, and to the
release of a diverse real-world gauge dataset. They achieved
pointer angle errors below 1° and while running at up to 25fps
on mobile devices [6].
III. RESEARCH FOCUS
This work addresses the fundamental challenge of au-
tomated interpretation of analogue gauges using computer
vision. As a proof of concept and to demonstrate the viability
of this idea, only pressure gauges of up to 10 BAR were
considered. The research investigates three distinct hybrid
approaches: OpenCV with Scikit-Image (traditional computer
vision), OpenCV with ResNet18 (modern residual learning),
and OpenCV with VGG19 (deep sequential architecture). This
comparative framework enables systematic evaluation of tra-
ditional versus deep learning methodologies while examining
the impact of architectural innovations (residual connections)
on classification performance. The choice of these approaches
is grounded in their theoretical significance. Scikit-Image
represents traditional computer vision techniques, VGG19
illustrates deep sequential architectures that are susceptible to
vanishing gradient issues [18], and ResNet18 demonstrates
modern advancements designed to overcome gradient flow
challenges. Their performance is evaluated using accuracy,
precision, recall, F1-score and mean average precision (mAP),
providing a comprehensive assessment across multiple dimen-
sions.
IV. REQUIREMENT ANALYSIS
Computer vision has vast industrial applications and has
steadily been growing in popularity in recent times. This
work’s scope is limited to image recognition, image processing
and deep learning models and their applications in digitizing
analogue gauges.
To be considered practical and viable, the proposed solution
must meet the following functional requirements: Images of
analogue gauge must be acquired from camera sensors.
1) Computer vision models should be used to analyse the
captured image to obtain the equivalent digital reading.
2) Digital value inference must have a precision targeting
±0.1 BAR accuracy
3) Real-time processing capability for industrial applica-
tions, with approximately 2 seconds processing time per
image.
4) The developed system should be able to work on low-
spec hardware such as microcontrollers or single board
computers
V. METHODOLOGY AND EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN
Analogue gauge digitization is formulated as a multi-class
classification problem where each discrete gauge reading (0-
10 BAR) represents a distinct class. This approach, while
discretizing continuous readings, provides robust performance
against visual noise and simplifies the mapping from visual
input to numerical output compared to regression-based needle
angle estimation methods [20]. The following sub-sections
discuss our research methodology.
A. Data Collection and Preparation
The data for this experiment were prepared as follows:
1) A custom dataset was curated by web scraping pressure
gauge images from Google Images. This was necessary
because, for the task of analogue gauge reading, there
is a significant lack of large, publicly available datasets,
a limitation also acknowledged by [6]. Three (3) types
of pressure gauges were selected as shown in Figure
1. These gauges had readings from 0 to 10 BAR (11
classes).
2) The 3 images were then synthesized to generate 33
image classes using Adobe Photoshop. 11 images per
class * 3 = 33. A sample of the synthesized image is
shown in Figure 2.
3) Finally, we augmented the resulting 33 images using
various techniques and ended up with 1,848 augmented
pressure gauge image variants.
Fig. 1. Three original gauges sourced from Google Images.
Fig. 2. Original (Left) and synthetic (right) image.
1) Data augmentation pipeline: The augmentation process
was designed to improve model robustness to real-world
variations in gauge imaging. Five augmentation processes were
carried out.
1) The images were randomly rotated by ±15° to simulate
different camera angles.
2) The images were scaled between 90% and 110% to
account for changes in camera distance.
3) Positional robustness was introduced through translation
of up to 10% of the image’s width and height along both
axes.
4) Perspective transformations were applied to mimic
changes in viewing angles.
5) Salt-and-pepper noise injection was used to simulate
sensor noise and environmental artifacts.
Fig. 3. Samples of augmented images.
2) Dataset Partitioning Pipeline: The dataset was then split
into an 80:20 ratio. 80% for training (80%, n=1.474) and 20%
for Validation (20%, n=374).
B. Image Processing
The following steps were taken to process the images in the
dataset:
1) Conversion to Grayscale
The images were converted to grayscale. Removing
colour information simplifies the images and enhances
the intensity. This step has been shown to help in
reducing computational complexity and is essential for
edge detection and further analysis, as reported in [7].
A comparison of the original vs gray scale version is
shown in Figure 4
2) Extraction of Region of Interest (RoI)
We isolated the gauge area from the background to focus
on the circular dial of the gauge and filter out irrelevant
parts of the image.
3) Gauge Labelling
Fig. 4. Original (left) image and Grayscale (right) image.
Traditionally, when using computer vision for analogue
gauge digitization, the model estimates the needle’s
angle to determine the reading as documented in [21]. In
contrast, this study used a classification-based approach,
treating readings as discrete labeled values. This ensured
that our computer vision models would be more robust
to visual noise and simplify the mapping from image
to value. To achieve this we framed this work as an
image classification problem and utilized deep learning
models (ResNet18 and VGG19). Being supervised learn-
ing models, we had to first manually label the images,
assigning each gauge image a class label that represents
its reading. For instance, if the gauge’s needle points to
’6’, we put it in class ’6’.
C. Models
As stated earlier, we explored and compared 3 hybrid
approaches in this work, namely, OpenCV with Scikit-Image,
OpenCV with ResNet18, and OpenCV with a VGG19. Py-
Torch framework was used to train and evaluate the deep
Learning models.
1) OpenCV
with
Scikit-Image:
This
approach
used
OpenCV to load and preprocess images and then applied
scikit-image for enhanced filtering and region analysis [8].
Scikit-Image is a Python library built on top of NumPy,
SciPy, and matplotlib. We tagged this the “Traditional com-
puter vision technique” as it employed a four-stage approach
for needle angle detection and classification. The stages are
summarized as follows:
• Canny edge detection with low and high thresholds of
50 and 150 respectively, was used to identify the needle
boundaries.
• Probabilistic Hough Line Transform was then used to
extract the needle line from the detected edges.
• Geometric computation was used to calculate the needle’s
angle relative to the gauge center.
• The obtained angles were mapped to discrete classes
using predefined angular intervals of 32.7 (360 divided
by 11) degrees per class, enabling classification across
11 classes spanning the full 360-degree range. This
systematic approach helped in uniform distribution across
the entire angular spectrum, with each class representing
an equal portion of the gauge’s measurement range.
2) OpenCV with ResNet18: This hybrid approach leveraged
OpenCV and ResNet18 (implemented in PyTorch). OpenCV
was used for image loading and preprocessing, specifically for
image resizing and conversion to grayscale, while ResNet18
was used for classification. Our implementation process can
be summarized as follows:
• The images were converted to to 224x224 pixels and
converted to 3-channel grayscale format to meet the input
requirements of pre-trained ResNet18.
• We utilized apre-trained ResNet18 backbone for feature
extraction, but still trained it on our dataset. By utilizing a
pre-trained model we were able to minimize the training
time and benefitted from transfer learning [18]. We froze
the ResNet model during the first initial 10 epochs before
being fine-tuned in subsequent training phases. In total we
trained the model using 100 epochs.
• The classification component of our model consisted
of a modified final fully connected layer that mapped
the 512-dimensional feature representations to 11 output
classes. We applied a dropout rate of 0.3 before the final
layer to mitigate overfitting and improve generalization
performance.
3) OpenCV with VGG19: Like in the previous model, we
also applied OpenCV to preprocess the images and convert
them to 224×224×3 RGB images. The converted images
were then passed as input to a VGG19 model pre-trained on
ImageNet for feature extraction.
• The
original
classifier
structure
of
25088→4096→4096→1000
was
modified
to
25088→1024→512→11 to accommodate the 11-class
classification task.
• We applied ReLU activation functions and dropout layers
throughout the network. Finally, to prevent overfitting we
applied a dropout rate of 0.5 across each of the fully
connected layers in the modified classifier.
4) Performance Metrics: To evaluate the performance of
the model, the following metrics were used:
• Accuracy - Measures how close the digitized value was
to the true pressure value (ground truth).

D. Visualization and Analysis Tools
The evaluation methodology encompasses comprehensive
performance assessment through multiple visualization and
analytical techniques, including confusion matrices to examine
class-wise performance and identify misclassification patterns,
ROC curves with corresponding AUC values to evaluate
binary classification performance for each individual class,
training dynamics plots that display loss curves and accuracy
progression throughout the training process.
VI. RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
The performance of the three proposed approaches imple-
mented in this work are presented in this section.
A. Comparative Performance Analysis
We start off by comparing ResNet18 and VGG19 as they
are both deep learning models. This comparison is important
because it highlights the relative strengths and weaknesses
of modern convolutional neural network architectures when
applied to the task of analogue gauge digitization. ResNet18,
with its residual connections, is designed to address the van-
ishing gradient problem and typically achieves higher accuracy
with fewer parameters, while VGG19, although deeper, is
computationally more intensive and less efficient in feature
reuse. Evaluating these models side by side

Similarity-based OSF Logic for Flexible SPARQL Query
Answering
Gian Carlo Milanese1,*, Gabriella Pasi1
1University of Milano-Bicocca, DISCo, Milan, Italy
Abstract
We present an updated version of fosf, a reasoner for fuzzy order-sorted feature (OSF) logic, with support for
flexible SPARQL query answering over RDF knowledge graphs. Fuzzy OSF logic is a knowledge representation
and reasoning language where feature symbols denote functions and sort symbols denote fuzzy sets. Sorts are
organized in a fuzzy subsumption relation that extends to OSF terms, record-like structures representing classes
of entities. The unification algorithm for these structures provides a calculus of fuzzy type subsumption. The
latest release of fosf introduces support for similarity-based reasoning by extending the OSF language with a
similarity relation among sorts, alongside a translation engine for compiling OSF terms into standard SPARQL.
Queries expressed as OSF terms undergo fuzzy ontology-aware rewriting prior to translation. This process
incorporates an OSF theory of sort definitions, feature domain and range declarations, and fuzzy subsumption and
similarity relations through fuzzy OSF constraint normalization. This rewriting enables flexible query answering
by returning approximate solutions, allowing queries that would otherwise be inconsistent with the underlying
ontology to yield relevant results.
Keywords
RDF knowledge graphs, SPARQL, Similarity-based reasoning, Order-sorted feature logic, Query rewriting
1. Introduction
We present an updated release of fosf,1 a reasoner for fuzzy order-sorted feature (OSF) logic, that
introduces similarity-based OSF reasoning alongside an ontology-aware translation engine for querying
RDF knowledge graphs (KGs) via SPARQL. Queries expressed as OSF terms undergo fuzzy constraint
normalization prior to translation into standard SPARQL. This process integrates ontological informa-
tion from a sort taxonomy, a sort similarity relation, sort definitions, and feature domain and range
declarations. The resulting query rewriting mechanism enables the retrieval of approximate solutions
for queries that would otherwise fail under strict ontological constraints.
Background
OSF logic is a knowledge representation and reasoning language introduced by Aït-
Kaci [1, 2]. It is based on sorts, which represent classes of objects, and features, which represent
functional attributes. Sorts are organized in a subsumption relation that extends to OSF terms, record-
like structures representing classes of entities and their constraints. Reasoning with OSF logic is based
on the normalization (or unification) of OSF terms, a procedure that aims to combine the constraints
expressed by one or more terms while taking the sort hierarchy into account. OSF logic is at the basis
of CEDAR [3], a Semantic Web reasoner that normalizes and optimizes queries expressed as OSF terms
before translating them into SPARQL, possibly leading to more efficient retrieval.
Fuzzy OSF logic [4] extends OSF logic by interpreting sorts and OSF terms as fuzzy sets, and by
generalizing the sort subsumption to a fuzzy subsumption relation among sorts, which is then extended
to OSF terms. The core reasoning algorithms of fuzzy OSF logic are implemented in the fosf Python
library [5], which supports fuzzy taxonomic reasoning, subsumption degree computation, and fuzzy
normalization and unification of OSF terms.

from fosf.parsers import parse_taxonomy
sim_tax_str = """
# Subsumption declarations

research_center < institution .
university < research_center .
researcher, lecturer, teacher < person .
professor < researcher, lecturer .
# Similarity declarations
teacher ~ lecturer = 0.5 ."""
sim_tax = parse_taxonomy(sim_tax_str)

Figure 1: Example of how a sort subsumption ⪯(black edges) and a sort similarity ∼(dotted green edges) are
parsed in fosf, and their graphical representation (where ⊥is omitted). After parsing, the two relations are
combined into a single fuzzy subsumption ⪯· (black edges and dashed red edges).
Contributions.
The new release of fosf introduces the following features: (i) support for a similarity
relation between sorts, which is integrated into the main reasoning algorithms of fuzzy OSF logic,
enabling similarity-based reasoning with OSF logic [6]; (ii) support for feature domain and range declara-
tions during OSF term normalization; (iii) querying RDF KGs through the translation of normalized OSF
queries into standard SPARQL. The normalization exploits fuzzy sort subsumption and sort similarity
relations to relax incompatible constraints and retrieve approximate solutions.
Related work.
Implementations of (crisp) OSF logic include the constraint logic programming
language LIFE [7] and the CEDAR Semantic Web reasoner [3]. Closely related formalisms include
description logics (DLs) and fuzzy DLs, which are supported by several reasoners (e.g., [8, 9, 10, 11, 12]).
The similarities and differences between OSF logic and DLs have been studied extensively [13, 14, 15,
16]. Similarity-based OSF logic is inspired by fuzzy unification in fuzzy logic programming, where
unification is guided by similarity or proximity relations (e.g., [17, 18, 19, 20, 21]); implementations
include Bousi∼Prolog [22] and FASILL [23]. In the Semantic Web community, various approaches
handle imprecise or flexible querying over RDF data, including fuzzy SPARQL extensions (e.g., [24, 25])
and query relaxation techniques (e.g., [26]). In this context, fosf applies similarity-based normalization
at the OSF logic level before compiling the resulting query terms into standard SPARQL.
2. Similarity-based OSF Taxonomic Reasoning
At the core of OSF logic is a sort taxonomy, a finite set of sort symbols 𝒮that is ordered in a lattice
(𝒮, ⪯, ⋏) with top element ⊤and bottom element ⊥. Similarity-based OSF logic [6] extends the sort
taxonomy with a similarity relation on sort symbols, that is, a fuzzy binary relation ∼: 𝒮× 𝒮→[0, 1]
which satisfies reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity.2 As described in [6], the information provided by
the sort subsumption ⪯and the similarity ∼can be combined into a single fuzzy subsumption relation
⪯· : 𝒮× 𝒮→[0, 1], according to the following informal inference, inspired by the similarity-based
approaches to logic programming (e.g., [18]):
if the sort 𝑠0 is subsumed by the sort 𝑠1
(i.e., 𝑠0 ⪯𝑠1)
and 𝑠1 is similar to the sort 𝑠2 with degree 𝛼
(i.e., ∼(𝑠1, 𝑠2) = 𝛼)
then 𝑠0 is subsumed by 𝑠2 with degree 𝛼
(i.e., ⪯·(𝑠0, 𝑠2) = 𝛼).
For example, if 𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑓𝑒𝑠𝑠𝑜𝑟s are 𝑙𝑒𝑐𝑡𝑢𝑟𝑒𝑟s, and 𝑙𝑒𝑐𝑡𝑢𝑟𝑒𝑟s are similar to 𝑡𝑒𝑎𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑟s with degree 0.5, then
we can conclude that 𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑓𝑒𝑠𝑠𝑜𝑟s are also 𝑡𝑒𝑎𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑟s with subsumption degree 0.5. As shown in [6], the

from fosf.reasoning import normalize_term
# Normalizing an OSF term according to subsumption + similarity only

print(normalize_term(t, sim_tax))

Figure 2: Normalizing an OSF term in fosf.

print(degree, nt)
# Output: 0.5 X0 : professor(teach_at -> X1 : university, research_at -> X1)

reflexivity, transitivity and strong antisymmetry, and such that a GLB 𝑠04𝑠1 exists for every 𝑠0, 𝑠1 ∈𝒮.3
As shown in Fig. 1, fosf supports parsing a sort subsumption relation ⪯and a sort similarity relation

simply a partial order, fosf works on a completion of ⪯· that does not need to be explicitly computed.4
By employing the graph encoding technique of [28] and optimized weighted graph traversal of [29], it
is possible to efficiently compute the GLB 𝑠0 4 𝑠1 and the subsumption degree ⪯·(𝑠0, 𝑠1) of two sorts 𝑠0
and 𝑠1 [5]. For instance, 𝑡𝑒𝑎𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑟4 𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑒𝑎𝑟𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑟= 𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑓𝑒𝑠𝑠𝑜𝑟and ⪯·(𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑓𝑒𝑠𝑠𝑜𝑟, 𝑡𝑒𝑎𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑟) = 0.5.
3. Similarity-based OSF Term Normalization
Sort symbols may be used with variables (also called tags) 𝑋0, 𝑋1 . . . ∈𝒱and features symbols
𝑓0, . . . , 𝑓𝑛∈ℱto build OSF terms. These are record-like representations of (fuzzy) sets of objects, such
as 𝑡= 𝑋0 : 𝑝𝑒𝑟𝑠𝑜𝑛(𝑡𝑒𝑎𝑐ℎ_𝑎𝑡→𝑋1 : 𝑖𝑛𝑠𝑡𝑖𝑡𝑢𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛, 𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑒𝑎𝑟𝑐ℎ_𝑎𝑡→𝑋1 : 𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑒𝑎𝑟𝑐ℎ_𝑐𝑒𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑟), which
denotes the class of people that teach at some institution 𝑋1 and carry out research at the same 𝑋1,
which is also a research center. In general, OSF terms may include redundant, or even contradictory,
information (e.g., the sort of 𝑋1 is specified twice in 𝑡). OSF terms that are well-behaved to this regard are
called normal OSF terms or 𝜓-terms [2], and they are also denoted 𝜓, 𝜓𝑖, and so on. The fosf reasoner
supports normalizing OSF terms according to a sort subsumption relation ⪯and similarity ∼: as shown
in Fig. 2, the term 𝑡can be normalized to 𝑝𝑒𝑟𝑠𝑜𝑛(𝑡𝑒𝑎𝑐ℎ_𝑎𝑡→𝑋1 : 𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑒𝑎𝑟𝑐ℎ_𝑐𝑒𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑟, 𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑒𝑎𝑟𝑐ℎ_𝑎𝑡→

The fosf reasoner also supports the normalization of OSF terms modulo an OSF theory of sort

should satisfy. Feature domain and range declarations have shape domain(𝑓) = 𝑠0 and range(𝑓) = 𝑠1,
and they ensure that, whenever 𝑡′ = 𝑋: ⊤(𝑓→𝑌: ⊤) is an OSF term, then 𝑋must be of sort 𝑠0 and
𝑌must be of sort 𝑠1. Overall, the (fuzzy) sort subsumption and similarity relations, the sort definitions,
and the feature domain and range declarations constitute the ontological component according to which
an OSF term can be normalized. Fig. 3 shows an example of parsing an OSF theory in fosf and
normalizing the OSF term 𝑡according to the theory. In the example, the domain declarations for the
features 𝑡𝑒𝑎𝑐ℎ_𝑎𝑡and 𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑒𝑎𝑟𝑐ℎ_𝑎𝑡enforce the tag 𝑋0 to be of sort 𝑡𝑒𝑎𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑟4𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑒𝑎𝑟𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑟= 𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑓𝑒𝑠𝑠𝑜𝑟,
and the sort definition for 𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑓𝑒𝑠𝑠𝑜𝑟thus enforces 𝑋1 to be a 𝑢𝑛𝑖𝑣𝑒𝑟𝑠𝑖𝑡𝑦. The constraints imposed
by an OSF theory may be satisfied up to a degree 𝛼∈[0, 1]. For instance, in the term nt of Fig. 3, 𝑋0
is of sort 𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑓𝑒𝑠𝑠𝑜𝑟rather than 𝑡𝑒𝑎𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑟(as required by the domain of 𝑡𝑒𝑎𝑐ℎ_𝑎𝑡) so that nt satisfies
the OSF theory with degree ⪯·(𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑓𝑒𝑠𝑠𝑜𝑟, 𝑡𝑒𝑎𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑟) = 0.5. Note that, without the fuzzy subsumption
⪯·(𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑓𝑒𝑠𝑠𝑜𝑟, 𝑡𝑒𝑎𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑟) induced by 𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑓𝑒𝑠𝑠𝑜𝑟⪯𝑙𝑒𝑐𝑡𝑢𝑟𝑒𝑟and ∼(𝑙𝑒𝑐𝑡𝑢𝑟𝑒𝑟, 𝑡𝑒𝑎𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑟), the GLB of
𝑡𝑒𝑎𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑟and 𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑒𝑎𝑟𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑟would instead be ⊥, and the normalization of 𝑡would fail.
4. Similarity-based OSF for SPARQL Query Answering
The fosf reasoner supports translating a (normalized) OSF term into SPARQL for instance retrieval
over an RDF KG. This translation is inspired by the query rewriting pipeline of CEDAR [3], in which an
OSF term query is preprocessed to ensure consistency and to potentially reduce the retrieval search
space before generating a SPARQL query. The fosf library extends this framework by integrating
sort definitions and the sort similarity relation ∼into the normalization, enabling similarity-based
query rewriting. Without the sort similarity, queries violating ontological constraints would be declared
inconsistent and return no results. Instead, fosf can rewrite OSF terms into queries that approximately
satisfy the OSF theory to some degree, thus enabling the retrieval of approximate solutions.
Consider again the query term 𝑡= ?𝑋0 : 𝑝𝑒𝑟𝑠𝑜𝑛(𝑡𝑒𝑎𝑐ℎ_𝑎𝑡→𝑋1 : 𝑖𝑛𝑠𝑡𝑖𝑡𝑢𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛, 𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑒𝑎𝑟𝑐ℎ_𝑎𝑡→
𝑋1 : 𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑒𝑎𝑟𝑐ℎ_𝑐𝑒𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑟), where 𝑋0 is marked with a question mark to denote instance retrieval. Under
standard OSF normalization, 𝑡is inconsistent because 𝑡𝑒𝑎𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑟⋏𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑒𝑎𝑟𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑟= ⊥, as discussed in Sec-
tion 3. Translating 𝑡directly to SPARQL without normalizing ignores the ontology entirely, yielding the
query in Fig. 4a, which fails to enforce domain/range semantics and sort definitions. In contrast, by taking
∼into account fosf normalizes 𝑡to 𝑋0 : 𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑓𝑒𝑠𝑠𝑜𝑟(𝑡𝑒𝑎𝑐ℎ_𝑎𝑡→𝑋1 : 𝑢𝑛𝑖𝑣𝑒𝑟𝑠𝑖𝑡𝑦, 𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑒𝑎𝑟𝑐ℎ_𝑎𝑡→
𝑋1), deriving an approximate solution that satisfies the OSF theory with a degree of 0.5 (Fig. 3). Fig. 4b
shows the resulting SPARQL translation. Providing approximate solutions for otherwise inconsistent
queries can be desirable in many scenarios. For example, users often do not possess full knowledge
of extensive ontologies, making an inconsistent result potentially surprising. Moreover, the inconsis-
tency of 𝑡arises from the closed-world assumption of OSF logic, where 𝑡𝑒𝑎𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑟⋏𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑒𝑎𝑟𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑟= ⊥
forces disjointness of the two sorts. Relaxing this requirement can be valuable in contexts where this
assumption does not hold, such as settings where domain knowledge can evolve.
From a practical standpoint, fosf handles OSF query parsing, normalization, and translation to
SPARQL. Base IRIs and prefixes can be specified prior to an OSF theory or query using Turtle-like syntax
(e.g., @base <IRI> . @prefix : <IRI> .). The syntax for OSF theories (including subsumption
and similarity declarations) and OSF terms supports base sorts like 𝑝𝑒𝑟𝑠𝑜𝑛(resolved via the base IRI), as
Figure 5: The web interface of fosf, displaying the OSF ontology composed of sort subsumption and similarity
declarations, sort definitions, and feature domain/range constraints (left), the target RDF KG facts (middle), and
the OSF query term (right). Action buttons enable users to inspect the taxonomy, display the translated query,
and execute the generated SPARQL, with options to toggle OSF query normalization and the similarity relation.
well as absolute IRIs (e.g., <http://example.org/person>) and prefixed names (e.g., ex:person).
The query generated by fosf can be executed over in-memory RDF graphs or remote SPARQL endpoints
using the rdflib and SPARQLWrapper libraries,5 or sent to any standard SPARQL query engine.
5. Demo Interface
We provide an interactive Web interface designed to demonstrate the query normalization and execution
pipeline of fosf.6 As shown in Fig. 5, users can specify custom OSF theories, target RDF KGs, and OSF
queries directly in the browser, or select from a list of pre-defined examples. The interface can visually
render the sort subsumption hierarchy, the sort similarity relation, and the resulting fuzzy subsumption
relation. Users can inspect the generated SPARQL queries and execute them directly against the RDF
KG to view retrieved instances alongside the approximation degree of the normalized query. Two global
toggles, for OSF query normalization and sort similarity, allow users to compare OSF terms, generated
SPARQL queries, and retrieval results with or without normalization and similarity-based reasoning.
6. Conclusion and Future Work
We have presented an updated release of fosf, extending fuzzy OSF logic with similarity-based
reasoning and ontology-aware SPARQL query generation. By integrating a sort similarity relation into
constraint normalization, fosf enables flexible query rewriting, deriving approximate solutions for
queries that would otherwise be declared inconsistent under strict ontological constraints.
While the current release of fosf provides a functional prototype, several limitations present avenues
for future development. Regarding performance, we are replacing the pure-Python reasoning core
with a C++ engine to improve execution speed and memory efficiency. To address the closed-world
assumption of OSF logic, where two sorts 𝑠0 and 𝑠1 are treated as disjoint whenever 𝑠0 4 𝑠1 = ⊥, we
plan to allow declarations of non-disjoint sorts within sort taxonomies, without the need to explicitly
name their GLB. Furthermore, we intend to improve the expressiveness of fosf by extending support
for disjunctive sorts and terms in both theories and queries, as well as enabling sort instances in OSF
query expressions. Finally, in addition to manually defined similarity relations, we plan to support
automated similarity estimation using techniques such as vector embeddings.

demonstration system.

SkillBridge: Cost-Aware Diagnosis and Repair of
Cross-OS Compatibility Defects in Agent Skills
Anjie Xu1,2,3, Zixing Wang4, Yifeng Cai1,2, Leye Wang1,2,*
1Key Lab of High Confidence Software Technologies (Peking University), Ministry of Education, China
2School of Computer Science, Peking University, Beijing, China
3Zhongguancun Academy, Beijing, China
4School of Computer Science, Northwestern Polytechnical University, Xi’an, China
anjiexu@stu.pku.edu.cn, leyewang@pku.edu.cn
*Corresponding author.
Abstract—LLM agents increasingly reuse executable capabili-
ties through skills, but a skill that works on one OS may fail
on another because OS assumptions are spread across guide
text, scripts, metadata, install contracts, and local entrypoints.
Diagnosing such failures by running every skill on every OS
is expensive: many executions spend model tokens, runner time,
and review effort before revealing whether the failure is truly OS-
related. We present SkillBridge, a contract-based workflow with
three stages: static analysis, dynamic validation, and repair. Skill-
Bridge first screens 3,270 skill-target-OS cases, covering 1,090
skills across Linux, macOS, and Windows, to find OS-sensitive
contract evidence. It then runs dynamic tasks and root-cause
review on selected cases to confirm whether a failure is caused
by an OS assumption, and repairs the contract field that caused
the failure, such as guide text, package scripts, dependencies, or
platform declarations. Repair raises the reviewer-judged target-
task pass rate from 30.6% to 38.4%, a gain of 7.8 percentage
points. A retrospective Linux/macOS budget analysis further
shows the efficiency effect: SkillBridge reaches 38 confirmed
OS issues with 185 dynamic validations, where uniform random
selection would require about 865 validations in expectation.
Index Terms—agent skills, cross-platform compatibility, static
analysis, dynamic analysis, automated repair
I. INTRODUCTION
Agents such as Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, and Open-
Claw are becoming practical interfaces for software work and
other tool-mediated tasks: they read files, call tools, run ter-
minal commands, and carry state across execution loops [1]–
[5]. To make these capabilities reusable, several agent systems
expose skills as a packaging unit for task-specific knowledge,
scripts, dependencies, and execution instructions [6]–[8].
A skill can contain a SKILL.md guide, examples, helper
scripts, metadata, install instructions, referenced commands,
local entrypoints, external dependencies, and assumptions
about the operating system where the harness runs. This makes
a skill a software-engineering artifact, not just a natural-
language prompt. Users expect the same skill to work on
Linux servers, macOS laptops, and Windows desktops, but
many skills are authored and tested on only one OS.
These assumptions surface as task failures that are difficult
to attribute. The same skill may pass on one OS and fail on
another, yet the difference may come from an OS assump-
tion, missing credentials, an unavailable service, a benchmark
fixture, or a non-OS agent planning error. The OS-specific
surface is often hidden inside the package: a guide may ask
the agent to run ./script.sh, a package may omit the
referenced entrypoint, an install contract may only mention
Homebrew or apt, or a script may depend on AppleScript [9],
Windows COM [10], POSIX paths [11], /proc [12], or
Windows naming rules and path limits [13], [14]. By the time
the agent discovers the mismatch dynamically, it has already
spent model tokens, runner time, and review effort.
Existing software portability work provides a foundation,
but it does not directly match this mixed artifact. Traditional
analyses focus on source code, APIs, system calls, tests, or
dependency declarations [15]–[17]. Agent benchmarks report
task-level pass/fail outcomes, but a failed task result is not
an OS root cause. Automated repair work typically patches
code, while skill repair may require coordinated changes to
guide text, scripts, metadata, install contracts, and support
declarations. The missing abstraction is a unit that connects
what the agent is told to read, install, and execute with the OS
assumption that explains a failure and the contract field that a
repair must change.
SkillBridge diagnoses cross-OS skill compatibility as a
contract problem. A dynamic failure is only a symptom; it
becomes an OS issue when review ties that symptom to an
operating-system assumption in the skill contract. This for-
mulation also turns efficiency into a selection problem. Static
evidence proposes which skill-OS pairs should receive dy-
namic validation, review decides the final label, and dynamic
execution is reserved for pairs that need runtime evidence.
We present SkillBridge, a workflow for cost-aware cross-
OS skill diagnosis and repair. SkillBridge builds a compact
contract, extracts and interprets OS-sensitive evidence for
each target OS, allocates dynamic budget to selected pairs,
and reviews root causes. Repairs edit the contract component
that caused the defect, such as command branches, wrappers,
install instructions, or support declarations.
Our evaluation covers 1,090 skills across three OSes, or
3,270 skill-target-OS cases. Static analysis screens these cases
for OS-sensitive contract evidence. A separate Linux/macOS
budget analysis shows that static-guided selection reaches the
same expected issue yield with 185 validations rather than

about 865 under uniform random selection.
The paper makes three contributions:
• We define the cross-OS compatibility problem for agent
skills: when the same skill task runs reliably on some
OSes but persistently fails on a target OS, it is a candidate
OS issue; review confirms the issue only when the failure
is caused by an OS-specific assumption in the skill
contract.
• We present SkillBridge, which uses static triage to focus
dynamic validation and a software engineering-inspired
multi-agent workflow to triage, patch, and review repairs.
• We evaluate SkillBridge on 1,090 public skills across
Linux, macOS, and Windows. We open-source our ex-
perimental code and data through the public SkillBridge
repository.1
II. PROBLEM DEFINITION
We study the following observable symptom: the same skill
is expected to run on O = {Linux, macOS, Windows}, but
it passes on some OSes and fails on others. This symptom
is insufficient by itself. We count an OS issue only when
the failure can be traced to the skill’s stated or implicit OS
assumptions.
The central object is the skill contract: everything the skill
exposes to the agent as the way to understand, install, and
execute the capability. We write this contract as:
C(s) = ⟨Gs, Ps, Ms, Ds, As⟩.
Here, Gs is guide text and examples; Ps is the package
surface, including files, scripts, wrappers, and referenced en-
trypoints; Ms is metadata and supported-platform declarations;
Ds is the dependency and installation contract; and As is
the set of OS-sensitive assumptions, including shell semantics,
commands, paths, permissions, GUI/session requirements, na-
tive applications, APIs, and platform guards. Assumptions in
As may be stated in Gs, implemented in Ps, advertised in
Ms, or required by Ds; the separate component lets review
name the OS assumption while repair edits the field that
exposes it. We merge files and referenced entrypoints into Ps
because the agent executes them as one package surface. These
assumptions are grounded in standard and vendor-documented
OS surfaces, including POSIX shell and utility behavior [11],
Windows path namespaces [13], AppleScript [9], COM [10],
and Linux procfs [12].
For each skill-OS pair (s, o) that receives validation, Skill-
Bridge preserves one evidence chain:

1https://github.com/TankTechnology/SkillBridge
Here, e(s, o) is the static evidence extracted from C(s) for
target OS o; h(s, o) is the static hypothesis used to select
the pair for dynamic checking; τ(s, o) is the dynamic trace
when the pair is run; y(s, o) is the reviewed label; and r
is an optional repair action. We use y(s, o) = confirmed
when review ties a cross-OS symptom to an OS assumption
in C(s), y(s, o) = excluded when the symptom comes from
a non-OS cause, and y(s, o) = uncertain when the evidence
is insufficient.
The formulation separates a dynamic symptom from a
compatibility defect. We write a reviewed OS issue as:
OSIssue(s, o) ⇐⇒symptom(τ(s, o)) ∧∃a ∈As.
violates(a, o) ∧explains(a, τ(s, o)).
Here, a is an OS-sensitive assumption in the skill contract.
violates means that the assumption is incompatible with the
target OS, and explains means that review can connect the
dynamic symptom to that violated assumption. Thus, a cross-
OS pass/fail difference is evidence, but it is not by itself an
OS-issue label.
The cost-aware validation problem, for a skill set S, is to
choose which skill-OS pairs receive dynamic traces under a
budget:

Because OSIssue(s, o) is unknown before dynamic execu-
tion and review, SkillBridge uses static evidence e(s, o) and
hypothesis h(s, o) as a proxy for this selection problem.
The same chain defines all three evaluation questions. RQ1
asks whether the pre-execution hypothesis h(s, o) can recover
labels that root-cause review later assigns as y(s, o). RQ2 starts
from confirmed labels and asks how a repair r : C(s) →C′(s)
changes aggregate reviewer-judged target-OS replay and the
per-pair outcome distribution. RQ3 asks whether the workflow
matters beyond that endpoint, comparing a direct-agent abla-
tion and budgeted selection policies that choose which (s, o)
pairs receive dynamic traces τ(s, o).
A confirmed issue must be explained by a violated OS
assumption in the contract. For example, a Windows failure
is an OS issue if the only executable path in Ps is a POSIX
.sh script [11]; a Linux failure is an OS issue if As depends
on an Apple-only application [9]; a macOS failure is an OS
issue if Gs uses GNU-only command flags without a BSD
fallback [18], [19]. Each proposed repair receives a scoped
replay label: the same target task is rerun after the contract
change, and the review stage assigns the replay judgment. The
label supports target-OS repair effectiveness, while unreplayed
OSes remain outside the claim.
III. METHOD: SKILLBRIDGE
The formulation imposes two requirements on SkillBridge.
First, SkillBridge must preserve the evidence chain from a
contract assumption to a runtime symptom and then to a re-
viewed label, which instantiates OSIssue. Second, SkillBridge
must allocate dynamic budget to pairs where low-cost static
evidence predicts OS-sensitive behavior, which approximates
Q∗
B. SkillBridge implements these requirements in four stages:
extract contract evidence from C(s), interpret that evidence
for each target OS, validate selected pairs dynamically, and
convert reviewed root causes into contract-preserving repairs.
The design adapts a common software-engineering pattern
to skills. Low-cost structural evidence guides expensive exe-
cution [20]; repair studies report both success and cost [21],
[22]; and inspection or review turns symptoms into auditable
labels [23], [24]. SkillBridge applies this pattern to a mixed
text-code-package artifact by treating guide text, package files,
metadata, dependencies, and OS assumptions as one contract
rather than as separate artifacts.
Figure 1 operationalizes the evidence chain as a multi-agent
workflow. The separation follows inspection and modern code
review [23], [24]: artifact generation and repair are separated
from root-cause labeling and replay judgment. Labels are
not inferred from inter-agent agreement. Each later stage
consumes an explicit packet and produces a scoped artifact,
such as a dynamic trace, reviewed label, contract edit, or
replay judgment. The review role is a workflow role in
SkillBridge, not maintainer acceptance; Section VI treats its
agent implementation as a reliability threat.
A. Design Invariants
Three invariants keep SkillBridge from confusing cheap
evidence with a compatibility label. Evidence precedes ver-
dicts: static analysis over C(s) is recall-oriented and never
assigns y(s, o), because low-cost evidence can select work
but cannot by itself assign an OS-issue label. Outputs are
contract-field localized: each warning names the component
that may be wrong, Gs, Ps, Ms, Ds, or As, so the result
can drive a concrete repair. Labels are reviewed: a dynamic
failure becomes a label only after root-cause review, because
credentials, services, task noise, and OS compatibility can
produce the same surface symptom.
Algorithm 1 makes the budget boundary explicit. Static
analysis can only enqueue (s, o, h) triples; SELECT chooses
a budgeted subset; REVIEW creates labels; and PLANREPAIR
runs only after a confirmed, repairable label. The algorithm
therefore returns reviewed labels and a repair-action set rather
than unreviewed static warnings. This separates three actions
that are often conflated in dynamic skill testing: screening,
labeling, and repair planning. BUILDCONTRACT materializes
the contract fields defined in Section II from the skill guide,
package surface, metadata, dependencies, and OS assumptions.
B. Static Analysis
Static analysis proposes which skill-OS pairs should enter
the dynamic-validation budget. For each pair (s, o), the ana-

final label y(s, o), and SELECT later enforces the budget B.
Algorithm 2 gives the procedure used by Algorithm 1.
The analyzer evaluates a rule set R over the contract. Each
rule ρ is attached to one contract component, such as Gs
or Ps, and is interpreted through four predicates. MATCH
extracts concrete OS-sensitive snippets, REACH keeps only
snippets used on the target-OS execution or installation path,
CONFLICT tests whether the snippet is incompatible with
the target OS, and FALLBACK suppresses snippets already
handled by a guarded branch, adapter, or explicit unsupported
declaration. A snippet fires only when it is matched, reachable,
conflicting, and not covered by a fallback.

Algorithm 2 stores each fired snippet as an evidence record
containing the implicated component, source location, rule,
and snippet. If no rule fires, the pair is skipped; otherwise, the
pair enters dynamic validation with ranked evidence. RANK
prioritizes executable blockers over wording mismatches,
cross-field contradictions over isolated mentions, missing fall-
backs over guarded branches, and repairable contract defects
over platform-intrinsic requirements. For example, a Windows
pair receives high priority when Ms claims Windows support,
Ps exposes only run.sh, and Gs instructs the agent to
execute it.

tures observed in a seed set of 30 problematic skills. An LLM

which the authors then reviewed manually. Table I summarizes
the six rule families, their target-OS interpretations, and repair
targets. These rules serve as screening heuristics rather than
independently validated predictors. A positive h(s, o) therefore
means “select this pair for dynamic validation,” not “this is
confirmed.” Review still decides y(s, o).
The analyzer does not simulate the agent, establish package
portability, or label a failure without execution evidence. It
exposes low-cost contract obligations before dynamic valida-
tion. Its main false-negative modes are runtime-generated OS
assumptions, live GUI or account-state failures, and dependen-
cies hidden behind remote services; these cases still require
dynamic validation and review.
C. Dynamic Validation
Dynamic validation asks an agent to execute generated tasks
for skill-OS pairs selected by h(s, o) under budget B. Dynamic
execution is expensive evidence, not the default first step for
every pair. The trace τ(s, o) records whether the selected pair
exhibits an execution symptom under the target OS.
Each dynamic run records the target OS, selected task, agent
transcript summary, exit status, timeout, observed command
errors, generated artifacts, and available token and timing
counters. The run record is broader than a pass/fail bit: review
needs enough context to distinguish an OS compatibility defect
from a missing account, unavailable service, benchmark gap,
or non-OS agent planning error.

D. Root-Cause Review and Repair
A failed dynamic run is only a symptom. SkillBridge joins

performs root-cause review. Inspired by differential testing,
the Review Agent compares task outcomes and artifacts

STAGE: Spatio-Temporal Augmented Graph
Expansion for Weakly Supervised Cross-Tweet
Event Causality Discovery
Hieu Minh Duong∗, Todd Gary†, Eugene Levin†, and Long Nguyen∗
∗University of Louisville, Louisville, Kentucky, USA
{hieu.duong, l.nguyen}@louisville.edu
†Meharry Medical College, Nashville, Tennessee, USA
{tpgary, elevin}@mmc.edu
Abstract—Causal relations in disaster-related social media of-
ten span independent posts, making cross-tweet causal discovery
difficult to supervise and model at scale. We propose STAGE, a
framework that separates scalable cross-tweet weak-supervision
construction from spatio-temporal relational learning over event
occurrences. Starting from local causal seeds, STAGE retrieves
semantically related event occurrences across tweets and uses
a causal scorer to construct weakly labeled cross-tweet pairs.
These pairs supervise a multi-head Graph Attention Network
over semantically enriched event representations and a spatio-
temporal context graph. We evaluate STAGE on California
Wildfire and Hurricane Harvey using human-gold cross-tweet
test sets and 15 baselines. Compared with local-only supervision,
the constructed cross-tweet supervision improves STAGE AUPRC
by 0.340 on Wildfire and 0.107 on Hurricane. STAGE achieves
in-domain AUROC of 0.885 on Wildfire and 0.710 on Hurricane.
Cross-disaster experiments reveal asymmetric transfer, highlight-
ing sensitivity to dataset-specific spatio-temporal shifts. These
results demonstrate the value of scalable cross-tweet supervision
combined with relational event modeling for causal learning
across fragmented disaster reports.
Keywords—Natural Language Processing, Causal Discovery,
Spatio-Temporal Graphs, Weak Supervision
I. INTRODUCTION
Discovering causal relationships in social media presents
a fundamental challenge, particularly for understanding how
real-world events unfold and escalate during disasters. Tra-
ditional causal extraction methods are fundamentally limited
for uncovering causal chains in social media streams because
they operate on isolated text units. Sentence-level approaches
rely on explicit linguistic cues that are rare in informal tweets.
Neural and LLM-based models capture semantic associations
but may conflate them with causation due to a lack of struc-
tural grounding [1]. Meanwhile, cross-document event linking
methods such as Zhao et al. [2] rely on richer document-level
context, while knowledge-augmented approaches may depend
on retrieved evidence [3] or structured event graphs [4],
making them difficult to apply directly to noisy, fragmented,
and high-volume disaster streams. Figure 1 illustrates this
cross-tweet setting, where a causal relation connects specific
event occurrences described in different tweets rather than the
tweets as whole units.

The core challenge is therefore to move beyond single-text
analysis and develop a method that can connect causal infor-
mation distributed across posts while exploiting the spatio-
temporal structure of an unfolding disaster. An effective
solution should not rely solely on explicit textual markers,
but should also exploit temporal, spatial, and semantic con-
text when reasoning about relations between specific events.
We introduce STAGE (Spatio-Temporal Augmented Graph
Expansion), a framework that combines scalable cross-tweet
weak supervision with spatio-temporal relational learning.
STAGE constructs weakly supervised cross-tweet event pairs
and models them through an event graph grounded in three
complementary signals: (1) temporal information that captures
temporal proximity and reporting context, (2) geographic
information that captures spatial relationships among events,
and (3) semantically enriched event representations that bridge
lexical variation across posts.
In this work, we use causal discovery in the task-specific
sense of identifying directed causal relations between real-
world event instances described across social media posts. The
prediction unit is an ordered pair of event occurrences, each
representing a specific event instance described in a particular
tweet. A cross-tweet pair therefore consists of two occurrences
drawn from different tweets, and the prediction determines
whether one causes the other and, if so, in which direction.
This formulation enables event-level reasoning rather than
treating entire tweets as causal units.
The framework separates cross-tweet supervision construc-
