tion from spatio-temporal graph learning. Cross-tweet candi-
date pairs are first generated from semantic neighborhoods
defined by event triggers and arguments, without temporal
or spatial constraints, providing the basis for scalable weak
supervision. STAGE then combines semantic, temporal, and
spatial information, applies semantic expansion across related
event descriptions, and constructs a graph whose contextual
edges capture spatio-temporal relationships. A Graph Atten-
tion Network propagates information over this structure before
predicting causal existence and direction for ordered event
pairs. Thus, temporal and spatial information contribute to
causal learning without determining which pairs enter the
candidate pool. Our contributions are threefold:
• We propose STAGE, a framework for cross-tweet causal
discovery that separates scalable cross-tweet supervision
construction from spatio-temporal relational learning over
event occurrences.
• We introduce a scalable weak-supervision strategy for
cross-tweet causal learning in which candidate event
pairs are constructed from trigger-and-argument semantic
neighborhoods and assigned weak causal labels by a fixed
causal scorer, while human-gold pairs are withheld from
model training and reserved for evaluation.
• We instantiate the relational learner with a spatio-
temporal event graph and multi-head GAT, and evaluate
the framework under in-domain weak supervision, local-
to-cross-tweet generalization, cross-disaster transfer, and
component ablations.
II. RELATED WORK
A. Causal Discovery in Natural Language
Early causal extraction relied on lexical and syntactic
patterns [5], semantic parsing for causal questions [6], and
feature-based classifiers using dependency and lexical cues
[7], with resources such as SemEval-2010 Task 8 support-
ing supervised relation learning [8]. Later work incorporated
external structure and data augmentation: LSIN uses induced
descriptive and relational graphs [9], while knowledge-guided
augmentation [10] and prompt-based auxiliary objectives [11]
improve event causality identification. Furthermore, recent
methods increasingly model richer event interactions. SemDI
formulates event causality as semantic dependency inquiry
[12]; ICCL uses contrastive demonstrations [13]; iLIF iter-
atively constructs and exploits an event causality graph [14];
and GLM4ECI evaluates LLM-generated statements for direc-
tional event causality identification [15]. More recently, Su et
al. propose a suggest–verify–revise framework with structural
refinement for document-level causality [16]. These methods
advance event causality identification, but primarily operate
within sentences or coherent documents, whereas disaster
tweets are short, noisy, and may distribute causal evidence
across independent posts.
B. Weak Supervision for Event and Relation Learning
Weak supervision reduces annotation cost by deriving labels
from indirect signals. Snorkel combines heuristic labeling
functions through a probabilistic label model [17], while dis-
tant supervision aligns textual mentions with knowledge-base
relations to construct large weakly labeled corpora [18]. For
event relations, Yao et al. derive weak temporal labels from or-
dering regularities [19], while Mirroshandel and Ghassem-Sani
infer temporal relations using bootstrapping and expectation
maximization over clustered documents [20]. Nath et al. study
cross-document event coreference using semantic transfer and
multimodal ensembles [21], and a recent survey identifies
weak supervision as an important direction for scalable event
causality learning [22]. These studies demonstrate the value of
indirect supervision, but semantic or temporal correspondence
does not by itself establish causality. Therefore, STAGE uses
semantic correspondence to construct candidate cross-tweet
event pairs and introduces temporal and spatial information
separately during relational learning.
C. Cross-Document and Cross-Tweet Event Linking
Cross-document event research links event mentions across
texts using semantic and structural evidence. Min et al. com-
bine local and global reasoning for cross-document event
coreference [23], while Xu et al. use heterogeneous graph
interactions for document-level event extraction [24]. Yao et
al. introduce argument-centric causal intervention to reduce
spurious reliance on lexical similarity in cross-document event
coreference [25]. Multi-document event extraction has also
combined large and small language models to connect het-
erogeneous documents [26].
In social-media settings, Dong et al. analyze cascading
disaster effects using textual and geospatial signals [27], while
Lenti et al. model probable causal drivers of climate activism
from Reddit and external events [28]. However, these settings
differ from explicit event-occurrence-level causal prediction
across independent tweets. Our prior CaST framework studies
spatio-temporal event causality within tweets and identifies
cross-tweet causal reasoning as an open direction due to the
absence of cross-tweet annotations [29]. STAGE addresses
this gap by constructing cross-tweet supervision and learning
relations between event occurrences distributed across posts.
D. Knowledge-Augmented and LLM-Based Causal Reasoning
External knowledge and language models provide additional
mechanisms for causal reasoning. Knowledge-graph methods
exploit graph structure to infer missing relations [30], while
retrieval-augmented generation introduces retrieved evidence
into pretrained language models [3]. Kiciman et al. show that
LLMs can perform several forms of causal reasoning [31],
although evaluation on causal extraction tasks continues to
reveal limitations in complex real-world text [32].
Structural guidance can improve such reasoning. Long et
al. use language models as imperfect experts for causal dis-
covery [33], while Roy et al. use Causal Event Graphs to
support language-based spatio-temporal reasoning [4]. SERE
retrieves structurally relevant demonstrations for LLM-based
event causality identification [34], and Zhao et al. introduce
potential-outcome and actual-causality grounding to mitigate

The Stability Gap in
Continual Reinforcement Learning
Sebastian Pusch, Matthia Sabatelli and Gido M. van de Ven
Department of Artificial Intelligence, University of Groningen
Groningen, The Netherlands
Abstract.
Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) aims to enable agents
to adapt to changing tasks while preserving previously acquired capabili-
ties. Evaluation often relies on final aggregate metrics that can hide tem-
porary performance degradation during adaptation. This work introduces
a simple CRL benchmark that varies observation representations while pre-
serving environment dynamics and rewards, supporting proof-of-concept
demonstrations, inexpensive experimentation, and easily reproducible san-
ity checks.
Using this benchmark, we demonstrate the stability gap in
CRL: a substantial drop in prior-task performance after the introduction
of new tasks, followed by partial or complete recovery. This pattern occurs
despite the agent having complete access to past tasks.
1
Introduction
Sequential training can severely degrade neural network performance on previ-
ously learned tasks, a phenomenon known as catastrophic forgetting [1]. Con-
tinual learning (CL) aims to adapt to changing tasks while retaining acquired
knowledge. Evaluation typically relies on task-boundary measures such as final
performance, forgetting, and backward transfer, which can overlook temporary
failures during adaptation. In supervised CL, De Lange et al. [2] identified the
stability gap: a sharp drop in previous-task performance after a task transition,
followed by partial or complete recovery. This gap can occur even when all past-
task data remain available [3], a setting referred to as incremental joint-training.
Whether a stability gap also occurs in continual reinforcement learning (CRL)
remains unexplored. Existing CRL evaluations emphasize final performance, or
they look at transfer and forgetting measured only at task boundaries or after
convergence [4]. Temporary performance drops may therefore have remained
hidden. To isolate these dynamics, we introduce a lightweight transformed-state
benchmark inspired by Permuted-MNIST [5]. Tasks share environment dynam-
ics, rewards, and action spaces but apply different orthogonal transformations
to the state representation. We compare value-based and actor-critic algorithms
across discrete and continuous action spaces, using frequent evaluation of past
tasks to test whether a stability gap arises in CRL.
2
Benchmark
We construct a controlled CRL benchmark in a way that can be applied to any
environment with vector observations.1 Each task shares the same dynamics,

Figure 1 presents the general benchmark construction (a) and its instanti-
ation on CartPole (b), which we use alongside InvertedPendulum for discrete
and continuous control, respectively. Both environments have four-dimensional
states (d = 4), and we construct three tasks (N = 3) for each. We verified
that with our experimental settings, all algorithms we consider can learn all

sequential fine-tuning. Panel (c) illustrates this for SAC-D.
3
Experimental setup
Algorithms
We evaluate DQN [6] and discrete SAC (SAC-D) [7] on CartPole,
and DDPG [8] and SAC [9] on InvertedPendulum. All algorithms are trained
and evaluated under an incremental joint-training paradigm: tasks are intro-
duced sequentially, and the agent continues to train on all tasks encountered
thus far. Unlike with methods that rely on limited replay or other approxima-
tions of prior-task experience, the agent thus retains full access to all past tasks,
making any stability gap especially notable. For all algorithms, we maintain a
separate replay buffer for each task and sample equal proportions of transitions
from these buffers for each update. At each task transition, we reset the replay
buffers and optimizer states while retaining the learned network parameters.
Then, we collect 1,000 transitions from each encountered task before resuming
network updates. We evaluate performance on all tasks every 15 environment
steps during the first 30,000 steps of each task and every 250 steps thereafter.
Performance on a task at a given timestep is measured as the mean return over
15 episodes.
For all experiments, we use the Adam optimizer, networks with two fully-
connected hidden layers of 256 units each, a batch size of 128, and a discount
factor γ = 0.99. We tune the learning rate separately for each algorithm, select-
ing the configuration with the highest mean return across all tasks at the end of
training, averaged over 10 seeds. Tuning consists of an initial logarithmic sweep
followed by up to three additional values near the best-performing region. The
selected learning rates are 10−4 for DQN, 3×10−4 for DDPG and SAC, and 10−3
for SAC-D. We then run the experiments with the selected learning rates on 50
new seeds. Regarding the exploration hyperparameters, for DQN we follow [6]
and employ an ϵ-greedy policy with an annealing schedule. In our experiments, ϵ
decreases from 1.0 to 0.05 over the first 10% of timesteps, after which it remains
constant. When it comes to SAC and SAC-D, we use automatic temperature
tuning as proposed in [10, 7], with target entropies of −da and 0.98 log |A|, re-
spectively. Here, da denotes the dimensionality of the continuous action space,
and |A| denotes the number of discrete actions.
Linear Interpolation

Results
All four algorithms exhibit a sharp, substantial drop in previous-task perfor-
mance after at least one task transition, followed by partial or complete recov-

Control experiments confirm that this pattern persists when
optimizer states and replay buffers are retained across task transitions, when
exploration parameters are reset at task transitions, and when returns are ag-
gregated across seeds using the interquartile rather than the arithmetic mean.

to those at the checkpoints, even though training shows pronounced transient

Conclusion
We demonstrate the existence of the stability gap in CRL: previous-task per-
formance can drop sharply following a task transition, even under incremental
joint-training. Consistent with prior work on unstable optimization trajectories
in supervised CL [11, 3], our finding shows that even an objective that jointly
incorporates all tasks encountered thus far is not, by itself, sufficient to main-
tain stable performance throughout training. The optimization trajectory also
matters.
This motivates future work on CRL methods that change the way
optimization is done, particularly during the updates following task transitions,
when the stability gap may emerge.
Additionally, we propose a simple benchmark for CRL in which tasks vary
only in their observation representations, while rewards and environment dynam-
ics remain fixed. Although this design does not capture the full range of task
changes encountered in CRL, its simplicity serves three purposes: (i) it supports
proof-of-principle demonstrations, as in this study; (ii) it provides a standard-
ized, inexpensive playground for initial iterations on new CRL methods; and
(iii) it offers an easily reproducible sanity check for new algorithms.

TwinLab-Bench: Evaluating AI Scientists
in Agentic Twins of Real Labs
Yang Wan1, Linchao Zhu∗1
1Zhejiang University
∗Corresponding author
 Project: https://twinlab-bench.github.io/
Abstract
AI agents are increasingly expected to act as AI scientists, which requires three increasingly open
abilities: carrying out a given computational workflow correctly, choosing the next measurements
from a given design space, and designing their own experiments. Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate
the first two abilities, in a terminal or in a closed loop that selects from predefined candidates.
Evaluating the third ability requires reliably executing an experiment that an agent designs, with
readings grounded in a real laboratory. We introduce TwinLab-Bench, which evaluates AI scientists
on self-designed experiments in 52 tasks from laboratories in the physical sciences, the life sciences,
and engineering. The benchmark supports more than 100 experimental action types, and the agent’s
report is scored by comparison with a hidden answer taken from real laboratory records. Each task
has its own TwinLab agent, an agent that serves as the environment and executes the experiments
that the tested agent designs, reading the raw materials of the laboratory and calling calculators
that are built from its records. Compared with a language model that sees only the task description,
the TwinLab agent almost eliminates readings that deviate from the real records and inconsistent
answers to a repeated request, and closed-book probes control for answers recalled from memory. We
find that these tasks remain hard for frontier models: the strongest, Claude Fable 5.2, averages a
score of only 45.0, and we conduct an empirical study of where it fails.

Introduction
AI is advancing science in more and more of the
research process, and the AI scientists that the
field now builds need three increasingly open
abilities (Gottweis et al., 2026; Ghareeb et al.,
2026). The first is carrying out a given compu-
tational workflow correctly, such as analyzing
a given dataset (Mitchener et al., 2025a; Chen
et al., 2025; Terminal-Bench-Science Team,
2026; Mitchener et al., 2025b). The second is
choosing the next measurements from a given

design space (Duan et al., 2025; Gandhi et al., 2025; Roohani et al., 2025; Wen & Liu, 2026). The third is
designing their own experiments, and automated laboratories are starting to run such experiments (Boiko
et al., 2023; Szymanski et al., 2023). The third ability is the hardest of the three, but few science benchmarks
test it.
Existing science benchmarks test whether an agent can recall knowledge (Laurent et al., 2024), work on given
data (Mitchener et al., 2025a), or search a given space (Duan et al., 2025), as figure 2(a) shows. These abilities
work on data that the task provides in advance, but the third ability, designing their own experiments, needs
an environment that returns real data for new experiments. Figure 2(b) orders these environments by how
close they come to a real laboratory. Fixed results support no new experiments. A simulator (Jansen et al.,
2024; Duan et al., 2025; Gandhi et al., 2025) or a replay (Roohani et al., 2025; Wen & Liu, 2026) returns
new results, which come only from written rules or from recorded experiments. The goal of the experiment
environment is a real laboratory, which returns real results for any experiment that an agent designs (Bran
et al., 2024; Tom et al., 2024). We move one step from simulators and replays toward this goal with a twin of
each real laboratory, and we build TwinLab-Bench on these twins.
A twin of a real laboratory has to return real readings for as wide a range of experiments as an agent may
design. Language models already play patients (Schmidgall et al., 2024) and users (Barres et al., 2025) in
agent evaluations, but they fall short when they play a laboratory. Given only the task description, a language
model has no basis for the numbers of this laboratory, and given the raw materials, it can still copy wrong

We propose the TwinLab agent to build a reliable
twin of each laboratory. The TwinLab agent is a
coding agent that serves as the environment, so it
uses tools to read the files of the laboratory and runs
programs on them. Each task has its own TwinLab
agent with the materials and the calculators of its
laboratory. For an experiment that the laboratory
performed, the TwinLab agent reads the raw materi-
als, often combining several records, and returns the
result that the laboratory recorded. For an exper-
iment that the laboratory did not perform, it runs
calculators, which are deterministic programs that
we write from the data of this laboratory, for exam-
ple by fitting a physical model to its measurements.
Each calculator extends the record only to nearby
settings, with a basis that we write down when we
build the task.
TwinLab-Bench consists of 52 tasks, and each task comes from the records of a real laboratory in the physical
sciences, the life sciences, or engineering. The tested agent, which we call the actor agent, receives the
notebooks, raw data, and interim conclusions that the laboratory had at one point of its work, requests
the experiments that it designs within a budget, and submits a report that we score by comparing it with
what the laboratory later found, as figure 3 shows for four tasks. Our experiments show three properties
of TwinLab-Bench.
(1) The score comes from the experiments, because without budget Opus 5.5 and
DeepSeek-flash pass none of the tasks. (2) The actor agent’s conclusion follows the true state of the laboratory
that it measures. (3) The twin predicts hidden recorded readings within a median error of 2.47% even outside
the recorded conditions, and it blocks all 9 attempts to exploit it.
On TwinLab-Bench, the strongest frontier model averages a score of only 45.0 out of 100. Opus 5.5 still loses
part of the score on decisions that it states in full before the run, and its most common decision error is
accepting a mechanism without a discriminating test.
Our contributions are threefold.
• TwinLab-Bench, a public benchmark that tests whether an agent can design its own experiments, built on
the records of real laboratories and released with its evaluation code.
• The twin of a real laboratory, made of a TwinLab agent, the raw records of the laboratory, and the
calculators that we write from these records.
• An empirical study that locates where frontier models lose score and which experimental abilities they lack.
2
Related Work
Benchmarks without new physical experiments. Most science benchmarks give the agent no laboratory for
running new experiments. Question sets test whether an agent recalls scientific knowledge (Rein et al., 2024;
Phan et al., 2026; Laurent et al., 2024, 2026) or how to change a published protocol (Sivakumar et al., 2026),
and data-analysis benchmarks hand the agent a dataset and a question (Chen et al., 2025; Mitchener et al.,
2025a). AI scientist systems such as Kosmos also automate this kind of analysis at scale (Mitchener et al.,
2025b). Terminal benchmarks (Merrill et al., 2026; Terminal-Bench-Science Team, 2026) and benchmarks of
automated machine-learning research (Chan et al., 2025; Wijk et al., 2024; Starace et al., 2025) let the agent

run new experiments, but these experiments are programs inside a computer. End-to-end systems already
write and review such research (Lu et al., 2026), and end-to-end research benchmarks run the agent on the
given data and code of a study (Xu et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2026). Benchmarks of these
four kinds cannot evaluate how an agent chooses physical experiments that cost time and consume scarce
materials.
Readings from simulation, replay, or a language model. Interactive environments answer the experimental
requests of an agent with readings from a simulation, a replay, or a language model. Text worlds and
equation models (Wang et al., 2022; Jansen et al., 2024; Duan et al., 2025; Gandhi et al., 2025; Rowstron
& Chadha, 2026) answer any request, and their readings follow the rules written into the environment.
EmbodiedLab (Gao et al., 2026) tests how agents operate instruments in a physics simulator on textbook
experiments, while TwinLab-Bench leaves out physical operation and tests experimental decisions on problems
from real laboratories. Replays of published measurements (Roohani et al., 2025; Wen & Liu, 2026) return
real readings, and the agent picks its next experiment among the recorded conditions. Learned world models
predict the outcome of an action (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018), and language models serve as such world models
for planning (Hao et al., 2023) and for text-based games (Wang et al., 2024). Language models also play
patients (Schmidgall et al., 2024) and users (Yao et al., 2025; Barres et al., 2025) in agent evaluations, and
they answer from general knowledge; evaluations of such simulators find that their feedback departs from real
environments and users (Liu et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026b). AgentBeats (Berkeley RDI, 2026) packages
a benchmark as an agent that sets the tasks, the environment, and the scoring for the agent under test.
TwinLab-Bench splits this role between a TwinLab agent that serves as the environment and a judge agent that
scores the report. These environments do not answer the experiments that an agent composes with readings
from the records of a real laboratory, so they cannot evaluate how an agent designs its own experiments.

3.1
Tasks
Task sources. We select the tasks from about 375 candidate sources, and each task is built on a real research
record, such as an open laboratory notebook, raw instrument exports, a paper with its supplementary material,
or a public dataset, as figure 3 shows. Most tasks are adapted from the records of one laboratory. In some of
them the laboratory itself met the problem and later solved it, and in the others the problem lies in the real
data of the laboratory. Their answers come from a later notebook entry, a publication, a correction, or a
reanalysis of the raw data. The few remaining tasks are grounded syntheses, as Appendix I describes.
Task construction. We choose a cutoff point in the record, which is a date or a clearly defined state of
the laboratory, and split the record into two parts. The data, protocols, and interim conclusions that the
laboratory had before the cutoff point are handed to the actor agent. What the source records show after the
cutoff point is given only to the TwinLab agent and to the judge agent, and we call this part the hidden truth.
An expert route taken from the record averages a score of 97.8 out of 100 when we replay it in the twin of
each task. Every task also passes a coverage review, which confirms that the standard experiments of the field
can be simulated, and Appendix I lists all tasks and their construction.
Task forms. The tasks take three forms. Most tasks are claim reviews, which ask the actor agent to decide
which conclusions of the laboratory hold and how to test them. Troubleshooting tasks ask for the cause of a
clear failure and a working procedure, and research-campaign tasks ask for an executable procedure toward a
research goal. Some tasks offer no experiments, and the actor agent analyzes only the raw records that the

FASTROVERVLA: FAST VISION-LANGUAGE-ACTION
EXECUTION FOR OFF-ROAD AUTONOMOUS DRIVING
Changtao Zhao1, Yingxue Guan1, Li Wang1,2,∗, Shijie Zhao3,
Yuhang Zhang3, Shengkai Zhang4, Qing Wang5, Ziying Song5,†
1School of Mechanical Engineering, Beijing Institute of Technology, Beijing 100081, China
2Chongqing Innovation Center, Beijing Institute of Technology, Chongqing 401120, China
3School of Mechanical Engineering and Intelligent Equipment, Chang’an University
4School of Electronic and Information Engineering, Beijing Jiaotong University
5School of Artificial Intelligence (School of Software), Yanshan University
∗Corresponding author: Li Wang (wangli_bit@bit.edu.cn)
†Project lead: Ziying Song
ABSTRACT
Off-road vision-language-action (VLA) models generate scene-conditioned plans, but frequent trajec-
tory updates can repeatedly invoke expensive multimodal inference. Reusing a prediction reduces
this demand while leaving its commands exposed to changes in vehicle motion. FastRoverVLA
addresses this mismatch by decoupling visual plan generation from motion-conditioned execution.
Its training-free interface maintains decoded plans between visual predictions. A speed–curvature
action buffer is aligned with measured motion at each update, integrated into a local trajectory, and
advanced by consuming the current action. The corrected remainder is written back to the buffer,
preserving motion corrections across successive updates. A bounded refresh rule normalizes speed
and curvature variations within a newly decoded plan and assigns a short or long reuse budget
according to the resulting plan-roughness score. The interface requires neither backbone features
nor an additional learned driving policy. Over a 3 s horizon, independent real-request evaluation
achieves average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) of 0.328/0.596 m
on ORAD-3D and 0.266/0.526 m on RELLIS-3D, reducing FDE by 18.0% and 36.7% at request
rates of 6.0% and 4.8%, respectively. These runs retain lower errors across four backbones and both
datasets and reduce Qwen3-VL request-processing cost by factors of 16.6 and 20.8 under serial replay,
while mechanism and motion-only controls identify persistent state correction as the main source of
the observed accuracy benefit. The source code and evaluation materials are publicly available at
https://github.com/ADEPT-ORG/FastRoverVLA.
Keywords Artificial Intelligence, Computer vision, Autonomous driving, off-road trajectory planning, recurrent
execution
1
Introduction
Off-road driving requires motion decisions in environments without fixed lane structure, where surface conditions,
visibility, and feasible routes can change within a journey [1–3]. Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect
visual observations and language-based reasoning to numerical actions or trajectories [4–7]. Their outputs must also
accommodate the vehicle motion that follows prediction. A scene-conditioned plan can remain relevant across several
trajectory updates, while its speed and curvature commands require continued adjustment to the measured state.
Coupling every trajectory update to a new prediction repeatedly invokes multimodal inference [8–11]. Efficient encoders
and inference pipelines reduce the cost of individual calls [12,13], while slow–fast systems combine expensive reasoning
with a faster planning path [6,14]. Action-chunk methods address continuity between predicted sequences through
temporal aggregation, constrained generation, or learned correction [15–17]. These developments leave a specific
execution problem at the decoded-action interface: retaining the motion corrections accumulated after a plan has been
generated, without another learned planner or access to the generative sampler.
A retained plan must account for two changes during reuse: commands are consumed as time advances, and measured
motion changes the state to which the remaining commands must be matched. Direct replay advances the sequence
without resolving this state mismatch. Realigning the original plan at each update incorporates current motion but

actions and the motion corrections retained in them (Fig. 1).
FastRoverVLA decouples visual plan generation from recurrent execution around a frozen vision-language model
(VLM) and a deterministic action adapter. The name combines “Fast” for reduced VLM inference demand, “Rover”
for off-road driving, and “VLA” for vision-language-action planning. Visual inference refreshes the action buffer,
while recurrent execution maintains motion-conditioned trajectories between refreshes. Each update aligns the retained
speed–curvature actions with measured ego motion, generates a local trajectory, consumes the current action, and writes
the corrected remainder back to the buffer. A bounded rule uses variation within the refreshed plan to assign its reuse
budget. The resulting interface separates visual plan generation from motion-conditioned trajectory updates without
modifying the backbone or training an auxiliary driving policy.
Evaluation on ORAD-3D [3] and RELLIS-3D [1] separates three questions: whether decoded plans benefit from
persistent correction, whether visual initialization adds information beyond motion history, and whether sparse refresh
reduces measured inference demand. Shared-prediction controls isolate the maintenance operations; motion-only
and matched-image controls examine initialization. Backbone transfer, disjoint-sequence evaluation, and a past-only
heading check test the stability of the execution effect. Independent real-request runs measure its computational
consequence under serial replay.
The main contributions are:
• FastRoverVLA introduces an action-level execution interface for off-road VLA planning. Maintaining a
decoded plan as a recurrent state separates visual prediction from motion adaptation, allowing local trajectory
updates between model requests without an additional learned driving policy.
• The interface combines state alignment, action consumption, and correction write-back to preserve measured-
motion updates in the retained plan. A bounded refresh rule assigns reuse budgets from normalized action
variation, controlling inference demand through the same decoded-action representation.
• Controlled replay and independent real-request evaluation cover two datasets and four backbones. In real-
request evaluation, Qwen3-VL reduces 3 s FDE by 18.0% and 36.7% relative to every-update execution, while
serial request-processing cost falls by factors of 16.6 and 20.8, respectively.
2
Related Work
2.1
Vision-Language-Action Planning
Robotic VLA models such as RT-2 and OpenVLA [18,19] connect vision-language representations to actions. Driving
planners UniAD and VAD [20,21] emphasize planning-oriented scene representations. LMDrive, DriveLM, DriveVLM,
and EMMA [4–7] incorporate language instructions, structured understanding, or hierarchical reasoning. AutoVLA,
2
FastRoverVLA
ORION, ReCogDrive, and SimLingo [8, 9, 11, 22] connect language or reasoning with numerical driving actions;
DriveMoE [10] specializes vision and action experts. ColaVLA, WAM-Flow, and Latent-CoT-Drive [23–25] explore
latent reasoning, parallel decoding, or world-model-based planning. Complementary work improves the information and
constraints used for planning: FocalAD [26] models decision-critical local interactions, and GraphBEV++ [27] aligns
camera–LiDAR features. GraphWorld and DriveFuture [28,29] use latent world-state or future-aware conditioning.
DriveWorld-VLA [30] integrates world modeling with VLA planning, while MindDrive [31] evaluates world-model-
generated candidates with a VLM. GuideFlow [32] constrains flow matching, and DIVER [33] applies reward-guided
diffusion to multimodal planning. These advances improve scene-conditioned plan generation, whereas decoded actions
must also remain consistent with the changing execution state. FastRoverVLA addresses this execution stage through
deterministic measured-motion updates to speed–curvature actions. Its frozen planner supplies new visual plans, while a
retained action buffer preserves corrections between predictions, separating plan maintenance from encoder, reasoning,
and decoding design.
2.2
Terrain-Aware Off-Road Planning
Off-road planning couples geometric clearance with physical traversability. BADGR and STEP [34,35] learn navi-
gation affordances or combine stochastic traversability with risk-aware planning. How Does It Feel?, V-STRONG,
and RoadRunner [36–38] learn terrain costs or traversability from visual, proprioceptive, or LiDAR observations.
TRAIL [39] supports joint path and speed optimization through continuous terrain representations; terrain-adaptive
MPC [40] incorporates vehicle–terrain interactions and online parameter estimates. OFF-EMMA [41] uses visual
prompts and self-consistent reasoning for off-road trajectory generation. RELLIS-3D, ORFD, and ORAD-3D [1–3]
provide evaluation settings with rugged terrain and varied visibility. These approaches determine where and how to
move, but measured vehicle motion can require adjustment without changing the selected route or terrain assessment.
FastRoverVLA complements terrain interpretation by updating decoded actions between visual predictions, maintaining
motion consistency without requiring new terrain labels or traversability estimates at every update.
2.3
Efficient and State-Consistent Execution
Temporal planners exploit cross-frame information: MomAD [42] carries trajectory and perception momentum,
MomADv2 [43] retains command-consistent memory and uses flow refinement, and MomWorld [44] propagates latent
future scene states. Efficiency methods improve visual encoding or model size [12,45], reduce reasoning [8,46,47], or
accelerate action generation and inference [13,48]. Slow–fast systems combine infrequent VLM planning with trajectory
refinement [6], learn adaptive activation and fusion [14], or schedule query, cache, and drop decisions [49]. These
mechanisms determine when guidance arrives, while action maintenance determines how decoded sequences evolve
during execution. ACT [15] ensembles overlapping predictions, and Diffusion Policy [50] generates receding-horizon
action sequences. RTC [16] asynchronously generates chunks while preserving committed actions and constraining
overlap through inpainting; REMAC [17] learns within-chunk corrections and preserves prefixes across chunks.
FastRoverVLA instead deterministically aligns a retained speed–curvature sequence with measured motion and writes
corrections back for subsequent updates. Its bounded refresh rule admits new visual plans, while intermediate updates
require neither sampler access nor an auxiliary learned planner. The focus is persistent state correction after decoding,
distinct from learned temporal planning, query scheduling, or new-chunk generation.
3
Methodology
FastRoverVLA maintains a speed–curvature action buffer between visual predictions (Fig. 2). A refresh initializes the
buffer from the current image, ego motion, and instruction. Subsequent updates align its actions with measured motion
and retain the corrected remainder until the reuse budget expires. A plan denotes the action sequence, and a trajectory
denotes the positions obtained by integrating that sequence.

4
Experiments
The experiments test whether motion-conditioned plan maintenance can reduce visual inference while preserving
trajectory accuracy in off-road driving. Comparisons across planning systems and frozen backbones establish overall
performance, while controlled ablations distinguish the effects of state correction, visual initialization, and refresh
scheduling. Cross-sequence tests and independent model requests then examine whether the accuracy and inference
savings persist beyond the shared-prediction replay.
4.1
Experimental Setup

and 650 frames from three sequences, respectively. Each frame anchors a motion history and its future ground-truth (GT)

timestamps and supporting history/future indices. Evaluation follows logged-state open-loop replay: measured motion

each backbone, all policies share the same evaluation frames and per-update processing. Every-update execution

Physics-Informed Feature Representations and Pretrained Tabular
Foundation Models for Generalizable Melt Pool Geometry Prediction
Rafid Enayet1, Imtiaz Ahmed2, and Md Habibor Rahman∗1
1University of South Carolina, Columbia, SC 29208, USA
2West Virginia University, Morgantown, WV 26506, USA
Abstract
Developing generalizable, data-efficient machine learning (ML) models for advanced manufacturing
processes remains a fundamental challenge in smart manufacturing systems, particularly when experimental
datasets are small and process-property relationships must transfer across materials and operating conditions.
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) exemplifies this challenge, where build quality is highly sensitive to
the coupled effects of laser processing conditions and thermophysical properties of the material, and
the melt pool geometry – encompassing width and depth – together with the prevailing melting mode
(conduction, transition, or keyhole) are critical determinants of process stability, defect formation, and
part integrity. Conventional data-driven models predict these responses directly from dimensional
process parameters, sometimes augmented by material properties. However, such representations encode
laser-material interaction physics only implicitly, limiting their ability to generalize across materials or
process conditions without retraining. This study investigates whether physics-informed dimensionless
parameters – specifically normalized enthalpy and Peclet number, derived by combining laser processing
conditions with material thermophysical properties – provide a more transferable and effective feature
representation than raw process parameters for data-driven melt pool modeling. A systematic benchmark
is conducted across three material systems (316L stainless steel, IN625, and IN718 nickel-based alloys)
and their combination, evaluating seven models spanning classical ML algorithms – Gaussian Process,
Support Vector Machine, Random Forest, and XGBoost – and three pretrained Tabular Foundation
Models – TabPFN, TabDPT, and TabICLv2 – for both regression of melt pool depth and width and
classification of melting modes. The results demonstrate that dimensionless representations improve
predictive performance across most evaluated conditions, with the most substantial improvement observed
in cross-material melt pool depth prediction, where the model achieved an 𝑅2 of 0.96. Moreover, the study
finds that pretrained tabular foundation models consistently outperform classical ML baselines under
both feature representations, demonstrating that synthetic pretraining priors transfer effectively to the
structured, physics-governed relationships of LPBF. These findings establish that combining physically
meaningful dimensionless representations with modern pretrained tabular models offers a principled
strategy for building generalizable process-property models under limited experimental data, with direct
implications for accelerating process-window identification and reducing reliance on material-specific
trial-and-error experimentation in laser-based manufacturing systems.
Keywords: Foundation Models; Machine Learning; Additive Manufacturing; LPBF; Melt Pool Prediction
∗Corresponding author: habiborrahman@sc.edu
1
arXiv:2611.26235v1  [cs.AI]  19 Nov 2026
1
Introduction
Integrating machine learning (ML) into advanced manufacturing systems has emerged as a transformative
approach to accelerate product design and process development, enable real-time quality control, and reduce
reliance on costly trial-and-error experimentation [22, 35, 40]. Within this paradigm, a persistent challenge
is building models that generalize reliably beyond the specific material system and operating conditions on
which they were trained [7, 39]. This is a major concern in industrial practice: data-driven process-property
models calibrated for one alloy must typically be retrained from scratch when the material changes, an
expensive requirement given the cost and time associated with manufacturing experiments [38]. The root
cause of this fragility lies not in data scarcity alone – though that is endemic to advanced manufacturing
processes – but also in the choice of input representation. Process parameters such as laser power, scan speed,
and beam diameter carry implicit dependencies on material thermophysical properties that the model must
reconstruct from limited observations, often failing to generalize across material systems [18, 25]. Addressing
this challenge in a principled way requires both rethinking how domain physics are encoded into the feature
space and evaluating whether emerging data-efficient modeling architectures can provide the inductive biases
needed to offset the structural disadvantage of small, material-specific datasets.

of melt pool cross sections ranging from conduction to keyholing mode [43].
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is one of the most industrially significant and methodologically
demanding contexts for examining these questions. As an established metal additive manufacturing (AM)
process that can produce geometrically complex, near-net-shape components from a broad range of engineering
alloys, LPBF has attracted considerable attention for aerospace, biomedical, and energy applications [3, 34].
The quality and structural integrity of LPBF-built parts depend critically on the melt pool geometry formed
during laser scanning, as shown in Figure 1. The melt pool width and depth govern inter-layer bonding,
determine the onset of defect modes – lack-of-fusion porosity, balling, and keyhole collapse – and establish
the thermal gradients responsible for microstructure evolution [21, 41]. Beyond geometry, identifying the
prevailing melting mode (conduction, transition, or keyhole) is essential for defining stable processing
windows, since each regime is associated with distinct defect mechanisms and part-quality outcomes [13, 14].
Despite this importance, systematically characterizing melt pool behavior experimentally across the full
process parameter space is prohibitively time-intensive and requires extensive single-track campaigns for each
new material. [32]. The combination of small experimental datasets, complex multi-physics interactions,
and the need to transfer knowledge across materials makes LPBF an ideal and demanding benchmark for
evaluating generalization strategies in manufacturing ML systems.
Recognizing the limitations of purely physics-based analytical models, researchers have applied a broad
2
range of ML methods to melt pool geometry prediction in LPBF [26]. Early efforts employed Gaussian Process
(GP), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), and multivariate adaptive regression splines
using laser power, scan speed, and beam diameter as inputs, demonstrating that data-driven models can surpass
the Rosenthal analytical solution in accuracy [1, 24, 31]. Subsequent works broadened input sets to include
layer thickness, powder characteristics, and material properties – density, specific heat, thermal conductivity,
and melting temperature – with multi-material studies across 316L stainless steel, Ti-6Al-4V, and AlSi10Mg
showing accuracy gains when physics-inspired material descriptors were incorporated alongside process
parameters [25, 30]. The MeltpoolNet framework showed that adding absorptivity coefficients to process
parameters improved cross-dataset prediction of melt pool width and depth [1], while physics-informed deep
learning approaches have been applied to molten pool morphology prediction in directed energy deposition
[4]. For melting regime classification, ML models trained on process parameters have been used to distinguish
conduction, transition, and keyhole conditions, enabling data-driven process map construction [33]. Faegh et
al. (2025) identified physics-based feature engineering as one of three principal strategies for incorporating
domain knowledge into ML models – alongside physics-constrained architectures and physics-based loss
functions – and highlighted cross-material generalization as a central open challenge [10]. Despite this
progress, a consistent limitation remains: models trained on a single material generalize poorly to other alloys,
and studies conducted on a systematic, controlled benchmark comparing physics-informed dimensionless
input representations against raw process parameters across multiple ML algorithms and material systems
with rigorous grouped evaluation remain largely underexplored [19, 38].
To address the generalization challenge, the authors utilized the dimensionless numbers derived from first
principles of laser-material thermal interaction. The normalized enthalpy, introduced by Hann et al. (2011)
[12] and evaluated by King et al. (2015) [20] specifically for LPBF conditions, encodes the ratio of deposited
laser energy density to the enthalpy of melting – a material-agnostic quantity that absorbs the thermophysical
properties of the alloy directly into the feature. The Peclet number represents the ratio of convective to
conductive heat transport, characterizing the relative influence of scan speed and thermal diffusivity on melt
pool shape [8]. Critically, both numbers are computable from independently measurable quantities – laser
parameters and material properties – without any melt pool observations, preserving their role as genuine
predictive inputs rather than response-derived descriptors. Analytical studies have demonstrated that plotting
normalized melt pool depth and width against normalized enthalpy and Peclet number collapses data from
diverse alloys onto common trend lines – an outcome that requires individual calibration curves for each
material when raw process parameters are used instead [12, 26, 27]. A dimensionless scaling law for melt
pool width in LPBF further demonstrated that dimensional analysis-based representations can characterize
melt pool width in a beam-size-independent, material-spanning manner [45]. Physics-informed ML for LPBF
wall thickness prediction has also shown that models incorporating dimensionless numbers achieve lower
prediction error than purely data-driven counterparts while requiring fewer training points [28]. Nevertheless,
no prior work has used normalized enthalpy Δ𝐻/ℎs and the Peclet number 𝑃𝑒as direct ML feature inputs in a
systematic, multi-model, multi-material regression and classification benchmark to the best of the authors’
knowledge – a gap that limits the field’s understanding of when and why physics-informed representations
outperform raw process parameters in practical data-limited scenarios.
Alongside input representation, the data scarcity inherent to LPBF experiments motivates evaluation
of ML architectures that are specifically designed to perform well with limited training data [9]. Gaussian
process regression has been the conventional choice in this setting because of its probabilistic predictions
and sample efficiency, and it has been applied to melt pool geometry and process property prediction across
several LPBF systems [19, 26]. However, GPR performance depends critically on kernel selection and
hyperparameter optimization, and isotropic kernels may inadequately capture the anisotropic sensitivity of
melt pool dimensions to inputs spanning very different physical scales – a limitation that becomes pronounced
when training datasets are small and input ranges are wide [36]. A fundamentally different approach has
recently emerged in the form of pretrained Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs), which learn a general prior
3
over tabular regression and classification tasks by training on millions of datasets, then apply that on new
datasets without dataset-specific gradient updates [16]. TabPFN demonstrated that this in-context learning
paradigm outperforms all prior ML methods – including gradient-boosted trees tuned for four hours – on
datasets with up to 10,000 samples, making accurate predictions in seconds [16]. Related models TabDPT
[23] and TabICLv2 [29] extend this paradigm with improved scalability and architectural refinement. Given
the importance of data-efficient learning strategies for advanced manufacturing, pretrained TFMs represent
a concrete recent realization of this direction. While TFMs have begun to appear in materials discovery
and biomedical applications [17], their application to LPBF process-property modeling with data-scarce
environments has been limited, leaving open the question of whether synthetic pretraining priors transfer
effectively to the structured, physics-governed relationships of laser-based manufacturing processes.
This study addresses three connected gaps in the literature. First, while dimensionless numbers have
been applied analytically to melt pool scaling, they have not been evaluated as direct ML input features in a
controlled, multi-model benchmark. Second, the generalization advantage of physics-informed dimensionless
representations relative to dimensional process parameters has not been quantified empirically across multiple
material systems with rigorous, group-based data partitioning that prevents process-condition leakage. Third,
pretrained tabular foundation models have not been evaluated on LPBF process-property prediction, leaving
their transferability to manufacturing contexts unestablished. The specific contributions of this work are the
following:
1. A systematic benchmark comparing dimensionless inputs against process parameters and material
properties for melt pool and depth and width regression and melting mode classification across three
material systems – 316L stainless steel, IN625, and IN718 alloys – and their combination;
2. Evaluation of pretrained tabular foundation models (TabPFN, TabDPT, TabICLv2) alongside established
baselines (GPR, SVR, random forest, XGBoost) for LPBF melt pool prediction;
3. Empirical demonstration that dimensionless inputs substantially improve cross-material generalization,
providing quantitative ML-level evidence for a hypothesis previously supported only by analytical
scaling arguments; and
4. Identification of the physical boundary conditions under which dimensionless representations outperform
process parameters and material properties as inputs – and the cases where they do not – with mechanistic
interpretation.
Together, these findings offer a principled, evidence-based framework for designing generalizable, data-
efficient ML systems for LPBF process-window identification and qualification, with direct implications for
smart manufacturing systems operating across diverse materials and processing conditions. The remainder of
this paper discusses the methodology, including the datasets and prediction models, in Section 2, presents the
findings in Section 3, and concludes in Section 4.
2
Methodology
Two experimental datasets were harmonized into a common schema, and two distinct feature representations
were constructed: one using dimensional process parameters with material properties, and one using physics-
informed dimensionless parameters. When dimensional inputs were used, the regression targets were the
directly measured melt pool depth (𝑑) and width (𝑤) in physical units. When dimensionless inputs were
used, both the inputs and the targets were kept dimensionless for internal consistency, where the melt pool
depth and width were normalized by the laser spot radius to formulate normalized melt pool depth (𝑑∗) and
width (𝑤∗) respectively. This choice ensures that the model operates entirely within a dimensionless space,

which is a fundamental requirement of dimensional analysis: a physically consistent model expressed in
dimensionless variables must have both its inputs and outputs in dimensionless form, so that the functional
relationship is independent of the system of units and can be generalized across process conditions and
materials [12, 26]. Seven machine learning models spanning tree ensembles, kernel methods, and pretrained
tabular foundation models were evaluated under both representations for regression of melt pool width and
depth and for classification of the prevailing melt pool mode. Figure 2 summarizes the workflow.
2.1
Experimental Data
Two single-track experimental datasets were used. The first was reported by Hofmann et al. (2026) [14],
providing 316L stainless steel single-track measurements under systematic variation of laser power, scan
speed, spot diameter, and powder layer thickness. A working subset of 210 observations with no layer
thickness was used. The authors referred to the dataset as ‘316L’ later in this study. The second dataset
was collected by Weaver et al. (2023) [43] and published by NIST (National Institute of Standards and
Technology) from laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) experiments on bare plates of IN625 and IN718 alloys,
conducted across two LPBF platforms while systematically varying laser power, scan speed, and spot diameter.
Tracks were cross-sectioned, metallographically prepared, and chemically etched, after which melt pool width
and depth were measured from optical micrographs, where width is the maximum lateral extent and depth is
the maximum subsurface dimension of the solidified track. All 250 observations were used after applying
complete-case filtering across all required features and targets. The second dataset has been referred to as
‘IN625+IN718’. Concatenation of both working datasets yielded a combined dataset of 460 observations used
for the multi-material benchmark, which has been referred to as the ‘Combined’ dataset.
Units were harmonized before modeling and numeric conversion was applied to all required predictors
and targets. The paired regression benchmark enforced complete cases across both feature representations
and both geometric targets, ensuring that all models were evaluated on an identical set of observations. Spot
diameter was verified to be strictly positive, and normalized geometric targets were audited against their
corresponding physical measurements to confirm consistency. Repeat measurements at the same process
condition were retained as independent observations and assigned to the same process-condition group for
splitting purposes.
5
2.2
Featurization
Two feature representations were constructed and compared systematically across all models. The following
subsections discuss the features and labeling of the melt pool modes.

Sightline: Calibrated Data-Flow Summaries for
LLM-Integrated Applications
ZIHAO XU, UNSW Sydney, Australia and Southern Cross University, Australia
YUEKANG LI, UNSW Sydney, Australia
RUITAO FENG, Southern Cross University, Australia
HAIFENG SHEN, Southern Cross University, Australia
Programs increasingly call large language models (LLMs), filling prompt placeholders with program values
and consuming the output. Such a call crosses the boundary between natural language and programming
language (NL/PL). To follow data across it, an analysis needs a data-flow summary of which placeholders
the output uses, but no code describes what the model does. Analyses of these LLM-integrated applications
therefore taint every output with every input, creating spurious flows, or ask a second model to label each call,
which is costly. We prove, and mechanize in Lean 4, that a placeholder flows to the output of a transformer, to
first order, only through the attention that reads it (no reading, no flow), and that a faint reading or sensitivity
cannot certify that a placeholder does not flow. Unlike reading, the log-probability gradients and Fisher signals
of existing methods vanish on confident outputs, and single-span removal fails on duplicated content. Our tool,
Sightline, reads a recorded call in one forward pass, learns from labels which reads are uses, and calibrates
the pruning to miss at most a chosen fraction 𝛼of true flows, on average over call sites, when deployment is
exchangeable with calibration. On 2,103 unseen repository families and four models, Sightline is the most
accurate summary against the seven closest methods and a hidden-state probe. Calibrated at 𝛼= 1%, it misses
about 1% of true flows and prunes 43.9–65.6% of spurious flows, 1.6 to 2.6 times as many as the best baseline,
and still 43.8–60.1% when calibrated on another collection. Through an open surrogate, it reads models treated
as closed about as accurately as they read themselves, without their labels. In the information-flow control of
an LLM agent, it removes about half of the labels from inputs that do not flow.
CCS Concepts: • Theory of computation →Program analysis; • Security and privacy →Information
flow control; • Computing methodologies →Natural language processing.
Additional Key Words and Phrases: data-flow summaries, taint analysis, information-flow control, LLM-
integrated applications, attention, conformal prediction, mechanized proofs
1
Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) are now components of ordinary programs. A program calls a model
through an API at an LLM call site. It fills the placeholders of a prompt template with run-time
values, such as a user query or a retrieved document, and then consumes the output, for example
by storing it, sending it, or passing it to a tool. Programs built this way are called LLM-integrated
applications [42, 71].
Program analyses that follow data, such as taint tracking, slicing and information-flow con-
trol [52], must know at every call which inputs reach the output. When the code of a callee is
unavailable or too costly to analyze, they rely on a data-flow summary of it, as taint analyses do for
framework code [5, 6]. LLM-integrated applications need these analyses as much as conventional
software, because they pass untrusted input into prompts and act on the outputs, which has led to
injection and code-execution vulnerabilities [32, 42].
However, no code describes what happens inside an LLM call. The model transforms the prompt
in its weights rather than in program text, a crossing that prior work calls the boundary between
natural language and programming language (NL/PL) [71]. For each call, an analysis needs to

University, Australia, ruitao.feng@scu.edu.au; Haifeng Shen, Southern Cross University, Australia, haifeng.shen@scu.edu.au.

2
Zihao Xu, Yuekang Li, Ruitao Feng, and Haifeng Shen

Fig. 1. A call site from the new batch. The query (A) decides the confident output Q, and the delimiter (B) is
read but unused. Each cell shows the verdict of a method at its threshold, green if right and red if wrong.
know which placeholders the output uses, and no summary answers this question. In practice, on
call sites from 2,103 open-source repository families (repositories with their forks), 12–14% of the
placeholders do not reach the output, because the model ignores them, lacks the context to use
them, or refuses. Every such placeholder that an analysis assumes to flow spreads a label to data
that the output never used (label creep [52]). A useful summary must miss few true flows, must
prune the placeholders that do not flow, must be cheap enough to compute for every call, and must
state how often it may miss. This missing summary at the NL/PL boundary is the gap we address.
Figure 1 shows the problem on one call site with two placeholders. The output is a short decision
that the first placeholder determines and that the model emits with near certainty. The model also
reads the second placeholder, but its output does not use it. A correct summary thus reports the
first placeholder and prunes the second.
Existing techniques do not produce this summary. Program analyses either treat the output of
an LLM call as opaque, which truncates every flow through it, or taint it as a whole, as a taint
source [32] or by merging the labels of all inputs into it [14]. Conservative merge never misses a
flow, but labels then spread to data that the output never used. Black-box per-call labeling asks LLM
labelers to read the prompt and the output [71]. It judges each call directly, but one labeler costs
about 10k tokens and 13 seconds per placeholder (§5.5) and runs offline. White-box methods use the
computation of the model instead. Context attribution removes parts of the input, as ContextCite
and TracLLM do [13, 65], sometimes fitting a linear model to the effects, or reads attention, as
AttnTrace and AT2 do [12, 64]. White-box information-flow control bounds the flow with gradients
and Fisher information, as Geometric Information Flow (GIF) does [55], or screens dependencies
with attention, as RTBAS does [74]. Gradient and Fisher sensitivity carry a factor 1 −𝑝, where 𝑝is
the probability of the output token, so they vanish when the model is confident, and removal fails
when content is duplicated (§3.4). Confident decisions are common at call sites, since for one in
five outputs of Qwen3-8B [72] the model leaves less than 1% of probability to other tokens. On the
call of Figure 1, the gradient- and Fisher-based methods miss the first placeholder for this reason.
The attention-based methods avoid this factor but report the second placeholder, because a model
can read an input without using it. None of them comes with a miss guarantee per call site.
Building such a summary is hard for three reasons. ❶The callee has no code. Program analyses
derive summaries from the code of the callee, so at an LLM call they fall back to truncation or
conservative merge. It is unclear which evidence about the computation of a model can bound
the flow at all. ❷Models read more than they use. Like the delimiter of Figure 1, a placeholder can
be read but not used. Reporting every placeholder that the model reads thus also reports many
placeholders that do not flow. Measuring how much the output changes when a placeholder is
Sightline: Calibrated Data-Flow Summaries for LLM-Integrated Applications
3
removed or perturbed reports fewer, but it misses flows when the model is confident or when its
content is duplicated. ❸A faint signal can hide a true flow. In code, an analysis prunes an input safely
when no dependence connects it to the result. At an LLM call, attention reads every placeholder at
least a little, and a placeholder that is read only faintly, or whose removal changes nothing, can
still decide the output. Any summary that prunes may therefore miss a flow, and an analysis can
rely on it only if the summary also states how often it misses.
To address these challenges, we present Sightline, which summarizes a recorded call by reading
the attention of the model. Although the model has no program text, its computation has a fixed
structure, and that structure decides where information can travel. In a transformer, a placeholder
flows to the output, to first order, only through the attention that reads it, hence no reading,
no flow. For ❶, we prove this property for every layer, in the way taint propagates along dependence
edges in code, with attention as the edges. This tells which evidence to read, and Sightline records in
one forward pass how much the output reads each placeholder, while the guarantee of the summary
comes from calibration. For ❷, we prove that a head can read a placeholder heavily without using
it, so Sightline learns from labeled calls which reads are uses, with a pruning readout over the
reading of every attention head. For ❸, we prove that faint reading, faint gradients and removal
without effect can each occur on a placeholder that decides the output, so Sightline states how
often it misses. It sets its threshold from labeled call sites of other repositories with conformal
prediction [19, 62], so that, when new call sites come from the same distribution as these, a true
flow of a randomly drawn call site is missed with probability at most a chosen 𝛼, such as 1%.
We fit Sightline on an old batch of 8,105 placeholder–output pairs and evaluate it on 19,672
new pairs from 2,103 repository families that training never saw, on four open models including a
Mamba2 hybrid [15]. Sightline is the most accurate summary on all four models (81.1–86.7 Macro-F1,
the mean F1 score of the two classes), significantly so on the three transformers, where it leads
the best of the seven closest methods by 4.5 to 6.2 points. Given the same labels and call features
(lengths and placeholder count), all seven baselines and a hidden-state probe stay significantly
behind, so the precision comes from the readout on reading. It holds up where the existing signals
fail, with an area under the ROC curve (AUROC) of 99.0–100.0 on duplicated content, against
54.0–68.8 for leave-one-out removal (LOO), and a lead of 19 to 34 points over the Fisher signal
on the most confident outputs. Calibrated to miss about one true flow in a hundred, it prunes
43.9–65.6% of the spurious flows that conservative merge reports, 1.6 to 2.6 times as many as the
best baseline, and still 43.8–60.1% when calibrated on the old batch. It costs one forward pass
per call (0.12–0.20 s), and since reading needs only the recorded tokens, an open surrogate reads
models treated as closed about as accurately as they read themselves, without their labels. In the
information-flow control of an LLM agent, it removes about half of the label creep and lets no
attack call through an integrity policy, which blocks side-effecting calls that carry untrusted labels.
Together, these results show that reading carries program analyses across the NL/PL boundary
with a summary that is accurate, calibrated per call site, and cheap enough for every call.
In summary, we make the following contributions.
• What one forward pass can certify about flow through an LLM call. Relative to the
information-flow semantics of GIF, we show that attention routes soundly over-approximate
local flow (§2.2) through an LLM call. We also show that a faint reading or sensitivity cannot
certify that a placeholder does not flow. All thirteen results are mechanized in Lean 4 [46] (§3.6),
and §5 confirms their predictions.
• Calibrated data-flow summaries across the NL/PL boundary. To the best of our knowledge,
Sightline is the first white-box data-flow summary for LLM calls whose miss rate is calibrated
4
Zihao Xu, Yuekang Li, Ruitao Feng, and Haifeng Shen
per call site, and through an open surrogate it reads models treated as closed about as accurately
as they read themselves, without their labels (§4).
• Evidence on unseen programs. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first evaluation
of white-box flow signals on real LLM call sites of open-source programs. On repositories
that training never saw and on four models, Sightline is more accurate than the seven closest
methods, holds up where the theory predicts that the existing signals fail, and helps a downstream
information-flow client (§5).
2
Background
This section defines the call sites we summarize, what a correct summary is, and the transformer
notation that the theory in §3 uses.
2.1
LLM Call Sites
An LLM call site is a program point that sends messages to a language model. The messages come
from a prompt template, and the template contains placeholders that the program fills with run-time
values, such as a user query, a retrieved document, or a conversation history. Each call renders the
template into a prompt, which the model reads as tokens 𝑥1, . . . ,𝑥𝑃. Each placeholder then occupies
a span of positions 𝑆⊆{1, . . . , 𝑃}, and the model produces the output tokens 𝑦1, . . . ,𝑦𝑛. We call
the pair of the rendered prompt and the output that the model actually produced a recorded call.
A data-flow summary of the call tells the consuming analysis which placeholders the output
carries. Runtime taint tracking and information-flow control propagate labels through the call with
it [14, 16], and offline analyses use it to follow data through recorded calls. Because whether the
model uses a placeholder depends on the values and on what the model generates, we compute
the summary for each recorded call, as dynamic taint tracking does for each execution of ordinary
code.
2.2
Problem Formalization
To judge a summary, we need a notion of flow that matches what the consuming analysis cares
about, namely whether the output carries the content of a placeholder or a decision derived from it.
We adopt the notion of reach of prior black-box summaries of LLM calls [71].
Definition 2.1 (Reach). A placeholder 𝑆of a recorded call reaches the output 𝑦if 𝑦visibly reflects
the content of 𝑆, namely if𝑦copies or transforms that content (for example, by rewriting, translating,
or summarizing it) or if the content determines a decision, a selection, a computed value, the format,
or a quantitative property of 𝑦. Otherwise, 𝑆does not reach 𝑦. This is the case when 𝑦shows no
observable use of 𝑆, for instance because the model ignored it, lacked the context or the capability
to use it, or refused the request.
Reach is a semantic property of one recorded call, and it is what black-box per-call labeling decides
when LLM labelers read the prompt, the placeholder and the output [71]. We write 𝑟(𝑆) ∈{0, 1}
for the reference label, and we call a placeholder with 𝑟(𝑆) = 1 a true flow and one with 𝑟(𝑆) = 0 a
non-flow. The theory in §3 also uses local flow, the sensitivity of the output to small perturbations
of the placeholder and the mutual information that such perturbations carry to the next token [55].
The two notions differ, since a confident decision can reach the output while its local flow is almost
zero (§3.4), and we state for each result which notion it concerns. For an analysis that propagates
labels, reach is the notion that matters, because a decision derived from a placeholder must carry
its label even when the model was certain.
Definition 2.2 (Summary). A summary of a recorded call reports a subset of its placeholders
as flowing to the output and prunes the others. A miss is a true flow that the summary prunes.
Sightline: Calibrated Data-Flow Summaries for LLM-Integrated Applications
5
A spurious flow is a non-flow that the summary reports. The pruning ratio of a summary is the
fraction of non-flows that it prunes.
The two summaries that analyses use today sit at the extremes of this definition. Conservative
merge reports every placeholder, so it never misses a flow but has a pruning ratio of zero. Truncation
reports nothing, so it prunes every non-flow and misses every true flow. A useful summary must
prune non-flows while missing few true flows (challenges ❶and ❷).
A summary that decides from evidence will sometimes err (challenge ❸), so we ask for a bound
on its misses. The bound should hold at the granularity at which an analysis consumes summaries,
namely the call site.
Definition 2.3 (𝛼-calibration per call site). A summary is 𝛼-calibrated per call site if, for a call site
drawn from the deployment distribution and a true flow drawn uniformly from the true flows of its
recorded calls, the probability that the summary misses the flow is at most 𝛼, where the probability
also ranges over the data on which the summary was calibrated.
We state the bound per call site rather than per pair because the true flows of one call site share a
template and tend to be missed together, so a rate averaged over pairs can be dominated by a few
call sites.
Scope. We summarize one recorded call at a time, which is what runtime monitors and offline
analyses consume, and these analyses compose the summaries along the program and across the
steps of an agent.
2.3
Attention in Transformers
The theory in §3 relies on one structural fact of the transformer [61], so we fix the notation
here for the decoder-only models we study. To read a recorded call, we run the model once on
[𝑥1, . . . ,𝑥𝑃,𝑦1, . . . ,𝑦𝑛−1] with teacher forcing, so every position sees exactly the tokens of the
recorded call. The output-predicting positions 𝑄= {𝑃, . . . , 𝑃+ 𝑛−1} are the positions whose next
token is an output token. A model with 𝐿layers of 𝐻heads keeps a residual stream ℎℓ

Preprint
REGIONAGENT: TWO-STAGE PREFERENCE
OPTIMIZATION FOR REGIONAL IMAGE RESTORATION
Weiyu Zhou1
Jiacong Tang1
Tao Hu1
Axi Niu1
Jinqiu Sun1
Peng Wu1
Wei Dong2
Qingsen Yan1,*
1 Northwestern Polytechnical University
2 Xi’an University of Architecture and Technology
* Corresponding author.
ABSTRACT
Images under non-uniform coupled degradations require diverse restoration ca-
pabilities for different degraded regions. Existing methods employ globally uni-
form operations, potentially overlooking regional differences and causing incom-
plete restoration or even damage to image content. Moreover, a degraded region
may require successive restoration actions, and earlier actions may alter residual
degradation characteristics or introduce artifacts, potentially hindering subsequent
restoration. To address these challenges, we propose RegionAgent, an adaptive
restoration framework that trains a Vision-Language Model (VLM) through two-
stage preference learning to generate a region-specific restoration action at each
iteration. Specifically, we first train the VLM to select an action suited to the
current region through step-level Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), using
preferences derived from immediate restoration feedback to supervise only the
differing component in each action pair. To account for the effects of current
actions on subsequent restoration, we then apply trajectory-level DPO, using pref-
erences derived from complete trajectory scores to supervise the sole differing
action in each trajectory pair. Furthermore, as conventional image-pair datasets
do not directly provide preferences over regional restoration decisions, we con-
struct a regional restoration preference dataset comprising 10K action pairs and
20K trajectory pairs for two-stage VLM training. Experiments across multiple
datasets demonstrate strong restoration performance under both mixed and sin-
gle degradations. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of two-stage
preference learning in improving restoration quality.
1
INTRODUCTION
Image restoration aims to recover clean images from observations affected by degradations such as
blur, haze, rain, or low light. Deep learning-based methods have advanced this task through spe-
cialized models for individual degradation types (Ren et al., 2021; Zamir et al., 2021; Yan et al.,
2025) and all-in-one networks for multiple restoration tasks (Li et al., 2022; Potlapalli et al., 2023)
(Figure 1(a)). However, real-world images can contain coupled degradations that vary in type and
severity across regions. Applying uniform restoration operations to the whole image may overlook
regional differences and damage unaffected content. Within an affected region, removing one degra-
dation can leave others unresolved, requiring successive restoration operations. The effectiveness of
later operations then depends on how earlier ones change the image (Chen et al., 2024; Zhu et al.,
2025; 2026).
To make restoration more adaptive, instruction-guided methods allow users to specify restoration
goals (Conde et al., 2024) and target regions (Liu et al., 2025). Restoration agents automate tool
selection and revise image-level plans using restoration feedback (Chen et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025;
Lin et al., 2025) (Figure 1(b)). As an alternative to sequential tool invocation, Beyond Sequential
Tools learns image-level expert weights through preference optimization for single-pass restoration
(Xiong et al., 2026). However, these approaches focus on user-specified regions or image-level
decisions, rather than learning to select regions and configure their restoration autonomously.
1
