Figure 1: Conceptual comparison of restoration paradigms. (a) Task-specific and all-in-one models
restore the whole image. (b) Image-level agents select tools using iterative feedback. (c) RegionA-
gent selects regions and expert configurations for adaptive local refinement.
We therefore introduce RegionAgent, an adaptive restoration framework in which a Vision-Language
Model (VLM) selects regions and configures their restoration from the current image state (Fig-
ure 1(c)). At each iteration, a localization network predicts a heatmap of residual degradations and
uses it to propose candidate regions (Figure 2). The VLM then selects one of these regions and
specifies its restoration configuration based on the current image.
Each refinement action specifies a target region, weights for combining restoration experts, and
the strength of the local correction. We train the VLM through two stages of Direct Preference
Optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2023): step-level DPO followed by trajectory-level DPO. Step-
level DPO learns which configuration choices suit the current region by comparing their immediate
restoration effects, applying the preference loss only to the component that differs between paired
actions. Trajectory-level DPO then trains the VLM to account for the effects of current choices
on subsequent restoration. It uses complete-trajectory scores to supervise the sole differing action
between paired trajectories. Since conventional image-pair datasets lack preferences over regional
restoration decisions, we construct a dataset of action and trajectory preference pairs for two-stage
training.
Executing these actions produces restored crops whose direct writeback can introduce boundary
artifacts and structural discontinuities. Our Degradation- and Structure-Guided Residual Fusion
Module (DSRF) integrates the difference between each restored crop and its current counterpart as a
residual correction. Spatial masks regulate this correction according to restoration needs and image
structure, while Laplacian pyramid blending promotes smooth transitions across scales. The VLM
then generates its next action from the fused image.
Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate strong restoration performance under both mixed
and single degradations. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:
• We introduce RegionAgent, an adaptive restoration framework whose VLM generates re-
gional actions from the current image state to address non-uniform coupled degradations.
2
Preprint
• We develop two-stage DPO: step-level DPO adapts restoration configurations to current
regional needs, while trajectory-level DPO uses complete-trajectory feedback to guide cur-
rent restoration actions.
• We construct a regional restoration preference dataset comprising 10K action pairs and 20K
trajectory pairs. It includes controlled comparisons that vary a single configuration com-
ponent or a single trajectory action, providing targeted supervision for regional restoration
decisions beyond conventional degraded–clean image pairs.
2
RELATED WORK
Adaptive Image Restoration.
All-in-one models condition shared restoration networks on degra-
dation representations and learned prompts (Li et al., 2022; Potlapalli et al., 2023), while vision-
language approaches incorporate visual-textual features for degradation diagnosis and restoration
guidance (Luo et al., 2024; Ai et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2024). Instruction-guided methods extend
this control to user-defined goals (Conde et al., 2024) and region-specific restoration (Liu et al.,
2025). Restoration agents automate tool selection and sequencing (Yu et al., 2018), using multi-
modal diagnosis and quality feedback to revise their plans (Chen et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025; Lin
et al., 2025). Recent systems integrate restoration with assessment (Chen et al., 2026) or couple
planners with LoRA-based tools (Li et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026), while OPERA jointly optimizes
planning and tool execution using restoration rewards (Zhu et al., 2026). As an alternative to sequen-
tial execution, Beyond Sequential Tools learns image-level expert weights for single-pass restoration
through a DPO-trained allocation branch (Xiong et al., 2026). RegionAgent instead selects regions
and configures their restoration autonomously from the updated image at each iteration.
Preference Optimization.
Preference optimization applies to restoration outputs and decision
policies. DSPO aligns super-resolution generators with semantic-instance preferences (Cai et al.,
2025), whereas TTPO guides diffusion sampling with test-time preferences without model training
(Li et al., 2026b). Within policy outputs, fine-grained objectives weight tokens or target local-
ized differences (Christopoulou et al., 2025; Hasan et al., 2025), and DiTTo separates preference
supervision across degradation reasoning, restoration order, and tool calls (Choi & Oh, 2026). For
sequential decisions, Hierarchical Preference Learning combines trajectory-, step-, and action-group
objectives (Gao et al., 2026), while Critical Step Optimization uses successful policy continuations
to verify alternative actions for action-level DPO (Li et al., 2026c). Our refinement pairs vary one
configuration component from a shared image state; trajectory pairs vary one action while fixing the
region and other actions. The losses target the differing component and full action, respectively.

PROBLEM FORMULATION

from the current restoration state. A refinement action specifies a region rt from the candidate region

values. The process returns the current image upon STOP or at the iteration limit Tmax.

two-stage DPO for learning these decisions (Secs. 3.4–3.5).

We train a lightweight U-Net Localizer fω, with parameters ω, to localize residual degradations. To

inputs or intermediate restoration results and their corresponding clean images.

SUPERVISION CONSTRUCTION
Conventional image-pair datasets provide degraded images and clean targets, but do not directly
provide preferences over regional restoration decisions. We therefore construct a regional restoration
preference dataset containing action and trajectory pairs to support two-stage DPO.
To control search cost, we first restore each newly proposed region with one expert at a time, with
every trial starting from the same current image. We fuse each restored crop at the allowed fusion
strengths and score the resulting images using the one-step utility Ustep, which measures restoration
gains relative to the current image after accounting for penalties. We rank regions by their highest
utility across these trials and expand expert configurations in the top two regions.

no-reference metrics (MANIQA, MUSIQ, and CLIP-IQA). We normalize and clip each metric gain
separately. For full-reference metrics, we equally combine full-image and selected-region gains,
whereas no-reference metrics use full-image gains. We average the resulting gains across the six
metrics and subtract penalties for halo degradation, boundary artifacts, action cost, repeated states,
and degradation below Base.

Budget Internalization: Fixed-Budget RLVR Trades
Test-Time Scaling for In-Budget Accuracy
Ilia Zavidnyi 1,2, Alexander Kovrigin 1, Arina Puchkova 1, Kirill Gelvan 1, Sergey Titov 1
1JetBrains Research • 2Czech Technical University in Prague • ilia@zavidnyi.com
Reasoning models often become more accurate when they can generate longer answers at test time.
This behavior is known as test-time scaling. However, RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) usually
trains them with a fixed rollout cap. We find that this cap changes model behavior, not only training
cost. After training, models use few additional tokens beyond the training budget. They outperform
the base models near that budget, but their accuracy stops improving and falls below the base
model at larger budgets. The rollout cap thus becomes a learned constraint, that limits model’s
test-time scaling. We call this effect budget internalization. We observe it across Qwen3.5-4B,
Gemma4-E2B, and Nemotron-3-Nano-4B and two reasoning training tasks: mathematical reasoning
and diverse, procedurally generated problems. This effect also transfers from math training to
science and coding tasks. Training-objective level ablations on Qwen3.5-4B show that most changes
recover little test-time scaling. Stronger KL regularization and lower training-data truncation
preserve more scaling, but stronger KL reduces in-budget accuracy. Forcing an answer on truncated
training rollouts largely removes budget internalization, but also removes most of the in-budget
gain. SFT on artificially truncated traces reproduces budget internalization, whereas SFT on
naturally short traces does not, which shows that the effect is not specific to RL. This result links
budget internalization to length-censored post-training rather than to an RL-specific objective term.
Thus, a rollout cap does not only control training cost. It can trade low-budget gains for lower
performance when additional inference compute is available.

1 Introduction
One promise of reasoning models is that they can solve harder problems when given more tokens at
test time (Guo et al., 2025; Snell et al., 2025). This makes test-time compute a useful scaling axis: a
deployment can spend more compute when a problem is difficult or when higher accuracy is required.
Unlike test-time scaling, RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) usually does not let the model reason until it
emits an end-of-sequence token. Instead, training uses a fixed rollout cap, often below the length of the
model could otherwise utilize(Team et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025; He et al., 2025). This is usually done to
cut training costs, since it can scale quadratically with the sequence length (Aghajohari et al., 2026). The
resulting model is then often evaluated at only one budget, at or close to the training cap. This evaluation
shows whether training helps near that budget, but not whether the model can still benefit from more
compute. A model can look better than its base model at the training budget and become worse when
both receive a larger budget.
We show that this failure occurs after fixed-budget GRPO on two hard reasoning training tasks: competition
mathematics (AIME, DeepScaler Luo et al. (2025)) and diverse procedurally generated reasoning problems
(Reasoning Gym Stojanovski et al. (2025)). For Qwen3.5-4B trained with a 4k rollout cap, the model moves
from a large gain over the base model at the matching evaluation budget to a large deficit when given
more tokens (4K: +34.8 pp; 64K: −30.2 pp, averaged over three training seeds). Gemma4-E2B (Gemma
Team, 2026) and Nemotron-3-Nano-4B (NVIDIA, 2026) show the same saturation after math training,
and Reasoning Gym training reproduces it for all three models. A similar pattern also transfers from
math training to GPQA-Diamond (Rein et al., 2024) and LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2025). We call this
effect budget internalization: the training budget becomes part of the model’s learned behavior rather
than remaining only a limit on training cost.
Budget internalization changes how RLVR results should be interpreted. Accuracy measured only at the
training cap can hide a reversal in model ranking. Increasing the deployment budget may then fail to
recover the base model’s performance, even though the base model benefits from the same additional
compute. The training cap can therefore trade future test-time scaling for better performance at the
budget used during training.
Our goal is to investigate budget internalization and understand why it occurs. To do this, we measure
accuracy and output-length curves across model families, training caps, and reasoning benchmarks. We
then run training ablations to study which training choices affect above-budget scaling. This analysis
makes three contributions:
• We show that fixed-budget training hurts test-time scaling. Across Qwen, Gemma, and
Nemotron, AIME accuracy improves near the training cap but stops improving at larger budgets.
Across all six checkpoints, gains over the base model range from +11.7 to +46.7 pp at the training cap,
while deficits at the largest evaluation budget shown for each model range from −17.2 to −35.0 pp.
• The effects of fixed-budget RLVR transfer beyond the training task and can improve
efficiency. For Qwen’s 8k-trained checkpoint, the high-budget differences from the base model are
much smaller (GPQA, 64K: −2.2 pp; LCB-v6, 64K: −1.0 pp). At the same time, mean output length
falls compared to the base Qwen3.5-4B from 11.15k to 4.56k tokens on GPQA and from 38.32k to
8.31k on LiveCodeBench. Gemma and Nemotron show the same pattern of much shorter responses
with smaller accuracy differences on these tasks. Therefore, losing some test-time scaling is not always
harmful and can reduce inference cost while retaining similar accuracy.
• Our ablations reveal a persistent trade-off between in-budget gains and test-time scaling.
We examine objective variants, truncation handling, KL regularization, and SFT approaches. Scaling
remains impaired under alternative length normalization and overlength penalties, but improves when
truncation exposure is reduced or KL anchoring is strengthened. The scoring of truncated rollouts
strongly affects budget internalization, suggesting that the responses reinforced during training matter
more than any single GRPO objective term. SFT experiments support this interpretation: scaling
is retained with naturally completed trajectories, but deteriorates with artificially shortened ones.
We release all our trained checkpoints (including ablations) at https://huggingface.co/collections/JetBrains-Resea
rch/budget-internalization.
2
Despite these partial mitigations, no tested intervention combines the full in-budget improvement with
the base model’s high-budget performance.
Budget internalization is therefore neither always good nor always bad. It is harmful when a task requires
longer reasoning to solve harder problems, but useful when the same accuracy can be reached with fewer
tokens on tasks where the model tends to overthink. Evaluating only at the training cap cannot distinguish
these cases. We therefore recommend reporting accuracy and output length at several budgets, so that
the effect of fixed-budget training is clear before choosing a model for deployment.
2 How Fixed-Budget Training Changes Test-Time Scaling
We study Qwen3.5-4B, Gemma4-E2B, and NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-4B. We run GRPO on the Deep-
ScaleR math dataset with 4k and 8k rollouts cap for Qwen, and 1k and 2k caps for Gemma and Nemotron.
We additionally train Qwen with 4k cap and Gemma and Nemotron with 2k caps on Nemotron-RL-
ReasoningGym-v1 (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026), which contains 15,000 examples from 104 procedurally
generated and verifiable Reasoning Gym environments (Stojanovski et al., 2025). These runs use the
same training hyperparameters as the corresponding DeepScaleR runs. We choose these caps below the
budgets at which the base models usually complete their AIME responses, so base-model generations
are frequently truncated at every chosen cap; Appendix Table 12 reports the exact rates. We evaluate
the selected checkpoints on AIME 2024 and 2025. We then test whether the resulting behavior transfers
to out-of-domain benchmarks, GPQA-Diamond and LiveCodeBench v6. All runs use the NeMo RL
framework (NeMo RL); the reward verifies the final answer and assigns zero reward to rollouts that end
at the cap without one.
We run all evaluations with the Inspect AI framework (UK AI Security Institute, 2024) and report
avg@k, the accuracy averaged over k sampled generations per problem, with the evaluation budget as
the generated-token limit. For DeepScaleR/AIME, each model/cap condition uses seeds 42, 43, and 44,
evaluated at both its in-budget validation-selected checkpoint and final step 300 (Appendix I). Other
experiments retain the original single-seed checkpoints and base-model evaluations. Appendix A reports
the complete training and evaluation configuration.
2.1 Fixed-Budget Training Limits Test-Time Scaling

The behavior transfers from both training datasets to GPQA-Diamond, a graduate-level science benchmark,
and LiveCodeBench v6, a code-generation benchmark with hidden tests (Figure 3). The trained checkpoints
gain accuracy near their training budget and saturate while producing shorter responses, although the
high-budget damage is smaller than on AIME. On GPQA and LiveCodeBench, both Qwen checkpoints
preserve much more of the base model’s high-budget accuracy than on AIME (GPQA at 64k: 4k-trained:
−9.1 pp, 8k-trained: −2.2 pp; LCB-v6 at 64k: 4k-trained: −9.0 pp, 8k-trained: −1.0 pp). Gemma’s
1k-trained checkpoint follows the same pattern on GPQA (16K: −1.0 pp) and LiveCodeBench (16K: −8.2
pp). Its 2k-trained checkpoint also remains close to the base model on GPQA (16K: −1.3 pp) and reduces
the LiveCodeBench deficit (16K: −5.1 pp). Nemotron’s 1k-trained checkpoint exceeds the base model
on GPQA at high budget (64K: +1.0 pp) but not on LiveCodeBench (64K: −9.0 pp). Its 2k-trained
checkpoint strengthens the GPQA improvement (64K: +4.0 pp) and narrows the LiveCodeBench deficit
(64K: −4.2 pp). Reasoning Gym checkpoints follow the same pattern: Qwen remains below the base model
on GPQA (64K: −6.7 pp) and LiveCodeBench (64K: −3.8 pp), as does Gemma (GPQA, 16K: −4.4 pp;
LCB-v6, 16K: −4.6 pp), while Nemotron slightly exceeds the base model on GPQA (64K: +0.7 pp) but
not on LiveCodeBench (64K: −4.8 pp). Because these differences are smaller, Appendix G additionally
reports pass@3 curves for a more stable comparison. We hypothesize that these tasks often require less
extended reasoning, so the base model sometimes overreasons rather than making productive use of
additional tokens.

often overreasons until it reaches the cap and fails to produce a final answer. Table 2 shows that this is

Next, we apply the reverse intervention to the 4k-trained checkpoint to test whether its loss of test-time
scaling only reflects early stopping. We remove its end-of-thinking delimiter and final answer, append
Wait, and ask it to continue the same trace, repeating this intervention up to four times under a 64k
cap. Relative to ordinary decoding of the same checkpoint, forcing up lowers accuracy at the 4k training
budget (AIME, 4K: −36.1 pp; GPQA, 4K: −51.0 pp; LCB-v6, 4K: −5.1 pp) and produces the same or
only modestly higher accuracy at 64k (AIME, 64K: 0.0 pp; GPQA, 64K: +2.7 pp; LCB-v6, 64K: +5.0
pp), despite using 2.58–2.74k more tokens (Appendix C.2). Stating the budget explicitly in the prompt
offers no reliable alternative, as models not trained on such cues largely ignore them (Appendix B).
Budget forcing can therefore improve base-model accuracy at a matched total token allowance, while
making the trained model spend more tokens does not restore its test-time scaling. This suggests that
fixed-budget training genuinely compresses the reasoning needed to reach its answers rather than only
teaching the model to stop early. Appendix C.1 gives complete examples of both procedures, while
5

Nemotron.
2.4 Budget Internalization
Fixed-budget training therefore has three distinct effects: it can improve low-budget accuracy, make
reasoning more economical, and reduce how much the model benefits from additional inference compute.
We call the last effect budget internalization. A model internalizes its training budget when, above that
budget, its base model continues to use more tokens and improve with additional compute while the
trained model’s response length and accuracy largely saturate.
3 What Affects Budget Internalization?

FrontierOR Challenge White Paper 2026
Version 1.0, 20 November 2026
The FrontierOR Challenge: Agentic Algorithm Design for
Operations Research
Organizers
Hai Wang, Bretislav Hajek, Chonghe Jiang, Minwei Kong,
Ao Qu, Huatian Gong, Bo Dong
Cynthia Barnhart, Jinhua Zhao
frontieror.competition@gmail.com
Abstract
Operations research (OR) relies on algorithms that experts tailor to each problem: a new
routing, scheduling or network design problem can take weeks of specialist work before it
is solved well at scale. Large language model (LLM) agents now write, test and improve
code, but whether they can design algorithms that scale to realistic instances is open: in
the FrontierOR benchmark’s one-shot evaluation, the strongest model matches Gurobi,
with an objective within 1% of Gurobi’s and no slower, on only 39% of the large instances.
The FrontierOR Challenge asks teams to build agentic workflows that design, test, and
improve algorithms for many optimization problems at once. Stage 1 releases 60 of the
benchmark’s 180 audited problems, spanning six application categories and five formulation
types, in weekly rounds of 15; Stage 2 introduces new problems outside the benchmark,
with unseen instances. Two tracks are ranked separately: in the Main track we run the
submitted algorithms in a network-isolated sandbox with open-source dependencies only; in
the Self-hosted track teams solve the instances on their own machines, with any software,
within a timed window. Every solution is checked for feasibility, and a feasible solution
scores the ratio of its objective to a frozen known reference, averaged over hidden instances.
Keywords: Operations research, combinatorial optimization, LLM agents, automated
algorithm design, competition
1. Introduction
The FrontierOR Challenge1 asks teams to build agentic workflows that design, test, and
improve algorithms for optimization problems, instead of hand-tuning a single algorithm.
The main scientific question is the following: “Can an LLM agent design algorithms that are
feasible, good and fast on instances it has never seen, across many optimization problems
and under a fixed compute budget?”
Optimization problems span many categories, such as routing, scheduling and network
design. For each of them, the OR literature studies specialized algorithms: decompositions,
branch-and-price, problem-specific heuristics. General-purpose solvers help, but a correct
formulation often still requires a deep understanding of the domain. Within a one-hour time
limit, Gurobi does not reach optimality on 46% of the large FrontierOR instances (Kong et al.,
2026a). LLM-driven program search has started to change this. FunSearch (Romera-Paredes
et al., 2024) and AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025) found new constructions by evolving
1. https://frontieror-challenge.com
© 2026 H. Wang et al.
arXiv:2611.26171v1  [cs.AI]  19 Nov 2026
Wang et al.
programs, and EoH (Liu et al., 2024) and ReEvo (Ye et al., 2024) evolve heuristics for
combinatorial problems. In optimization modeling, AlphaOPT builds and refines a library of
reusable insights based on solver feedback to guide LLMs in formulating new problems (Kong
et al., 2026b). Benchmarks measure the gap that remains: CO-Bench (Sun et al., 2026),
HeuriGym (Chen et al., 2026), ALE-Bench (Imajuku et al., 2025) and FrontierOR (Kong
et al., 2026a) all find that agents trail expert algorithms and commercial solvers, and that
consistency across problems is the weakest point. In FrontierOR’s one-shot setting, a model
writes one program per problem from its statement, with a few self-debugging rounds on
execution errors. In the latest evaluation, the strongest model, Claude Fable 5, returns a
feasible solution within 1% of or better than Gurobi’s reference objective, in no more than
Gurobi’s wall-clock time, on 39% of the large instances across all 180 problems. Results in
this competition may differ, since the Main track allows only open-source libraries, whereas
in FrontierOR the generated algorithms could call Gurobi.
The competition captures a practical scenario: a practitioner faces a new decision problem
with a written statement, a data format, and a deadline, and needs an algorithm that works
on unseen instances. Each team receives the problem definitions, builds a pipeline that turns
each one into an algorithm, and is scored on hidden instances. The competition runs in two
stages: a qualification on 60 problems from the FrontierOR benchmark, released 15 per week,
and a final on new problems, and in two tracks: the Main track, where we run the submitted
algorithms under fixed compute with open-source dependencies, and the Self-hosted track,
where teams solve the instances on their own infrastructure with any software, including
commercial solvers.
We expect the competition to contribute (1) a public comparison of agentic algorithm
design methods under one protocol, with independent checkers and hidden instances; (2) ev-
idence for practitioners on whether an agent can replace weeks of expert work on a new
problem; (3) new problems and instances for the OR community, through a call for contri-
butions; and (4) released problems, checkers and descriptions of the top teams’ methods
after the competition.
2. Related Competitions
Earlier competitions at the intersection of machine learning and OR focused on one part
of the pipeline.
NL4Opt (Ramamonjison et al., 2022) asked for formulations of small
linear programs from text. ML4CO (Gasse et al., 2022) replaced heuristic components
inside a MIP solver on three datasets. The DIMACS Implementation Challenges2 and the
ROADEF/EURO Challenge3 pose one problem per edition to human algorithm designers,
as do the AtCoder Heuristic Contests,4 which ALE-Bench (Imajuku et al., 2025) later used
to evaluate AI systems.
To our knowledge, no earlier competition combines four features: one workflow must
cover many problems at once, so that generality is rewarded over tuning for a single problem;
on the Main track, the scored submission is algorithm code that the organizers run on
hidden instances under fixed compute, rather than a formulation or a set of solutions; every
2. http://dimacs.rutgers.edu/programs/challenge/
3. https://www.roadef.org/challenge/
4. https://atcoder.jp/
2
FrontierOR Challenge
solution passes an independent checker that recomputes the objective; and the final stage
tests transfer to problems outside the published benchmark. The Self-hosted track scores
uploaded solutions instead.
3. Competition Format
Teams
Participants enter through the competition portal as teams of one or more people.
Each person holds only one account and belong to only one team at a time. A team chooses
the Main or Self-hosted track when it is created. Registration and team formation close
at 23:59 EST (UTC-5) on 27 December 2026. Teams may change their track before this
deadline; afterward, their track is fixed for the competition.
Stage 1: Qualification
Stage 1 runs from 00:00 EST (UTC-5) on 4 January 2027 until
23:59 EST on 31 January 2027. Sixty problems are released in four weekly rounds of 15.
The rounds open at 00:00 EST on 4, 11, 18 and 25 January, respectively, and each remains
open for exactly seven days. A submission covers only the currently open round. Main-track
submissions must be accepted by the portal before the round closes; their evaluation may
finish afterward. Self-hosted uploads must meet the applicable instance, submission-window,
and round deadlines. Teams follow a public leaderboard that accumulates results across
rounds.
Main Track: Algorithm Design
Teams submit algorithm code, the scored submission,
which we run in a sandbox with no network, 2 vCPU and 4 GB of memory. Only open-source
dependencies are allowed. The overall champion comes from this track.
Self-hosted Track: Tool-Augmented Solving
Teams solve the instances on their own
machines, by any means, including commercial solvers, and upload solutions within a timed
window. The uploaded solutions are scored; we verify the solutions, not the process.
Qualification for Stage 2
Finalists are selected separately within each track using the
final Stage 1 ranking across all 60 problems, after eligible submissions have been evaluated
and eligibility checks have been completed. Teams are ranked by score S, highest first, and
then by normalized time U, lowest first (Section 5). The number of finalist places in each
track is TBA and will be announced when Stage 1 ends. If teams remain tied on both S and
U at the qualification cutoff, all such tied teams advance, even if this increases the number
of finalists.
Stage 2: Final
Stage 2 takes place on 8–14 February 2027 and introduces new problems
outside the published benchmark, with unseen instances. Main-track finalists submit both
their algorithm code and the source code of the agentic framework used to produce it.
Self-hosted finalists submit solution files only. Final rankings are determined on a private
final dataset. Detailed Stage 2 rules will be published on 1 February 2027, when Stage 1
ends, and will specify the exact development and submission deadlines, submission formats,
and verification requirements.
Leaderboards
Each stage has one leaderboard per track; the two tracks are never
compared. Each problem category and each formulation is also ranked on its own (Section 4).
Baselines run by the organizers appear as unranked reference bands (Section 7).
3
Wang et al.
4. Datasets
Source
The problems come from the FrontierOR benchmark (Kong et al., 2026a): 180
problems derived from methodologically diverse papers in leading OR venues. Its audited
release (FrontierOR Team, 2026) covers all 180, with 1,080 instance/reference pairs, each
reference accepted by the problem’s checker. Every problem comes with a natural-language
statement, instance and solution schemas, a feasibility checker, instances with 102 to 107
variables and constraints, and reference solutions computed with Gurobi. Each problem has
a slug named after its source paper, such as barnhart2000.
Stage 1 Problems
The organizers select 60 of the 180 problems for Stage 1, none of
them from the testing stage, chosen to cover diverse problem classes, formulations, objective
directions and algorithm runtimes. Each problem has two labels (Table 1): a category, the
application domain it comes from, and a formulation, the mathematical form of the model
behind it. A round’s problems stay hidden until the round opens.
Table 1: Problem categories and formulations. Every problem has one of each. The examples
are illustrative.
Category
Example problems
Routing
vehicle routing variants, dial-a-ride, orienteering
Production & Inventory
lot sizing, production planning
Scheduling
crew scheduling, machine scheduling
Packing & Partitioning
bin packing, cutting, set partitioning
Graph & Quadratic Optimization
graph partitioning, quadratic assignment
Network Design & Location
multicommodity flow, facility location
Formulation
Model
Combinatorial
discrete choices of routes, sequences, sets or assignments
Mixed-integer
linear models with integer and continuous variables
Quadratic
quadratic objective or constraints
Stochastic
uncertain data given by scenarios or distributions
Robust & bilevel
worst case over an uncertainty set, or a leader and a follower
Instance Sets
Each problem has three disjoint sets of instances. Public instances are
published for development and accessible to registered teams; they are never scored. Private
Main instances score the Main-track submissions and are never published. Private Self-hosted
instances score the Self-hosted track; Self-hosted teams receive them during a submission, so
they are kept apart from the Main set. Instances are generated iteratively: random instances
are generated for each problem, their difficulty is evaluated with Gurobi, and generation
continues until the set has the desired difficulty.
Reference Objectives
Each private instance has a reference objective z∗: a good checker-
accepted objective. Reference solutions are computed with long-running Gurobi solves or
specialized algorithms for the given problem.
4
FrontierOR Challenge
Example
Appendix A gives a complete problem from the testing stage, barnhart2000:
its statement, instance schema and solution schema.
Contributions
Anyone registered may propose a new problem, or new instances for an
existing problem. Each contribution should include a description, related work and files.
Each contribution is reviewed individually and used to extend the benchmark. Accepted
contributions are credited to the contributors.
5. Evaluation Metrics
Each solution is checked, scored by its ratio to its instance’s reference, and the instance
scores are averaged into a submission score. Only private instances count.
Feasibility
The checker verifies every constraint and recomputes the objective from the
decisions. A reported objective value that disagrees with the recomputed one beyond the
objective tolerance is rejected; otherwise, the recomputed value z is the one scored. In the
testing stage and Stage 1, each problem’s checker is published with it, as the evaluation runs
it, so teams can check feasibility themselves; Stage 2 checkers are not published. Teams see
the verdict for each instance.
Instance Score
A feasible solution with objective z is scored against the reference objective
z∗. A solution is better than the reference when z < z∗for minimization and z > z∗for
maximization. The score is

For positive objectives, minimization scores z∗/z and maximization scores z/z∗; for negative
objectives the two ratios swap. Either way, matching the reference scores 1, a worse solution
less and a better one more, up to the cap of 2. When z and z∗have opposite signs, or either
is 0, a ratio has no meaningful scale: a better solution scores 2, an equal one 1 and a worse
one 0. An instance scores 0 when there is no feasible solution: the algorithm exceeded the
time limit or the memory limit, crashed, wrote no readable solution, or the checker rejected
it.
Tolerances
Each problem’s checker sets its own tolerances. Constraints, including integral-
ity, must hold within an absolute tolerance, typically 10−5. The reported objective value
must agree with the recomputed objective within a relative tolerance, usually 0.5%, depend-
ing on the problem. The score adds no tolerance of its own: z = z∗only when the two values
are identical, and only an objective of exactly 0 counts as zero.
Time Limits
The score rewards quality only, so speed is enforced through the time
limits instead. Each problem falls into one of three time classes, with a limit of 10 seconds,
60 seconds or 5 minutes per instance. The classification is based on problem difficulty and
application domain. The testing stage uses 60 seconds for every problem.

Submission Score
A submission covers the problems Pr of one round r. Let Ip be
the private instances of problem p in the team’s track; every one of them is scored. The
submission’s problem scores and its round score are

In each round, exactly one submission counts: the team’s completed sub-

a round’s result is never assembled from the best problem scores of different submissions.
Among submissions with equal Rr, the one with the lower time Ur (below) counts, then the

Ranking
Teams are ranked by S, highest first. Scores are compared without rounding,

6

Discussion
The ratio is simple to explain and normalizes each instance by its own reference,
so problems with objectives of very different magnitude can be averaged. It has known
limits, which we accept for the first edition: it is not invariant to a constant offset in the
objective, so a problem whose objective is mostly a fixed cost compresses all teams near 1
and weighs less in the ranking than its equal weight suggests; and weak references inflate
scores up to the cap.
6. Evaluation Protocol
Algorithm Contract
A Main-track submission is a zip or tar.gz archive of up to 4 MB
with one folder per problem, named by its slug, each holding a solve.py. Each folder is
mounted on its own, so algorithms cannot share code. The sandbox runs
python solve.py --problem <slug> --instance /work/in/instance.json \
--output /work/out/solution.json --time-limit <seconds>
and expects a JSON object with a numeric objective value and the decisions the problem’s
solution schema defines. Algorithms are Python only; teams who want another language use
the Self-hosted track.
Environment
Our images run Python 3.12 or 3.14 with NumPy, SciPy, pandas, NetworkX,
OR-Tools, PuLP, HiGHS and Pyomo, and their full lockfiles are published. A team may add
up to 50 open-source packages from PyPI, within the documented installation and resource
limits; they are installed once before the first run, outside the time limit, and reused by later
submissions with the same list.
Main-Track Execution
Each instance runs in its own gVisor5 sandbox with no network,
2 vCPU, 4 GB of memory, 1 GB of disk, a read-only algorithm folder and the problem’s
time limit (Figure 1). Each problem’s public instances run first; if the algorithm fails on
one, the problem’s private instances are skipped and score 0. The checker then verifies each
solution. Teams see each instance’s score or the reason it scored 0, but no algorithm logs,
objective values or run times for private instances, since these could reveal the instances.
Self-hosted Submissions
Opening a submission starts a time window long enough to
solve every private instance of the round one after another, each within its time limit plus
the grace below, plus 15 minutes. The team starts each private instance separately. The
instance submission process consists of: starting the evaluation window, downloading the
instance data, solving the instance locally, and uploading th

1University of Science and Technology of China 2Shanghai AI Laboratory
{tangyinhao,fangyq}@mail.ustc.edu.cn, {sunyanan}@pjlab.org.cn
Abstract
Post-training recursive self-improvement (RSI)
iteratively improves a target capability, op-
erationalized by a fixed anchor benchmark,
through repeated intervention, training, and
evaluation. Yet most loops use the anchor’s
aggregate score as their sole observation, so
early gains give way to stalled progress and
repetitive exploration. When this anchor-only
feedback ceases to reveal actionable gaps, a
plateau may reflect an exhausted observation
rather than an exhausted capability. We in-
troduce adaptive observation (AdaObs), an
observation-side mechanism of harness evo-
lution that keeps the anchor objective fixed
while adapting the active observation. At a
plateau, a controller refines diagnostic gran-
ularity, escalates difficulty, and adds related
tasks; validated increments are fused back into
training, while every checkpoint remains eval-
uated against the anchor. Across eight inde-
pendently optimized anchors in long-context
reading comprehension and instruction follow-
ing, AdaObs raises the mean score from 66.4 to
73.7 under a matched data budget, outperform-
ing FixedObs, the anchor-only baseline. The
evolved harness further improves the seven-
task average on the independent PostTrain-
Bench across two agent backends. These re-
sults identify observation adaptation as a miss-
ing mechanism of harness evolution for sus-
taining post-training RSI.
1
Introduction
Post-training increasingly takes the form of a
feedback-driven search over data and training deci-
sions rather than a fixed recipe (Jaech et al., 2024;
Guo et al., 2025; Bai et al., 2026). In this fram-
ing, an agent drives the search: it inspects model
failures, proposes a targeted intervention, trains a
new checkpoint, and reads benchmark outcomes

to decide what to try next. Because training and
evaluation are repeatable, the agent can run this
cycle many times, each result sharpening the next
intervention. We study this closed-loop process as
recursive self-improvement (RSI): each run targets
a designated model capability, a fixed benchmark
anchors the objective, and experimental feedback
connects successive interventions. By accumulat-
ing validated gains across rounds, such a loop can
keep finding productive steps even after the recipe
has exhausted its most obvious opportunities.
In practice, however, autonomous post-training
loops often lose momentum. Recent studies report
that early gains give way to stalled progress and
repetitive exploration: agents keep launching near-
identical training variants on a plateaued bench-
mark instead of rethinking their approach, so that
“execution is solved, rethinking is not” (Lim et al.,
2026; Rank et al., 2026). In the conventional set-
ting, the same anchor serves two roles: it defines
the fixed optimization objective and provides the
loop’s sole observation. We refer to this anchor-
only setting as FixedObs. Its aggregate score can

indicate whether an intervention helped, but often
not which capability gap remains or what interven-
tion should come next. Existing systems mainly
evolve what the loop acts on or how it acts, in-
cluding training data (Du et al., 2026; Wang et al.,
2026), synthesis code (Zhang et al., 2026a), and
agent-side harness components (Lee et al., 2026),
while keeping the observation used for experiment
selection fixed. We identify this as a missing di-
mension of harness evolution: when anchor-only
feedback ceases to reveal actionable gaps, a plateau
may reflect an exhausted observation rather than
an exhausted capability.
We therefore decouple the fixed anchor objec-
tive from the active observation used to guide op-
timization. We introduce adaptive observation
(AdaObs), an observation-side mechanism of har-
ness evolution. Every checkpoint remains evalu-
ated against the anchor, but when progress plateaus,
a controller adapts the diagnostic evidence that
guides the next intervention through an ordered
ladder: (L1) refining diagnostic granularity to ex-
pose failure modes hidden by the aggregate score,
(L2) escalating to harder difficulty levels that re-
store headroom, and (L3) adding related tasks that
reveal transferable gaps. The controller consults
experiment memory and skips concrete updates
that have already failed. Validated increments dis-
covered under these cumulative observations are
merged into the retained training set within each
run, redirecting optimization toward the anchor
without moving the objective (Figure 1).
We realize this policy as a fully autonomous
loop on production training infrastructure, running
repeated full-parameter SFT. Across long-context
reading comprehension and instruction following,
we optimize eight anchor benchmarks indepen-
dently. With the same starting data and training
recipe and a comparable data budget, AdaObs out-
performs FixedObs on all eight, raising their mean
score from 66.4 to 73.7. The evolved harness also
transfers unchanged to PostTrainBench, improving
its seven-task average by up to 6.9 points.
Our analyses expose the mechanism behind
these gains. Diagnostic refinement (L1) makes
heterogeneous failures visible: decomposing ag-
gregate feedback into behavioral indicators reveals
a supervision-format mismatch that drives over-
length, truncated answers. Difficulty escalation
(L2) moves the active observation to harder subsets,
whose increments transfer asymmetrically back to
easier subsets and the anchor. Lateral expansion
(L3) introduces complementary tasks whose su-
pervision continues to improve the anchor after
anchor-only optimization has saturated. Together,
these results show why no single observation re-
mains uniformly informative: progress resumes
when the harness shifts to an observation that re-
veals a new, transferable gap. On the agent side,
persistent harness updates also reduce recurrent
failures such as capability misdiagnosis, data con-
tamination, and redundant exploration across both
backends. To summarize, our key contributions are
as follows:
• We identify observation adaptation, evolving
the diagnostic evidence used to select interven-
tions while preserving a fixed anchor objective,
as an overlooked observation-side mechanism
of harness evolution.
• We instantiate this principle as a three-level
ladder of diagnostic refinement (L1), diffi-
culty escalation (L2), and cumulative expan-
sion to related tasks (L3), coordinated by a
plateau-triggered controller that accumulates
validated increments and avoids failed interven-
tions through experiment memory.
• Across eight separately optimized anchors,
AdaObs sustains gains beyond anchor-only
feedback and the evolved harness transfers un-
changed to PostTrainBench across tasks and
agent backends, with analyses showing that
each lever resumes progress by exposing a new,
transferable capability gap.
2
Related Work
Autonomous and agentic post-training.
Recent
work asks whether LLM agents can automate post-
training. PostTrainBench (Rank et al., 2026) tasks
agents with budgeted research, data synthesis, and
training-code iteration, documenting failures such
as contamination and reward hacking. Data-centric
systems optimize this loop: DataMaster (Du et al.,
2026) tree-searches over curation strategies, Cura-
teEvo (Wang et al., 2026) rewrites policies from
failed trajectories, LaMDAgent (Yano et al., 2025)
searches over pipelines, and LoopTool (Zhang
et al., 2026c) closes a probe-synthesize-retrain loop
for tool use.
Across 1,338 trajectories, agents
master execution but rarely re-assess strategy at
plateaus (Lim et al., 2026): “execution is solved,
rethinking is not.” These systems evolve data, cu-
ration code, or pipelines while holding evaluation
2
fixed. We instead adapt the observation to escape
these plateaus.
Self-improving and self-evolving agents.
Be-
yond data, many systems recursively revise their
own artifacts: self-improving harnesses (Zhang
et al., 2026a; Lee et al., 2026), self-modifying
agent code (Zhang et al., 2026b), and evolving
skills, memory, or context (Wang et al., 2023;
Ouyang et al.); SEAL (Zweiger et al., 2026) lets
a model generate its own finetuning data and self-
edits. A common choice is to keep the evaluator
outside the evolving loop to prevent reward hack-
ing (Lin et al., 2026). Our work is complementary:
we fix the objective and its verification discipline
but let the loop adapt what it observes, at what gran-
ularity, at what difficulty, and over which tasks.
Evolving evaluation, curricula, and difficulty.
Two adjacent halves of the literature touch our idea.
On the measurement side, benchmarks are made
dynamic to resist saturation: AutoBencher (Li
et al.)
searches for harder benchmarks, Aren-
aBencher (Liu et al., 2025) evolves items via multi-
model competition, and DyVal (Zhu et al.) gener-
ates controllable-difficulty samples, while nearly
half of surveyed benchmarks saturate as models
improve (Akhtar et al.).
On the training side,
self-play and curriculum systems adapt what to
train on: Absolute Zero (Zhao et al., 2026), R-
Zero (Huang et al., 2026), Tome-Math (Fang et al.,
2026), SPICE (Liu et al.), and SCOPE (Kwan et al.,
2026) generate tasks at the learner’s frontier, and
rubric- or reward-evolving methods co-evolve the
reward with the policy (Iacob et al., 2026; Shao
et al.). The former target leaderboard compara-
bility; the latter evolve the training distribution or
reward directly, whereas we adapt the observation
that selects which increments to train on while
keeping the anchor objective fixed. We unite these
halves inside a single RSI loop. Because fixed feed-
back loses information as models improve (DeV-
illing, 2025; Chen et al., 2026), a plateau triggers
adaptation of the observation, across granularity,
difficulty, and task set, to expose hidden capability
gaps and re-open gains on the target capability.
3
Method
We
cast
post-training
as
a
recursive
self-
improvement (RSI) loop that iteratively trains and
re-evaluates a model, linking runs through an ex-
periment memory (§3.1). The loop stalls when its
feedback goes stale: a plateau may reflect an ex-
hausted capability, but it may also mean that the
loop is viewing that capability through an uninfor-
mative lens. We address the latter case by evolving
two parts of the loop on different timescales—the
active observation changes when progress plateaus
(§3.2), while the agent harness changes when re-
curring failures surface (§3.3).
3.1
The self-improvement loop
We optimize a base model M0 toward target ca-
pabilities C. Each iteration executes seven stages:
OBSERVE collects feedback from the latest check-
point under the active observation; ANALYZE iden-
tifies a capability gap; PLAN turns it into a minimal,
falsifiable data intervention; PRODUCE generates
the corresponding SFT increment by synthesizing
new data or downloading a public dataset; VALI-
DATE applies quality, provenance, and contamina-
tion gates; TRAIN runs full-parameter SFT on the
base data plus all retained increments; and EVAL-
UATE scores the resulting checkpoint. Successive
iterations are connected by the evaluated check-
point and an experiment memory M, which stores
confirmed conclusions and negative results so the
loop does not repeatedly propose interventions that
have already failed. This closes the loop: each
checkpoint seeds the next iteration, and M carries
forward what earlier rounds learned.
An observation is Or = (Br, δr, gr), where Br
is the benchmark set, δr selects its active tiers or
subsets, and gr controls the diagnostic resolution.
We distinguish a fixed anchor observation Oanc,

both, the active score testing the current hypothe-
sis and the anchor score guarding the unchanged
objective. An increment is retained if it improves
either score within a small anchor-regression toler-
ance, accumulating in ∆⋆.

The controller first

can reveal an actionable defect without collecting

L2:
difficulty escalation.
If finer diagnosis
yields no new gap, the controller keeps the task
identity fixed and adds a harder difficulty tier δ⋆
of its own choosing to the active observation, us-
ing a held-out reference model as a guide so the
chosen tier stays within an informative pass-rate
band: hard enough to provide headroom, but not
so hard that it ceases to provide useful feedback.
The previously observed tiers are retained along-
side it, so the observation accumulates difficulty
rather than replacing it. The selection rule is given
in Appendix B.1.
L3: lateral expansion.
If the within-benchmark
options are exhausted, the controller selects an un-

added tasks stay in the cumulative observation and
the target remains fixed in Oanc. This lateral view
can expose transferable sub-skills the original task
did not isolate, without discarding earlier evidence.

Each candidate is replayed on two sets of logged
iterations: a repair set containing the targeted fail-

successful decisions. The best candidate is commit-
ted only if it repairs the target cases, preserves the
regression buffer, and passes interface, provenance,
and prompt-budget checks; otherwise the active
harness is unchanged. The evaluator, anchor ob-
servation, and validation gates remain immutable,
preventing the harness from improving by chang-

full controller appear in Appendix B.2.
A deterministic execution layer submits dis-
tributed training and evaluation jobs, validates

It makes no scientific decisions, but enables the
loop to run unattended on a production cluster; im-

Experiments
4.1
Setup
Base model.
Our main post-training study
starts from Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-base (Qwen Team,
2026a) and uses full-parameter SFT throughout.
We optimize each benchmark as its own anchor,
running a separate loop that holds that benchmark
fixed as the target. Within each loop, the fixed-
observation route (FixedObs) and our adaptive-
observation route (AdaObs) start from the same

ChronoPatch: Black-Box Energy-Latency Attacks on Vision-Language Models
Jiawei Xing
Shandong University
Li Wang
Shandong University
Xiangtao Meng
Shandong University
Chuanchao Zang
Shandong University
Rui Wen
Institute of Science Tokyo
Zheng Li
Shandong University
Abstract
Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed as
generative inference services, where autoregressive decoding
makes response length a key determinant of latency and com-
putational cost. This creates an availability risk: adversarial vi-
sual inputs can prolong generation and increase serving over-
head. Existing energy-latency attacks typically rely on gra-
dients, logits, or token-level feedback, leaving open whether
such risks persist when an attacker observes only the final
response. We present ChronoPatch, a black-box attack that
induces prolonged VLM generation requiring only the final
response. It discovers visual delay anchors through response-
length-guided evolutionary search, then minimizes perturba-
tion magnitude through subspace-calibrated decision-based
optimization. Across four open-source VLMs, ChronoPatch
increases inference latency by 47.86%–293.34% and GPU
energy consumption by 41.44%–249.70% under a 5% spatial
budget. It also induces more repetitive outputs, as reflected
by increased n-gram repetition ratios. On three commer-
cial VLM APIs, ChronoPatch increases response length by
37.6%–81.5% and client-observed latency by 1.82×–2.29×
under query budgets of 500 per API. These results reveal
a generation-based availability risk that persists under final-
response-only access and motivate generation-aware safe-
guards for deployed generative AI services.
1
Introduction
Large vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly de-
ployed as multimodal inference services, serving as the
perception and reasoning components in embodied agents,
autonomous perception pipelines, and interactive decision-
making systems [5,8,20,21,40]. In these deployments, avail-
ability depends not only on response quality but also on pre-
dictable latency and computational cost. Delayed perception
or excessively long responses can postpone downstream deci-
sions and increase serving overhead.
This exposes a security-relevant risk in autoregressive
VLMs [1, 4, 24]. Given an image and a textual prompt, a

generation under final-response-only black-box access.
VLM generates its response token sequentially until an end-
of-sequence (EOS) token is emitted or the generation budget
is exhausted [14,32]. Since each generated token incurs an ad-
ditional decoding step, generation length is a key determinant
of inference latency and energy consumption [14, 19]. Ad-
versarial inputs that delay response termination can therefore
amplify inference cost without modifying model parameters
or textual prompts. We refer to this threat as an energy-latency
attack [30].
Prior energy-latency attacks demonstrate that adversarial in-
puts can amplify VLM inference costs, but differ in their feed-
back assumptions and attack surfaces. White-box methods
such as NICGSlowDown [10] and Verbose Images [14] rely
on model internals or gradients, whereas VLMInferSlow [34]
optimizes visual perturbations using continuous feedback
such as output logits. Recent approaches also induce exces-
sive reasoning through visual scene-text triggers [17], jointly
optimize images and textual prompts [26], or exploit serving-
side KV-cache and scheduling mechanisms [33]. In contrast,
ChronoPatch focuses on localized visual perturbations with a
fixed textual prompt, using only completed-response length
as optimization feedback, without gradients, logits, or inter-
mediate decoding signals. This raises a central question: Can
an attacker substantially amplify VLM generation cost using
only final-response feedback?
1
arXiv:2611.26117v1  [cs.CR]  19 Nov 2026
We study this final-response-only black-box setting and
identify two challenges. First, no natural adversarial initializa-
tion is available to reliably induce prolonged generation. The
attacker must discover effective visual delay patterns using
only response-length feedback. Second, once a visual delay
anchor is found, the attacker must reduce its perturbation mag-
nitude while preserving prolonged generation, despite lacking
intermediate feedback to guide refinement.
To address these challenges, we propose ChronoPatch, a
two-stage energy-latency attack framework. Phase I, delay-
anchor discovery, uses response-length-guided evolutionary
search over visual patterns and locations to identify visual
delay anchors that induce prolonged generation. Phase II,
perturbation refinement, starts from these anchors and pro-
gressively reduces perturbation magnitude within the fixed
editable region while preserving the long-generation effect.
It employs subspace-calibrated decision-based optimization
to adapt the exploration scale to the effective dimensional-
ity of the editable region, enabling more reliable boundary
estimation under spatial constraints.
We evaluate ChronoPatch on four representative open-
source VLMs across three benchmark datasets, measuring
generation length, inference latency, and GPU energy con-
sumption. Under a perturbation budget of 5% of the image
area, ChronoPatch increases end-to-end inference latency
by up to 293.34% and GPU energy consumption by up to
249.70% on MSCOCO. The generated responses also ex-
hibit repetitive degeneration, particularly on Qwen3-VL and
InternVL3. We further evaluate ChronoPatch on three com-
mercial VLM APIs under a reduced query budget, observ-
ing response-length increases of 37.6%–81.5% and client-
observed end-to-end latency reaching 1.82×–2.29× that of
clean requests, demonstrating that over-generation remains
externally observable in deployed services.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
• We identify a final-response-only energy-latency threat
in VLM services, showing that generation cost can be
amplified using only returned response lengths, without
access to model internals or intermediate feedback.
• We propose ChronoPatch, a two-stage attack framework
that discovers visual delay anchors from response-length
feedback and refines them into low-distortion perturba-
tions under constrained visual modification.
• We evaluate ChronoPatch on four open-source VLMs,
three benchmark datasets, and three commercial APIs,
demonstrating latency and energy amplification on open-
source models, as well as response-length and client-
observed latency amplification on commercial APIs un-
der limited perturbation and query budgets.
2
Related Work and Preliminaries
2.1
Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs)
Modern VLMs typically combine a vision encoder with a
pretrained large language model (LLM) through an alignment
module, enabling autoregressive generation conditioned on
visual and textual inputs. This architecture supports diverse
multimodal tasks, including image captioning [21,22], visual
question answering [5,24], and multimodal reasoning [40].
For availability analysis, autoregressive decoding is partic-
ularly relevant: the LLM generates tokens sequentially until
an end-of-sequence (EOS) token is emitted or the generation
budget is exhausted. Since computational cost scales approx-
imately with the number of generated tokens [19], delayed
response termination directly increases inference latency and
energy consumption.
2.2
Energy-Latency Attacks
Energy-latency attacks target system availability by increas-
ing inference-time resource consumption rather than degrad-
ing model accuracy. Sponge examples [30] increase neural
network computation costs through inefficient activation pat-
terns. Building on this idea, subsequent works extend re-
source amplification to autoregressive generation: NICGSlow-
Down [10] delays response termination in image-captioning
models, while AutoDoS [39] induces excessive generation in
text-only LLMs.
Recent studies reveal similar vulnerabilities in VLMs. Ver-
bose Images [14] uses visual perturbations to delay response
termination, while RE-CITE [13] induces repetitive genera-
tion. VLMInferSlow [34] explores black-box energy-latency
attacks using zeroth-order optimization, but assumes access
to both generated text and token-level logits to guide per-
turbation updates. Other approaches exploit distinct attack
surfaces: Overthink-Triggered Slowdown [17] induces ex-
cessive reasoning in robotic LVLMs, Joint Pixel-Prompt Op-
timization [26] jointly optimizes visual perturbations and
prompts, and Rethinking Latency DoS [33] targets serving-
side KV-cache utilization and scheduler behavior. In contrast,
ChronoPatch optimizes localized visual perturbations with a
fixed textual prompt, using only completed-response length as
feedback, without requiring gradients, logits, or intermediate
decoding signals.
2.3
Threat Model
Target VLMs. We consider autoregressive VLMs deployed
as multimodal inference services. The attacker submits image-
text queries to a target model and observes only final re-
sponses, with each image optimized independently under a
fixed generation configuration. We evaluate open-source mod-
2
els for systematic analysis and commercial APIs to assess
attack applicability under query-limited access.
Adversarial Goal. The adversary aims to compromise ser-
vice availability by crafting visual perturbations that delay
response termination and induce excessive generation, thereby
increasing inference latency and computational resource con-
sumption without modifying textual prompts.
Adversary Capability. We consider a final-response-only
black-box setting in which the attacker can modify input im-
ages but observes only completed responses, using response
length as the sole optimization feedback. Textual prompts and
generation settings remain fixed, with no access to model inter-
nals or intermediate signals. Latency and energy are used only
for evaluation. All attacks, including those on open-source
models, follow this restricted access assumption. Perturba-
tions are confined to a limited spatial region and refined to
minimize their masked ℓ2 magnitude.
3
Methodology of ChronoPatch
3.1
Design Intuitions
ChronoPatch addresses two challenges in the final-response-
only black-box setting. Since autoregressive VLMs incur
additional decoding computation for each generated token,
delaying response termination directly increases inference
latency and energy consumption. However, without access to
gradients, logits, or intermediate decoding signals, discover-
ing inputs that induce prolonged generation and refining them
under restricted visual modifications remain challenging.
Delay-Anchor Discovery. The first challenge is identify-
ing visual patterns that induce prolonged generation using
only final-response feedback. Although evolutionary search
has been effective in discovering inputs that trigger long con-
tinuations in the text domain [16], directly extending it to
high-dimensional visual inputs is challenging [2]. We there-
fore adapt population-based exploration to visual patches,
selecting and evolving candidates according to their observed
response lengths. This process discovers visual delay anchors:
localized patterns that delay response termination and amplify
generation cost.
Perturbation Refinement. The second challenge is reduc-
ing perturbation magnitude while preserving the attack effect
within a restricted spatial budget. Existing decision-based
methods, such as Boundary Attack [7] and HopSkipJumpAt-
tack [9], primarily explore the full image space. When only
a small editable region is available, such exploration pro-
vides limited useful variation within the constrained subspace,
making boundary estimation less effective. This motivates
calibrating the exploration process according to the effec-
tive dimensionality of the editable region, thereby improving
query efficiency.

The ChronoPatch Framework

and placement using response-length feedback. In Phase II,
it refines the anchor within a fixed spatial mask using binary
response-length feedback, reducing perturbation magnitude
while preserving prolonged generation.
