SenseAlign: Learning Decision-Aligned Predictive Representations for Active
Urban Sensing with UAVs
Weijiang Xionga, Nikolas Geroliminisa,∗
aUrban Transport Systems Laboratory (LUTS), EPFL, Lausanne, 1015, Switzerland
Abstract
Active urban sensing orchestrates a mobile sensor fleet to proactively inspect a dynamic road network and gather critical
information for system management. This problem simultaneously requires understanding the complex spatio-temporal
evolution and making decisions with partial observations. In this work, we focus on active sensing in a large-scale
urban road network with utilities grounded in dynamic traffic states, while prior work has rarely considered these
factors jointly. We propose SenseAlign, a Reinforcement Learning-based (RL) framework that learns decision-aligned
predictive representations for coordinating an urban sensing drone fleet. SenseAlign first trains a privileged teacher
agent that exploits future ground-truth traffic for optimal sensing choices. The student agent has an auxiliary branch
that learns to predict future traffic with partial observations, in addition to the RL-trained actor and critic branches.
During student learning, our framework matches the action distributions of the teacher under ground-truth and student-
predicted future traffic, while keeping the teacher’s observations unchanged. Such a design shapes the latent space
for decision-making instead of prediction alone. At inference time, the student agent has no overhead as all this
learning is done in training. We conduct comprehensive experiments with the real road network of central Barcelona
containing 1570 road segments, and demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms the baselines on multiple
utility formulations. The codebase will be made publicly available upon paper acceptance.
Keywords: Urban transportation, Active sensing, Drones, Reinforcement Learning, Representation Learning
1. Introduction
Urban transportation networks are complex systems with spatio-temporal correlations, and their management builds
upon the knowledge of network states and dynamics. Traditional solutions usually rely on fixed sensor infrastructure,
e.g., loop detectors and surveillance cameras, where decent coverage requires substantial investments and continuous
maintenance. Considering the complex spatio-temporal evolution of congestion and the inherent stochasticity of urban
traffic system, sparse fixed sensors cannot always provide a reliable monitoring under the varying conditions. As a
result, urban traffic sensing with aerial sensors has been gaining increasing attention in recent years (Barmpounakis
and Geroliminis, 2020; Fonod et al., 2025). Drone monitoring can better capture the onset of a traffic breakdown,
queue dissipation and propagation of stop-and-go waves. They provide a more complete description and more precise
measurements of traffic dynamics, particularly for the locations without loop detectors (Xiong et al., 2025). These
observations are particularly valuable for microscopic traffic modeling, as the detailed trajectories reveal multi-agent
interactions such as merging, lane changes, intersection queues, bus stops and turning maneuvers (Kim et al., 2026).
Those high-quality vehicle trajectory data have supported many studies in microscopic traffic, including parameter
extraction (Zhou et al., 2026; Sica et al., 2026), trajectory prediction (Mohebbi et al., 2025) and traffic flow estimation
(Song et al., 2026). Meanwhile, trajectory data can also enable the research in consistent macro-micro traffic flow
modeling (Wang et al., 2024) and analyzing the capacity drop in the infrastructure (Han et al., 2026). On broader
aspects, drone-based observations have created wider social-economic values in emission analysis (Pascual-Anglès
et al., 2026) and sustainability (Barmpounakis et al., 2025).
∗Corresponding author.
Email addresses: weijiang.xiong@epfl.ch (Weijiang Xiong), nikolas.geroliminis@epfl.ch (Nikolas Geroliminis)
arXiv:2611.26109v1  [cs.AI]  19 Nov 2026
Although aerial platforms have promising potential in urban sensing, full spatial coverage is hardly possible under
realistic resource constraints. Therefore, the drone fleet must optimize the movements to actively inspect the most
valuable areas according to the monitoring requirements. In this work, we study the problem of active urban sensing,
where a swarm of drones moves over a city to monitor network conditions as they evolve. We consider two types
of sensing tasks that are essential for understanding the system dynamics: detecting congestion-change events and
estimating the Macroscopic Fundamental Diagram (MFD) (Geroliminis and Daganzo, 2008). The former aims to
observe roads as congestion emerges or dissipates, while the latter requires measurements that represent the aggregate
flow and density of the road network. Both tasks require the fleet to coordinate its movements based on partial
observations and uncertain states, since traffic conditions in unobserved areas remain unknown and previously collected
measurements become outdated. Thus, effective sensing depends on understanding how the network evolves and how
this evolution changes the value of visiting different locations.
The problem of modeling traffic evolution has long been a central topic in spatio-temporal forecasting, with
graph-based methods learning dependencies across connected roads and successive observations (Li et al., 2018). For
active sensing, such predictive knowledge can help the fleet anticipate traffic conditions at the locations it will reach
after moving. We therefore introduce traffic prediction as an auxiliary task for a reinforcement learning (RL) agent,
teaching the model to understand traffic dynamics from partial observations. Since the ultimate goal is to allocate the
drone fleet, prediction accuracy does not strictly translate to the value in decision-making. For example, a small error
near a congestion transition can change which road should be visited, while a larger error at another location may have
little influence. Therefore, an ideal predictor should provide decision-friendly forecasts, following the principle of
Smart Predict-then-Optimize (SPO) (Elmachtoub and Grigas, 2022).
Based on these observations, we propose SenseAlign, an RL-based framework that learns decision-aligned predictive
representations for drone-based active urban sensing. A privileged teacher is first trained with access to future ground-
truth (GT) traffic, giving it great advantage on the monitoring task (Chen et al., 2020). We then train a student model to
make decisions while having no privileged information. In addition to the standard RL training with Proximal Policy
Optimization (PPO) (Schulman et al., 2017), the student is augmented with three tasks for representation learning:
• Future traffic prediction, for understanding the dynamics and propagation of network traffic
• Knowledge distillation, for imitating the behavior of a privileged model while having only partial information
• SPO-inspired decision alignment, for preserving the traffic information most relevant to choosing the observations
These objectives jointly shape the shared latent space, and allow the learned model to make better monitoring decisions.
Experiments on a large-scale urban road network show that SenseAlign outperforms PPO and the other evaluated
baselines on congestion-change monitoring and MFD estimation. Ablation studies have further verified the contribution
of each module, showing the necessity of learning decision-aligned representations.
2. Related work
2.1. Drone-based monitoring
Drones are favorably utilized in inspection and monitoring across wide application domains. For landslide
inspection, routing models maximize collected geological information while requiring visits to high-priority sites (Fang
et al., 2023). Shen et al. (2020) adapt drone routes to changing vessel locations for air pollution surveillance, and Liu
et al. (2026) schedule flights to continuously cover a sea area. Other applications include infrastructure inspection
(Yang et al., 2025), agriculture (Tang et al., 2025; Velusamy et al., 2021), maritime monitoring (He et al., 2026) and
wildfire monitoring (Merino et al., 2012). Specifically in the transportation domain, drone swarms have been adapted
in smart cities for traffic monitoring (Khan et al., 2020). With the support of computer vision (Fonod et al., 2025), that
footage is particularly valuable for analysis of emissions (Espadaler-Clapés et al., 2023), travel behavior (Zhu et al.,
2024) and road safety (Outay et al., 2020).
With limited flight resources, drone-based traffic monitoring requires decisions about both spatial coverage and
observation value. Christodoulou and Kolios (2020) plan tours that cover a prescribed road network with as few
drones as possible under flight-time constraints. For traffic-responsive navigation, Huang et al. (2021) direct drones
to gather around detected road blockages, while Yahia et al. (2022) guide a drone toward observations that reduce
2
uncertainty in traffic and incident estimates on a freeway. For network-level monitoring, Wang et al. (2022) optimize
peak-hour monitoring routes using time-varying road profits, Theocharides et al. (2024) aims to estimate per-region
MFD with drones, and Chow (2016) formulates repeated visits as information refreshes in a stochastic arc-inventory
routing problem. Learning-based controllers prioritize event-arrival uncertainty under partial observability (Khamidehi
and Sousa, 2021) or combine changing traffic importance with observation age (Maljkovic and Geroliminis, 2025).
Since drones have become an important factor in urban logistic infrastructure (Tan et al., 2026), drone monitoring
is often considered with other urban applications. Bai and Feng (2026) and Xu et al. (2023) propose to leverage the
observations from existing ground vehicles to have better monitoring quality. Lyu et al. (2026) jointly optimize drone
routes for urban monitoring, data collection, and parcel delivery. Xu and Geroliminis (2026) consider both monitoring
and parcel delivery drones with rolling-horizon planning, and a follow-up work coordinates local detours to collect
road information whose value grows over time (Zhu et al., 2026).
Despite this progress, existing works either optimize geometric coverage without traffic dynamics, assume the
system states are fully known, study traffic-responsive actions on limited road structures, or define monitoring utility
according to predefined priorities and known information-growth models. However, a large-scale urban network can
hardly be fully observed, and the predefined scores are not directly connected with the underlying network traffic.
Therefore, we study the monitoring problem under dynamic traffic and partial observability, and define the monitoring
utility using the evolving traffic states.
2.2. Multi-agent planning
In general, coordinating a drone fleet to monitor an evolving road network is a multi-agent planning problem, whose
central challenge is to define the value of obtained information and plan actions accordingly.
Informative path planning (IPP) aims to plan trajectories for multiple robots to maximize collective information
gain in an unknown environment while respecting resource constraints (Popovi´c et al., 2024). Some earlier works have
derived their objectives using information theory, such as mutual information, for environment sensing with single
or multiple robots (Singh et al., 2009; Hitz et al., 2014). Many learning-based methods rely on Gaussian processes
(GP) for system modeling and decision-making. Cao et al. (2023) use a GP-based belief state and train an RL agent
to minimize the predicted uncertainty, and Deolasee et al. (2024) further enhance the framework with a prediction
module to anticipate future belief in a dynamic system. Later, Ma et al. (2025) combine a physics-based model with a
linear Gaussian system using Bayesian Filtering to monitor water pollution dispersion. The objective of IPP is also
tightly connected to GP, as many works aim to minimize the uncertainty of the learned GP (Zhao et al., 2025; Lew
et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2023). Some works instead build an auxiliary reward with GP-based uncertainty reduction, but
target discovering a set of static targets in the environment (Vashisth et al., 2024, 2026).
Persistent monitoring plans repeated observations to maintain information about an evolving environment. Early
studies often impose restrictive assumptions that limit the agents’ motion space. For example, Smith et al. (2012)
optimize the robot motion along predefined loops, and Yu et al. (2015) plan cyclic visits, with the visiting order and
time intervals subject to optimization. Their monitoring objectives are often time-dependent accumulation or random
event arrivals, without grounding in the actual process of a specific system. Rezazadeh and Kia (2021) extend the
problem scope and consider the distribution of rewards on a spatial graph and optimize paths for multiple mobile
agents. Pinto et al. (2022) assume that the internal states of monitored targets follow linear stochastic dynamics
and define observation quality as a function of the distance between agents and targets, thereby optimizing agent
trajectories in continuous space. Zhang et al. (2025a) propose a decentralized optimization method that accounts
for drone communication ranges when optimizing their spatial allocation. In contrast to these optimization-based
approaches, Mishra et al. (2025) use a graph neural network (GNN) to model inter-agent correlations and train the
monitoring agent with multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). Rather than abstract events or information, STAMP
and COMPASS focus on monitoring specific moving objects (Wang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025b). They combine
Gaussian processes with deep learning to model target dynamics and use reinforcement learning to train agents to
optimize their sensing positions.
MARL offers a general learning architecture for coordinating agents under distributed observations (Yu et al., 2022).
Specifically, MAGPPO combines CNN-based spatial encoders with graph-attention communication to learn persistent
coverage policies using penalties that accumulate at unobserved locations (Chen et al., 2021). The Multi-Agent
Transformer (MAT) generates joint actions autoregressively (i.e., one-by-one) instead of simultaneously (Wen et al.,
3
2022), such that subsequent agents need to consider the actions of previous agents and avoid conflicts. We adapt
MAGPPO and MAT as baselines for the traffic-monitoring tasks.
Compared to existing works, we study the monitoring problem of a partially observable urban traffic system, whose
complexity is beyond the capacity of classical models but learnable with deep neural networks (Xiong et al., 2026).
Our monitoring objectives are defined with dynamic traffic states instead of heuristics or static weights, which requires
the agent to understand the underlying traffic system rather than exploiting the predefined rules. Our method takes an
RL-based approach and provides insights on how to shape the latent representation space with predictions, and how the
predictions can better contribute to decision-making.
3. Problem formulation and Monitoring Objective
This section will formulate active sensing under the framework of RL (Section 3.1), and define the rewards that are
grounded on dynamic system traffic, i.e., changes of road congestion (Section 3.2) and the MFD (Section 3.3).
3.1. Reinforcement Learning Setup
In general, we consider an active urban sensing environment where a drone fleet moves over an evolving road
network to collect measurements for its specified sensing tasks. The road network is represented by a graph G, where
the nodes are road segments and edges represent road connections. The urban space is discretized into non-overlapping
grids, and a drone hovering over a grid cell can obtain perfect traffic information of all roads within. We aim to
coordinate the drones to collect spatially distributed, high-resolution traffic observations at the most informative
locations and time. Throughout the derivation, we use i to index roads, j to index drones, t to index time, and z to index
grid cells; bold lowercase and uppercase symbols denote vectors and matrices.
State and Observation. Let Xt ∈RN×C denote the network-wide traffic state at time t, with N road segments and C
feature channels per segment. Its element xi,t, contains the traffic state of road i at time t, where the state has two
channels (C = 2) for traffic flow and density, denoted by qi,t and ki,t. The spatial grid of the road network contains Z
non-empty cells in total, and the drone fleet consisting of M drones are not allowed to observe empty cells or overlap
on the same cells. Let z be the index of grid cell, and let cz ∈Z2 denote the grid coordinates of cell z. Therefore, at
each time step, the available new observations are the traffic states of roads covered by the whole drone fleet:
Ot = {xi,t : ∃j, g(i) = zj,t},
(1)
where g(i) is the index of the grid cell containing road i, and z j,t is the cell index occupied by drone j at time t.
To provide more context information, the observations Ot are augmented with memories from earlier visits in the
same episode and additional metadata. Concretely, for every road, the complete inputs include the current measured
flow and density, time of day, historical traffic, drone positions and coverage mask, last-observed values, observation
age, and whether the road has ever been observed (more details in Section 4.2). Unobserved traffic states are set to zero
before normalization, and they are identified by the binary coverage mask.
Agents and Actions. The drone fleet relocates synchronously after monitoring current locations for a time window, and
the movements follows a centralized policy π(ut | Ot), where ut collects the actions from all M drones. For the next
step, a drone j can choose to stay in its current cell zj,t or move to another accessible cell within grid distance ρ by
taking action u j,t = (∆x, ∆y):
czj,t+1 = czj,t + u j,t,

where ∆x and ∆y are integers, allowing movement in either direction along each grid axis. We assume that moving
within this range will not affect the monitoring quality of the target cell, and we do not consider the observations during
the movements to the target cell, which could be used to improve monitoring quality in future works. In this work,
we focus on the drone allocation problem based on the traffic dynamics, and assume that the deployed drones have
sufficient endurance to complete the approximately two-hour monitoring mission.
4
Reward. The reward or utility is a numerical description of the monitoring objective, and is also the major signal to
guide the improvement of the monitoring agent. Following the general practice in RL, the objective of active urban
sensing is learning a policy π to maximize the expected rewards with temporal discount:

3.2. Congestion-change Event
Urban traffic congestion typically emerges at certain locations, where the travel demand often exceeds the available
capacity, such as intersections, merging areas, or capacity-constrained links. These bottlenecks can act as initial
congestion hotspots, from which congestion progressively propagates acr

Pareto-Optimal and Strategyproof
Data-Sharing Between Competitors
Morgan Colin-Mourre1
Felipe Garrido-Lucero2
Patrick Loiseau1
1. Inria, Fairplay joint team, Palaiseau, France
2. IRIT, Université Toulouse Capitole, Toulouse, France
Abstract
We study data-sharing among firms competing in the same market through the quality
of their predictive models.
We model firms’ profit through two main components,
precision and market share, where the former depends on the firm’s own number of
datapoints and the latter depends on the endowments of all firms. We characterize
Pareto-optimal contracts as those in which at least one firm receives all of the other
firms’ datapoints. We then propose a parametric family of data-sharing contracts and
show that, under any of them, the relative market shares of all firms remain constant,
eliminating the negative effect of sharing data with competitors and equalizing all firms’
gains relative to the no-sharing scenario. We further show that one contract within this
family satisfies both Pareto-optimality and strategyproofness against firms attempting
to under-declare the size of their initial endowment. Finally, using a real-world dataset,
we empirically test the gain in profit for all firms under the contract described above,
and show that data-sharing is particularly beneficial when the machine learning task is
harder or when firms’ initial endowments are closer to homogeneous.
1
Introduction
Modern machine learning and deep learning algorithms increasingly rely on larger and larger
amounts of training data, making it harder for firms to possess the required volumes of data
on their own. Data-sharing has risen as an established solution in the literature, allowing
different data-owners to collaborate in order to train common models (Donahue and Klein-
berg, 2021; Hu et al., 2019; Imakura et al., 2021). Still, a main issue is often ignored in
the data-sharing literature, namely that data-owners within the same market are usually
competitors selling the same products, and might therefore be reluctant to share. Indeed,
successful data-sharing requires data-owners to find each other’s data useful, typically re-
quiring them to serve overlapping customers, putting them in direct competition for those
same customers. Still, if competitors manage to enter into data-sharing agreements, they
could all gain access to more data; in turn, this would result in better models, leading to
more clients and higher sales (Hagiu and Wright, 2023).
In markets such as e-commerce search engines or recommendation systems (Ricci et al., 2015;
Zhang et al., 2019), firms engage in quality-based competition (Taylor, 2013). A firm whose
model has a larger predictive power will capture more clients (Hagiu and Wright, 2023). In
arXiv:2611.26108v1  [cs.AI]  19 Nov 2026
M. Colin-Mourre, F. Garrido-Lucero and P. Loiseau
such settings, differences in the quality of the models and of the offers produced are the pri-
mary factors guiding customer choice, while price-competition is much less prevalent. Search
engines usually provide search results to clients at zero cost (Taylor, 2013), and in recom-
mendation systems, prices are often a fixed feature of the products being recommended.1
Data-sharing between competitors might therefore seem counterintuitive, as giving data to
a competitor will directly improve their model and help them increase their market share at
the firm’s expense.
Despite its economic significance, this dilemma has been little studied in the academic lit-
erature. Tsoy and Konstantinov (2023) work on a similar question but focus on price-based
or quantity-based competition, where additional data reduces production costs or increases
products’ utilities. On the contrary, we examine a setting where firms are competing on
model quality directly and where additional data has an immediate competitive impact, al-
lowing a firm to steal market share from its competitors. In Federated Learning (Donahue
and Kleinberg, 2021; Kairouz and McMahan, 2021), several recent papers have suggested
methods for competing firms to collaboratively build machine learning models without ex-
changing raw data (Huang et al., 2024).
However, managing competition while respect-
ing privacy-constraints often requires highly sophisticated infrastructures, whether through
monetary transfers (Nguyen et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2020) or structural or coalition-based
approaches (Chen et al., 2024; Tan et al., 2024). In contrast, our work demonstrates that
when direct data exchange is possible, a simpler partial data-sharing contract can be suffi-
cient to incentivize cooperation. Finally, our work also connects to the Information Design
literature, which has increasingly examined sharing of consumer signals or market states
between competitors (de Zegher and Lo (2020); Gradwohl and Tennenholtz (2022),(2023));
however, in their models, the information shared consists of real-time market signals, while
we focus on the sharing of training data prior to market interactions.
Contributions. In this article we consider a set of firms competing in the same market.
We formalize the firms’ dilemma of sharing data with their competitors by decomposing the
profit of a firm into two components, its market share, interpreted as the probability that a
new client entering the market chooses to visit the firm, and its precision, related to its ability
to close the sale once a client visits the firm. The precision of a firm always increases when
engaging in data-sharing, but its market share might decline if competitors gain too much
precision themselves. To capture a broad range of data-sharing arrangements, we introduce
partial and asymmetric data-sharing, allowing firms to share less than their full dataset and
to share different amounts from one another.
The main contributions of the article are the following.
• We introduce a novel model of data-sharing under competition where a firm’s profit directly
depends on the precision of all firms within the market.
• We show that in our setting, there always exists a data-sharing contract under which all
firms end up better off with respect to the no-sharing setting (Theorem 2).
1In the real-world data coming from a hotel recommendation system used in Section 5, the price of a
hotel is fixed by the hotel itself, and is considered a fixed feature that the recommendation system cannot
change.

• We propose a parametric family of data-sharing contracts that ensures all firms obtain
an equal gain from data-sharing, eliminating the negative effect of sharing data with
competitors, and we prove that a particular contract within this family is both Pareto-
optimal (Theorem 4) and strategyproof (Theorem 5 and Proposition 6).
• We provide an empirical study on real-world data quantifying the gains in profit for firms
under the aforementioned contract beyond the theoretical assumptions required to estab-
lish our results, and show that data-sharing is particularly beneficial whenever the machine
learning task is harder or firms possess similar datasets before sharing.

HIUNI: HARMONIZING UNDERSTANDING AND GEN-
ERATION IN SHARED VISUAL SPACE
ERNIE Team, Baidu Inc.
Project Page: https://ernie-research.github.io/HiUni
ABSTRACT
Unified multimodal models aim to support visual understanding and generation
within a single framework. However, prevailing approaches often separate their
visual representations or backbone computation to accommodate the different re-
quirements of these two tasks, which limits the degree of unification. In this pa-
per, we present HIUNI, which revisits this design choice and explores whether a
pretrained vision language model can be directly extended into a unified model
with extensive parameter sharing. Specifically, HIUNI reuses the same language-
aligned ViT and dense Transformer backbone for both capabilities, while confin-
ing task-specific computation to the output side. Yet such a design introduces two
key challenges. Generation in pixel space is difficult to optimize, and semantic
abstraction in pretrained ViT discards fine spatial details required for synthesis.
To address these challenges, HIUNI introduces a Pixel Diffusion Head tailored to
direct pixel-space optimization and a lightweight HiGate pathway that provides
fine-grained spatial details near the output stage. Extensive experiments show
that HIUNI achieves a similar average understanding score to the pretrained VLM
while attaining competitive performance on image generation and editing. Con-
trolled comparisons and analyses further demonstrate that a single dense backbone
can effectively support both capabilities without task-specific backbone computa-
tion, highlighting a simpler path toward unified multimodal modeling.
1
INTRODUCTION
Image understanding translates visual content into language, whereas visual generation synthesizes
images from textual descriptions. An ideal unified multimodal model (UMM) is expected to support
both capabilities within a single framework and facilitate cross-task interaction between them (Kang
et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026). However, most existing UMMs still maintain two separate visual rep-
resentation spaces with dedicated encoders. The understanding branch extracts high-level semantics
via a language-aligned Vision Transformer (ViT), while the generation branch learns fine-grained
spatial details with a Variational Autoencoder (VAE). As highlighted by Janus (Wu et al., 2025b),
forcing two divergent encoding objectives into one representation triggers severe task interference.
Bagel (Deng et al., 2025) further introduces a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture that sep-
arates task-specific computation within the backbone, establishing a modular paradigm adopted by
recent studies (Agarwal et al., 2026; Diao et al., 2026; Yan et al., 2026).
Although this separation preserves individual performance, it limits direct interaction through shared
visual representations. Recent studies further suggest that closer sharing of visual representations
can promote stronger interaction between the two capabilities with an appropriate backbone de-
sign (Zheng et al., 2025; Su et al., 2026). These observations motivate us to revisit whether such
architectural separation is indeed necessary: Can a shared visual space internally harmonize under-
standing and generation without relying on task-specific backbone computation?
Recent advances offer promising opportunities to address this question using a single visual encoder
for both understanding and generation (Liu et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026a). Conventional genera-
tion models heavily rely on VAE latents, yet these features are optimized primarily for reconstruction
and are less aligned with the high-level semantics required for understanding (Wu et al., 2025e; Ma
et al., 2026a). Conversely, modern pixel-space diffusion models demonstrate that high-quality gen-
eration can also be achieved without VAE latents (Li & He, 2026; Yu et al., 2026), opening a new

and task-specific MoT modules for understanding and generation. (b) TUNA constructs a shared

path towards shared visual representations. Going one step further, some encoder-free architectures
process raw pixels for both understanding and generation (Liu et al., 2026a; Diao et al., 2026), but
the absence of pretrained visual semantic priors makes optimization substantially less stable and less
data efficient. An alternative choice is to reuse language-aligned ViT as the shared visual encoder,
given its strong semantic representations and direct compatibility with standard Vision Language
Model (VLM) infrastructures. Nevertheless, adapting such an architecture to image generation in-
troduces a spatial bottleneck. VLMs typically employ a patch merger after ViT to compress visual
tokens, doubling effective patch size from 14/16 to 28/32 (Bai et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). Such
aggressive spatial pooling, together with the semantic abstraction of deep ViT layers, improves un-
derstanding efficiency, but weakens fine-grained information needed for high-fidelity synthesis.
Following this direction, we introduce HIUNI, a UMM initialized from a pretrained VLM that ex-
tends image understanding to generation through a shared semantic visual pathway. Understanding
and generation use the same visual encoder, token representation, and dense backbone. Task-specific
computation is confined to the output modules. For image generation, we observe optimization insta-
bility when applying a standard DiT to pixel-space diffusion in our early experiments. We therefore
design a dedicated Pixel Diffusion Head with a simplified modulation for pixel-space generation. To
compensate for spatial information weakened by patch merging and deep semantic abstraction, we
incorporate a lightweight gating module (HiGate), inspired by Cheers (Zhang et al., 2026b), which
directly routes uncompressed pixel-level features to the pixel diffusion head. This residual pathway
supplies local spatial cues for image generation while leaving semantic modeling in the shared visual
encoder and backbone.
We comprehensively validate HIUNI on image understanding, image generation, and image editing.
HIUNI retains strong visual understanding capabilities inherited from the pretrained VLM while in-
corporating image generation into the shared backbone. It also achieves the highest overall Chinese
score on Qwen-Image-Bench among the compared UMMs, together with competitive image edit-
ing performance. More importantly, further architectural comparison reveals the trade-offs between
shared and task-specific backbone computation. While task-routed MoT improves generation over a
same-scale dense backbone under matched training settings, a larger shared dense backbone with a
comparable total parameter count achieves substantially stronger understanding while maintaining
competitive generation. These results suggest that scaling a shared dense backbone within a shared
visual space offers a simple and promising path toward unified multimodal modeling.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
• We propose HIUNI, which provides a new perspective on building UMMs from pretrained
VLMs. Understanding, generation, and editing share the same language-aligned encoder
and dense backbone, while task-specific computation is limited to the output module.
• We develop a Pixel Diffusion Head tailored to direct pixel-space generation, together with
a lightweight HiGate pathway that complements the shared semantic representation with
fine-grained spatial details.
• Extensive experiments show that HIUNI maintains strong understanding while achieving
competitive generation and editing performance. Controlled comparisons further highlight
that a shared dense backbone has the potential to effectively support both understanding
and generation without task-specific backbone computation.
2
Preprint
2
RELATED WORK
Unified Multimodal Models. UMMs are intended to support visual understanding and generation
within a single model. Existing UMMs mainly follow two paradigms according to how images
are represented and generated. Autoregressive models tokenize images into discrete visual tokens
and model text and vision under a unified autoregressive objective (Team, 2024; Cui et al., 2025; Wu
et al., 2025e; Team et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b). This formulation provides a simple and scalable
interface across modalities, but discrete tokenization may lose subtle visual details required for high
fidelity image synthesis. Another line of work follows the Transfusion paradigm (Zhou et al., 2025),
which retains the autoregressive prediction of language while applying diffusion or flow matching
to continuous visual features for image generation (Deng et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026b; Yan et al.,
2026). More recently, pixel-space diffusion further demonstrates that strong image synthesis can be
achieved without VAE latents (Li & He, 2026; Yu et al., 2026), and local details can be recovered
from noisy pixels to complement global semantic modeling (Chen et al., 2026b; Ma et al., 2026b),
opening a more direct path toward shared visual representations. Together, these advances shift
an important architectural question toward how visual representations and backbone computation
should be shared between understanding and generation.
Visual Unification. The architectural design of UMMs depends on how visual representations and
backbone computation are organized. Many existing models maintain separate visual spaces due to
the different requirements of understanding and generation, where a language-aligned ViT provides
semantic features for understanding, and a reconstruction-oriented VAE preserves fine-grained de-
tails for generation (Wu et al., 2025b; Deng et al., 2025). To reduce this separation, recent studies
explore more unified visual pathways. TUNA cascades a VAE encoder with a representation encoder
to construct a shared visual representation, while TUNA-2 further removes both encoders for pixel
space modeling (Liu et al., 2026b;a). Cheers decouples semantic representations and local details
through a unified visual tokenizer and gated detail residuals in generation head (Zhang et al., 2026b).
HYDRA adopts a progressive ViT, and UniSpace introduces reconstruction aware patch represen-
tations into a pretrained ViT (Zhang et al., 2026a; Yan et al., 2026). These designs reduce visual
separation, but differ in their use of pretrained visual encoders and task-specific backbone computa-
tion. For example, UniSpace still adopts task-specific Transformer experts, while encoder-free mod-
els such as SenseNova remove both ViT and VAE but retain an MoT backbone (Yan et al., 2026;
Diao et al., 2026). In another related direction, RepFusion processes noisy visual representations
through a pretrained VLM, but relies on a separate diffusion Transformer for representation-space
generation (Pan et al., 2026). HIUNI reuses the ViT and patch merger of a pretrained VLM and
shares their output representation and a single dense backbone across understanding and generation,
without separate generative visual encoders or task-specific backbone computation.
3
METHOD
Image understanding and generation differ substantially in their input and output forms, but both
rely on semantic alignment between visual content and language. HIUNI therefore separates shared
semantic modeling from task-specific prediction. Specifically, we seek to let the visual encoder and
multimodal backbone provide a common semantic pathway for both capabilities, while introducing
generation-specific processing only when detailed visual signals need to be reconstructed. This
design allows understanding and generation to share the visual and backbone computation without
requiring separate semantic representations.
Following this principle, HIUNI is built upon a pretrained VLM and extends it with image generation
capability while reusing its pretrained visual encoder and backbone architecture. Both understanding
and generation use the same language-aligned ViT, the same visual tokens after patch merging, and
the same dense backbone. Textual outputs are predicted by the native language modeling head, while
image synthesis is handled by a new Pixel Diffusion Head. No separate semantic visual encoder or
task-specific backbone is involved. To compensate for the spatial information weakened by patch
merging and deep semantic abstraction, HIUNI further adopts a lightweight gating module, termed
HiGate, which routes raw features from the noisy image to the diffusion head. The residual branch
supplies local spatial cues to complement the shared semantic representation without modifying the
main semantic computation. Figure 2 illustrates the overall architecture.

Figure 2: Overview of HIUNI. Starting from a pretrained VLM, HIUNI shares the same visual
encoder and dense backbone across understanding, generation, and editing. Language understanding
is handled by a language modeling head, while image synthesis is performed by a Pixel Diffusion
Head. To bridge semantic representations and pixel-level details, HiGate provides a lightweight
residual pathway that supplies local spatial cues weakened by visual compression.
3.1
UNIFIED MULTIMODAL ARCHITECTURE
Shared Visual Encoding.
HIUNI adopts a language aligned ViT from the pretrained VLM as the
only visual encoder for both understanding and generation. Let E denote the ViT and M denote the
patch merger, which compresses the ViT outputs into visual tokens. For an input image x, the visual
tokens are obtained as Z = M(E(x)). The same pathway is used for clean images in understanding
and visual conditioning, as well as noisy target images in generation. Consequently, both tasks are
grounded in the same visual token space without requiring separate or task-specific encoders.
Shared Dense Backbone.
The shared visual tokens are further processed by the same dense back-
bone for both understanding and generation. Text embeddings and visual tokens are organized into
a multimodal sequence S and processed by a single dense Transformer B, yielding H = B(S).
Attention mask allows bidirectional interaction within each image, while text tokens retain causal
attention for autoregressive prediction. After the shared backbone, task-specific prediction is han-
dled on the output side. For image understanding, the language modeling head projects hidden states
corresponding to textual outputs onto the vocabulary space. For image generation, hidden states at
the target visual positions are passed to the pixel diffusion head for image prediction.
3.2
PIXEL-SPACE IMAGE GENERATION
Pixel Diffusion Head.
Diffusion directly in pixel space poses additional optimization challenges
compared with conventional latent diffusion, as the model must predict high dimensional pixel sig-
nals while maintaining semantic consistency and fine spatial structure (Jiang et al., 2026; Li & He,
2026). Consistent with these observations, we observe frequent loss spikes when using a standard
DiT (Peebles & Xie, 2023) with repeated AdaLN modulation in our early experiments. In subse-
quent development runs, a simplified design without block-wise AdaLN exhibits smoother training
trajectories. Motivated by this observation, we remove AdaLN from the DiT blocks, reducing the
diffusion head to a standard Transformer architecture.
Timestep conditioning enters through an explicit time token and a final modulation layer. Inspired
by recent works (Ma et al., 2025; Team, 2025), for timestep t, a sinusoidal encoding ϕ(t) is mapped
by a two layer MLP to a time embedding et ∈RDb, where Db denotes the hidden dimension of
the backbone. The resulting vector replaces the embedding of the <time> token and is processed
together with the multimodal sequence by the shared backbone. The backbone hidden states for the
target visual positions, together with the time token representation, are projected to the diffusion
hidden dimension D and processed by N Transformer blocks.
4
Preprint
At the output of the diffusion head, we retain a single timestep modulation before pixel prediction. A
separate two layer MLP maps the same sinusoidal encoding ϕ(t) to a diffusion time embedding ct ∈
RD. This embedding is further projected to channel wise scale and shift parameters as [γt, βt] =
Wmod SiLU(ct) + bmod. Let Fout ∈RNg×D denote the target visual features at the output of the
diffusion head. The final modulation is given by ¯Fout = (1+γt)⊙LN(Fout)+βt. After modulation,
a linear projection predicts the corresponding pixel patches. With a ViT patch size of 16 and a spatial
merge factor of 2, each generated token predicts a 32 × 32 RGB region, corresponding to a flattened
patch dimension of Np = 3×32×32. Finally, the predicted patches are rearranged into image space
to obtain ˆx0. In this way, the head removes repeated block-wise AdaLN while preserving timestep
conditioning through the shared backbone and final modulation layer.
HiGate.
Although the unified visual tokens carry strong semantics, the patch merger reduces their
spatial resolution, while deeper ViT layers increasingly favor abstraction over local texture. Such
compression is well suited to understanding but may discard cues important for pixel-level recon-
struction. To complement the semantic pathway, HIUNI introduces a lightweight HiGate module,
inspired by Cheers (Zhang et al., 2026b), which directly injects low-level pixel information into the
diffusion head without introducing an additional visual encoder.
Specifically, the noisy image xt ∈R3×H×W branches into two pathways before ViT patch em-
bedding. The main pathway encodes xt through the ViT, patch merger, and the shared backbone
to obtain semantic features, while a lightweight residual branch directly preserves its local pixel
content. In the residual branch, each 2 × 2 group of 16 × 16 RGB patch is concatenated into
Rt ∈RNg×Np, following the same spatial layout as the target visual tokens. A linear projection
maps these raw pixel features to the diffusion hidden dimension D, producing Pt ∈RNg×D. The
aligned pixel features Pt are then fused with the target features Fg ∈RNg×D through HiGate. A
lightweight MLP predicts a token wise gate gt ∈RNg×1, and the residual fusion is formulated as
eFg = LN(Fg+gt⊙LN(Pt)). Only the target visual positions are updated by this residual injection,
and the resulting features continue through the Pixel Diffusion Head. In this manner, the residual
pathway supplies fine-grained spatial cues for image synthesis, while high-level semantic modeling
remains in the unified ViT and shared backbone.

Unified Task Formulation.

Controlling the Humanoid Robot H1-2 With a Simulated
Biologically Plausible Network
Fatima Atwi, Constant Roux, Christian Bergaud and Olivier Stasse
Abstract—Biologically inspired neural oscillators
have already made humanoid robots walk, spiking
networks have controlled simulated humanoids, and
spiking models can reproduce the activity of in-vitro
neural cultures. Whether a network grounded in
such a culture and trained by biologically plausible
learning rules can keep a full-size humanoid balanced
in closed loop remains, however, an open question.
We study this problem by proposing a biologically
inspired spiking network, trained by different learning
schemes, compared in simulation and deployed on
the H1-2 Unitree humanoid. These schemes differ
in how recurrent weights are trained. Ordered from
most to least biologically faithful, they are: a fixed
reservoir mimicking an in-vitro neural culture, where
recurrent weights are kept frozen and only a linear
readout is trained, the same network but with its
synapses trained by reward-modulated spike timing
dependent plasticity and eligibility propagation, and
finally backpropagation through time as a non bio-
logical baseline for comparison. All schemes relied on
distillation of a reinforcement learning expert policy
with dataset aggregation. In simulation, we show that
e-prop reached a 100% survival rate, matching back-
propagation through time, whereas both the fixed
reservoir and the reward-modulated STDP, though
the closest to biological cultures, plateaued at a much
lower performance (~43.7% and ~11% survival). We
explore in further detail which trends a real culture
could and could not produce until now. Finally we
demonstrate brief bipedal stepping on the full size
humanoid H1-2: the e-prop network produces genuine
bipedal walking for 3–9 s, but every hardware trial
ended in a fall, so the hardware evaluation remains
preliminary and the distilled policy is not yet viable
on the real robot.
I. Introduction
In the field of Humanoid Robotics, since the semi-
nal work of [1], it has become almost standard to use
DeepRL to generate policy to make humanoid robots
walk in a robust way. The policy is evaluated in a
massively parallel GPU simulator. On the other hand, bi-
ological neural networks have also been used to perform
computation using the Reservoir Computing paradigm.
For instance in [2], an organoid, and more precisely a
brain organoid, is trained to perform speech recognition
and nonlinear equation prediction. The long term ques-
tion is to understand if a robot can be controlled by a
biological neural network using a similar approach to the
one proposed by [2].

A first problem is organoid reproducibility, as their
production yields highly variable results. A more con-
trolled production of biological neurons is the 3D as-
sembly of neural networks [3] where biological neurons
are grown between beads. Biologically inspired neural
oscillators have made humanoid robots walk [4], [5], and
spiking architectures have coordinated arm and locomo-
tor control of a simulated humanoid [6], but they were
not constrained to match a culture that can actually be
grown. As producing such cultures takes time, the more
humble question addressed here is whether a plausible
model of a 3D neural assembly, trained by biologically
plausible rules, can control a humanoid robot.
From this, the learning schemes we explore in this
work span a range from most to least biologically plau-
sible. Starting off with a fixed reservoir with a trainable
linear readout [7], [8], closest to a real culture assembled
on a multi-electrode array (MEA) in the connectivity
patterns, topology, and network parameters [9], [10].
Next, the same network but with the internal synapses
trained using reward-modulated spike timing dependent
plasticity (R-STDP) [11], [12], matching the dopamine
based learning believed to occur in the basal ganglia. We
then train the same network using eligibility propagation
(e-prop) [13], a biologically plausible approximation of
backpropagation through time (BPTT) that keeps local
eligibility traces and combines them with per neuron
feedback. Finally, we also explored BPTT [14] as a non-
biological strong baseline for evaluation.
We observe all different schemes on the same hu-
manoid locomotion task and in the same control pipeline
featuring a proportional derivative (PD) controller and

II. Related Work
A. Humanoid Locomotion and the expert policy
Humanoid locomotion is dominated today by rein-
forcement learning based policies, along with model
based predictive control. Such policies are often trained
in many parallel environments and then deployed on
hardware in a suitable control pipeline. Our expert policy
used to teach the SNN is such RL-based policy with
constraints as terminations (CaT) [15]. Our aim is not
to outperform the expert policy rather to check whether
we can reproduce its performance on the SNN trained
with biologically plausible methods.
B. Neuromorphic Locomotion
The closest previous work related to the present paper
is [6]. In [6] the authors propose a SNN architecture to
perform an arm motion together with walking. They also
provide a distillation procedure from a policy encoded
in an ANN to a SNN. It was validated in simulation
using IsaacSim. The SNN simulator used in [6] is Nengo.
Compare to this work our contribution is threefold:
a demonstration on a real humanoid H1-2, a close
grounding to a 3D assembly of neural network, and the
biological plausibility of the learning rule itself, on a task
requiring continuous balance. Note that the authors of
[6] are using models recognized as being close to models
of biological arm and walking control.
Neural oscillators (CPGs) generate a repeating gait
rhythm and have driven closed-loop walking on a real
humanoid in non-spiking form [4], and simpler robots
such as quadrupeds and snake robots in spiking form.
Another application is spiking neural models trained by
surrogate gradient RL [16], and three-factor rules have
been applied to adaptive robotic control [17]. However,
none of these up to our knowledge have achieved a full
size humanoid balanced walking in closed loop based on
an SNN trained by biologically plausible rules.
C. 3D Neural Assembly and Reservoir Computing
Our neural model is based on the work of [9], where
the authors discuss the proper modeling methods for a
neuron and for the connectivity patterns within a 3D
neural assembly. Moreover, the geometry and recording
methods of our 3d neural model were inspired by the
work of [18] where a 3D engineered platform is developed
for stimulating and recording from a 3D neural culture.
Finally, the usage of a fixed neural reservoir with a linear
readout, which was our baseline approach, follows the
famous reservoir computing paradigm [7], [8]: where an
input fed into a highly dimensional recurrent neural net-
work gets projected into a rich space from which a simple
readout produces an output. Its internal weights are
kept random and fixed and only the readout is trained,
avoiding credit assignment in recurrent connections.
D. Learning Rules for Spiking Neural Network
Training spiking neural networks is not an easy
task as spikes are non differentiable entities. That is
why surrogate gradient backpropagation through time
(BPTT) [14] is used in a lot of applications but is not
biologically plausible as we cannot propagate error back
in time with real neural cultures. Biologically plausible
alternatives we explored include reward modulated spike
timing dependent plasticity, where synapses marked as
eligible would be updated based on a global neuro-
modulator. Another approach relies on dedicated credit
assignment instead of a global reward, one such method
is the eligibility propagation (e-prop) [13]. This method
approximates the behavior of BPTT but using a biolog-
ically plausible learning instead. All training methods
used are based on behavioral cloning of the expert CaT
policy with dataset aggregation (DAgger) [19].
III. Setup
A. Robot Used and Simulation Setup
The dataset used for behavioral cloning was collected
by running the expert CaT policy [15] in MuJoCo [20]
including different velocity commands and directions to
ensure a diverse dataset. CaT is evaluated there on
a quadruped and applied here to the H1-2 with the
framework of [21]: PPO in Isaac Lab, 4096 parallel
environments and of order 3 × 108 environment steps at
the same 50 Hz control rate, with exponential velocity-
tracking rewards and regularisation penalties, and CaT
constraints on contacts, joint limits and gait style of
which only time-out and illegal base contact act as
terminations. The robot used is the 27-joint Unitree H1-2
humanoid, and our model controls 12 joints required for
walking at 50 Hz control loop rate, with a PD controller
τ = kp(qref −q) + kd( ˙qref −˙q)
(1)
where τ is the torque applied at each actuated joint, q
and ˙q are the measured joint position and velocity, qref
is the target position produced by the network readout,
˙qref the target velocity, and kp, kd are the stiffness and
damping gains, taken unchanged from the expert policy.
In our setup ˙qref = 0, so the derivative term acts as pure
damping on joint motion.
B. Observation and Action Spaces
The controller reads a 45-dimensional observation vec-
tor made up of: base angular velocity, projected gravity,
velocity commands, 12 joint position errors with respect
to the default, joint velocity errors and last actions. In
return, it outputs a scaled action vector of the 12 target
joint positions.
IV. Network Model
A. Neuron model
To capture the essential dynamics of a cortical neuron
while keeping the network tractable, we use the current-
based leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) model [22]. Each
neuron behaves as a leaky container of charge: incoming
synaptic and stimulus currents accumulate on its mem-
brane potential v. Once v crosses a specific threshold
Vth the neuron fires a spike and its potential is reset.
It is unable to fire again for a brief refractory period,
simulating the sodium-channel recovery time that keeps
real neurons from firing immediately [22]. The model
is called leaky because, with no input, v decays back
toward its resting value with time constant τm. For more
biological plausibility, it is ensured that synaptic currents
decay exponentially too with different time constants. To
achieve spike frequency adaptation (SFA), an adaptation
current is included [22], making it harder for a neuron
to fire the more it has recently fired. The equations
describing the neuron model are:

ALTRA-TEST: AN ALTERNATIVE ANNOTATOR TEST
FOR LLM JUDGES WITHOUT SHARED ANNOTATORS
Nagham Omar1, Rotem Dror2, Almog Gueta3, Avigdor Gal1, Roi Reichart1, Nitay Calderon3
1Faculty of Data and Decision Sciences, Technion
2Faculty of Computer and Information Science, University of Haifa
3Google Research
nagham.omar@campus.technion.ac.il, rdror@is.haifa.ac.il,
avigal@technion.ac.il, roiri@technion.ac.il, nitayc@google.com
ABSTRACT
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges and graders to re-
place human annotators, raising the question of when such replacement is statis-
tically justified. To support such decisions, the Alternative Annotator Test (ALT-
TEST) was introduced for dense settings where all items are annotated by the same
annotators. However, in many large-scale annotation settings, items are annotated
by different subsets of annotators. We therefore propose the Alternative Annotator
Test with Resampled Annotations (ALTRA-TEST), a statistical test that does not
require that all items are annotated by the same annotators. ALTRA-TEST uses a
bootstrap that resamples items, draws k human annotations for each item, and sub-
stitutes one of them with an LLM annotation. This produces paired all-human and
mixed human–LLM panels. A replacement is supported when the inter-annotator
agreement (IAA) of the mixed panel is statistically non-inferior to the IAA of the
all-human panel, i.e., when the LLM preserves the signal that the human annota-
tors share. We establish that ALTRA-TEST is a consistent test of asymptotic level
α. We then evaluate it through simulations and real-world experiments in which
we test 18 LLMs and 5 prompting techniques on 20 datasets across text, image,
audio, and video. Across these evaluations, about 100 items often suffice for the
test. In simulations, where we know whether the LLM is a better or a worse anno-
tator than the humans, ALTRA-TEST makes more correct replacement decisions
than existing baselines. In real-world data experiments, LLMs pass the test in
about half of the setups, depending mainly on the task. Since replacement is not
always justified, we encourage researchers to test it for their task.
1
INTRODUCTION
Creating labeled datasets has long depended on human annotation, one of the slowest and most
expensive stages of the AI pipeline (Ding et al., 2023; Tan et al., 2024). Researchers use human an-
notations to train models and to evaluate them, and they draw empirical conclusions from both (Mei
et al., 2026; Omar et al., 2026b), so annotation quality directly affects the validity of the resulting
models and findings. Large language models (LLMs) offer an appealing alternative: they can an-
notate quickly, cheaply, and at a scale that is difficult to achieve with experts or even with crowd
workers (Chiang & Lee, 2023; Gilardi et al., 2023; T¨ornberg, 2023; Nahum et al., 2025). Indeed,
LLMs are increasingly used as annotators, judges (LLM-as-a-judge), and raters (Zheng et al., 2023;
Wei et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Wu, 2025; Mei et al., 2026).
In many AI applications, such as response quality evaluation, there is no ground truth to check
labels against (unlike, e.g., checking whether code runs or a math answer is correct), and human
judgment defines the correct label (Raykar et al., 2010; Paun et al., 2018). Human annotations can
serve two different goals. In most cases, they are used to train, evaluate, or judge models. This
requires one target per item, so what matters is the signal that the annotators share, and not the
variation between individual annotators. In other studies, the disagreement is itself the object of
study, and the goal is to capture the different perspectives of the annotators (Aroyo & Welty, 2015;
Basile et al., 2021; Uma et al., 2021; Plank, 2022). In this paper, we focus on the first goal, although

we also propose adaptations of our test for the second. Replacing human annotators with LLMs is
therefore useful only if the replacement preserves this shared signal (Egami et al., 2023; Gligoric
et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). However, it is not guaranteed that LLMs preserve it. They have
been shown to disagree with experts even when their responses appear fluent or confident (Zhou
et al., 2024; Griot et al., 2025; Szymanski et al., 2025; Tseng et al., 2025; Wu & Aji, 2025; Omar
et al., 2026a), and to systematically diverge from annotators in subjective tasks (Lissak et al., 2024;
Elangovan et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). Accordingly, using an LLM as an alternative to humans
requires statistical justification for the replacement (Bavaresco et al., 2025; Calderon et al., 2025b).
Since there is no ground truth to compare with, researchers assess human annotation quality using
inter-annotator agreement (IAA) (Hayes & Krippendorff, 2007; Klie et al., 2024): if independent
annotators consistently agree above chance, the task is well-defined, and the labels capture a mean-
ingful shared signal rather than random noise (Artstein & Poesio, 2008; Krippendorff, 2011). Even
when IAA is modest, as in subjective tasks where some disagreement is inherent (Basile et al.,
2021; Davani et al., 2022; Plank, 2022; Sap et al., 2022; Fleisig et al., 2023), agreement clearly
above chance still indicates a shared, if noisy, signal. LLM annotations are typically evaluated using
accuracy, F1, or correlation with a majority-vote label (Ziems et al., 2024; Bavaresco et al., 2025;
Elangovan et al., 2025; Guerdan et al., 2025). However, since some disagreement is inherent, in-
dividual human annotators also disagree with the majority-vote label, so even a human would not
score perfectly on these metrics. Their ceiling depends on the task, and without knowing it, it is un-
clear whether a given score is good or poor. As a result, such measures cannot provide a statistically
grounded replacement decision. A replacement test should therefore mirror how we evaluate human
annotation quality, and test whether the LLM keeps the IAA over all human annotations statistically
non-inferior to that of the humans.
Two recent works formulate human replacement by LLMs as a statistical procedure, the Alternative
Annotator Test (ALT-TEST; Calderon et al. (2025b)) and the Statistical Turing Test (STT; He et al.
(2025a)). Both assume a representative set of items, which we call the evaluation set, each labeled
by multiple human annotators. Crucially, they also require the same group of annotators to label
every item in this set. However, this requirement is restrictive, and in many common annotation
settings it does not hold. In crowdsourcing, workers sometimes choose their assignments and may
stop after a few items. In preference annotation, a large pool of participants contributes only a few
judgments each, and in demanding tasks, such as verifying the factuality of a long document, an
annotator can complete only a few items. Finally, many existing datasets omit the identities of the
annotators (Siththaranjan et al., 2024). In all of these settings, researchers observe multiple human
2
labels for each item, but the items are not all labeled by the same annotators, making existing tests
inapplicable. Indeed, 11 of our 20 datasets do not satisfy their requirements.
In this work, we introduce the Alternative annotator test with Resampled Annotations (ALTRA-
TEST1; Figure 1), which does not require that the same annotators label all the items in the evaluation
set. The test uses a paired percentile bootstrap: in each bootstrap sample, it resamples items with
replacement, draws k human annotations per item, and constructs a mixed panel by replacing one
human annotation with the LLM annotation. Unlike existing tests, it resamples the annotations
within each item, and therefore never uses the identities of the annotators. It then tests whether the
mixed-panel IAA is non-inferior to the human-only IAA. An adaptive margin permits a small IAA
loss proportional to the observed human disagreement, so the same test applies to objective tasks,
in which annotators agree strongly, and to subjective tasks, in which some disagreement is inherent.
E.g., our calibrated default of c = 0.1 allows at most a 10% increase in disagreement. We say that
an LLM passes the test when we reject the null hypothesis that the mixed-panel IAA is inferior.
We theoretically establish that ALTRA-TEST is a consistent test of asymptotic level α, i.e., as the
number of items grows, it accepts valid replacements with probability approaching 1 and falsely
accepts invalid ones with probability at most α. We then use simulations, in which items have
a latent gold label that annotators observe with noise, and we control whether the LLM is more
or less noisy than the humans. This enables us to evaluate the replacement question directly, as we
measure each procedure’s better-model pass rate and worse-model pass rate (i.e., correctly accepting
simulated LLMs that are less noisy than simulated humans versus falsely accepting noisier ones). In
the setup that the existing tests require, in which the same annotators label all items, ALTRA-TEST
dominates ALT-TEST and STT, with a higher better-model pass rate at any given worse-model pass
rate. We also evaluate the ALTRA-TEST in the setup that motivates it, in which the items are not
all labeled by the same annotators, and there, its pass rates remain the same. The simulations also
calibrate the default margin constant to c = 0.1 and show reliable behavior with around 100 items.
In addition, we evaluate the ALTRA-TEST on 20 real-world datasets across text, image, audio, and
video, spanning objective and subjective tasks with a wide range of human IAA levels. We test
18 LLM judges and 5 prompting techniques. Under the default CoT setting, LLMs pass the test
in 71 of 201 judge–dataset pairs (35.3%); when each judge uses its best prompting technique, this
increases to 95 of 201 (47.3%). We find that replacement is strongly dataset-dependent, and in many
passing cases the LLM not only passes the test but increases IAA. Consistent with the simulations,
sample-size analyses show that around 100 items often suffice for LLMs that pass with 300 items.
We encourage researchers to apply the ALTRA-TEST before delegating annotation to an LLM.
As the test examines whether the LLM preserves the signal that the annotators share, its result is
meaningful only when this signal exists, and we recommend applying it when human agreement is
at least fair (IAA ≥0.2). We hope it supports more explicit and statistically justified decisions.
2
RELATED WORK
IAA as a proxy for human annotation quality.
When ground-truth labels are unavailable, re-
searchers commonly assess annotation quality through IAA (Artstein & Poesio, 2008; Krippendorff,
2011). In this work, we use Krippendorff’s α, a standard chance-corrected IAA coefficient that
supports multiple annotators, missing annotations, and nominal or ordinal labels (Hayes & Krippen-
dorff, 2007; Krippendorff, 2011). IAA scores should be interpreted relative to the task: objective or
well-specified tasks are expected to yield high agreement, while difficult, ambiguous, or preference-
based tasks may yield lower but still meaningful agreement (Pavlick & Kwiatkowski, 2019; Plank,
2022; Lissak et al., 2024). This interpretation depends on the purpose of annotation. When dis-
agreement is itself the object of study (Aroyo & Welty, 2015; Basile et al., 2021; Uma et al., 2021;
Plank, 2022), forcing high IAA may remove the variation that the study aims to measure. Our focus
is different (see Section 1), and for such studies we propose variants of our test (see Section 3.2).
Even in subjective tasks, such as response-preference annotation, where human IAA may have an
inherent ceiling, positive and non-negligible IAA (e.g., 0.2 or higher) indicates that the annotations
carry a shared signal that an LLM replacement should reflect. We test whether LLMs preserve it.
1
naghamo/altra-test
3
Testing whether LLMs can replace human annotators.
Various methods propose correcting or
calibrating model-generated labels (Angelopoulos et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2026),
but they do not decide whether replacement is justified. Two recent procedures address replacement
as a statistical decision. ALT-TEST (Calderon et al., 2025b) holds out each annotator in turn and
tests whether an LLM is non-inferior to that annotator in its agreement with the remaining annota-
tors. STT (He et al., 2025a) tests whether human and mixed human–LLM panels are statistically
equivalent. Both require the same annotators to label all the items, a requirement that often does not
hold (see Section 1). ALTRA-TEST removes this requirement. Like ALT-TEST and unlike STT, it
answers a non-inferiority question. This fits the replacement decision, since LLM annotations are
much cheaper than human ones, and researchers may prefer an LLM even at the cost of a small loss.
An equivalence test does not accept an LLM that increases IAA, even if it captures the shared signal
more reliably than a typical annotator. Like STT, it uses bootstrap resampling, but unlike both, it
does not replace all annotations of a single annotator. Instead, for each sampled item, it draws k
human annotations, replaces one with the LLM annotation, and bases the decision on a percentile-
bootstrap statistic. Its margin also differs. ALT-TEST uses a fixed margin that is chosen according to
the type of the annotators, and STT derives its margin from the agreement gap between two groups
of humans, while the margin of ALTRA-TEST adapts to the observed human disagreement. When
all three tests can be applied, ALTRA-TEST dominates both (see Section 4).
3
METHOD
Setup and notations.
Let k ≥3 be the panel size used by the test, and let D = {x1, . . . , xN} be
a dataset of N items. For each item xi, we observe Mi human annotations Hi = {hi,1, . . . , hi,Mi},
with Mi ≥k. We do not require annotator identities, and we use each item’s annotations only as a
set of labels. The LLM annotation is f(xi). For each item, let yi,h be a panel of k annotations from
Hi, and let yi,m be formed by replacing one annotation in yi,h with f(xi). Stacking these item-level
panels gives two annotation matrices: the human-only matrix Yh and the mixed matrix Ym, both of
dimension N ×k. Let R be an agreement or reliability score applied to an annotation matrix, where
higher values indicate a more reliable annotation panel. We define 1−R as the disagreement level.
In the main experiments, we use Krippendorff’s α, the standard chance-corrected IAA coefficient
for nominal and ordinal labels; we give its formal definition in Appendix C.1. Finally, we define:
Rh = R(Yh),
Rm = R(Ym),
∆= Rm −Rh.
The substitution gap ∆measures the effect of replacement; a positive value means that the mixed
panel is more reliable than the human-only panel.
3.1
THE ALTRA-TEST
The ALTRA-TEST tests whether an LLM can replace one human annotation per item without reduc-

iteration samples N items with replacement, draws k human annotations for each sampled item,
replaces one of them with the LLM annotation, and compares the reliability of the human-only and

Knowledge Graphs

Abstract
Knowledge graphs on the Web are incomplete, and SPARQL an-
swers a query only from the stored triples. Large language models
(LLMs) can predict missing facts, but an LLM returns names instead
of IRIs and requires one call per binding of a query variable. We
present GenSPARQL, a generative extension of SPARQL 1.1 with
an operator GENOP that binds values generated by an LLM to query
variables during query evaluation. A similarity join maps generated
names to entities of the graph, and the query planner invokes the
LLM only for the bindings selected by the other graph patterns
and filters. In a web workbench, attendees query two graphs built
from Wikidata and inspect generated values, mapped entities and
LLM calls. In our evaluation with three open-weight LLMs, the
embedding similarity maps 83% of the entities named by the LLMs
and yields only one incorrect match.
CCS Concepts
• Information systems →Resource Description Framework
(RDF); Query languages; Entity resolution; Incomplete data.
Keywords
SPARQL, RDF, Large Language Models, Knowledge Graphs
1
Introduction
Knowledge graphs on the Web, such as Wikidata [13], are incom-
plete [5]. SPARQL is the W3C-recommended query language for
knowledge graphs in RDF [4]. A SPARQL query matches its graph
patterns only against the stored triples [10]. For example, Figure 1
shows an excerpt of a knowledge graph of the 2026 FIFA World
Cup with teams, groups and players from Wikidata. The query
SELECT ?pos WHERE { ?p ex:playsFor wd:Q79800 ; ex:position ?pos }
asks for the positions of the Argentine players and returns an empty
result, because the graph models no playing positions.
Large language models (LLMs) acquire factual knowledge during
pretraining on Web documents such as Wikipedia articles [11]
and generate candidate answers to questions about facts that a
graph lacks, such as the positions and the World Cup titles of
players. Extending the answers of a SPARQL query with values

generated by an LLM poses three obstacles. First, an LLM returns
entity names as strings, whereas the graph identifies entities by IRIs,
such as wd:Q615 for Lionel Messi. A SPARQL graph pattern relates
a generated name to an entity only through an identical label and
therefore cannot match variants such as Emiliano Martinez to the
label Emiliano Martínez. Second, an LLM also generates names of
entities outside the graph and names that denote no entity at all [6].
A name outside the graph can resemble the label of a different
entity, so a comparison that tolerates variants can also produce
incorrect matches. Third, a prompt with a query variable yields one
LLM call per binding, such as one call per player.
Four lines of existing work combine LLMs with queries over
knowledge graphs. Text-to-SPARQL systems employ an LLM to
translate a question in natural language into a SPARQL query [3],
whose answers remain restricted to the stored facts. Work on LLM-
augmented knowledge graphs [8] materializes facts inferred by an
LLM in the graph before query evaluation and therefore spends LLM
calls on all entities of the graph, including entities that no query
reads. Retrieval-augmented generation over knowledge graphs [9]
retrieves facts from the graph as context for an LLM and returns the
answer of the LLM as text with names instead of IRIs, so a SPARQL
query cannot use the named entities in further graph patterns.
GraphDB invokes an LLM inside a SPARQL query through magic
predicates and binds the generated text to a variable as a literal [7].
The query itself has to relate the literal to an entity of the graph. The
mapping of generated names to entities of the graph thus remains
outside the query engine.
We present GenSPARQL, a generative extension of SPARQL.
GenSPARQL extends the SPARQL algebra with the operator GENOP,
which invokes an LLM during query evaluation and binds the gener-
ated values to query variables. Within the query engine, a similarity
join [2] can map generated names to entities of the graph. A name
matches an entity if the similarity between the name and a label of
the entity reaches a threshold 𝜃. The answer then contains the IRIs

planner schedules GENOP after the triple patterns that contain no
variable bound by GENOP and after the filters over variables bound
by the same triple patterns. The LLM is therefore invoked only for

The demonstration applies GenSPARQL to the World Cup graph
and a graph of Nobel laureates from Wikidata. In a web workbench
(Section 3), attendees write GENOP queries, choose the LLM and the
threshold 𝜃, and inspect the matched entities and the number of
LLM calls of each query.1 A recorded mode on the project page
requires no LLM.
2
GenSPARQL
In this section, we define the operator GENOP (Section 2.1) and the
similarity join that maps generated names to entities of the graph
(Section 2.2) and describe the query planner and the implementation
in Apache Jena (Section 2.3).
2.1
The GENOP Operator
Syntax. We extend the grammar of SPARQL 1.1 [4] with GENOP.
For a prompt string 𝑝, output variables ?v1, ..., ?vk, an IRI 𝑚that
identifies an LLM and a threshold 𝜃∈[0, 1], the expression
GENOP(𝑝, (?v1, ..., ?vk), 𝑚, 𝜃)
is an element of group graph patterns. The argument 𝜃is optional
and defaults to a threshold 𝜃0. GENOP expressions occur only out-
side EXISTS and NOT EXISTS. A placeholder {?x} in 𝑝refers to
the query variable ?x. A GENOP expression is in context mode if 𝑝
contains placeholders, and in base mode otherwise.
Semantics. The algebra of GenSPARQL extends the SPARQL
algebra [4] with GENOP patterns and similarity joins. A GENOP pat-
tern has the form GENOP𝜃(𝑝, ¯𝑣,𝑚, 𝑃), where 𝑝, ¯𝑣= (?𝑣1, . . . , ?𝑣𝑘), 𝑚
and 𝜃are the arguments of a GENOP expression and 𝑃is a graph pat-
tern. GENOP extends the solutions of 𝑃with values that the LLM 𝑚
generates for ¯𝑣. In a query, 𝑃is implicit and consists of the elements
of the enclosing group that contain no variable of ¯𝑣. The elements

Query Planning and Implementation
The planner orders the elements of a group as in the translation of
Section 2.1, so GenSPARQL sends one prompt for every solution
of 𝑃in context mode and a single prompt in base mode. Filters

precede 𝐺1 and remove solutions before the prompts. In Figure 2(a),
the LLM is invoked for the 26 Argentine players out of the 1,248
players in the graph, wherever GENOP stands in the group.
GenSPARQL extends the query engine ARQ of Apache Jena [1]
with a parser for the syntax and compiles a query into the algebra of
Section 2.1. The engine evaluates GENOP, the similarity join, FILTER
and every OPTIONAL, MINUS or UNION that contains GENOP, and ARQ
evaluates the other operators. GenSPARQL sends prompts to the
Anthropic API, to OpenRouter and to OpenAI-compatible APIs,
including those of the inference servers vLLM and Ollama for self-
hosted models. The prompts request the generated tuples as a JSON
array that is empty if the LLM has no answer. GenSPARQL obtains
embeddings from OpenAI-compatible APIs and falls back to the
Jaccard similarity if the embedding model fails. The default thresh-

the HTTP service. The workbench offers the World Cup graph

planner and with GENOP evaluated first, and shows the LLM
calls of both orders (Section 4).
(4) Writing new queries and uploading graphs. Attendees will

and patterns of their choice. Attendees can also upload a
graph of their own as a Turtle file.
Live and recorded modes. In the live mode, the service evaluates

Evaluation
We built the World Cup graph and the Nobel graph from Wikidata

laureates. We evaluated GenSPARQL on both graphs with the open-

thinking mode and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 at temperature 0 in the
inference server vLLM. The embedding similarity used the model
bge-large-en-v1.5. The repository contains the queries, the gold
standard from Wikidata and the results.
