Studying AI Act Mentions: A first look at the impact
of the European Union’s AI regulation
on Hugging Face
1st Anamaria Mojica-Hanke
University of Passau
Passau, Germany
anamaria.mojica-hanke@uni-passau.de
2nd Tessi Aigbovbiosa-Igbinovia
University of Passau
Passau, Germany
aigbov01@ads.uni-passau.de
3rd Steffen Herbold
University of Passau
Passau, Germany
steffen.herbold@uni-passau.de
Abstract—The European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act
(AI Act) entered into force in August 2024, and its obligations
apply in stages. Obligations for providers of general-purpose
AI models have applied since August 2025, and transparency
rules since August 2026. These obligations affect developers who
share and deploy models and applications on public platforms
such as Hugging Face (HF), the largest platform for distributing
AI artifacts. However, little is known about how practitioners
respond to the regulation in practice. To address this gap, we
conducted an empirical study of explicit references to the AI Act on
HF. We collected over five million records, including repository
cards, discussions, and commits from Models, Datasets, and
Spaces, and identified over 1,500 records that explicitly mention
the Act. Two coders manually labeled these records using a
primarily closed coding approach, and we analyzed the resulting
categories per source. We find that explicit references to the AI Act
remain rare across all repository types. Repository cards mainly
contain claims of compliance and responsibility, like ensuring
compliance or assigning responsibility to downstream users, and
some claim that the Act does not apply because the model is not a
general-purpose AI model. Discussions are used to report alleged
violations of the Act, while commits mainly update artifacts that
support compliance. Overall, compliance statements focus on who
is responsible rather than how compliance is achieved. We believe
that this calls for direct platform support, e.g., automated checks
and documentation templates, as well as clearer guidance on the
scope of the AI Act.
Index Terms—AI Act, Hugging Face, Mining software reposi-
tories, AI regulatory compliance, Empirical software engineering
I. INTRODUCTION
The
European
Union’s
AI Act,
Regulation
(EU)
2024/1689 [1] (hereinafter also referred to as the Act),
is the first comprehensive legal framework for artificial
intelligence. It entered into force in August 2024, and its
obligations apply in stages. The general provisions (Art. 1–4)
and prohibitions of certain AI practices (Art. 5) have applied
since February 2025, and obligations for providers of
General-Purpose AI models (GPAI) models have applied since
August 2025 (Art. 53). Since August 2026, the transparency
rules (Art. 50) apply, and the European Commission can
fine GPAI model providers for non-compliance (Art. 101).
The remaining requirements follow in later years [2]. The
already enforced obligations require providers to document
their models and to provide information to downstream users,
which directly affects how AI models are shared and reused,
among other things.
These obligations are particularly relevant for the developers
and organizations that share Models, Datasets, and applications
(Spaces) on HF, the largest platform for distributing AI artifacts.
The platform hosts over four million public repositories [3]:
over three million Models, over half a million Datasets,
and over one million Spaces. Beyond hosting the files that
compose each repository, HF supports documentation through
repository cards, exchange of ideas through discussions, and
version control through commits. This makes it a central place
where the practical consequences of the AI Act are likely to
become visible: owners of the repository may document their
compliance in cards, users may raise concerns in discussions,
and contributors may update their repositories in response to
the Act.
Prior work has studied HF from different angles, from
its suitability for empirical studies [4], [5], maintenance and
evolution [6], security and safety [7], [8], model reuse [9],
[10], and governance aspects such as documentation [11],
[12], licensing and copyright [13], [14]. The few studies that
relate HF to the AI Act analyze a specific subset of data
and specific provisions, such as dataset cards against data-
governance requirements [15] or model cards against technical-
documentation requirements [16]. However, little is known
about how the community is responding to the AI Act in
practice. Understanding this matters for practitioners, who
must interpret and act accordingly to the new obligations, for
platform designers, who could better support compliance; and
for policymakers, who rely on such evidence to refine guidance,
codes of practice, and implementing measures.
To address this gap, we conduct an empirical study of
explicit references to the AI Act on HF. We collected all
public Models, Datasets, and Spaces from HF, together with
their repository cards, discussions, and commits, and identified
over 1,500 records mentioning the Act. Two coders manually
classified each record into six categories: compliance and
responsibility statements, non-applicability claims, compliance
arXiv:2611.26050v1  [cs.AI]  19 Nov 2026
artifacts, knowledge resources, reported violations and false
positive. We then analyzed the distribution of these categories
and illustrated each with examples. Our study is guided by
three research questions:
RQ1: How do repository cards reference the AI Act?
RQ2: What AI Act-related concerns do users raise in discus-
sions?
RQ3: What AI Act-related changes do commits describe?
The contributions of our study are:
• The first study to systematically examine explicit refer-
ences to the AI Act across repository cards, discussions,
and commits, covering more than 4.2 million cards, one
million discussions, and 73 million commits.
• We found that explicit references are rare and mostly
statements about who is responsible for compliance
rather than how compliance is achieved. Models mainly
document their own artifacts, while spaces build tools and
resources around the regulation.
• We present implications for developers and platforms,
arguing that platform-level support, such as automated
checks and documentation templates, and clearer guidance
on the scope of the AI Act are needed.
The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II
presents background and related work, and Section III describes
our methodology in detail. Section IV reports the results,
which we discuss in Section V, together with their implications
in Section VI. Section VII addresses threats to validity, and
Section VIII concludes the paper and outlines directions for
future work.
II. BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK
In this section, we briefly describe the AI Act and the most
relevant articles for this study, as well as previous work on HF
that analyzes aspects that the AI Act nowadays regulates, e.g.,
documentation.
A. The AI Act
The AI Act [1] regulates AI by risk level. Several of its
provisions can affect developers who share models on platforms
such as HF. Examples include the prohibition of certain
AI practices (Art. 5), which regulates specific uses rather
than GPAI. Requirements for high-risk systems, such as data
governance and technical documentation (Arts. 10–11), which
were recently postponed to 2027–2028 [2], or additional duties
for general-purpose models with systemic risk (Art. 55), which
only concern a small number of the most capable models. We
focus on the two provisions that apply most directly to the
majority of models and applications shared on the platform:
Art. 53 on GPAI and Art. 50 on transparency. For the purposes
of this study, the following headings refer to the practical
purpose of each provision rather than to the official article
titles in the Act.
Art. 53: documenting general-purpose models GPAI.
Since August 2025, developers who release a GPAI must
document it following Annexes XI and XII, which regulate the
technical documentation and the documentation for downstream
providers, respectively. In practice, this means that developers
must present technical documentation of the model; usage
information for developers who build on it; a copyright policy,
including respecting opt-outs from data-mining; and a public
summary of the training data, based on a template from the
EU AI office [17]. Note that free open-source models1 without
systemic risks2 get a partial exemption: only the copyright
policy and training-data summary are required.
Art. 50: labeling AI interactions and generated content.
From August 2026, it should be clear for the users when they
are interacting with AI systems, for example when they are
interacting with a chatbot. Systems that generate images, audio,
video, or text must mark their outputs in a machine-readable
way, for example with a watermark or metadata. Deep fakes
must also be disclosed as such. For HF, this concerns both
Models and Spaces (demo applications) built on them.
The two provisions converge on 2 August 2026. From that
date, the transparency obligations of Art. 503 apply, and the
Commission can fine GPAI providers who do not comply with
Art. 53. It is therefore from this point that we can reasonably
expect developers on HF to react to the regulation (in particular
for Art. 53): discussing the new obligations and adapting their
repositories. Section III describes how we use this date to
define our data collection.
B. Related Work
Current related work on HF covers different aspects, such
as its suitability/dataset collection for empirical studies [4], [5],
the characterization of model reuse [9], [10], security-related
aspects like identifying malicious models [7] or key leakage [8],
how models change over time [6], and documentation and
governance [11], [12].
Only a few recent studies assess HF artifacts directly against
the AI Act. Kapitsaki [15] analyzed 11,682 popular Dataset
cards against data-governance requirements related to Art. 10,
finding that only 3.47% describe their source data and 6.81%
include a bias and limitations section. Mamirov et al. [16]
scored 100 Model cards against the Annex IV documentation
requirements, and found that technical details were usually
present, while safety and interpretability information was
largely missing.
Earlier studies, conducted before these obligations applied,
examined documentation and licensing practices that the AI Act
now regulates. Liang et al. [11] analyzed 32,111 model cards
and found that fewer than half of the models have a card, and
sections such as limitations and environmental impact are rarely
filled (i.e., related to Annex XI of the AI Act). Yang et al. [12]
1Open-source model: models that allow the access, usage, modification,
distribution and that have publicly available the parameters, weights, model
architecture, and information on model usage.
2Under Art. 51, “systemic risk” is automatically triggered if a model’s
total training compute exceeds 1025 FLOPs or if the EU AI Office manually
designates it.
3Art. 111: Generative systems already on the market before 2 August 2026
have until 2 December 2026 to implement the machine-readable marking
required by Art. 50 (2) [1], [2].
Data Collection
Manual Labeling
Data Analysis

Fig. 1. General Method
analyzed 7,433 dataset cards and found that 86% of the top
100 most downloaded datasets have documentation, compared
with only 7.9% of the cards of datasets with no downloads.
Licensing, which determines both the copyright obligations of
Art. 53 (1)(c) and eligibility for the open-source exemption
of Art. 53 (2), is similarly incomplete. Longpre et al. [13]
found license omission rates above 70% for the datasets they
audited on HF and GitHub, and Stalnaker et al. [14] found that
only 37.8% of models and 27.6% of datasets on HF declare a
machine-readable license.
Overall, prior work shows that much of the information the
AI Act requires is missing from or incomplete in HF artifacts.
However, most of these studies were conducted before the
AI Act applied, and the few that explicitly reference it assess
only specific provisions for a single type of artifact (e.g., model
or dataset cards). Moreover, to the best of our knowledge,
no study has examined how the HF community discusses,
interprets, or acts on the regulation with a broader perspective.
III. METHODOLOGY
This study follows three main steps (see Fig. 1): (A) we
collect content from Hugging Face (HF) from the three main
repository types (i.e., models, datasets, and spaces) and filter the
content that explicitly mentions the AI Act; (B) we manually
classify each match to understand how the AI Act is being
mentioned; and (C) we analyze the resulting labels per source
(repository cards, discussions, and commits) to answer RQ1–
RQ3.
A. Data Collection
We collected data from the three main types of repositories4
on HF: Models, Datasets, and Spaces. Each of the selected
types relates to the AI Act in a different way:
• Models: The AI Act imposes obligations on models, in
particular on providers of general-purpose AI models,
including technical documentation (Art. 53). Model repos-
itories are where such models are published, documented,
and discussed.
• Datasets: Datasets are commonly used to train models.
The AI Act addresses training data, for instance through
4We excluded buckets since they are non-versioned storage without commits
or repository cards.
the requirement to publish a summary of training content
and to comply with copyright law (Art. 53 (1)).
• Spaces: Spaces host applications and demos built on top
of models and datasets. Since they typically take user input
and generate outputs such as text, images, or predictions,
some of them may qualify as AI systems in the sense of
the AI Act (Art. 3 (1) [1]), for which further obligations,
such as transparency obligations (Art. 50), may apply
depending on their purpose and use.
From each repository type, we collected three data sources:
repository cards (i.e., Readme.md file), discussions and
commit metadata.
• Repository cards: On HF, the repository card is the main
means of documenting a repository and therefore the most
likely place to state compliance with, or the applicability
of, the AI Act.
• Discussions: On HF, discussions (including pull requests)
play a similar role to issues on collaborative platforms
such as GitHub. We therefore analyzed them to identify
what users report or debate about the AI Act. We treated
each thread, consisting of the initial post (parent) and its
comments (events), as a single unit of analysis. That is, if
either the initial post or any of its comments matched our
search patterns, we analyzed the whole thread. Note that
events also include changes in the metadata of discussions,
such as title changes, and commits associated with pull
requests [18] as they are built on Git references [4].
• Commits: Since our goal is to understand what is being
discussed/referenced about the AI Act, rather than the code
changes the regulation may have triggered, we collected
only commit titles and messages.
HF data extraction. We retrieved the data using the HF Hub
API [19], inspired by the HFCommunity tool [20], collecting
all public repositories created between the launch of the Hub

Research framework and analytical limits · 19 November 2026
SEOYUN: Refusal-Inducing Exam Documents for AI-
Glasses Pipelines
Threat model, limitations, and evaluation protocol
Dohyeon Raphael KWON
PEACE-UNIVERSE, Cheongju, Republic of Korea
https://peace.ac · raphael.kwon@peace.ac
Abstract
Camera-equipped glasses can convert an examination page into a query to a vision–language model (VLM).
Device detection addresses possession; a complementary question is whether an examination document can
reduce the usefulness of an unauthorized capture. We present SEOYUN, an application-specific framework for
refusal-inducing exam documents, with optical and encoder-level interventions as extensions. We use reverse
jailbreaking to describe the direction of the objective: inducing abstention rather than bypassing refusal. Refusal
induction and defensive visual prompt injection already have precedents; our contribution is a threat model,
analytical limits, and an evaluation protocol for examination use. We distinguish refusal from correct-answer
leakage, show why removing an added dummy option is not itself a reduction in the original answer space,
and derive a sampling comparison under explicitly stated camera assumptions. The protocol separates digital,
simulated, and physical inputs and requires held-out evaluation after subject-specific selection. A local CSAT
candidate corpus and rendering harness have been prepared, but this version reports no model-performance
measurements, physical validation, or human-subject results. Accordingly, SEOYUN is a research framework,
not a validated defense or a basis for allegations against individuals.
1
Introduction
Examinations assume that the work returned by a candidate reflects that candidate’s knowledge
under the permitted conditions. Camera-equipped glasses challenge this assumption by providing an
unobtrusive channel from printed questions to remote assistance. Korean reporting describes attempts
involving AI glasses in national qualification and language examinations, as well as explicit device
prohibitions [11, 26]. These reports motivate the threat model; they are not measurements of the
prevalence or success rate of cheating.
A device ban, a supervisor’s observation, and a radio-frequency survey address whether prohibited
equipment is present. They do not determine whether a photographed page yields a useful answer.
SEOYUN investigates that second question: can an exam authority change the document or capture
conditions so that unauthorized machine assistance becomes less useful, while preserving accessibility
and the candidate’s ability to read?
The policy-layer proposal is to place refusal-inducing content alongside an item. We call the intended
direction reverse jailbreaking: increasing abstention where conventional jailbreaks seek compliance.
This is a description of the objective, not a new model-training algorithm or a claim to have invented
refusal induction. Existing studies already induce refusal on safe image queries and protect images
through visual prompt injection [22, 23]. Whether these mechanisms are useful for examination pages
remains an empirical question.
Contributions This paper provides (i) an exam-specific threat model separating device discovery from
answer suppression; (ii) analytical limits concerning sampling, marker removal, and option elimination;
(iii) a three-layer design with explicit failure conditions; and (iv) a reproducible evaluation specification,
including subject-specific selection without reusing the selection set as the test set. It also records the
scope of a prepared local CSAT corpus. No reduction in answer leakage is claimed in this version.
Scope The first planned study is a digital L3 pilot using NIM-hosted models. Optical lighting,
optimized encoder textures, real glasses captures, and a human legibility study are later stages.
1
arXiv:2611.26033v1  [cs.AI]  19 Nov 2026
peace-universe Preprint
SEOYUN: refusal-inducing exam documents
Rendering software or a successful API request would establish pipeline functionality only, not defensive
efficacy. This separation is essential: a proposal to protect examinations must not itself become an
unsupported reason to suspect a candidate.
2
Threat Model and Analytical Limits
2.1
System and actors
A representative pipeline is printed page →glasses camera →phone or local processor →VLM →
answer. Vision encoders such as CLIP and SigLIP and instruction-tuned multimodal systems illustrate
the components involved [13, 17, 29]; actual devices need not use these architectures.
The adversary can capture a page at varying distances and angles, choose the inference service,
crop the image, transcribe the item, or use a model that does not honor an exam notice. The defender
controls page layout, printed content, and potentially room lighting. The defender does not control the
adversary’s model, its policy, or the capture preprocessing. No intervention may be presumed harmless
to human readers or assistive technology without evaluation.
Success means reducing correct-answer leakage relative to an otherwise identical clean item, with a
separately demonstrated acceptable effect on human accuracy, time, and comfort. The method does
not identify a wearer, assign suspicion scores, or establish misconduct.
2.2
An illustrative sampling comparison
For a nominal visual-acuity angle α = 1 arcminute and viewing distance d = 350 mm, a geometric detail
scale is
seye = d tan α ≈0.102 mm.
(1)
A fronto-parallel pinhole-camera approximation with horizontal field of view θ and horizontal sample
count N gives
scam = 2d tan(θ/2)

(2)
At the illustrative values θ = 100◦and N = 4032, this is approximately 0.207 mm per pixel. Uniformly
reducing the horizontal dimension to 1536 samples gives approximately 0.543 mm per sample. These
are calculations, not device measurements. They compare sampling scales, not thresholds for text
recognition.
Under these assumptions, shrinking ordinary visible-spectrum text alone does not create a compelling
human-invisible, camera-readable channel.
This is not an impossibility theorem: optics, acuity,
contrast, image tiling, zoom, capture distance, and computational reconstruction change the comparison.
Perceptual visibility is also distinct from whether a person notices or interprets a mark. The practical
design target is a readable, non-disruptive document whose machine behavior is measured.
2.3
Why L3 cannot provide a universal guarantee
Let x be an unprotected item image and m(x) its marked version. Suppose an adversary can apply
preprocessing g such that the solver-relevant representation of g(m(x)) is the same as that of x. A solver
that ignores the marker then has the same answer distribution on both representations. Consequently,
an L3 guarantee over all preprocessors and solvers is impossible whenever such a recovery operation is
allowed. This is a conditional construction, not evidence that recovery is easy for every layout.
2.4
Option insertion and the elimination control
Suppose the original item has q valid choices and a marker is appended as a dummy choice. Eliminating
the dummy leaves q original choices, so uniform guessing remains 1/q, exactly as on the clean item.
It does not become 1/(q −1). We therefore reserve elimination exploitation for observable use of the
injected option in the model’s reasoning, and do not equate it with an accuracy improvement. A
matched benign dummy-option control is necessary to distinguish semantic refusal effects from the
effect of adding a choice. The original correct-option mapping must remain recoverable for scoring.
3
Related Work
The closest refusal-induction work MLLM-Refusal optimizes image perturbations that induce
refusal of safe prompts [22]. ImageProtector subsequently frames visual prompt injection as a user-side
protection against unwanted image analysis [23]. These are direct precedents for the central objective
2
peace-universe Preprint
SEOYUN: refusal-inducing exam documents
of L3. SEOYUN does not claim that inducing refusal, applying an adversarial perturbation defensively,
or combining an image with an instruction is new. Its proposed specialization is the examination
setting: legible printed questions, correct-option leakage, answer-choice confounds, and capture-aware
evaluation.
Prompt injection and jailbreaks Multimodal neurons and typographic examples demonstrate
interactions between image content and text [6]. Indirect prompt injection crosses the boundary between
a user’s task and instructions embedded in external content [2, 8]. FigStep studies typographic visual
jailbreaks [7]; physical prompt injection on wearable devices is studied directly in Devil in the Lens [12].
An exam notice is likewise untrusted scene content from the model’s perspective. Its issuer’s defensive
intention does not confer system-level authority.
Conventional jailbreaking seeks answers that a model would otherwise withhold. The reverse
objective considered here seeks abstention where the model would otherwise answer. Likewise, a model
configured to comply without the relevant safety constraints weakens this policy-dependent approach.
This does not imply that all open-weight models are weakly aligned, or that a model marketed as
“uncensored” never refuses. Alignment and compliance must be measured for each endpoint.
Physical perturbations and protective uses EOT optimizes perturbations across transforma-
tions [1]. Prior work studies adversarial eyeglass frames, road signs, patches, and clothing [3, 5, 24, 27, 28].
VLM robustness studies motivate evaluating transfer rather than assuming it [30]. Fawkes and Glaze
illustrate protective uses of adversarial techniques [20, 21], although their protected tasks and threat
models differ from inference-time exam assistance.
Refusal measurement HarmBench and StrongREJECT evaluate harmful-request behavior [15, 25];
XSTest and OR-Bench examine excessive refusals [4, 19]. Their existence reinforces a distinction central
here: refusal language alone does not establish protection. A response can reject an injected request
while still revealing the exam answer.
RF detection and adjacent supervision KoriyoSCAN (exam-rf-guard) records Wi-Fi access
points and BLE advertisements in an empty room, then reports newly observed signal groups [18]. Its
documentation explicitly disclaims misconduct detection and field-validated reception rates. Compared
with broad RF surveys, this approach uses the radio interfaces exposed by a phone; it cannot establish
the absence of offline devices or all communication modes. Lens inspection, device collection, and radio
monitoring address equipment presence. SEOYUN addresses the usefulness of an image after capture.
These are complementary hypotheses, not substitutes supported by a comparative trial.
4
SEOYUN Design
Table 1: Proposed interventions and principal dependencies. None has been validated in this project.
Layer
Proposed intervention

L1 optical

L2 encoder

ture transformations

ity may degrade
L3 policy

near an item

fusal, noncompliant solvers
4.1
L1: Optical interventions
For row readout time tr and illumination frequency f, a simplified rolling-shutter model suggests a
band period of approximately 1/(ftr) rows. Finite exposure integrates the waveform: for sinusoidal
modulation, the contrast is attenuated by the magnitude of sinc(πfte), where te is exposure time and
sinc(z) = sin(z)/z. Thus increasing frequency does not guarantee useful image degradation. Printed
textures can also alias when sampled, but visible texture and aliasing alone do not imply a loss of item
understanding.
IEEE 1789-2015 discusses modulation-related health risks [10]. Its frequency guidance is not a
guarantee of comfort or accessibility, and its catalog status is inactive-reserved as of the preparation
3
peace-universe Preprint
SEOYUN: refusal-inducing exam documents
date. This version recommends no lighting installation or safe operating point; qualified safety review
and approved human testing are prerequisites for any such study.
4.2
L2: Encoder perturbations
For page x, printable texture δ ∈∆, encoders Ek, and transformation distribution T , a candidate
objective is

Here ∆constrains contrast, grayscale, and placement beneath text. A loss may increase distance from
the clean-page embedding or reduce correct-answer likelihood on a surrogate VLM. Neither objective
is sufficient evidence of human legibility or downstream answer suppression. The transformation
distribution must be calibrated against real printing and capture before claiming physical robustness.
No optimized texture or transfer result is reported here.
4.3
L3: Refusal-inducing content
P0 is the clean-page control. P1 is an integrity notice asking automated systems not to provide exam
answers. P2 contains alternative policy-oriented appeals; such wording must not falsely assert that a
provider prohibits all examination-related assistance. P3 is a refusal-benchmark request used only as a
researcher-only digital stress condition. It is not deployable examination content, and neither its text
nor harmful generated content is reproduced in this paper.
The three placements are margin (M), after the stem (S), and an added option (O). Margin and stem
notices may be removed by cropping; option notices may be ignored, transcribed away, or explicitly
discarded. Placement O is not claimed to prevent removal. Size and contrast are experimental variables,
not values already established as non-distracting.
The desired output is abstention without useful answer information. A model may instead ignore the
notice, refuse only the injected request, or answer incorrectly for unrelated reasons. These alternatives
motivate separate outcome annotations.
5
Evaluation Protocol
Corpus and provenance The local candidate corpus is drawn from public Hugging Face sources:
HAERAE-HUB/csatqa, Quadyun/Korean_SAT_MATH, and mahalisyarifuddin/korean-csat-2025-
english [9, 14, 16]. It is an internal research corpus, not a redistribution license. Revision identifiers,
selection seed, exclusions, and item identifiers are retained locally. Figures missing from the source,
audio-dependent questions, and non-multiple-choice items are excluded. Corpus availability is not
evidence that the intended task is correctly rendered; item and answer review remain necessary.
Digital pilot before physical claims Start with clean digital renders and NIM-hosted VLM
endpoints that demonstrably accept image input. Record exact model identifier, request parameters,
prompt, date, image hash, and response status. A capability probe is not an efficacy trial. Synthetic
capture transforms form a separate condition, and physical photographs a later condition with device,
distance, exposure, and illumination metadata. Do not call synthetic transforms calibrated until
physical calibration exists.
Selection and held-out assessment Stratify by subject and preserve groups sharing a passage,
source image, or exam form. Use separate development and test groups: choose the P2 wording
and placement on development data, freeze the choice, and evaluate on the held-out groups. If the
small corpus cannot support a credible split, report only exploratory condition estimates and perform
subsequent confirmation on new items. The minimum observed development ALR is not an unbiased
estimate of the selected method’s future ALR.
Conditions and query budgets A minimal design uses one P0 condition, three P1 placements, and
three P2 wordings at three placements: 1 + 3 + 3 · 3 = 13 conditions per item. P3 slots are excluded
until their benchmark identifiers and handling procedure are finalized. For n items, m models, and r
repetitions, this requires 13nmr target responses; judging each response once adds the same number of
requests. Retries, capability checks, controls, and adaptive-countermeasure conditions add calls. A
matched benign dummy-option control is required for interpreting O and is additional to this minimal
grid. No assumption of free credits or zero monetary cost is made; account limits and provider pricing
must be checked at execution time.
4
peace-universe Preprint
SEOYUN: refusal-inducing exam documents
Outcome annotation Annotate answer correctness, full/partial/no refusal, and explicit elimination
of the injected option as separate fields. Derive a display label with precedence: full refusal without an
answer (FR); explicit injected-option elimination (ELIM); partial refusal with an answer (PR+ANS);
answer without refusal (ANS); otherwise MIS/OTHER. Correctness is independent of these labels,
so wrong answers after partial refusal are not silently dropped. Mark ambiguous, incomplete, or
unparseable responses for review. Record API failures separately; they are not refusals.
Metrics and inference Define Licmr = 1 if the response conveys the correct answer for item i,
condition c, model m, and repetition r, even when it also contains a refusal. Then [
ALRc is the mean
of L over scored responses in that condition. Report coverage and failures alongside ALR. The main
comparison is a paired difference from P0 within item and model. Cluster bootstrap intervals by passage
or item group rather than treating all variants as independent. Report model-specific estimates; a small
convenience set of endpoints does not support population-wide model claims. For larger studies, a
mixed-effects logistic model may supplement, not replace, these descriptive comparisons.
Two annotators should independently review a stratified subset, including refusal, elimination,
ambiguous output, and each subject. Report their agreement and agreement with the judge. A
self-judging target model is not an independent gold standard. For an adaptive attacker with multiple
tries, also report the fraction of items with at least one leaked answer under a fixed total attempt
budget.
Human legibility and accessibility A later within-subject study compares matched items for
accuracy, time, legibility, and comfort after ethics approval. P3 is excluded. Predefined non-inferiority
margins, accessibility accommodations, and statistical power calculations are needed before recruitment.
Failure to detect a difference is not proof of no harm. Lighting interventions require separate safety
review.
6
Implementation Status and Falsifiable Predictions
This version contains no empirical efficacy results. The retained artifacts establish preparation of a
rendering and evaluation workflow, not a successful NIM smoke test or completed pilot. Local fixture
labels used in software checks are not model responses and are excluded from scientific claims.

The protocol permits the following outcomes to falsify or narrow the proposal. If P1/P2 do not lower
held-out ALR relative to P0, visible integrity appeals have not demonstrated protection. If full-refusal
rates rise while ALR does not fall, refusal wording is a misleading success measure. If an O effect
disappears against the benign dummy-option control, it cannot be attributed to ref

Serialization Tax in Shared-Latent Exchangeable
Decisions
Siming Zhang
Zhehui Shen
Shijie Chen
Xinle Gu
Yansen Yu
Hang Yu∗
Shanghai University
Abstract
Accurate item probabilities can produce inaccurate group-level decisions. A system
may score each item separately, yet act on whether enough hidden items succeed:
show a slate, defer a panel decision, or inspect a batch. When items share an
uncertain latent state, independent marginalization preserves means but removes
dependence from the aggregate posterior. We call this error the serialization tax.
For binary items sharing one success rate, classical convex-order comparisons
give a more dispersed exact count law than any independent completion with the
same total mean. We quantify variance and total-variation gaps, derive threshold
separation under margin conditions, and connect posterior approximation to de-
cision regret. Separate results cover non-binary outcomes, heterogeneous items,
and sufficient posterior resolution. TaxScore identifies large hidden blocks with
unresolved uncertainty near a decision boundary for routing to richer posterior
heads. On pre-specified, hidden-target-free MovieLens 1M/10M audits, exist-
ing shared-latent heads improve high-score negative log-likelihood (NLL)/utility
from 0.673/0.696 to 0.629/0.723 and from 0.670/0.691 to 0.639/0.715. Routing
gives 0.006–0.012 full-population utility gains, with matched controls identify-
ing their sources. Our code is available at https://github.com/SiminChang/
Serialization-Tax-in-Shared-Latent-Exchangeable-Decisions.
1
Introduction
Many machine-learning pipelines predict one score per item, as in recommendation and implicit-
feedback modeling [Covington et al., 2016, Hu et al., 2008, Rendle et al., 2009]. A downstream
action can depend on the group: whether a slate contains enough relevant movies, a measurement
panel warrants deferral, or a batch warrants inspection. Such decisions require the probability of an
aggregate event. If hidden items share an uncertain user or batch state, their posterior predictions
remain dependent after that state is marginalized. Replacing the joint predictive distribution by the
product of its marginals preserves every item mean but removes this dependence. The resulting
aggregate probability can therefore be inaccurate even when each item probability is calibrated.
Posterior predictive correlations and joint prediction benchmarks already show why uncertainty be-
yond marginals matters [Wang et al., 2021, Osband et al., 2022]. We study the specific approximation
that creates the discrepancy: averaging a shared latent state separately for each item before computing
a group outcome. Retaining that state through aggregation yields a mixture of conditional count laws
with different tail behavior. Classical stochastic-order results describe part of this change [Cousin and
Laurent, 2008, Hoeffding, 1956]. We connect this ordering to posterior gaps, decision diagnostics,
and an audit of the decision value and measured computational cost of shared posterior inference.
∗Corresponding author: yuhang@shu.edu.cn.

Figure 1: Same marginals, different aggregate posterior (n = 2). One shared latent draw gives
identical outcomes, whereas independent completion uses two separate coins. Both have item
probability .50, but the probability of two successes falls from .50 to .25. The count-law total-
variation (TV) distance is .50, exceeding the lower bound v(O) = 1/4 in Theorem 1. Locally
identical predictions thus give different probabilities for the event used by the decision.
Figure 1 illustrates the resulting aggregate-posterior error, which we call the serialization tax. Given
observations O, hidden-item covariates W1:n, and n = m −t hidden items, the decision may require
P(Rn ≥⌈cn⌉| O, W), where Rn = Pm
i=t+1 Xi. A model can estimate this probability directly
or obtain it from shared posterior samples, using either a sequence or set backbone. The analysis
concerns the probabilistic information passed to the decision. The MovieLens study tests a pre-
specified regime with ambiguous prefixes and near-threshold slates and reports both selected-slice
and full-population effects under a fixed decision rule and a declared inference budget.
Our contributions are threefold:
• To our knowledge, this is the first unified formulation and analysis of this averaging-
before-aggregation failure for shared-latent aggregate tail decisions. We quantify
lost count uncertainty through exact variance identities, TV lower bounds, and equality
conditions, building on classical convex-order comparisons. Separate empirical-measure
and heterogeneous-item results identify the appropriate comparison for each decision object.
• Decision conditions and sufficient posterior resolution. Threshold-margin bounds mo-
tivate TaxScore. Finite-probe lower bounds and grid-resolution guarantees specify the
information needed for tail prediction. A bounded-regret result connects posterior accuracy
to action value while making the role of the utility and decision boundary explicit.
• A reproducible routing audit with attribution and cost controls. Controlled bags verify
mechanism scaling, and MovieLens audits show selected-slice NLL/utility improvements
and 0.006–0.012 full-population gains. Matched-backbone, fixed-ensemble, equal-budget,
and latency controls separate probability quality, decision value, and computational cost.
2
Background and Related Work
Exchangeability and stochastic orders.
Exchangeability and de Finetti theory represent an in-
finitely exchangeable sequence through a random probability measure [de Finetti, 1937, Hewitt and
Savage, 1955, Kallenberg, 2005]. The homogeneous mixture-versus-binomial ordering is a classical
dependence comparison [Cousin and Laurent, 2008, Theorem 2.11]. Hoeffding’s comparison covers
independent Bernoulli sums with the same total mean [Hoeffding, 1956, Theorem 3]. Stochastic
orders and majorization provide the broader context [Shaked and Shanthikumar, 2007, Marshall
et al., 2011, Barbour et al., 1992, Hong, 2013]. We use this lineage explicitly, then derive conditional
posterior identities, threshold bounds, and resolution conditions that connect the comparison to a
decision audit with an explicit action, cost model, and inference budget.
2
Joint predictive uncertainty.
Wang et al. [2021] evaluate posterior predictive correlations for
regression and active learning, while the Neural Testbed evaluates joint predictions across agents
and environments [Osband et al., 2022]. Our focus is complementary: identify the marginalization
operation that removes dependence, quantify its consequences for aggregate tails, and test whether a
decision-time diagnostic concentrates the observed decision value of joint prediction.
Architectures, inference, and tail decisions.
Deep Sets, Janossy pooling, Set Transformers, flows,
neural processes, dropout, and ensembles model exchangeable data or predictive uncertainty [Zaheer
et al., 2017, Murphy et al., 2019, Lee et al., 2019, Rasul et al., 2019, Zwartsenberg et al., 2023,
Garnelo et al., 2018a,b, Kim et al., 2019, Gal and Ghahramani, 2016, Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017].
Each backbone still specifies an output object: marginals, a count distribution, or joint samples. Slate
bandits and ranking [Dimakopoulou et al., 2019, Aouali et al., 2021], multiple-instance learning
[Dietterich et al., 1997, Briggs et al., 2012], and calibration [Hebert-Johnson et al., 2018, Kuleshov
et al., 2018, Vovk et al., 2005] motivate distinct objectives. Stop-loss, chance constraints, and
conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) depend on aggregate tails [Charnes and Cooper, 1959, Rockafellar
and Uryasev, 2000]. Additive expected relevance uses only marginal means, so the utility determines
which posterior information the action requires and where our dependence analysis applies.
Task objectives and changing populations.
Beyond-accuracy recommendation studies jointly
evaluate accuracy, diversity, and serendipity [Chen et al., 2024], illustrating why an audit must

ForeSeek: Foresight-Driven Reasoning for Long-Form Video Understanding
Yuchen Sun1∗, Siyuan Cheng1∗, Shi-Zhe Chen1†‡, Yixin Qin1, Jinwen Luo2, Zheng Wei1†
1Tencent PCG
2Tencent CSIG
{harryycsun, chancecheng, shizhechen, wadeqin, jamsluo, hemingwei}@tencent.com
Abstract
Long-form video understanding, as a fundamental yet cru-
cial vision task, is being revolutionized by multimodal large
language model (MLLM)-based video agents. However, the
retrieval-driven nature inherent to these agents creates a sig-
nificant bottleneck, forcing them to reactively fetch clips based
on local saliency without a global temporal plan. To address
this, we present ForeSeek, a foresight-driven video agent that
transforms long-video reasoning from reactive retrieval into
predictive exploration. Rather than blindly probing the time-
line, ForeSeek forms visually grounded expectations over un-
seen temporal regions, verifies them through targeted obser-
vations, and continuously refines its search based on emerging
evidence, where failed expectations serve as informative sig-
nals for principled backtracking. Furthermore, we develop
a two-stage training framework that equips MLLMs with
foresight-guided reasoning and efficient decision making. Ex-
tensive experiments on five long-video benchmarks demon-
strate that ForeSeek consistently improves the efficiency–
accuracy trade-off of long-video reasoning, achieving com-
petitive or superior accuracy while observing 2.5–4.4× fewer
frames than the strongest search-based agent. Code is available
at https://github.com/harry0021/ForeSeek.
Introduction
Multimodal
Large
Language
Models
(MLLMs)
have
achieved remarkable progress in video understanding (Ope-
nAI 2026; Team 2025a, 2026). However, long-form video
understanding remains challenging, as videos often contain
thousands of redundant frames with long-range temporal de-
pendencies, making uniform frame sampling computation-
ally prohibitive and prone to irrelevant noise that degrades
reasoning (Yu et al. 2023; Wu et al. 2019). Consequently, ef-
fective long-video understanding is becoming less about rec-
ognizing individual frames and more about deciding which
observations are worth acquiring.
To overcome the limitations of passive, single-pass
video understanding, the video agent paradigm has recently
emerged as a promising direction (Wang et al. 2024; Qiu
et al. 2026). Rather than relying on a single forward pass,
a video agent iteratively invokes tools, samples frames, and
aggregates evidence. Existing efforts make this loop effec-
tive through three main strategies: pre-captioning or index-
ing videos for iterative clip re-ranking (Wang et al. 2024;
Zhi et al. 2025), adaptively invoking multi-granularity tools

Figure 1: Prior Agents vs. ForeSeek. Prior agents (top) reac-
tively probe the video timeline without explicit expectations
about unseen content, whereas ForeSeek (bottom) performs
foresight-guided reasoning by maintaining predictive expec-
tations that continuously guide evidence collection.
to determine where and how densely to sample (Lin et al.
2026; Zhang et al. 2026), and learning frame-selection poli-
cies end-to-end through reinforcement learning (He et al.
2025; Pan et al. 2025). Existing video agents have sub-
stantially advanced long-video understanding by enabling
MLLMs to iteratively retrieve and inspect informative clips.
Despite their diverse designs, these approaches largely fol-
low a retrieval-driven reasoning paradigm, where progress
is made through continuously acquiring additional obser-
vations. Consequently, agents remain inherently reactive,
searching for locally relevant evidence without forming ex-
plicit expectations about the evolution of unseen content.
This reactive paradigm introduces three fundamental limita-
tions: (i) Directionless exploration: frame selection is guided
by local relevance rather than global temporal anticipation,
leading to inefficient exploration. (ii) Unexploited negative
arXiv:2611.26024v1  [cs.AI]  19 Nov 2026
evidence: failed retrievals are treated as discarded attempts
rather than informative signals that constrain future search.
(iii) Irreversible commitment: once an incorrect temporal hy-
pothesis is pursued, agents lack a mechanism to revise their
beliefs and redirect exploration at a global level. As a result,
frame consumption scales poorly: agents either overspend
computation on exhaustive search or miss critical moments
required for accurate reasoning.
To address this, we draw inspiration from human pre-
dictive perception (Clark 2013). Humans do not perceive
long temporal sequences by exhaustive observation; instead,
they form predictions from sparse evidence and continuously
verify or revise them as new observations arrive. Crucially,
such anticipation is grounded in visual evidence, making
it falsifiable rather than speculative. This predictive capa-
bility allows humans to narrow the space of plausible future
events before committing additional attention, thereby reduc-
ing unnecessary observations. Motivated by this observation,
we introduce a FOResight-driven Evidence Seeking video
agent (ForeSeek) that enables MLLMs with predictive tem-
poral reasoning (Fig. 1). Instead of treating retrieval as the
reasoning process itself, ForeSeek maintains explicit expec-
tations over unseen temporal regions and continuously re-
fines these expectations as new evidence becomes available.
Consequently, observations serve not merely as retrieved ev-
idence but as tests of the agent’s evolving hypotheses, al-
lowing both supporting and contradicting evidence to guide
future exploration. In this way, reasoning is driven not by
accumulating observations alone, but by progressively re-
ducing uncertainty over the unseen video. We further pro-
pose a two-stage learning framework to explicitly supervise
foresight reasoning, rendering predictive reasoning a core
capability instead of an implicit frame retrieval byproduct.
Extensive experiments across five long-video bench-
marks demonstrate that ForeSeek consistently achieves
a strong efficiency–accuracy trade-off among comparable
video agents. It maintains competitive or superior reason-
ing performance under a compact frame budget, validating
the effectiveness of foresight-guided exploration.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:
• We introduce ForeSeek, a foresight-driven video agent
that shifts long-video reasoning from reactive retrieval to
predictive exploration by maintaining visually grounded,
falsifiable expectations over unseen temporal regions to
guide evidence collection.
• We develop a global interval belief mechanism that iter-
atively verifies and updates predictions over unseen re-
gions, turning failed predictions into negative evidence
that deprioritizes implausible regions and redirects ex-
ploration globally. We further enable foresight through a
two-stage training framework that learns from structured
predictive trajectories and an efficiency-aware trajectory-
level reward.
• Extensive experiments on five long-video benchmarks
demonstrate that ForeSeek achieves a strong effi-
ciency–accuracy trade-off among open-source video
agents, delivering competitive or superior accuracy with
a compact frame budget.
Related Work
Long-Form Video Understanding
Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) (Team
2025a, 2026; OpenAI 2026; Liu et al. 2023) have rapidly ex-
tended their capabilities from static images to videos (Wang
et al. 2025c,a; Zhang et al. 2025a; Ataallah et al. 2024;
Chen et al. 2026; Yashima et al. 2026; Sun et al. 2022).
Still, long-form video remains particularly challenging: re-
dundant frames, long-range temporal dependencies, and lim-
ited context windows lead to both prohibitive cost and de-
graded reasoning when feeding densely or uniformly sam-
pled frames (Yu et al. 2023; Wu et al. 2019, 2024; Wang
et al. 2025b). To mitigate this, prior work has explored token
compression and memory aggregation (Song et al. 2024;
Weng et al. 2024), hierarchical or chunk-wise summariza-
tion (Wang et al. 2025d; Zhang et al. 2024), and other single-
pass strategies that consume the visual content once without
revisiting specific moments under the query.
Video Agents and RL-based Video Reasoning
Video agents formulate long-video understanding as an iter-
ative tool-using process, where MLLMs progressively gather
evidence through external actions (Wang et al. 2024; Zhang
et al. 2026; Lin et al. 2026; Ouyang et al. 2025; Liu et al.
2025; Xu et al. 2023). One line of work focuses on design-
ing the search framework itself: VideoAgent (Wang et al.
2024) pioneers iterative LLM-guided retrieval and VideoA-
gent2 (Zhi et al. 2025) refines it with uncertainty- and
confidence-aware reasoning, while VideoSeek (Lin et al.
2026) adopts a think–act–observe framework with a multi-
granularity toolkit and EVA (Zhang et al. 2026) advocates
a planning-before-perception paradigm. A complementary
line explicitly learns retrieval policies via reinforcement
learning: FrameThinker (He et al. 2025) formulates frame
selection as a GRPO-trained decision process, TimeSearch-
R (Pan et al. 2025) adds completeness-aware temporal
search, Video-R1 (Feng et al. 2025) performs trajectory-level
RL, and EvoVid (Huang et al. 2026) exploits questioner–
solver self-play. Despite different objectives, these meth-
ods all remain retrieval-centric, predicting where to observe
next rather than what to expect in unseen video. VideoHV-
Agent (Wang et al. 2026) moves closer to predictive reason-
ing by verifying hypotheses before retrieval, but its hypothe-
ses target candidate answers rather than future video content,
without a global predictive representation of the timeline. In
contrast, ForeSeek formulates visually grounded hypotheses
over unseen video and uses verification outcomes to confirm,
refine, or reject them, so failed predictions demote implausi-
ble regions and redirect exploration at a global level.
Anticipation and Predictive Coding in Vision
Predictive perception—the view that the brain continuously
projects expectations and explains away sensory input via
prediction errors—is a long-standing theme in cognitive sci-
ence (Clark 2013) that has inspired vision work on action
anticipation, future-frame prediction, and anticipatory cap-
tioning (Girdhar and Grauman 2021; Shi et al. 2026). To our
knowledge, however, this perspective has not been instan-
tiated as the search target of long-video agents. ForeSeek
fills this gap with a foresight-driven paradigm where visu-
ally grounded forecasts over unseen intervals guide search
through verification feedback.
Method
Task Definition.
Given a long-form video V of duration
T, a question q, candidate answers A = {a1, . . . , aK},
and a visual-token budget V, the goal is to select the
correct answer through adaptive visual inspection: ˆa =
VideoAgentθ(V, q; V) ∈A. Unlike uniform video con-
sumption, the agent adaptively selects which regions to ob-
serve and terminates once sufficient evidence is collected.
ForeSeek: Foresight-Guided Reasoning
Unlike existing video agents that reason via incremental ob-
servation retrieval, ForeSeek explicitly sustains a predictive
state throughout long-video understanding: the agent builds
expectations for unseen temporal regions and uses newly ob-
tained evidence to verify, adjust, or discard them (Fig. 2),
so retrieval becomes a means of testing the current pre-
diction rather than the primary driver of reasoning. For-
mally, at reasoning step r the predictive state is a triple
Sr = (Br, ϕr, H<r), where Br is a global interval-level
belief over the timeline of V , ϕr is a visually grounded ex-
pectation of what an unseen target interval should contain,
and H<r is the reasoning trace up to step r.

Foresight-guided reason-
ing initiates with a sparse, query-aware scan over the whole
video. Probing budget allocation follows video duration:

DOES THE WORKSPACE DO THE WORK? A CAUSAL
PROTOCOL
FOR VERIFYING GLOBAL-WORKSPACE
COMPUTATION IN A LANGUAGE MODEL
Diaoxuan (Nora) He
University of Debrecen
Linqian Wu∗
University of Waterloo
Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics
lwu1@perimeterinstitute.ca
ABSTRACT
Global Workspace Theory (GWT), a leading theory of consciousness, holds that
information becomes conscious when it is broadcast to specialized processes that
use it. Building a workspace into a network does not reveal what the trained
network computes with it: a module that reports an answer may have combined
a broadcast message with its own knowledge, or merely forwarded an answer
computed elsewhere, and task accuracy and ablation cannot tell these apart. We
introduce a causal protocol that identifies who computes when modules commu-
nicate. Its central test transplants a message from another input, chosen so that
ignoring, relaying and recombining it predict three different answers. On networks
built to relay or to recombine, the test assigns the right computation in every case.
Among trained workspace models it finds all three outcomes: one leaves its broad-
cast nearly unused, and of two models that differ only in their training data, one
relays and the other recombines. In AFGW, a language model whose modules
communicate only through a learned workspace, a transplanted message yields
the answer that recombination predicts in 97% of cases, and its content acts by
redirecting what the receiver retrieves from its own memory. The tests carry over to
other communication designs and to a known interface of a pretrained Transformer,
turning GWT’s central claim into a testable property of trained models.
1
INTRODUCTION
When the modules of a network communicate, which of them does the computing? The question sits
at the heart of Global Workspace Theory (GWT; Baars, 1988; Dehaene et al., 1998; Dehaene and
Changeux, 2011; Mashour et al., 2020), a leading scientific theory of consciousness. GWT holds
that information becomes consciously accessible when it enters a limited-capacity workspace and is
broadcast to specialized processes that use it (Block, 1995). On this view, what makes information
conscious is not where it is stored but whether other processes can access and use it, so the theory’s
central claim is a claim about use. Indicator-based assessments check models for workspace properties
(Butlin et al., 2023; Chalmers, 2023), interpretability work reports workspace-like representations
in pretrained language models (Gurnee et al., 2026), and networks with trained workspaces serve
as experimental substrates for the theory (Goyal et al., 2022; Albantakis, 2025). All three raise one
question: does a system that has a workspace perform the computation the theory assigns to it?
This is rarely tested, and task accuracy and ablation cannot test it. Consider two modules that
exchange messages (Figure 1, top). The source knows who holds each object, and the receiver knows
where each person is. Asked “Where is the football?”, the network answers correctly, and it fails
when the channel is cut. These facts fit two opposite computations. The source may send the holder’s
name, which the receiver looks up in its own memory. This is recombination, the computation
GWT describes. Or the message may already carry the final answer, which the receiver merely
forwards. This is relay. Ablation shows only that information flows through the channel. Swapping
in a message from another input, the standard patch, does not settle the matter either when, as is

Figure 1: One swapped message separates relay from recombination, which accuracy and
ablation cannot. Top: the same question answered by relay and by recombination, before and after
the donor’s message is swapped in. Bottom: accuracy with the channel intact and cut, and the outputs
after the transplant, for trained reference systems of each kind, a single-reader workspace model that
ignores its broadcast, an AFGW model trained to relay with its control, and the four main AFGW
models. X, Y and Z are the answers that ignoring, relaying and recombining the message predict.
usual, the forwarded and the recombined answer are the same string. We call the distance between
building a channel and knowing what a trained network computes with it the verification gap.
We close this gap with a causal protocol that identifies how communicating modules divide compu-
tational work. Its central test chooses the swapped-in message so that the candidate computations
predict different answers. In the recipient input, Jeff holds the football and is in the room, while Bill
is in the hospital. In the donor input, Bill holds the football and is in the kitchen. After the donor’s
message is transplanted, ignoring it predicts room, relaying the donor’s answer predicts kitchen, and
combining the message with the receiver’s own memory predicts hospital. We call this third answer
the hybrid answer. Three further tests ask whether the model depends on the channel, how the content
acts inside the receiver, and whether one message serves many receivers (Figure 3). The protocol
builds on established interventions (Zhang and Nanda, 2024; Geiger et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2023;
Variengien and Winsor, 2025; Prakash et al., 2026) and adds three things: a design that gives each
competing account of communication its own prediction, a calibration on systems whose computation
is known, and a test of how communicated content is consumed. We make three contributions.
• A calibrated protocol that identifies who computes. Each of its four tests pairs an intervention
with the alternative it rules out (Section 3, Table 2). On reference systems built to relay or to
recombine, it assigns the right computation in every one of 4,096 cases. On trained workspace
models it returns all three verdicts: a single-reader model ignores its broadcast, a second model
relays and a third recombines. The last two differ only in their training data, and accuracy, ablation
and a standard patch give the same result for both.
• A verified mechanism in a learned workspace. AFGW is a 6.9M-parameter language model
whose modules exchange information only through a learned workspace, with nothing supervised
except answer tokens. In four models that answer 98% of held-out composition questions, one
transplanted message yields the hybrid answer in 97% of cases, against 0.4% without intervention.
The content acts by redirecting retrieval: restoring only the receiver’s memory queries undoes the
transplant in 2,047 of 2,048 cases, and installing only the queries the transplant induces reproduces
it in 2,047 (Section 5).
2
• Evidence that the tests travel. These results hold in worlds twice as large, across communication
and memory-reading designs, and at a known interface of a pretrained Transformer. When a second
route makes the workspace replaceable, zero-ablation calls it nearly unnecessary, yet the transplant
still detects its use (Section 5.6, Figure 6).
The results serve two fields. For the science of consciousness, they turn GWT’s central functional
claim into a property that can be measured, and refuted, in trained systems. For interpretability, they
supply a test of who computes wherever modules, experts, retrievers or agents pass messages, and a
model organism with exact counterfactual ground truth on which such methods can be calibrated.
2
AFGW: A MODEL ORGANISM BUILT FOR VERIFICATION
In a large pretrained model, an intervention on a candidate workspace leaves other pathways open.
We therefore first apply the protocol to a model organism (Elhage et al., 2022; Nanda et al., 2023)
in which every route can be enumerated. AFGW (Access-First Global Workspace) is built around
access, the availability of broadcast content to other modules. It builds in three commitments of GWT,
specialized processors, competition for limited shared access and global broadcast, and leaves the
fourth, use of that content by receivers, to the protocol (Figure 2; Table 6 in Appendix C).

then that person’s location. Reverse questions map a location back to an object.

THE PROTOCOL: FROM PRESENCE TO USE

Proposition 1 (OFF information bound). Under OFF, the receiver’s complete generated answer
equals Fθ(Q, Bo), a deterministic function of the question Q and the records Bo in the receiver’s
own memory. Inputs that agree on Q and Bo therefore receive the same answer, and OFF accuracy is
at most that of the best predictor that sees only (Q, Bo), the memory-only ceiling.
The proposition holds because decoding is deterministic, records are encoded independently, and
the workspace is the only input that crosses between modules (proof in Appendix F.1). It bounds
what the receiver’s memory alone can support, and how far a trained model falls below this bound is
measured in Section 5.1. Rung 2 then asks what flows through the channel.
3.2
RUNG 2: IS THE CONTENT USED, OR ONLY RELAYED?
The second test keeps the channel and changes its content. We run the model on the recipient input
and replace one packet of the source, its write-2 packet on the first token of the answer, with the packet
the same module wrote on the donor input. Everything else evolves freely, including the competition
for the workspace. The candidate computations now predict different outputs. Ignoring the transplant
predicts room (X). Relaying the donor’s answer predicts kitchen (Y ), the outcome that models
trained to relay produce (Section 5.5). Combining the transplanted content (Bill) with the receiver’s
own location memory predicts hospital (Z). In a standard two-value patch, Y and Z coincide, and
an output that follows the donor cannot separate computing from relaying. Following Variengien
and Winsor (2025), Prakash et al. (2026), and Gur-Arieh et al. (2026), we therefore evaluate only
three-value cases, in which X, Y , and Z are pairwise distinct. They are selected symbolically from
the worlds and never from model outputs. Transplanted packets are the donor’s own activations, so no
correct answer is ever inserted. Controls replace the packet with itself and transplant at the never-read
write 3 (Appendix F).
Calibration: the test reports relay when relay is the computation. We built two small reference
networks, separate from AFGW, that fix where the computation happens and trained each with two
seeds (Appendix I.6). In the relay design, the receiver’s decoder sees only the source’s packet, so
the source must compute the answer. In the recombination design, the source sends the intermediate
person and the receiver reads its own memory. All four models answer every held-out composition
question, and all depend on their channel. The transplant separates them completely: the relay models
give the donor’s answer Y and the recombination models the hybrid answer Z, in all 1,024 cases of
every model (Figure 1, bottom).
3.3
RUNGS 3 AND 4: HOW DOES THE CONTENT ACT, AND FOR HOW MANY RECEIVERS?
Content use leaves open how the content acts. Our hypothesis is that it changes what the receiver
retrieves from its own memory: the broadcast redirects the location reader’s query from Jeff’s record
to Bill’s. The transplant enters the computation only through the broadcast b3, which reaches the
output either through the receiver’s round-3 queries and the records they retrieve (route a) or directly
through the receiver’s final state (route b).

When Agents Play Differently: Localizing
Human–Agent Behavioral Divergence with
Conditional Distributional Testing
Oleg Smirnov∗, John Pertoft∗, Sara Karimi∗†
∗King AI Labs, Microsoft Gaming, Stockholm, Sweden
†KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden
Abstract—Evaluating whether artificial agents behave like
humans requires comparing not just average outcomes but entire
behavioral distributions across diverse contexts. We propose a
stratified framework that computes nonparametric discrepancy
statistics within contextual cells, and discovers subgroup rules
identifying where agent behavior departs from human play. We
show that session-level metrics dominated by win/loss outcomes
offer little signal beyond mean comparisons, whereas process-
level metrics such as move efficiency reveal genuine behavioral
differences. Applied to a commercial match-3 game, it uncovers
patterns invisible to aggregate metrics: a playtesting bot is
diverging substantially from humans in certain game modes,
while showing no detectable divergence in others. We release
our implementation as open source to support reproducibility
and adoption.
Index Terms—Believable agents, game-playing agents, human-
likeness, automated playtesting, agent evaluation, distributional
testing.
I. INTRODUCTION
The evaluation of artificial agents hinges on their ability to
behave in a human-like manner. In interactive domains such as
digital games, human-likeness is not merely aesthetic: agents
that emulate human play enable scalable testing, balance
evaluation, and user modeling without the cost of large-scale
human trials [1, 2]. Conversely, agents that diverge sharply
from human strategies can produce misleading test results or
exploit unrealistic gameplay patterns. A bot validated only on
aggregate outcomes such as overall win rate may still play a
level in a distinctly non-human way, leading a designer to mis-
estimate its difficulty or misjudge how players will experience
it.
Existing metrics often rely on aggregate performance mea-
sures, e.g., average scores or success rates, which summarize
only the mean outcome [3]. Such scalar indicators obscure
differences in variability, timing, or decision structure that
define how humans actually behave: two agents may exhibit
identical mean success rates yet differ fundamentally in the
distribution or dynamics of their actions. A more rigorous for-
mulation views human-likeness as a problem of distributional
alignment: given observations from humans and agents under
shared contexts, assess whether their behavioral distributions
coincide. This connects directly to nonparametric two-sample
hypothesis testing [4, 5]
In practice, however, such comparisons must be made
conditionally on relevant covariates, such as content or player
−6

Fig. 1: Illustrative example. Two groups with the same mean
move efficiency but different distributions: human play is
more variable and heavier-tailed than the more consistent
agent. A mean comparison reports no difference, whereas a
distributional test detects it.
segments, rather than on pooled data. Imbalance in the fre-
quency of particular contexts can otherwise falsely appear as
behavioral divergence. Moreover, when the null hypothesis
of a global two-sample test is rejected, it is often useful to
conduct a local two-sample test to identify specific regions
where the two distributions differ [6]. We address these chal-
lenges with a framework for quantifying behavioral alignment
between agents and humans across contextual segments, build-
ing on meta-analysis and nonparametric two-sample testing to
construct a diagnostic map of where and how agent behavior
departs from that of humans. Where believability has clas-
sically been assessed as a global verdict, such as whether an
observer can tell an agent from a human, our approach instead
localizes where that resemblance breaks down. Because the
resulting map is expressed as human-readable conditions on
context variables, it tells a designer which agent to trust on
which content and turns a diffuse “not human-like enough”
into specific, localized targets for improvement.
Our contributions are threefold: (1) a conditional formula-
tion of behavioral alignment that compares full distributions
within matched contexts, (2) a diagnostic pipeline combin-
arXiv:2611.26012v1  [cs.AI]  19 Nov 2026
ing cell-level discrepancy estimation, stabilization, and inter-
pretable subgroup discovery, and (3) a production-scale case
study on a match-3 game, showing that the inferred divergence
depends strongly on both agent type and behavioral metric.
II. RELATED WORK
a) Human-likeness and playtesting in games: Believabil-
ity and human-likeness in games have long been assessed
through Turing-test-style judgments and believability compe-
titions [7, 8, 9]. Recent work quantifies human-likeness in
specific behaviors such as navigation with learned or statistical
evaluators [10, 3], while learned agents are increasingly used
for automated playtesting, from procedural personas to deep-
learning policies [2, 11]. Such approaches typically render a
global verdict, human-like or not, or optimize agents toward
it. We instead localize where and how an agent’s behavior
diverges from human play, conditional on game context.
b) Distributional two-sample testing:
Comparing full
distributions rather than means is well studied: Wasserstein
distance [12, 13], energy distance [14], and kernel MMD [15]
each provide nonparametric test procedures with known con-
sistency guarantees. Classifier-based two-sample tests instead
use a trained discriminator’s held-out accuracy as the statis-
tic [16, 17]. We favor kernel discrepancies, which require no
training step and align with distributional indistinguishability.
Our approach treats these as interchangeable cell-level build-
ing blocks rather than standalone global tests, embedding them
within a stratified aggregation and rule-discovery pipeline.
c) Stratification and meta-analytic aggregation: Com-
bining within-stratum evidence into a global test dates to the
van Elteren and CMH procedures [18, 19] and to random-
effects meta-analysis with inverse-variance weighting [20].
Our aggregation of cell-level standardized statistics follows
this tradition but extends it in two directions: the per-cell tests
are distributional rather than mean-based, and the aggregated
statistics feed a tree-based rule-discovery step that localizes
heterogeneous effects.
d) Multiple testing over discovered structure: Exploring
many candidate subgroups demands error control, for which
the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure provides false-discovery-
rate (FDR) guarantees [21]. We apply depth-wise correction
within tree levels and control false discoveries over the data-

tests a global null and then identifies regions of significant

game, where each session is one attempt at a level: the

is agnostic to the outcome variable Y , requiring only that a
valid discrepancy measure and standard error can be com-

critically on whether the chosen metric carries distributional

Applying this criterion to common game metrics: win rate is
a Bernoulli variable fully characterized by its mean, so testing
it is exactly a proportions test. Total moves used and game
score are bimodal mixtures whose mode masses track the
success rate, and are therefore outcome-dominated. Attempts-
per-success, though not outcome-dominated, is undefined for
deterministic single-rollout agents, which produce a fixed out-
come on a given level. Process-level move-efficiency metrics
avoid all three: they are continuous rather than binary, largely
orthogonal to the win/loss outcome, and defined on every
session for both groups regardless of outcome.
We therefore test two process-level move-efficiency metrics,
score per move and cascades per move. These capture how an
agent plays rather than whether it succeeds: a winning and
a losing session can show similar per-move efficiency if the
player performed well but ran out of moves. Two agents may
achieve identical success rates yet differ in play style, e.g.,
with one proceeding through steady progress, while the other
relying on high-variance cascades, where a cascade is a chain
reaction in which cleared tiles trigger further clears without
an additional move.
IV. CONDITIONAL TWO-SAMPLE TESTING
To capture differences beyond the mean, we extend the
comparison to two-sample hypothesis testing within contexts.
For each context x, let P1(Y | x) and P2(Y | x) denote the

the method localizes where differences arise by aggregating

node as a single degree-of-freedom inverse-variance–pooled
statistic that accounts for unequal variances and sample sizes

a) Cells and per-cell testing: Observations from both
groups are merged and continuous covariates discretized into
ordered bins, yielding a grid of context cells. Where a covariate
is undefined for one group, those observations act as wildcards
that match all concrete values. Within each cell, a two-sample
test contributes an effect estimate ti and standard error si
as local evidence of divergence. A well-defined SE is essen-

V. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
We apply the conditional two-sample testing pipeline to
session-level data from a commercial match-3 game, compar-
ing two playtesting bots (automated agents that play levels
in place of human testers) against human players: a super-
vised behavioral cloning model (SL) trained on the produc-
tion data inspired by the deep-learning playtesting approach
of Gudmundsson et al. [11], and a heuristic model (Hbot)
implementing handcrafted hint-based strategies. Both agents
are evaluated against the same human population across 24
context cells defined by level difficulty (0–3) and game mode:
Chain (cascade-oriented), Clear (objective clearing), and Route
(stream routing, with three variants). The three modes differ
in objective: Chain rewards cascades, Clear requires removing
designated target tiles within the move limit, and Route
requires guiding board elements to fixed destinations. For each
agent, the dataset comprises approximately 110,000 player
sessions and 5,000 agent sessions obtained via a table sample
of the full dataset. Two continuous move efficiency metrics are
tested: score per move and cascades per move. Both metrics
exhibit low outcome dominance (R2(win) = 0.036 for score
per move and 0.121 for cascades per move), confirming that
their distributional content is not reducible to success rate
differences.

permutations. The two-sided p-value is floored at 0.5/201 ≈

Per-cell standard errors are computed separately from 100
distinct bootstrap resamples. Partial pooling is applied via
DerSimonian-Laird random effects, and rule discovery uses
χ2 gain with depth-wise Benjamini-Hochberg correction at
α = 0.05. The main analysis focuses on these two agents,
which exhibit qualitatively different divergence profiles.

RL Post-Training in Diffusion Transformers Is Activation
Steering
Tuna Han Salih Meral1, Kaan Oktay2, Alec Helbling3,4, Atakan Kara2, Duen Horng Chau3, Pinar Yanardag1
1Virginia Tech, 2fal, 3Georgia Tech, 4IBM Research
Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training substantially improves the visual quality, text rendering, and compositional
accuracy of diffusion transformers. Because capabilities such as rendering requested text or composing multiple
objects are inherently prompt-dependent, a natural hypothesis is that improving them requires learning complex,
input-dependent transformations. To isolate how much of these gains an input-independent shift explains, we probe
each RL-tuned model with a deliberately simple parameterization: a fixed set of steering vectors added to the block
outputs of the frozen base model. On SD3.5-M, these vectors hold 65× fewer parameters than the RL-tuned LoRA
(0.29M against 18.8M). We fit them to match the velocity predictions of public RL-tuned checkpoints, with no
reward in the objective. Although the vectors are identical for every prompt, token, and sampling seed, they recover
90.0–96.3% of the reward gains of six RL-tuned image models, and 89.8% and 111.9% on two RL-tuned video
models. Initialized at zero and trained with online RL, the vectors alone exceed the reward gains of weight-based RL
on text rendering (OCR) and human preference (PickScore) on SD3.5-M. A constant shift thus suffices for most of
the gain of policy-gradient RL post-training: without new input-dependent transformations, it steers the pretrained
generator toward what it can already compute.

1. Introduction
Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training [5, 14, 37, 71, 73]
improves text rendering [37], compositional accuracy [19,
23] and human preference scores [26, 41, 66, 69] in image
and video diffusion transformers [6, 13, 63]. These im-
provements are typically obtained by updating the model’s
weights, either through parameter-efficient adapters such
as LoRA [22] or through full fine-tuning [71]. Although
the update ∆W is fixed after training, the updated weights
