linear layer W, token inputs zi and zj, and block outputs hi and hj. Base + s adds the same s (black) to every token of both prompts; s
changes only with the block, guidance pass, step bin and stream. In the RL-tuned model, the weight change gives each input its own shift,
∆Wzi̸ = ∆Wzj (gray). In block ℓ, s is one vector and ∆W a matrix: on SD3.5-M, all 188 vectors together hold 0.29M parameters, 65×
fewer than the RL-tuned LoRA’s 18.8M.
W + ∆W act on each token’s input, so different prompts
and tokens produce different activation changes. This flexi-
bility seems natural for visual generation, where the words to
render and the objects to compose change with every prompt.
But is this input dependence actually necessary to obtain the
gains of RL post-training?
Surprisingly, we find that most of the reward improve-
ment of a diverse collection of RL-tuned image and video
generators can be reproduced by freezing every pretrained
weight and adding a small set of fixed steering vectors to
the model’s activations. We fit these vectors to match the
velocity predictions of each RL-tuned model, with no reward
in the objective; simply averaging the activation changes
that RL induces recovers far less of the gain. For a given
RL-tuned model, the same vectors are used for every prompt,
every sampling seed, and every token (Fig. 2). In total, they
have 1.5% of the parameters of a rank-32 LoRA on SD3.5-
M, and they do not depend on the requested text, objects, or
composition. Yet they can make the frozen generator render
requested phrases, satisfy compositional constraints and im-
prove preference scores much as its RL-tuned counterpart
does (Figs. 1 and 5). On six RL-tuned image models span-
ning SD3.5-M and FLUX.1-dev, multiple RL algorithms,
LoRA and full fine-tuning, and rewards including PickScore,
HPSv2.1, OCR, and GenEval, these fixed activation shifts
recover 90.0–96.3% of the RL reward gain. The result ex-
tends to video: on two RL-tuned video generators, the same
intervention recovers 89.8% and 111.9% of the gain.
We next ask whether RL can learn such constant shifts
directly from the reward in diffusion transformers. We freeze
the generator and run Flow-GRPO [37] with only the steering
vectors trainable, starting from zero. The trained vectors
reach 104.6% and 103.6% of the gains of the OCR-tuned
and PickScore-tuned SD3.5-M models, so RL achieves both
gains by learning only a small set of constant vectors, without
updating any pretrained weight.
How can one constant intervention produce different im-
provements for different prompts? The steering vectors carry
no prompt information, so the prompt-specific part of the
change must come from the frozen generator. Inside the
transformer, attention, normalization and MLP layers mix
the constant vector with prompt-dependent representations,
so its effect on the output can depend strongly on the prompt.
On SD3.5-M, we trace how the shift reaches the image:
through what image tokens read from text tokens in joint
attention. When image tokens read the text keys and values
of the unsteered base model instead, with everything else
unchanged, most of the OCR and PickScore gains disap-
pear. The same replacement removes most of the gains of
the OCR-tuned and PickScore-tuned models, so the steering
vectors and RL reach the image by the same route. The
text stream, the conditional guidance pass and the early sam-
pling steps carry most of the gain: vectors fitted to these
parts alone, with 531× fewer parameters than the rank-32
LoRA, recover 89.5% of the RL gain on OCR and 73.7% on
PickScore (Sec. 5).
These results suggest a different view of RL post-training
in visual generators: a constant shift suffices to steer gener-
ation toward most of the RL gain, and the frozen generator
does the prompt-specific work. Although RL’s weight up-
dates produce input-dependent activation changes, most of
their reward gain is reproduced without new input-dependent
transformations beyond those the base model already com-
putes. Our main contributions are:
• We show that fixed steering vectors, fitted with no reward
in the objective, recover most of the gain of eight RL-tuned
image and video models, including two full fine-tunes.
• We find that matching the RL-tuned model’s velocity re-
2
covers far more of the gain than adding its average activa-
tion change.
• We train only the steering vectors of a frozen SD3.5-M
with Flow-GRPO and exceed the reward gains of the RL-
tuned OCR and PickScore models, with images rated on
par with theirs in a user study.
• We trace how a constant shift yields prompt-specific gains:
on SD3.5-M, it reaches the image through what image
tokens read from text, as RL’s change does.
2. Related work
RL post-training of diffusion transformers. Reward fine-
tuning raises a score of a diffusion model’s samples by
backpropagating the score through the sampler [11, 51], by
learning from preference pairs [62] or with policy gradi-
ents [5, 14]. Policy gradients [64] need only one score per
sample, and their group-relative form in Flow-GRPO [37]
and DanceGRPO [71] now post-trains image and video
diffusion transformers [6, 13, 63]. The rewards include
OCR accuracy [37], GenEval [19] and T2I-CompBench [23]
scores, and preference models trained on human judg-
ments [10, 26, 41, 66, 69]. Other studies report side effects
on color saturation [45] and output diversity [3]. We ask
what RL changes inside the model to produce these gains.
Where RL acts. Studies of RL in language models ask
where its update sits. RL fine-tuning updates a small subnet-
work [44], reaches most of its gain with few trained parame-
ters [43] and keeps the model close to the base model [52].
Alignment tuning mainly changes the stylistic or first tokens
of each answer [34, 48], and RL raises the probability of an-
swers that the base model already samples [72]. Venhoff et
al. [61] close most of the gap to RL-trained reasoning mod-
els with classifier-gated steering vectors: a classifier decides
where to add each reasoning behavior. Sinii et al. [54, 55]
train steering vectors with RL on a math reward and match
or nearly match full RL fine-tuning, and Vakada et al. [60]
do the same with label-free rewards. We fit ours to a given
RL-tuned model to measure how much of its gain a constant
recovers, and also train them with the reward (Sec. 4.6). We
study diffusion transformers, in which a reward gain is a
prompt-specific change of a whole image or video.
Activation steering. Activation steering adds a fixed vec-
tor to a model’s hidden states, taken from contrasting
prompts [31, 49, 58, 74] or optimized [8, 56]. In image
models, a fixed direction in deep features edits image con-
tent [59], and similar, often gated, additions steer diffusion
models [15, 29] and diffusion transformers [27]. Task arith-
metic [25] adds the weight difference of a fine-tuned model,
which is constant in weight space but changes the activations
of each input differently. In concurrent work, First-Order
Steering [28] turns such a weight update into steering vectors
to first order. Adila et al. [1] find the block output, where
our steering vectors sit, an expressive place for such shifts.
We instead fit steering vectors to the velocity predictions of
a given RL-tuned model.
Constants in a network. Many adaptation methods change
a frozen model through parameters that are the same for ev-
ery input. At the input, prompt tuning [30] trains soft prompt
tokens, textual inversion [16] fits a word for a new concept
and ReNeg [32] learns a negative embedding on a reward.
RaTE [9] fits one prompt token to a Flow-GRPO model by
flow matching. Inside the network, prefix tuning [33] and
P-Tuning v2 [39] prepend learned keys and values to atten-
tion layers, and ReFT [67] learns interventions on hidden
representations. BitFit [4] and (IA)3 [36] train biases and
channel scales, DiffFit [68] tunes the biases and scales of a
diffusion transformer and Calibri [57] tunes the block gates
of diffusion transformers on a reward. BitFit and DiffFit
train biases with the task loss to adapt a model to new data,
whereas we fit steering vectors at the block outputs to an
existing RL-tuned model to measure how much of its gain
they reproduce.
3. Method
3.1. Preliminaries
Diffusion transformers. The base model, the RL-tuned
model and the steered base model are diffusion transform-
ers [46] trained by flow matching [35, 40]. Each predicts
a velocity v at the noisy latent xt = (1 −t)x0 + tϵ, with
the clean latent x0, the noise level t ∈[0, 1] and Gaussian
noise ϵ ∼N(0, I). Let vθ denote the base model, vθRL
the RL-tuned model and vθ,s the steered base model. The
sampler takes N sampling steps from t = 1 to 0, one per
discrete noise level. We use N = 40 on SD3.5-M [13], as in
Flow-GRPO [37].
Guidance passes. Classifier-free guidance (CFG) [21] com-
bines the conditional pass for the prompt y and the uncon-
ditional pass for the empty prompt ∅as v∅+ w(vc −v∅),
with CFG scale w. FLUX.1-dev [6] is guidance-distilled and
runs a single pass per sampling step.
Token streams. SD3.5-M processes image and text tokens
in two streams. In joint attention [13], every token attends to
both streams.
3.2. Steering vectors
A steering vector is a constant vector added to a model’s
hidden states at inference, which changes the model’s output
without changing its weights [49, 56, 58]. In a model of L

TIDECACHE: EFFICIENT HYBRID LLM SERVING WITH TRANSPARENT
CACHE MANAGEMENT AND LAYER-WISE STREAMING
Jinbin Luo 1 Xiaozhe Yao 2 Shang Yang 1 Zhijian Liu 3 Song Han 1 Qinghao Hu 1
1Massachusetts Institute of Technology
2ETH Zurich
3University of California, San Diego
ABSTRACT
Hybrid architectures have become mainstream among open-weight language models. Their global-attention and
bounded-state layers maintain heterogeneous caches whose demands vary with context length and concurrency.
We present TideCache, a serving system on CPU–GPU superchips with three components for allocating GPU
memory among caches and managing their residency across GPU and host memory. The Transparent Cache Pool
redistributes physical pages among cache components behind fixed virtual addresses, preserving cache layouts
and backend interfaces. The Cache Streamer uses computation intervals provided by bounded-state layers to
prefetch the next global-attention layer’s prefix into GPU slots shared across global-attention layers, reducing
GPU residency while overlapping layer-wise transfers with computation. Generated KV remains resident. The
Request Scheduler selects resident or streamed execution and triggers capacity adjustments according to request
size and queue state. Together, they let HBM released by streaming accommodate other cache components and
additional requests. Implemented in SGLang and evaluated on GB300 and GH200 across seven model/platform
configurations, TideCache completes up to 2.04× as many agent turns, reduces overall P50 per-token latency by
20–59%, and improves agent P50 TTFT by 1.40–3.05× compared with SGLang with HiCache.
1
INTRODUCTION
Hybrid architectures have become mainstream among open-
weight language models. Kimi K3 (Kimi Team, 2026),
Ring-2.6 (Li et al., 2026), GLM-5.3-Flash (Z.ai, 2026),
Qwen3.8 (Qwen Team, 2026) and GPT-OSS (OpenAI,
2025) keep a global-attention layer only once every few
layers and fill the rest with sliding-window attention or re-
current layers such as Mamba, Gated DeltaNet and Kimi
Delta Attention (Gu & Dao, 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Kimi
Team, 2025). We refer to the latter as bounded-state layers,
since their cache memory per request is bounded indepen-
dently of context length. These models serve everyday chat,
coding agents, document analysis and automated data label-
ing. Such applications differ in context reuse, interaction
structure, arrival patterns and concurrency (Lin et al., 2024;
Xiang et al., 2026). A coding agent accumulates tool outputs
across turns, document analysis retains reference material,
and chat or labeling services may process many indepen-
dent requests. These behaviors create different demands on
global-attention KV, window caches and recurrent states; no
application label alone determines which component limits
serving capacity.
CPU–GPU superchips offer a larger memory hierarchy for
these workloads by coupling GPU memory with host mem-
ory through high-bandwidth interconnects. The bandwidth
of this link has grown by an order of magnitude in five

Existing systems improve hybrid models’ memory utiliza-

et al., 2023). Static partitioning reserves a fixed budget for

vLLM’s Hybrid KV Cache Manager, reduce this imbal-

sharing an arena across cache layouts can require changes

with attention backends and other serving features.
A complementary line of work uses offloading to reduce
GPU memory residency. HiCache (Xie, 2025) preserves
reusable contexts in a hierarchical cache and restores them
for later execution, reducing repeated prefill computation.
However, restored prefixes remain GPU-resident during
subsequent decoding. HiSparse (Xie et al., 2026) reduces
active requests’ GPU footprint by fetching selected KV
entries during decode, but is specialized for sparse attention.
General offloading systems such as FlexGen and Pie (Sheng
et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024) support larger inference batches
through tensor placement and transfer scheduling, but do
not leverage the cache access patterns of hybrid models.
To this end, we present TideCache, a hybrid-model serving
system with three components: the Transparent Cache
Pool, a Cache Streamer, and a Request Scheduler. Our
key observation is that bounded-state layers create inter-
vals of computation during which the historical KV of the
next global-attention layer is not yet needed. The Cache
Streamer exploits idle CPU–GPU bandwidth during decode
to prefetch host-resident prefixes into GPU slots shared
across global-attention layers (Figure 1b). Overlapping
these transfers with computation expands effective global-
KV capacity: requests with reusable host-resident prefixes
shrink their GPU footprint, while newly generated KV stays
resident. To make the released capacity available to other
cache components, the Transparent Cache Pool redistributes
physical pages behind the reserved virtual addresses of the
hybrid subpools. The Transparent Cache Pool transparently
supports existing cache layouts and attention backend inter-
faces, without requiring changes to either. The two memory
mechanisms work together: layer-wise KV streaming frees
HBM that can hold window caches and recurrent states
for additional requests, and a larger decode batch provides
more computation with which to overlap subsequent trans-
fers. The Request Scheduler coordinates these mechanisms,
selecting resident or streamed execution and triggering sub-

We implement TideCache in SGLang and evaluate seven
model/platform configurations on GB300 and GH200 su-
perchips without model-specific kernel changes. Across
mixtures of Chat and Coding Agent traffic, TideCache com-
pletes up to 2.04× as many agent turns, reduces overall
P50 per-token latency by 20–59%, and improves agent P50
TTFT by 1.40–3.05× compared with SGLang with HiCache.
The Transparent Cache Pool achieves 96.3–113.6% of the
turns of the better of two hand-tuned partitions at each fixed
load; under a shifting workload on GH200, the full system
completes 59% more agent turns and reduces agent P50
TTFT by 78% relative to SGLang with HiCache. At equal
batch size, the system adds at most 6.3% to decode-step
latency.
This paper makes three contributions:
• We identify idle partition capacity and idle decode-time
CPU–GPU bandwidth as two opportunities in hybrid serv-
ing.
• We design the Transparent Cache Pool, the Cache
Streamer and the Request Scheduler, and build them be-
hind fixed virtual addresses in SGLang.
• We evaluate seven model/platform configurations on two
superchip platforms across varying workloads.
2
BACKGROUND
2.1
Hybrid Model Inference
An autoregressive model runs a prefill phase, which builds
per-layer state for the input, and a decode phase, which
produces one token per request per step and updates that
state. What the state is depends on the layer (Figure 2). A
global-attention layer lets every token attend to all earlier
positions, so its Key–Value (KV) cache grows with the
context. A bounded-state layer keeps a state whose size is
independent of the context (Peng et al., 2022): a sliding-
window layer keeps the KV of the most recent window, and
a recurrent layer such as Mamba, Gated DeltaNet or Kimi
Delta Attention keeps a fixed-size state updated in place.
The model stacks the hybrid block of Figure 2 repeatedly,
placing one global-attention layer every few bounded-state
layers. We call the data each layer type keeps a cache
TideCache: Efficient Hybrid LLM Serving with Transparent Cache Management and Layer-Wise Streaming
3
component: global-KV, window KV and recurrent state;
where the distinction does not matter we write state for the
two bounded components. For Ring-2.6-1T at TP4 with
BF16 caches, a 67K-token context uses about 0.72 GiB of
global-KV per GPU, while one recurrent-state slot occupies
35 MiB. The evaluated SGLang configuration budgets five
such slots per running request for admission (175 MiB, or
0.17 GiB), independent of context length.
2.2
Hybrid Cache Management
Serving systems reuse the cached state of a prefix to avoid
prefilling it again. In a hybrid model a global-KV hit alone
is not enough: a bounded-state layer can resume only from
a checkpoint at the matched position, so every component
must be consistent at the same boundary. SGLang’s unified
radix cache coordinates matching, insertion and eviction of
all components under one prefix tree (Zheng et al., 2024;
Huang et al., 2026), and its memory pool owns the tensors
and decides how much GPU memory each component re-
ceives, either through a partition fixed at start-up or through
a unified pool whose boundary moves at run time (SGLang
Team, 2026). HiCache extends the tree to host memory:
evicted prefixes and checkpoints are backed up there and
loaded back before a session’s next turn runs (Xie, 2025).
TideCache replaces only the memory-pool layer and inherits
the radix cache and HiCache.
2.3
Offloading on CPU–GPU Superchips
On Grace superchips the GPU reaches host memory over
NVLink-C2C; one GB300 GPU reads pinned host memory
at 211 GB/s, and four GPUs reading concurrently reach
182–192 GB/s each. Two ways of using this path differ
in what stays on the GPU. Request-level restore copies a
session’s prefix back once before the turn runs; the prefix
is then resident for the whole turn (Xie, 2025). Layer-wise
loading keeps on the GPU only the layers about to execute
and transfers the rest again in every decode step (Xu et al.,
2024); it is hidden only if each layer’s copy finishes before
that layer starts, which depends on how much compute
separates the layers that need the data.
3
MOTIVATION
3.1
Cache Demand Depends on the Workload
Different workloads stress different parts of a hybrid
model’s cache. A busy chat or data-labeling service may
have many requests active at once, each requiring its own
window KV or recurrent state. Coding agents or document
analysis may instead retain substantial context, increasing
the global-KV footprint per request. These examples de-
scribe demand patterns, not fixed application categories.
For N running requests with mean context ¯c, global-KV
demand grows with N¯c, whereas bounded-state demand

grows only with N. A fixed partition can therefore exhaust
one component while leaving another underused. Figure 3 il-
lustrates this imbalance using Ring-2.6-1T under SGLang’s
default partition. The state pool limits concurrency to 61
requests even when most of global-KV remains unused.
Conversely, at 64K tokens per request, global-KV holds
only 17 requests while most of the state pool remains un-
used. A different partition moves these limits but retains
the tradeoff: giving more memory to one component leaves
less for the others. In a mixed workload, demand shifts with
each request source’s arrival rate, so a partition tuned for
one mix can become a bottleneck for another. Repartition-
ing cannot increase the GPU’s total cache budget: when
combined demand exceeds HBM capacity, it only changes
which requests wait.
3.2
The CPU–GPU Link Is Idle During Decode
HiCache uses host memory between turns: a session’s prefix
is restored in full before its next turn is admitted and stays
resident until the turn ends. During decode, which domi-
nates the turn, the host-to-device link carries almost nothing.
Its capacity is large: a GB300 GPU reads host memory at
211 GB/s, so one 57 ms decode step of Ring-2.6-1T at the
loads of Section 5 could move about 12 GB per GPU at that
bandwidth. A hybrid model can use this capacity because
only its global-attention layers read the prefix. Between two
of them, 7 bounded-state layers on Ring-2.6 compute with-
out needing any global-KV, so the next layer’s prefix can
be transferred in that interval and the previous layer’s can
be discarded. A request served this way needs device mem-
ory for a few global-attention layers at a time rather than
for all of them. More computation per decode step allows
more transfer to overlap. Diverse workloads can create this
opportunity: concurrent requests enlarge the decode batch
while other requests retain reusable host-resident prefixes.
The relevant properties are batch computation and cache
demand, rather than application identity.

4
DESIGN
Motivated by the observations in Section 3, we build Tide-
Cache, a serving system with three components. The Trans-
parent Cache Pool (TCP, Section 4.1) repartitions GPU
memory at run time by moving physical pages to the cache
component that blocks admission. The Cache Streamer
(Section 4.2) serves streamed requests by copying each
global-attention layer’s prefix into a shared slot just before
that layer runs. The Request Scheduler (Section 4.3) decides
whether the first request in SGLang’s waiting queue (the
head request) runs with its prefix resident on the GPU or
streamed from host memory, and which cache component
blocks it if neither fits. All three operate on one memory lay-
out whose defining property is that every cache component
keeps fixed virtual addresses: attention backends, the page
table, CUDA graphs and HiCache address the cache as they
always have, and TideCache only changes which physical
pages back an address and which host rows are present at
an address during a step.
Figure 4 presents TideCache’s architecture. The Request
Scheduler controls admission to the resident and streaming
regions, shown by its two labeled arrows, and dispatches
admitted requests to the inference engine. The data plane ex-
poses virtual cache layouts, physical GPU memory and host
cache. The Transparent Cache Pool manages a shared arena
of GPU pages, repartitioning it among cache components
as demand changes. For the head request, the scheduler
selects resident or streamed execution, or reports the block-
ing cache component to the Transparent Cache Pool for
growth between forward passes. Before each forward pass
the Cache Streamer assigns slot rows to the batch’s streamed
prefixes and prepares their copies, while HiCache restores
resident prefixes and backs up finished turns as before.
4.1
Transparent Cache Pool
As Section 3.1 shows, a fixed partition can block requests
even when another cache component has unused capacity.
The Transparent Cache Pool addresses this imbalance by dy-
namically repartitioning a shared GPU physical page arena
among global-KV, window KV and recurrent state. Each
cache component has a subpool: a fixed virtual address
range backed by a variable number of physical pages. To
grow a subpool, the Transparent Cache Pool maps additional
arena pages into its virtual range; to shrink one, it unmaps
pages that no active request uses, making them available to
another subpool. This adjusts capacity without relocating
live data or changing its virtual addresses.
The physical arena is allocated once in 2 MiB pages through
the CUDA virtual memory API (NVIDIA, 2026b). Each
subpool reserves more virtual address space than any phys-
ical share it will receive, and its tensors span this reserva-
tion. The allocator uses only rows whose backing pages
are mapped. Rows retain SGLang’s index addressing, so
forward passes are independent of physical page locations.
Transparent dynamic sharing.
Table 2 contrasts how dy-
namic sharing affects existing cache interfaces.1 SGLang’s
Unified Memory Pool (UMP) allocates global-KV and
bounded state from opposite ends of a raw uint8 buffer.
It packs all layers’ KV for a page into one page envelope;
reclaiming fragmented space can require copying live en-
velopes and updating address mappings. This page-major
layout requires stride-compatible attention backends and
logical-to-physical index translation (SGLang Team, 2026;
Zhang & SGLang Team, 2026). In this revision, UMP re-
jects HiCache and LMCache: host pools are not initialized,
and host offloading lacks logical-to-physical slot transla-
tion (SGLang Contributors, 2026). vLLM’s Hybrid KV
Cache Manager shares uniformly sized pages among cache
groups without relocating live blocks (vLLM Team, 2026;
vLLM Team and Inferact, 2026). KV-transfer connectors
must implement SupportsHMA to handle per-group block
lists and their asynchronous release (vLLM Contributors,
2026).
These designs expose pool-specific layouts or grouping to
cache consumers. TCP confines repartitioning to physi-
cal page mappings. It preserves per-layer tensors, virtual
addresses and cache indexing, enabling copy-free reparti-
tioning without pool-specific adaptation of attention back-
ends or HiCache. The same virtual layout natively supports
aliased mappings for layer-wise streaming (Section 4.2),
preserving existing cache interfaces.

Bio-PM-Guided Synthetic IMU Generation
Deepali Singh, Deepesh Parpani, Aviral Gupta
College of Information and Computer Sciences
University of Massachusetts Amherst
Amherst, USA
{deepalisingh, dparpani, aviralgupta}@umass.edu
Abstract—Collecting and labeling inertial measurement unit
(IMU) data for human activity recognition (HAR) is expensive,
and models trained on one group of subjects often fail to
generalize to unseen individuals. Even with balanced data, clas-
sifiers struggle to distinguish dynamically similar activity classes
and benefit from targeted augmentation. We explore whether
synthetic IMU data generated in the representation space of a
pretrained biosignal encoder, Bio-PM [1], can serve as a practical
augmentation source. Rather than synthesizing raw signals, we
leverage Bio-PM’s frozen encoder to convert 10-second IMU win-
dows into token embedding sequences and train class-conditional
decoders in this space: (1) an autoregressive transformer decoder
that predicts tokens sequentially, and (2) a diffusion decoder
that learns the token distribution through a denoising objective.
We analyze generation realism through distributional metrics
and embedding-space visualizations, evaluate downstream utility
through leave-one-subject-out HAR classification, and present
a PatchDecoder for approximate raw waveform reconstruction.
Our diffusion decoder achieves a Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-
Real (TSTR) macro-F1 of 0.68, demonstrating that generated
tokens are realistic enough to train a classifier that transfers to
real data. Combining synthetic-token augmentation with a 320-
dimensional gravity-aware feature representation raises LOSO
macro-F1 from 0.729 to 0.809 over a real-only baseline across 51
subjects on the WISDM benchmark, with statistically significant
gains concentrated in the most challenging activity classes. These
results demonstrate that high-fidelity generation in a pretrained
encoder’s representation space is achievable and practically
useful for cross-subject HAR augmentation. Source Code is
available here: Google Drive Link
Index Terms—Human activity recognition, inertial measure-
ment units, synthetic data augmentation, diffusion models, self-
supervised learning, token embeddings, cross-subject generaliza-
tion, wearable sensing
I. INTRODUCTION
Human activity recognition (HAR) from wrist-worn iner-
tial measurement unit (IMU) sensors supports a range of
health monitoring and behavioral analysis applications. De-
spite strong benchmark performance, cross-subject generaliza-
tion remains a persistent challenge as classifiers trained on
one subject population frequently fail on unseen individuals,
a gap directly measured by leave-one-subject-out (LOSO)
evaluation.
Synthetic data augmentation offers one path toward broader
generalization, yet generating realistic IMU signals directly
is difficult given complex temporal structure, subject-specific
motion styles, and device-placement variability. An alternative
is to generate in a pretrained model’s representation space,
where activity-relevant structure is already encoded. Bio-PM
[1], a Transformer encoder pretrained via masked movement-
segment reconstruction on the NHANES wrist-IMU corpus
(approximately 28,000 hours, 11,000 participants), provides
this foundation. Its token space is semantically organized by
activity and exhibits no subject-level clustering, making it a
natural target for class-conditional generation without subject
conditioning.
We train class-conditional generative decoders directly in
Bio-PM’s token space, using the frozen encoder as a quality
oracle. A key challenge is that Bio-PM produces contextual,
BERT-like representations in which each of the 192 tokens per
window encodes global temporal context, making this a richer
but more complex distribution to model than a standard latent
space. We develop and compare two decoders: (1) CAR-IMU,
a Class-conditional AutoRegressive decoder, and (2) CD-
IMU, a Class-conditional Diffusion decoder, evaluating both
distributional realism and downstream LOSO classification
utility on the WISDM benchmark.
The main contributions of this paper are as follows:
• We propose CAR-IMU, which generates synthetic Bio-
PM token sequences autoregressively, and characterize a
distributional shift requiring per-class affine calibration to
resolve.
• We design CD-IMU, a diffusion decoder that eliminates
the calibration dependency of CAR-IMU, achieving high
distributional realism without post-hoc correction.
• We provide systematic generation quality analysis across
both decoders using cosine similarity, Fr´echet distance
(FD) in Bio-PM token space, maximum mean discrep-
ancy (MMD), variance ratio, and Train-on-Synthetic-
Test-on-Real (TSTR) evaluation.
• We demonstrate that augmenting a LOSO HAR classifier
with CD-IMU synthetic tokens, using a 320-dimensional
feature representation and confusion-aware augmentation,
yields statistically significant improvements over the real-
only baseline across 51 subjects on WISDM.
• We present a PatchDecoder for approximate reconstruc-
tion of raw IMU waveforms from synthetic token se-
quences, extending the pipeline toward signal-level syn-
thesis.
II. DATASET AND BIO-PM
A. WISDM Dataset
We use the WISDM wrist accelerometer dataset [2], com-
prising recordings from 51 subjects performing six activ-
arXiv:2611.26607v1  [cs.LG]  19 Nov 2026
Fig. 1: UMAP activity clusters on real data tokens generated
by Bio-PM
ities: Walking, Jogging, Upstairs, Downstairs, Sitting, and
Standing. Raw signals are sampled at 20 Hz and segmented
into non-overlapping 10-second windows, yielding 12,514
windows with approximately balanced class distribution. All
experiments follow a leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) protocol,
training on 50 subjects and evaluating on the held-out subject
across all 51 folds.
B. Bio-PM Encoder Pipeline
Each window is encoded using two frozen Bio-PM mod-
ules. The accelerometer encoder applies a bandpass filter
and projects the signal into 192 movement-element patches,
each represented as a 64-dimensional token embedding via
a bidirectional Transformer, producing a token sequence of
shape 192 × 64. The gravity encoder applies a low-pass filter
and maps the DC component to a 64-dimensional gravity
embedding via a CNN, and appends it as a key to the same
token store.h5. Neither encoder is fine-tuned at any stage so
they serve exclusively as a frozen feature extractor and quality
oracle for generation.
C. Bio-PM Token Space Inspection
To validate the token space before training any decoder, we
compute nearest-neighbor same-class accuracy and visualize
the mean-pooled token embeddings using UMAP. As shown
in Fig. 1, activity classes form well-separated clusters with no
subject-level structure. A nearest-neighbor classifier achieves
90% same-class accuracy in this space, confirming semantic
richness. The absence of subject separation means that a
decoder conditioned only on activity class is sufficient, and
no subject conditioning is required. These properties make
Bio-PM’s token space a viable target for class-conditional
generation. Despite approximate class balance (≈16.6% per
class), the dataset exhibits significant representation overlap.
Baseline analyses reveal high confusion rates between ac-
tivities sharing fundamental motion patterns: Walking and
Upstairs are confused 22%–27% of the time, while Downstairs
is confused with Sitting and Standing up to 23% of the time.
III. CAR-IMU: AUTOREGRESSIVE DECODER
A. Architecture and Training
CAR-IMU is a class-conditional autoregressive transformer
that generates synthetic Bio-PM token sequences one position
at a time. A learned activity-specific prefix token CLS c is
prepended to the token sequence, providing class conditioning.
The model consists of four causal Transformer layers with
multi-head attention, where each position attends only to
preceding positions. An output projection head maps each
hidden state back to the 64-dimensional token space. Training
follows a next-token prediction objective using mean squared
error (MSE) loss, with teacher forcing applied during training
and autoregressive rollout at inference. The model is trained
for 50 epochs using AdamW with a cosine learning rate
schedule on the 12,514 real token sequences from the token
store. The resulting model has 137K trainable parameters, with
all Bio-PM encoder weights frozen throughout.
B. The Calibration Problem
Raw CAR-IMU tokens exhibit a distributional shift from
real tokens. While centroid directions are roughly aligned,
per-class means and variances differ measurably. We quan-
tify generation realism using Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-Real
(TSTR) evaluation, where an MLP classifier is trained entirely
on synthetic tokens and tested on real data. Uncalibrated CAR-
IMU tokens yield a TSTR macro-F1 of 0.22, confirming the
shift is large enough to mislead a downstream classifier. To
close this gap, we apply per-class affine calibration, shifting
and scaling each synthetic class distribution to match the mean
and standard deviation of the corresponding real class:

After calibration, TSTR macro-F1 improves to 0.63 (more
details in Table
V), demonstrating that the representational
structure is present but distributionally offset. While calibra-
tion resolves the shift post-hoc, it requires access to real token
statistics and does not address the underlying generation gap.
C. Architectural Limitations
While computationally efficient and highly effective for
high-variance locomotion activities, the CAR-IMU architec-
ture introduces structural challenges beyond distributional
shift:
• Class Signal Fading: Because the class embedding is only
injected at position 0, the conditioning signal dilutes over
the 192-step sequence.
• Autoregressive Drift: Prediction errors compound over
time. This disproportionately affects static and less pe-
riodic activities (e.g., Sitting, Standing, Downstairs) that
lack the self-correcting periodic rhythms naturally found
in activities like Walking.
Together, these limitations, (1) distributional shift requiring
post-hoc calibration, (2) class signal fading, and (3) autoregres-
sive error compounding, motivate CD-IMU: a diffusion-based
decoder that conditions on class identity at every denoising
step and learns the full token distribution directly, without
relying on calibration.
IV. CD-IMU: CLASS-CONDITIONAL DIFFUSION
DECODER
A. Architecture
CD-IMU is a class-conditional denoising diffusion model
operating over Bio-PM token sequences. The forward process
adds Gaussian noise to real token sequences over T = 1000
timesteps using a linear schedule (β1 = 10−4, βT = 0.02).
The reverse process is parameterized by an 8-layer bidi-
rectional Transformer that directly predicts the clean token
sequence ˆx0 from the noisy input xt, the timestep t, and the
activity class c.
Class and timestep conditioning are applied at every layer
via Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) [3], modulating
each layer’s activations using scale and shift parameters from
a concatenated class and sinusoidal timestep embedding. This
ensures class conditioning persists throughout the full network
depth, directly addressing the signal fading of CAR-IMU.
Bidirectional attention with no causal mask is consistent with
Bio-PM’s contextual encoding.
The training objective combines three losses:
L = Lx0 + w(e) (Ldist + Lfreq)
(2)
where Lx0 is the MSE between predicted and real clean
tokens, Ldist is a per-class mean and variance alignment term,
Lfreq penalizes spectral discrepancy along the sequence axis,
and w(e) is a linear warmup weight ramped from 0 to 1 over
the first 15 epochs to prevent regularization from dominating
before the model learns basic denoising. Generation uses
deterministic DDIM sampling [4] with 200 steps.
B. Architectural Ablation
An earlier variant introduced a Spectral FFN branch and
an aggressive spectral loss coefficient βfreq=5.0, causing the
spectral loss to dominate reconstruction at a ratio of approx-
imately 1369 : 1 and preventing convergence. Additionally,
checkpointing on validation loss caused the best checkpoint to
be saved at epoch 1 due to a favorable initialization, yielding
a model that generated class-agnostic tokens.
CD-IMU resolves these failures by reducing βfreq to 0.05,
removing the Spectral FFN, applying uniform regularization
weights across classes, and checkpointing on average cosine
similarity from periodic generation evaluations rather than
validation loss.
V. CLASSIFICATION EXPERIMENTS
A. CAR-IMU Augmentation Strategies
We evaluate CAR-IMU synthetic tokens across four aug-
mentation experiments that vary calibration, feature dimen-
sionality, and augmentation strategy. Features are extracted
from the 192-token sequence in four configurations as sum-
marised in Table I. The gravity embedding encodes device
orientation and is particularly discriminative for postural ac-
tivities such as Sitting and Standing, which are difficult to
separate using accelerometer statistics alone.

For each experiment, we explored three classifier architec-
tures: logistic regression, a three-layer MLP, and an MLP
with an attention pooling layer over the token sequence.
Final results for CAR-IMU augmentations are reported for the

CD-IMU tokens are evaluated under two strategies. As

VI. RECONSTRUCTION PIPELINE
The reconstruction pipeline maps synthetic Bio-PM to-
ken sequences back to approximate raw IMU waveforms.
Rather than reconstructing at the window level, we exploit
the direct correspondence between each Bio-PM token and
the movement-element patch it was computed from, treating
reconstruction as a per-token regression problem.
A. PatchDecoder Architecture
PatchDecoder is a shared-backbone MLP applied indepen-
dently to each of the 192 tokens in a sequence. Given a
64-dimensional token, a three-layer backbone with GELU
activations produces a 256-dimensional hidden representation,
which is passed to four task-specific heads: (1) a waveform
head predicting the 32-sample normalized patch signal; (2) an
axis head classifying the accelerometer axis (X, Y , or Z); (3) a
position head predicting the patch’s temporal location within
the window; and (4) a duration head predicting the original
patch length before normalization. The model is trained on
approximately 1.4M patch-level pairs using a composite loss
combining MSE and cosine similarity on the waveform, cross-
entropy on the axis, and MSE on position and duration.
B. Waveform Stitching
At inference, each predicted 32-sample patch is resampled
to its predicted duration via cubic interpolation, placed at its
predicted position on its predicted axis in a (300 × 3) output
buffer, and averaged where patches overlap. A per-class gravity
DC offset derived from real data is added to restore low-
frequency orientation content. The final output is a (300 × 3)
approximate IMU waveform per synthetic token sequence.
C. Limitations
Because each token is decoded independently without ac-
cess to neighboring tokens, the decoder cannot enforce tempo-
ral continuity across patch boundaries, resulting in discontinu-
ities in the stitched waveform. Amplitude attenuation is also
observed, as the per-token regression averages overlapping
patches rather than preserving peak dynamics. Addressing
these limitations through a context-aware decoder and overlap-
add stitching is left as future work.
VII. EVALUATION
A. Decoder Results
Table V compares token generation quality across CAR-
IMU (uncalibrated), CAR-IMU (calibrated), and CD-IMU.
Calibration substantially improves CAR-IMU’s TSTR score,
confirming that the representational structure is present but
distributionally offset. CD-IMU achieves a higher TSTR than
calibrated CAR-IMU without any post-hoc correction, demon-
strating that the diffusion objective learns the token distribution
directly. Cosine similarity for calibrated CAR-IMU is 1.0 by
construction, since calibration matches each class mean, so
it is not informative for that column. The near-unity cosine
similarity and low FD scores of CD-IMU across all six
activity classes confirm that CD-IMU synthetic tokens are
distributionally close to real tokens in Bio-PM’s representation
space.
Fig. 2 shows t-SNE and UMAP projections of real and
CD-IMU synthetic tokens. Synthetic tokens for each class are
tightly co-located with their real counterparts, and the raw
token-level visualization confirms alignment at the individual
patch position level rather than only at the window mean.
B. Classification: CAR-IMU

Depth Pro 2: Sharp and Temporally
Consistent Metric Monocular Depth
Peiyun Hu, Marko Mihajlovic, Lyndon Duong, Lahav Lipson, Wei Dong, Amaël Delaunoy, Stephan R. Richter,
Vladlen Koltun
Apple
WepresentDepthPro2, anapproachtoestimatingdensemetricdepthforimagesandvideoatfullresolution. Byanalyzing
prior methods for monocular depth estimation, we find that they commonly trade off temporal consistency and boundary
sharpness: multi-frame methods favor consistency, single-frame methods favor sharpness. To overcome this trade-off,
we train a single, scalable network that processes both images and video and predicts depth maps at native resolution.
Depth Pro 2 produces depth maps that are metrically accurate, sharp, and temporally consistent all at once, outperforming
prior work in all of these dimensions. We release a family of models that define a new Pareto frontier in terms of metric
accuracy, sharpness, temporal consistency, and runtime.
https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-depth-pro-2/
1
Introduction
Consider the meerkat (Figure 1). You may have recorded it on a recent holiday and are watching it now
on your high-resolution screen. While you admire the sharp details of the meerkat, you find the background
leaves distracting and regret not having recorded the video at a shallower depth of field. Applications that
synthetically blur the background could help, but to reliably separate the meerkat from its background, they
require a depth map for every frame (Bertalmío et al., 2004; Peng et al., 2022).
Picking a suitable method for estimating depth from monocular videos is surprisingly difficult. Methods
designed for single images can provide high-resolution depth maps with sharp occlusion boundaries.
In-
finiDepth (Yu et al., 2026), for instance, reasonably delineates the fur (third column of Figure 1). Yet its
predictions are temporally inconsistent as it processes each frame separately and places the meerkat at dif-
ferent distances over time. A method designed for video, such as π3 (Wang et al., 2026b), reliably places the
meerkat at a consistent distance across frames (last column of Figure 1). But it operates at a lower resolution
than the input video, which smooths over the fur.
This trade-off between sharp boundaries and temporal consistency pervades monocular depth estimation.
Figure 2 presents the state of the art on boundary sharpness and temporal consistency, measured over the
Sintel and Spring datasets (Butler et al., 2012; Mehl et al., 2023). (We choose these datasets for their dense,
high-resolution ground truth on video sequences.) We find that single-image methods cluster at the top
left and multi-frame methods cluster at the bottom right. That is, depth maps from single-image methods
feature the sharpest boundaries but are unstable over time, while depth maps from multi-frame methods are
stable but overly smooth. Multi-frame approaches are commonly optimized for stability through temporal
attention over many frames (Wang et al., 2025a, 2026b), video diffusion priors (Hu et al., 2025; Shao et al.,
2025; Yang et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2026), and video training data (Wang et al., 2023). This biases the
methods towards longer temporal context and costly diffusion, which require substantial resources (memory
and runtime) and necessitate operating at reduced resolution, thus oversmoothing boundaries.
In this paper, we present Depth Pro 2, a method that estimates sharp, metric, and temporally consistent
depth from monocular images and video.
Depth Pro 2 outperforms both single-image and multi-frame

methods in boundary sharpness and temporal consistency (see Figure 2), as well as in metric depth accuracy
(see Section 4). The key idea is an architecture that processes a flexible number of frames jointly at their
native resolution. The joint processing stabilizes depth temporally. Operating at native resolution preserves
sharp boundaries. In contrast to training with complex multi-stage curricula (Chen et al., 2025; Chou et al.,
2025; Lin et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2023), we train Depth Pro 2 on clips of 1 to 32 frames, mixing image,
video, and multi-view datasets. By training on single images alongside video, Depth Pro 2 learns to infer
metric scale from individual frames. By training on videos with a temporal consistency loss, it learns to keep
its estimates stable across frames.
Depth Pro 2 predicts inverse depth normalized by the focal length, and uses the focal length of input images
to recover metric depth (Bochkovskii et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2023a). To reliably estimate metric depth when
the focal length is not provided, we train a focal length estimator, following Depth Pro (Bochkovskii et al.,
2025). In contrast to Depth Pro, however, we design our focal length estimator to be lightweight to facilitate
streaming video processing. Our focal length estimator runs at 118 fps at 1080p on a B200 and is more
accurate than prior estimators.
To support a broad set of applications that may vary in the relative importance of accuracy and latency, we
release a family of models ranging from 24M to 872M parameters. In the streaming setting, where frames
arrive one at a time, our smallest model (Depth Pro 2-S) runs at 53 fps at 1080p on a B200 (Figure 12),
faster than the 30 fps at which most videos are recorded. Our largest model (Depth Pro 2-H+) runs at 8 fps
2
on 1080p video and outperforms all prior work in terms of metric depth, boundary sharpness, and temporal
consistency, on both images and video (Section 4).
2
Related work
Zero-shot metric depth. Early work trained on single-domain datasets with known camera intrinsics for
domain-specific metric depth prediction (Eigen et al., 2014; Eigen & Fergus, 2015; Liu et al., 2016). Ranftl
et al. (2022, 2021) pioneered training on diverse cross-domain mixtures of datasets for generalist monocular
depth estimation. While this substantially increased generality and enabled zero-shot deployment across
domains, their formulation relaxed the estimated depth from metric to relative. Subsequent work focused
on recovering metric depth while retaining strong generalist performance (Yin et al., 2023b,a). One line of
work developed approaches for handling arbitrary camera models (Piccinelli et al., 2024, 2025b,a). Another
predicted point clouds to supervise via depth-affine losses (Wang et al., 2025c,d; Kong et al., 2026). Metri-
cAnything pretrained on large-scale diverse depth completion to forego reasoning about camera intrinsics (Ma
et al., 2026). Depth Pro demonstrated strong metric depth estimation through a separate field-of-view esti-
mator, which can be trained without any depth supervision (Bochkovskii et al., 2025). We build on the Depth
Pro approach and train a lightweight field-of-view estimator that outperforms prior work while substantially
reducing the estimator’s size to enable accurate field-of-view and metric depth estimation at high frame rates.

Sharp depth.
A line of work processes
images in tiles at multiple scales to obtain
sharper depth predictions (Bochkovskii et al.,
2025; Li et al., 2024a,b, 2026; Miangoleh
et al., 2021). Kong et al. (2026) lift point esti-
mates into sparse voxels and apply sparse 3D
convolutions to iteratively refine local geome-
try and sharpness. Yu et al. (2026) represent
depth as a neural implicit field that can be
queried at arbitrary resolution, but require
sparse metric depth as additional input to
predict dense metric depth. He et al. (2026);
Ke et al. (2024); Pavlovic et al. (2026) lever-
age latent diffusion priors and synthetic train-
ing data for predicting sharp depth bound-
aries.
To avoid artifacts from decoding la-
tents, Xu et al. (2025) denoise in pixel space
through a cascade of diffusion transformers.
In contrast to prior work that combines mul-
tiple scales or iteratively refines predictions,
Depth Pro 2 predicts sharp boundaries at na-
tive resolution via a single pass through a vi-
sion transformer.
Stable depth. Single-image methods are in-
consistent when applied to individual video
frames separately.
To produce consistent
depth maps over video sequences, researchers
have proposed specialized modules (Piccinelli et al., 2026; Chou et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b; Zhang et al.,
2019), plug-and-play stabilization (Wang et al., 2023), and spatiotemporal heads (Chen et al., 2025). An-
other line of work fine-tunes video diffusion models for temporally consistent depth prediction (Hu et al.,
2025; Shao et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025b), or adapts them into deterministic single-step regressors (Zhang
et al., 2026). Instead of relying on custom modules or computationally heavy video diffusion priors, we adapt
a single-image vision transformer (ViT) (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) to handle a flexible number of frames and
penalize inconsistency between predictions during training.
Another line of work takes inspiration from classic 3D reconstruction and optimizes depth jointly with camera
3
poses (Wang et al., 2024, 2025a, 2026a,b; Lin et al., 2026). To improve the consistency of reconstructed
geometry, these methods are commonly optimized for handling large sets of views, which in turn limits their
ability to process images at high resolution, a key requirement for producing sharp depth maps.
In contrast, Depth Pro 2 estimates metric depth from a flexible number of input frames and processes them
at native resolution to produce significantly sharper occlusion boundaries. To enable processing of multiple
images, we simply adapt a subset of the self-attention layers of our transformer to attend over tokens from
multiple views without introducing additional parameters. Variants of this idea have been used in video
transformers (Bertasius et al., 2021; Arnab et al., 2021), multi-view recognition (Chen et al., 2021; Lee et al.,
2025), and generation (Khachatryan et al., 2023; Shi et al., 2024). Most closely related, Depth Anything
3 (Lin et al., 2026) rearranges tokens so that pretrained DINOv2 attention operates across views for feed-
forward reconstruction. Unlike these approaches, we design our network to predict metric depth at native
resolution.
3
Method
3.1
Architecture
Overview. The architecture of Depth Pro 2 is depicted in Fig. 3. It consists of a multi-view transformer
that ingests a single image or multiple frames of a video, processes them jointly, and decodes them to an
inverse depth map per input image or video frame. Following Depth Pro, our depth estimation network
predicts inverse depth normalized by focal length, and we combine it with a known or estimated focal length
to predict metric depth (Bochkovskii et al., 2025). A separate field-of-view estimator processes the input
image(s) and predicts the field-of-view per image, which we convert to the focal length. If the focal length is
known a priori, e.g., through EXIF data, we use that instead of running the field-of-view estimator.
Lightweight multi-frame depth estimation network. We design our depth estimation network to be
lightweight and to flexibly handle a variable number of images, starting from a ViT variant pretrained for
single-image processing (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021; Siméoni et al., 2026). Since temporal stability requires
an architecture that aligns predictions across frames, our model shares information across jointly processed
frames via cross-attention, alternating blocks of within-frame self-attention and cross-frame attention (Wang
et al., 2025a; Lin et al., 2026). (See Fig. 3, 1 .) Since early blocks in multi-view transformers tend to encode
low-level features and only later blocks approximate feature matching (Starý et al., 2026), we restrict the
first 1/3 of the L transformer blocks to self-attention operating only over tokens from the same frame for
higher efficiency. The remaining 2L/3 blocks alternate between within- and cross-frame attention. When
encoding spatial positions of tokens processed by the transformer, we specifically omit any encoding of frame
order, making our network equivariant to frame permutation. This allows flexible processing of any number
of frames and directly reusing the attention weights from single-image pretrained encoder checkpoints (Lin
et al., 2026) without adding transformer blocks that need to be trained from scratch for multi-view processing.
Native resolution processing. Boundary sharpness correlates with the resolution at which frames are
processed (Miangoleh et al., 2021; Bochkovskii et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2026). We therefore design Depth Pro
2 to operate at the full native resolution of the input image or video. To this end, we initialize our multi-
view transformer from DINOv3 weights, as DINOv3 is trained specifically to produce dense, high-resolution
features (Siméoni et al., 2026). An input image is split into patches of size 16, and each patch is embedded
as a token. We encode each token’s spatial position through a 2D rotary embedding over their coordinates.
Instead of normalizing coordinates per axis (Siméoni et al., 2026), which would discard any information about
the image’s aspect ratio, we divide both axes by the longer side. The position (x, y) of a patch (i, j) within
a grid of size h × w is thus
y′ = 2(i + 1
2)/ max(h, w) −1,

DPT decoder. A DPT decoder (Ranftl et al., 2021) decodes features extracted per frame into inverse depth
maps. (See Fig. 3, 2 .) Following DPT, we extract tokens after several transformer blocks, assemble them
into feature maps at different resolutions, and project them to a common channel dimension. Depending on
the size of the multi-view transformer, we adjust the positions at which we extract features, and scale the

et al., 2025).
Focal length estimation.
Our multi-view transformer predicts inverse depth normalized by the focal
length (Bochkovskii et al., 2025). Converting this prediction to metric depth therefore requires the focal
length. The focal length is often recorded in EXIF metadata; when it is not, we estimate it with a separate,
lightweight vision transformer. This estimator predicts the field of view along the shorter image side, from
which the focal length follows given the length of that side in pixels. To minimize the overhead, we build
the estimator on DINOv3 ViT-S/16 (Siméoni et al., 2026) and fine-tune it end-to-end on Flickr photographs
with EXIF focal lengths (Thomee et al., 2016). The estimator has 23.5M parameters and, for a 1080p frame,
adds about 8%, 3%, 1%, and 0.5% to the compute of Depth Pro 2-S, Depth Pro 2-B, Depth Pro 2-L, and
Depth Pro 2-H+, respectively. For multi-view input, we assume a constant focal length and take the median
of the per-frame estimates. On the zero-shot benchmark of Bochkovskii et al. (2025), our estimator attains a
mean δ25 of 88.6%, compared to 71.7% for Depth Pro (Table 6). Appendix A.2 describes the training setup,
Appendix E.4 analyzes design choices, and Table 6 compares the estimator to prior work.
3.2
Training
Training data. Depth Pro 2 is trained on a diverse set of 19 datasets with a strong focus on synthetic
ground truth. See Table 7 for the full list. To preserve the sharpness of ground-truth depth maps, we avoid
any interpolation of ground-truth depth during training, as averaging over depth discontinuities breeds flying
pixels (Bochkovskii et al., 2025). To expose our model to a broad set of image sizes and aspect ratios, we crop
and sample images at varying strides. During training, we use ground-truth camera intrinsics (focal length)
and adjust accordingly depending on how we crop or subsample. Controlled experiments in the supplement
(Section E) show that training without resampling improves boundary accuracy by more than 5 percentage
points over Depth Pro’s resizing.
To handle both images and video, Depth Pro 2 is trained on clips with varying length, of which all frames are
processed jointly. Images are treated as clips of length 1; for video and multi-view datasets, a clip contains
up to 32 frames. (We use frame for both video frames and views.) For each clip, we draw the source dataset i
with probability pi ∝n1/T
i
, where ni is the size of dataset i and T = 2 (Arivazhagan et al., 2019). To avoid
5
overfitting to small datasets, we cap their sampling weight.
Batching. To efficiently train with varying resolutions and clip lengths, we batch by tokens. Each GPU
receives a fixed budget of 73,728 tokens, e.g., 18 frames at 1024×1024. When a clip leaves part of the budget
unused, we fill the remainder with further clips of the same resolution.
Training objective. Our loss is the unweighted sum of four terms:
L = Lmae + Lssi + Lmge + Lmvc.
(3.1)
Lmae is a trimmed L1 loss on focal-normalized inverse depth. It anchors metric depth, and we apply it only
to sources with metric ground truth. Lssi is a trimmed L1 loss after normalizing prediction and ground truth
independently to zero median and unit mean absolute deviation (Ranftl et al., 2022). We apply it to all
datasets. Both trimmed losses discard, per image, the fraction τ of pixels with the largest loss, with τ = 1%
on synthetic data and τ = 10% on real data, since the noise level on real data is higher. The multi-scale
gradient term Lmge matches first-order gradients of the normalized depth maps over a Gaussian pyramid of
M = 3 scales (Bochkovskii et al., 2025). These gradients are reliable only where depth boundaries are exact,
so we apply Lmge only to synthetic data. Next we describe the multi-view consistency term Lmvc.
Multi-view self-consistency. To stabilize predictions across frames, we introduce a multi-view consistency
loss Lmvc. Our formulation is inspired by Luo et al. (2020), who warp points via their predicted depth and
penalize deviations from estimated optical flow. For robustness, we replace optical flow with correspondences
given by ground-truth camera poses

Represented but misread: Post-training changes how language
models read out what they represent
Jochen Laubrock
University of Potsdam
19 November 2026
Abstract
Does post-training change what a language model represents, or how this representation is read
out into an answer? We compared linear probes with the models’ own answers, analyzed with signal
detection theory, in six open-weight base models and their post-trained versions. For judgments
of whether German texts were written by a human or an AI, probes and word n-gram classifiers
separated the classes well, but the answers did not and often ordered the texts inversely. Post-training
lowered the sensitivity of the answers on average (Δd′ = −0.34 across model families; −0.29 across
three prompts). It also changed the use of a stated base rate: Base models shifted their log-odds by less
than the stated change in prior odds, most post-trained models by more. In two models with stage-
wise checkpoints, the change occurred during supervised fine-tuning, model stitching implicated
the early layers, and from mid-depth on internal states at positions after the text, not those of the
text, transferred the change between checkpoints. Because our corpora cannot be shared, we add a
case reproducible from public data, the truth of negated statements. Here, post-training acted in the
opposite direction: Probes decoded truth at or near ceiling in every model, the answers of several
base models did not use it, and post-training repaired them; by mid-depth the repair resided at the
positions after the statement; below it, the representation of the statement contributed, strongly in
one of four models. In a training study, adding 2,000 correctly labeled authorship judgments of news
texts to otherwise identical fine-tuning data improved the answers on our newspaper and textbook
corpora and inverted them on the chats, where they followed a news-trained probe of the base model.
Post-training thus changed how a judgment is read out of what a model represents, and a small
training signal can set its direction.
1 Introduction
What does post-training change in a language model? After pretraining on large text corpora, language
models are turned into assistants in several stages of post-training: supervised fine-tuning (SFT), in
which the model learns to imitate example dialogues, and stages that optimize it for human or AI prefer-
ences, e.g., direct preference optimization (DPO), in which it learns to prefer the better of two candidate
answers. An influential view holds that these stages add little knowledge: A model learns what it knows
during pretraining, and post-training mainly teaches it in which format and style to respond. Zhou et
al. (2023) formulated this as the superficial alignment hypothesis, and several findings are consistent
with it, among them that a few well-chosen examples or a suitable prompt to a base model can produce
much of the behavior of a fully post-trained model (Lin et al., 2023), and that instructions change how
a model expresses information more than how it encodes it (Waldis et al., 2026). If this view is correct,
1
arXiv:2611.26584v1  [cs.CL]  19 Nov 2026
post-training should leave a model’s internal representations largely intact while changing how they
are read out into an answer. This distinction matters beyond its theoretical interest: A model whose
answers no longer reflect what it represents knows something but says something else, which is a cen-
tral concern for assessing the honesty of language models. Testing the distinction, however, requires a
judgment for which we know what the model should represent, can measure whether it does, and can
pinpoint where the representation diverges from the answer.
We argue that judging the authorship of a text, i.e., whether it was written by a human or generated by
an AI, is such a test case, for several reasons. The correct answer is known for every text, so that both
the model’s representation and its answer can be scored against the same ground truth. Authorship is a
property of the input text, which the model reads in full before it answers; the information is therefore
available in principle and does not depend on retrieving facts from memory. Whether the distinguishing
information is present can be established independently of the model, with simple text statistics. Texts
can be chosen that the models are unlikely to have seen, or cannot have seen, during training, which
rules out memorization. Humans make the same judgment, which connects the question to a long
tradition of research on human judgment. The judgment is also of practical relevance, because AI-
generated text has become hard to tell apart from human writing in education, journalism, and science,
human readers perform close to chance (Clark et al., 2021; Jakesch et al., 2023; Jones & Bergen, 2025;
Köbis & Mossink, 2021; Porter & Machery, 2024), and detectors trained specifically for this purpose
are in wide use (Thai et al., 2025). Human judgments rely on plausible but invalid heuristics, such as
taking references to personal experience or first-person pronouns as signs of human authorship (Jakesch
et al., 2023), and only readers who frequently use language models for their own writing appear to
detect AI-generated text reliably (Russell et al., 2025). Because the texts that make authorship a clean
test case cannot be shared, we complement it with a second judgment on public data that meets the
same requirements and can be reproduced in full: whether a statement is true, for statements with and
without negation (Marks & Tegmark, 2024).
One might expect language models to do better. They produce such texts themselves, and the regular-
ities that distinguish their output from human writing are, in principle, available to them. However,
language models asked directly whether a text was written by a human or by an AI are weak and biased
judges: Their errors lean in one direction, and the direction differs between models and model gener-
ations (Bhattacharjee & Liu, 2024; Yuan et al., 2026). When GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 judged transcripts of
Turing-test conversations, their accuracy was even below chance (Rathi et al., 2024). In pilot work with
the German chat messages used here, four commercial models judged each message with five prompt
versions and rated their confidence. Two of them, GPT-5.4 and Claude Opus 4.6, had written the AI
messages themselves. None of the four models recognized these messages: With any prompt version,
each model called at most 16% of them AI, and the two generators called at most 7% and 14% of their
own messages AI. The confidence ratings ordered the messages below chance in the smallest model
(GPT-5.4-mini: AUC = .20–.34) and at or above chance in the larger ones (GPT-5.4: .53–.73; Claude Son-
net 4.6: .63–.76; Claude Opus 4.6: .69–.90). Why would a model that writes like an AI fail to recognize
AI-written text, and why would the training that makes it a helpful assistant make it worse at this?
Two classic frameworks from psychology are helpful in asking this question precisely. Signal detection
2
theory separates the sensitivity of a judge, i.e., the ability to distinguish signal from noise, from the cri-
terion, i.e., the tendency to give one answer rather than the other (Macmillan & Creelman, 2004). A
bias toward answering “human” only shifts the criterion for all texts alike; it cannot make the evidence
for “AI” stronger for human than for AI texts. Sensitivity below chance therefore indicates that the
evidence on which the judgment is based is ordered inversely. Brunswik’s lens model adds the distinc-
tion between the validity of the cues that a stimulus offers and the way in which a judge utilizes them
(Brunswik, 1956; Karelaia & Hogarth, 2008). Poor judgments can result from a lack of valid cues or
from valid cues that are not used, or used in the wrong way. For human judges, the utilization of cues
can only be inferred from their judgments. For language models, it can be examined directly, because
their internal representations are accessible. The judgment of a language model can then be described
by two lenses in series (Figure 1): In a first lens, the cues of the text are encoded in the model’s internal
representation; in a second lens, this representation is read out into an answer to the question. Splitting
the judge side of the lens model in this way has precedents in research on personality judgment, which
distinguishes the detection of cues from their utilization (Funder, 1995), and in neuroscience, which dis-
tinguishes the information that a neural population encodes from the information that is read out for
behavior (Panzeri et al., 2017). Because psychology and machine learning often use different words for
the same idea, and sometimes the same word for different ideas, Appendix A lists the correspondences
between their terms.
A brief description of how a language model processes a prompt may be helpful for readers from psy-
chology. The prompt is split into a sequence of tokens (words or parts of words), and in each of its
several dozen layers the model computes an internal state for every position of this sequence. Through
the attention mechanism, the state at a position can draw on the states at all earlier positions, but not on
later ones. The answer is generated from the state at the last position after the final layer. In a prompt
that presents a text and then asks a question about it, information about the text can therefore reach the
answer only through the positions that follow the text, i.e., those of the question and of the cue for the
answer (Figure 2A). We refer to these parts of the prompt as the text positions, the question positions,
and the last position. All analyses and interventions reported below are carried out on these internal
states of an artificial neural network, i.e., of a computer program whose every state can be recorded,
replaced, and restored.
This possibility has been used to show that language models often represent more than they say. Simple
linear classifiers (“probes”) trained on a model’s internal activations can recover properties such as the
truth of a statement (Burns et al., 2024; Hu & Levy, 2023; Marks & Tegmark, 2024) or the correctness of
the model’s own answers (Orgad et al., 2025) better than the model’s answers do, and prompting a model
for a judgment can underestimate what it knows (Hu & Levy, 2023). The same dissociation has been
reported for authorship: Models encode whether they wrote a text themselves although they fail to report
it (Y. Zhou et al., 2026), and a direction in the residual stream that tracks self-authorship can be used to
steer what a model claims to have written (Ackerman & Panickssery, 2025; see also Panickssery et al.,
2024). Interpretability research at the scale of frontier models has made the same distinction between
the presence of a feature and the behavior it supports (Templeton et al., 2024), and has identified a
small subspace of representations that a model is able to verbalize, whose content is shaped by post-
training (Gurnee et al., 2026). Why represented information fails to reach the answer is less clear. One

the text, some of which are valid and some of which are not (dashed). In the first lens (encoding), the
model integrates these cues into its internal representation; whether the ground truth can be decoded

of the prompt in reading order (the instruction, the text to be judged, the question, and the position at
which the answer is produced), and the vertical axis shows the layers of the network. (A) Information
flow: through attention, later positions read information from earlier ones. The answer is produced at

(dark tiles) and the last position itself, which also reads the text directly at every layer (the schematic
shows only the route via the question). (B) Steering, sketched in a two-dimensional version of the high-
dimensional representation space: human texts (open circles) and AI texts (triangles) differ along an
AI–human direction (arrow between the class means). Steering moves the state of one text along this
direction (diamonds) and measures how the model’s answer changes; the dashed line marks where the
answer switches. The two need not be orthogonal: the angle between the AI–human direction and the
model’s decision boundary determines how strongly a shift along the direction changes the answer. If

(C) Model stitching combines the lower layers of one checkpoint (here the base model, blue) with the

the base model’s states at the question positions).
5
recent account attributes such gaps to a miscalibrated decision threshold (Villuri et al., 2026), i.e., to the
criterion in terms of signal detection theory, which cannot explain sensitivity below chance. Another
line of work shows that steering along a direction that discriminates a concept can promote the opposite
behavior (Torop et al., 2026), which suggests that the readout of represented information can itself be
reversed.
What post-training does to this relation has been studied mainly by comparing base and post-trained
models. Representations learned during pretraining largely transfer to the post-trained model (Kissane
et al., 2024), fine-tuning tends to enhance existing mechanisms rather than to create new ones (Prakash
et al., 2024). Model diffing, i.e., the systematic comparison of the internal representations of a base
model and its post-trained version, has been carried out with crosscoders, sparse dictionaries of fea-
tures that are learned from both models at once and reveal which features are shared and which are
specific to one of them (Lindsey et al., 2024). It suggests that much of what chat fine-tuning adds is
concentrated at the tokens of the chat template (Minder et al., 2026; see also Leong et al., 2025), i.e.,
the special tokens that mark the beginning and the end of the user’s and the assistant’s turns and that,
in a prompt, lie between the user’s text and the answer. Likewise, exchanging the key-value cache,
i.e., the stored internal states of earlier positions that later positions read, between fine-tuned and base
models transfers fine-tuned behaviors mainly through system-prompt and template positions (Loos &
Eberle, 2026), and crossing the lower and upper layers of base and post-trained models has shown that
changes in the late layers can depend on altered earlier computation (Y. Zhou, 2026). For example, the
representation of whether a model is being evaluated, tracked across the published checkpoints of one
model, is already present in the base model and amplified during supervised fine-tuning (Heidari et al.,
2026). To our knowledge, however, these approaches have not been combined to ask, for a judgment
with known ground truth, whether post-training changes the representation of a property or the way
in which the answer reads it out, and where in the network this happens. Models whose developers
released checkpoints after every stage of post-training make this possible. Combining the lower layers
of one checkpoint with the upper layers of another, a technique known as model stitching (Bansal et al.,
2021; Lenc & Vedaldi, 2015), locates a change in depth; exchanging internal states between checkpoints
at selected positions of the prompt, an application of activation patching (Heimersheim & Nanda, 2024;
Meng et al., 2023; Vig et al., 2020), locates it in the prompt.
Here we use authorship judgments as a test case for representation versus readout under post-training.
We studied six open-weight base models and their post-trained versions with three corpora of German
texts: chat messages that students wrote for this study and that were never published, so that they cannot
have been part of any training data; segments of articles from a local newspaper that, to our knowledge,
were not available in digital form and are therefore unlikely to have been part of the training data; and
summaries of textbook chapters. First, we tested whether the information that distinguishes AI from
human texts is available in the models’ representations, and compared it with simple text statistics. Sec-
ond, we measured with signal detection theory how the models’ own answers use this information,
how post-training changes it from stage to stage, whether labeled examples can correct it, and whether
a stated base rate moves the answers as it would for an ideal observer. Third, we located the effect of

Text-Aware, Vision-Blind: How Multimodal Image Editing Systems
Handle Unsafe Inputs
Ziqing Yang1 Yixin Wu2,3 Michael Backes1 Yang Zhang1*
1CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security
2The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
3The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Abstract
Multimodal image generation systems have made rapid
progress and increasingly emphasize content safety. How-
ever, their safety mechanisms tend to rely on a single modal-
ity and lack joint consideration of both visual content and
text prompts, particularly in instruction-guided image edit-
ing, where the uploaded image may itself carry risk. We
thus introduce EditSafetyBench, a benchmark that mea-
sures system-level safety awareness of advanced image edit-
ing systems, containing 5,940 image-instruction pairs, cover-
ing safe and unsafe images across 11 risk categories and three
edit intents. We then probe the benchmark dataset on four
systems, including Gemini, GPT, Qwen API, and Qwen Lo-
cal. Based on our evaluation, we observe a systematic text-
vision safety mismatch: Gemini and GPT refuse 87.1% and
81.6% cases containing unsafe-intent editing prompts, while
only refusing 24.2% and 22.4% cases with both unsafe im-
ages and neutral instructions. At the category level, most
risks are considered inconsistently by different systems, e.g.,
GPT allows 70.4% editing attempts of unsafe political con-
tent while Gemini only allows 34.8%. Notably, sexual con-
tent shows the strongest visual sensitivity, likely benefiting
from mature NSFW identification works. Our findings high-
light the need for safety guardrails that jointly reason over
both visual and textual modalities in image editing systems.
Disclaimer: This paper contains examples of unsafe content.
We blur unsafe images and provide only redacted unsafe-
intent editing instructions. Reader discretion is advised.
1
Introduction
There are emerging commercial multimodal generation
platforms that provide both text-to-image generation and
instruction-guided image editing [7, 18, 29].
All major
providers emphasize content safety in their policies [1,8,19],
yet existing safety mechanisms on these platforms are de-
signed primarily around text: they analyze the prompt but
largely overlook the visual input [9, 12, 21].
Image edit-
ing, however, requires jointly considering the visual con-
