tent and the textual intent to make appropriate safety deci-
sions [20,30]. For example, a user who uploads a violent im-
age and requests “improve the image quality” or “mask the
violent part” poses a safety question that cannot be resolved
by analyzing the instruction alone.
Despite this challenge, text-visual safety in image editing
remains underexplored. Existing safety benchmarks [15,34]
primarily target single-modality threats rather than the cross-
modal interaction inherent to image editing. Concurrent ef-
forts have begun to explore adversarial attacks and guardrails
for editing models [11, 20], but few works directly measure
whether deployed systems account for visual input risk in
non-adversarial, naturalistic editing scenarios.
We thus introduce EditSafetyBench,
a benchmark
that measures system-level safety awareness in instruction-
guided image editing systems. We define a system as a de-
ployed editing pipeline that may include the model, safety
filters, and API wrappers [31]. We consider three system
decisions: allow, refuse, or error.
Specifically, we con-
struct the EditSafetyBench dataset by pairing safe and un-
safe images with neutral, risk-reducing, and unsafe-intent
1
arXiv:2611.26569v1  [cs.CR]  19 Nov 2026
edit instructions across 11 risk categories, yielding 5,940
image-instruction pairs. Then we probe the dataset on four
systems that are based on multimodal large language mod-
els (MLLMs): Google’s Gemini [7], OpenAI’s GPT Im-
age (GPT) [18], Alibaba’s Qwen Image Edit API (Qwen
API) [29], and Qwen Image Edit Local Model (Qwen Lo-
cal) [29]. We obtain the following main findings:
(a) Text-Vision Safety Mismatch. Gemini and GPT refuse
81.6–87.1% of unsafe-intent edits but only refuse 22.4–
24.2% of unsafe images with neutral instructions, revealing
more awareness on text modality (see Figure 1).
(b) Text Intent Overrides Visual Risk. Although unsafe
images with neutral-intent edits have a higher moderation
score than safe images with unsafe intent, system decisions
ignore this: the safe-vs-unsafe allow rate gap is only 0.2–
0.4% under unsafe-intent edits for Gemini and GPT, indicat-
ing text intent dominates safety filtering.
(c) Category-Level Visual Sensitivity. Most risk categories
show cross-platform awareness inconsistency, e.g., GPT al-
lows 70.4% of unsafe political content while Gemini only
allows 34.8%. Notably, sexual content shows the strongest
visual sensitivity among all categories, likely benefiting from
mature NSFW detection studies.
Contributions. Our contributions are as follows:
• We formulate the system-level safety awareness prob-
lem for image editing, focusing on the deployed
pipeline rather than isolated model capabilities.
• We introduce EditSafetyBench, a controlled bench-
mark pairing safe/unsafe images with three edit intents
across 11 risk categories and evaluate on four systems
from three providers.
• Based on our findings, we urge the development of
safety guardrails that jointly reason over both visual and
textual modalities in image editing systems.
2
Related Work
Multimodal Image Generation. Multimodal image gener-
ation has evolved from text-to-image diffusion models [24,
26] to unified systems that support both generation and
instruction-guided editing [3,33]. Commercial systems such
as Gemini [7], GPT Image [18], and Qwen [29] now offer
image editing as production endpoints wrapped in layered
safety architectures [31].
Platform Policy. We survey three main platforms [1, 8, 19]
and map their content policies to 11 risk categories. These
policies have broad coverage for hate, violence, and sexual
content but weaker attention to categories like self-harm and
political content. Details can be found in Appendix B.
Content Moderation. Content moderation has been widely
studied, especially for individual modalities [5,6,27,28]. For
multimodal image generation, existing safety guardrail re-
search mainly focuses on preventing unsafe generation from
text prompts [5, 22, 25, 32].
Image content moderation is
also studied from BERT-based classifiers [5] to VLM-based
LlavaGuard [10] and SafeVision [30]. However, multimodal
content moderation requires considering the joint of both vi-
sual and text modalities [13,16]. For example, HoliSafe [13]
measures both visual and textual inputs of VLMs. To the
extent of our knowledge, however, there is a lack of work fo-
cusing on image editing, which requires considering both the
input image and editing prompts and measuring the safety of
their outcomes.
Multimodal Safety Benchmarks. Existing benchmarks fo-
cus on identifying unsafe content [2,15,34] or text-to-image
safety generation [14]. MM-SafetyBench [15] tests whether
multimodal models generate unsafe text responses to image-
text inputs, and VLGuard [34] evaluates jailbreak robust-
ness through safety fine-tuning of vision-language models
(VLMs). Image safeguarding approaches reason about un-
safe visual content using VLMs [2]. Two concurrent works
from early 2026 also address image editing safety: IES-
Bench [11] studies adversarial jailbreak attacks on editing
models through visual prompts, while Piao et al. [20] propose
policy-adaptive image guardrails using edited image pairs.
In contrast, EditSafetyBench measures system-level safety
awareness under non-adversarial, naturalistic editing scenar-
ios, focusing on whether deployed systems jointly consider
visual content and textual intent.
3
EditSafetyBench
3.1

tion T (natural language text), an image editing system S pro-
duces a response:

• Allow: The system returns an edited image, indicating

• Refuse: The system rejects the request through explicit

• Error: System failures (e.g., timeout or server error) do

Note that we evaluate system-level safety decisions, not

Scope.
We target the safety awareness of existing real-

3.2
Benchmark Construction
As shown in Figure 3, our EditSafetyBench pipeline
includes collecting safe/unsafe images, designing image-
agnostic edit instructions, and system probing.
Image Collection. We draw images from UnsafeBench [23],
which provides safe and unsafe examples across 11 risk
categories (Hate, Harassment, Violence, Self-Harm, Sex-
ual, Shocking, Illegal Activity, Deception, Political, Pub-
lic and Personal Health, Spam). These categories originate
from OpenAI’s content policy [19] and align with the poli-
cies of three major commercial platforms we surveyed (Ap-

To ensure unambiguous safety labels, we apply a moder-

the maximum category score as each image’s overall mod-
eration score. We then select safe images with the lowest
scores and unsafe images with the highest scores within each
category, ensuring that safe images are unambiguously be-
nign and unsafe images carry genuine risk rather than bor-
derline cases.
Within each of the 11 × 2 = 22 category-
safety cells, we sample 30 images with balanced provenance
(15 human-crafted, 15 AI-generated), giving 11 × 2 × 30 =
660 images in total.
This yields 330 safe images (mean

producing a 372.58× separation (see Figure 4). The bal-

Edit Instruction Design. EditSafetyBench uses general,
image-agnostic edit instructions rather than image-specific
ones. This design is critical: by applying identical instruc-
tions to both safe and unsafe images, any behavioral dif-
ference between the two groups can be attributed to visual
content, not instruction phrasing. For each of the three in-
tent types defined in Section 3.1, we write three concrete
prompts, yielding a fixed bank of nine prompts per image
(see Appendix C).
Benchmark Assembly. Each of the 660 images is paired
with all nine prompts, producing 660 × 9 = 5,940 image-
instruction pairs.
The balanced design (30 images per
category-safety cell, identical prompts across systems) en-
ables category-level statistical analysis and controlled cross-
platform comparison.
We additionally collect 200 natu-
ral images from MagicBrush [33], a large-scale instruction-
guided real image editing dataset, as a held-out control set
for validating safe-image behavior (Section 4.7).
System Probing. For every image-instruction pair, we query
each system and normalize the response to the decision la-
bels defined in Section 3.1: Allow (edited image returned),
Refuse (request blocked), or Error (technical failure).

Implementation. All images are preprocessed to 2048px

mechanism is opaque. Note that all three metrics (SOR, UIR,

4.2
Overall Performance
Table 1 summarizes the main results across four systems.
Gemini and GPT actively refuse 41.5–43.9% of requests on
unsafe images, while both Qwen variants show near-zero ex-
plicit refusal. Qwen API blocks 6.8% of requests through
persistent platform-level errors, suggesting a basic content
wrapper. The three metrics reveal a clear pattern: all systems
with any safety filtering achieve high UIR but low UNR, in-
dicating text-driven rather than vision-aware safety. We an-
alyze this pattern along three dimensions: text-vision inter-
action (Section 4.3), edit intent (Section 4.4), and image risk
category (Section 4.5).
4.3
Text-Vision Safety Mismatch
As shown in Table 1, Gemini and GPT achieve high UIR
(87.1% and 81.6%), refusing most unsafe-intent edits regard-
less of whether the input image is safe or unsafe. However,
their UNR is only 24.2% and 22.4%: even when the input
image contains violence or hate, these systems allow neutral
edits such as “improve the image quality” (Figure 1). Qwen
API exhibits a similar pattern at lower magnitude (UIR 7.2%,
UNR 12.0%), suggesting it applies basic text-level content
filtering.
This mismatch also manifests as over-refusal on safe im-

held-out validation in Section 4.7 further confirms this, e.g.,
SOR of Gemini drops from 14.0% to 3.6% on topically neu-
tral images.

DETERMINISTIC TEMPORAL EMBEDDING FOR CALCIUM IMAGING TRACE
EXTRACTION
Qi Gao1,2, Julius Beichert3,4, Miriam Ratliff 3,4, and Karl Rohr2
1Core Facility Platform Mannheim, CF LIMa, Medical Faculty Mannheim, Heidelberg University, Germany
2Biomedical Computer Vision Group, BioQuant, IPMB, Heidelberg University, Germany
3Department of Neurosurgery, University Hospital Mannheim, Heidelberg University, Germany
4Clinical Cooperation Unit Neurooncology, German Cancer Consortium (DKTK), German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ), Germany
ABSTRACT
Reliable extraction of calcium-dependent fluorescence traces
in calcium imaging sequences requires identifying pixels
whose fluorescence intensity reflects the same underlying
cellular activity. We present a deterministic temporal embed-
ding framework that maps pixel-wise fluorescence traces to
a low-dimensional representation in which temporally coher-
ent sources form spatially coherent regions. Starting from
a fuzzy-neighborhood graph and spectral initialization, we
optimize a class-balanced cross-entropy objective using exact
sparse attraction and a deterministic particle-mesh decom-
position of the dense repulsive interaction with sparse edge
compensation, avoiding stochastic negative sampling. The
resulting latent representation is spatially decoded into reli-
able source supports for trace extraction without imposing an
explicit cellular shape prior. Experiments on synthetic and
in vivo two-photon calcium imaging data demonstrate robust
recovery of irregular and spatially touching sources together
with efficient deterministic embedding optimization.
Index Terms— Calcium Imaging, Trace Extraction, Em-
bedding
1. INTRODUCTION
Calcium imaging enables the observation of intracellular cal-
cium dynamics across large populations of cells and provides
a widely used readout of cellular activity. Downstream bio-
logical analysis requires determining a reliable fluorescence
or calcium activity trace associated with each underlying cel-
lular source. Accurate and reproducible source support es-
timation for trace extraction is therefore a central step from
raw calcium imaging data to quantitative analysis of cellular
dynamics.
Existing calcium imaging trace extraction methods can
generally be classified into three categories.
First, widely
used ROI- and clustering-based methods identify active cel-
lular regions and subsequently extract their temporal sig-
nals (e.g., PCA/ICA-based cell sorting [1], Suite2p [2],
and MIN1PIPE [3]).
A second category of methods for-
mulates source extraction as a spatio-temporal decomposi-

(b) Frame 110

(d) Deterministic PM

tion problem. Constrained nonnegative matrix factorization
(CNMF) [4], CNMF-E [5], and CaImAn [6] jointly estimate
spatial footprints, temporal components, and background ac-
tivity, and are particularly effective when their source and
background models match the imaging modality. Third, more
recently, deep learning methods have been used to learn
spatio-temporal features for neuron detection and segmenta-
tion directly from calcium imaging sequences (e.g., STNeu-
roNet [7], SUNS [8], and DeepWonder [9]). These methods
have improved automation, scalability, and segmentation ac-
curacy, but they generally rely on spatial source models, on
morphology learned from annotated or simulated neurons,
or on assumptions tailored to commonly studied neuronal
imaging settings.
Here, we consider two-photon calcium imaging data of
1

glioblastoma cells, in which active cellular sources may be
irregular, elongated, branching, curved, heterogeneous in
brightness, and frequently touching or spatially connected
(cf. Fig. 1(a,b)). In such data, a static or maximum-intensity
projection may merge distinct cells, and morphology alone
is generally insufficient to define source identity.
In con-
trast, pixels belonging to the same active cell often exhibit
a common blinking pattern over time, whereas neighboring
cells can display distinct and asynchronous temporal dynam-
ics. This motivates treating source identification as a high-
dimensional temporal representation problem rather than as
a purely spatial image segmentation problem.
In our pre-
liminary work, we noticed that UMAP [10] applied directly
to raw pixel-wise fluorescence traces produced remarkably
compact latent regions corresponding to blinking cells, with
neighboring cells often mapped to distinct latent values even
when being in direct spatial contact (cf. Fig. 1(c)). However,
standard UMAP uses stochastic low-dimensional optimiza-
tion, which is undesirable when the embedding itself serves
as the basis for reproducible downstream source extraction.
In this work, we introduce a deterministic temporal em-
bedding framework inspired by UMAP for calcium imag-
ing trace extraction. Pixel-wise raw fluorescence traces are
represented by complementary Euclidean and cosine fuzzy-
neighborhood graphs, which are adaptively fused to retain
both waveform and amplitude information. Starting from a
spectral initialization used in UMAP, we optimize a class-
balanced cross-entropy objective in which sparse graph at-
traction is computed exactly, while the dense repulsive in-
teraction is decomposed into a global particle-mesh (PM)
field and an exact sparse edge compensation term. This for-
mulation avoids stochastic negative sampling and enables
deterministic low-dimensional optimization.
The resulting
latent representation is decoded into spatially coherent can-
didate source supports, which are then selected based on
temporal activity, without imposing an explicit cellular shape
prior. Experiments on synthetic data with ground truth and
real in vivo calcium imaging data demonstrate robust recov-
ery of irregular and spatially touching sources and reliable
extraction of their fluorescence traces.
2. METHODS
2.1. Temporal fuzzy graph and spectral initialization
We start from the raw fluorescence trace of each spatial pixel
in an image sequence of T frames. No temporal centering
or spatial smoothing is applied, as both operations can sup-
press or mix source-specific temporal structure. We construct
fuzzy neighborhood graphs from the raw traces using the stan-
dard UMAP neighborhood construction [10] with 15 nearest
neighbors. Two graphs are computed independently, using
Euclidean and cosine distance. The Euclidean graph retains
amplitude-dependent information, whereas the cosine graph
emphasizes waveform similarity and is less sensitive to mul-
tiplicative intensity variation within a source. The proposed
representation combines these complementary relationships.

guish signal-bearing components from noise [15]. The ACF
is used only as a post-embedding activity measure and is not
part of the embedding optimization. Finally, the fluorescence
trace of each accepted source is obtained as the frame-wise
mean intensity over its selected support.
3. EXPERIMENTS
Data. We evaluated the method on a synthetic dataset and
an in vivo calcium imaging sequence.
The synthetic data
consists of a sequence of 44 irregular cells with 180 frames of
256×256 pixels, including isolated and touching cells, het-
erogeneous shapes and fluorescence patterns, asynchronous
calcium events, static distractors, and multiple noise sources
(Fig. 2(a,b)). The in vivo data was acquired using a mul-
tiphoton microscope from an awake, head-fixed NMRI-
nude mouse with a chronic cranial window [16, 17] and
implanted BG5 glioblastoma cells expressing GCaMP7b and
tdTomato [18]. The image sequence consists of 980 frames of
512×512 pixels with a spatial resolution of 0.59 µm per pixel
and a frame interval of 0.94 s (Fig. 1(a,b)). We employed the
GCaMP7b (green) channel for analysis.
Implementation details. In all experiments, we set D = 3
to enable direct RGB visualization of the latent coordinates.
For PM optimization, we employed a 64×64×64 mesh with
bounds fixed from the spectral initialization and a 75% margin
on each side. The optimization used β =4 and ran for 120 it-
erations with a linearly decaying step size ηt =0.1(1−t/120).
Results on synthetic data. We studied three variants of our
method using Euclidean, cosine, and adaptive fused temporal
graphs (PM-Euclidean, PM-Cosine, and PM-Adaptive) and
performed a comparison with Suite2p [2] and CaImAn [6].
Predicted and ground-truth source supports were matched
one-to-one by the Hungarian algorithm using an IoU thresh-
old of 0.30. We report F1 score and recall for all cells and
for the subset of touching cells.
Recall quantifies source-
recovery completeness, whereas F1 additionally penalizes
false positives.
As shown in Tab. 1, PM-Adaptive achieved the best over-
all F1 score while recovering all ground-truth cells.
PM-
Euclidean also reached perfect recall (1.000), but its lower F1

excluding static distractors; extracted supports from (c) Suite2p [2], (d) CaImAn [6], and (e) PM-Adaptive; and (f) spatial
visualization of the PM-Adaptive embedding. In (b)–(e), different colors denote distinct source supports; in (f), the three latent

score indicates more false positives. PM-Cosine reduced false
positives, but missed several cells. PM-Adaptive avoids this
trade-off by combining the complementary information cap-
tured by the Euclidean and cosine temporal graphs. The ad-
vantage was most pronounced for touching cells, where PM-
Adaptive achieved 1.000 for both F1 and recall, substantially
outperforming CaImAn and Suite2p.
The visual results in Fig. 2 are consistent with these quan-
titative results. Suite2p produces a visibly incomplete set of
source supports, while CaImAn recovers most cells but shows
remaining errors in crowded regions. PM-Adaptive produces
source supports that more closely match the ground truth, in-
cluding those for touching cells. In addition, the spatial visu-
alization of the PM-Adaptive embedding shows distinct latent
representations across cell regions. The latent representation
is subsequently decoded into the extracted supports.
Results on real calcium imaging data. We further evalu-
ated the method qualitatively on the in vivo calcium imaging
sequence. Since exhaustive manual annotation of all active
cells is not available, we focus on the spatial supports and the
corresponding extracted fluorescence traces. Compared with
Suite2p, CaImAn produced a more interpretable result and is
therefore shown as the baseline in Fig. 3. For visualization,
we display the top 100 accepted CaImAn components ranked
by trace SNR and the top 100 PM-Adaptive supports ranked
by the ACF activity feature.
While both methods identify numerous fluorescent struc-
tures, PM-Adaptive produces spatially coherent supports for
a wide range of irregular, elongated, and closely adjacent cell
morphologies (Fig. 3(b)). This behavior is also reflected in
the PM-Adaptive embedding (Fig. 1(d)), where neighboring
cellular structures exhibit distinct latent representations. This
can be attributed to the fact that the proposed method relies
primarily on temporal similarity and does not impose an ex-
plicit cellular shape prior during source discovery. The ex-
tracted traces of the top-ranked PM-Adaptive supports show
distinct transient and sustained fluorescence dynamics across
cells. The support IDs in Fig. 3(b) correspond directly to
those in the trace plot in Fig. 3(c), illustrating the spatial ori-
gin of the recovered temporal signals.

graph and spectral initialization, we compared the time for
embedding optimization for the real calcium imaging data.
On a MacBook Pro with an Apple M1 Pro and 16 GB unified
memory, UMAP required 148.3 s, whereas PM-Adaptive re-
quired 22.8 s and was about 6.5 times faster. This gain was
obtained with a CPU implementation. The particle-mesh op-
erations are highly parallelizable and may benefit further from
a GPU implementation.
4. SUMMARY
We presented a deterministic temporal embedding framework
for calcium imaging trace extraction that combines adaptive
Euclidean–cosine fuzzy graphs with particle-mesh optimiza-
tion of a class-balanced cross-entropy objective. The method
separates temporally distinct sources in a low-dimensional
latent space and converts the resulting spatially coherent
regions into reliable cellular supports without imposing an
explicit cellular shape prior. Experiments on synthetic and in
vivo data demonstrated robust recovery of irregular and spa-
tially touching sources together with efficient deterministic
optimization. The strong downstream performance obtained
with a simple spatial decoder further suggests that source
separation is achieved primarily in the temporal embedding
rather than through complex spatial post-processing.

ments.
Compliance with ethical standards: The animal experi-

Regierungspr¨asidium Karlsruhe (G110/21). This work is a

The Window Lever: Longer Observation Windows
Outweigh the Observed Effects of Data, Capacity,
and Architecture in Customer Behavior Forecasting
Tara Sowrirajan∗
Yanqiao Wang
Amazon
Abstract
In our experiments on long-horizon customer-behavior forecasting, a longer obser-
vation window outweighed the observed effects of more data, more capacity and
newer architectures. The window is the weeks of history a model sees before the
week it forecasts from. Going from an 8- to a 16-week window adds a raw +0.070–
0.107 log-space R2 in every family at 1M. Matched test cohorts, which score the
same customer-weeks at every window, show this raw comparison understates
the gain in every family they cover. The direction holds on five public datasets,
four spanning over a year (ridge and our transformer on all five). On our internal
data, longer windows admit up to 10% more and colder training customers, which
matching does not fix. Our design does not separate window length from calendar
coverage, because every test anchor (the week a forecast is made from) falls in
one eight-week band. On training-period anchors, the weekly ridge probe’s gain
persists outside the holiday season, keeping about 72% of it. We therefore report a
robust positive association with longer windows and do not identify the magnitude
of a calendar-independent history effect. Of four internally registered predictions,
the only fully blind one failed. An activity-mixture model predicted +0.014 from
24 to 32 weeks; the weekly-aggregate probe returned −0.0004. For the sequence
families, the other three levers are about an order of magnitude smaller, bounded
and unresolved. Their observed effects are at most 0.006 between the nominal
1M and 10M tiers and 0.0052 among five sequence families at 16 weeks with
clocks as built, both single-seed on the full test split, and 0.006 for capacity on
three-seed means. These are observed intervals, not equivalence bounds. Our claim
is the order-of-magnitude contrast between the window and those bounds. A team
building on this class of data should start by lengthening the window.
1
Introduction
The usual levers for a sequence model are more data, more parameters and a newer architecture [Ka-
plan et al., 2020, Hoffmann et al., 2022], while history length is usually fixed or treated as a capacity
setting (§3). We compare them on an industrial task, forecasting a customer’s activity from their
event history [Fader et al., 2005, Wang et al., 2019, Li et al., 2022], and of the levers we tested,
history length, the one usually fixed, moves accuracy most. Two lessons carry over. A longer window
changes who is scored, biasing raw comparisons either way; scoring every window on one matched
cohort removes that bias on the test side (training cohorts still grow). A cheap ridge fit on activity
aggregates shows the history gain on every dataset we tried (toy model in §C).
Whether any of these levers binds is not a new question. How much event history a churn model
needs has been asked directly [Ballings and Van den Poel, 2012], and observation-window sufficiency
∗Corresponding author: tarastar@amazon.com
Preprint.
arXiv:2611.26521v1  [cs.LG]  19 Nov 2026
is under active study (§3). However, the question is rarely answered under controlled conditions.
Interventions ship sequentially, on moving populations, and improvements can be hard to attribute
when several parts of the modeling pipeline change at once. We run a controlled comparison of
these commonly modified axes. We hold fixed the export, the test anchor weeks, the target (364-day
forward activity, log(1+y)-transformed, scored in log-space R2), and the evaluation. We then sweep,
one factor at a time, the axes the field usually credits: model family (eight, from a single-feature
linear model to a decay-gated recurrent model [Mei and Eisner, 2017]), population scale (the nominal
1M/5M/10M sampling tiers, §4.1), capacity, and training objective. The training recipe is held fixed
within each family but not across families (Table 13). We also sweep the length of the observation
window, and it is the largest lever we measured. We internally registered four falsifiable commitments
on whether the window gain survives matching and how it bends as the window grows, each with its
falsifier fixed before the evaluation that decided it. The one fully blind prediction failed on its own
falsifier, and the other three held (Table 1).
Doubling the observation window from 8 to 16 weeks moves log-space R2 by +0.070–0.107
at the 1M tier in every family we train.
The families are the transformer, GRU [Cho et al.,
2014], LSTM [Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997], time-biased attention, a decay-gated recurrent
model [Mei and Eisner, 2017], boosted trees [Ke et al., 2017], a 6-feature ridge, and a single-feature
linear model. Time-biased attention replaces the ODE-evolved keys and values of ContiFormer [Chen
et al., 2023b] with a learned time-decay bias on the attention logits. The two continuous-time
baselines, labeled ContiFormer and Neural Hawkes in our tables, are simplified stand-ins for the
cited models. In the main runs the inter-event interval they consume is identically zero, so their time
mechanisms contributed nothing (§E.5). On this end-anchored export, where every input window
ends at the week its forecast is made from, doubling the window also shifts which calendar months
the input covers (§6).
The other levers move the metric substantially less (Figure 1). Among them, the training objective
and time representation (the transformer’s positional encoding) give the largest gains. Both are
smaller than the window gain, and we quantify them below. Moving from the nominal 1M to the 10M
sampling tier changes sequence-model levels by ≤0.006, seed 42. The exception is the 6-feature
ridge, whose level dips 0.016–0.028 at 10M while its window gain stays intact (§2.7). The recurrent
models train on a fixed-size sample at every tier, so their differences across tiers measure population
composition at a fixed training-set size rather than a response to more data (§2.1). The measured
window gain is similar across the population tiers we evaluate: +0.0737 at 10M vs. +0.0731 at
1M (both 3-seed, Huber). Doubling width or depth moves the metric by ≤0.005 at 8 weeks, seed
42. Against the window’s +0.070–0.107 gain, the observed customer-scale and capacity changes
are approximately an order of magnitude smaller. These are one-factor-at-a-time bounds inside the
fixed 2-layer, width-128 (d128) recipe, except that the realized learning-rate schedule is not matched
across tiers (§6). We scale customers at fixed capacity and capacity at fixed data (1M tier), and
never grow capacity and data together, so we measure no compute-optimal configuration. Two of
our own measurements are also about as large as these bounds. The three-seed detection floor for
this class, 0.0059, sits above the architecture band reported below and within a factor of 1.2 of the
customer-scale and capacity bounds. Re-selecting checkpoints in log space, the space we report in,
moves validation scores by +0.002 to +0.009. The top of that range exceeds every one of these
bounds, and the shift does not cancel out of the capacity contrast. These three axes are therefore
bounded but unresolved, and we read none of them as a null (§6).
In these experiments, observation-window length moved the metric by roughly an order of magnitude
more than sequence-architecture choice did, on observed effect sizes rather than interval bounds. With
the Huber objective at M16 (a 16-week window), five sequence architectures land within ∼0.005 of
each other with their clocks as built (0.5525/0.5522/0.5508/0.5478/0.5474, seed 42, full test split). A
separate test that gives each continuous-time model a working clock detects no gain for ContiFormer
and helps Neural Hawkes, by +0.0116 (95% t interval over three seeds +0.0102 to +0.0130), about
twice that band. These paired runs are not bridged to the main ones, so where Neural Hawkes would
land among the five with a working clock is not measured (§E.5). Because those baselines ran at their
own training budgets, we read that band within families rather than as a cross-family ranking (§2.7).
With the MSE objective and 3-seed means, the three families we retrained land within ∼0.0025
(transformer 0.5875 / GRU 0.5863 / LSTM 0.5850, §2.8). The architecture spread observed at shorter
windows narrows substantially by 16 weeks: the decay-gated recurrent model starts 0.015 below the
transformer at 8 weeks and closes most of that gap by 16 weeks (seed 42).
2
Through 16 weeks, matching the test customers across windows makes the window gain larger
(§2.3). We re-evaluate the already-trained checkpoints on matched cohorts, which hold the same
customer-weeks at every window, with identical targets and a constant R2 denominator. The matched
∆(M16−M8) is +0.096, against +0.075 on the full set (Huber, seed 42 for both; the 3-seed full delta
is +0.073). The raw 8-to-16-week comparison understates the gain in every objective and family
measured, and the same pattern holds at 10M (+0.094 matched vs. +0.075 full); both matched
ladders replicate at three seeds.
A confound we do not resolve. A longer window changes more than composition. The calendar
months the input covers move with it. Every test forecast is made from one of three anchor weeks,
four weeks apart (2025-02-24, 2025-03-24, 2025-04-21; §4.1). Each input window ends at one of
these three dates, all inside a single ≈8-week band, so lengthening the window can only extend it
backward into particular calendar months. Only at the earliest anchor does an 8-week window cross
the turn of the year, and then by two days. At that anchor, 16 weeks is the shortest window we test that
reaches the prior November, which the latest anchor reaches only at 24 weeks. The 24- and 32-week
windows reach into the preceding autumn and summer. Window length and calendar coverage are
therefore not separated in this design, against a target that is a 364-day forward aggregate. The
matched cohorts, the activity decomposition, and the objective and family sweeps all hold those three
anchor weeks fixed, and the Taobao dataset (§2.12) spans nine days in total. We therefore ran an
anchor-varying control.
That control is void under its own registered criterion. When we vary which calendar months the
added block covers, the 8-to-16-week gain is +0.18731 at the 2025-02-24 anchor, +0.14910 at
2025-03-24 and +0.04793 at 2025-04-21 for MSE seed 123, and +0.21159/+0.16369/+0.05818
for MSE seed 456. At both seeds the gain is monotone in calendar position, the ordering a seasonal
mechanism predicts. The earliest-minus-latest contrast is +0.13938 (customer-clustered bootstrap
95% CI [+0.12459, +0.15432]) and +0.15341 (95% CI [+0.13851, +0.16930]), both excluding
zero, and a 200-draw same-cohort placebo that shuffles the anchor labels never attains it. We
nonetheless do not interpret it, because the criterion we committed before running the control fails
in every setting. That criterion voids the contrast if the per-anchor R2 spread at M8, before the
added block enters, exceeds 0.010. At both objectives and three seeds each (6 settings, 18 per-anchor
values) the spread is 0.0562/0.0562/0.0623 on MSE and 0.0367/0.0378/0.0420 on Huber. That is
3.7–6.2× the bound, so the criterion voids all six. The numbers show why the criterion exists. In all
six settings the anchors are ordered identically by baseline difficulty and by calendar position (M8
R2 = 0.224/0.248/0.280 at MSE seed 123). The anchor with the most headroom is therefore also the
one whose added block covers the holiday period, and we cannot exclude headroom as an explanation
of the ordering. Algebraically, 37–46% of each contrast is carried by the M8 model, which contains
no added block at all. On Huber, the latest anchor’s added eight weeks are worth −0.00451 to
+0.01407, small or slightly negative. We report every per-anchor figure in this paragraph only as a
record of what failed and by how much. We do not interpret any of them as a calendar measurement.
These figures come from the uniquely keyed matched cohort, the n = 233,038 rows with a unique
target value in each window’s test split. Its selection drops the zero-target rows, so its levels are not
comparable to any full-set R2. In a post-hoc check we renormalize each anchor’s gain by its own
remaining variance, (R2(16) −R2(8))/(1 −R2(8)). The two MSE seeds’ earliest/latest ratios then
move only from 3.91 to 3.63 and from 3.64 to 3.36, so a proportional headroom effect accounts for
roughly 7–8% of the ordering. That check does not change the void verdict.
The window gain’s direction holds in every pooled analysis we report and at every anchor on MSE. Its
magnitude, however, remains confounded with calendar coverage and is not identified as a calendar-
independent history effect (§6). We conclude from the control that, on this end-anchored export,
the test anchors in one eight-week band cannot separate window length from calendar coverage at
either objective. For the transformer runs, a calendar-balanced test set cannot be recovered from this
export. For the weekly-aggregate ridge probe of §E.4, and only for it, the export’s training period
partly separates window length from calendar coverage. We refit the probe on training-period anchors
and score it on held-out training customers. Its 8-to-16-week gain on holiday-free anchors is then
0.72 (95% interval [0.69, 0.75], covering score-side sampling only) of its gain on anchors in the test
anchors’ weeks of the year (the test calendar), so by the probe’s pre-stated rule the gain persists
outside the holiday season (§A). This is a validation-style estimate from a linear probe, not from the
transformer or the test set, so the share of the window gain due to history remains unidentified.
3
The gain from a longer window bends, and where it bends tracks how active the customer is. At 24
weeks the measurement is closer to the saturating curve’s prediction than to the log-linear curve’s,
missing the first by 0.005 and the second by 0.066. We committed both falsifiable predictions before
any 24-week evaluation. The two forms were near-tied on the data they were fit to, and the curvature
inside the fit range had already strained the log-linear form. The 24-week point therefore tests
whether the better in-sample form extrapolates, rather than testing two live hypotheses (§4.5). A
weekly information curve built from a single cohort extract (§2) puts the pooled plateau at 22–24
weeks on the test calendar (the marginal week is worth +0.0001 R2 by k=22–24 weeks). When the
probe is refit on training-period anchors, its returns diminish on both holiday-free and test-calendar
anchors. The sharp bend persists on test-calendar anchors, scored on all their held-out customers, but
is not shown to persist on holiday-free ones (§A) or on any public dataset of §B on which we assess
the bend. The pooled law, however, is consistent with a mixture, and decomposing it by customer
activity yields a result on how to allocate history. The bend moves with customer activity, sharply
and monotonically across the top five deciles. The top activity decile saturates with a half-saturation
point of 3.9 weeks, while the bottom half of the cohort shows no detectable bend within 16 weeks
and is still climbing at the window edge. Higher-activity customers realize their predictive gains
earlier, and lower-activity customers keep benefiting from added history over more of the measured
range. Consistent with the mixture reading inside the window, the pooled curve is visibly not a single
exponential (the fitted exponential underfits in the direction the per-decile mixture predicts). An
internally registered 32-week extension bounds the allocation result. Past 24 weeks, the per-decile
refits find small remaining gains everywhere (+0.012–+0.021, with the lightest deciles at a third
of the mixture’s predicted +0.045–+0.059), and the pooled curve is flat. The advice to allocate
history by activity therefore applies only within the window. By ∼6 months, on the test calendar,
the weekly-aggregate probe finds little left in longer history at any activity level. On the nine-day
public dataset of §2.12, a far sparser one, the saturating form is favored on fit error while the bend
sits at or beyond the edge of the observable window. An internally registered 32-week transformer
test corroborates that the deep model decelerates too. Its 24-to-32-week gain lands on the saturating
prediction and misses the log-linear one. That test ran at one seed and compared models trained on
different cohort extracts (§2.5). No single observation horizon is budget-efficient across customer
activity levels. Within the first few months, “how much history a customer needs” is a per-decile
quantity, predictable from activity and converging on a saturating law. A uniform 24 weeks is still
accuracy-optimal on this grid, so allocating history by activity pays off in budget alone (§2.6).
Against our rotary encoding as implemented, time representation produces the largest model-side
improvement we measured. It clears the customer-scale, capacity, and architecture bounds, and it
composes with the window lever. MS-RoPE, a multi-scale variant of rotary positional encoding
(RoPE) [Su et al., 2024], constrains the rotary frequencies to bands aligned with physical time (hours,
days, weeks, years). Across three seeds, MS-RoPE gained 0.021 in log-space R2 over our integer-
position RoPE implementation. In all three rotary variants we compare, including the learnable
control below, the coordinates of each rotary pair use different frequencies (§E.3), so the gain over
correctly paired RoPE remains unmeasured. MS-RoPE also sits above an unconstrained learnable-
frequency control on 3-seed means, by a margin within the control’s own seed spread. The MS-RoPE
and objective gains are nearly additive: stacking MS-RoPE with the best loss reaches 0.6060±0.0006
log-space R2 (3-seed; 96% of the additive gain). Against the stronger tabular baseline we ran (a
fixed-hyperparameter LightGBM gradient-boosted ensemble on six aggregate features, hereafter
GBM), that stack widens the transformer’s margin over it by ≈2.3× on the matched cohort (≈4×
full-split; §2.11). Explicit physical-time representation lifts the level at every window; it is not how
the model exploits a longer window (§2.10).
Our contributions:
• The observation window is the largest lever we measured. At the 1M tier, all eight model
families gain +0.070–0.107 log-space R2 from a longer window (two of the eight ran with an
inert time mechanism, §E.5). The gain replicates across all three population tiers in every family
evaluated at all three. These figures pool three test anchors inside a single eight-week band, so
window length and calendar coverage are not separated here (§6). The direction replicates on a
nine-day public dataset for linear and deep families, where longer windows also enlarge the eligible
training set (§2.12), and holds for a weekly-aggregate ridge probe on four public datasets that each
span more than a year, and for the paper’s transformer on all four, each read on its own (§B). On
4
those four datasets, rows are held fixed across windows, so their gains do not come from more
training rows.
• Observed effects of scale, capacity, and architecture are much smaller than the window’s;
scale and capacity are unresolved at the precision of these experiments, and architecture
effects are small but not zero. On 3-seed means these three axes move the sequence families by
≤0.007 (architecture at matched objective). We use ≤0.007 throughout as one band for these
three axes, with the architecture bound taken at 16 weeks and the clocks as built. Each axis was
varied alone, with the training recipe fixed within each family apart from the realized learning-rate
schedule of the tier contrast, and measured

Simple Private Noisy SGD is Minimax-Optimal
under Population Strong Convexity
Valentin Roth∗
Marco Avella Medina†
October 2026
Abstract
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is at the center of modern machine learning and is known
to be statistically minimax-optimal in many regression settings, e.g., for convex Generalized
Linear Models (GLMs). Yet, it is unknown whether its simplest differentially private Noisy
SGD counterpart fulfills similar favorable guarantees even on strongly convex losses. We resolve
this question affirmatively. We upper bound the parameter estimation error for a single pass
of Noisy SGD with a fixed stepsize schedule and constant batch sizes on smooth and strongly
convex Lipschitz losses over a compact convex domain under Renyi DP. Specialized to strongly
convex GLMs, our error bounds match minimax lower bounds we derive based on the Score
Attack framework. In particular, this provides the first minimax-optimal rate for Noisy SGD
in private logistic regression, avoiding poly-logarithmic terms present in existing results. Our
analysis is versatile as it relies on standard convex analysis and establishes the same rates in
expectation and with high probability.
1
Introduction
Many supervised machine learning tasks can be formulated as stochastic convex optimization (SCO)
problems. In regression, e.g., a population risk LP (θ) := E [Ln(θ)] := E

is to
be minimized, where Xi are i.i.d. observations from a prespecified distribution with true parameter
ϑ ∈Θ ⊆Rd that shall be recovered. In times of big data, SCO is mostly solved using stochastic
gradient-based optimization procedures where LP is approximated using the loss ℓevaluated on a
subsample of the observations instead of the whole empirical risk Ln. For classical regression models,
stochastic gradient descent (SGD) can be shown to achieve statistically optimal performance when
recovering ϑ through an SCO with properly specified loss components ℓ(Polyak and Juditsky, 1992;
Bach and Moulines, 2013; Toulis et al., 2014). When data privacy guarantees like approximate,
Gaussian or Renyi differential privacy (DP) (Dwork, McSherry, et al., 2006; Dong et al., 2022;
Mironov, 2017) need to be enforced, the picture is less clear even in simple convex and strongly
convex settings. This work focuses on the simplest possible case, regression problems that can be
solved through SCO with strongly convex and smooth Lipschitz losses with a single pass of SGD.
Objective perturbation solves such problems by privatizing the empirical risk through noise and
solving this new optimization problem using standard convex optimization methods.
Similarly,
output perturbation algorithms solve the non-private problem first, e.g., using SGD and afterwards

privatize the estimate by adding noise. Both approaches are known to be optimal for recovering
the empirical/population risk minimizer for strongly convex and smooth problems (See Chaudhuri
et al., 2011; Kifer et al., 2012; Talwar et al., 2014 for objective and Zhang et al., 2017; Lowy and
Razaviyayn, 2021 for output perturbation).
Noisy SGD-type algorithms follow another approach and privatize every single gradient within the
iterations of SGD via additive Gaussian noise. This approach was introduced by Song et al., 2013
and later popularized under the name of DP-SGD by Abadi et al., 2016. Initially, the privacy of
such algorithms was shown through composition theorems or privacy amplification by subsampling.
Privacy guarantees based on amplification by subsampling analyze Noisy SGD’s privacy when mini-
batches are sampled uniformly at random, with or without replacement or using Poisson sampling
(Abadi et al., 2016; Mironov et al., 2019; Wang, Balle, et al., 2019; Dong et al., 2022; Bu et al.,
2020). In a concurrent line of work, the privacy amplification by iteration guarantees in Feldman,
Mironov, et al., 2018; Feldman, Koren, et al., 2020 tighten privacy bounds by analyzing the Renyi
DP leakage when only releasing the last iterate after one pass of Noisy SGD over the data, with
fixed disjoint batches. Most recently, works by Chourasia et al., 2021; Altschuler and Talwar, 2022;
Ye and Shokri, 2022 introduced convergent Renyi DP bounds, for full-batch and mini-batch Noisy
SGD, where the privacy loss on (strongly) convex and smooth losses eventually stops growing after a
fixed number of iterations. Likewise, Bok et al., 2024 proved this phenomenon under Gaussian DP.
Such convergent Renyi DP bounds extend to non-convex and also non-smooth losses (Asoodeh and
Diaz, 2023; Altschuler, Bok, et al., 2024; Kong and Ribero, 2024; Chien and Li, 2025; Liang et al.,
2026). Unfortunately, the generic convergent privacy bounds seem to be too weak for optimal utility
guarantees under strong convexity.
For instance, the privacy bounds requiring strong convexity
like Altschuler, Bok, et al., 2024, Theorem 5.1 are stated for constant stepsizes, tie the privacy
inducing noise to a lower bound on the batch size or introduce excess polylog(n) factors. Others like
Bok et al., 2024, Theorem 4.2 and Ye and Shokri, 2022, Theorem 4.2 do not provide closed form
expressions required for deriving precise guarantees. They also all impose strong convexity on the
loss components ℓ. However, in Rd with d > 1, the components ℓused for parameter estimation
for important regression models – like generalized linear models (GLMs)1 – are not strongly convex
without regularization. In turn, the empirical risk Ln or population risk LP may still be strongly
convex.
As a consequence, the (almost) optimal utility guarantees for gradient-based algorithms in the
literature rely on simpler privacy bounds and make up for this through algorithm design such as
complicated batch size schedules etc.
Bassily et al., 2014 systematically study the optimization
performance of several algorithms. Thereby, they provide an (ε, δ)-DP optimization lower bound of
order
d
ε2n2 Bassily et al., 2014, Theorem 5.5 and show that full-batch Noisy SGD achieves this rate
up to polylog(n) in n2 iterations (Bassily et al., 2014, Theorem 2.4). Ultimately, their guarantees
transfer to statistical estimation in GLMs (Bassily et al., 2014, Theorem F.4). Feldman, Koren, et
al., 2020 shave off this remaining polylog(n) using only n samples through a complicated algorithm
that repeatedly solves auxiliary optimization problems (Feldman, Koren, et al., 2020, Theorem 5.1).
Alternatively, they provide a version of Noisy SGD that performs a single pass over the observations
with an elaborate batch sizing scheme (Feldman, Koren, et al., 2020, Theorem 5.4), whose privacy is
governed by privacy amplification by iteration. Yet, this algorithm again suffers an excess polylog(n)
factor. Likewise, the parameter estimation upper bounds for GLMs in Wang, Zhang, et al., 2021;
Cai et al., 2025 suffer from such polylogarithmic factors.
It is unclear whether a simple and practical gradient-based algorithm can achieve statistical optimal-
1See, e.g., Nelder and Wedderburn, 1972 for an introduction.
2
ity under privacy. We resolve this question affirmatively, relying on Feldman, Koren, et al., 2020’s
privacy amplification by iteration Renyi DP guarantee. Concretely, we show that a single pass of
Noisy SGD with fixed batch sizes achieves minimax estimation rates for parameter estimation in
strongly convex GLMs. We verify the optimality of our upper bound derived using simple convex
analysis techniques through a matching lower bound obtained via the Score Attack framework (Cai
et al., 2025). Our work thereby contributes to a growing body of literature that evaluates the sta-
tistical performance of (full batch) Noisy SGD on regression problems under privacy (Wang, Zhang,
et al., 2021; Cai et al., 2025; Avella-Medina et al., 2023; Brown et al., 2024; Marchis and Loh,
2025; Bombari et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025). To the best of our knowledge, the minimax-optimal
bound for linear regression in Bombari et al., 2025 is the only other purely Noisy SGD-based utility
guarantee for GLMs without excess polylogarithmic factors. Given that their proofs rely on deter-
ministic equivalents in the high-dimensional proportional regime where d/n →c ∈(0, ∞), we want
to highlight the simplicity of our analysis.

Hybrid Retrieval for Government Scheme Search in English and Marathi
Aishwarya Gunjal1,2
Kanchan Khemnar1,2
Pawan Poojary1,2
Pranav Kulkarni1,2
Raviraj Joshi2
Manish Khodaskar1
1Pune Institute of Computer Technology, Pune, India
2L3Cube Labs, Pune, India
{gunjalaishwarya625, kanchankhemnar170, pawanpoojary989,
pranavkulkarni1115, ravirajoshi}@gmail.com; mrkhodaskar@pict.edu
Abstract
Retrieving
government
schemes
requires
matching citizens’ information needs to for-
mal administrative descriptions, often across
languages and terminology. We present a bilin-
gual search system for Maharashtra govern-
ment schemes and public services that com-
bines BM25 retrieval with sentence-embedding
similarity through equal-weight score fusion.
The system indexes aligned English–Marathi
scheme descriptions and supports multilingual,
Marathi-focused, and translation-mediated se-
mantic configurations. Evaluation on manu-
ally curated bilingual queries compares BM25,
dense retrieval, and hybrid retrieval using In-
dicSBERT and MahaSBERT. BM25 provides
a strong baseline with a mean reciprocal rank
(MRR) of 0.864. Hybrid retrieval increases
MRR to 0.872 with IndicSBERT and 0.879
with MahaSBERT, whereas the corresponding
dense-only systems achieve 0.663 and 0.655.
MahaSBERT-based fusion also increases preci-
sion from 0.781 to 0.808 while matching BM25
recall at 0.946. These results support the com-
plementary use of lexical and semantic signals
in this collection, while showing that improve-
ments over a strong lexical baseline are modest
and metric-dependent. The study provides an
application-focused analysis of hybrid retrieval
for bilingual public-service information access.
1
Introduction
Government schemes and public services are com-
monly described using formal names, departmental
terminology, and procedural language. Citizens
may instead express their needs through short de-
scriptions of a problem or desired benefit. A query
such as “financial help for farmers” need not share
the wording of a scheme described as providing
agricultural credit. This vocabulary mismatch mo-
tivates retrieval methods that combine exact term
matching with semantic representations.
The problem also has a multilingual dimension.
A citizen may search in Marathi while relevant de-
scriptions are available in English or in translated
administrative language. A useful retrieval system
must accommodate this variation without losing the
discriminative value of scheme names, categories,
and domain-specific terms. Bilingual records pro-
vide a common document inventory, but translation
alone does not resolve mismatches between a user’s
phrasing and an official description.
BM25 provides an established lexical rank-
ing function that rewards informative query-term
matches (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009). Sen-
tence embedding models offer a complementary
mechanism by representing queries and docu-
ments in a shared vector space (Reimers and
Gurevych, 2019). In Marathi, MahaSBERT pro-
vides language-focused representations, while In-
dicSBERT supports multiple Indian languages
(Joshi et al., 2023; Deode et al., 2023). However,
semantic similarity need not imply that a scheme
satisfies a user’s specific requirement. Combin-
ing lexical and semantic signals therefore requires
empirical evaluation against a lexical baseline.
We develop a hybrid search system for a collec-
tion of 64 Maharashtra government schemes and
public services in English and Marathi. The sys-
tem combines field-weighted BM25 scores with
sentence-embedding similarity and presents ranked
records with their source links. We investigate
whether fusion improves retrieval over either com-
ponent and whether the choice between a Marathi-
focused and a multilingual encoder affects the re-
sulting ranking.
Our contributions are:
• A bilingual retrieval pipeline integrating cor-
pus collection, English–Marathi alignment,
lexical indexing, and semantic search for gov-
ernment schemes and public services.
• A comparison of BM25, IndicSBERT-based
retrieval, MahaSBERT-based retrieval, and
1
arXiv:2611.26514v1  [cs.LG]  19 Nov 2026
their hybrid combinations on 150 manually
curated queries.
• An analysis of the magnitude and metric de-
pendence of hybrid gains, distinguishing im-
provements over dense-only retrieval from
improvements over an already strong lexical
baseline.
2
Related Work
Lexical and semantic retrieval.
BM25 esti-
mates relevance from term occurrences, inverse
document frequency, and document-length nor-
malization (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009). It is
well suited to exact terminology but does not ex-
plicitly represent semantic relationships between
different expressions. Contextual encoders such
as BERT provide the basis for learned text repre-
sentations (Devlin et al., 2019); Sentence-BERT
adapts contextual encoding to produce indepen-
dently computable sentence vectors (Reimers and
Gurevych, 2019). These representations support
similarity-based retrieval, although their effective-
ness depends on the relationship between the em-
bedding training objective and the target retrieval
task. MiniLM uses self-attention distillation to ob-
tain compact Transformer encoders (Wang et al.,
2020), providing a basis for efficient sentence-
embedding configurations.
Dense Passage Re-
trieval (DPR) explicitly trains a dual encoder on
question–passage relevance pairs (Karpukhin et al.,
2020), illustrating the distinction between general
sentence similarity and retrieval-specific supervi-
sion.
Representations for Indian languages.
Indic-
NLPSuite develops corpora, evaluation bench-
marks, and pretrained multilingual models for In-
dian languages (Kakwani et al., 2020). MuRIL
introduces Indian-language pretraining that incor-
porates translated and transliterated sentence pairs
(Khanuja et al., 2021). More generally, multilin-
gual sentence embedding spaces can be learned
through knowledge distillation with parallel sen-
tences (Reimers and Gurevych, 2020). LaBSE
combines multilingual pretraining with translation-
based alignment to learn language-agnostic sen-
tence embeddings (Feng et al., 2022). MahaSBERT
and HindSBERT apply sentence-level training with
translated natural language inference and seman-
tic similarity data to Marathi and Hindi (Joshi
et al., 2023). IndicSBERT extends sentence rep-
resentation learning across multiple Indian lan-
guages using multilingual BERT (Deode et al.,
2023). These models motivate a comparison be-
tween language-focused and multilingual represen-
tations for Marathi administrative text. Their per-
formance on general similarity tasks does not, by
itself, establish their relative effectiveness for re-
trieving specific public benefits.
Hybrid score fusion.
Hybrid retrieval combines
lexical and semantic relevance estimates. Recip-
rocal rank fusion aggregates rank positions rather
than raw relevance scores (Cormack et al., 2009),
providing an alternative to score-level interpolation.
Bruch et al. (2024) analyze fusion functions, includ-
ing convex combinations of lexical and semantic
scores, and demonstrate the importance of treat-
ing score combination as a retrieval-design choice.
Our system uses a fixed, equal-weight combina-
tion rather than introducing a new fusion algorithm.
The contribution lies in its bilingual public-service
application and the comparison of encoder choices
against a shared lexical baseline.
Multilingual
and
cross-domain
evaluation.
Mr. TyDi evaluates dense retrieval in typologi-
cally diverse languages and finds that dense sig-
nals can improve sparse–dense hybrids even when
the dense retriever is weaker than BM25 in iso-
lation (Zhang et al., 2021). BEIR examines re-
trieval across heterogeneous tasks and domains
and identifies BM25 as a robust zero-shot baseline
(Thakur et al., 2021). Complementary multilin-
gual resources address how retrieval data are con-
structed: mMARCO translates the MS MARCO
passage-ranking dataset (Bonifacio et al., 2021),
whereas MIRACL provides native-speaker rele-
vance annotations for monolingual retrieval across
diverse languages (Zhang et al., 2023). The distinc-
tion is relevant to bilingual public-service search,
where translated document coverage and native-
language relevance judgments serve different pur-
poses. These findings motivate comparison against
a strong lexical system and caution against trans-
ferring encoder rankings directly from general sim-
ilarity benchmarks to a specialized collection. Our
evaluation addresses a bilingual administrative do-
main rather than the broader benchmark settings
studied in these resources.
2
3
Bilingual Scheme Collection
3.1
Collection and Preprocessing
The collection contains 64 distinct government
schemes and public services gathered from Maha-
rashtra government portals, including Aaple Sarkar,
and scheme information repositories. Each record
comprises a title, description, and source URL, to-
gether with category information used for retrieval
and filtering. The collection covers 14 domain
categories, including agriculture, health, housing,
education, revenue, transport, welfare, and indus-
try.
We remove HTML markup and navigation con-
tent using BeautifulSoup and regular-expression-
based cleaning. Text normalization standardizes
whitespace and punctuation and corrects encoding
artifacts. Potential duplicates are identified through
fuzzy matching of names and descriptions; pairs
with similarity scores above 85% are manually re-
viewed and merged when they refer to the same
record. Entries lacking a title or description are cor-
rected from their source or excluded. The resulting
scheme identifier is shared across the two language
versions.
3.2
English–Marathi Alignment
The English records are translated into Marathi
using the Google Translation API with domain-
specific glossaries. Translation is performed in
batches, followed by terminology consistency
checks and native-speaker review of a 20% sam-
ple. The aligned collection contains 64 English
records and 64 corresponding Marathi records, rep-
resenting 64 underlying schemes rather than 128
independent schemes.
Table 1 summarizes the collection. Description
lengths vary substantially, reflecting differences in
the amount of procedural and service information
associated with individual records. This variation
motivates document-length normalization in lexi-
cal retrieval and consistent record construction for
semantic indexing.
4
Retrieval Framework
4.1
Architecture
Figure 1 summarizes the retrieval pipeline. Offline
processing produces the aligned records and their
lexical and semantic indexes. At query time, the
interface accepts an English or Marathi query and
optional category, date, or department filters. The

4.2

The lexical component uses BM25 in Elasticsearch

• MahaSBERT (Joshi et al., 2023) pro-

Hybrid Ranking
Let eSlex and eSsem denote normalized lexical and

the weight is optimal for this domain.
Candidates from the lexical and semantic
branches are combined and reranked using the hy-

branch at 2,000 candidates. For this 64-record col-
lection, that cap exceeds the corpus size and there-
fore imposes no additional depth truncation. The
evaluation consequently concerns ranking within a
small collection rather than large-scale candidate
generation.
5
Experimental Setup
5.1
Queries and Relevance Judgments
The test set comprises 150 manually curated
queries: 75 in English and 75 in Marathi. Each
query is associated with one or more relevant
schemes in the collection. All configurations are
evaluated against the same query-to-scheme rele-
vance mappings. We compare the shared BM25
baseline, the two dense-only retrievers, and the
corresponding hybrid configurations.
The query set evaluates retrieval from the
fixed collection. It does not measure whether a
user meets a scheme’s eligibility requirements or
whether retrieval leads to a successful application.
These outcomes require evidence beyond query–
document relevance.
5.2
Evaluation Metrics
We use standard relevance-based retrieval mea-
sures (Manning et al., 2008). Mean reciprocal rank
(MRR) measures the position of the first relevant
result. If rq is the rank of that result for query q,

that are relevant; recall reflects the proportion of

metrics capture different aspects of retrieval, so an
improvement in one does not imply an improve-
ment in the others.
6
Results and Discussion
6.1
Comparison of Retrieval Strategies
Table 2 reports the retrieval results. BM25 achieves
an MRR of 0.864, exceeding IndicSBERT-only re-
trieval at 0.663 and MahaSBERT-only retrieval at
0.655. Lexical matching is therefore a strong base-
line in this collection, and replacing it with dense
similarity alone reduces the measured ranking ef-
fectiveness.
Both hybrid configurations obtain higher preci-
sion and MRR than BM25. IndicSBERT-based
fusion increases precision by 0.014 and MRR by
0.008, while recall increases from 0.946 to 0.950.
MahaSBERT-based fusion increases precision by
0.027 and MRR by 0.015, while recall remains
0.946. Its MRR gain over BM25 is approximately
1.7% relative to the baseline. These results support
a benefit from combining relevance signals, but do
not show strict improvement on every metric.
The gains over dense-only retrieval are substan-
tially larger. MahaSBERT-based fusion increases
MRR from 0.655 to 0.879, an absolute difference
of 0.224, or approximately 34.2% relative improve-
ment. IndicSBERT-based fusion increases MRR
from 0.663 to 0.872, an absolute difference of
0.209. Distinguishing these comparisons is im-
portant: the large improvements over dense-only
retrieval do not characterize the smaller improve-
ment over BM25.
6.2
Effect of the Semantic Encoder
IndicSBERT obtains higher precision, recall, and
MRR than MahaSBERT in the dense-only setting.
Under hybrid fusion, MahaSBERT instead yields
the highest precision and MRR, while IndicSBERT
yields the highest recall. The encoder ranking there-
fore depends on the retrieval configuration and eval-
uation metric.
A possible explanation is that an encoder’s use-
fulness in fusion depends on which candidates it
promotes relative to BM25, rather than only on
its standalone ranking. The results are compatible
with complementary relevance signals, but do not
isolate the mechanism responsible for the change
in ordering. They also do not establish language-
specific superiority from the aggregate bilingual
scores.
6.3
Implications for Public-Service Search
Administrative descriptions contain names, cate-
gories, and terms that can make lexical matching
effective. Semantic representations may contribute
when users paraphrase those descriptions, but can
also assign high similarity to schemes with related
topics and different purposes. The observed results
favor retaining lexical evidence while supplement-
ing it with an embedding-based signal. This qual-
itative pattern is consistent with the complemen-
tary sparse and dense signals observed in Mr. TyDi
(Zhang et al., 2021), although the collections and
evaluation settings differ.
Qualitative error analysis identifies ambiguous
queries and semantically similar schemes across de-
partments as challenging cases. A retrieved record
can be topically related without satisfying a user’s
intended benefit or eligibility condition. Source
links and explicit scheme details therefore remain
important for interpreting results. The system sup-
ports discovery of potentially relevant information
rather than automated eligibility determination.
7
Conclusion
We presented a bilingual hybrid retrieval system
for 64 Maharashtra government schemes and pub-
lic services. The system combines field-weighted
BM25 with sentence-embedding similarity through
equal-weight normalized score fusion. On 150 En-
glish and Marathi queries, MahaSBERT-based hy-
brid retrieval achieves the highest precision (0.808)
and MRR (0.879), while IndicSBERT-based hybrid
retrieval achieves the highest recall (0.950). BM25
remains a strong baseline, with MRR 0.864, and
substantially exceeds both dense-only systems.
The main finding is that hybrid retrieval provides
modest, metric-dependent improvements over lexi-
cal retrieval in this collection, rather than a uni-
form advantage on all measures.
Future work
should evaluate larger and more diverse scheme
collections, domain-specific representation learn-
ing, and query-dependent fusion weights, along-
side direct assessment of user information needs
and eligibility-sensitive retrieval.

Grid Cells as Spectral Successor Features:
A Reusable Basis for Continual Reinforcement Learning
´Elodie Cˆot´e-Gauthier
McGill University and Mila – Quebec AI Institute
Doina Precup
McGill University and Mila – Quebec AI Institute
Isabeau Pr´emont-Schwarz
Universit´e Laval and Mila – Quebec AI Institute
Abstract
Continual reinforcement learning requires agents to adapt when the task changes while
reusing what they know about the environment. Successor features separate dynamics from
task-specific reward, but their effectiveness depends on the choice of base features. Taking
the identification of entorhinal grid cells with eigenvectors of the successor representation
as a design principle, we build this basis from eigenvectors of the transition matrix of a
fixed reference policy. With such a basis, the successor features at a state-action pair are
a linear combination of the base features at that same pair, which is not true in general,
and the coefficients are known in closed form: each successor feature is its base feature
multiplied by θi = 1/(1 −γλi), where λi is its eigenvalue. The long-term return is thus
predicted from the same features as the immediate reward, no successor-feature network
or replay buffer is needed, and adapting to a new task reduces to a linear regression on
the reward. The agent acts greedily on the action values of the reference policy, which is
one step of policy improvement over it and suffices to reach a single goal. In a two-goal
gridworld, with the uniform random walk as reference policy, whose eigenvectors are the
low-frequency Laplacian eigenvectors, agents built this way maintain near-maximal return
across every change of goal, whereas SimpleSF and DQN lose most of their return at each
change.
Keywords: successor representation, grid cells, Laplacian eigenfunctions, spectral meth-
ods, continual reinforcement learning
1. Introduction
Continual reinforcement learning requires an agent to reuse knowledge across tasks when
only the reward changes, without relearning the world from scratch. Successor features
(Barreto et al., 2017) address this by decomposing the value function into task-independent
dynamics and task-specific reward weights, but their effectiveness depends critically on
the feature basis. We ask whether grounding that basis in the spectral geometry of the
transition structure, specifically in the eigenvectors of the random-walk graph Laplacian,
makes successor-feature learning faster and simpler.
The choice is motivated by neural coding in the hippocampal–entorhinal system. Dayan
(1993) introduced the successor representation (SR) as a predictive state representation that
generalises between states with similar successors, and Stachenfeld et al. (2017) proposed
that hippocampal place cells encode the SR while entorhinal grid cells correspond to its
eigenvectors, so that the SR functions as a predictive map.

Contributions.
(i) In general, the successor features at a state-action pair cannot be
computed from the base features of that pair alone. They can when the span of the base
features is invariant under the transition matrix of the policy, as a linear combination with
coefficients in closed form, and when the base features are eigenvectors of that matrix, each
successor feature is its base feature multiplied by a constant. Successor features then need
not be learned, and the long-term return is predicted from the same features as the immedi-
ate reward (Section 2.1). (ii) Computing these features for a fixed reference policy, while the
agent acts greedily on the action values of that policy, makes the basis independent of the
agent’s behaviour. The price is that the agent performs one step of policy improvement over
the reference policy rather than following the optimal policy, which still suffices to reach
a single goal (Section 2.2). With the uniform random walk as reference policy, the basis
is made of the low-frequency Laplacian eigenvectors, which must be built over state-action
pairs, because invariance under the averaged transition operator does not imply invariance
under each per-action operator (Sections 2.3 and 2.4). (iii) In a continual-learning gridworld,
agents that act greedily on the action values of the uniform random walk, with the tran-
sition graph either given or estimated from their own transitions, maintain near-maximal
return across changes of goal, where SimpleSF and DQN do not (Section 3).
1.1. Background
Setting.
We consider a Markov decision process with finite states S, actions A, transition
probabilities P(s′ | s, a) and discount γ ∈(0, 1). Since the agent needs action values, we
work directly with state-action pairs z = (s, a). A policy π induces a transition matrix
between pairs, P π
zz′ = P(s′ | s, a) π(a′ | s′) for z′ = (s′, a′), and we write wj := E[r(zj)] for
the expected immediate reward of pair zj.
The successor representation.
The SR of π (Dayan, 1993) counts, for every starting
pair, the expected discounted number of future visits to every pair:

Successor features.
The SR has one entry per pair of state-action pairs, which does not
scale to large or continuous state spaces. Successor features (SFs) (Barreto et al., 2017)
compress it with n base features ϕ(z) = (ϕ1(z), . . . , ϕn(z)):

SR is the special case of one-hot features, for which w is the reward of each pair, as in

temporal difference, and it changes whenever π does.
2
Grid Cells as Spectral Successor Features
The graph Laplacian and grid cells.
The transitions of the environment also define a
graph whose nodes are the pairs, in which z = (s, a) is joined to every pair (s′, a′) available
at the state s′ that a leads to. With W its adjacency matrix and D the diagonal matrix of
its degrees, Prw = D−1W is the transition matrix of the uniform random walk on the graph,
and I −Prw its Laplacian. The eigenvectors of this Laplacian with the smallest eigenvalues
vary slowly along the graph and describe its large-scale geometry; they are the proto-value
functions of Mahadevan (2005). Because the SR of the random walk, (I −γPrw)−1, is a
function of Prw, it has the same eigenvectors (Stachenfeld et al., 2017; Machado et al., 2018).
These shared eigenvectors are the functions that Stachenfeld et al. (2017) identify with grid
cells.
1.2. Related work
Laplacian eigenvectors have also been used in reinforcement learning independently of the
neuroscientific connection: as proto-value functions for value approximation (Mahadevan,
2005; Mahadevan and Maggioni, 2007), for option discovery (Machado et al., 2017), and
for reward shaping (Wu et al., 2019). Machado et al. (2018) rely on the same equivalence
between the SR and the Laplacian as we do, but in the opposite direction: they learn the
SR, from pixels if needed, in order to extract its eigenvectors, which then define intrinsic
rewards for exploration. We start from the eigenvectors and derive the successor features
from them. Vijayan et al. (2026) also learn Laplacian eigenfunctions online from pixels,
with an ALLO-based objective (Gomez et al., 2024) weighted by novelty, and turn them
into options that drive exploration towards novel states in sparse-reward Atari and ProcGen
games. Touati et al. (2023) compare many base features for successor features in zero-shot
reinforcement learning and find Laplacian eigenfunctions to be a reliable choice among
them, second overall to forward-backward representations, which learn the features and
the successor features jointly. They still learn the successor features with a network, for
a family of greedy policies, a step our construction removes. Our graph has the topology
of the off-policy state-action graph of Osentoski and Mahadevan (2007), but we weight its
edges differently (Appendix D) and symmetrise it instead of using a directed Laplacian.
They found that Laplacian bases built on this graph approximate action values with far
fewer functions than a state basis copied once per action. In their setting the copied state
basis remains usable, if less efficient, because Q(λ) learns the effect of each action in the
weights. In ours it cannot distinguish actions in general, because the dynamics are fixed
in closed form and only the immediate reward is learned, so the action must be carried by
the basis itself (Section 2.4). Finally, SimpleSF (Chua et al., 2024) learns successor features
directly from pixels by combining a temporal-difference loss with a reward-prediction loss,
which avoids representation collapse without pretraining.
Its network must nonetheless
reorganise when the task changes, whereas our successor features are computed rather than
learned. We use SimpleSF as our main baseline, together with DQN (Mnih et al., 2015) as
an agent that learns no successor structure.
2. Spectral successor features
Two separate choices remove the two problems of Section 1.1: that ψπ must be learned, and
that it must be relearned whenever the policy changes. Base features whose span is invariant

form (Section 2.1). Computing them for one fixed policy, while the agent acts greedily on

changes (Section 2.2).

The dynamics now enter only through the basis and the constants θi, both computed once.
The only quantity left to learn is w, by a linear regression of the immediate reward on the

2.2. Two policies: a fixed reference policy and a greedy acting policy

the agent’s policy changes. We therefore separate the two roles that a policy plays. A

The acting policy changes continuously, as w is learned and whenever the goal moves, but

be any fixed policy: the uniform random walk, whose transition matrix depends only on the
graph of the environment (Section 1.1), a policy learned on an earlier task, or the agent’s

our experiments.
