Related Work
Learning to Defer (L2D)
Early work on classifiers that can choose to reject or abstain instead of making
a prediction (Chow, 1957) inspired more recent work on how to model what happens after the classifier
abstains (Madras et al., 2018), with Mozannar & Sontag (2020) deriving the first consistent surrogate loss
for the problem. This work has been expanded in recent years to address several limitations, including mis-
calibration (Verma & Nalisnick, 2022; Cao et al., 2023), underfitting (Narasimhan et al., 2022), realizable
consistency (Mozannar et al., 2023), sample complexity (Charusaie et al., 2022), data scarcity (Hemmer et al.,
2023), and deferral to multiple experts (Verma et al., 2023). However, these approaches do not consider the
‘messiness’ of modeling human experts—as we do—and could just as well be applied to a black-box API.
L2D for Sequences and Populations
L2D has also been extended to the difficult settings of sequential
tasks and encountering novel experts. Regarding the former, Sequential Learning-to-Defer (Joshi et al., 2023)
5
incorporates temporal dynamics by framing deferral as a sequential decision-making problem, employing
model-based reinforcement learning. This work, however, is primarily concerned with the sequential nature
of the prediction task itself and not robustness to expert drift, which is our primary concern. Regarding the
latter, Learning to Defer to a Population (Tailor et al., 2024) uses meta-learning to adapt to never-before-
seen experts at test-time. Their motivation is to be robust to novel experts (with the novelty not being a
function of time), whereas we are concerned about modeling the temporal drift of a known expert.
Temporal Shifts in Human Performance
In many high-stakes domains, human performance shift
over time (due to fatigue or other cognitive factors) are well-documented and widely studied. Fatigue is
extremely common in high-stakes domains and long-horizon tasks, such as radiology (Bruni et al., 2012),
automated driving (Figalová et al., 2024), air traffic control (Peukert et al., 2023), and flying planes (Pan
et al., 2022). Beyond affecting surface-level performance on these tasks, fatigue physically affects the brain,
causing reduced alertness and vigilance that can be measured directly, e.g. using EEG signals (Figalová
et al., 2024). We extend L2D to be adaptive to these variations in human performance.
L2D with Time-Varying Experts
Recent work has also begun to relax the assumption of a static
expert. Zhang et al. (2026) model expert accuracy as a parametric function of cumulative workload and
learn a deferral policy with constrained reinforcement learning under a coverage budget. Montreuil et al.

Exact Bayesian layers via characteristic functions
William H. W. Thompson
∗1, Guillaume St-Onge
2, Laurent Hébert-Dufresne
1,3,4, and
Jean-Gabriel Young
†1,3,5
1Vermont Complex Systems Institute, University of Vermont
2School of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, University of Ottawa
3Department of Computer Science, University of Vermont
4Santa Fe Institute
5Department of Mathematics and Statistics, University of Vermont
November 20, 2026
Abstract
Bayesian neural networks provide principled uncertainty estimates, but training them with
Monte Carlo sampling can be expensive. Sampling-free variational inference algorithms make
training Bayesian neural networks feasible, but existing approaches assume a Gaussian output
distribution, which can be inaccurate in applied problems. Here, we introduce CF-Prop, an
uncertainty propagation method that uses characteristic functions to compute the exact output
distribution of a Bayesian ReLU layer, without any sampling, even for non-Gaussian predictive
densities. Because CF-Prop propagates characteristic functions, the evidence lower bound—the
objective of variational training—can be computed in closed form for a broad class of likelihoods,
including the Gaussian, Poisson, and Gamma. This allows us to implement an efficient variational
inference algorithm, CF-VI. On CIFAR-100, CF-VI achieves the lowest calibration error of any
tested method, improving on the next best method by about 35%. On a heavy-tailed insurance
claim dataset, CF-VI accurately captures tail uncertainty that is severely underestimated by
both other sampling-free methods and Monte Carlo methods.
1
Introduction
Neural networks are the least reliable when training data is scarce. Bayesian Neural Networks
(BNNs) offer a principled way to deal with the fundamental uncertainty of this data regime [Mitros
and Mac Namee, 2019, Kristiadi et al., 2020]. They quantify both epistemic uncertainty, which
arises from limited knowledge of the model, and aleatoric uncertainty, which is due to the inherent
randomness of the data-generating process. They excel in high-stakes, safety-critical applications
[Ghoshal et al., 2021, Ding et al., 2021], perform well with limited data, prevent overfitting [Depeweg
et al., 2018], and can increase fairness and reduce bias [Doherty et al., 2023].
∗wthomps3@uvm.edu
†jean-gabriel.young@uvm.edu
1
arXiv:2611.26426v1  [stat.ML]  19 Nov 2026
BNNs quantify epistemic uncertainty by introducing a posterior distribution p(θ | D) over
the model parameters θ, given training data D. Propagating this uncertainty to the output η is
required for training and inference. Stochastic methods, such as Bayes by Backprop [Graves, 2011,
Blundell et al., 2015], estimate it by sampling weights. Sampling-free methods, such as Deterministic
Variational Inference (DVI) [Wu et al., 2019], CovProp [Wright et al., 2024], and Variational Bayesian
Last Layers (VBLL) [Harrison et al., 2024], replace sampling with moment propagation, which
removes noise at the cost of assuming a specific functional form for the pre-activations.
We argue that these methods break down exactly where uncertainty quantification matters most.
Indeed, DVI, CovProp and VBLL assume that the predictive distribution and the variational family
are Gaussians. However, many applied problems require accurate estimates of tail probabilities—the
probability of a 100-year flood or a multi-million-dollar insurance claim—for distributions that are
often far from Gaussian. This Gaussian assumption shows up in two places in these methods: the
likelihood, which captures aleatoric uncertainty, and the distribution of the network, which captures
epistemic uncertainty. But in practice, the likelihood can be skewed, in Gamma regressions for claim
sizes, for example. And the distribution of the network output also tends to be skewed in these cases,
because tail predictions are often dominated by a few rarely active neurons. Hence, non-Gaussian
variational families are required to properly handle these cases. Any propagation method that
models either distribution as Gaussian can severely underestimate tail risk. In practice, the BNN
literature uses many other variational families: spike-and-slab families for sparsification [Hubin and
Storvik, 2019], scale mixtures for shrinkage [Louizos et al., 2017, Ghosh et al., 2019], and multimodal
mixtures [Dusenberry et al., 2020, Miller et al., 2017]—though current sampling-free propagation
methods are incompatible with these families.
We introduce CF-Prop, an exact and sampling-free method for uncertainty propagation in a
single-layer Bayesian perceptron that uses characteristic functions (CF). The forward pass of the
layer is expressed in the Fourier domain, making the predictive density tractable. We use this
propagation algorithm as the backbone of a new method, Variational Inference via Characteristic
Functions (CF-VI). CF-VI extends sampling-free variational inference beyond the Gaussian regime by
expressing the predictive density of the Bayesian layer exactly and in closed form. It allows for both
non-Gaussian predictive distributions and non-Gaussian variational families. It can accommodate
any likelihood and any variational family with a tractable characteristic function.
CF-VI can be used to train a fully exact Bayesian perceptron or as an exact Bayesian last layer on
a sampling-free or stochastic trunk. We show that CF-VI performs well on traditional benchmarks
such as UCI regressions, and provides state-of-the-art uncertainty quantification on classification
tasks with a large number of labels such as CIFAR-100. We also show that CF-VI performs
exceptionally well in uncertainty quantification for neural GLMs commonly used in the actuarial
sciences. In particular, we show that for a Gamma regression task on heavy-tailed data—predicting
the size of insurance claims—other methods severely underestimate uncertainty in the tails of the
distribution. In contrast, our method provides an exact description of the tail uncertainty. CF-VI
is also computationally efficient: In many common cases, it adds only a modest overhead to the
training of a fully deterministic neural network.
Our contributions are as follows:
1. An exact expression for the output distribution of a Bayesian ReLU layer using characteristic
functions.
2. CF-VI, a sampling-free variational inference method compatible with any mean-field variational
family and a broad class of likelihoods.
2
3. Lower training and inference cost than other sampling-free methods on UCI benchmarks, at
comparable NLL.
4. The best calibration among tested methods on CIFAR-100.
5. Accurate tail uncertainty on heavy-tailed regression, where other tested methods underweight
tail risk.
2
Background: Uncertainty propagation
Given a distribution q(θ) over the full set of model parameters θ, uncertainty propagation computes
the induced distribution of the network output at an input xn, q(η | xn), the latent predictive
distribution, which is needed both to train a BNN and to make predictions. The latent predictive
distribution quantifies epistemic uncertainty in the prediction due to uncertainty in the model
parameters. The model also includes a likelihood p(yn | η), which links the latent output η to the
observation yn and models the aleatoric uncertainty, the irreducible noise in the data. Combining
the two gives the posterior predictive distribution, q(yn | xn) = Eη∼q(η|xn)[p(yn | η)] =
R p(yn |
η) q(η | xn) dη.
Directly calculating the probability density function of the activations of a BNN is so compu-
tationally expensive that it is rarely implemented. Instead, training and inference of BNNs rely
on stochastic sampling [Graves, 2011, Blundell et al., 2015] or sampling-free approximations. We
review sampling-free methods below.
2.1
Moment propagation
Even when the full density q(η | xn) is intractable, its moments might be easy to compute. Moment
propagation methods derive exact or approximate expressions for the moments of the activations of
a single hidden layer, then moment-match, assuming that the distribution of the activations is well
described by a Gaussian sharing these moments.
Two methods are relevant here: deterministic variational inference (DVI) and covariance propa-
gation (CovProp). Wu et al. [2019] develop DVI expressions for the first and second moments of
the activation distribution and derive an asymptotic approximation for the correlation between
activations. DVI generally tracks the full covariance structure among all h hidden units, with O(h3)
complexity. A diagonal method (dDVI) can also be implemented by ignoring covariance, reducing
DVI’s cubic complexity with layer width to linear complexity.
Wright et al. [2024] extend this work. CovProp expresses the moments as a power series in
the correlation coefficient. The resulting method can, in principle, attain an arbitrarily accurate
representation of the first two moments, provided that enough terms are computed in the power
series. In practice, CovProp requires at least 4 terms to outperform DVI.
Both DVI and CovProp can be applied to arbitrarily deep networks, although approximation
error compounds for deeper networks: even after 5 layers, DVI’s predictive distribution is distorted
significantly. Competitive benchmark performance is attained only for very shallow networks of 1 or
2 layers [Wu et al., 2019].
3
2.2
Variational Bayesian last layers
Variational Bayesian last layers (VBLLs) [Harrison et al., 2024] are another sampling-free approach.
This is an example of Bayesian last-layer methods [Kristiadi et al., 2020], which have many of the
benefits of a fully Bayesian neural network. They use a deep deterministic “trunk” to generate
low-dimensional features, which are then fed as inputs to a shallow Bayesian network. VBLLs are a
sampling-free variational approach where only the linear readout is Bayesian.
While VBLLs are efficient, they have limited expressiveness. VBLLs capture uncertainty only in
the linear readout; they cannot account for uncertainty through a full non-linear layer. Like moment
propagation methods, VBLLs restrict the predictive distribution of the output η to a Gaussian,
and thus cannot account for any skew or heavy tails. A VBLL classifier, for example, can only
express uncertainty around decision boundaries that are linear in the learned features. While highly
efficient, the linear method cannot properly forecast uncertainty when data is sparse.
2.3
Failure of Gaussian assumptions
Moment propagation is a good approximation only when two assumptions hold: the likelihood is
Gaussian, and the latent predictive distribution q(η | xn) is Gaussian. Many common scenarios
violate one or both, including typical configurations of the UCI regression benchmarks frequently
used to evaluate Bayesian neural networks.
First, we consider the assumption that the likelihood is Gaussian. If it is not, the expected
log-likelihood Eη∼q(η|xn)[log p(yn | η)] is no longer determined by the first two moments of q(η | xn).
For the Poisson and Gamma likelihoods with a log link, the expectation contains exponential
moments, E[eη] and E[e−η]. These are sensitive to the tails and only weakly constrained by the first
two moments.
The second assumption, that the latent predictive is Gaussian, rests on the central limit theorem.
When the linear readout sums many weakly correlated activations together, the predictive will be
approximately Gaussian. Wu et al. [2019] argue that the correlation between hidden units remains
weak enough during training for this to hold approximately, and in a heteroscedastic regression with
two hidden layers of 128 units they show close agreement between the Monte Carlo sampled and
the moment-matched Gaussian activations. However, many commonly used architectures have last
layers with fewer than 128 units: the network used later in the same paper for the UCI regression
benchmark has a single hidden layer of 50 units.
Layers of this size (50 units) show meaningfully non-Gaussian predictive distributions, especially
in the tails. In Figure 1, we train networks with a deterministic hidden layer followed by a Bayesian
hidden layer using CF-VI with a mean-field Gaussian family, varying the layer’s width from 8 to 256
units, and apply CF-Prop, DVI, and CovProp to the same trained network to isolate the differences
that can be attributed to propagation alone. All methods model the mean correctly, but DVI and
CovProp underestimate the tails. Averaged over test inputs, their error is small, but at individual
inputs it can be large. At the width of the example in Wu et al. [2019] (128 units), the average total
variation between DVI and Monte Carlo is 0.017, while its worst case over inputs is 0.064. CF-Prop
matches the Monte Carlo baseline throughout.
The worst-case failures occur where training data is scarce. Figure 3 below shows that moment
propagation works well in distribution but fails to generalize correctly. Moment propagation is thus

3
CF-Prop: Exact uncertainty propagation via characteristic func-
tions
We develop an exact description of the predictive density for a perceptron with ReLU activations. We
express the forward pass of a network in the Fourier domain via characteristic functions, the Fourier
transforms of probability density functions. This approach builds on prior work from Pilipovsky
et al. [2023], which expresses the action of the non-linear activation function in the Fourier domain
using Hilbert transforms. That work was focused on the output density of a deterministic perceptron
with random input. Here, we adapt the method to calculate the predictive density of a random
network with a deterministic input. Our network consists of a hidden layer of ReLU units with
random weights and biases, followed by a deterministic linear readout. It can be used on its own, as
a trained perceptron, or as a Bayesian last layer.
3.1
Characteristic functions
Characteristic functions can be used to propagate the full distribution of uncertainty. The CF ϕX(t)
of a random variable X is defined as:

FEA solver integration of a composite World Model
with a Spiking Neural Network memory Block for
computationally efficient modelling of defects and
variabilities
Bassam El Saida,∗, Adam Sobeyb,c
aBristol Composites Institute, University of Bristol, Bristol, United Kingdom
bUniversity of Southampton, Southampton, United Kingdom
cAlan Turing Institute, London, United Kingdom
Abstract
Each fiber-reinforced composite structure has a unique material architec-
ture. The manufacturing methods used and the presence of defects lead to
local variations which require material-scale models that can resolve the re-
sponse in real time at every location in the structure. Concurrent multi-scale
schemes such as Finite Element Squared (FE²) provide this capability, but at
a prohibitive computational cost for large structures as the number of inte-
gration points and time increments scales with size. Replacing the material-
scale models with surrogates has been studied extensively to mitigate these
computational limitations. A surrogate model must represent an arbitrary
local architecture including defects, track the irreversible material state over
a number of increments that is not known in advance, remain stable when
driven recursively by the surrogate’s own predictions, and operate within the
memory available at every integration point of a structural model. In this pa-
per, a Composites World Model based on Multi-Modal Spiking Transformer
(MMST) architecture is designed to meet these requirements. The architec-
ture combines a de-noising β-Variational Auto-encoder that learns the mate-
rial architecture including defects, a Spiking Neural Network (SNN) memory
block that efficiently tracks the long-term internal state of the material, and
transformer blocks that learn the short-term applied strain state. The sys-
∗Corresponding author
Email address: bassam.elsaid@bristol.ac.uk (Bassam El Said)
Preprint submitted to Elsevier
November 20, 2026
arXiv:2611.26419v1  [cs.LG]  19 Nov 2026
tem is trained in three stages: material architecture encoding, base training
on short time windows, and recursive fine-tuning with scheduled sampling
to suppress cumulative error drift. The trained model is disassembled at
inference and coupled to a non-linear FE solver, enabling structural scale
simulation of composites containing embedded defects. Benchmarks against
experimental results for IM7/8552 laminates under tension, compression and
transverse shear, for pristine and wrinkled composites, show that the SNN
memory block successfully tracks the material internal state and results in
prediction errors between 0.4% and 4.8%.
Keywords:
Multi-scale modelling, Composite materials, Spiking neural
networks, Transformer architecture, Finite element analysis, Manufacturing
defects
1. Computationally efficient damage prediction of composite ma-
terials under quasi-static loading
Efficient and safe composite design is dependent on failure prediction.
The mechanical response: stiffness, damage initiation and damage progres-
sion [1–3], are entirely determined by the internal architecture of the material.
However, accurate and reliable numerical simulation of composite material
behaviour is a challenging task due to a number of factors relating to how
these materials are manufactured. During manufacturing, the internal ar-
chitectures deform to conform to the structural geometry, leading to locally
varying architectures and material properties. Additionally, manufacturing
processes often introduce localized defects (wrinkles, gaps and voids), adding
a further layer of property variability which can be stochastic in nature [4–
8]. The material properties measured independently from the structure and
manufacturing processes do not describe how the material will behave as
part of a structure, since their properties do not include the impact of the
geometric features and presence of defects and variabilities [9, 10].
A second level of complexity originates from the multi-scale nature of
the materials’ mechanical response. Damage events often initiate at the Fi-
bre/Matrix scale, as a result of the interaction between the architectural fea-
tures and the applied loading conditions [11, 12]. An example is transverse
cracks appearing in a matrix pocket inside a 3D woven composite. These
material-scale damage events do not correlate directly with structural-scale
performance [13], but as loading increases these small cracks progress and
2
interact gradually leading to structural scale failure[14, 15].
The separa-
tion between material-scale and structure-scale damage events means that
to quantify structural failure behaviour in composites it is essential to ob-
serve the failure progression at the material architecture length scale for a
period of time. Predicting damage initiation based on failure of an individ-
ual constituent (fibre and matrix) will greatly underestimate a composite
structure load carrying capacity. This challenge is a multi-scale problem,
where the complete response of a structure is a function of the structural-
scale loads and damage progression on the material-scale. This progression
is non-linear in nature, due to the stress distribution at the material-scale as
a result of damage progression, and the associated change in structure-scale
loading condition.
Currently, capturing the history dependent non-linear behaviour of hi-
erarchical materials requires time-dependent FEA simulations using phe-
nomenological models based on the material constituents properties and
observed damage modes [16, 17]. These models, while accurate, are com-
putationally prohibitive for structural-scale simulations. It necessitates high
fidelity simulation at every location in a structure. For large scale struc-
tures such as aircraft wings (60–80 m) and wind turbine blades (60–100 m),
a high-fidelity simulation might require millions of evaluations of the mate-
rial constitutive law for each time iteration. This makes the computational
expense of these models prohibitive as a design tool [18, 19]. Concurrent
multi-scale schemes such as Finite Element Squared (FE²) [20] provide this
capability, but at a cost that scales with the number of integration points
and time increments, since a Representative Volume Element (RVE) model
has to be solved for each integration point. This computational cost becomes
prohibitive for large structures.
Replacing the material-scale models with surrogate models has been stud-
ied extensively to mitigate these computational limitations. However, these
surrogates must satisfy requirements imposed by the FE solver beyond ac-
curately representing the material response. Here, the surrogate model must
represent an arbitrary local architecture including defects, track the irre-
versible material state over a number of increments that is not known in
advance, remain stable when driven recursively by the surrogate’s own pre-
dictions, and operate within the memory available at every integration point
of a structural model.[18, 21, 22]. This challenge has been addressed previ-
ously using Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN) [23–25], which are designed
to model time series data based on internal memory mechanisms. RNN are
3
associated with high computational expense in both training and inference
as each neuron has a memory. In practice, RNN-based surrogates have been
demonstrated predominantly on academic-scale problems [26], and their be-
haviour when deployed at every integration point of a structural model has
received little attention. Integrating RNN surrogates with FE solvers will
lead to prohibitive memory requirements. This arises from the need to main-
tain the history of each integration point in the form of a complete copy of
an RNN network’s internal memory unique to each integration point. While
the memory cost of an individual copy of an RNN can be small, this ex-
pands rapidly as the number of integration points reach 100 of thousands or
millions, as is the case for industrial scale FE models.
Another limitation of history dependent material surrogate models is
that they have been shown to suffer from error drift over long predictions.
This means that for long FEA simulations, errors will start accumulat-
ing as the simulation progress often leading to erroneous results for failure
prediction[27]. Here, small stress-prediction errors will lead to errors in the
subsequent FE steps, Internal Force Vector calculations and global equilib-
rium, which in turn will lead to further errors in strain and stress predictions
for the next time step.
Transformers are an alternative to RNNs, which has seen considerable
success in Large Language Models (LLMs), and have success in materials
application [28, 29]. However, Transformers are difficult to reconcile with
the incremental nature of multi-scale solvers. Modern LLMs support context
lengths of 105 to 106 tokens, but that capability is provisioned for a single
instance evaluated once per query.
In a multi-scale FEA simulation, the
model is instead evaluated at every integration point at every increment,
and a context must be maintained for each integration point independently.
This is further complicated by the fact that the number of increments and
the strain step are not known in advance, since FE solvers adapt the time
step to maintain stability. Retaining this information, or the full stress-strain
history for each integration point, will lead to the same excessive memory
requirements observed for RNN. These issues have been addressed in long-
context LLMs by reducing the unbounded history into a fixed-length context
[30, 31]. World Models are an example of such architectures which employ an
encoder/memory/predictor model [32, 33]. Under this modeling paradigm,
the history is encoded and then submitted to a memory module which stores
the “world state” and provides a context for the transformer prediction.
In this paper, a novel Multi-modal Transformer Architecture with a Spik-
4
ing Neural Network memory block (MMST) is proposed for multi-scale simu-
lation of hierarchical materials. Inspired by World Model type architectures,
the proposed model has the ability to learn the material architecture, history
dependencies, and mechanical response. The use of a memory block in this
architecture gives the overall system the ability to integrate seamlessly with
a non-linear FEA solver without being burdened by the transformer con-
text size. To achieve robust performance in an FEA simulation environment,
the full system is trained in three subsequent stages: Material Architecture
Pretraining, Base Training (short-term) and Recursive Training (long-term).
Finally, the paper covers the efficient integration of the trained system in the
time integration loop of FEA solvers, with comparisons against experimental
results of composite material with defects and variabilities.
2. Deep Learning Powered Multi-Scale Modelling
2.1. Multi-scale Modelling Requirements for Deep Learning Models
Numerical approaches for nonlinear multi-scale modelling of strongly het-
erogeneous materials often employ computational homogenisation, with FE2
[20] based approaches being the most common. This family of approaches
link a structural-scale model with a number of material-scale models. Each
material-scale model represents the material architecture in the vicinity of
the macro-scale integration point. FE2 approaches involves two main stages:
Homogenisation and Localisation.
Homogenisation. Each macro-scale integration point is assigned a material
constitutive behaviour based on the local underlying architecture. This con-
stitutive behaviour could take the form of a constitutive material tensor or
stresses calculated at the integration point. Representative Volume Element
(RVE) models are built to represent the local material architecture and it
is impact on the constitutive behaviour. The RVE models are solved under
the applied strains to calculate full field stress/strains. Most commonly used
approaches involve 1st Order Homogenisation (1OH), which links an RVE
to a macro-scale integration point. The full field stresses are homogenised
following,

model coordinates y. EX are the macro-scale strains and ε(X, y) are the
material-scale strains and V is the RVE volume. Using this homogenisation,
the RVE response, which is defined by 3D stress and strain fields, is com-
pressed into average stress/strain at the macro-scale integration point. Here,
it is worth noting that more recently Second Order Computational (2OH) ho-
mogenisation has grown in popularity for modelling strongly heterogeneous
materials [34, 35]. In 2OH approaches, the average strains/stresses and their
spatial gradients are passed between the length scales, as opposed to the aver-
ages only for 1OH. While these approaches are very robust to scale-separation
challenges, they are associated with an exceptionally high dimension strain
space, which poses a unique challenge for surrogate modelling, and will be
out of scope for this work.
Localisation. forms the second step in the FE2 loop. At each time step, the
macro-scale model is solved using the homogenised properties mapped from
the RVE models to integration points. The macro-scale strains are extracted
and then applied as boundary conditions to the RVE models. These material-
scale models are then solved and homogenised to predict the constitutive
behaviour for the next macro-scale time-step.
Running the full FE2–1OH loop, involves solving the macro-scale model
and every associated RVE model at each FEA solver time step, followed by
computational homogenisation and information exchange between the length
scales.
An overview of the FE2 loop is shown in Figure 1.
Due to the
number of models involved in this approach, this process is computationally
prohibitive for any practical scale models. Consequently, FE2 models use
is primarily limited to benchmarking multi-scale modelling techniques. All
practical applications of FE2 involves some form of approximation of the
full loop. Of interest for this work, is the family of approaches where the
RVE models are replaced with a time-dependent surrogate[36, 37]. Here, the
surrogate model replaces the RVE models in the online FE2 loop. To fulfil
this role, such surrogates need two key capabilities :
• Represent the response of the underlying material architecture. For
example, in a composite, a surrogate should be able to predict the ma-
terial response including stiffness, damage initiation and failure, while
taking into account the local lay-up and the presence of any defects
and variabilities.

These functionalities are carried out per integration point, which is a con-
siderable computational challenge for most deep learning models due to mem-
ory cost. The deep learning approach proposed in this paper was constructed
from the ground up for FEA solver integration. Consequently, memory man-
agement requirements and time integration challenges were given priority
during model architecture and training.
2.2. Spatial / Temporal Deep Learning System Architecture
Multi-scale modelling of progressive damage in a hierarchical material is
a combined temporal/spatial learning task, where the model needs to learn
both the material architecture and material state. To tackle both learning
tasks and develop a memory efficient deep learning approach, the proposed
system is constructed from a number of modular blocks, each focusing on one
task. The proposed architecture is inspired by World Models, and builds on
the model conceptualisation by LeCun [38].In this formulation,the learning
7
of a dynamic environment is decomposed into three tasks: an encoder which
compresses a high dimensional observation into a latent space, a memory
which carries the internal state of the environment forward in time, and a
predictor which maps the current state and input to the next observation.
This decomposition can be mapped onto the components of a multi-scale
material problem. The material architecture is the spatial observation to be
encoded, the damage state is the environment state to be tracked over time,
and the stress is the quantity to be predicted. In a multi-scale simulation
problem, the role of the controller in a World Model, is assumed by the Finite
Element Solver, which supplies the strain increment at each step, and is not
learned. This mapping aligns with the conventional phenomenological dam-
age models for composites, where the material response is calculated from
the applied strains and a set of internal state variables which track damage
initiation and progression [16, 17]. In this sense, the memory block plays the
role that the damage state variables play in a conventional constitutive law.
A separate memory instance is required for every integration point in the
structural model, and the internal state of each instance must be retained
between solver increments. For a wind turbine blade or an aircraft wing, this
can extend to millions of integration points. Consequently, the memory block
is the component which determines whether the framework can be deployed
at structural scale. Here, the size of the neuron internal state, rather than
accuracy alone, becomes a governing design constraint.
In a multi-scale simulation the history is comprised of two components
with different origins. The first is the strain, which is imposed by the FE
solver as a result of the structural boundary conditions and the global equilib-
rium state. The strain is therefore a forcing term supplied to the environment
and is not predicted by the model. The second is the stress, which is gener-
ated by the model and returned to the solver, where it is assembled into the
internal force vector and consequently contributes indirectly to the strains
applied at the following increment. Here, a small error in the surrogate pre-
dicted stress can propagate into the strains subsequently imposed by the
solver, and over a large number of increments this leads to the cumulative
error drift previously observed for recurrent models of composite materials
[27]. To mitigate this error drift, a recursive training stage is employed where
the composite model is trained using it is own stresses predictions as input.

Preprint
SEQUENTIAL ANYTIME VALID TESTS FOR EFFICIENT
INFERENCE-TIME ALIGNMENT
Vishesh Kumar Singh & Sayak Ray Chowdhury
Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur, India
{visheshk24,sayakrc}@iitk.ac.in
ABSTRACT
Inference-time alignment methods, such as Best-of-N (BoN), improve language
model outputs by generating many candidates per prompt and selecting among
them using a reward model. The cost is largely wasted, since a fixed budget is
applied uniformly across prompts, even though the computation required by dif-
ferent prompts varies widely. Adaptive methods halt generation once sampled
answers appear settled, but their thresholds are tuned heuristics with no statisti-
cal control over early-stopping errors. Instead, we seek an anytime-valid stopping
rule that takes a permitted Type-I error tolerance α as input, guaranteeing that gen-
eration halts only when an answer is certified to hold genuine majority dominance
(θa > 1/2) under the generator’s distribution. To build such a rule, we aggre-
gate candidates by their final answers using a reward-weighted self-consistency
(RWSC) score and treat the decision of when to stop as a sequential test over the
resulting clusters. Wald’s sequential probability ratio test (SPRT) is the natural
tool for such a test, and when applied to the RWSC clusters, it yields SPRT-RWSC,
which performs well empirically. Yet its guarantee does not hold here, since the
leading answer shifts as sampling proceeds, and the run is continuously moni-
tored. Our main contribution replaces Wald’s test with an anytime-valid construc-
tion that resolves this issue: it maintains a betting supermartingale (an e-process)
for every answer the policy produces, bounding the probability of ever certifying a
non-dominant answer by α, uniformly over time and across all answers, however
many the policy produces. We call the resulting rule e-RWSC: the RWSC scores
drive the bets, which affect only how quickly a dominant answer a⋆is certified, not
the validity of the guarantee; and certification takes O
�log(1/α)/dKL(θa⋆||1/2)

samples. Experiments across several language models, datasets, and reward mod-
els confirm the predicted 1/dKL scaling of per-response cost, and show that accu-
racy also improves over baselines at substantially lower token cost.
1
INTRODUCTION
Inference-time alignment has emerged as the practical alternative to fine-tuning, in which one re-
peatedly generates responses from the existing language model (e.g., a policy) and selects among
them. Best-of-N (Beirami et al., 2025) selection scores each response with a reward model and re-
turns the one with the highest score. Self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022) takes a majority vote over
final answers. Both are effective, but expensive: their cost is N full generations per prompt, and N
must be large enough for the hardest prompt in the workload. Since inference is the dominant cost
of deployed language models, the token budget spent on selection should be minimized.
A fixed budget of N is uniform across prompts, while the computation required by prompts varies
enormously. On a prompt where the policy immediately concentrates on a single answer, ten samples
are enough, whereas on a prompt on which the policy remains genuinely divided, even a thousand
samples are not sufficient. Fixed-budget selection, therefore, results in both over- and underspending
of tokens. Adaptive methods address this by halting generation once the sampled answers look
settled, e.g., stopping when a posterior over answer frequencies concentrates (Aggarwal et al., 2023;
Wan et al., 2025), when the marginal value of another sample falls below its cost (Kalayci et al.,
2025), or when a budget estimated from a short burn-in is exhausted (Raman et al., 2026). In every
case, the halting rule is a tuned threshold with no control over the probability of stopping on the
1
arXiv:2611.26413v1  [cs.LG]  19 Nov 2026
Preprint
non-dominant answer. Moreover, they must be re-tuned for each new policy, reward model, and
benchmark.
One would instead like an anytime-valid stopping rule that takes a formal error level α as input and
adapts the token budget accordingly, guaranteeing that the probability of erroneously certifying a
non-dominant answer (θa∗≤p†) is strictly bounded by α. The rule must be defined based on a
computable statistic of the generations. Since many distinct reasoning traces can yield the same
final answer, we group responses by their final answers and frame the stopping rule at the answer
level. We introduce Reward-Weighted Self-Consistency (RWSC), which scores each cluster by the
softmax-weighted mass of its members’ reward scores, so that a cluster is favored both for containing
many responses and for highly rewarded ones. Let a∗denote the highest-scoring cluster (the leading
answer) at the current step. Framing stopping as the question – is a⋆genuinely the dominant answer,
or merely ahead by chance? – makes it a sequential hypothesis testing problem. Wald’s sequential
probability ratio test (SPRT) is the classic solution: as each new response arrives, one accumulates
evidence for or against the leader and stops once it crosses a boundary (Wald, 1945). It performs
strongly in practice, but remains a heuristic here, without any rigorous error-control guarantee.
Wald’s guarantee assumes hypotheses that are fixed in advance, tested by a single terminal decision,
and none of these holds here. Writing θa for the probability that a fresh response yields answer a, the
rates defining the test are estimated from the same responses the test then examines, rather than fixed
beforehand. The leading answer a∗is itself a function of the sampled responses, so the parameter
under test, θa∗, shifts whenever the leader does, forcing the test to restart. And the statistic is
checked after every response, not at a single stopping point. Each of these voids the error control that
Wald’s boundaries nominally provide. We resolve this with anytime-valid inference (Ramdas et al.,
2023), whose guarantees hold under continuous monitoring and arbitrary stopping. We maintain a
separate betting supermartingale for each final answer the policy produces, instantiating one when
that answer first appears and assigning it a weight from a fixed, summable sequence. Since the
weights sum to 1, they split a single error budget across answers, regardless of how many arise.
Ville’s inequality (Ville, 1939) then bounds by α the probability that a non-dominant answer (θa ≤
1/2) is ever certified, uniformly over time and over a growing set of answers. This addresses each
failure of SPRT. A change in the leading answer is irrelevant, since every answer accumulates its
own evidence. Continuous monitoring is an inherent property of Ville’s inequality, so checking the
boundary after each response incurs no additional cost.
Validity requires only that the bets be predictable, each computed from earlier responses before
the next one is sampled. The reward model sets each bet based on the current RWSC score of the
answer cluster, which buys efficiency when the scores are accurate. The gain has a precise form:
under the log-optimal Kelly betting (Kelly, 1956), evidence for a dominant answer accrues at a rate
dKL(θa||1/2), so certification takes about log(1/α)/dKL(θa||1/2) sampled responses. An accurate
RWSC score bets near-optimally and approaches this rate, while an inaccurate or hacked score bets
poorly and slows the certification. But it never crosses the boundary in expectation under the null,
since validity does not depend on the estimate being correct.
The efficiency of the stopping rule, therefore, adapts to the prompt. The number of tokens spent
scales with its difficulty: an answer the policy strongly favors (θa > 1/2) is certified in a few
responses, whereas one near the decision boundary θa = 1/2 takes many, often more than the
budget allows, in which case the procedure certifies nothing and falls back to standard aggregation.
Either way, the practitioner fixes the error-control probability α once, and the number of responses
adjusts itself to each prompt. We summarize our contributions as follows.
(i) We cast early stopping as a sequential hypothesis-testing problem and introduce SPRT-RWSC,
which applies Wald’s test to determine when the leading answer has converged. It operates on
Reward-Weighted Self-Consistency (RWSC): an answer-level aggregation rule that scores answer
clusters by reward-weighted mass, and recovers majority voting and Best-of-N as extreme cases. It
works well in practice, but Wald’s error guarantee does not hold in this setting (Section 2).
(ii) We propose E-RWSC, an anytime-valid stopping rule that accumulates evidence over all an-
swers through separate e-processes. It controls the Type-I error (certifying an answer that is not
dominant under the policy) at a user-specified level α, uniformly over time, and over an unknown
set of answers. The guarantee holds for any predictable choice of bets, so the reward model, which
sets them through RWSC scores, governs only efficiency and never validity. Under a plug-in es-

prompt’s difficulty (Section 3).
(iii) An empirical study on 5 Language Models (Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3-8B, Phi-3-
Mini-4K, Mistral-24B) with 4 Reward Models (ArmoRM, FsfairX, Skywork V1, Skywork V2)
over 4 Benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH500, MMLU, CruxEval) showing that realized certification
error stays below the nominal level, that per-response cost follows the predicted 1/dKL scaling with
prompt difficulty, and that E-RWSC matches or outperform several baselines at substantially lower
average cost (Section 4). For example, with Qwen-2.5-3B as the language model, ArmoRM as the
reward model, and a maximum generation budget capped at 512, on the MATH500 Benchmark, we
achieve an 8.2% absolute accuracy gain over BoN with a 61.7% smaller budget.
Related work. A line of work improves which response is chosen from a pool: reward-weighted
selection with a temperature (Verdun et al., 2025), ensemble reward models normalized across mem-
bers (Coste et al., 2024), and step-level search or process verification that refine how each candidate
is generated and scored (Qiu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024; 2025; Lee et al., 2025a). RWSC draws
on the first two but aggregates over final answers rather than individual candidates. Our contribu-
tion concerns the orthogonal question of how many candidates to generate. The adaptive stopping
methods (Aggarwal et al., 2023; Wan et al., 2025; Kalayci et al., 2025; Raman et al., 2026; Sun
et al., 2024) share a common limitation: their halting rules are tuned thresholds resting on distri-
butional assumptions, with no control over the probability of stopping on the wrong answer. Con-
Sol (Lee et al., 2025b), like SPRT-RWSC, applies Wald’s test to halt self-consistency generation,
but compares only the top two answers and uses static priors. Two recent works give anytime-valid
certificates for self-consistency: MMC (Cordero-Encinar & Duncan, 2025) certifies the empirical-
leader mode via paired e-processes and couples this with test-time training, and CITE (Ota et al.,
2026) certifies a fixed target as the unique mode with a matching minimax lower bound. Unlike
reward-agnostic mode certifiers (MMC, CITE), E-RWSC uses reward-informed betting to certify
strict majority dominance (p† ≥0.5), achieving 94.5% accuracy on certified early stopped answers
vs. 88.9% for MMC with a lower budget.

Each response y carries a chain of reasoning terminating in a final answer, extracted by a function

Abstract
The transition from fossil fuels presents significant challenges in energy management.
The era of simply activating gas power plants to meet electricity demand or refuelling
vehicles with petrol in a matter of minutes is coming to an end. To ensure a sustain-
able energy future, it is crucial to reduce energy consumption when possible and to
synchronize electricity consumption and storage with the production from sources with
low greenhouse gas emissions. Effective energy management in residential settings can
help achieve these goals. This thesis explores a variety of energy management meth-
ods used to manage batteries, heat pumps, and other energy-related systems. The
thesis presents three simulation cases alongside one real-world experiment to compare
energy management done through simple rules, optimization, and machine learning
methods. Furthermore, this thesis introduces TreeC, a novel machine learning-based
method that learns understandable yet efficient energy management strategies, ap-
plicable to many cases. The thesis concludes with a comprehensive analysis of the
benefits of energy management methods in electrified residential settings.
The three key contributions of this thesis can be summarized as follows: 1) The devel-
oped TreeC method demonstrates competitive performance compared to a variety of
energy management approaches, such as model predictive control and reinforcement
learning, across a diverse set of energy management problems.
The understand-
ability TreeC’s energy management strategies greatly improves the transparency and
trustworthiness of machine learning-based energy management. 2) The real-world
experiment highlights the need to validate energy management methods on actual
hardware and not solely on simulations. Both TreeC and model predictive control
performed worse than in simulations, due to, respectively, insufficiently representa-
tive training data and the real-time input data not being reliable enough. 3) Energy
management algorithms reduce costs in electrified Belgian dwellings, particularly in
poorly insulated dwellings, electric vehicle chargers, and photovoltaic installations.
However, on average, these cost savings do not yet outweigh the current costs and
effort required to implement such algorithms.

Statistical Inference with Ill-Conditioned Random Weight Neural
Network Sieves
Giovanni Ballarin
∗
Lyudmila Grigoryeva
†
Lukas Gonon
‡
November 20, 2026
Abstract
Random weight neural networks (RWNNs) are shallow networks whose hidden-layer
parameters are randomly generated and then kept fixed, while only the output coefficients
are estimated. Conditional on the sampled parameters, RWNN regression is a linear sieve
problem with random approximation space. We show that such random sieves cannot remain
uniformly well-conditioned as their dimension grows. For parametrized feature families
satisfying polynomial covering and Lipschitz conditions, the eigenvalues of the population
covariance matrix are proven to have polynomial upper bounds determined by the covering
geometry of the parameter space, leading to a vanishing smallest eigenvalue. We develop
approximation, estimation, and inference theory that explicitly treats the ill-conditioning.
Under a β-H¨older source condition, we obtain both faster-than-Monte-Carlo L2 approximation
rates and new L∞approximation bounds based on stratified sampling. We then derive
improved consistency guarantees for ridge-regularized least squares driven by ridge effective
dimension, spectral, and leverage-based stability conditions. For inference, we establish
asymptotic linearity and Gaussian limits for linear functional directions while allowing
the smallest eigenvalue of the population covariance matrix to vanish. Nondegeneracy is
directional: we characterize it with a ridge-normalized Rayleigh quotient and extend it
to smooth functionals via Riesz representation. Consistency of ridge-adjusted variance
estimators is proved, yielding feasible studentized inference. Numerical experiments illustrate
the deterioration of random-feature conditioning and the finite-sample behavior of the
resulting estimation and inference procedures.
Keywords: random weight neural networks, random feature sieves, nonparametric estimation,
spectral ill-conditioning, ridge regression, functional inference

1
Introduction
Random weight neural networks (RWNNs) are shallow neural networks whose hidden-layer
parameters are randomly drawn and subsequently kept fixed, so that only the coefficients of
the linear output layer are estimated from the data (Gonon et al., 2023). Neural networks of
this type have been applied very successfully in a variety of settings; we refer in particular to
the seminal works on random feature models (Rahimi and Recht, 2007) and extreme learning
machines (Huang et al., 2006). Conditional on the sampled parameters, estimation under squared
loss is a linear least-squares problem over the random finite-dimensional space spanned by the
K hidden units. When the same sequence of hidden-layer parameters is used as K increases,
these spaces are nested and form a random sieve, which we study within the framework of
nonparametric sieve regression (Grenander, 1981; Gy¨orfi et al., 2006; Chen, 2007; Tsybakov,
2009). However, the population covariance matrix of the randomly generated features need not
remain well-conditioned as K increases: additional hidden units may improve approximation
while introducing substantial redundancy in the feature representation. Understanding the
statistical consequences of such ill-conditioning, particularly for inference on functionals of the
regression function, is the central problem addressed in this paper.
2
Approximation properties of random neural networks have been studied under different
assumptions on the target function and the distribution of the hidden-layer parameters (Rahimi
and Recht, 2008; Gonon et al., 2023; Neufeld and Schmocker, 2023; Liu et al., 2025; De Ryck
et al., 2025; Mehmood and Gonon, 2026). In the context of positive definite kernels, Bach
(2017) established approximation guarantees for random feature expansions in terms of the
spectral properties of the associated integral operator, including results in L2 and L∞. Related
quantitative approximation results for shallow neural networks include those for general activation
functions (Siegel and Xu, 2020), for Sobolev classes with ReLU activations (Mao et al., 2026),
and for non-polynomial activations on noncompact domains (Neufeld and Schmocker, 2026).
Statistical convergence rates for random feature estimators have been established in several
settings (Rudi and Rosasco, 2017; Carratino et al., 2018; Gonon, 2023; Lanthaler and Nelsen,
2023). In particular, Braun et al. (2024) establish an expected squared L2(X) error bound
of order O((log n)4n−1/2) for a shallow neural network estimator learned by gradient descent,
under suitable Fourier-decay assumptions on the regression function. They obtain the same rate
for a truncated linear least-squares estimator with randomly sampled hidden-layer parameters.
Mei and Montanari (2022) derive precise asymptotics for random features ridge regression.
Conditional on the sampled features, a ridge-regularized RWNN estimator is a finite-rank kernel
ridge regressor, for which Cheng et al. (2023) give sharp non-asymptotic bounds on the test
error.
From the kernel point of view—the original setting of the random features approach of Rahimi
and Recht (2007)—statistical inference for kernel ridge regression has been studied in the recent
literature, including uniform confidence bands based on Gaussian and bootstrap approximations
(Singh and Vijaykumar, 2023) and asymptotic normality for linear functionals, including point
evaluations and derivatives (Tuo and Zou, 2024). These results concern regularization in a
prescribed reproducing kernel Hilbert space, and existing inferential results involving sampled
features address particular estimation targets and statistical models; see Shen and Bellec (2020);
Steland (2021); Guignard et al. (2021) for recent discussions. In contrast, we develop a theory of
functional inference for growing RWNN sieves that accommodates increasingly ill-conditioned or
singular population feature covariance matrices.
Randomly generated features present a fundamental and distinctive structural obstacle: a
uniform positive lower bound on the population covariance eigenvalues cannot be sustained
as the number of features increases. In fact, we show that, for parameterized feature families
satisfying polynomial covering and Lipschitz conditions, the eigenvalues of the population feature
covariance matrix satisfy polynomial decay upper bounds determined by the covering dimension
of the parameter space, uniformly over feature realizations. In particular, its smallest eigenvalue
necessarily converges to zero as the number of features increases. Related spectral ill-conditioning
has been investigated by Ming and Yu (2026), who establish rapid singular-value decay for
random-feature discretization matrices associated with Fourier and hyperbolic tangent features.
Our results instead concern the population regression covariance matrix under general covering
and Lipschitz conditions.
Unlike an L2(X)-orthonormal series sieve, whose population Gram matrix is IK, an RWNN
sieve does not generally have an orthogonal feature representation. Standard sieve inference
typically relies on suitably normalized bases and control of their population Gram matrices
(Newey, 1997; Chen, 2007; Belloni et al., 2015; Chen and Christensen, 2015). Importantly,
our spectral deterioration results are not restricted to randomly generated features: they hold
uniformly over arbitrary choices of hidden-layer parameters within the prescribed compact
feature family and therefore also apply to fully trainable shallow networks satisfying these
restrictions. Our subsequent statistical analysis focuses on RWNNs. In this setting, both spectral
deterioration and the resulting regularization bias must be accounted for explicitly.
We develop a framework for statistical inference with random sieves and RWNNs based on
ridge normalization, in which the relevant quantities are measured relative to the regularized
3
population covariance matrix. Two key results guide our analysis. First, the same covering
geometry that induces spectral decay also controls the ridge effective dimension, which governs
the stochastic estimation error and is sublinear in the nominal sieve dimension under suitable
ridge scaling. This effective dimension plays a role analogous to that of its counterpart in
kernel ridge regression (Caponnetto and De Vito, 2007; Rudi and Rosasco, 2017). Second, and
more importantly for inference, global spectral nondegeneracy is not required. We formulate
a sufficient nondegeneracy condition along the functional direction, relative to the ridge level,
through a ridge-normalized Rayleigh quotient. Together with conditions controlling empirical
covariance stability, approximation, and ridge bias, we derive asymptotic normality conditional
on the sampled hidden-layer parameters, in Pθ-probability, even when the smallest eigenvalue of
the population feature covariance matrix converges to zero. Under additional conditions ensuring
consistency of the ridge-adjusted variance estimator, we obtain feasible studentized inference.
The framework also accommodates irregular sieve functionals, such as point evaluation, whose
normalizing variance may vary with the sieve dimension and need not remain bounded.
1.1
Preview of contributions
The main contributions of this paper concern four interconnected aspects of growing RWNN
sieves: approximation by randomly generated features; spectral properties and L2(X) estimation;
asymptotic inference for linear and smooth functionals; and uniform estimation under prediction-
space stability conditions. Throughout this subsection, Pθ denotes the law of the sampled hidden-
layer parameters, OPθ refers to this law, and OP refers to the joint law of the observations and the
hidden-layer parameters (see Subsection 1.2 below). Table 1 summarizes selected approximation
benchmarks from the literature and the principal approximation, spectral, estimation, and
inference results established in this paper.
First, we establish L2 approximation rates for RWNNs under a β-H¨older direct source
condition. Adapting the control-neighbors Monte Carlo construction of Leluc et al. (2025) to
the RWNN integral representation yields an approximation error of order OPθ(K−1/2−β/(d+1)),
improving upon the classical Monte Carlo order K−1/2. Under the additional conditions of the
generic sieve theory developed in Appendix E, this improvement yields an oP (n−1/4) convergence
rate for the constrained unregularized sieve estimator, ensuring that quadratic remainder terms
are negligible at the √n scale in smooth-functional inference. We also derive approximation
guarantees for integral Sobolev classes (see Subsection 3.2). Furthermore, we establish sup-norm

Simulation-pretrained autoencoders versus PCA for
compressing multimode fibre transmission matrices
Callum J. Wilson1*, Terry Wright1, Qing Yang2, Zhong Wen2, Michael P. Pound3,
and George S.D. Gordon1
1OPTIMlab, Department of Chemical Engineering and Biotechnology, University of
Cambridge, United Kingdom
2State Key Laboratory of Modern Optical Instrumentation, Department of Optical
Engineering, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China
3School of Computer Science, University of Nottingham, United Kingdom
Abstract
Multimode optical fibres can image through a thin, flexible probe once their transmission
matrix (TM) has been measured, but a TM is large and must be re-measured whenever the fibre
moves. A compact model of feasible TMs would make storing and re-estimating them cheaper,
so we ask how compactly TMs can be represented, and from how few measured TMs. Here we
benchmark a permutation-equivariant autoencoder, pretrained on simulated fibres and adapted
to measured TMs, against principal component analysis (PCA). At 62× compression, adapting
the pretrained autoencoder with just two measured TMs reconstructs the TM of a 50 µm fibre
well enough to focus light at 98% of the ideal enhancement, and it stays accurate when the
TMs are shifted by 25 pixels or zoomed by 10%, which quickly degrades a linear basis. It is
not, however, a better compressor: PCA is about ten times more accurate when fitted on all
163 real TMs (1.1% against 11.9% error on held-out TMs) and is already more accurate from
ten. The autoencoder’s value is as a prior when few or no real TMs exist: with none it reaches
29% error, against 91% for PCA fitted on the same simulation. Transfer to a different fibre is
only partial. The most important extension, not yet tested, is to recover pixel-basis TMs from
fewer measurements than a full TM, which would turn the pretrained prior from a compressor
into a measurement-saving tool.
1
Introduction
Multimode fibres (MMF) guide many spatial modes of light through a core larger than a single-
mode fibre, and have been proposed as cost-effective, ultrathin (<0.1 mm diameter) endoscopes
[1], promising subcellular-resolution imaging deep inside tissue [2]. However, MMFs suffer image
distortion from bending, movement, and temperature drift [3–7]. Provided the fibre is stable, this
*Corresponding author: cw2011@cam.ac.uk
1
arXiv:2611.26391v1  [physics.optics]  19 Nov 2026
behaviour is characterised by its transmission matrix (TM), such that Eout = TM ·Ein; knowing the
TM allows these distortions to be corrected [8, 9]. TMs are large objects: captured experimentally
in the pixel basis, i.e. as the field at each camera pixel rather than in the fibre’s mode basis, a single
TM in this work occupies approximately 48.7 MB (complex64, 42,025×145 elements). Compressing
TMs into a compact latent representation — while retaining sufficient information for downstream
reconstruction — is therefore practically important for storage, transmission, and real-time TM
inference [10].
Conventional TM calibration also requires access to the distal end of the fibre [8], stable reference
arms, and careful alignment, limiting applicability to in vivo environments [11]. However, single-
ended TM calibration is an active research area and showing promise [12]. Measuring one TM with
145 input patterns takes approximately 1–2 minutes on our setup, excluding fibre repositioning and
alignment checks, and this scales at least linearly with the number of input patterns; because the TM
changes whenever the fibre is disturbed, it must be remeasured at each new fibre state. A compact
representation of the family of TMs a fibre can take, built from simulation and a few calibration
measurements, could instead serve as a prior from which the current TM is estimated from limited
information, with prior work already suggesting this is possible when using mode basis TMs [13, 14].
The rationale is that fewer degrees of freedom require fewer measurements to determine the current
TM. Here we test the prerequisite: how compactly TMs can be represented, and from how few real
TMs.
Principal component analysis (PCA) is a linear method that is fast to fit and requires no iterative
training. Each column of a pixel-basis TM is a speckle pattern, and PCA has been used to compress
speckle patterns [15]. Because every output speckle is a linear superposition of the fibre’s guided
modes, all speckles lie in a subspace whose dimension is set by the number of modes and is far smaller
than the number of camera pixels.
A pixel-basis TM is therefore expected to be compressible,
with the limit set by the mode count. Skvarenina et al. extracted a bend-resolved modal basis
from speckle-field correlation matrices using successive singular value decompositions [16], exploiting
redundancy between speckle fields measured within a bend state. The redundancy in our setting is
of a different kind. A TM has 145 columns, fewer than the ≈V 2/2 modes supported by the 50 µm-
core step index fibre used here (V = 2πa NA/λ ≈52 for core radius a = 25 µm, NA = 0.22 and
λ = 660 nm), so the columns of a single TM are generically linearly independent and a decomposition
across them removes no redundancy. Instead, each column is a vector of 42,025 complex pixels that
lies in the fibre’s shared mode subspace, and that subspace can be learned only by pooling speckles
from many TMs. Autoencoders are a nonlinear counterpart to PCA: an encoder network maps the
data to a low-dimensional code and a decoder network reconstructs the data from it [17], so they
can capture structure that a linear subspace cannot. Whether a nonlinear autoencoder can improve
on this linear baseline, and in which data regimes, remains unclear.
Deep learning autoencoders are widely used for image compression [18, 19], and may be suited to
TMs, which are themselves speckle-pattern images when captured in the pixel basis; convolutional
networks have already been used to extract spatial features from multimode-fibre speckle patterns
[20]. However, Zheng et al. [21] reported that convolutional layers are ill-suited to compact mode-
basis TMs, whose correlations are non-local, and used a learned invertible basis transform with
self-attention to obtain sparse latent representations.
Our setting differs in basis and aim: we
compress pixel-basis TMs, in which each column is a speckle image with local spatial structure, and
compare against PCA, a dimension-reducing linear baseline.
2
Training such a model requires a large corpus of TMs [11] spanning the expected distribution
of fibre states, but collecting experimental TMs at scale is slow and instrument-intensive, making
physics-based simulation an attractive data source. A key practical advantage of simulation is that
TMs can be generated and stored in the mode basis, where dimensionality reflects the number of
guided modes rather than camera pixels. In this work, simulated TMs occupy only 1.19 MB per
matrix — roughly 41× smaller than their experimental counterparts — and can be converted to the
pixel basis on the fly during training, avoiding any storage bottleneck.
A critical question is whether a model pretrained on simulated TMs transfers to experimental
data, which carries real-world noise, calibration artefacts, and physical imperfections absent from
simulation. Fibres of different lengths present an additional challenge: simulating a 5 m fibre ac-
curately requires substantially more compute than simulating a 1 m fibre, raising the question of
whether cheaper 1 m simulations provide a useful pretraining signal for experimental 5 m TMs. We
therefore construct 5 m TMs by multiplying five 1 m simulated TMs (“composite” TMs), and ask
whether these provide a useful pretraining signal.
Here, we compare a simulation-pretrained autoencoder with PCA on pixel-basis TMs of a 5 m
multimode fibre, and ask seven questions:
1. How redundant is a pixel-basis TM: how much can PCA compress it, and what sets the limit?
2. Can “composite” simulated TMs, formed by multiplying several 1 m simulated TMs, provide
a useful pretraining signal for 5 m experimental TMs?
3. Does a nonlinear autoencoder compress TMs better than PCA at the same latent size?
4. How many real TMs does each approach need, and where does a pretrained prior help?
5. How large is the simulation-to-experiment gap, and can a pretrained model bridge it where a
linear basis cannot?
6. Do the models transfer to a different fibre, and can one model serve several? We evaluate a
second, larger-core fibre.
7. Do the remaining reconstruction errors matter for focusing and imaging, and what survives
geometric drift, such as camera shift and zoom?
The autoencoder here serves as a vehicle for studying the simulation-pretraining workflow itself:
pretrain on simulated TMs, then adapt to a fibre using few or no real TMs. The questions above
concern how many real TMs this workflow needs, which we expect to be relevant to other TM
models, although we test only this architecture. In our data, PCA is hard to beat when real TMs
are available, whereas a simulation-pretrained autoencoder is most useful when they are not.
2
Materials and Methods
2.1
Simulated data
Multiple simulation techniques exist, such as: the transfer matrix method (TMM), which models
the fibre as a sequence of infinitesimally small segments and uses a spatial translation between
segments to simulate the mode coupling induced by bending [22]; pyMMF [23]; and the beam
3
propagation method (BPM) [24], which numerically solves the full propagating field and, in our
experience, scales poorly to the fibre lengths and segment counts required here. We adopt TMM
here, as it has been validated against experimental MMF transmission matrices in prior work from
our group [3, 14], and its computational cost scales with fibre length — a property this paper exploits
directly when comparing cheap 1 m simulations against costly 5 m simulations. The simulated fibre
had the following properties: fibre length 1 m, numerical aperture 0.22, refractive index 1.457,
wavelength 632.8 nm (the experimental laser was 660 nm; this mismatch was unintentional and
means the simulated fibre has V ≈55 against ≈52 for the experiment, which we treat as part of the
simulation-to-experiment gap), core diameter 50 µm, with the number of guided modes kept being
386 (scalar LP modes with one polarisation and one azimuthal orientation). Simulated TMs were
generated using randomly assigned bend radii and directions which are saved alongside the mode-
basis TM and can be traced. Each generated 1 m mode-basis TM must have a 2-norm condition
number calculated using singular value decomposition (SVD) of less than 250 to remain in the
dataset. 5,000 simulated 1 m TMs were generated and split 80:10:10 into training, validation and
test sets with a fixed seed (as for the experimental data), so no 1 m TM appears in more than one
split.
The 5 m fibre was simulated as a composite: each 5 m TM is the product, in the mode basis,
of five 1 m TMs drawn without replacement from the same split’s pool, with the product taken
in the propagation order of the fibre. The five indices of every composite were drawn once with
a fixed seed and stored, so every run uses identical composites. Training sets of 500, 1,000 and
2,000 composites are nested prefixes of one list, and the validation and test sets each contain 250
composites. Composite TMs are built on the fly during training: the stored 1 m TMs are loaded,
multiplied, and converted to the pixel basis. Mode amplitudes for 145 fixed random orthonormal
input patterns are propagated through the composite, and a fixed mode-to-pixel matrix maps the
output to the 205 × 205 camera grid, giving a 42,025 × 145 pixel-basis TM. Gaussian amplitude and
phase noise was then added to each TM, with the amplitude and phase noise levels drawn uniformly
from 1–15% and 0.01–0.1 rad per TM. Each TM was normalised by its largest singular value.
2.2
Experimental data
Experimental data (204 TMs) was collected using a 5 m multimode fibre (50 µm core diameter,
numerical aperture 0.22). These 204 TMs were created by randomly altering the bend state of the
MMF, whose ends were fixed to an optical table. Light from a 660 nm laser was modulated using a
spatial light modulator, which displayed 145 input patterns, each generating a tilted plane wave at
the fibre input. The 145 inputs are mutually orthogonal (the correlation between every pair is zero),
and the number was limited by the stability of the setup over the measurement time. A single mode
fibre carried the reference beam, which was interfered with the beam exiting the fibre at the distal
facet to measure the phase by off-axis holography. A charge-coupled device (CCD) collected the
resulting output speckle. Each element of both the simulated and experimental TMs is a complex
number a + bi. The TMs were normalised independently by their own largest singular value. Both
simulated and experimental data scaling studies use nested datasets, for example the 50 TM dataset
would contain the exact same TMs in the 25 TM dataset, plus 25 extra. This ensures that the effect
of more data is isolated, not the data itself. The training, validation, test sets were split 80:10:10,
resulting in 163, 20, 21 TMs, respectively.
4
2.3
Second-fibre experimental data
To test transfer to a different fibre, we used 164 TMs measured by two of the authors [1] on a larger-
core fibre (105 µm core, 1,024 input patterns, 64 × 64 output pixels), split 131, 16, 17 into training,
validation and test sets. These TMs are not part of our public release and can be requested from the
authors who measured them (Z.W. and Q.Y.; see [1]). Of the 1,024 inputs we kept the 145 with the
highest mean column power, averaged over the training TMs, to match the 145 inputs of the original
data. The same 145 inputs were used for every TM in the training, validation and test sets. Each
output field was upscaled to 205 × 205 by zero-padding its two-dimensional Fourier spectrum, and
each TM was divided by its largest singular value, as for the original TMs. We call these the raw
second-fibre TMs. A coherent speckle is band-limited: its spectrum fills a disc in spatial frequency
whose radius is set by the aperture, here the fibre’s numerical aperture [25, Ch. 6], while the core
diameter sets the field of view [26]. A larger core therefore fits more speckle grains across the frame,
so the second fibre’s speckle patterns carry finer spatial structure than those of the 50 µm fibre: the
Fourier disc holding 99% of a speckle’s power contains πr2
99 ≈4,300 complex degrees of freedom,
against about 800 for the original data. The two fibres differ in many ways (core size, mode count,
setup and input patterns), so to test the effect of the larger core’s finer speckle on its own, we also
made band-limited second-fibre TMs. Before upscaling, each output field was low-pass filtered in
the Fourier domain with a disc of radius R = 15 cycles per frame (raised-cosine edge over two bins),
chosen so that the number of modes per speckle matches the original data (Supplementary Note
S1). Band-limiting discards spatial detail, so errors on band-limited and raw TMs are not directly
comparable.
2.4
Model architecture
The encoder and decoder are trained without skip connections between them, ensuring the com-
pressed latent representation is a complete and self-contained encoding of the transmission matrix
(Figure 1). This design choice allows the decoder to be used independently of the encoder — for
instance, reconstructing a transmission matrix from a latent vector obtained by means other than
the trained encoder — a property that would be precluded by skip connections directly propagating
encoder activations into the decoder. The decoder is also deliberately not a mirror of the encoder:
it contains no attention, only a linear layer and convolutions, which makes decoding fast when it is
used on its own. Without skip connections, error may increase.
The autoencoder is permutation equivariant over the input patterns. A TM of shape 42,025×145
is treated as 145 two-channel (real and imaginary) 205 × 205 images, each processed independently
with shared weights; the channel attention acts across feature channels within a single speckle, never
across inputs. Reordering the columns of a TM therefore reorders the reconstruction in the same
way, so the model does not depend on the order of the input basis. This matters for three reasons.
First, the columns of a TM have no canonical order, since they depend on how the input patterns
are chosen. Second, the same weights can be pretrained on simulated inputs and then applied to
an experiment, or to another fibre, that uses a different set of input patterns: in this work a model
pretrained on simulated TMs with random orthonormal input patterns is fine-tuned on, and applied
to, experimental TMs measured with tilted plane waves, and to the second fibre’s TMs measured
with a different set of inputs. Third, each TM supplies 145 training examples, which makes better
use of a small number of TMs than treating a whole TM as one sample. The cost is that correlations
5
between different input patterns are not exploited.
The architecture follows preliminary tests on smaller 256×256 TMs, run before the experimental
data were collected. In those tests Linformer-style [27] coarse channel attention matched full channel
attention after fine-tuning (45.3% against 44.6% experimental error) with a smaller attention matrix,
and a one-dimensional convolutional encoder failed to train (Supplementary Table S1 and Figures S1–
S3). A complex-valued autoencoder of the same design did not match the two-channel (real and
imaginary) model on the pixel-basis TMs. At the same latent size (2,704 real numbers per speckle,
i.e. 8 complex against 16 real channels) it failed to train under our recipe (101% error after fine-
tuning, against 7.5%), and with twice as many latent numbers (16 complex channels) it trained but
gave a higher fine-tuned error (13.1%) (Supplementary Table S2). These were single runs under
earlier protocols, so we use them to motivate the design and not to rank architectures.
The compression rate of the autoencoder is controlled by the number of channels in the latent
space, the feature map size is fixed throughout. A single TM has shape [145, 2, 205, 205] (real),
some example compression rates and latent tensor shapes below:
1. Compression rate 62×: [145, 8, 13, 13] (real)
2. Compression rate 124×: [145, 4, 13, 13] (real)
Note that each speckle pattern was padded to size [208, 208] to allow for more natural convolution
feature reduction.
2.5
PCA baseline
Each TM was treated as 145 speckle vectors, each holding the real and imaginary parts of its
42,025 pixels (84,050 reals). A single PCA was fitted over all speckles of the training TMs, after
subtracting their mean, so the basis is shared across columns and across TMs. A TM was compressed
by projecting each speckle onto the first k components and reconstructed from those coefficients.
The 62× setting uses k = 1,352, matching the autoencoder latent of 8 × 13 × 13 = 1,352 reals; with
fewer than k+1 training speckles, k is capped at one less than the number of speckles. PCA involves
no iterative training and was fitted once for each training set, so no seeds apply. Errors are scored
with Eq. 1.
2.6
Training and finetuning
All models were trained with AdamW and gradient-norm clipping (maximum norm 1.0), minimising
the phase-aligned error of Eq. 1. The final configuration (encoder widths [24, 48, 72], one attention
head, Linformer projection length k = 24, pretraining learning rate 1.35 × 10−3, pretraining batch
size 4, fine-tuning learning rate 1.49 × 10−4, weight decay 1.27 × 10−6) was chosen by a Bayesian
search (Optuna, TPE sampler) [28] over these quantities with validation error after fine-tuning as
the objective. Altogether 27 trials were undertaken. Sections 3.1.2– 3
