A Complete Geometric Message-Passing
Architecture for Point Clouds
Nadav Dym1, Tal Amir1, Gia Chi Dang2, and Christopher Morris2
1Technion – Israel Institute of Technology
2RWTH Aachen University
Three-dimensional point clouds are a fundamental data modality, and a large
family of machine learning architectures has been developed to respect their natural
symmetries to rigid motions and permutations.
A principled way to compare
these architectures, which vary widely in complexity and cost, is through their
expressive power. That is, an architecture is complete if it can distinguish any two
inputs not related by the symmetries it respects. Simple distance-based message-
passing networks are known to be incomplete, and while there exist complete
alternatives, they typically rely on computationally intensive mechanisms like high-
order representations of the rotation group or higher-order Weisfeiler–Leman-type
tests.
In this work, we devise a novel, simple, equivariant message-passing architecture
for point clouds, and prove that it is complete. We complement our theoretical
result with experiments showing that our architecture separates challenging point
clouds that distance-based message passing provably cannot distinguish. Our results
suggest that high-order equivariant features may not be necessary to enhance the
expressivity of point cloud architectures, and can help settle completeness for other
equivariant architectures for which such results are currently unknown. We give
initial evidence for this by proving completeness of a slightly modified version of
SEGNN.
1. Introduction
Three-dimensional point clouds are a fundamental data modality. They represent shapes in
computer vision and molecules in cheminformatics and physical simulation [Schütt et al.,
2017, Qi et al., 2017]. Learning tasks defined on this modality, from shape classification and
generation to the prediction of molecular properties and interatomic forces, are correspondingly
of broad interest. As a result, a large and growing family of machine learning architectures has
been designed for point clouds, many of them built to respect the clouds’ natural symmetries,
i.e., invariance or equivariance to rigid motions and to permutations of the points [Thomas
1
arXiv:2611.26384v1  [cs.LG]  19 Nov 2026
et al., 2018, Satorras et al., 2021, Deng et al., 2021, Batatia et al., 2022, Schütt et al., 2017,
Brandstetter et al., 2022].
This proliferation of architectures, which vary widely in complexity and computational cost,
raises a natural question: what, if anything, is gained by using a more expressive and more
costly architecture? A principled way to address this question is to analyze an architecture’s
expressive power theoretically, through the notion of completeness. An architecture is complete
if it can distinguish between any two inputs that are not related by the symmetries it respects.
Completeness is motivated by its close ties to approximation, i.e., an architecture that cannot
separate two distinct point clouds cannot approximate a function that assigns them different
values, while, conversely, a complete architecture can be shown to be a universal approximator
of invariant functions [Chen et al., 2019, Dym and Gortler, 2025]. Thus, completeness is a
natural requirement for general-purpose point cloud networks where universal approximation
properties are desirable.
Distance-based message passing neural networks (MPNNs) for point clouds are a family of
simple and natural architectures for which (in)completeness is well understood. Such networks
achieve invariance by applying the permutation-invariant message-passing mechanism of graph
neural networks to pairwise distances, a rigid-motion invariant. Concretely, MPNNs iteratively
update rotation- and translation-invariant node features h(t)

the point cloud, the mapping ψ is permutation-invariant, and a global, permutation-invariant
representation of the point cloud is obtained by summing, or otherwise pooling, the final
node features hi. Popular architectures of this kind include SchNet and Molecular Graph
Convolutions [Schütt et al., 2017, Kearnes et al., 2016].
Distance-based architectures were shown to be incomplete for three-dimensional point
clouds [Pozdnyakov and Ceriotti, 2022, Li et al., 2023], which motivates the search for more
expressive architectures. Many modern successful architectures retain the message-passing
mechanism, but, besides the invariant features h(t)

two families.
1. Euclidean equivariant MPNN. Message passing networks whose equivariant features
yi are themselves vectors in R3. These vectors are typically obtained from the previous
generation’s features by elementary equivariant operations, such as weighted linear
combinations or cross products. Successful methods in this category include EGNN
and Vector Neurons [Satorras et al., 2021, Deng et al., 2021]. Prior to this work, no
completeness results were known for such networks.
2. High-Order equivariant MPNN. These methods instead use the irreducible represen-
tations of the rotation group, which gives a rich family of equivariant features of dimension
2ℓ+ 1, with ℓany non-negative integer. There are many methods using this approach,
including Tensor field networks, SEGNNs, and MACE [Thomas et al., 2018, Brandstetter
et al., 2022, Batatia et al., 2022]. Such methods are typically more time-consuming than
those of the first category, but they often attain very good results. Theoretically, the use
of high-order MPNNs is justified by the fact that, for high enough order features, this

construction is complete [Dym and Maron, 2021, Maennel et al., 2024]. However, the
theoretical estimates of the representation order necessary to attain this guarantee are
unrealistically large [Hordan et al., 2026].
Main contribution.
Our main contribution in this paper is a new, provably complete and simple
architecture from the Euclidean equivariant category. In its simplest form, the architecture
constructs two equivariant features yi,1 and yi,2 at each index, and uses them, together with
their cross product yi,1 × yi,2, to define a basis for R3 onto which the remainder of the point
cloud is then projected; see Figure 1. The key technical difficulty in proving completeness is
analyzing the case where the three vectors yi,1, yi,2 and yi,1 × yi,2 fail to form a basis. We
show that this occurs only for balanced configurations, in the sense of Leech [1957], and we use
Leech’s classification to prove completeness in this setting as well.
In addition, we show that a somewhat modified version of the steerable graph neural network
(SEGNN) of Brandstetter et al. [2022] can emulate our architecture with irreducible features of
order one, and thus is complete.
Finally, we complement our theoretical analysis with synthetic experiments showing that our
architecture can separate challenging pairs from the literature that distance-based message
passing provably cannot distinguish.
Significance.
We present a simple equivariant architecture with completeness guarantees. In
this manuscript, we report only preliminary, toy-scale results for this architecture, but we
are optimistic that it may perform well on real-world tasks. We believe, however, that the
significance of this work extends beyond the specific architecture itself. Ultimately, this result is
a theoretical breakthrough showing that completeness can be attained in much lower complexity
than what was previously suspected. We believe our proof will help establish completeness for
many other architectures for which completeness is currently unknown, either by showing that
their architecture can simulate ours, or by incorporating ideas from our proof. Our result on
SEGNN is a first result in this direction.
Additionally, we have proved that Euclidean equivariant MPNNs are sufficient to approximate
all invariant functions, so that at least theoretically, high-order equivariant MPNNs are not
needed. This should encourage researchers to revisit whether these more complex constructions
are truly needed in practice, or whether some engineering refinements could make Euclidean
architectures just as effective as high-order ones.
3
1.1. Related work
We now discuss related work that has not been mentioned in the introduction.
Equivariant frame constructions.
Our networks are based on the construction of a local
equivariant basis, or frame. This idea has appeared in works such as [Luo et al., 2022, Du et al.,
2022]. What distinguishes our work is that we can establish global separation even when the
equivariant vectors remain dependent.
Completeness via 2-WL.
An alternative way to construct a local basis is to construct, for
every pair of points i, j, a basis derived from the points xi, xj. This idea is the basis of some
complete constructions for point clouds [Hordan et al., 2024b, Nigam et al., 2024, Kurlin, 2027],
and proofs that geometric order-two Weisfeiler–Leman tests [Hordan et al., 2024b, Delle Rose
et al., 2023], and subgraph networks [Li et al., 2025], are complete. They are also used to
define a frame averaging operator in [Dym et al., 2024, Pozdnyakov and Ceriotti, 2023]. While
these approaches can also guarantee completeness, their disadvantage is their high complexity,
stemming from the need to store and update features for every pair of nodes. In comparison,
our complete model maintains features only for individual nodes.
Theoretical Comparison of Equivariant Architectures.
Joshi et al. [2023] and Sverdlov and
Dym [2025] show that sparse geometric MPNNs which use equivariant features are more
expressive than those that only rely on invariant features. Our analysis gives a similar picture
with regard to completeness when using all pairwise interactions. Cen et al. [2024] argue that
high-order representations are necessary for symmetric inputs, where Euclidean permutation-
invariant and rotation-equivariant features vanish. The implications of these results are for
specific applications where one is interested in recovering the orientation of the input. However,
for tasks that involve computation of invariant functions like molecular energy or point cloud
classification, our results prove that Euclidean Equivariant message passing is universal. These
results can probably be extended to universality results for equivariant functions, using the
work of Villar et al. [2021], Hordan et al. [2024a], but we leave this for future work.
2. Background
We introduce our notation and the symmetry and completeness notions used throughout the
paper.
Basic notation.
Let N := {1, 2, . . .} and [n] := {1, . . . , n}, for n ∈N. We write vectors and
matrices in boldface using x and A, respectively; scalars and individual matrix entries are
unbolded. Vectors are columns, and tuples of vectors and scalars denote their concatenation
when used as neural-network inputs. We use u·v = u⊤v and ∥u∥for the Euclidean inner product
and norm, and Ik for the k × k identity matrix. The unit sphere is S2 := {u ∈R3 : ∥u∥= 1}.
The notation {{· · · }} denotes a multiset, retaining repeated elements and their multiplicities.
Function names are not bolded, including when their outputs are vectors.
4
Attributed point clouds.
For fixed n, d ∈N, a charged or attributed point cloud is an ordered
tuple
X = ((xi, qi))i∈[n] ∈V[3, d, n], where V[3, d, n] := (R3 × Rd)n.
Here, xi ∈R3 denotes the position of the i-th point, and qi ∈Rd carries rotation-invariant
information on that point. We will refer to qi as a charge. We write ri := ∥xi∥and, when
ri > 0, call ui := xi/ri the direction of xi.
Rotations, permutations, and congruence.
A proper rotation is a matrix R ∈R3×3 that is
orthogonal and has a positive determinant. The group of proper rotations in three dimensions is
denoted by SO(3). Let Sn be the permutation group on [n], and set Gn := SO(3) × Sn. Its left
action on point clouds applies the rotation R to all positions, while simultaneously permuting
the positions and charges. Formally,


i∈[n].
A point-cloud isomorphism from X to X ′ is a pair (R, π) ∈Gn satisfying X ′ = (R, π)∗X. Two
clouds are congruent, written X ∼= X ′, if such an isomorphism exists.
We note that in most practical settings, we are also interested in translation symmetry.
In some settings, we are also interested in reflection symmetry. Our architecture and theory
apply directly to rotations, permutations and, after centering the cloud, translations; with a
straightforward adaptation to account for reflections, by averaging over ±X, they also apply to
the full orthogonal group, where universality is preserved (Appendix E).
Invariance, equivariance and geometric operations.
A map F is invariant if F(g∗X) =
F(X), for every g ∈Gn. It is equivariant if transforming the input induces the prescribed
transformation of its output.
For example, for R ∈SO(3), and vectors u, v ∈R3,
(Ru) · (Rv) = u · v,
(Ru) × (Rv) = R(u × v).
Consequently, inner products are invariant and cross products are equivariant. The signed triple
product (u × v) · w is invariant under proper rotations and changes sign under an orthogonal
transformation with determinant −1. It therefore retains orientation information that pairwise
distances and inner products alone do not retain.
Completeness and universality.
A family F of invariant maps is complete, or separates orbits,
if every noncongruent pair X, X ′ is distinguished by some map F ∈F. The separating map
may depend on the pair. A single invariant map F is globally separating on M ⊆V[3, d, n] if
F(X) = F(X ′)
⇐⇒
X ∼= X ′,
for all X, X ′ ∈M.
Equivariance alone does not imply either separation property. Finally, a family is universal
for continuous invariant functions on a compact domain if it approximates every such function
uniformly to arbitrary accuracy. We establish family completeness first, then a continuous
globally separating neural representation, and finally universality by adding a feed-forward
neural network readout.
5
3. A Complete Geometric Message-Passing Architecture for Point
Clouds
We define a Gn-invariant architecture via an all-to-all message-passing architecture on the
attributed point clouds introduced in Section 2. We note that the architecture we introduce now
is an abstract and minimal architecture for which completeness can be obtained. A concrete
neural parameterization is given in Section 5, including extensions to enable global separation
and universality guarantees.

The functions ϕ0 and ϕ1 combine a vector input with a multiset of vectors to produce a
feature vector; ϕ2 maps a multiset of vectors to a vector. The scalar-valued functions ψ1 and
ψ2 determine the message weights. All nodewise functions are shared across points, and the

The intuition behind this construction is as follows. The first step, Equation (2), encodes
all available rotation-invariant information via a message-passing aggregation to obtain the
rotation-invariant feature hi. The second step, Equation (3), then produces two equivariant
vectors, yi,1 and yi,2. Together with their vector product yi,1 × yi,2, these three vectors (may)
form a basis for R3. The third step then records the properties of this basis via the Gram matrix,
and the projection of the point cloud onto this basis, to obtain another rotation invariant
feature zi. Finally, the last step aggregates all node invariant features to obtain a final global
representation E(X).
We denote by F(d) the family of all maps E obtained from (2)–(5) by varying these functions
and their feature dimensions. The multiset functions accept multisets of any finite size, so each
E ∈F(d) is defined on clouds with any number n of points.
4. Completeness theorem
We now state our main result, i.e., the message-passing architecture from Section 3 is invariant
and complete.

Theorem 4.1 (Charged-cloud completeness). For every fixed d, n ≥1, any function E ∈F(d)
is SO(3) × Sn invariant on V[3, d, n]. Moreover, F(d) is complete, i.e., if X, X ′ ∈V[3, d, n] are
two non-congruent point clouds, then there exists E ∈F(d) such that E(X)̸ = E(X ′).

1. Equivariant linear independence is enough. The first idea behind the proof is well known

Evidence from a Multi-Regime Causal Discovery Benchmark: UCMT
Algorithms, Comparative Performance, and Controlled Ablation
Studies
Mahyar Eslami
UCMT Labs, Canada
8 November 2026 (revised 19 November 2026)
Research manuscript (not peer-reviewed)
Abstract
We present an internal, pre-registered evaluation of the UCMT causal discovery algorithm family alongside
established alternatives across heterogeneous benchmark regimes, complemented by a separately pre-registered,
controlled study of UCMT v2 Global components. The contribution is both empirical and methodological: a
family-stratified comparison of three actively developed algorithm configurations and targeted evidence about
which internal stages affect their outcomes. In the main benchmark, UCMT v2 Global has higher directed
F1 than NOTEARS and DAGMA in selected real, semi-synthetic and Gaussian-network comparisons at the
paired-run level, while trailing leading permutation-search methods in other settings. The BOSS-based UCMT
v4 produces a CSuite-specific directed-F1 improvement over BOSS (mean paired difference +0.279; pair-level
Holm p < 0.001), but the dataset-level adjusted result is not significant (p = 0.188). In a separate fixed-skeleton
ablation, UCMT v2 Global exceeds an adapted R2-SortnRegress orientation baseline on standardized iSCM
data (directed F1 0.537 vs 0.468, dataset-level Holm p = 0.031); absolute orientation accuracy is 0.563 and
there is no established broad advantage over RESIT, ANM or DirectLiNGAM. Controlled ablations show that
sparsity and BIC-based refinement materially affect some outcomes, whereas the examined arbitration and
automatic regime-selection mechanisms do not yield confirmed general improvements. We report performance
shortcomings, multiple-testing correction, runtime costs, evaluation limitations and reproducibility checks. The
results support UCMT as an implemented and empirically investigated algorithm family, not a claim of overall
superiority, independent validation or demonstrated commercial impact.
Competing interests.
This report was prepared by UCMT Labs, which develops the UCMT algorithms evaluated
here. The author is the founder of UCMT Labs and the developer of the UCMT algorithms, and has a financial
interest in their commercial use.
Evaluation status.
Both studies are internal, not peer-reviewed or independently replicated.
The main
benchmark and the later component experiments have different datasets, seed counts, methods and confirmatory
families; their estimates are not pooled.
Intellectual property.
Only high-level algorithm descriptions and aggregate evaluation results are included.
Detailed implementations and research settings remain confidential as trade secrets.
1 Introduction
Causal discovery from observational and interventional
data is evaluated on few real datasets with trusted
ground truth [23, 8] and on many synthetic generators
whose artefacts can be exploited [21]. We present an
internal benchmark, pre-registered before execution, in
which the UCMT family of algorithms is compared with
established methods. The aim is to build a verifiable
picture of where the UCMT family is useful, where it is
not yet competitive, and which measured changes follow
from its development. The public benchmark overview,
methodology and comparative summaries are available
at https://ucmtlabs.com/benchmarks. This page is
a public results landing page, not a deposit of raw exe-
cution records or source code. No pooled ranking across
families is produced. The paper offers three contribu-
tions: (i) a heterogeneous, family-specific comparison of
v2 Global, v3 and a BOSS-based v4; (ii) separately pre-
registered mechanism-level experiments on v2 Global;
and (iii) an explicit translation of benchmark evidence
into testable requirements for robust analytical software
rather than unvalidated claims of business impact.
2 Benchmark design
Datasets.
Five families of part 1 (completed as far as
the part-2 gap filling allowed) are analysed separately:
real data (two Sachs versions and three Causal Chamber
sets), semi-synthetic data (CausalAssembly stations and
a SERGIO network [10, 7]), DREAM4 [17], bnlearn
Gaussian networks [24] and CSuite [9]. Part 2 adds
three families, analysed separately and never pooled
1
arXiv:2611.26383v1  [cs.LG]  19 Nov 2026
with the others: synthetic ER/SF (8 datasets), iSCM
(6) and misspecification (4), chosen mechanically before
the run, 3 seeds, 10 core methods (UCMT v2 Global,
v3, v4, BOSS, GRaSP, PC, DirectLiNGAM, DAGMA,
NOTEARS, empty graph); rankings there cover these 10
methods only. Discrete bnlearn and Tübingen families
were not run for UCMT and are not interpreted.
Methods.
PC, FCI [27], GES [5], GIES [11], GRaSP
[13],
BOSS [1],
LiNGAM-type methods [25, 26],
NOTEARS [30], DAGMA [2], CAM [4], SCORE [22],
DAS [18], NoGAM [19], AVICI [16], DiBS [15], SDCD
[20], DCDI [3], ENCO [14], DECI [9], Sea [29], plus
Empty, random and sortability baselines [21].
UCMT algorithms (general description).
UCMT
v2 Global is UCMT Labs’ own algorithm, developed
in-house; v3 is a variant of v2 Global with additional
post-processing; v4 is a hybrid built on BOSS with an
additional orientation step. The descriptions are general
by design; the source code is confidential.
Protocol.
Pre-registration of settings, 10 seeds per
dataset, standardised data, one thread per job, one-hour
cap per job, UCMT dataset priors off, AVICI limited
to 1,000 rows. Part 1 ended at its deadline, 2026-11-
06 (it was interrupted on the host and its deadline
moved by the time lost). Part 2 is a 24-hour pilot under
Amendment 3 (pre-registered before any part-2 job) and
used about 27 minutes of the budget; no job timed out.
Metrics and statistics.
SHD under a favourable
convention (an undirected predicted edge on a true
edge costs 0) and a strict convention (cost 1), directed
F1, skeleton F1 and runtime. Ranks follow Demšar
[6] (Friedman and Nemenyi); paired comparisons use
Wilcoxon signed-rank tests [28] with Holm correction
[12], and a dataset-level test where at least six datasets
exist.
3 Results
No method is separable from the first-ranked group
in any family. On real data (five datasets) all UCMT
variants have higher mean SHD than the empty graph
(significant at pair level after Holm for UCMT v4 only)
although their directed F1 (0.31 to 0.34) is far above
it; with the four datasets of the earlier version all three
were significant. On real-data favourable SHD UCMT
v4 is significantly worse than (higher favourable SHD,
pair-level Holm p < 0.05) UCMT v2 Global and UCMT
v3 (50 pairs each), FCI, PC, SDCD and Sea (20 pairs
each: these four ran on two of the five datasets only)
and the Empty graph (50 pairs, Holm p 0.040).
Part 2 and cross-family robustness (Q5).
In the
three part-2 families each UCMT variant is inside the Ne-
menyi top group of the ten core methods on favourable
SHD, strict SHD and directed F1 (top group 7 to 10 of
10 methods; with four misspecification datasets the test
cannot separate any methods). UCMT runtime grows
more slowly with the number of variables than that of
BOSS and GRaSP on the ER/SF subset (log-log slopes
1.8 against 2.8, D from 10 to 50). The pre-registered
robustness question asked whether UCMT v2 Global is
the most consistent fully directed method across fam-
ilies on directed F1, with a normalised mean rank rf
of at most 0.50 in every part-2 family; it is not (rf
= 0.59, 0.60 and 0.57), so the claim is unproven. Q5
was formulated after inspecting the part-1 results; on
the part-1 families it is exploratory, and the confirma-
tory test is the pre-registered Q5 on the part-2 families.
CPDAG-output methods are penalised by directed F1
for undirected edges, so the comparison is across output
types; UCMT v4 (CPDAG output) has a lower worst-
family rank than v2 Global in both parts, and on SHD
v2 Global does not stand out (worst-family normalised
rank W = 0.65 on both favourable and strict SHD).
4 Controlled UCMT v2 Global component
study
Design
and
scope.
A second study was pre-
registered on 2026-11-06 before the main-run outcomes
were inspected and completed on 2026-11-07.
It is
distinct from the multi-algorithm benchmark above.
It evaluated raw and standardized inputs using
dataset-level paired analyses with two-sided Wilcoxon
signed-rank tests, Holm adjustment within pre-specified
confirmatory families, and two-stage bootstrap confi-
dence intervals. The study logged 6,234 job records
in the main and post-hoc queues plus 694 attempted
CAM-GAM pruning comparisons. Among its evalu-
ation groups were 12 classic synthetic, eight iSCM,
eight misspecification, seven pooled real/Gaussian
datasets, and four exploratory D=50 datasets. Dataset
seeds are correlated within datasets and were not
treated as independent confirmatory units. Evaluation
used 10 seeds on smaller datasets and four or five at
larger dimension. The primary validation compared an
instrumented run with an unwrapped production run;
no production source file was edited. This study does
not represent independent replication.
4.1
A bounded positive orientation re-
sult
On eight standardized iSCM datasets (80 dataset-seed
instances), UCMT v2’s production orientation stage on
the same true skeleton as its comparator achieved mean
directed F1 of 0.537 versus 0.468 for the adapted R2-
SortnRegress order, a paired mean difference of 0.068
(95% bootstrap interval 0.022–0.119). Orientation ac-
curacy was 0.563 versus 0.468, a difference of 0.094
(95% interval 0.045–0.147). The two dataset-level Holm-
adjusted p-values were 0.031. This supports a narrowly
specified comparative result on low-sortability iSCM
data; it does not establish high absolute accuracy, ro-
bust causal orientation across regimes, or superiority to
the broader set of baseline methods. All comparisons
used adapted baselines constrained to the same skele-
ton and therefore do not compare published algorithms’
native graph outputs.

deployable offering would additionally need validated un-

From Benchmarks to the Bench:
Preference, Correspondence and Selectivity in Bidirectional
Drug–Target Screening
Jiangjie Qiu1,†, Chengrui Xu1,†, Xiaonan Wang1,*
1Beijing Key Laboratory of Artificial Intelligence for Advanced Chemical Engineering Materials, State Key
Laboratory of Chemical Engineering and Low-Carbon Technology, Department of Chemical Engineering, Tsinghua
University, Beijing 100084, China.
†These authors contributed equally to this work and share first authorship.
*Corresponding author: Xiaonan Wang, email: wangxiaonan@tsinghua.edu.cn.
Abstract
Identifying active molecules for known targets and potential targets for existing drugs is central to drug
discovery and repurposing. Drug–target interaction (DTI) models can rank vast numbers of drug–target
pairs, but limited experimental capacity restricts testing to a small number of candidates. We compared the
bidirectional recommendations of 13 released systems across 711 molecular structures of FDA-approved drugs
and 614 human proteins. For the same target or drug, pairs of models produced completely disjoint Top-10
molecule and protein lists in 77.8% and 70.1% of comparisons, respectively. Even where recommendations
overlapped, agreement between some systems largely reflected recurring preferences for the same candidates.
Published inhibition measurements for 79 molecules and 65 kinases revealed that some systems enriched
active candidates, yet their hit yields changed little when recommendations were matched to different drugs
or targets, whereas other systems lost substantially more hits. Some of the former systems also rarely ranked
both molecules and kinases correctly when two drugs favoured different kinases. We further retrained the
same architecture on the same data, with the training objective fixed and random seeds varied. Despite
similar test performance, mean pairwise Top-10 overlap on a separate screening catalogue was about two
candidates. Our study moves DTI model evaluation beyond benchmark performance to assess whether model
predictions can guide meaningful experimental decisions in drug discovery and target identification.
Introduction
Mapping interactions between small molecules and biological macromolecules underpins chemogenomics and drug
discovery. Drug–target interaction (DTI) prediction is used in forward ligand screening to identify molecules
active against a given protein target1;2. Reverse target screening asks which proteins a known active molecule
or approved drug may act on. Identifying these targets can suggest new uses for a drug or help explain
off-target effects3;4. In molecule selection, the protein is the query and molecules are the candidates. In
protein selection, these roles are reversed. DTI models can evaluate vast numbers of possible molecule–protein
pairs5–11, but experimental budgets and throughput limit how many can be tested, even in emerging self-driving
laboratories12–14. The usefulness of a candidate list depends on the experimental objective. For an initial screen,
measurable activity may be the main criterion. Target identification asks which proteins a molecule acts on,
while selective probe development also requires distinguishing its activity on the intended target from activity
on alternatives. The pairs selected for testing determine which new measurements enter the next round of a
closed-loop experiment12;13.
DTI models are commonly evaluated using aggregate prediction metrics or their ability to recover known
interactions11;15. Previous studies have shown that predictions can be influenced by ligand and target preferences,
as well as biases in training and evaluation datasets16–19. For example, two systems may recommend the same
molecule because both rank it highly for many targets. We therefore reassign one system’s recommendation lists
across queries to measure how much agreement remains. Finding active candidates does not establish whether a
model’s recommendations yield more hits for their intended drug or target than they would if assigned to other
queries. Understanding these distinctions requires examining both the candidates selected for testing and their
measured outcomes, rather than relying on aggregate prediction performance alone.
Selectivity requires comparing activity across alternative partners. Kinase profiling studies have shown that
1
arXiv:2611.26369v1  [cs.LG]  19 Nov 2026
compounds can differ substantially in their activities across targets20;21. When two molecules and two proteins
exhibit crossed measured preferences, a strict evaluation requires all four comparisons to be correct: the model
must identify the preferred molecule for each protein and the preferred protein for each molecule. Recommenda-
tions may also change when a model is retrained. Studies of underspecification and predictive multiplicity have
shown that models with similar aggregate performance can disagree on individual predictions22–24. Whether
such differences change the candidates selected for testing, and whether different selections lead to different
measured outcomes, cannot be determined from aggregate test performance alone.
We address these questions through three complementary analyses (Fig. 1). Comparing 13 released systems on a
common catalogue of 711 molecular structures of FDA-approved drugs and 614 human proteins, we find that
most cross-system Top-10 comparisons share no candidates, while much of the agreement between some systems
persists when complete recommendation lists are reassigned across queries. Using published single-concentration
inhibition measurements for all 79 × 65 molecule–kinase pairs in a subset of the Kinase Inhibitor Repurposing
Hub (KIRHub)25, we find that some systems enrich active candidates yet recover nearly the same number of
hits whether their recommendations are evaluated for their original queries or reassigned among queries. Other
systems lose substantially more hits under the same comparison. Some systems showing the former pattern
also rarely recover crossed preferences between molecules and kinases in both screening directions, revealing a
marked difference between finding activity and correctly ranking selective pairings. We additionally examine
how alternative candidate-selection rules affect these outcomes. To assess reproducibility, we repeated training
with different random seeds while holding the data split, encoders, architecture and objective fixed. The models
had similar test performance, but their Top-10 lists shared only about two candidates on average in pairwise
comparisons on a separate screening catalogue. On the measured overlap between this catalogue and the kinase
panel, no seed shows a clear advantage in mean hit yield.
A model may identify active candidates without reliably distinguishing the drug–target preferences relevant to a
particular investigation, while similar predictive performance can lead to substantially different experimental
choices. We evaluate these differences through activity yield, query-associated gain, recovery of crossed preferences
and stability across training runs. These measures relate a model’s recommendations to the biological comparisons
required by the experiment.

remain ≤20% at 1 µM. Arrows indicate the four required strict orders. Ties fail. The 26,114 qualifying units share

3
Results
Bidirectional recommendations from released prediction systems
Under a common candidate pool and budget, released prediction systems proposed different experimental
candidates for the same query. We compared thirteen systems using their supplied weights and specified input
and output configurations (Table 1). The common matrix contained 711 molecules, 614 proteins and 436,554
pairs, with valid scores from every system. For each protein query, we selected the ten highest-ranked molecules.
For each molecule query, we selected the ten highest-ranked proteins. Candidates were ranked using each system’s
own scores.
Table 1. Released prediction systems and evaluated outputs. Each row represents one system under its specified
inference configuration. Ensembles of released models are treated as single systems. Scores differ in training objective and
scale and are used to rank candidates within each system.

We compared all 78 distinct pairs formed by the 13 systems. Across all queries, these pairs yielded 47,892
molecule-selection and 55,458 protein-selection comparisons. Top-10 lists were completely disjoint in 77.8% of
molecule-selection comparisons and 70.1% of protein-selection comparisons. Thus, in most comparisons, choosing
a different system changed all ten candidates proposed for the same query and testing budget. For each system
pair, we also averaged the number of shared Top-10 candidates across queries. The medians of these 78 averages
were 0.2289 molecules and 0.3390 proteins, both below one shared candidate per ten recommendations.
To assess sensitivity to specific input and output configurations, we repeated the analysis after excluding
DrugCLIP, DTBind, GraphBAN and CheMLT-F, while keeping the candidate pools unchanged. In this nine-
system subset, Top-10 lists were completely disjoint in 78.49% of molecule-selection comparisons and 67.39% of
protein-selection comparisons (Supplementary S3). We next reassigned one system’s complete recommendation
lists across queries, preserving the candidates and their order within each list. Comparing the observed overlap
with the exact reassignment reference quantifies how much agreement is retained through recurring candidate
preferences and how much is associated with the original query correspondence.
Persistent candidate preferences and query-dependent agreement
We first measured how much of each system’s recommendation could be recovered from persistent candidate
preferences. In molecule selection, BALM’s ten most frequent molecules occupied 84.9% of its Top-10 slots,
compared with 7.8% for DrugCLIP. In protein selection, the ten most frequent proteins from MAMMAL pKd
occupied 87.6%. We fitted a fixed query-blind ranking from mean candidate percentile ranks in other query
groups, without using the current query. On held-out queries, this ranking recovered 8.76 of the Top-10 proteins
from MAMMAL pKd and 7.53 of the Top-10 molecules from BALM. The corresponding recoveries for Nesso-1
were 0.36 proteins and 2.18 molecules. Persistent preferences thus reproduced different fractions of the systems’
recommendations (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. S1).
4
To separate sources of agreement, we preserved candidate identity and each list’s internal order while reassigning
one system’s query correspondence. For MAMMAL pKd–BALM, the molecule-selection correlation was 0.4217,
with an exact reassignment reference of 0.4201. The corresponding protein-selection values were 0.3789 and
0.3784. MAMMAL pKd–ADME-DTI shared 3.736 Top-10 proteins on average, versus a reference of 3.748. Most
agreement for these pairs remained after query reassignment (Fig. 2c,d).
Across all 78 pairs, median query-aligned agreement increments for Spearman correlation were 0.00233 and
0.00177 in the two directions, and median Top-10 increments were 0.0181 and 0.0252. Some pairs showed
stronger query alignment. For Nesso-1–DTBind protein rankings, the whole-list correlation was −0.0974. Their
Top-10 lists shared 1.000 candidates on average, compared with a reference of 0.3745, an increment of 0.6255.
MAMMAL pKd–BALM also showed similar observed and reference correlations on a separate 128 × 128 catalogue
sharing no molecule or protein identities with the common catalogue (Supplementary S3 and Table S7). The
increment quantifies query-aligned excess agreement between systems. It does not measure either system’s query
dependence alone, because systems with different query-dependent responses can also have a small increment.
These label-free analyses distinguish sources of agreement, while measured activity is needed to assess whether
query correspondence accompanies additional hits.
Activity enrichment and correspondence gain
The retrospective functional panel separated activity enrichment from correspondence gain. The selected KIRHub
subset comprised 5,135 single-concentration measurements for 79 molecules and 65 kinases25. A hit was defined
as at least 70% inhibition at 1 µM. In total, 628 pairs met this criterion. Hit yield was the mean number of hits
among the selected candidates per query. With five candidates per query, uniform selection gave an expected
U = 0.611 hits. All queries were retained, including 15 molecules and 10 proteins without measured hits.
We asked whether each list yielded more hits for its original query than when reassigned to other queries.
Matched hit yield, G, was the mean Top-5 hit yield under the original query correspondence. Reassigned hit
yield, R, was the exact mean after complete recommendation lists were reassigned within evaluation folds. The
identity G −U = (R −U) + (G −R) separates excess yield into enrichment retained after reassignment, R −U,
and correspondence gain, G −R. The latter measures the additional hit yield associated with the original query
correspondence within this panel, budget and reassignment scheme.
MAMMAL pKd and BALM protein lists yielded 1.114 and 1.329 hits per five candidates, above the uniform
reference, but their correspondence gains were only 0.025 and −0.001. Nesso-1 yielded 2.354 hits with a gain
of 1.466, and SCOPE light yielded 1.962 with a gain of 1.069. UniDTI yielded 0.908 molecule hits and 0.456
protein hits, the latter below the uniform expectation of 0.611. Its correspondence gains were 0.044 and 0.073,
with both conditional resampling intervals including zero. Figure 3 and Supplementary Table S8a provide the
complete comparison. Activity enrichment with low correspondence gain for MAMMAL pKd and BALM also
persisted in the nine-system subset.
To assess dependence on pairs found in the two audited BindingDB source extracts, we evaluated a complete
57-molecule × 65-kinase subpanel after excluding their exact pair matches. MAMMAL pKd and BALM protein
lists yielded 1.000 and 1.246 hits, above the uniform reference of 0.563, with correspondence gains of 0.030
for both. Nesso-1 and SCOPE light retained protein-selection gains of 1.429 and 0.936. In molecule selection,
MAMMAL pKd yielded 0.415 hits, below the uniform reference, whereas BALM yielded 0.815 with a gain of
−0.052. Nesso-1 and SCOPE light had molecule-selection gains of 1.258 and 0.217, respectively (Supplementary
Tables S1d and S8b).
A query-blind baseline fitted to mean candidate preferences on development queries yielded 1.292 molecule hits
and 1.291 protein hits on held-out queries (Supplementary Table S10). The ranking was fitted on development
queries that were separate from the evaluation queries. Unlike R, which uses evaluation measurements to interpret
completed recommendations, this baseline generates recommendations from development-query scores alone. It
therefore demonstrates activity enrichment without conditioning on the current query. Neither enrichment nor
correspondence gain, however, tests whether scores recover reciprocal preferences among alternative partners.
Strict crossed selectivity
We next tested strict crossed selectivity in measured two-molecule/two-protein units. A unit qualified when both
preferred pairs had at least 70% inhibition at 1 µM and both crossed pairs had at most 20% inhibition. Strict
recovery required all four molecule-wise and protein-wise orders to be correct, with ties counted as failures. The
primary panel contained 26,114 qualifying units, involving 64 molecules and 55 proteins. Figure 4a illustrates
the criterion with ruxolitinib, lenvatinib, NTRK3 and CSF1R.

HiSA: Sparsifying the Hidden Dimension of RoPE Attention in LLMs
Ambroise Borbely * 1 2 Mathieu Salzmann 1 Olivier Verscheure 2
Abstract
Attention in large language models (LLMs) scores
every query against every key with a full dot prod-
uct. We investigate whether this dot product must
be computed completely for attention to be effec-
tive. We propose Hidden Sparse Attention (HiSA),
which keeps the query and key projections intact
but only computes a partial dot product, follow-
ing a static, parameter-free rule set by the token
positions: attention becomes sparse in the hidden
(feature) dimension, an axis much less explored
than token sparsity, rather than over tokens as in
almost all sparse attention methods. Based on the
structure of rotary position embeddings (RoPE),
we decompose keys and queries into parts which
can be omitted when computing attention. By
training LLMs from scratch with HiSA, we find
that this partial dot product does not hurt but im-
proves performance compared with the complete
product while computing only about a third of the
query–key products. During inference HiSA im-
proves decoding speed and shrinks memory foot-
print. We also extend HiSA to FlashAttention-3
kernels for training and inference. Finally, we
motivate our approach by showing that dense at-
tention learns to suppress the attention score parts
that HiSA drops. Code is available at https:
//github.com/ambroise-b/hisa.
1. Introduction
The attention layer (Vaswani et al., 2017) of a large lan-
guage model compares every query with every key via a
dot product over the full head dimension. Most work on
making attention cheaper keeps this dot product intact and
instead reduces the set of keys a query looks at. Strategies
to do so include fixed patterns (Child et al., 2019), sliding
windows (Jiang et al., 2023), KV-cache eviction (Xiao et al.,
2024; Zhang et al., 2023), and query-dependent token selec-
*Corresponding author.
1EPFL, Switzerland 2Swiss Data Sci-
ence Center, EPFL and ETH Zurich, Switzerland. Correspondence
to: Ambroise Borbely <ambroise.borbely@epfl.ch>.
Preprint. November 20, 2026.
tion, training-free (Tang et al., 2024) or learned (Yuan et al.,
2025). In this work, we investigate an orthogonal ques-
tion: whether attention requires computing the complete
query–key dot product.
Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) (Su et al., 2024), used
by many modern LLMs (Grattafiori et al., 2024; Yang
et al., 2025; Team Olmo, 2025; DeepSeek-AI, 2026; Gemma
Team, 2026), give this question a natural structure. RoPE
rotates each two-dimensional frequency pair of the query
and the key by an angle proportional to its position. Because
rotations compose, the two rotations combine into a single
one that encodes the relative distance between the query and
the key. High-frequency pairs complete many turns within a
few tokens, whereas low-frequency pairs barely rotate over
the whole context.
The score parts of fast pairs are therefore highly sensitive to
the exact distance between the query and the key, whereas
language does not follow an exact structure over distant
words or tokens, and sequences can be long. This raises
the question of whether every pair needs to be computed at
every relative distance. We show that high-frequency pairs
are not necessary for the model when distance between
tokens is large, and that removing them is harmless or even
beneficial.
Our Hidden Sparse Attention (HiSA) method turns this
hypothesis into an attention rule: the dot product of each
frequency pair l between a query and a key is kept only when
the rotation induced by RoPE is below an angle budget Φ, a
hyperparameter that we set to 90◦by default. The query and
key projections are unchanged and what becomes sparse
is the hidden dimension of the dot product. The sparsity
pattern follows from the RoPE frequencies and the positions
alone: it has no learned parameter and needs no selection
step, unlike sparse attention methods that score, route or
select keys at runtime. For a given query, fast pairs only see
nearby keys, slow pairs see far.
We propose HiSA, a new sparse attention architecture that
is sparse in the hidden dimension rather than over tokens.
Our contributions can be summarized as follows:
• Based on the structure of RoPE, we develop HiSA, a
sparse attention in the hidden dimension that com-
putes a partial query–key dot product. Its sparsity pat-

• For existing models, we show that a pretrained dense
model can be converted to HiSA by continued train-
ing and matches dense continued training (Section 4.5).
• From an interpretability perspective, we show that the
score parts that HiSA drops correspond to those
that dense attention learns to suppress during train-
ing (Section 5): the rule is not only motivated by the
geometry of RoPE, but measured in what dense models
learn.
2. Related Work
Attention and RoPE.
Attention (Vaswani et al., 2017)
with RoPE (Su et al., 2024) encodes relative positions by
rotating query and key pairs at spaced frequencies θl =
b−2l/d. Barbero et al. (2025) show that Gemma 7B uses
the highest frequencies for positional attention patterns and
suggest that the lowest carry semantic information; Men
et al. (2024) and Liu et al. (2024) relate the RoPE base to
the usable context length, and Wang et al. (2026a) learn
per-head frequencies. Exact attention is made fast by the
IO-aware FlashAttention kernels (Dao et al., 2022; Dao,
2024; Shah et al., 2024), which we extend.
Sparse attention over tokens.
Static patterns and sliding
windows (Child et al., 2019; Beltagy et al., 2020; Zaheer
et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2023) restrict each query to a subset
of keys. For inference, KV-cache eviction keeps attention
sinks and recent tokens (Xiao et al., 2024) or heavy hitters
(Zhang et al., 2023), and Quest (Tang et al., 2024) selects
cache pages per query. Recent methods are trained with the
sparsity in place, using block-sparse kernels: NSA (Yuan
et al., 2025) combines compressed, selected and sliding-
window branches, and MoBA (Lu et al., 2025) routes each
query to the top-scoring blocks of keys.
Sparsity in the hidden dimension.
Several inference
methods exploit the feature dimension, but mostly as a proxy
for selecting tokens. SparQ (Ribar et al., 2024) and Loki
(Singhania et al., 2024) approximate the scores with a few
query components or a low-rank key projection, select the
top keys, and then compute the full dot product over them;
Double Sparsity (Yang et al., 2024) calibrates important
channels offline and FASA (Wang et al., 2026b) uses a few
dominant RoPE frequency chunks for the same purpose.
The final attention of these methods is sparse over tokens,
not in the hidden dimension. ThinK (Xu et al., 2025) does
compute the final score on fewer features, by pruning key-
cache channels, but chooses them from the content and
applies the same pruning to all but the most recent tokens.
All of these methods are applied after training. Sparse Fea-
ture Attention (Xie et al., 2026) trains models whose queries
and keys keep only their k largest-magnitude features, cho-
sen per vector from the content; HiSA instead fixes the
kept parts by the positions alone, through the RoPE rotation
angles.
Two concurrent works also restrict each RoPE pair to a
window proportional to its wavelength. ATFlash (Hayashi
et al., 2026) applies such windows to pretrained models
without training (two periods by default) and ports them
to FlashAttention-4 prefill and FlashInfer decode, with
speedups that grow with context length. WavePrune (Du
et al., 2026) restricts each pair to one rotation period, both
2
HiSA: Sparsifying the Hidden Dimension of RoPE Attention in LLMs
training-free and when pretraining GPT-2 models from
scratch, with FlashAttention-based forward and backward
kernels. WavePrune explains the window by the aliasing
that fast pairs cause in the attention maps of pretrained
models. Both works skip computation and key reads, but
neither reduces the KV cache: every key and value stays in
memory. HiSA differs in three ways. It trains with much
tighter budgets (a quarter period at 90◦), where the partial
product clearly improves the loss at the training length. It
turns the rule into an actual KV-cache reduction, for keys
per chunk and for values beyond the reach. Moreover, an
interpretability analysis of dense models explains why the
dropped pairs are not needed: dense training itself learns to
suppress them.
Long-context extension.
RoPE models are extended by
interpolating positions (Chen et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2024)
or raising the base (Xiong et al., 2024), followed by contin-
ued pretraining on long documents mixed with short data
(Xiong et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2025). We follow this recipe
to study HiSA beyond its pretraining length.

Token-sparse attention

LEARNING FROM CONTEXT: LEAVE-ONE-OUT PREDIC-
TION IN JUMP DIFFUSIONS
Christian Wald
INSA Lyon, Centrale Lyon, Université Lyon 1, Université Jean Monnet,
CNRS, ICJ UMR5208, 69621 Villeurbanne, France
ABSTRACT
Continuous diffusion models generate discrete data through stochastic dynamics
in an embedding space. We consider jump diffusions that additionally reset coor-
dinates to embeddings of categorical values. A coordinate’s own corrupted state
can make prediction easy, potentially reducing the pressure to learn dependencies
between coordinates. We study leave-one-out (LOO) prediction, in which each
coordinate is predicted from the corrupted states of the other coordinates. We show
that, under stated assumptions, jump diffusions with complete coordinate resets and
state-independent clocks preserve the prescribed marginals when reset destinations
use exact LOO probabilities and the drift uses the full endpoint posterior. We
further show that this drift can be constructed from LOO probabilities by analytic
likelihood completion without additional network evaluations. We evaluate unre-
stricted, LOO, and completed predictions on Text8 and LM1B text generation and
ZINC250k molecular graph generation. LOO-based variants improve key genera-
tion metrics over matched unrestricted controls on all three datasets. Controlled
interventions assess reliance on local inputs and context, and we analyze the effect
of analytic likelihood completion.
1
INTRODUCTION
Generating text and molecular graphs requires learning dependencies between discrete coordinates.
Continuous (jump) diffusion models approach this task by corrupting token embeddings and learning
to predict their endpoints (Li et al., 2022; Dieleman et al., 2022; Gulrajani & Hashimoto, 2023;
Jutras-Dubé et al., 2026). Yet a coordinate’s own noisy embedding can reveal its target without
requiring the model to learn the surrounding dependencies. A masked position in masked diffusion
or flow matching provides no such local token evidence (Sahoo et al., 2024; Gat et al., 2024). For
continuous models, increasing noise to remove this shortcut can also destroy useful context (Pynadath
et al., 2026a). We ask whether excluding a coordinate from its own prediction, so called leave-one-out
(LOO) prediction, encourages useful contextual learning, and how to do so while preserving the
intended probability path.
We study LOO prediction in embedding-space jump diffusions, where continuous motion is combined
with jumps to token embeddings. Let Y = (Y1, . . . , YL) be a token sequence, Xt = (X1,t, . . . , XL,t)
its corrupted embeddings in continuous space at time t, and denote by X−i,t all coordinates except i.
For a token a, the full and LOO posteriors are
pi,t(a | x) = P(Yi = a | Xt = x),
qi,t(a | x−i) = P(Yi = a | X−i,t = x−i).
Predicting qi,t requires estimating Yi without access to Xi,t. Our four-token parity experiment
illustrates why this can matter: low full-state prediction loss can precede learning the dependence
needed for joint generation (Table 1).
Excluding local inputs is established in blind-spot denoising (Batson & Royer, 2019; Laine et al.,
2019) and discrete diffusion (Sun et al., 2023; Gourevitch et al., 2026; Casado Noguerales et al., 2026).
For a broader overview of related work, see Appendix A. The gap we address is how to use these
qi,t(a | x−i) predictions in processes with both a continuous drift and coordinate resets, i.e. jumps to
the token embeddings. In this case the input of the network provides noisy contextual information
1
arXiv:2611.26359v1  [cs.LG]  19 Nov 2026
before discrete decisions. Continuous motion resumes after each reset, and later resets can replace an
earlier, possibly wrong, hypothesis. LOO makes the last point particularly meaningful: the learned
reset distribution qθ,i,t(a | x−i) depends only on the surrounding state x−i, so an incorrect local state
xi at time t cannot directly influence this reset distribution.
The distinction between pi,t and qi,t is essential. Posterior averaging of conditional generators uses the
full posterior pi,t(a | x) (Holderrieth et al., 2025), whereas LOO training learns qi,t(a | x−i) without
using xi. We show that substituting the latter into the drift can change the prescribed marginal path
(Example C.2). For jump diffusion, however, exact LOO jump probabilities qi,t(a | x−i) preserve
the correct probability curve when the drift retains the full posterior, under the assumptions of
Proposition 3.2. Analytic likelihood completion combines LOO predictions with the local corruption
likelihood to recover the full posterior. Thus one network can supply both prediction roles without
additional network evaluations.
We compare unrestricted, raw LOO, and completed predictors on Text8, LM1B, and ZINC250k.
LOO improves key generation metrics over matched unrestricted controls, while completion’s
effect depends on the path and dataset. Local-state and subject–verb interventions test contextual
information use, see Section 4.
Our contributions are:
• A marginal-preservation result for complete coordinate resets using LOO destinations and
full-posterior drift, with a counterexample for substituting LOO probabilities into the drift.
• A repeated-reset Brownian bridge whose marginals converge to the data law, using one LOO
network and analytic likelihood completion for the two prediction roles.
• Matched-budget experiments on Text8, LM1B, and ZINC250k showing when LOO improves
over unrestricted prediction and when raw LOO drift outperforms completion despite lacking
a marginal-preservation guarantee.
• We demonstrate empirically that LOO drift without analytic completion can help recover
from wrong predictions at earlier time steps, offering a possible explanation for its better
performance in some experiments despite lacking a marginal-preservation guarantee. Con-
trolled LM1B interventions show that a token’s own noisy input can dominate unmasked
predictions and final token choices, even when it conflicts with context. On LM1B, LOO
improves subject tracking and the usefulness of older word order in generated text.
2
CONDITIONAL PATHS AND LEAVE-ONE-OUT PREDICTION
Let V be a finite vocabulary and let pdata ∈P(VL) be a data distribution on sequences of length
L. Choose a random variable Y = (Y1, . . . , YL) ∼pdata, and consider an embedding e : V →Rd.
For recovery of token sequences, we assume that e is injective. Write E(Y ) = (e(Y1), . . . , e(YL))
and for x = (x1, . . . , xL) ∈RdL let xi←z denote x with position i replaced by z i.e. xi←z =
(x1, . . . , xi−1, z, . . . , xL). We write x−i = (x1, . . . , xi−1, xi+1, . . . , xL) for the sequence with

For each process below, write pt = L(Xt) for its state law and pi,t(a | x) = P(Yi = a | Xt = x) for
the endpoint posterior at position i.

Mamba Flow Matching Neural Processes:
Linear-Time Inference for Irregularly Observed
Spatial Fields
Cosmo Santoni∗
Giovanni Charles
Timothy James Hitge
Oliver John Watson
Elizaveta Semenova
Imperial College London
Abstract
Interpolating a spatial field, such as daily maximum temperature, from sparse and
irregularly located observations is a recurring task across the environmental and
health sciences. The standard tool, Gaussian-process kriging, refits hyperparame-
ters and solves an O(N 3) system for every new field. When many related fields
are observed, such as daily maps from one sensor network, neural processes (NPs)
instead learn the interpolation map from past fields and predict a new field in a sin-
gle forward pass. Joint-predictive variants, which sample whole fields rather than
independent values at each location, typically rely on self-attention over context
and query points, incurring O(K2) compute in the combined point count K and
capping practical use at a few thousand points. State-space models offer a linear-
time alternative, but a direct state-space adaptation compresses the context into a
single hidden state before reading queries, reducing the information available to the
decoder. We propose MambaFlowNP, a joint-predictive NP with linear compute,
trained with a conditional flow-matching objective. A multi-directional Mamba-2
scan reads context and query tokens in a single shared sequence, so each query’s
velocity is read from its own scan position rather than from a compressed context
summary, and because queries only read the scan state, predictions are consistent
across query sets. MambaFlowNP is competitive with the strongest attention-based
joint-predictive baselines on synthetic Matérn Gaussian-process benchmarks, and
across regional and continental-scale NOAA temperature interpolation tasks it
attains the lowest RMSE, the lowest CRPS and near-nominal coverage on every
tier, while running 114–784× faster than the strongest joint-predictive baseline.
A single forward pass scales to 106 points on one NVIDIA L40S GPU in under
a second. This makes joint prediction computationally feasible for continental-
scale, irregularly sampled sensor networks, with predictive quality evaluated up to
K=5,580.
1
Introduction
Modelling continuous spatial fields from discrete, scattered sensor data remains a fundamental chal-
lenge in spatial statistics and probabilistic machine learning. Examples include inferring temperature
from weather stations (Vaughan et al., 2022), disease prevalence from sentinel sites (Weiss et al.,
2025), and rainfall between rain gauges (Li et al., 2023). Gaussian-process kriging is the standard
approach, but it refits hyperparameters and solves an O(N 3) system for every new field. When many
related fields are observed, as with daily readings from a fixed sensor network, neural processes (NPs;
Garnelo et al., 2018b) cast this as amortised inference, in which the network is trained on many
∗Corresponding author: cosmo.santoni@imperial.ac.uk
40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026).
arXiv:2611.26355v1  [cs.LG]  19 Nov 2026
datasets drawn from a data-generating process and, given a new dataset, performs inference in a
single forward pass without further optimisation. An episode is one dataset together with a random
split into context observations and query locations at which values are to be predicted. Factorised NPs
infer the parameters of an independent Gaussian distribution at each query (Garnelo et al., 2018a),
whilst latent-variable NPs introduce a global latent variable (Garnelo et al., 2018b) through which all
cross-query dependence passes. In contrast, a fully joint-predictive NP directly models the conditional
distribution of the values at all query locations together, via autoregressive (Nguyen and Grover,
2022), diffusion (Dutordoir et al., 2023) or flow (Abu Hamad and Rosenbaum, 2025) parametrisa-
tions. Most existing fully joint-predictive instances employ self-attention over the concatenation
of N context and M query locations, with compute scaling as O(K2), where K = N + M. Flow
Matching NP (FNP) (Abu Hamad and Rosenbaum, 2025) and Transformer NP (TNPA) (Nguyen and
Grover, 2022) are representative, and FNP exhausts GPU memory at 16,384 points and TNPA at
65,536 (Table 8). As an alternative to self-attention transformers, state-space models (SSMs) such as
Mamba-2 (Dao and Gu, 2024) run a recurrent scan in O(K) time, FLOPs, and activation memory.
However, a naive adaptation of these models compresses the context into a single hidden state, a
bottleneck that we show degrades accuracy on synthetic and NOAA tasks (§6.4).
MambaFlowNP (MFNP) avoids this compression by maintaining a hidden state at every token
position throughout a multi-directional state-space scan (Figure 1). Context and query tokens share
a single sequence, and the model predicts a flow-matching (Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023)
velocity at each query location. A single joint-predictive draw for all the query locations requires
batched ODE integration of the velocity, which typically entails tens of network function evaluations
(NFE) (Table 13). MFNP mitigates this cost via a single round of reflow distillation (Liu et al., 2023)
to enable inference with only one NFE. As in latent-variable NPs, dependence between queries is
carried by a shared latent, here a random-function initial condition transported by the learned flow
(§4.3).

Contributions.
1. We introduce MambaFlowNP (MFNP), a joint-predictive NP that processes observations and pre-
diction locations together in a shared sequence, scanned in multiple directions. Its computational
cost grows linearly with the total number of points.
2. Through controlled ablations, we identify and quantify a single-state compression bottleneck
in state-space NPs. A variant that compresses the context into one terminal hidden state has
10–17% higher MSE than the full model on synthetic tasks and 58–65% higher MSE on NOAA.
This finding motivates MFNP’s use of hidden states at individual query positions.
2
3. Across three NOAA temperature interpolation tiers, MFNP achieves lower RMSE and CRPS than
the strongest joint-predictive baselines, with sampling speedups of 114–784×. We separately
assess the contributions of reflow distillation and the linear-time scan to these speedups.
4. We demonstrate computational scalability to 106 points, with a single forward pass completing
in under a second on one NVIDIA L40S GPU. Each forward pass requires O(K) compute,
where K is the total number of context and query points. All tested quadratic-time baselines
exceed GPU memory at this scale.

2
Background
2.1
Neural processes
A neural process defines a conditional distribution p(YQ | XC, YC, XQ) over target values YQ ∈
RM at query locations XQ ∈RM×D, given a context of N input–output pairs XC ∈RN×D,
YC ∈RN. Let K = N + M denote the total number of points. We tokenise each point separately,
so K is also the sequence length. Training is episodic. Each iteration samples a dataset from a
stochastic process, partitions points into context and query, and fits the predictive distribution against
the ground-truth query values. At test time, the context and query locations of a new dataset are
passed through the trained model in a single forward pass. NPs do not specify an explicit prior and
then apply Bayes’ rule; instead, they learn an implicit prior over functions from the data-generating
stochastic process during episodic training, and the forward pass through (XC, YC) acts as an
amortised update producing an approximation to the posterior predictive p(YQ | XC, YC, XQ) over
the query locations. We use predictive and posterior predictive interchangeably for this distribution.
2.2
Conditional flow matching and reflow distillation
Flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023; Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2023; Liu et al., 2023) models
approximate a velocity field ut that transports samples from a source distribution p0 to the conditional
data distribution p1(Y1 | c) ≡pdata(Y1 | c), where c = {XC, YC, XQ} denotes the neural process
conditioning. Here Y1 equals the query values YQ ∈RM targeted by the predictive, so Yt ∈RM is
indexed by the query locations. The velocity field is determined by a choice of conditional flow path
or interpolant Yt = atY1 + btY0,

(e.g. Euler). Drawing inspiration from work on data-dependent source distributions (Tong et al.,
2024; Kollovieh et al., 2025), we use a query-geometry-dependent Gaussian source distribution
p0(Y0 | XQ) = N(0, Σ(XQ)), obtained by evaluating a random-feature Gaussian-process draw
at the query locations. This gives a spatially correlated source, of rank at most F, that shortens
the transformation from source samples to smooth spatial fields (§4.2). The network also receives
a per-draw latent z and routing offset o (§4), which we omit from the notation vθ(Yt, t, c). The
gradient equivalence above assumes a network without these inputs. With them, the minimiser of
LCFM is E[Y1 −Y0 | Yt, t, c, z, o] rather than ut; reflow and CRPS fine-tuning (§4.2) then fit the
one-step map directly. We use the linear interpolant at = t, bt = (1 −t), with conditional velocity
dYt
dt = Y1 −Y0. Although this conditional flow has straight trajectories, the underlying velocity
field typically induces curved trajectories, leading to inaccurate results with few solver steps (Liu
et al., 2023; Geng et al., 2025). To obtain high-quality samples with fewer steps, we use reflow
distillation (Liu et al., 2023). A pre-trained teacher model generates coupled (Y0, ˆY1) pairs, and the
student model is optimised on LCFM against these couplings rather than independently drawn source
and target samples. The full training pipeline is described in §5.2 and Appendix H.
3
Related work
Factorised and latent-variable NPs.
Conditional Neural Processes (Garnelo et al., 2018a) encode
the context with a permutation-invariant set encoder and predict independent Gaussian distributions
at query locations. Latent-variable NPs (Garnelo et al., 2018b) introduce dependence across queries
through a shared Gaussian latent, trained under a variational ELBO. Attentive NP (Kim et al.,
2019) replaces mean-pooling with cross-attention from each query to the context. Convolutional
Conditional NPs (Gordon et al., 2020) use grid-based convolutions to encode translation equivariance,
an inductive bias suited to stationary spatial fields. AR-CNP (Bruinsma et al., 2023) introduces
cross-query dependence by sampling from a CNP autoregressively, requiring M sequential forward
passes for M queries.
Joint-predictive NPs.
Gaussian NPs (Bruinsma et al., 2021) explicitly model cross-query cor-
relations through a joint Gaussian predictive. TNPA (Nguyen and Grover, 2022) decodes queries
autoregressively under causal self-attention. NDP (Dutordoir et al., 2023) and FNP (Abu Hamad
and Rosenbaum, 2025) use transformer backbones trained with score-based diffusion (Song et al.,
2021) and flow-matching (Lipman et al., 2023) objectives, respectively. In these transformer models,
self-attention incurs O(K2) compute per network evaluation. Spatial coordinates enter through token
embeddings, whereas MFNP also uses them to determine the scan order.
Mamba on point sets.
Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2023) and Mamba-2 (Dao and Gu, 2024) introduced
selective state-space models with input-dependent gating and computational cost linear in sequence
length. VMamba (Liu et al., 2024) scans regular image grids in four directions. MFNP adapts
this four-direction scheme to irregular point sets through two Hilbert orderings and their reversals.
PointMamba (Liang et al., 2024) serialises 3D point clouds along Hilbert curves for supervised
shape analysis, while Voxel Mamba (Zhang et al., 2024) applies Hilbert serialisation to sparse voxels
for 3D detection. These methods use spatial scans for visual recognition tasks. MFNP applies
multi-directional scans to amortised joint-predictive inference for continuous 2D fields, with episodic
training over varying numbers of context and query points (N, M).
Scalable GPs and spatial statistics.
Exact GP inference for kriging requires an O(N 3) covariance
factorisation for N observed locations. Sparse variational GPs (Titsias, 2009), Vecchia approx-
imations and nearest-neighbour GPs (Vecchia, 1988; Datta et al., 2016), and structured kernel
interpolation (Wilson and Nickisch, 2015) reduce this computational burden, and the SPDE approach
4
represents Matérn fields as sparse Gaussian Markov random fields (Lindgren et al., 2011). These
approaches make inference within an individual field more tractable, but each still fits hyperparam-
eters per field. NPs amortise inference across fields. Episodic training learns a map from context
observations to a predictive distribution, which can then be applied to a new field without further
optimisation.
In-context learning and prior-fitted networks.
NPs learn to infer from context observations
without updating their parameters at test time. Prior-fitted networks (Müller et al., 2022) similarly
train transformers on datasets sampled from a prior to approximate the posterior predictive. Mamba
has also been shown to learn regression tasks in context (Grazzi et al., 2024).
MFNP builds on established components, namely Mamba-2 scans (Dao and Gu, 2024), Hilbert
serialisation (Liang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024), conditional flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023),
GP-based source distributions (Kollovieh et al., 2025), and reflow distillation (Liu et al., 2023). Our
contributions are the shared context–query scan for joint-predictive neural processes and the analysis
of how scan routing affects predictive performance.
4
MambaFlowNP
MFNP processes irregularly placed observations in one or two dimensions with an O(K) neural
recurrence. A direct SSM-based NP adaptation compresses the context into a single fixed-dimensional
hidden state and conditions a query decoder on that state. MFNP avoids the compression by
maintaining a hidden state at every token position throughout the scan. Context and query tokens
share the sequence, so each query is decoded from its own position. The single-state ablation forces
the context through one hidden vector before reading queries (§6.4).
4.1
Architecture
For each joint draw, a shared latent z determines the random initial values at the query locations and
conditions the network. Given the current query values Yt, flow time t and context c, the network
computes the velocity vθ(Yt, t, c) in the four stages shown in Figure 1.
(1) Tokenise. For each point, we concatenate a coordinate embedding computed using frozen Random
Fourier Features (Rahimi and Recht, 2007) with its scalar value, which is the observed value at a
context point or Yt,i at a query. Context and query tokens use separate linear projections.
(2) Route. We use Hilbert curves (Sagan, 1994; Butz, 1971) to order the combined context and query
points so that nearby locations tend to remain close in the sequence. Two orderings, π1 and π2, use
the original and swapped coordinate axes. Together with their reversals, they form
Π = {π1, πrev
1 , π2, πrev
2 }.
A shared random offset o shifts the routing grid to reduce artefacts at fixed curve boundaries. In
one dimension, we scan points in ascending and descending coordinate order, repeating these two
orderings to fill the four direction slots (Appendix B).
(3) Scan. A Mamba-2 block propagates information through a recurrent hidden state. Context tokens
write to the recurrent state. Query tokens read the state at their own positions but do not write to it,
since they enter the scan with zero input and zero step size; the block has no short convolution. A
single L-layer stack of Mamba-2 blocks, with parameters shared across directions, processes each

TRCF: Temporal-Reference Complementary
Forecasting for Irregular Multivariate Time Series
Xudong Zuo1,*, Shusen Ma1,*, Qirui Chen1, Bing Fan2, Yun-Bo Zhao3,†
1Institute of Advanced Technology
2School of Computer Science and Technology
3Department of Automation
University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, China
chenqirui@mail.ustc.edu.cn
bingfan@mail.ustc.edu.cn
ybzhao@ustc.edu.cn
Abstract—Irregular multivariate time series forecasting sup-
ports healthcare monitoring, environmental analysis, and activity
recognition. Channel-independent (CI) approaches capture each
variable’s temporal patterns but do not explicitly use observations
from other variables. Channel-dependent (CD) modeling exploits
relationships among variables, yet asynchronous measurements
make these relationships difficult to learn. Incorporating cross-
variable information while preserving each variable’s irregular
history therefore remains a key challenge. We propose Temporal-
Reference Complementary Forecasting (TRCF), a framework that
augments a compact CI forecaster with a complementary CD
branch. ANCHOR aggregates observed values and timestamps at
shared temporal locations, retaining observation support to form
compact CI features. BRIDGE constructs complementary features
through history completion. It first estimates each variable’s
historical values from its own observations, then uses differences
between other variables’ observed and estimated values at nearby
times to correct missing entries. The completed history preserves
observed values and is encoded to supply context alongside the
direct CI representation. Finally, the two representations are
fused, combined with the query-time embedding, and passed to
a shallow multilayer perceptron for forecasting. Experiments on
four real-world datasets show that TRCF achieves the lowest mean
squared error and mean absolute error in the main benchmark
comparison, while reducing measured peak inference memory by
17.28%–87.98% relative to APN.
Index Terms—Irregular time series, forecasting, temporal
aggregation, incomplete data.
I. INTRODUCTION
Irregular multivariate time series (IMTS) forecasting supports
healthcare monitoring, environmental analysis, and human
activity modeling [1], [2]. In these applications, measurements
are collected at unequal intervals, and different variables may be
recorded at different times. A clinical record, for example, may
contain frequent heart-rate measurements alongside occasional
laboratory tests. The resulting histories contain both the
evolution of individual variables and relationships among
variables, but these sources of information are only partially
observed. Effective forecasting therefore requires learning
temporal patterns from the available measurements and using
relevant information across variables despite irregular sampling.
Temporal aggregation offers an effective way to represent
such histories. APN uses time-aware patch aggregation to
*Equal contribution.
†Corresponding author.
(a) Uneven observation support
Weights

(b) Asynchronous cross-variable context
