Fig. 1.
Two core challenges in IMTS forecasting: (a) uneven
observation support and (b) asynchronous cross-variable context.
encode observed values and timestamps, followed by a shallow
prediction network [3]. It follows a channel-independent (CI)
strategy: each variable is represented using its own observations.
This provides a direct path from irregular measurements to
forecasts without first completing the history. However, a
strictly CI predictor cannot directly use another variable’s
observations to supplement an incomplete target history. When
observations of the target are sparse, related variables may
provide useful additional context.
Channel-dependent (CD) modeling makes this information
available by explicitly connecting variables. GraFITi represents
irregular observations through a graph, while t-PatchGNN
combines temporal patching with cross-variable graph mod-
eling [2], [4]. For irregular histories, however, the available
relationships depend on when each variable was measured. A
related variable may have no observation at the time when
the target needs additional context, even though a nearby
arXiv:2611.26351v1  [cs.LG]  19 Nov 2026
measurement could still be informative. Figure 1(b) illustrates
this difficulty. Incorporating cross-variable information into
a direct predictor therefore requires a way to obtain useful
context from observations recorded at different times.
History completion provides one way to construct aligned
representations. Interpolation-Prediction Networks map irregu-
lar observations to reference times [5], while BRITS and SAITS
estimate missing values through recurrent and attention-based
models [6], [7]. A completed history contains both recorded
values and model estimates. We use this history to supply
auxiliary features alongside a separate representation of the
original observations. This raises two questions: what should
other variables contribute beyond the target’s own temporal
pattern, and how can that information be obtained when their
measurements occur at different times?
We address these questions by using each variable’s own
temporal estimate as a reference for constructing cross-variable
context. An observed residual measures the difference between
a historical measurement and this estimate. Residuals from
other variables then provide correction signals relative to their
respective temporal patterns. To make these signals available
at missing positions, we relay the nearest observed residual
along each variable’s time axis. This construction assumes that
a nearby historical deviation may remain informative, with its
influence reduced as temporal distance increases. The resulting
cross-variable corrections refine the historical estimates and
provide a completed history for auxiliary encoding.
Based on this idea, we propose Temporal-Reference Com-
plementary Forecasting (TRCF), which augments a compact
CI forecaster with a complementary CD branch. TRCF uses
APN’s lightweight prediction architecture [3], replacing its
aggregation with ANCHOR and adding the context branch
BRIDGE. ANCHOR summarizes each variable’s measured
values and time features at a small set of shared temporal
locations. It also retains normalized observation support to dis-
tinguish summaries formed from different sampling patterns, as
illustrated in Figure 1(a). BRIDGE constructs a shared historical
grid, forms temporal estimates from each variable’s own history,
and corrects missing entries using distance-weighted residuals
from other variables. The correction excludes the target’s
own residual, and observed grid entries remain unchanged. A
variable encoder converts the completed history into auxiliary
features, which are fused with the direct representation for
forecasting. The model is trained jointly with forecasting and
historical reconstruction objectives.
Experiments on HumanActivity, USHCN, PhysioNet P12,
and MIMIC-III show that TRCF achieves the lowest mean
squared error (MSE) and mean absolute error (MAE) in the
main benchmark comparison. Relative to APN, it reduces
MSE by 2.54%–10.06% and measured peak inference memory
by 17.28%–87.98%. Controlled comparisons distinguish the
contribution of compact direct encoding from that of con-
structed context and examine whether additional model capacity
explains the gains.
Our contributions are as follows.
• We develop ANCHOR, a compact CI encoder that aggre-
gates measured values, timing, and normalized observation
support at shared temporal locations. With matched slot
counts, it achieves lower mean forecasting errors with
fewer parameters than the adaptive-patch encoder on all
four datasets.
• We develop BRIDGE to construct complementary histori-
cal context through temporal estimation, distance-weighted
residual relay, and target-excluded cross-variable correc-
tion. The completed history supplies auxiliary features
while the direct path continues to encode the original
irregular observations.
• We evaluate forecasting accuracy and inference resources
across four datasets, with component, capacity, and super-
vision controls. The results identify gains from compact
direct encoding on USHCN and additional benefits from
constructed context on the clinical datasets, including
under matched parameter budgets.
II. RELATED WORK
a) Representing irregular histories: Irregular forecasting
methods differ in how they turn observations into inputs
for prediction. Continuous-time models such as GRU-ODE-
Bayes evolve hidden states between observed events [1].
GraFITi represents sparse observations as a graph, t-PatchGNN
combines temporal patching with adaptive graphs, and Hi-Patch
uses hierarchical patches [2], [4], [8]. These representations
retain temporal or relational detail at different granularities.
APN uses direct time-aware aggregation followed by a compact
channel-independent predictor [3].
b) Observation support:
Reference times and sam-
pling intensity have a long role in irregular representations.
Interpolation-Prediction Networks use multiple Gaussian band-
widths at evenly spaced reference times to encode smooth
signals, transients, and observation intensity [5]. Warpformer
learns multiscale alignment for clinical histories [9]. KAFNet
aggregates pre-aligned features with Gaussian kernels; its
released implementation learns widths and centers initialized
on a uniform grid [10]. DNBNet corrects basis responses
for sampling density and fuses temporal resolutions [11].
CTLite computes continuous-time moments at fixed decay
scales and suppresses poorly supported slope estimates [12].
ANCHOR combines Gaussian pooling at fixed reference times
with explicit observation support in a compact direct encoder.
Shared widths keep its temporal parameters independent of the
number of variables, while each slot retains pooled value–time
features and normalized support.
c) Cross-variable modeling: PatchTST shares parameters
across independently processed channels [13], whereas Cross-
former and iTransformer explicitly model relationships between
variables [14], [15]. DUET uses separate clustering mechanisms
for temporal heterogeneity and channel relationships [16].
CTLite applies a low-rank correction that discounts stale
sources and depends on the target’s observation state and
forecast distance [12]. In irregular histories, the available
cross-variable information also depends on when each source
was measured. BRIDGE addresses source availability before
variable encoding. It relays nearby historical residuals along
each variable’s time axis and uses other variables’ residuals to
correct missing entries. The resulting history supplies context
alongside the direct observation features.
d) Historical completion and forecasting: BRITS and
SAITS reconstruct incomplete histories through bidirectional
recurrence and attention [6], [7]. Interpolation-Prediction Net-
works learn cross-variable interpolation jointly with supervised
prediction and reconstruction [5]. Completion and downstream
learning are therefore established approaches. ImputeBench’s
finding that no recovery method is uniformly best also motivates
testing completion by its forecasting contribution and resource
cost [17].
TRCF keeps completed history alongside a separate direct
representation. In BRIDGE, shared temporal convolutions
estimate a reference for each variable [18]; a target-excluded
ridge operator then corrects missing entries from residual
sources. The exclusion follows the leave-one-out identity [19,
Sec. 5.4.2]. Capacity-matched interpolation and temporal-
context controls test whether the full construction adds value
beyond simpler completion. The context-only comparison
separately tests the value of retaining the direct path.
III. PROBLEM FORMULATION AND DESIGN PRINCIPLE
A. Forecasting task
Variable n has Ln observed time–value pairs (ti,n, xi,n).
Together these form the history O for the N variables.
Observation counts can differ by variable, and all historical
timestamps precede the forecasting window. Given future query
times Q, the model returns byk,n for variable n at query qk.
Predictions are evaluated only where a future measurement is
available. We use the dataset’s prepared values and normalized
timestamps, with the same preprocessing and splits for the
APN and TRCF comparisons.
B. Direct evidence and constructed context
TRCF assigns two representation roles to O. In ANCHOR,
the direct summary consists of K feature slots, which aggregate
observed value–time features. In BRIDGE, the auxiliary
summary starts from G value-grid cells, containing within-cell
means X ∈RG×N and observation mask M ∈{0, 1}G×N.
Soft slots do not fill missing values; the grid supports historical
completion and variable encoding. The direct summary there-
fore retains features derived only from recorded observations,
whereas the completed grid supplies aligned context that
includes model estimates. Keeping both representations lets the
predictor use constructed context without replacing its direct
evidence.
IV. METHOD
A. Direct representation and constructed context
Figure 2 shows how TRCF combines direct observation
features with context from a completed history.
ANCHOR maps each variable’s recorded values and times-
tamps to K feature slots and a direct representation hCI

BRIDGE constructs a separate G-cell value grid, completes

encodes the result as zn. The forecast head combines the
direct evidence and constructed context with the query-time
embedding.
B. ANCHOR: temporal aggregation under uneven support
ANCHOR uses actual timestamps to summarize observations
around K shared temporal locations. Each summary contains
values, time features, and the amount of observed support.
The slot centers are fixed, and their widths are learned from

1 
Perfumer: A Large Language Model-based Agentic Framework 
Accelerating Structural Relaxation and Electronic Band Prediction for 
First-Principle Calculation 
Zhiwei Li1,†, Yuhao Zhou2,†, Yikai Yang1, Haonan Wang1, Qing Ye2,  
Jiancheng Lv2,∗ and Kazunari Matsuda1,∗ 
 
1Institute of Advanced Energy, Kyoto University, Uji, Kyoto 611-0011, Japan 
2DICALab, School of Computing, Sichuan University, China 
 
†These authors contributed equally to this work. 
∗Corresponding authors: Jiancheng Lv, and Kazunari Matsuda  
E-mail: lvjiancheng@scu.edu.cn; matsuda@iae.kyoto-u.ac.jp  
 
2 
Abstract 
First-principles structural relaxation and band calculations require substantial 
computation and expertise. Here we present Perfumer, a large language model-based 
agentic framework that couples Quantum ESPRESSO with two predictive models. Across 
tested structures, pre-relaxation with Perfumer-relax model followed by QE refinement 
yielded a 2.75-fold overall speedup over QE alone. Perfumer-band model combines a 
periodic graph neural network with a latent Hermitian spectral head returns 12 band 
energies at any requested wavevector, preserving reciprocal lattice periodicity and time-
reversal symmetry without constructing Hamiltonian. Trained on 125,153 self-curated 
band structures, Perfumer-band model reaches a median per-material mean absolute error 
of 0.157 eV on 2,607 test materials, including lanthanide, actinide and magnetic 
compounds, from held-out composition families spanning 85 elements, taking about 97 ms 
per material on two consumer CPU cores. The agent turns natural-language requests into 
relaxation-to-band workflows, from a single uploaded structure to automatically 
constructed new candidates and returns predicted properties. 
 
3 
Introduction 
Advances in computational methods have made first-principles calculations an 
important tool in modern research, enabling the prediction of physical and chemical 
properties across a wide range of materials, including insulators, semiconductors and 
metals. Within all the methods, Density functional theory (DFT) provides a practical 
framework for first-principles predictions of structural energetics and electronic 
properties1,2. Widely used implementations include Quantum ESPRESSO (QE)3–5 and the 
Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP)6. In a typical workflow connecting crystal 
structures to electronic bands, structural relaxation requires repeated self-consistent 
evaluations of energies and atomic forces. Band structure calculations then evaluate 
electronic eigenvalues for the relaxed geometry along selected paths in reciprocal space. 
These calculations can become costly when screening many candidate materials or 
modelling large supercells, including moiré structures. 
 
Machine learning (ML) offers routes to accelerating individual stages of these 
workflows. Neural networks, including graph neural networks (GNNs), predict materials 
properties and interatomic interactions from atomic structures and local environments7–10, 
supported by publicly available datasets such as the Materials Project11. For structural 
relaxation, learned interatomic potentials supply energies and forces for iterative 
optimization12–14, whereas DeepRelax predicts relaxed structures from initial 
configurations15. Equivariant architectures such as NequIP and MACE, together with 
broadly pretrained MACE models, extend these approaches to diverse atomic 
environments16–18. For electronic-structure prediction, DeepH learns DFT Hamiltonian 
matrix elements in a localized atomic-orbital basis19, an approach further developed 
through equivariant networks20–22. Other methods, including graph Transformer models, 
predict band structures directly from crystal structures23. These approaches establish 
complementary ways to reduce the numerical effort required for structural and electronic 
calculations. 
 
4 
Large language models (LLMs) offer a complementary means of coordinating scientific 
workflows through agents equipped with computational tools24–27. In materials research, 
multiagent systems have combined atomistic simulations and GNN surrogates for alloy 
design28,29. GENIUS integrates LLMs with domain knowledge to generate QE inputs and 
uses early execution feedback to validate and repair simulation protocols30. MatSciAgent 
coordinates specialized tools for materials data retrieval, crystal structure generation and 
molecular dynamics simulations31. Such systems translate natural-language requests into 
computational operations and can reduce the manual effort required to configure and 
connect scientific tools32. Automating calculation setup and execution33,34 does not, by 
itself, reduce the cost of the underlying numerical calculations. An integrated relaxation-
to-band workflow must therefore address numerical efficiency and task coordination 
together. It must also transfer structures and calculation settings consistently between 
stages and distinguish model predictions from quantities refined through first-principles 
calculations. These requirements motivate combining specialized numerical models with 
an agent that coordinates their use within a common workflow. 
 
Here we present Perfumer, an LLM-based agentic framework that integrates model-
assisted structural relaxation and electronic band prediction with QE. The agent interprets 
natural-language requests, prepares computational inputs, coordinates tool execution and 
summarizes numerical outputs. Perfumer-relax model uses a learned interatomic potential 
to pre-relax atomic structures before QE refinement under specified convergence criteria. 
Perfumer-band model combines a periodic GNN with a latent Hermitian spectral head that 
yields selected band energies as eigenvalues at specified reciprocal space points. This 
representation is trained against reference band energies without reconstructing an orbital-
resolved Kohn–Sham Hamiltonian. Its training data cover 91 elements, including all 15 
lanthanides and six actinides, as well as magnetic compounds described by spin-polarized 
bands. The modules can operate independently or sequentially, with the QE-refined 
geometry passed to Perfumer-band model for electronic band prediction. We assess 
relaxation efficiency against unassisted QE, evaluate band prediction on held out 
composition families and illustrate task coordination through natural-language workflow 
examples. 
5 
Results 
Perfumer framework and training data 
Perfumer connects natural-language requests to structural relaxation and electronic band 
prediction through an LLM coupled to the Perfumer Harness (Fig. 1). The LLM interprets 
tasks and coordinates tool calls, while the numerical calculations are performed by 
Perfumer-relax model, QE and Perfumer-band model. The harness integrates these 
specialized tools with general purpose utilities for WebSearch, WebFetch and file access, 
alongside a scientific database component including prediction setup for commonly used 
materials. Tool outputs are returned to the LLM to guide subsequent operations and 
generate the response. 
 
For a combined relaxation-to-band task, Perfumer-relax model first performs model-
assisted pre-relaxation. QE then refines the atomic geometry under user defined 
convergence criteria, and Perfumer-band model predicts selected band energies from the 
refined structure along the requested reciprocal-space path. The Perfumer-band model 
predicts 12 electronic bands per spin channel. For nonmetals, these comprise the six highest 
valence bands and the six lowest conduction bands; for metals, they comprise 12 bands 
near the Fermi level. The two predictive modules can also operate independently. Users 
can submit follow-up requests through the same interface to extend or revise the task. The 
Perfumer agent connects task coordination, first-principles structural refinement and 
model-based band prediction within a modular workflow. 
 
We also constructed separate training datasets for the two models (Fig. S1). For the 
Perfumer-relax model, we generated a dataset from QE structural relaxation calculations 
performed on the supercomputer system. Each validated ionic step was stored as a separate 
record pairing the atomic configuration with the corresponding Cartesian force labels. For 
the Perfumer-band model, each record associates a crystal structure and a reciprocal space 
path with 12 selected band energies per spin channel. The curated band dataset contained 
130,367 material records and collected data from the Materials Project, JARVIS-DFT, 
AFLOW and NOMAD11,35–37. We grouped band structure records by reduced chemical 
6 
formula and assigned each group to the training, validation or test set. This allowed us to 
assess how well Perfumer-band model predicts band energies for compositions unseen 
during training38,39. Dataset construction, target definitions and training procedures are 
described in Methods. 
 
Architecture and evaluation of Perfumer-relax model 
The Perfumer-relax model is based on a MACE interatomic potential fine-tuned on a 
curated dataset of QE structural relaxation trajectories. The fine-tuned model performs 
structural pre-relaxation of perturbed or unrelaxed structures, after which QE refines the 
resulting geometry under the prescribed convergence criteria (Fig. 2a). To quantify the 
benefit, we relaxed each test structure twice on the same compute allocation, with QE alone 
and with 100 Perfumer-relax steps followed by QE refinement (Fig. 2b). For the 553 tested 
structures, comprising 241 metallic and 207 non-metallic bulk crystals and 92 two-
dimensional materials with randomly displaced atoms and 13 displaced 3 × 3 two-
dimensional supercells, the total wall time fell from 277.8 h to 101.1 h, a 2.75-fold 
reduction. The reduction was 3.05-fold for metals, 2.44-fold for non-metals, 2.66-fold for 
two-dimensional materials and 8.24-fold for two-dimensional supercells.  
 
Al6Ir2, an eight-atom intermetallic among the metals in Fig. 2b, illustrates how pre-
relaxation reduces the QE simulation time (Fig. 2c,d). QE alone required 419.1 s and 22 
force evaluations. With 40, 100 and 200 model steps, the combined pre-relaxation and QE 
refinement times were 257.7, 54.1 and 53.5 s and the QE force evaluation counts fell to 14, 
4 and 4, corresponding to speedups of 1.63, 7.75 and 7.84 (Fig. 2c). The final structures 
agreed with the QE only result to within 4.5 × 10−4 Å, with a largest single atom deviation 
of 6.0 × 10−4 Å (Fig. 2d). 
 
Architecture and evaluation of Perfumer-band model 
The Perfumer-band model predicts selected electronic band energies from crystal 
structures, known physical conditions and reciprocal space queries through a periodic 
7 
latent Hermitian representation (Fig. 3). A periodic crystal encoder comprising eight 
message-passing layers of hidden width 640 and global atom attention produces a crystal 
representation 𝑔 and atom representations {ℎ!} . These representations support two 
complementary branches that construct the latent spectral matrix. 
 
The periodic matrix branch decodes structure-dependent coefficients for an expansion 
in integer Fourier modes. In parallel, an independent query branch combines Fourier 
features of the reciprocal space coordinate with query-to-atom attention to generate a 
Hermitian residual. For each requested spin channel, the model constructs: 
𝐻"(𝒞, 𝐪) = 𝐻#,"(𝒞) + 𝛿"(𝒞)𝐼+ / 0𝑇𝐦,"(𝒞)𝑒!&'𝐦⋅𝐪+ 𝑇𝐦,"
* (𝒞)𝑒+!&'𝐦⋅𝐪3

+ 𝛾𝑅"(𝒞, 𝐪). 
Here, 𝒞 denotes the crystal structure and the declared calculation and band selection 
conditions, 𝐪 is the fractional reciprocal coordinate, and ℳ is a fixed set of integer 
frequency vectors. The trainable parameters are denoted by 𝜃, and † denotes the conjugate 
transpose. Both 𝐻#," and the query-dependent residual 𝑅" are Hermitian; δθ(C) is a scalar 
reference offset predicted by a separate head, which shifts all energies of a channel together, 
and the learnable scalar gate 𝛾 controls the residual contribution. The scaled residual 𝛾𝑅" 
corresponds to Δ𝐻(𝐪) in Fig. 3. The selected band energies are obtained from the ordered 
eigenvalues of the resulting 16 × 16 matrix, which carries two buffer bands below and two 
above the 12 requested bands: 
𝐸?.(𝒞, 𝐪) = 𝑠/𝜆.0&[𝐻"(𝒞, 𝐪)],  𝑛= 1, … ,12, 
where 𝑠/ is the energy scale determined from the training data, and λk denotes the kth 
smallest of the 16 eigenvalues; the two lowest and two highest act as buffer bands that are 
never compared with reference energies. Hermiticity ensures real eigenvalues, and the 
integer Fourier representations enforce reciprocal lattice periodicity. Because the 
coefficient matrices are real and the query residual is symmetrized between q and −q, the 
predicted energies at q and −q are identical by construction, as required by time-reversal 
symmetry. Each reciprocal space query is evaluated independently at fixed input conditions. 
The model is trained end to end against reference band energies using an objective that also 
penalizes errors in dispersion shape, amplitude and adjacent point energy differences. The 
8 
latent matrix is learned through its eigenvalues. Details of the training objective and output 
conventions are provided in Methods. 
 
On the test set of 2,607 material records spanning 85 elements, the Perfumer-band model 
achieved a median per-material mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.157 eV. Among the 80 
element groups represented by at least ten test records, 77 had median MAEs below 0.30 
eV. The median MAEs were 0.127 eV for the 394 records containing lanthanides, 0.223 eV 
for the 71 records containing actinides and 0.200 eV for the 1,025 spin-polarized records. 
Fig. 4a summarizes the element-resolved results: each cell reports the median MAE for 
test records containing that element, with 𝑛 indicating the corresponding number of records. 
Prediction and export for the full test set took 327.5 s in a single run on two cores of an 
Intel Core i9-13900H CPU. The median prediction time was 96.9 ms per material. Fig. S2 
presents the corresponding median prediction time for records grouped by element, 
illustrating variation in processing time across these groups.  
 
We also compared electronic band structures obtained using QE, the Perfumer-band 
model and Fable 5.2 (max, conversation in Claude Science) for WSe2 by using the same 
JSON input file. The QE calculation and model prediction are conducted on two cores of 
the same CPU. The result of band structures and corresponding computation times are 
compared in Fig. S3a and b, respectively. Perfumer-band model achieved a band energy 
MAE of 0.086 eV relative to the QE reference, compared with 0.306 eV for Fable 5.2, 
corresponding to a 72.0% reduction in MAE. The prediction time was 0.043 s for the 
Perfumer-band model, compared with 91.3 s for QE and 319 s for Fable 5.2 (whole 
conversation time). These timings correspond to speedups of approximately 2,100-fold 
relative to QE and 7,400-fold relative to Fable 5.2. These results demonstrate moderate 
band structure accuracy combined with rapid prediction and modest computer resource 
requirements. Moreover, we compared the predicted and DFT reference band structures for 
selected materials from the test set (Fig. 4b-c, Fig. S4a-d). For the metal DyIn3 and the 
non-metal Ba2HoO6Ta in Fig. 4b-c, Perfumer-band model achieved mean absolute errors 
of 0.038 and 0.035 eV, respectively. In both cases, the predicted bands closely follow the 
9 
reference dispersions along the sampled reciprocal space paths. These examples illustrate 
the model’s ability to predict band energies and dispersion features for held-out 
compositions, complementing the aggregate assessment of generalization across the test 
set. 
 
Integrated relaxation-to-band workflow 
The Perfumer agent translated a natural-language request into a coordinated workflow 
for structural relaxation and electronic band prediction (Fig. 5). To facilitate practical use, 
we also developed a software package that enables users to access and run the integrated 
workflow (Fig. S5). For the WSe2 monolayer example included with the software, the 
request was “Please relax the atomic positions of the included WSe2 example structure, 
calculate its band structure and provide me with a standard QE input.” The LLM 
(DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017) planned the task as structure inspection, pre-relaxation with 
the Perfumer-relax model followed by QE refinement, band prediction with the Perfumer-
band model and export of a QE input file. QE converged in two ionic steps to a maximum 
force of 0.015 eV Å−1, and Perfumer-band model predicted 12 bands along Γ–M–K–Γ for 
the QE-relaxed geometry, with a band gap of 1.48 eV (QE PBE reference: 1.54 eV). The 
LLM integrated the relaxation log and the predicted bands into a response to the original 
request within about 5 min, illustrating the connection between task planning, numerical 
evaluation and result reporting. 
 
The second example extended this workflow to the search for new materials (Fig. 6). 
The request was “Please identify new materials for chip applications from wurtzite GaN 
(mp-804) and perform the relax–band workflow for the selected candidates. Relax the 
candidates one at a time, and predict each candidate’s bands right after its own relaxation.” 
The LLM imported the wurtzite GaN structure from the Materials Project, generated 12 
candidate structures by Ga → Al, Ga → In, Ga → Sc and N → P substitutions and screened 
them by their predicted bands. It then relaxed five selected structures (AlN, two symmetry-
equivalent AlGaN2 structures, ScGaN2 and Ga2PN) one at a time, with Perfumer-relax 
model pre-relaxation followed by QE refinement, and predicted the band structures of each 
10 
relaxed geometry with the Perfumer-band model. All five relaxed structures reached 
maximum forces no more than 0.0091 eV Å−1, with predicted band gaps of 1.554 to 3.234 
eV; while the ScGaN2 and Ga2PN compositions do not occur in the band-model dataset. 
The final output combined summaries with structure files and QE input/output logs, and 
the whole run took 15 min. This example demonstrated the extension from processing a 
supplied structure to constructing and evaluating a candidate set within the goal of finding 
new materials. 
Discussion 
We have developed Perfumer, an LLM-based agentic framework that integrates model-
assisted structural relaxation, QE refinement and electronic band prediction within a 
modular computational workflow. The Perfumer-relax and Perfumer-band models address 
distinct numerical tasks, while the LLM coordinates input preparation, tool execution and 
result reporting. This organization connects natural language interaction with specialized 
predictive modules and established first-principles software. 
 
Across 553 structures with randomly displaced atoms, model-assisted pre-relaxation 
followed by QE refinement reduced the total relaxation time by a factor of 2.75 relative to 
unassisted QE, counting structures on which both routes reached the same final geometry. 
On 2,607 test materials from held-out composition families, Perfumer-band model 
achieved a median per-material mean absolute error of 0.157 eV and took a median of 96.9 
ms per material on two CPU cores. These materials span 85 elements, including all 15 
lanthanides and six actinides, and 1,025 of them are spin-polarized, most of which are 
magnetic; the median errors were 0.127 eV for records containing lanthanides, 0.223 eV 
for those containing actinides and 0.200 eV for the spin-polarized records. These 
evaluations quantify the relaxation efficiency and band prediction accuracy of the two 
numerical predictive models. 
 
The integrated workflow passes refined structures between modules and consolidates 
numerical results and calculation files into a response to the user’s request. By coupling

OceanCoder: A Verification-Guided Large Language Model for
Automated Simulation Modelling in Ocean Engineering
Can Xuea,†, Changhong Hea,b,†, Ziyi Suna, Anliang Gea,∗, Shimin Yua,∗and Bingchen Lianga
aCollege of Engineering, Ocean University of China, Qingdao, 266100, China
bSchool of Mechanical Engineering and Automation, Beihang University, Beijing, 102206, China
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Ocean engineering
Automated simulation modelling
Large language models
Engineering verification
Reinforcement learning
A B S T R A C T
Numerical simulation is important in ocean engineering, but model construction requires expert
knowledge. Large language models support automated modelling, but code syntax and successful
execution alone do not establish whether generated models and results meet engineering requirements.
We present OceanCoder, a Qwen3-8B-based large language model for automated simulation modelling
in ocean engineering. To address specialised programming requirements and scarce training data, we
develop an extensible data construction pipeline producing 12,000 verified supervised fine-tuning
(SFT) examples across 12 engineering task categories. A three-layer verification framework checks
model inputs against engineering parameters and task constraints, verifies completion of required
simulation analyses, and assesses the engineering plausibility of computed outputs. Its outcomes
provide graded rewards for group relative policy optimisation (GRPO), guiding the model towards
engineering task completion. We also construct the first benchmark for automated modelling in ocean
engineering, covering out-of-distribution tasks and real-world engineering cases. Experiments and
ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the data pipeline, verification framework and reward
design. OceanCoder outperforms both base models and the closed-source comparison, with Pass@1
increasing from 0% for the base model to 46.77% after SFT and 51.43% after GRPO. These results
support engineering verification as a training signal for automated simulation modelling.
1. Introduction
Numerical simulation helps engineers assess loads and
motions in mooring systems, marine risers and subsea
installation operations (Hall and Goupee, 2015; Ja’e et al.,
2022; Kallinger et al., 2026). Building these models still
requires specialist knowledge. Users must define component
connections and physical properties, set environmental con-
ditions, and choose the analysis steps and results to extract.
A change in structural configuration or operating sequence
can require corresponding changes to the program, even
when an existing script is available. Generating simulation
programs from engineering task descriptions could reduce
this preparation effort and make specialised software easier
to use.
Large language models (LLMs) offer a way to translate
such descriptions into programs. Studies in ship design, finite-
element analysis and computational fluid dynamics (CFD)
show how natural-language requirements can be converted
into design parameters or simulation workflows (Choi et al.,
2026; Hou et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2026). However, an
executable program may still perform a different analysis
from the one requested. A solver can run successfully after a
program has changed a line property or extracted the wrong
response quantity. Assessing automated modelling therefore
requires checking whether the model and its results meet
the engineering requirements, in addition to checking code
syntax and execution.
Project leader: Changhong He.
∗Corresponding authors
geanliang@126.com (A. Ge); yushimin@ouc.edu.cn (S. Yu)
†These authors contributed equally to this work.
We present OceanCoder, a Qwen3-8B-based large lan-
guage model for automated simulation modelling in ocean
engineering. OceanCoder takes a natural-language descrip-
tion of engineering conditions and analysis requirements and
generates a complete OrcaFlex program to build the model,
run the analyses and extract the results. We develop this
capability by first training on verified examples and then using
engineering verification of generated programs to provide
further training feedback.
Training OceanCoder requires paired examples of an
engineering task and a program that correctly implements it.
Such public data for specialised ocean engineering simulation
software are scarce. Seed-based generation can expand
training examples (Wei et al., 2024b,a), but engineering
parameters must remain consistent. For example, water depth,
endpoint coordinates and line lengths in a catenary model
must describe a compatible geometry. We therefore build a
data construction pipeline that expands expert-designed seed
cases within engineering constraints and generates each task
description and reference program from the same physical
parameter record. Each pair is verified before entering
the training corpus. The resulting corpus contains 12,000
supervised fine-tuning (SFT) examples across 12 categories
of static analysis, dynamic response and offshore operations.
The corpus can be extended by adding seed cases with their
parameter constraints and verification rules.
Training on verified examples cannot prevent all mistakes
in new programs. In Figure 1, an SFT-generated lowering
program changes the prescribed line properties. It completes
the simulation, but its error in predicting the first seabed-
contact time exceeds the task tolerance. To identify errors of
this kind, we introduce a three-layer engineering verification
Page 1 of 22
arXiv:2611.26333v1  [cs.LG]  19 Nov 2026
OceanCoder: Verification-Guided Simulation Modelling
framework covering inputs, processes and outputs. It checks
the constructed model against the given parameters and task
constraints, confirms that the required analyses have been
completed, and checks the reported response quantities and
their numerical values against task-specific criteria. These
checks assess whether the computed results are consistent
with the specified engineering problem. A successful run
is accepted as a completed task only when it passes the
engineering checks.
The verification results also provide feedback for improv-
ing the model. Earlier code-generation studies have used
program outcomes and execution feedback as reinforcement-
learning signals (Le et al., 2022; Gehring et al., 2025).
After SFT, we use the engineering verification outcomes
as rewards for online group relative policy optimisation
(GRPO). Programs that fail to run, run but fail engineering
checks, or complete the task receive different rewards. This
graded feedback retains information about partial progress
while reserving full reward for complete task acceptance.
During training, generated programs run in OrcaFlex, and
their verification results supply the rewards used to update
the model.
We also construct the first benchmark for automated
modelling in ocean engineering, covering out-of-distribution
tasks and real-world engineering cases to assess generali-
sation and practical applicability. Its 665 tasks cover core
parameter variations, structural variations and engineering
cases adapted from public project descriptions and technical
materials. Each model generates one program per task
without using simulator feedback to repair it. All programs
are evaluated using the same engineering acceptance criteria.
This protocol assesses the modelling capability acquired
through training. The benchmark and its evaluation resources
will be released together.
The experiments compare OceanCoder with base and
leading closed-source models under this protocol. Indepen-
dent manual audits compare the verifier’s decisions with hu-
man inspection of generated programs and results. Controlled
reward ablations examine the contribution of intermediate
verification feedback to training. OceanCoder outperforms
the evaluated comparison models, with the proportion of
tasks completed on the first attempt (Pass@1) increasing
from 46.77% after SFT to 51.43% after GRPO.
The main contributions are as follows.
1. OceanCoder for automated simulation modelling.
A Qwen3-8B-based model translates natural-language
engineering requirements into complete OrcaFlex pro-
grams for model construction, analysis execution and
result extraction.
2. Verified and extensible training data. A seed-based
pipeline preserves engineering parameter relationships
and agreement between task descriptions and reference
programs, providing 12,000 verified examples across
12 task categories.
3. Engineering verification as training feedback. A
framework checks model inputs, analysis completion
and computed outputs, and turns the outcomes into
graded GRPO rewards that guide model training.
4. Benchmark and evaluation protocol. A 665-task
benchmark applies common engineering checks to all
evaluated models. Manual audits and controlled reward
ablations assess verifier reliability and the contribution
of training feedback.
2. Related work
2.1. Large language models for engineering
simulation
Automating engineering simulation involves translating
natural-language requirements into solver inputs and coordi-
nating numerical analyses. Language models support these
tasks through structured interfaces, retrieval and agent coordi-
nation. LLM-as-UI converts user requests into parameters for
modular ship design (Choi et al., 2026). AutoFEA combines
planning and example retrieval to generate finite element
solver inputs (Hou et al., 2025). For computational fluid
dynamics (CFD), OpenFOAMGPT and ChatCFD use domain
knowledge and iterative correction to configure simulation
cases (Pandey et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2026). MetaOpenFOAM
2.0 and Foam-Agent organise simulation and post-processing
through task decomposition and agent coordination (Chen
et al., 2025; Yue et al., 2026). LLM-based residual dynamics
also augment marine-vessel predictive control (Zeng and
Zhang, 2026). These studies assign language models specific
roles in interpreting requirements, constructing cases and
supporting engineering decisions.
Domain-specific supervision supports different engineer-
ing tasks. OceanGPT uses ocean-domain instruction data
(Bi et al., 2024). ALL-FEM fine-tunes models on verified
FEniCS scripts for finite element workflows (Deotale et al.,
2026). Simulation-generated data also train neural networks
to predict riser fatigue (Sivaprasad et al., 2023). Program
generation requires reliable pairs of engineering requirements
and executable implementations. Self-Instruct generates and
filters instructions, Magicoder constructs tasks from source-
code snippets, and SelfCodeAlign selects generated solutions
through execution tests (Wang et al., 2023; Wei et al.,
2024b,a). For engineering simulation, execution testing must
be accompanied by consistency between physical parameters,
task descriptions and program implementations. When a task
contains coupled parameters, independent changes to the
description or program can make an otherwise executable
example inconsistent with the specified engineering prob-
lem. To preserve this consistency during data expansion,
OceanCoder generates descriptions and reference OrcaFlex
programs from shared physical parameter records, subject to
engineering constraints.
2.2. Engineering verification and learning from
feedback
Successful execution does not establish whether a pro-
gram satisfies its intended requirements. The test-oracle
problem concerns how to judge the correctness of observed

simulation solution.
program behaviour (Barr et al., 2015). EvalPlus shows that
expanded tests detect functional errors missed by the original
test suites (Liu et al., 2023). In optimisation modelling,
even agreement with a reference objective value can conceal
an incorrect constraint set. Constraint injection addresses
this problem by checking feasible and constraint-violating
solutions alongside objective values (Luo et al., 2026). Com-
putational verification addresses both code implementation
and numerical-solution accuracy (Oberkampf and Trucano,
2002). These distinctions motivate checking the engineering
specification as well as program behaviour.
The same verification criteria can guide learning as
well as evaluation. Constraint injection uses verification
outcomes for synthetic-data filtering and reinforcement-
learning rewards (Luo et al., 2026). CodeRL combines
unit-test outcomes, graded rewards and a learned critic
(Le et al., 2022). RLEF trains models to use execution
feedback during iterative refinement (Gehring et al., 2025).
CODERL+ uses variable-level execution feedback (Jiang
et al., 2026). OraclePhys examines how different forms of
finite-element-based supervision and verification feedback
affect learning in structural mechanics (Li et al., 2026). The
appropriate feedback depends on the task. Unit-test outcomes,
formulation constraints and structural responses each assess
different requirements. For OrcaFlex modelling, the relevant
checks concern the constructed physical system, completion
of the required analyses and extraction of the requested
responses. OceanCoder’s three-layer verification framework
performs these checks and distinguishes execution progress
from complete task acceptance. The resulting verification
states provide graded rewards for online GRPO, linking
model updates to engineering task completion.
2.3. Benchmarks for automated simulation
modelling
Benchmarks differ in the tasks they assign and the evi-
dence they use to judge success. DS-1000 evaluates program-
ming with scientific Python libraries, and BigCodeBench
tests diverse function calls and complex instructions (Lai
et al., 2023; Zhuo et al., 2025). SciCode assesses research pro-
gramming problems curated by scientists (Tian et al., 2024).
Simulation benchmarks extend this evaluation to numerical
software and its outputs. FEABench checks COMSOL-based
multiphysics models, physical settings and numerical results
(Mudur et al., 2025). CFDLLMBench covers CFD knowl-
edge, solver implementation and OpenFOAM workflows
(Somasekharan et al., 2026). SimulCost evaluates simulation
parameter tuning under accuracy and computational-cost
constraints (Cao et al., 2026). LiveCodeBench additionally
evaluates code generation, self-repair, execution and output
prediction using time-segmented problems (Jain et al., 2025).
These settings assess distinct programming and simulation
requirements.

Interaction budgets further affect what a benchmark mea-
sures. A single-attempt setting assesses the initial response,
whereas feedback-based settings also assess error diagnosis
and correction. To measure the modelling capability acquired
through training, the OceanCoder benchmark fixes the inter-
action budget. Each model makes one attempt to generate a
complete OrcaFlex program for each task, without simulator-
feedback repair. During evaluation, verification outcomes
determine acceptance without being returned to the model
for another generation attempt. Its 665 tasks cover parameter
variations, structural variations and engineering contexts.
Common checks of model inputs, analysis completion and
requested outputs define acceptance for every model. The
resulting comparisons separate performance across task vari-
ations while retaining a consistent definition of engineering
task completion.
3. OceanCoder framework and training
procedure
3.1. Task definition and framework overview
OceanCoder addresses the task of generating complete
OrcaFlex programs from natural-language specifications of
physical systems, required analyses and requested responses.
Each program uses OrcFxAPI, the Python interface to
OrcaFlex, to build the model, run the analyses and extract
the results (Orcina Ltd., 2025). Task completion requires
agreement with the engineering specification throughout this
process, including the model configuration, analysis steps
and reported responses.
Figure 2 presents the data construction, training and
evaluation framework. We expand expert-designed seed cases
within engineering constraints and use the same parameters
to generate each task description and reference program.
Verified pairs are used for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of
Qwen3-8B. Since programs generated after SFT can still alter
specified inputs or extract unintended responses, subsequent
training uses engineering verification of generated programs
as feedback. Three-layer verification checks model inputs,
analysis completion and outputs. The verification outcomes
determine graded rewards for online group relative policy
optimisation (GRPO). The trained OceanCoder checkpoints
and comparison models are evaluated on a separate bench-
mark using the same engineering acceptance criteria. Each
model makes one attempt to generate a complete program for
each task, without simulator-feedback repair.
3.2. Engineering-constrained data construction
We construct training examples by expanding expert-
designed seed cases, as shown in Figure 3. A seed defines
the physical objects and their connections, the analysis
procedure and the response quantities to extract. These
elements establish the task family within which additional
cases are generated. The corpus covers 12 categories grouped
into static analysis, dynamic response and offshore operations,
as listed in Table 1. Each category contains ten seed families,
with 100 expanded examples per family, producing 1,000
examples per category and 12,000 examples in total. The
seed therefore provides both an engineering specification and
a complete program structure that can implement admissible
variations of that specification.

Conformal Selection for Hierarchical Streaming Data
Zhenyuan Suna∗, Chengyao Yub∗, Ruixing Mingc†, Bingyi Jingd,e
aSchool Mathematical Sciences, Peking University;
bDepartment of Statistics and Data Science,
Southern University of Science and Technology;
cSchool of Statistics and Data Science, Zhejiang Gongshang University;
dSchool of Artificial Intelligence, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen;
eShenzhen Loop Area Institute
Abstract
Many real-world tasks involve making sequential decisions about whether to select candidates
before their responses of interest are revealed. In this work, we address the online selection
problem in the context of hierarchical data, where candidates arrive sequentially from different
populations. This extends existing online conformal selection frameworks beyond the standard
i.i.d./exchangeable data assumption. The primary challenge lies in constructing valid statistics
for each candidate sequentially under the hierarchical data structure. To this end, we first
develop Online Hierarchical Selection (OHS), a distribution-free method that enables principled
candidate selection for hierarchical data streams. Specifically, we introduce methods to construct
rank-based e-values for both between-group and within-group samples, and apply averaged
e-values to the online e-BH procedure. We then develop OHS with feedback (OHSF), which
boosts the power of OHS by leveraging potential response feedback. Theoretically, the proposed
methods achieve false discovery rate control under mild hierarchical exchangeability and data
arrival assumptions at any time. We also generalize methods to broader settings, such as data
with covariate shift and selection under effect-related responses. Extensive experiments on both
simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.
1
Introduction
Many scientific discovery and decision-making tasks involve selecting candidates with desired
outcomes sequentially from a data stream before their outcomes are observed. This paper focuses
such online selection problem in the context of hierarchical data, where the streaming candidates
can be organized into groups and i.i.d./exchangeability only holds within and across groups. Such
data structure is common in reality:
• In multi-center clinical studies, patients are grouped by hospitals or study sites, which may
have distinct populations and outcome distributions (Higgins et al., 2009).
• In cluster-randomized trials, individuals are nested within villages, cities, or schools and share
a cluster-specific treatment or environment (Su and Ding, 2021).
• In repeated assessment, the same data point may receive multiple ratings or annotations,
creating observations nested within the assessed unit (Stutz et al., 2023).
∗Co-first authors.
†Corresponding author.
1
arXiv:2611.26328v1  [stat.ML]  19 Nov 2026
While selections concern spending scarce resources such as experimental capacity, follow-up budgets,
and patient slots, we aim to develop principled online selection procedures that rigorously control
false selections under the hierarchical steaming data.
The fast-developing artificial intelligence presents great promise in assisting decision-making due
to its excellent predictive power across a wide range of fields (Dara et al., 2022; Watson et al., 2023;
Price et al., 2025). For the online selection task, a promising way is to leverage machine-predicted
outcomes to select those desired candidates. However, such decisions are commonly based on
black-box predictive models, which can not control false selections. To achieve principled selection,
conformal selection (CS) (Jin and Candès, 2023) provides a model-agnostic framework for selecting
candidates with large outcomes in offline settings, which converts predictive scores into conformal
p-values and applies the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995) to
select candidates with false discovery rate (FDR) control. Numerous studies have extended CS
to different settings (Gui et al., 2024, 2025; Bai et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2026a; Jin and Candès,
2026). Recently, to tackle the online setting where candidates arrive sequentially, Liu et al. (2026)
developed an online extension of CS by applying the online BH procedure (Xu and Ramdas, 2024) to
conformal p-values. Other works, including Fischer et al. (2026); Lu et al. (2026), further generalized
the online selection method and extended the online selection problem to settings with feedback.
Despite these remarkable advancements in principled candidate selection, none of these works
address the selection problem under hierarchical streaming data. The statistical challenge is that
these methods mainly rely on the i.i.d./exchangeable data assumption, and the failure of this
assumption will directly affect the validity of test statistics, such as conformal p-values. One
of the most related works is Lee and Ren (2025), which generalizes CS (Jin and Candès, 2023)
to hierarchical data. Specifically, they introduce methods to construct subsampling/hierarchical
conformal e-values and subsequently apply the e-BH procedure (Wang and Ramdas, 2022) to provide
FDR control, where the e-value is a competitor of the p-value and has been widely applied to
hypothesis testing with complex data structures (Yu et al., 2024a, 2026b; Gablenz and Sabatti, 2025).
However, their method is designed for offline settings, and their statistics can not be directly applied
to online selection procedures, such as online e-BH. Extending conformal selection for hierarchical
streaming data therefore needs novel techniques. This paper aims to address this gap.
1.1
Our Contributions
In this paper, we develop online selection frameworks for hierarchical streaming data, covering
both settings with and without response feedback. For the no-feedback setting, we propose Online
Hierarchical Selection (OHS), which constructs two complementary rank-based e-values for each
arriving candidate. Specifically, we construct a within-group e-value obtained by comparing the
threshold score of the candidate with null calibration scores from the same group, and a between-
group e-value by comparing it with one uniformly sampled null representative from each eligible group
other than the candidate group. The two e-values are combined through a prespecified weighted
average, allowing OHS to leverage information from both within- and between-group comparisons.
We then apply online e-BH to the combined e-values and progressively expand the selection set
as new candidates arrive, without revoking previous selections. For settings requiring immediate
and irreversible decisions, we further develop Online Hierarchical Selection with Feedback (OHSF).
After each decision, we incorporate every newly revealed null observation into the reference pool of
the corresponding group, regardless of the selection outcome, and apply randomized e-LOND (Xu
and Ramdas, 2024) to the resulting hierarchical e-values for subsequent decisions. We also extend
the proposed frameworks to accommodate covariate shift, effect-related responses, and the arrival of
previously unseen groups.
2
Theoretically, we establish finite-sample FDR control for both OHS and OHSF under the
corresponding assumptions. For OHS, we establish the validity of the within-group and between-
group rank-based e-values under score monotonicity. For OHSF, we establish FDR control for
immediate decisions based on feedback-updated reference pools, without requiring the score function
to be monotone in the response. We further establish FDR guarantees for extensions to covariate
shift, effect-related responses, and previously unseen groups under their respective conditions.
The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 formulates the problem and introduces
the data assumptions. Section 3 develops the OHS and OHSF, and establishes their theoretical
results. Section 4 extends the proposed methods to settings, including data with covariate shift,
selection under effect-related responses, and selection for unseen groups. Simulation results and real
data applications are presented in Sections 5 and 6, respectively. Section 7 provides the discussions.
All proofs are provided in appendix.

Predicting Surface Displacement Fields of Laser Powder Bed Fusion
Parts Using STL-Derived Graphs and Part-Level Descriptors
Saima Ahmed Suhi1, Lang Yuan1, and Md Habibor Rahman∗1
1Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of South Carolina, Columbia, SC 29208, USA
Abstract
Predicting part distortion before fabrication remains a key challenge in the Laser Powder Bed Fusion
(LPBF) process. Thermomechanical simulation is commonly used to predict such distortion by modeling
thermal and mechanical responses, but it can be computationally demanding for repeated design evaluation.
In response, this work predicts the three-dimensional surface displacement field of LPBF parts directly
from their STL derived graphs employing a two-branch Graph Attention Network (GAT). One branch
combines normalized geometric information from connected vertices of a densified STL surface mesh
using learned attention weights; the other encodes 12 part-level descriptors characterizing mass distribution,
geometric contact area with the build plate, overhang, size, and shape. Training labels are transferred
from displacement fields simulated using ANSYS ADDITIVE PRINT onto the STL surface vertices
through a Gaussian-kernel weighted average. The GAT model was evaluated on 117 parts with a 5-fold
cross-validation split by parts, achieving an 𝑅2 of 0.946 and a MAE error of 0.0178 mm for displacement
magnitude. Compared with the node-wise MLP, GAT increases 𝑅2 from 0.913 to 0.946, with the largest
component-wise improvement occurring in the build direction, where 𝑈𝑧𝑅2 increases from 0.903 to 0.939.
GAT also achieves higher predictive accuracy than GraphSAGE (displacement-magnitude 𝑅2 = 0.936) and
Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) (displacement-magnitude 𝑅2 = 0.934) in all five folds. Additionally,
an ablation study evaluates the contribution of each descriptor group by removing it individually and
retraining the model. Removing the mass-distribution descriptors reduces displacement-magnitude 𝑅2
from 0.946 to 0.900, while removing descriptors of geometric contact with the build plate and overhang
reduces it to 0.920. These comparisons indicate that combining information from connected surface
vertices with part-level geometric descriptors improves accuracy. By linking CAD geometry directly
to surface nodal displacement with graphs and global descriptors, the approach supports faster design
iteration, earlier identification of distortion-prone features, and more informed LPBF production planning.
Keywords: Laser powder bed fusion; Geometric descriptors; Distortion prediction; Graph attention network;
Surface mesh; Process simulation.
1
Introduction
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) enables the fabrication of metal components with complex geometries, but
maintaining dimensional accuracy remains a major challenge [13]. Repeated localized heating and cooling
during the build process produce nonuniform thermal expansion and contraction, leading to residual stress
and part distortion [9, 33]. Predicting distortion before printing enables early assessment of part geometries
∗Corresponding author: habiborrahman@sc.edu
1
arXiv:2611.26323v1  [cs.LG]  19 Nov 2026
and helps guide design modifications to improve dimensional accuracy. Distortion is commonly predicted
using finite-element simulations, including thermomechanical models and simplified approaches based on
inherent or assumed strains [12, 26]. These simulations capture the mechanisms governing residual stress and
distortion within parts, but running a simulation for each part can take hours to days, depending on geometric
complexity, mesh resolution, and the modeling approach [19]. In practice, designers compare many variants,
orientations, and support design strategies before printing, so running a full simulation for every candidate
slows the design iteration and is often deferred until later in the design process [31]. A faster approach that
predicts distortion directly from the design geometry would allow candidate geometries to be screened before
starting the manufacturing process. Data-driven surrogate models offer an alternative to repeated numerical
simulation of thermal and mechanical responses in Metal Additive Manufacturing (MAM). Some existing
approaches use geometric encodings and process parameters to predict part-level quantities or categories,
such as peak deviation, feature recognition, and geometry clusters [2, 35]. Although useful for assessing
overall part behavior or grouping geometries, these outputs cannot indicate the distortion region.
Beyond part-level predictions, studies are increasingly using geometric representations and process
parameters to learn spatially resolved responses [22, 24]. Under fixed material, process, and boundary
conditions, part geometry influences distortion through its effect on heat transfer, temperature evolution,
and mechanical constraint [3, 15]. During LPBF part fabrication, the surrounding material and build-plate
attachment restrict thermal contraction, while the part shape determines available heat-dissipation paths
and the stiffness resisting deformation [23, 34]. The resulting displacement field therefore depends on how
material is distributed along the build direction, how much of the part is attached to the plate, and how much
of its surface is unsupported or down-facing. These are properties of the geometry itself, suggesting that a
model with an adequate geometric information can learn spatially resolved distortion without explicit thermal
inputs. Researchers have used voxel grids, signed distance fields, and point clouds for this purpose [11, 28],
but voxelization trades resolution for computational cost [29] and produces stair-stepped surfaces, while point
clouds do not explicitly encode surface connectivity.
Triangulated surface meshes, by contrast, are the native format of design files (e.g., STL) and explicitly
encode connectivity between surface vertices. These meshes can be converted into graphs by treating surface
vertices as nodes and mesh edges as connections between them, thereby preserving the spatial relationships
among neighboring vertices [37, 38]. By aggregating information from connected vertices, graph-based
models can capture spatial dependencies relevant to predicting temperature and displacement fields across
a part. For example, Mozaffar et al. (2021) used a graph-based framework to predict thermal histories
[24] in Directed Energy Deposition (DED), while subsequent studies by Raut et al. (2025) and Choi et al.
(2025) investigated the transferability of graph-based thermal prediction in LPBF and DED, respectively
[10, 27]. These studies demonstrate how mesh connectivity, spatial coordinates, and information about
heat-source locations and boundary conditions can be utilized to predict temperature changes over time at
different locations within a part. Graph-based modeling has also been extended to spatial prediction of
residual stress and distortion. For example, Li et al. (2026) developed a Graph Attention Network (GAT)
to predict three-dimensional residual stress in DED workpieces using nodal coordinates and temperature
information [22]. Chen et al. (2026) introduced a DeepONet-GNN framework that integrates sparse
temperature histories with structural features, including spatial coordinates, boundary conditions, and initial
displacements, to predict distortion along the build direction [8]. Lee et al. (2025) developed GraphCompNet,
which uses point-cloud representations and incorporates part-position information to predict and compensate
for manufacturing-induced shape deviations [21]. Collectively, these studies demonstrate the potential of
graph-based models to capture spatial relationships and incorporate structural and process-related information
for distortion prediction. In a related but distinct application, Giovenali et al. (2026) introduced PAGE-Net,
which integrates local mesh features, global geometric descriptors, and printing parameters to estimate
manufacturing resource requirements in fused filament fabrication [16]. Although developed for a different
2
prediction task, PAGE-Net demonstrates the feasibility of combining local mesh representations with global
geometric descriptors within a graph-based learning framework.
Previous studies have manifested the potential of graph-based models for predicting manufacturing-
induced distortion and integrating local and global geometric information, but the combined use of these
representations to predict full-field LPBF displacement directly from part geometry remains underexplored.
Such an approach could enable early assessment of geometric distortion without requiring thermal histories,
process-state measurements, or additional simulations for individual parts at the prediction stage. To bridge
this gap, this study proposes a two-branch Graph Attention Network (GAT) that combines local surface
features and connectivity with twelve part-level geometric descriptors to predict displacement at each surface
vertex, without requiring simulation results as inputs during inference. The study develops an STL-based
surrogate for predicting three-dimensional surface displacement fields of LPBF parts under specific material
and process conditions. A densified STL surface provides both the prediction graph and the locations at
which simulation-derived displacement labels are assigned. Gaussian-kernel weighted transfers displacement
vectors from the corresponding VTK1 simulation surface to the STL vertices, bridging the different design
and simulation discretizations. The contribution extends beyond the architectural combination by assessing
the label-transfer procedure and controlling the predictive inputs. Held-out reconstruction tests assess label
transfer accuracy, while comparisons with a capacity-matched node-wise MLP and alternative graph operators
examine the value of message passing. Additionally, a descriptor drop-group ablation retraining identifies the
complementary information supplied by part-level geometry descriptors. Together, these analyses establish
and evaluate a geometry-informed workflow for predicting LPBF surface displacement from STLs, supporting
its potential use in design-stage distortion screening. The primary objectives of this study are the following:
1. Develop a two-branch graph attention network framework to predict full-field three-dimensional surface
displacement in LPBF directly from STL-derived mesh geometry and geometric descriptors under
fixed material and process conditions, enabling design-stage distortion assessment without requiring
additional process simulations for individual predictions.
2. Construct and validate a simulation-to-STL displacement-transfer workflow using surface densification
and Gaussian-kernel-weighted averaging to generate reliable training labels on the design mesh.
3. Evaluate the effectiveness of graph-based feature aggregation and the contribution of part-level geometric
descriptors to prediction accuracy through controlled model comparisons and descriptor-group ablation
studies.
2
Methodology
This section describes how the training data were generated and how the model was built, trained, and
evaluated as illustrated in Fig. 1. The process simulation is used only offline to supply the displacement labels.
Subsection 2.1 describes the dataset; Subsections 2.2–2.2.5 describe how each STL–simulation pair becomes
a labeled surface graph with part-level descriptors; Subsections 2.3–2.4.1 present the network, its training,
and the evaluation protocol.
2.1
Dataset
This study uses an extension of the LPBF simulation dataset reported in [5, 6]. It comprises 117 parts with
features such as slots, steps, and chamfers (Fig. 2), each provided as an STL file with the corresponding

STL densification

Scalable Fault Vulnerability Analysis for
ReRAM-Based Process-in-Memory CNN
Accelerators
Aniseh Dorostkar, Hamed Farbeh, Hamid R. Zarandi,
Meysam Sharifzadeh
Department of Computer Engineering, Amirkabir University of
Technology (Tehran Polytechnic), Tehran, Iran.
*Corresponding author(s). E-mail(s): farbeh@aut.ac.ir;
Contributing authors: a dorostkar@aut.ac.ir; h zarandi@aut.ac.ir;
msharifzadeh@aut.ac.ir;
Abstract
Resistive random-access memory (ReRAM)-based processing-in-memory (PIM)
accelerators offer a highly efficient platform for parallel matrix-vector mul-
tiplications (VMM) in neural networks, leveraging analog computation, high
density, low leakage, and non-volatility. However, their susceptibility to per-
manent faults, such as stuck-at-high (SaH ) and stuck-at-low (SaL) resistance
states, permanently corrupts the convolutional neural networks (CNNs) weights
mapped onto ReRAM cell conductance values, thereby degrading inference accu-
racy and leading to system unreliability in safety-critical applications. Fault
injection is a commonly used technique to assess the vulnerability of neural
networks by systematically injecting faults into individual parameters and mea-
suring the resulting accuracy degradation. Although this method is accurate,
it is prohibitively time-consuming and computationally expensive, especially for
large-scale CNNs. In this paper, we propose a fast, scalable, and analytical
framework to quantify the fault vulnerability of convolutional neural networks
deployed on ReRAM-based PIM accelerators. This method quantifies vulnerabil-
ity at different granularities, including weights, kernels, and layers, without the
need for exhaustive simulation, enabling the design of fault-tolerant accelerators
for edge and safety-critical applications. The comparison between the results of
the proposed vulnerability score (VS) metrics with performance metric of CNNs
captured with fault injection simulations confirms the effectiveness of our pro-
posed method. Unlike exhaustive fault injection, which requires days or weeks,
whereas the proposed approach achieves a speedup of about 104 × −105×,
1
arXiv:2611.26307v1  [cs.AR]  19 Nov 2026
enabling fast and accurate vulnerability analysis for large-scale CNNs within only
a few minutes or hours.
Keywords: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), fault vulnerability,
processing-in-memory (PIM), resistive random-access memory (ReRAM), sensitivity
analysis
1 Introduction
Deep neural networks (DNNs), and in particular convolutional neural networks
(CNNs), have achieved high attention and great performance in classification, detec-
tion, and recognition tasks in various domains such as healthcare, autonomous driving,
space applications, and other safety-critical systems [1]. Their success is primarily
due to their ability to extract complex features through deep, multi-layered archi-
tectures, which is based on computationally intensive vector-matrix multiplication
(VMM). To achieve high accuracy, the complexity of CNNs increases, which in turn
leads to significant growth in computational cost, memory requirements, and energy
consumption.
Despite the widespread use of traditional computing platforms, including central
processing units (CPUs), graphics processing units (GPUs), and field-programmable
gate arrays (FPGAs), for convolutional neural networks (CNNs), these platforms
increasingly face performance bottlenecks, particularly with respect to memory band-
width and power consumption. Resistive random-access memory (ReRAM)-based
Process-in-Memory (PiM) accelerators have emerged as a promising candidate that
provide high parallelism and energy efficiency for large-scale CNNs inference. ReRAM
devices, fabricated at the nanoscale, can be seamlessly integrated into crossbar arrays,
providing an efficient solution for implementing large numbers of synaptic connections
in neural networks [2, 3] and graph processing [4]. ReRAM crossbars can perform mas-
sively memory-intensive VMM operations in parallel and have been widely adopted in
accelerators for CNN such as ISAAC [5], PRIME [6], and PipeLayer [7].
ReRAM-based accelerators face critical reliability challenges due to the limitations
of technology fabrication. Accordingly, they suffer from non-idealities such as process
variations (PVs), limited write endurance, discrete and limited number of conductance
states, sources of noise, and non-linearity of current-voltage characteristics [8–10].
Transient and permanent faults, such as stuck-at-high (SaH ) and stuck-at-low (SaL)
faults, introduce significant errors in VMM computations, ultimately degrading CNN
inference accuracy. As CNNs are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications,
ensuring reliable inference becomes essential, as even a single fault may propagate
through the network and compromise the correctness of the entire system [11]. There-
fore, it is critical to investigate and analyze the vulnerability of CNN models deployed
on ReRAM-based accelerators to transient and permanent faults, particularly SaH
and SaL faults, at the level of weights, kernels, and layers. Such analysis is crucial for
understanding the fault behavior of each kernel or layer and for ensuring the design
2
of robust CNN models or the design of a fault-tolerant ReRAM accelerator suitable
for safety-critical systems.
To investigate the reliability of CNNs, there is some fault injection and analytical
model to analyze the vulnerability of CNNs to permanent or transient faults across
a variety of hardware platforms, including CPUs, GPUs, FPGAs, Tensor Process-
ing Units (TPUs), Application-Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs) [1, 12–15] and
ReRAM-based PIM accelerators [11, 16, 17].
Traditional fault injection provides an accurate way to assess the vulnerability
of neural networks by systematically injecting faults and measuring the resulting
accuracy drop or loss increase [15, 18]. However, this approach is computationally pro-
hibitive for large-scale CNNs with millions of parameters. Several work have attempted
to reduce the complexity of fault injection simulations [19, 20]. In practice, most fault
injection studies rely on random fault injection into a subset of layers, kernels, or
parameters.
However, conducting a comprehensive analysis that covers all weights, kernels,
and layers requires simulating faults and re-executing inference for every parame-
ter. Therefore, exhaustive analysis requires running inference and fault simulation for
every parameter, kernel, and layer, which is impractical for large-scale and deep mod-
els. Therefore, alternative approaches are necessary to enable scalable and efficient
vulnerability analysis.
In CNNs, specific components, such as certain neurons, weights, kernels, and lay-
ers, exhibit higher computational significance, influencing overall model efficiency and
accuracy. Consequently, faults occurring in different components have unequal impacts
on the network’s output. Despite ongoing advancements in neural network resilience, a
significant gap remains in accurately identifying the most critical weights, biases, ker-
nels, and layers whose faults lead to substantial accuracy degradation in PIM-based
ReRAM CNN accelerators.
In this work, we propose a comprehensive framework to analyze fault sensitivity
for ReRAM-based PIM accelerators for CNNs. Our method introduces an element-
wise sensitivity metric that estimates the vulnerability of individual weights and
biases across different CNN layers under stuck-at faults (SAFs), leveraging both first-
and second-order gradient approximation. Furthermore, the framework provides a
fast, scalable, and efficient mechanism to rank the vulnerability of weights, kernels,
and layers, which can be utilized in the design of fault-tolerant PIM-based ReRAM
accelerators. The main contributions to this article are as follows:
1. We provide a scalable, fast, and efficient vulnerability analysis framework for SAFs
occurring in ReRAM-based PIM accelerators targeting large scale CNNs.
2. We introduce a sensitivity metric that combines first- and second-order gradient
terms to capture both linear and curvature effects of weight perturbations caused
by SAFs.
3. We analyze the sensitivity of different CNNs at three levels of granularity, i.e.,
element-wise, kernel-wise, and layer-wise, enabling a hierarchical ranking of network
components.
4. We conduct a comprehensive analysis of CNN parameter sensitivity across diverse
network topologies and scales, revealing that vulnerability to permanent faults
3
depends on fault type and magnitude, network architecture, layer configuration,
distance from the output, and the role of learning parameters such as weight or
bias.
5. We validate the proposed sensitivity metrics through systematic fault injection sim-
ulations, demonstrating their effectiveness in evaluating CNN performance under
faults.
The remainder of this article is organized as follows. Section 2 provides background
information on neural networks, ReRAM-based PIM accelerators, reliability considera-
tions, and fault models associated with ReRAM-based architectures. A comprehensive
discussion of related work is presented in Section 3. Our proposed vulnerability anal-
ysis framework is detailed in Section 4. Extensive analysis and evaluations using our
scalable framework, along with validation results, are provided in Section 5. Finally,
Section 6 concludes the paper.
2 Preliminaries
2.1 Convolutional Neural Networks
CNNs are composed of a sequence of convolutional (CONV) and pooling layers, along
with optional layers such as batch normalization (BatchNorm) for feature extraction,
followed by a small number of fully connected (FC) layers (typically fewer than three)
for classification. The trainable parameters, namely, the kernels and biases in CONV
layers, as well as the weights and biases in FC and BatchNorm layers, are adjusted
during the training phase. The main computations in CNNs are dominated by multi-
dimensional convolution and VMM, primarily carried out in the CONV and FC layers.
In FC layer, each neuron receives weighted input from all activations of the previous
layer, equivalent to a VMM, added by a bias passed through an activation function
σ, (commonly sigmoid, ReLU, or tanh) to compute the neuron output (as shown in
Fig. 1(a)). The operation of an FC layer can be formulated as:
