2.2 ReRAM-based PIM Accelerators
ReRAM is a non-volatile memory technology that operates by switching the resistance
state of its cells. A typical 1T1R cell consists of a resistive switching device based on a
metal–insulator–metal (MIM) structure, integrated with an access transistor (shown
in Fig 2(a)). Depending on the applied voltage pulses, the device can switch between
different resistive states, by the formation and rupture of conductive filaments within
the insulating layer. Reading the cell requires only a small read voltage that does not
disturb the current cell state.
A ReRAM crossbar array (shown in Fig. 2(b)) is constructed by arranging multiple
ReRAM cells at the intersections of perpendicular word-lines and bit-lines. The main
operation of ReRAM-based neural network accelerators is VMMs, which are executed
natively in the analog domain. In this process, input vectors are applied as voltages
to the rows of the crossbar, while the stored conductance values represent the weight
matrix. According to Ohm’s law, the product of input voltages and conductance values
yields the corresponding multiplication results. By Kirchhoff’s current law, the cur-
rents along the bit-lines are naturally accumulated to generate the final vector-matrix
product [21].

For executing matrix–vector multiplication in a FC layer, the input vector is mapped
to input voltages V , while the weight matrix of dimension (H, W) is mapped to the
conductance values of the ReRAM crossbar.
To execute convolutional operations within ReRAM crossbars, the convolution
kernels are first flattened and transformed into equivalent matrix representations. The
resulting weight matrix of dimension (Cin × KW × KH, Cout), where each column
corresponds to the weights of a kernel, is mapped to the conductance values of the
crossbar array. Similarly, the IFM is unrolled into an input voltage matrix of size
(H × W, C × K × K), which is applied to the rows of the crossbar.
Since the number of parameters and the corresponding matrix dimensions differ
across layers, the weight matrices may not match the size of a single crossbar. When the
dimensions of the weight matrices (both FC and CONV layers) and inputs exceed the
size of the crossbar, the matrices and inputs are partitioned into blocks matching the
crossbar size and mapped across multiple crossbars. Consequently, depending on the
6
CNN architecture, an appropriate mapping strategy is required to map weight matrices
across a hierarchy of crossbars, tiles, and memory banks within the ReRAM-based
accelerator.
Since ReRAM cells can only store non-negative conductance states, signed neu-
ral network weights are implemented using a dual-crossbar architecture. In this
scheme, positive and negative weights are mapped to separate crossbars, while
the corresponding cells in the dual crossbar are set to the minimum conductance
value [6, 22, 23].
2.3 Fault Model and Reliability of ReRAM-based
Accelerators for CNNs
In ReRAM-based PIM accelerators, the learning parameters of neural networks are
mapped to the conductance of ReRAM cells. Consequently, any variations or defects
in ReRAM cells directly lead to variations in the neural network parameters, thereby
affecting inference accuracy and system reliability.
The reliability of ReRAM accelerators is influenced by data-dependent and data-
independent factors. Data-dependent factors include the mapping of weights and
biases to conductance values of ReRAM cells, scaling of inputs into voltages, process-
variations (cell-to-cell and cycle-to-cycle variations), resistance drift, quantization
errors, and device faults such as stuck-at-high (SaH ) and stuck-at-low (SaL). In con-
trast, data-independent factors are related to peripheral circuitry and fabrication
technology, including access transistors or selectors, ADC/DAC resolution, sneak-path
currents, and parasitic resistances.
ReRAM faults are commonly categorized into transient and permanent types.
Transient faults are temporary and reversible, typically caused by external distur-
bances such as high-energy particles, temperature fluctuations, resistance drift, or
read/write disturbance [1, 24–26]. These faults alter cell resistance temporarily with-
out causing physical damage and ReRAM cells can still function. Permanent faults,
however, are persistent and result from irreversible physical damage caused by limita-
tions in fabrication (e.g., oxide thickness variations, forming-stage defects, or reduced
feature sizes [27, 28]) or limited write endurance [29, 30]}. The forming process of
ReRAM cells is particularly sensitive, as high-voltage stress is applied to establish con-
ductive filaments in devices. Defects such as over-forming or short defects [28] often
cause the resistance of cell to becomes irreversibly stuck-at high-resistance (SaH ),
stuck-at low-resistance (SaL), or more generally, stuck-at value (SaV ) states. Exper-
imental studies report that approximately 9.04% of ReRAM cells exhibit SaH and
1.75% exhibit SaL [28].
Even after successful fabrication and initial testing, additional faults can occur
during operation due to limited endurance, especially after repeated write-0 or write-1
pulses [30, 31]} or wear-out, which cause damaging the device or transistor.
3 Related Work
Faults occurring during neural network execution can lead to errors in the output.
Prior studies have focused on the software- and hardware-based investigation and
7
analysis of various types of faults and errors associated with these networks. Impor-
tantly, faults originating from different network layers or parameters have been shown
to have varying impacts on the network’s output accuracy and overall performances.
Software-based fault injection tools typically evaluate neural network reliabil-
ity without considering the underlying hardware. For example, TensorFi [32] and
PyTorchFi [33] are open-source fault injection tools built on TensorFlow and PyTorch,
respectively. These frameworks enable the injection of both transient and perma-
nent faults at the algorithmic-level. TensorFi injects the faults at the data path of
neural networks, while PyTorchFi modifies neuron activations and weights at spe-
cific locations. However, their functionality is limited to random data modifications,
and they are unable to provide a detailed vulnerability analysis across CNN mod-
els or hardware platforms. In contrast, GPU-oriented tools such as SASSIFI [34] and
NVBitFI [35] perform fault injection at the instruction-level and can also be applied
to CNN workloads.

SKILL.PNG: Learning Agent Skills in Pixel Space
Maximilian Seeth
Hasso Plattner Institute
Technical University of Munich
max.seeth@tum.de
Chengzhi Martin Hu
Technical University of Munich
Helmholtz AI
cm.hu@tum.de
Marie Kempkes
Volkswagen Group Innovation
marie.kempkes@volkswagen.de
Paul R¨ottger
Hasso Plattner Institute
paul.rottger@hpi.de
Leo Schwinn
Technical University of Munich
Helmholtz AI
leo.schwinn@helmholtz-munich.de
Abstract
AI agents are commonly specialized for new tasks and do-
mains using skills, i.e. natural language instructions placed
in their context. However, the discrete nature of textual
skills prevents continuous optimization. Gradient-based ap-
proaches such as finetuning, on the other hand, are typi-
cally model-specific, preventing skill transfer across differ-
ent agents. Since many agents today are built on vision-
language models (VLMs), we can address these limitations
by introducing SKILL.PNG: a method for obtaining skill-like
image inputs whose pixels are optimized with gradient de-
scent through the vision encoder of a frozen VLM. Image
skills are compatible with any VLM, and a single image
can be optimized jointly for an ensemble of models. We
show that SKILL.PNG significantly outperforms state-of-the-
art textual skills optimized using frontier LLMs in 9 of 16
settings (across 4 VLMs and 4 benchmarks) while requir-
ing only 64 to 256 image tokens instead of roughly 900 to
2000 text tokens at inference time. Hybrid skills, i.e. text
and image skills jointly optimized, further improve agent
performance. Moreover, an image optimized with an ensem-
ble of VLMs can successfully transfer across the models in
the ensemble. SKILL.PNG thus presents the first agent skill
that can be optimized with gradient descent while retain-
ing transfer benefits of text skills. Our code is available at:
https://github.com/omseeth/skill.png
1. Introduction
Skills, natural language instructions placed in a model’s
context, have become a common way to specialize agents for
new tasks, tools and domains. Beyond writing them by hand,
recent work refines skills in loops where a large language
model (LLM) proposes edits and keeps those that help the
Figure 1. Three ways to improve agents. Text skills work with
any model but cannot be optimized with gradients. LoRA is trained
with gradients, but is model-specific. SKILL.PNG (ours) encodes
the skill as an image, optimized with gradients through one or more
frozen models, and transfers across them.
agent [1, 3, 20, 32]. Relying on large and capable, often
proprietary LLM optimizers is costly, though, compared to
gradient-based optimizations, which are much more sample-
efficient, as shown in adversarial research [6, 24, 29].
One way to bypass discrete search is to optimize in con-
1
arXiv:2611.26296v1  [cs.LG]  19 Nov 2026
tinuous parameter or embedding spaces instead. Finetuning
with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [16] learns updates of a
model’s weights, and visual prompt tuning [17] learns con-
tinuous prompt tokens in a model’s embedding space. Both
methods are model-specific, either by merging new weights
or inserting embeddings, requiring white-box access. How-
ever, parameters from a model’s latent space are not skill ar-
tifacts that can be easily handed to other agents via its input.
Therefore, we introduce SKILL.PNG, which brings
gradient-based optimization to skills while staying in the
input space. Many agents are built on vision-language mod-
els (VLMs), and every VLM accepts images. SKILL.PNG
continuously optimizes the pixels of an image through the
vision encoder of a frozen VLM and keeps them in the valid
image domain (Fig. 1). A model provider can, for exam-
ple, optimize skill images for its newest model in-house and
release them alongside it. Users then simply attach these
images, potentially along with text skills, to their queries
without the need to access the agent’s weights again. For
open-weight models, skills can also be optimized and shared
by users directly.
Across four VLMs and four benchmarks spanning ques-
tion answering, tool use, research-level mathematics and
planning, SKILL.PNG outperforms text skills from SkillOpt,
an LLM optimization loop [32], in 9 of 16 settings signifi-
cantly. It improves on the model without a skill by up to 37.8
benchmark points, while requiring only 64 to 256 image
tokens instead of roughly 900 to 2000 text tokens. Text and
image skills can also be combined: optimizing an image
with a text skill already in context adds 6.1 to 15.5 points
on three of four benchmarks. Finally, one image optimized
jointly for Qwen3.5-4B and Gemma-4-E4B-it improves both
models, allowing the image to transfer between the two. In
summary, our contributions are:
• The introduction of SKILL.PNG, a gradient-based agent
skill insertable via the input space of a frozen VLM, which
requires neither weight changes nor white-box access at
deployment;
• an ensemble objective with per-model gradient normal-
ization that optimizes a transferable image for VLMs of
different families;
• evaluation of image skills against LLM-optimized text
skills on four VLMs and four benchmarks, covering multi-
modal skill combinations, transfer across models, and an
interpretation attempt of image skills.
2. Related Work
Our approach combines image optimization via frozen
VLMs with agent skills.
Agent skills. Skills are reusable natural language instruc-
tions and resources that help agents perform specific tasks,
use tools, and adapt to new domains. Beyond manually writ-
ing skills, obtaining skills more systematically is comparable
to prompt optimization [13, 31, 35], where large language
models (LLMs) are tasked with providing better instructions.
Work in skill optimization has therefore developed increas-
ingly complex pipelines to deploy LLM optimizers for skill
writing [1, 3, 20, 31, 34]. However, all of these approaches
stick to text editing and inefficient sampling from LLMs.
Image optimization.
A new line of work has be-
gun to explore multimodal skills. These works typically
develop a combination of text and screenshots or visual
highlighting that guides agents like an illustrated manual
[18, 30]. However, they rely on manual or only partially
automated selections of suitable illustrations. Generating
image perturbations through gradient-based updates is there-
fore much closer to visual prompting [4, 12], which has
mostly been used in AI safety contexts to jailbreak VLMs
[2, 5, 6, 9, 10, 28, 33]. In contrast to this work, we attempt
to elicit a more general behavioral effect through images
that goes beyond the narrow target of producing a single
adversarial output from VLMs. Moreover, this behavior is
intended to improve agents instead of breaking them. Clos-
est in spirit to our work is ART [8], which also optimizes an
image through a frozen VLM to increase task performance;
we instead consider the image as an agent skill, compare it
with optimized text skills, combine both, and optimize one
image jointly for VLMs of different families.
3. Method
Let fϑ : X →Y denote a vision-language model (VLM)
with trainable parameters ϑ. To optimize an image skill,
fϑ is provided with the image Iskill, text Ttext (i.e. system
message, user request, and previous tool outputs), and target
answer Ttarget as input:

3.1. Ensemble Optimization
To obtain a transferable skill in pixel space, we optimize one
shared Iskill jointly against an ensemble of K frozen VLMs

target, processes Iskill with its own vision module, and yields

4. Experimental Setup
4.1. Benchmarks
We evaluate on four benchmarks. SearchQA [11] poses
Jeopardy! questions together with web snippets retrieved
for clues. The agent’s answers are scored by exact match.
TRAJECT-Bench [15] is a tool use benchmark for everyday
tasks. The agent must emit every required tool call from
a set of tools that also contains 10 distractors. An answer
counts as correct only if both the selected tools and their re-
quired parameters match exactly. LiveMathematicianBench
(LiveMath) [14] asks five-way multiple-choice questions on
theorems from recent arXiv papers, scored by accuracy. T1
[7] covers multi-turn travel planning: at a user turn, the agent
writes Python code against flight, hotel, restaurant and attrac-
tion tools. The code is executed and scored by exact match
of the resulting benchmark cache states. All benchmarks use
fixed train/validation/test splits, and all reported scores are
on our test split. We share further benchmark details in the
Supplementary Material.
4.2. Vision-Language Models
We optimize skill images for four VLMs: Qwen3.5-4B [27],
Qwen3.5-9B [27], Gemma-4-E4B-it [26] and Nemotron-3-
Nano-Omni-30B-A3B (Nemotron-3) [21], all kept frozen
in bfloat16. Images are optimized with reasoning disabled,
and unless stated otherwise, models are also evaluated in
non-reasoning mode.
A VLM’s preprocessor resizes any image that does not
match its patch grid or token budget, which would place a
resampling step between Iskill and the vision encoder. We
therefore set H × W per model to the smallest square size
that its preprocessor passes through unchanged, so that every
optimized pixel reaches the encoder as is: 256 × 256 for
Qwen3.5, the minimum pixel count of its dynamic resizing;
512 × 512 for Nemotron-3, below which its preprocessor
upscales to a minimum of 1024 patches; and 768 × 768
for Gemma-4-E4B-it, to which its preprocessor maps every
square image to fill a fixed soft-token budget. This gives 64,
256 and 256 image tokens, for each VLM respectively.
Iskill is initialized to uniform mid-gray and then optimized
with Adam for 80 epochs over the training split, with a batch
size of 12 and a learning rate of 0.03 that decays to zero on a
cosine schedule. We lower the momentum term to β1 = 0.5
(β2 = 0.999) so that each update follows the current gradient
more closely (consider our ablation on β1 in Sec. 5.2). Every
100 steps, the image is scored on the validation split with
the benchmark metric, and the best-scoring image is kept
for testing. If no image beats the model without a skill on
validation, we report the No Skill score, marked with ∗in
the tables.
4.3. Baselines
LLM-Skill is a text skill that GPT-5.5 writes in a single pass
from a description of the benchmark, its system prompt and
five training examples, without feedback from any target
model. One such skill per benchmark is therefore shared
by all models. SkillOpt [32] creates a text skill from scratch,
with GPT-6 Luna – as a cheaper alternative to GPT-5.5 –
reflecting on each target model’s rollouts on the training split
and keeping only edits that raise the validation score. Both
skills are appended to the system prompt. Because none of
the VLMs we tested allows images in the system prompt,
all images must be injected with the first user request. The

Who Moved My Z Boson? Revealing Resonance Features Inside a Neural
Network
Kevin A. Urqu´ıa-Calder´on 1 Midori Kato 1 Inar Timiryasov 1 Oleg Ruchayskiy 1
Abstract
Methods used in mechanistic interpretability have
revealed human-aligned concepts inside language
and image models.
In this paper, we search
for physics concepts inside a neural a genera-
tive collider physics model trained on real LHC
data (ShellFlow). We discover features inside
ShellFlow that represent resonances, such as
the Z, J/ψ, and Υ. The network was never told
which muons come from a resonance, it was only
trained to generate the kinematics of the final-state
particles. We use these features to alter aspects of
the Z boson: we change its mass between ∼80
and 105 GeV, and removing such a feature from
the neural network produces a broader Z peak.
In both cases the rest of the invariant mass spec-
trum remains mostly unchanged. The feature was
built from the gradients of the neural network, and
its selectivity was built using pattern recognition
methods. A generative particle physics model
trained on unlabeled data can be modified inter-
nally to change a physical quantity.
1. Introduction
Language and image models learn internal directions that
align with human concepts, and adding such a direction to
the activations, a steering vector, changes what the model
produces in a controlled way (Mikolov et al., 2013; Park
et al., 2024; Turner et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024; Zou
et al., 2023; Templeton et al., 2024; Sofroniew et al., 2026).
The same idea has been carried to image diffusion mod-
els (Haas et al., 2024; Gaintseva et al., 2026; Konovalova
et al., 2026) and to models of the natural sciences (Simon
& Zou, 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Dimitrievikj & Wells,
2025; Fear et al., 2025), including particle physics (Faucett
et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2024; Bonnet-Guerrini et al.,
2026b). Generative models are now also trained directly on
1Niels Bohr Institute, University of Copenhagen, Jagtvej 155A,
DK-2200, Copenhagen, Denmark. Correspondence to: Kevin A.
Urqu´ıa-Calder´on <kevin.urquia@nbi.ku.dk>.
Preprint. November 20, 2026.
real collision data from the Large Hadron Collider (LHC).
ShellFlow (Kato et al., 2026) is a Riemannian flow-
matching model trained on ATLAS Open Data (ATLAS
Collaboration, 2025a). It accurately reproduces the kine-
matics of LHC collisions, and most remarkably, it also
replicates inter-particle correlations, such as the invariant
mass spectrum of muon pairs, in particular the J/ψ, Υ, and
Z peaks. This raises a question: can a physical quantity,
like the mass of a resonance, be steered along a direction in
such a model? Such a direction would let us test whether
a generative model trained on collision data has learned
the physics of a resonance, and change a single physical
parameter of the generated sample without retraining.
In most of the steering literature, the effect of a steering
vector is judged by a classifier or a similarity score (Turner
et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024; Gaintseva et al., 2026;
Konovalova et al., 2026). These scores are used because
of a major limitation inherent in images or text: there is no
rigorous ground truth, so it is impossible to measure how
much a quantity changes. You cannot measure how much
a smile has changed in a picture. A generator of collision
events does not have this limitation: its output is a set of
four-momenta, on which a physical observable, such as the
invariant mass of a muon pair, can be measured.
In this paper, we search for a direction in ShellFlow that
is aligned with the concept of the Z boson. We aim to find
a steering vector that changes the mass of the Z boson and
leaves the rest of the dimuon spectrum unchanged. We find
its shape by doing a Taylor expansion of the invariant mass
with respect to the activations of the network, and keeping
only the linear term. We then argue that such steering vec-
tors are the ones that give the largest second moment of the
gradients, the derivatives of the invariant mass with respect
to the activations. We use a Fukunaga–Koontz transform
(FKT) (Fukunaga & Koontz, 1970) to find the vector along
which this second moment is the largest for the Z, and the
smallest for the other parts of the invariant mass spectrum.
We scale and add this vector to the muon tokens and study
the generated events.
We use this vector to change the mass of the Z boson with-
out changing much the J/ψ and Υ peaks, or the continuum.
This steering of the mass is predictable: we can select the
1
arXiv:2611.26291v1  [hep-ph]  19 Nov 2026
Who Moved My Z Boson?
mass of the Z pole itself. However, the steering also broad-
ens the Z peak. Furthermore, we test if this is a direction
that the network uses to construct its internal concept of the
Z boson, by ablating the direction in the residual stream,
where we find that the model generates a broader Z bosons
without this direction.
2. Previous work
Activation steering.
Early works looking for linear direc-
tions that point to concepts inside of a model were (Mikolov
et al., 2013; Alain & Bengio, 2016; Kim et al., 2018), later
formalised as the linear representation hypothesis (Park
et al., 2024). Such linear directions were then used to steer
the output of a model in (Subramani et al., 2022; Turner
et al., 2023) with the use of steering vectors. Steering vec-
tors have been built in the literature in different ways such
as: differences of activations (Turner et al., 2023; Rimsky
et al., 2024; Arditi et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023), a PCA of dif-
ferences of activations (Zou et al., 2023), sums of attention-
head outputs (Todd et al., 2024), sparse-autoencoder fea-
tures (Templeton et al., 2024), and vectors optimised by
gradient descent (Subramani et al., 2022; Dunefsky & Co-
han, 2025). Our steering vectors were obtained from a
generalized eigenproblem that contrasts classes, on the gra-
dients of the model’s own output. The closest methods to
ours are (Beaglehole et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026), which
take eigenvectors of the “Average Gradient Outer Product”
of a classifier trained on the activations. Attribution patch-
ing (Nanda, 2023; Syed et al., 2024) also uses gradients with
respect to the activations, but to locate the components and
circuits responsible for a behaviour, not to build a steering
direction.
Steering in diffusion and flow-matching models.
Vari-
ous steering analyses have been done on diffusion and flow
matching models. This includes finding steering vectors
in audio (Staniszewski et al., 2026) and video (Hong et al.,
2026) models. However, by far, the most work has been
done in text-to-image work, with methods using differences
of mean activations between contrasting prompts (Gaint-
seva et al., 2026; Konovalova et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026),
sparse-autoencoder features (Surkov et al., 2025; Kim &
Ghadiyaram, 2025), and, in unconditional image models,
gradients (Haas et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026). We steer
a Riemannian flow-matching generator of collision events
that is conditioned on the particle content of the recon-
structed event, rather than on text like most of the examples
highlighted before. This also provides us a more rigorous
approach to what the ground truth is with respect to what
we are steering, and can even properly check if the steering
respects physical laws.
Interpretability in natural science models.
A growing
body of work has studied interpretability in the natural sci-
ences. In biology, many studies have found and/or steered
interpretable features of protein language models (Simon &
Zou, 2025; Villegas Garcia & Ansuini, 2025; Huang et al.,
2025; Parsan et al., 2025). In chemistry, steering vectors
have been found in chemical language models (Dimitrievikj
& Wells, 2025). In physics, interpretability methods have
been applied to models of partial differential equations (Fear
et al., 2025; Patil et al., 2026), weather (MacMillan & Ouel-
lette, 2025), quantum many-body states (Qi & Earls, 2026),
cosmology and astronomy (Ocampo et al., 2025; Ocampo
& Ca˜nas-Herrera, 2026; Bonnet-Guerrini et al., 2026c; Wu
& Walmsley, 2025), and nuclear structure (Kitouni et al.,
2024). In particle physics, they have been applied to jet
classifiers (Faucett et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2024; Rai
& Ganguly, 2026), to parton distributions (Kriesten et al.,
2024; Bonnet-Guerrini et al., 2026a), to the latent space of
a jet variational autoencoder (Collins, 2021), to jet-tagging
transformers (Tiourine & Thais, 2026), and for a neutrino-
telescope foundation model (Bonnet-Guerrini et al., 2026b).
This paper, to our knowledge, presents the first application
of steering vectors to a generative particle-physics model.

3.2. ShellFlow
In a previous work we introduced ShellFlow (Kato
et al., 2026), a Riemannian conditional flow-matching trans-
former that generates the kinematics of reconstructed col-
lider events, given the particle composition of the event.
It was trained on unlabelled real data: a mixed dataset of
the two-to-four-lepton (ATLAS Collaboration, 2025c) and
the 1LMET30 (ATLAS Collaboration, 2025b) skims of the
ATLAS Open Data 13 TeV release (ATLAS Collaboration,
2025a). We trained only on events with, at most, eight
particles. In total the dataset has ∼825 million events; the
training-validation split is 95/5.
The model has two different manifolds, one for massless
particles (electrons, muons, and photons) and another for
massive particles (jets). The massless manifold is R ×

A Statistical Framework for Training Data
Auditing of Large Language Models
Shengjie Niua ∗, Yeheng Gea ∗, Jian Huanga,b†
aDepartment of Data Science and Artificial Intelligence, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University
bDepartment of Applied Mathematics, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University
November 20, 2026
Abstract
Training-data auditing asks whether data of interest were used to train a large lan-
guage model (LLM), a question central to privacy auditing, copyright protection, and
benchmark-contamination detection. These concerns are particularly relevant to the
use of copyrighted books and scientific papers in pre-training, as well as synthetic text
and medical question–answer records in fine-tuning. In practice, training membership
signals may be concentrated in only a few passages of a long document, making it
important to aggregate evidence within each document without diluting these localized
signals. Beyond individual documents, auditing a target collection requires an overall
assessment based on the document-level evidence. In this paper, we propose a uni-
fied statistical framework for document-level membership inference, target-collection
global auditing, and suspicious-subset identification. We integrate complementary
chunk-level membership evidence with Cauchy combination to construct document
scores for document-level membership inference. The document scores and their
calibrated p-values further enable an overall assessment of training-data collection use
and the identification of suspicious documents through multiple testing. Under the
stated exchangeability conditions, we establish finite-sample validity of document-level
p-values, type-I error control for global auditing, and false discovery rate control
for subset identification. Case studies on BookTection, Pile–arXiv, Cosmopedia,
and HealthCareMagic demonstrate the effectiveness and reliability of the proposed
framework in auditing pre-training and fine-tuning data.
Keywords: Membership inference; multiple testing; large language model; training data
auditing.
∗Co-first authors.
†Corresponding author.
1
arXiv:2611.26264v1  [stat.ML]  19 Nov 2026
1
Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) are trained on vast text corpora whose composition is often
undisclosed (Brown et al. 2020). Their ability to memorize and reproduce training content
raises privacy and copyright concerns (Tang et al. 2024, Duarte et al. 2024), while the
inclusion of benchmark evaluation data can compromise model assessment (Oren et al. 2023).
These concerns motivate training-data auditing, which seeks to determine whether particular
texts were used during training (Shi et al. 2024). Membership inference (MIA) (Shokri
et al. 2017) formulates this question as a binary decision between member and non-member
status. This task is fundamentally a statistical decision problem: the auditor must extract
membership signals from limited and heterogeneous model outputs, aggregate diverse and
dependent evidence, and translate the aggregate into membership decisions with controlled
error rates. Meeting these requirements calls for principled statistical methodology for
training-data auditing at both the document and collection levels. Accordingly, we develop a
unified statistical framework for training-data auditing that addresses three complementary
objectives: document-level membership inference, global auditing of a target collection, and
identification of suspicious subsets.
The first objective is document-level auditing: determining whether a specific document
was included in the target model’s training set.
Documents such as scientific papers
and Wikipedia pages can span thousands of tokens, while membership signals may be
concentrated in localized paragraphs (Chen et al. 2026). Auditing such documents therefore
involves extracting evidence from smaller units, referred to as chunks, and aggregating
it at the document level (Puerto et al. 2025). For each chunk, auditing methods derive
membership evidence statistics from model outputs, such as perplexity and log-probability-
based scores. These statistics exploit differences in model fit: the overfitting nature of large
language models can lead to lower prediction loss on training text than on non-member
2
text, corresponding to lower perplexity and higher average token log-probabilities (Maini
et al. 2024). These statistics may be dependent across chunks within the same document,
making evidence combination and aggregation statistically challenging.
The second objective is target-collection global auditing: examining evidence of training-
data use across a collection of documents. Dataset inference (Maini et al. 2024) addresses
this objective by testing whether any members of the target dataset were used for training.
This problem is particularly relevant to data owners, businesses, and rights holders seeking
to verify large-scale use of their data. For example, a scholarly publisher may suspect
that its journal corpus was used in LLM pre-training, while an AI company may seek to
determine whether its proprietary reasoning dataset was used to fine-tune a competitor’s
model. However, the statistical tests and uncertainty estimates used by these approaches
rely on independence assumptions and lack corresponding validity guarantees for collections
of dependent documents.
The third objective is suspicious-subset identification. It determines which specific
documents in a target collection are likely to be training members. Existing dataset-level
methods mostly provide aggregate conclusions about collection-level usage and have paid
comparatively little attention to itemized evidence. In copyright and compliance auditing,
rights holders and auditors often need an itemized list of suspicious documents to support
data-use claims and guide further verification. Because such a list may support legal or
regulatory action, the proportion of false inclusions must be controlled. We formalize
this requirement through false discovery rate (FDR) control under dependent document
signals (Benjamini & Hochberg 1995). The result is an itemized list in which the expected
proportion of false accusations is bounded by a prespecified level q, yielding evidence reliable
enough to support legal, regulatory, or organizational review.
In this paper, we propose a multi-level statistical framework for training-data auditing, as
3
illustrated in Figure 1. The framework unifies the three auditing objectives by translat-
ing chunk-level membership evidence into document-level conclusions and collection-level
decisions. These transitions introduce distinct statistical challenges. Within a document,
heterogeneous and dependent chunk-level statistics complicate aggregation, which may dilute
localized membership signals or amplify noisy evidence (Chen et al. 2026). Across documents,
the signals are also dependent because all documents are scored by the same fitted rule
and calibrated against the same non-member collection. This dependence among document
scores complicates both the calibration of global tests and FDR control for suspicious-subset
identification. To address these challenges, we integrate complementary statistical tools
into a unified auditing framework: Cauchy combination (Liu & Xie 2020) aggregates local
evidence into document scores sensitive to localized signals, and empirical calibration against
held-out non-member documents then provides a basis for individual membership testing.
At the collection level, an Energy permutation test (Székely & Rizzo 2013) is applied to
assess distributional departures from non-member behavior, while the Benjamini–Hochberg
(BH) procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg 1995) is considered to select suspicious documents
using the calibrated document-level p-values. Under the stated exchangeability conditions,
which permit dependence among document scores, we establish type-I error control for
individual and global testing and FDR control for subset identification.
Our framework applies to both pre-training and fine-tuning data auditing. We study four
case studies to evaluate the proposed framework. For pre-training, we examine copyrighted
books from BookTection and scientific papers from Pile–arXiv, where auditing involves
aggregating local membership evidence across long documents. For fine-tuning, we examine
synthetic text from Cosmopedia and medical question–answer records from HealthCareMagic
to assess whether these data were used to fine-tune the pretrained models. Across these
case studies, we assess the framework’s detection performance and statistical reliability at
4
all the document, collection, and subset levels.
Our contributions are threefold. First, we formulate LLM training-data auditing through
three complementary statistical objectives: document-level membership inference, target-
collection global auditing, and suspicious-subset identification with explicit error control.
Second, we develop a unified framework that combines heterogeneous chunk-level evidence
and uses Cauchy combination to construct document scores sensitive to localized membership
signals. These scores support empirically calibrated individual testing, Energy-based global
auditing, and BH subset identification. Third, under the stated conditional exchangeability
conditions, we establish finite-sample validity of document-level calibration, type-I error
control for individual and global testing, and FDR control for subset identification. We
further quantify the additional error caused by departures from exchangeability.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the preliminaries,
the datasets, and formulates the auditing problems.
Section 3 presents the proposed
statistical auditing framework.
Section 4 establishes its theoretical guarantees under
conditional exchangeability and quantifies the effects of departures from these conditions.
Section 5 evaluates the framework through four case studies spanning pre-training and
fine-tuning data auditing. Section 6 concludes the paper.
2
Preliminaries, Datasets, and Problems
2.1
Preliminaries
Autoregressive Language Models
Autoregressive LLMs model by predicting each
token conditional on its preceding context (Brown et al. 2020). Let w = (w1, . . . , wL) denote
a token sequence of length L, and let w<t = (w1, . . . , wt−1) denote the prefix preceding
5
token wt. For a model with parameters θ, the sequence likelihood factorizes as
pθ(w) =
L
Y
t=1
pθ(wt | w<t),
(1)
where pθ(wt | w<t) is the conditional probability assigned to token wt. These models are
typically trained by minimizing the negative log-likelihood (NLL) of the training sequences.
These token-level conditional probabilities are also the quantities on which auditing is
based. Evaluating them for a given sequence requires a single forward pass rather than text
generation, and their negative logarithms are the per-token losses from which perplexity
and the other membership evidence statistics below are obtained.
Auditor Access
We consider a black-box setting in which the auditor can query the
target model with a token sequence and obtain the conditional probability of each token
given its preceding context. The auditor has no access to the model’s internal parameters or
the membership labels of the target documents. Such token probabilities can be obtained
through token-scoring APIs or self-hosted model interfaces. The Min-K% + + features used
in our experiments additionally require access to the full next-token predictive distribution
or the corresponding moments defined in Supplementary Section S1.
For fine-tuning data auditing, we additionally assume the auditor has black-box query access
to the model used to initialize fine-tuning, which serves as a reference model. This assumption
reflects a common scenario in which an organization fine-tunes a publicly available model
on private data, while the initial model remains available for querying (Touvron et al. 2023).
Comparing the outputs of the target and reference models provides evidence of changes in
model behavior associated with fine-tuning.
Membership Signals and Evidence
Training-data auditing uses observable model
outputs, such as token-level conditional probabilities, as membership signals. Auditing
6
methods transform these signals, optionally together with auxiliary information, into scalar
statistics that quantify membership evidence for a queried sequence. For example, perplexity
(PPL) summarizes how well the model predicts the sequence, whereas Min-K% focuses
on its least predictable tokens. Smaller PPL values and larger Min-K% values indicate
stronger membership evidence. Other methods incorporate reference-model outputs or
textual characteristics to adjust these statistics. These methods provide different aspects of
the model’s behavior, motivating us to combine their statistics into chunk-level membership
evidence for subsequent document-level auditing. The individual evidence statistics are
detailed in Supplementary Section S1.
2.2
Datasets
LLM training commonly involves large-scale pre-training followed by fine-tuning on selected
data, and our framework audits data use in either stage.
We study BookTection (Duarte et al. 2024) and Pile–arXiv (Gao et al. 2020) for pre-training
data auditing, and Cosmopedia (Ben Allal et al. 2024) and HealthCareMagic (Li et al. 2023,
HCM) for fine-tuning data auditing. Membership is defined with respect to the training
stage under audit.
BookTection comprises excerpts from 165 books, with roughly 34 original passages per
book. We use the benchmark’s Medium setting, which provides passages with a nominal
length of 128 tokens. Each book serves as a document-level inferential unit, with its passages
treated as chunks. Following the benchmark’s publication-date labeling rule, we treat 105
classic books published in or before 2021 as candidate members and 60 books published
in 2023 as non-members. Books published in 2022 are excluded because their membership
status is ambiguous under this rule. This benchmark allows us to evaluate how aggregating
passage-level membership evidence supports individual book auditing.
7
Pile–arXiv consists of full-text scientific papers from the arXiv component of The Pile (Gao
et al. 2020). The public release used here contains 79,046 papers from the first training
shard and 4,841 papers from the official held-out validation and test splits. Each record
contains a paper’s main text, mathematical expressions, references, and source metadata.
We treat each paper as a document-level inferential unit. For Pythia target models trained
on the corresponding Pile corpus, papers from the training partition are members, while
those from the held-out partitions are non-members.
Cosmopedia provides synthetic English text, including educational explanations, textbook-
style passages, and other expository content. We use its web_samples_v2 subset, which
contains 10,345,867 records generated from web-page excerpts.
Each record includes
generated text, a generation prompt, and metadata describing the source, format, intended
audience, and token length. We use the generated text as the document-level input and
fine-tune Pythia-2.8B on selected documents using the next-token prediction objective.
Documents used in this fine-tuning run are members, while withheld documents are non-
members.
HealthCareMagic (HCM) contains 112,165 health-care question–answer records, each
comprising an instruction, a patient question, and an answer. We treat each complete record
as a document-level inferential unit. We adapt Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct to the medical domain
through supervised fine-tuning, using the instruction and patient question as conditioning
context and the answer as the supervised response. Records used for gradient updates are
members, while withheld records are non-members.
2.3
Problem Formulation
Let Fθtarget denote the target LLM with parameters θtarget and trained on an undisclosed
corpus Dtrain. For a target collection Dtarget = {di}m

Time Series Structure Learning with Local Causal Parent Discovery
Jacqueline Maasch
Cornell Tech
jam887@cornell.edu
Shu Wan
Abel AI
shu.wan@abel.ai
Hank Zhu
Abel AI
hank.zhu@abel.ai
Huan Liu
Arizona State University
Zhiguang Wang
Abel AI
Abstract
Learning and inference on time series can pose significant statistical challenges, including autocor-
related observations, distribution shift over time, and the curse of dimensionality. These challenges
complicate the practical application of causal discovery algorithms, which already suffer from high
computational and sample complexity in the general case. To mitigate these issues, this work in-
troduces Iterative Temporal Parent Discovery (ITPD): a sound and complete constraint-based pro-
cedure for causal structure learning on multivariate time series with causal nonstationarity. ITPD
takes a local-to-global learning approach that discovers the global graph by sequentially discover-
ing the parent set for each variable. ITPD exploits temporal structural priors, graph partitioning,
and the local Markov condition to swap higher-order conditional independence tests for lower-order
alternatives. With an exact oracle, ITPD performed the least number of tests and used the smallest
average conditioning set sizes relative to baselines. In benchmarking simulations, ITPD sat on the
Pareto frontier with respect to F1 and wall-clock time and was faster than baselines on large graphs
(≥1000 nodes). For graphs with 2000 nodes, ITPD ran 2.3×, 9.1×, and 40.9× faster than iterative
IAMB, DF-PC, and PCMCI, respectively.
Keywords: Time series, causal discovery, graphical models
1. Introduction
Temporal data naturally arise in many high-impact domains, including biomedicine, signal process-
ing, meteorology, ecology, finance, prediction markets, and dynamical systems research. In these
settings, knowledge of how causal relationships recur and change over time can support decision-
making, forecasting, and intervention. In practice, temporal causal structure is rarely known a priori
and must be learned from data (Glymour et al., 2019). However, many advancements in statistics
and machine learning assume independent and identically distributed (iid) random variables and
some form of stationarity (Hastie et al., 2009), complicating their direct application to temporal
data with autocorrelation and distribution shift (Figure 1). Such challenges motivate the design of
special methods for time series analysis (Brockwell and Davis, 2009), including temporal causal
discovery algorithms (Assaad et al., 2022; Runge et al., 2023; Hasan et al., 2023).
This work considers the problem of temporal causal discovery under distribution shift. We
restrict our attention to the constraint-based paradigm, which uses sequential conditional indepen-
dence (CI) tests to infer graphical structure (Spirtes et al., 2001). This paradigm benefits from a
wealth of theoretical results, minimal innate parametric assumptions, and explainability. However,
constraint-based discovery suffers from several drawbacks in the general case, including high com-
putational complexity and high sample complexity (Shiragur et al., 2024).

The computational complexity of constraint-
based discovery is often measured with respect
to (wrt) the worst-case number of CI tests re-
quired (Spirtes et al., 2001). For the general
case, this is exponential wrt some graph pa-
rameter (e.g., total nodes, maximum in-degree,
etc.).
Unless assumptions are placed on the
data generating process, it has been shown that
the number of CI tests is lower bounded by a
value that is exponential in the maximum undi-
rected clique size of the essential graph (Mon´es
et al., 2026).
CI testing is known to be a
hard problem in the general case (Shah and Pe-
ters, 2020), with exponential sample complex-
ity wrt the size of the conditioning set. Expo-
nential time and sample complexity can prevent
tractable discovery on large data, motivating diverse strategies for pruning CI tests and reducing
their order (i.e., the number of variables in the conditioning set) (Shiragur et al., 2024; Kim and
Lee, 2026). We extend this effort to the time series setting, where high-dimensional data often arise.
The search space of time series directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) can be significantly reduced by
leveraging known problem structure, such as temporal structural priors or other graph parameters.
Exploiting structural priors for efficiency gains is a common strategy in local causal discovery
algorithms that only learn contextually relevant subgraphs (Maasch et al., 2024). This work applies
lessons from local structure learning to time series whose causal graphs are nonstationary. As an
inspiration point, we naively apply previously introduced local discovery algorithms (Tsamardinos
et al., 2003b; Maasch et al., 2025) in iterative fashion to obtain the global graph. As these local
discovery algorithms were not intended for global time series discovery, this naive approach can
entail extraneous CI tests or unnecessarily large conditioning sets. To mitigate this, we introduce an
iterative procedure that is tailored for nonstationary temporal graphs.
Contributions
Our methodological and empirical contributions are as follows.
§4 Local-to-global temporal causal discovery algorithms.
§4.2 Iterative Parent Discovery on Leaves (IPaDL). We present Algorithm B.2, a sound and
complete naive baseline that extends a previously introduced local parent discovery algo-
rithm to the nonstationary time series setting. We use the inefficiencies of this simplistic
adaptation as an inspiration and departure point for our core algorithmic contribution.
§4.3 Iterative Temporal Parent Discovery (ITPD). We present Algorithm 1, a sound and com-
plete causal discovery algorithm for nonstationary time series designed to reduce reliance
on high-order CI tests. Additionally, we provide support for manually-derived theoretical
results via AI-assisted autoformalization in Lean.
§5 Empirical validation and open code. Theoretical claims are numerically verified on synthetic
and semi-synthetic data. ITPD sat on the Pareto frontier wrt F1 and wall-clock time as well
as F1 and unique CI tests per variable. On graphs with 1000 to 2000 variables, ITPD was the
fastest running method tested. Code is available on GitHub.1
1. https://anonymous.4open.science/r/itpd-0FC0
Preprint, 2027
2
TIME SERIES STRUCTURE LEARNING WITH LOCAL CAUSAL PARENT DISCOVERY
§E.3 Negative results post-mortem. We provide a supplementary discussion of a systematic ablation
study, highlighting strategies that failed to contribute to improved efficiency in ITPD.
2. Related Works
Time Series Causal Discovery
Diverse strategies have been proposed for learning temporal struc-
ture from data. An historically dominant approach has been Granger causality and its variants
(Granger, 1969; Geweke, 1982), including neural Granger causality (Marcinkeviˇcs and Vogt, 2021;
Tank et al., 2022; L¨owe et al., 2022). Constraint-based algorithms have been extended to this setting,
including FCI (Entner and Hoyer, 2010). Most notably, the PCMCI family of algorithms extends
PC to causally stationary settings under causal sufficiency and latent variables, with and without
contemporaneous links (Runge et al., 2019; Runge, 2020; G¨unther et al., 2023; Runge et al., 2023).
Methods that assume functional causal models (Fujiwara et al., 2023) and neural methods also
abound (Pamfil et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2023). See Assaad et al. (2022); Hasan et al. (2023) for
thorough surveys on time series causal discovery.
Local Causal Discovery
Often, the problem setting for causal discovery does not necessitate
knowledge of the full graphical structure. Instead, learning local substructures is often sufficient to
answer the scientific questions of interest. This emphasis on tailored local discovery can yield more
computationally and sample efficient search procedures. Hence, local causal discovery (Cooper,
1997) is a popular strategy for many problems, including parent and child discovery (Gao and Ji,
2015), Markov blanket (MB) discovery (Tsamardinos et al., 2003a,b; Aliferis et al., 2010; Wang
et al., 2014), valid adjustment set discovery (Cheng et al., 2023; Gupta et al., 2023; Maasch et al.,
2024, 2025; Li et al., 2026), identifying necessary and sufficient explanatory variables (Cai et al.,
2023), and causal fairness analysis (Maasch et al., 2025). Local learning can also be used as a
subroutine for global causal discovery in static DAGs (Hiremath et al., 2024) and in the time series
setting (Fujiwara et al., 2023), as we do in the present work.
3. Preliminaries
Notation
We represent random variables by uppercase letters and their realizations by lowercase,
with sets of variables and vector-values in bold (e.g., V = v, V = v). Graphs are denoted by
calligraphic script (e.g., G). Given a variable V in DAG G, we denote its set of parents, children,
ancestors, descendants, nondescendants, and spouses in G as pa(V ), ch(V ), an(V ), de(V ), and
nd(V ), respectively. Let the ancestor set of a set be denoted an(S) := S
W∈S an(W). Sets c

pa(X) ⊆an(X) and ch(X) ⊆de(X). We denote the probabilistic independence of random
variables by ⊥⊥and the independence of nodes in G (d-separation) by ⊥⊥G. Let X →Y denote that
variable X is a direct cause of another variable Y , while X →· · · →Y denotes an indirect causal
path. The absence of a directed edge between X and Y is denoted X̸ →Y .
3.0.1. TEMPORAL CAUSAL MODELS
We consider structural causal models (SCMs) in the nonparametric structural equation models with
independent errors (NPSEM-IE) regime (Wang et al., 2025).

Definition 1 (Structural causal model (SCM), Bareinboim et al. 2022) An SCM is a tuple M :=
⟨U, p(u), V, F⟩where U is the set of exogenous variables explained by mechanisms external to M,
p(u) is the distribution over U, V is the set of endogenous variables explained by U ∪V, and F

4. Local-to-Global Time Series Discovery
This section introduces two algorithms: (1) IPaDL, a sound and complete yet naive extension of an
existing parent discovery algorithm (Maasch et al., 2025), which served as an inspiration point and
cheap baseline for this work; and (2) ITPD, a sound and complete constraint-based procedure that
overcomes some of the inefficiencies of IPaDL. While IPaDL is a pure causal partitioning algorithm
(Maasch et al., 2024), ITPD takes a combined strategy that leverages temporal structural priors and
the local Markov condition (Definition 3). To handle causal nonstationarity, ITPD does not assume
a recurring window graph as done in baselines PCMCI (Runge et al., 2019) and DYNOTEARS
(Pamfil et al., 2020), and instead learns the unique parent set for every node individually.

4.1. Data Settings: Stationary & Nonstationary Data
The proposed methods are applicable to two settings. While the nonstationary setting is the primary
focus of this work, a stationary setting can be assumed if desired. Let D denote our observational
dataset and N the number of variables observed at each of T time steps.
S1 Single multivariate time series with causal stationarity: D ∈RT×N. As in PCMCI, ITPD for
S1 assumes causal stationarity over a maximum lag of τmax and returns a window graph.
S2 Multiple multivariate time series with causal nonstationarity: D ∈RM×T×N, where M is the
number of replicate time series. In S2, ITPD does not assume causal stationarity and returns a
full time graph. Each T × N time series T is independently sampled M times from the joint
distribution: Tm

the same underlying dynamical system. Under faithfulness, this implies that each trajectory is
also an iid sample from the same SCM M with causal graph G.
S1 can arise in finance and prediction markets (e.g., only a single ground truth trajectory can be
observed for a given stock price). S2 naturally arises in panel data sampled from a population, as
commonly encountered in economics, sociology, epidemiology, and clinical research. In S2, repli-
cate trajectories can represent patients in a clinical trial, citizens in census data, users of a wearable
device, etc. Under S2, this work allows for causal nonstationarity. Natural examples where causal
nonstationarity can arise include gene regulatory networks, where regulatory relationships change
over development (e.g., in early embryonic stages versus senescence); ecological data, where pop-
ulations can collapse and exotic species can be introduced; and climate data, where new biotic and
abiotic causes can arise over geologic history (e.g., anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions).
4.2. A Naive Causal Partitioning Baseline
This work was inspired by the premise that one could iteratively run an efficient local parent dis-
covery procedure to obtain a global nonstationary graph. To this end, we devised a naive baseline
method against which to compare our final algorithm: Iterative Parent Discovery on Leaves (IPaDL;
Algorithm B.2). Based on a subroutine of the local causal partitioning algorithm LD3 (Maasch et al.,
2024) that we term Parent Discovery on Leaves (PaDL, pronounced paddle; Algorithm B.1), IPaDL
extends to the TiMINo setting for S1 and S2. Though sound and complete under sufficient con-
ditions (Theorem 13), PaDL was designed for a setting with different structural priors: namely,
no time-indexing and unknown relation between X and Y . Thus, naively applying PaDL to each
variable results in extraneous CI tests and unnecessarily large conditioning sets. IPaDL therefore
serves as a proof-of-concept that iterative local parent discovery is a viable strategy for temporal
graph learning, but thoughtful extensions are required for efficiency. See Appendix C for a com-
plete discussion with proofs. To our knowledge, this work represents the first case of leveraging
local causal partitioning for time series discovery. Additionally, this work uses causal partitioning

Attention Head Specialization:
Phase Transitions in Sample Complexity
Léo Catteau1, Odilon Duranthon1, Lenka Zdeborová1
1 Statistical Physics of Computation Laboratory,
École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL) CH-1015 Lausanne
Abstract
Attention heads specialize into distinct functions during training, often emerging in
stages together with sharp changes in model behavior. While this phenomenon has mostly
been studied as a function of training time, we ask how head specialization depends on the
amount of available training data. Empirically, we find that heads specialized to syntactic
relations in BERT emerge as the dataset size increases. We then study this phenomenon in
a solvable high-dimensional model of multi-head attention and establish that, in this model,
head specialization is a genuine phase transition in sample complexity, corresponding to a
non-analyticity in the test error and other observables. Depending on data structure and
regularization, specialization can follow uninformative head differentiation or occur through
a cascade of phase transitions that progressively recover weaker latent features, providing
a statistical form of simplicity bias. Finally, we relate these statistical transitions to the
stagewise emergence of specialized heads during online learning, disentangling statistical
from dynamical origins of head specialization.
1
Introduction
Multi-head attention is a central architectural ingredient of modern transformer models, enabling
multiple attention patterns to coexist within a single layer. Different heads learn to perform
distinct functions, while their collaboration allows implementing circuits that no individual
head captures alone. Empirical studies have identified such specialized heads across multiple
settings, including induction heads involved in in-context learning (ICL) (Olsson et al., 2022;
Yin and Steinhardt, 2025), heads specializing to different syntactic relations (Chen et al., 2024a),
and heads progressively differentiating into distinct functional roles during training (Wang
et al., 2025). Head specialization has predominantly been studied as a function of training time:
specialized mechanisms emerge at distinct stages of training, sometimes coinciding with sharp
improvements in performance or drops in training loss (Hoogland et al., 2025; Aoyama et al.,
2026).
Much less is known about specialization as a function of the amount of available training data.
Rather than asking when during training different heads specialize, one can ask how many samples
are needed for distinct specialized heads to emerge. This distinction separates a statistical
question about the information available in the dataset from the particular optimization dynamics
used to learn it. We investigate this question in BERT masked language models (MLMs), where
syntactic attention structure (SAS), characterized by heads specializing to different syntactic
relations (Clark et al., 2019), emerges during training alongside a sharp drop in loss (Chen
et al., 2024a). Empirically, training BERTSmall models from random initialization on datasets of
N sequences from BookCorpus and English Wikipedia reveals a clear phenomenology shown
in Fig. 1: as N increases, SAS emerges sharply over a characteristic range of dataset sizes,
accompanied by abrupt changes in the learning curves. For each dataset size, we fix the sequences

enabled by specialization of the heads.
Sample complexity provides a natural control parameter for asking whether such emergence
corresponds to a genuine phase transition. In the statistical physics of learning, one considers a
proportional high-dimensional limit in which the number of trainable degrees of freedom and
training samples grow together, D, N →∞at fixed α = N/D. This framework has a long history
in neural-network theory, where increasing sample complexity can induce phase transitions from
permutation symmetric to specialized solutions in the committee machine (Schwarze and Hertz,
1992; 1993; Aubin et al., 2018). In this limit, changes between qualitatively different learning
regimes can become sharp, with nonanalyticities of macroscopic observables at critical values
of α. For multi-head attention, this raises a precise question: can the emergence of specialized
heads be understood as a genuine phase transition controlled by sample complexity?
We answer this question in a tractable multi-feature variant of the single-location regression
(SLR) model (Marion et al., 2025; Sagitova et al., 2026), whose head-specialization dynamics
under online learning were characterized in Sagitova et al. (2026). The task is to retrieve one
token carrying a low-dimensional latent signal from a sequence of otherwise uninformative tokens,
using multiple attention heads that can specialize to different latent features. Here, instead of
following training dynamics, we study the associated empirical risk minimization (ERM) problem
as a function of sample complexity. Fig. 1 shows that this model exhibits behavior qualitatively
analogous to that observed in the BERTSmall experiment. Moreover, we show that, in this model,
head specialization occurs through phase transitions in sample complexity, characterized by
2
non-analyticities in the order parameters and prediction error at critical values of α.
The resulting phase diagram reveals a richer structure than a single specialization threshold.
At low regularization and low sample complexity, specialization is preceded by an unspecialized
phase with broken head-permutation symmetry, in which heads differ by fitting sample-specific
fluctuations without recovering distinct latent features. This illustrates that distinct attention
patterns alone do not imply specialization that improves generalization. For heterogeneous
signals, increasing sample complexity instead produces a cascade of specialization transitions:
heads successively recover latent features from strongest to weakest, so that increasingly subtle
structure requires increasingly more data. This provides a statistical counterpart of stagewise
learning and simplicity bias, arising here from the structure of the ERM solutions rather than
from a particular training dynamics.
Finally, we connect these equilibrium transitions back to the training-time phenomenology
from which we started (Olsson et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2025; Aoyama et al., 2026; Chen et al.,
2024a). In online learning, training time and the amount of observed data increase together,
entangling the statistical transition with optimization dynamics. In the solvable model, we show
how the critical sample complexities map onto the emergence of specialized heads along training.
This perspective suggests that some of the abrupt or stagewise emergence observed during
transformer training may reflect underlying statistical phase transitions, while distinguishing
these from phenomena that are genuinely dynamical and helping clarify how such transitions
manifest in learning dynamics.
Main Contributions
The main empirical result of the paper is the characterization of head
specialization in the number of training samples. In a tractable model of multi-head attention,
we then show that head specialization is a statistical phase transition in sample complexity,
and connect the equilibrium transition to specialization during training. Our main technical
contributions are:
• We derive a tight asymptotic characterization of the regularized ERM problem in the
proportional high-dimensional limit N, D →∞at fixed α = N/D, through closed self-
consistent equations for the errors and order parameters (Sec.3).
• We show that head specialization is a genuine phase transition in sample complexity.
Depending on regularization and signal structure, we uncover an unspecialized phase with
broken head-permutation symmetry, as well as a cascade of specialization transitions in
which increasingly weaker latent features are recovered with increasing sample complexity,
yielding a statistical form of simplicity bias (Sec.4).
• We establish a controlled correspondence between these equilibrium phase transitions
and the emergence of specialized heads during online learning, relating critical sample
complexities to training-time specialization and disentangling statistical from optimization-
dependent effects (Sec.5).
Notations.
We write [n] = {1, . . . , n}, δij for the Kronecker delta, and In for the identity
matrix. For a matrix A, Ai and A:j denote its i-th row and j-th column. We write ∥·∥2 for
the Euclidean norm, ∥·∥F for the Frobenius norm, and v⊗2 = vv⊤. We denote by N(µ, Σ) the
Gaussian distribution with mean µ and covariance Σ.
Related works
Empirical emergence and head specialization.
Specialized attention heads have been
observed across architectures and tasks, including induction heads associated with in-context
learning (Olsson et al., 2022; Yin and Steinhardt, 2025), syntactic heads in masked language
models (Chen et al., 2024a), and circuits studied in controlled synthetic settings (Singh et al.,
3
2024). A complementary literature studies when such capabilities and internal mechanisms
emerge during training, including abrupt changes in performance (Wei et al., 2022), stagewise
development and head differentiation (Hoogland et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025), and the
emergence time of induction heads (Aoyama et al., 2026). Such behavior can depend strongly
on data, initialization, and training trajectory: emergent capabilities can be transient (Singh
et al., 2023), vary across random seeds (Juneja et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2026), and depend on
the structure of the training data (Qin et al., 2025). While these works predominantly follow a
model through training, our BERT experiments instead hold dataset size fixed for each training
run, and study how syntactic head specialization changes across datasets of different sizes.
Theory of attention and head specialization.
Recent solvable models characterize learning
in attention architectures, including single-location regression (Marion et al., 2025; Duranthon
et al., 2026), sequence multi-index models (Troiani et al., 2025), attention-indexed models
(Boncoraglio et al., 2026), mapping to generalized Potts model (Rende et al., 2024), or hierarchical
models (Cagnetta and Wyart, 2024). Multi-head specialization has primarily been studied through
training dynamics (Chen et al., 2024b; Singh et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025; Sagitova et al.,
2026; Yüksel et al., 2026). Here we instead study specialization at equilibrium as a function of
sample complexity.
Phase transitions and specialization in neural networks.
Specialization as a sample-
complexity phase transition has a long history in committee machines, where increasing α = N/D
can induce transitions to solutions in which different hidden units align with distinct features
of the data (Schwarze and Hertz, 1992; 1993; Aubin et al., 2018; Pérez Ortiz et al., 2026).
Phase transitions have also been studied in solvable attention models (Cui et al., 2024); most
closely, Lavie et al. (2026) establish a sample-complexity transition for the emergence of a single
copy head. We instead study specialization of attention heads and the associated emerging
generalization capabilities.

Learn, Freeze, and Transfer an Activation Function
Across Architectures
Arun Prakash A
Nilekani Centre at AI4Bharat
Indian Institute of Technology Madras
a.arun283@gmail.com
Abstract
Transfer learning typically reuses knowledge acquired by a source network through
its learned weights. We investigate whether a learned activation function can also
be transferred and remain useful in networks trained from scratch. We study this
complementary form of transfer through a learn–freeze–transfer protocol, in which
the activation is optimized jointly with a source network in a single training run,
and is then frozen and reused in target networks trained from scratch. A pointwise
activation with globally shared parameters is independent of layer dimensions
and can therefore be incorporated into networks of different architectures trained
from scratch. We instantiate this protocol with FAct, a five-parameter activa-
tion represented by a two-harmonic truncated Fourier series, initialized from a
Fourier approximation of GELU and learned in a Vision Transformer (ViT) on
ImageNet-1K. When reused in a ViT of the same architecture trained from scratch
on ImageNet-1K, the frozen activation (Frozen FAct) improves top-1 accuracy
by 1.46 percentage points over GELU. Across four smaller target architectures
(standard ViT, Swin Transformer, linear-attention ViT, and MLP-Mixer) and four
image-classification datasets, it achieves the highest mean accuracy among eleven
activation functions in 15 of 16 settings under a common training configuration,
with improvements of up to 1.71 percentage points over the best conventional
activation. When the learning rate and weight decay are tuned separately for each
activation under the same search budget, Frozen FAct still ranks first in 11 of the 16
settings, second in four, and fourth in one. These results provide empirical evidence
that a learned activation function can retain its usefulness when transferred across
vision architectures, independently of the weights with which it was learned.
1
Introduction
Transfer learning typically reuses knowledge acquired by a source network through its learned
weights. We investigate whether an activation function learned jointly with a source network in a
single training run can also be transferred to target networks and remain useful. To this end, we use a
parameterized activation function whose coefficients are shared globally across all activation sites of
the network. Global sharing makes the number of activation parameters independent of network depth
and width, so the learned function can be reused in networks of different architectures. This yields
a complementary form of transfer, in which the learned activation, rather than the source-network
weights, is retained and reused.
Learnable activation functions allow the nonlinear transformation to adapt during training. Existing
parameterizations include adaptive slopes [10, 14], customized activation functions [23], rational
