Figure 1: Overview of the learn–freeze–transfer framework. (a) A five-parameter FAct activation, shared
across all MLP blocks, is learned jointly with a depth-6 ViT on ImageNet-1K. (b) The learned activation
coefficients are frozen after source training. (c) Only these coefficients, not the source-network weights, are
transferred to independently initialized target networks. Evaluation includes same-task transfer to a freshly
initialized copy of the source architecture (ViT-d6) and cross-architecture transfer to depth-2 targets (ViT-d2,
Swin-d2, LinViT-d2, and MLP-Mixer), with the activation coefficients fixed throughout target training. Transfer
performance for these settings is reported in Tables 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6.
functions [26], and kernel-based representations [30]. Their parameters may be assigned locally
to individual neurons or layers [1, 10, 15, 23, 26] or shared across multiple layers [14, 5]. These
approaches study how activation functions adapt within a network. In contrast, we examine whether a
learned activation can be retained and reused independently of the network in which it was optimized.
Prior work has reused activation functions beyond the setting in which they were obtained, but
mainly through automated search [29, 2, 32] or meta-learning [34]. To our knowledge, transferring an
activation learned in a single training run across architectures has not been studied. In our setting, the
activation is learned through end-to-end training with a single source network, without meta-learning
or a separate search. After source training, the activation is frozen and transferred to target networks
trained from scratch. Only its learned coefficients are transferred; the source-network weights are not
reused, and the activation remains fixed throughout target training (Figure 1). This protocol allows
us to examine whether a nonlinearity learned within one network remains useful across different
architectures and tasks.
We instantiate this protocol with FAct (Fourier Activation), a learnable activation represented by a
two-harmonic truncated Fourier series with five coefficients. A single set of coefficients is shared
across all MLP blocks of the network. The coefficients are initialized from a two-harmonic Fourier
approximation of GELU [11] and optimized jointly with the source-network weights. We refer to the
activation after source training, with its coefficients fixed, as Frozen FAct.
We evaluate Frozen FAct in two transfer settings. In the same-task setting, the activation learned by a
depth-6 Vision Transformer (ViT) [7] on ImageNet-1K [6] is reused in a ViT of the same architecture,
trained from scratch on the same task. In the cross-architecture setting, the same five coefficients
are used in four depth-2 target architectures: a ViT with global self-attention, a Swin Transformer
with shifted-window self-attention [22], a ViT with linear attention [16], and an attention-free MLP-
Mixer [35]. These targets contain approximately 100K parameters each and are trained on four
image-classification datasets: Fashion-MNIST [36], CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 [20], and Food-101 [3].
In the same-task setting, Frozen FAct improves ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy by 1.46 percentage
points over GELU. In the cross-architecture setting, it achieves the highest mean test accuracy
among eleven activation functions in 15 of the 16 architecture–dataset combinations under a common
training configuration, with improvements of up to 1.71 percentage points over the best conventional
activation. When the learning rate and weight decay are tuned separately for each activation under the
2
same search budget, Frozen FAct still ranks first in eleven combinations, second in four, and fourth
in one. Finally, on Swin targets of one to six blocks, a frozen, untrained Fourier approximation of
GELU does not reproduce these gains, indicating that the benefit comes from the learned activation
rather than the Fourier parameterization alone. In contrast to the SPLASH ablation of Tavakoli et al.
[33], these results show that a frozen learned activation can retain its benefit after transfer.
This work makes three contributions:
1. A learn–freeze–transfer protocol for activation functions. We formulate a complementary
form of transfer in which a globally shared activation is learned jointly with a source network
in a single training run, then frozen and reused in target networks trained from scratch, without
transferring source-network weights.
2. A globally shared activation suited for transfer. We instantiate the protocol with FAct, whose
five coefficients are shared across all MLP blocks, so that the learned activation can be placed in
networks of different architectures.
3. An empirical evaluation of activation transferability. We evaluate same-task and cross-
architecture transfer using three transformer architectures and an attention-free MLP-Mixer on
four image-classification datasets. We compare Frozen FAct with ten conventional activation
functions under common and activation-specific hyperparameter configurations, and we include a
control showing that the gains come from the learned activation rather than its parameterization.
2
Related Work
2.1
Transfer Learning
Transfer learning reuses knowledge acquired on a source task to improve learning on a target task [28].
In deep networks, this is typically done by reusing learned weights, either to initialize a target network
that is then fine-tuned or as fixed feature extractors [37]. Knowledge distillation transfers knowledge
between networks of different architectures, but it requires the source network during target training to
provide supervision [12]. In both cases, the transferred knowledge is carried by the source network’s
weights or outputs. We study a complementary setting in which only a learned activation function is
transferred, and the source network is not used during target training.
2.2
Learnable and Globally Shared Activation Functions
Learnable activation functions introduce parameterized nonlinear transformations whose parameters
are optimized jointly with the network weights. PReLU learns the slope of the negative input
region [10], and ACON provides a more flexible parametric formulation [23]. Padé activation
units represent the nonlinearity as a ratio of polynomials [26], while other approaches use adaptive
piecewise-linear functions [1] or kernel-based representations [30]. Learnable Fourier-type activations
have also been studied, with coefficients learned within the network in which they are used [17, 19,
31].
Activation parameters also differ in how they are shared. They may be assigned to individual neurons
or layers, or shared across multiple layers. Jagtap et al. [14] introduced globally adaptive activation
functions for deep and physics-informed neural networks, using a single trainable scaling parameter
that adjusts the activation slope across the network. Delfosse et al. [5] shared a common set of
rational-function parameters across layers to regulate activation plasticity in deep reinforcement
learning. These approaches show that sharing activation parameters within a network can be useful.
However, sharing alone does not show whether a learned activation can be separated from its source
network and reused in another network.
2.3
Reuse and Transfer of Activation Functions
Several studies have reused activation functions beyond the setting in which they were obtained.
Ramachandran et al. [29] discovered Swish by automated search on a small network and showed
that it transfers to larger models and other tasks. Bingham and Miikkulainen [2] used surrogate-
based search to find activation functions that transfer from small search tasks to larger models,
including ResNet-50 on ImageNet. Strack et al. [32] used gradient-based search and transferred the
3
resulting activations, with their constants fixed, to larger models of the same type and to new datasets.
Teney et al. [34] meta-learned activation functions through bilevel optimization across task episodes,
demonstrating transfer across algorithmic tasks and reuse in networks of different widths.
Reusing a learned shape does not always preserve its benefit. Tavakoli et al. [33] found that a fixed
activation mimicking the final shape of trained SPLASH units performed only on par with ReLU,
and concluded that the evolution of the shape during training was important. Although this was not a
transfer study, it suggests that freezing a learned activation may discard part of its benefit.
The present study differs from these works in two respects. First, the activation is learned in a
single conventional training run, without search or meta-learning. Second, the frozen coefficients are
transferred across architecture families, from a ViT to Swin, linear-attention, and MLP-Mixer targets,
without reusing source-network weights or updating the activation during target training.

This section evaluates whether a globally shared activation learned jointly with a source network
remains useful when transferred to independently initialized target networks. We first describe the
source and target architectures, datasets, and training protocol. We then examine the evolution of the
source-learned activation, its transfer to a network with the same architecture and task, and its transfer
across four target architectures with different attention and token-mixing mechanisms. Frozen FAct

Backbone Matters: Benchmarking Encoder–Decoder
Networks for Semantic Segmentation of Driving
Scenes on BDD100K
Ehsan Rassekh
Institute for Advanced Studies in Basic Sciences (IASBS), Zanjan, Iran
Email: rassekh.ehsan@gmail.com, rassekh.ehsan@spes.uniud.it
Abstract—Semantic segmentation gives an autonomous vehicle
a dense, pixel-level description of its surroundings and is a core
part of scene understanding. Most segmentation networks consist
of an encoder (the backbone) and a decoder, yet the backbone
is often chosen without a systematic comparison. This work
studies this choice on the BDD100K driving dataset. Four widely
used decoders (U-Net, FPN, LinkNet and PSPNet) are combined
with 13 backbones from six families (ResNet, VGG, DenseNet,
Inception, MobileNet and EfficientNet), and all 52 models are
trained with one common protocol. The best model, an FPN
decoder with an EfficientNet-B4 backbone, reaches 62.6% mean
intersection over union (mIoU), 89.8% accuracy and a loss of
0.092. Only two of the 52 models, both FPN with EfficientNet,
exceed the 56.9% mIoU reported with the BDD100K benchmark.
The effect of the backbone depends strongly on the decoder: the
same EfficientNet-B4 gives 42.6% mIoU with PSPNet but 62.6%
with FPN, and the gap between the best and the worst backbone
ranges from 12.0 points (U-Net) to 42.5 points (FPN). The results
and the scope of this study are discussed.
Index Terms—semantic segmentation, scene understanding,
autonomous driving, backbone, BDD100K, feature pyramid net-
work, EfficientNet
I. INTRODUCTION
Road safety is one of the strongest motivations for self-
driving technology. Traffic accidents cause about 1.3 million
deaths and 20–50 million injuries every year [1], and more
than 90% of crashes are linked to human error [2]. A self-
driving system is usually described as a pipeline of sensing,
perception and decision making [3]. Perception is a part where
deep learning can help a lot: a vehicle can only take safe
decisions if it understands the road, the lane markings, the
traffic signs, and the vehicles and pedestrians around it.
Semantic segmentation supports this understanding by as-
signing a class label (for example “road”, “sky”, “car” or
“pedestrian”) to every pixel of a camera image [4], [5]. For
driving, the data must cover many lighting and weather con-
ditions, and the model must find object boundaries precisely.
Modern segmentation networks follow an encoder–decoder
design. The encoder, called the backbone, extracts features
from the image; the decoder turns these features back into a
full-resolution label map. Many different backbones exist, but
in practice one is often chosen in advance and the comparison
focuses on the decoder.
This paper asks a simple question: how much does the
choice of backbone change the quality of semantic segmen-
tation for driving scenes, and does the answer depend on the
decoder? To answer it, this work presents a controlled study on
BDD100K [6], building on earlier work [7]. The contributions
of this work are:
• A systematic benchmark of 52 segmentation models: four
decoders (U-Net, FPN, LinkNet, PSPNet) combined with
13 backbones from six families, all trained with the same
protocol and reported with mIoU, pixel accuracy and loss.
• The finding that FPN with an EfficientNet backbone is
clearly the best combination in this study (62.6% mIoU
with EfficientNet-B4), while the same backbone performs
at the level of the other backbones with the other three
decoders.
• An analysis of backbone sensitivity, of the relation be-
tween mIoU, accuracy and loss, and of the scope of the
study, which points to concrete next steps.
II. RELATED WORK
A. Segmentation Architectures
Fully convolutional networks (FCN) [8] showed that a
classification network can be turned into a dense predictor.
Encoder–decoder networks such as SegNet [9] and U-Net [10]
then added a decoder that recovers spatial detail; U-Net also
copies encoder features to the decoder by skip connections
and was first designed for biomedical images. Several works
improve the use of context. PSPNet [11] pools the feature map
at several scales to collect global context. The DeepLab family
uses atrous (dilated) convolution and atrous spatial pyramid
pooling [12], [13], and DeepLabv3+ adds a light decoder [14].
HRNet [15] keeps a high-resolution representation through
the whole network. Feature Pyramid Networks (FPN) [16]
build a pyramid of features with a top-down path and lateral
connections; they were proposed for object detection and
are also effective for segmentation [17]. LinkNet [18] was
designed for efficiency: it links each encoder block to the
matching decoder block to keep the number of parameters low.
More recent work uses vision transformers and attention-based
decoders, such as SegFormer [19] and Mask2Former [20], and
modernized convolutional backbones such as ConvNeXt [21].
This paper focuses on classical convolutional encoder–decoder
networks, which remain a common baseline. Surveys of deep
segmentation are given in [5], [22]; for driving scenes, see [4],
[23], and [24] for a comparison of real-time networks.
arXiv:2611.26191v1  [cs.CV]  19 Nov 2026
B. Backbones
The encoder of a segmentation network is normally an
image-classification network used as a feature extractor.
ResNet [25] uses residual connections to train deep networks,
VGG [26] stacks small convolution filters, DenseNet [27]
connects every layer to all later layers in a block, and Inception
[28], [29] uses parallel filters of different sizes. MobileNet
[30], [31] uses depthwise separable convolutions to reduce
computation. EfficientNet [32] scales network depth, width
and input resolution together with one compound coefficient
instead of scaling a single dimension. Using pretrained back-
bones (transfer learning) is standard practice, because it lets
the segmentation model reuse features learned on a large
classification dataset such as ImageNet [33], [34]. Better
classification backbones usually transfer better to other tasks,
but the relation is not perfect [35], which is one more reason
to compare backbones directly.
C. Driving Datasets
Public datasets for urban scenes include CamVid [36],
KITTI [37], Cityscapes [38] and Mapillary Vistas [39].
BDD100K [6] contains 100K driving videos with ten tasks,
recorded in different cities, at different times of day and in
different weather. The BDD100K paper reports 56.9% mIoU
for a semantic segmentation model trained on segmentation
data alone, and 58.3% when it is trained jointly with object
detection data. The first number is used as a reference point
in Section V.
III. METHOD
A. Overall Design
Fig. 1 shows the pipeline. An RGB image is passed through
a backbone that is initialized with pretrained weights. A
decoder uses the backbone features to build a high-resolution
representation, and a final convolution with a softmax acti-
vation gives one probability per class for each pixel. Any
backbone can be combined with any decoder, so the pipeline
allows a controlled comparison where only one component
changes at a time.
B. Decoders
Four decoders are evaluated; they differ mainly in how they
bring information from the encoder to the output.
U-Net [10] has a contracting path and a symmetric expand-
ing path. At each step of the expanding path the feature map
is upsampled with an up-convolution and concatenated with
the feature map of the same resolution from the contracting
path.
FPN [16] has a bottom-up pathway (the backbone), a top-
down pathway and lateral connections (Fig. 2). The top-down
pathway upsamples semantically strong but coarse maps by a
factor of two with nearest-neighbor interpolation. Each lateral
connection applies a 1×1 convolution to the backbone map
of the same size and merges it with the upsampled map by
element-wise addition.
LinkNet [18] uses an initial 7×7 convolution with stride
two, followed by residual encoder blocks. The input of every
encoder block is linked to the output of the matching decoder
block, which recovers spatial detail with few extra parameters.
PSPNet [11] applies a pyramid pooling module to the
last feature map. The map is average-pooled into 1×1, 2×2,
3×3 and 6×6 sub-regions; each level is reduced with a 1×1
convolution, upsampled bilinearly, and concatenated with the
original map to combine local and global context.
C. Backbones and Transfer Learning
The study uses 13 backbones: ResNet-34 and ResNet-50
[25]; VGG-16 and VGG-19 [26]; DenseNet-121, -169 and
-201 [27]; Inception-v3 [28] and Inception-ResNet-v2 [29];
MobileNet [30] and MobileNetV2 [31]; and EfficientNet-B3
and -B4 [32]. Every backbone is initialized with ImageNet-
pretrained weights [33] and then trained for segmentation.
D. Data Preparation
The ground-truth masks of BDD100K are color images in
which each class has a fixed RGB color. For training, each
mask is converted into an integer label map by looking up the
color of every pixel in a table of class colors. The table has 22
label indices, including the “unlabeled” and “static” indices,
and every pixel receives the index of its matching color.

The study uses BDD100K [6], collected by the University

about 40 seconds each, recorded at 720p and 30 fps with
GPS/IMU data, on more than 50K rides in New York, the

B. Implementation and Training
All networks are implemented in Python with TensorFlow
[40] and Keras, using an open-source Keras/TensorFlow li-
brary of segmentation networks. The training protocol follows
[7], and all 52 models share the hyperparameters in Table I.
Training uses the Adam optimizer [41]. The experiments ran
on a server with an Intel Xeon Silver 4210R CPU (2.40 GHz),
128 GiB of memory, four Tesla K80 GPUs and one Tesla
V100S GPU (32 GB). Training and evaluating all 52 models
took about 130 hours in total on this machine.
V. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
A. Main Results
Table II and Fig. 3 give the mIoU of all 52 models, and
Table III gives their accuracy and loss. The best model is FPN
with an EfficientNet-B4 backbone. It reaches 62.6% mIoU and
the highest accuracy (89.8%), with a loss of 0.092. FPN with
EfficientNet-B3 is second (58.6% mIoU, 87.0% accuracy). The
next best model, FPN with DenseNet-201, reaches only 44.3%
mIoU, so the two EfficientNet models are separated from the
rest of the field by more than 14 points.

D. Accuracy, Loss and mIoU
Over the 52 models, mIoU and accuracy rank the models al-

and loss are also correlated (Spearman −0.77). However, the

F. Scope of the Study
This work is a controlled empirical comparison: all 52
models use one protocol, so the differences between them
come from the choice of backbone and decoder. The main

are a natural extension of the same benchmark.

This work compared 52 combinations of four decoders and
13 backbones for semantic segmentation on BDD100K. The
choice of backbone has a large effect, and this effect depends
on the decoder. FPN with an EfficientNet-B4 backbone was

gives the vehicle a better understanding of the road scene.

Invertible Transport Between Sample-Only Distributions
via Projected Characteristic Functions
Juan Gutiérrez1,2, Victor Gutiérrez-García2, José Luis Blanco-Murillo1,2
1Information Processing and Telecommunications Center
2ETSI de Telecomunicación, Universidad Politécnica de Madrid, Spain
{juan.gutierrez, v.ggarcia, jl.blanco}@upm.es
Abstract
Many useful latent distributions can be sampled but do not
have a tractable density. Such distributions may be repre-
sented by empirical collections of real-world observations or
generated by scientific simulators and black-box generative
models. These sample-only priors cannot be used directly in
likelihood-based normalizing flows, which require evaluat-
ing the prior density. We propose Projected Characteristic-
Function matching (PCF), a density-free framework for learn-
ing an invertible map between a data distribution and a prior
specified only through samples.
Our method aligns distributions using projected empirical
characteristic functions, eliminating the need for density es-
timation, adversarial training, or paired observations. To ad-
dress the non-uniqueness of the transport map, we introduce an
optional transport regularizer that selects lower-displacement
transformations while preserving endpoint alignment.
We benchmark PCF on controlled transports, sample-
efficiency studies, and high-dimensional alignment tasks. PCF
matches the accuracy of kernel MMD on the controlled bench-
mark and on raw-pixel MNIST–USPS at a cost linear in the
batch size, and it is more sample-efficient, achieving lower
endpoint error than MMD in 13 of 15 paired runs across li-
brary sizes. By avoiding pairwise kernel evaluation, it reduces
discrepancy memory by 29.8% and trains at batch sizes where
kernel MMD exceeds GPU memory. These results show that
PCF provides accurate and efficient invertible transport, par-
ticularly in sample- and memory-limited settings.
Introduction
Learning a transformation between two probability distribu-
tions from finite, unpaired samples is a fundamental prob-
lem in generative modeling, domain translation, simulation-
based inference, and representation learning. In many of
these settings, it is desirable for the transformation to be
invertible: samples should be transported in both directions,
and every generated observation should admit an exact rep-
resentation in the source space. Normalizing flows provide a
natural framework for learning such transformations through
compositions of invertible functions or continuous-time dy-
namics (Dinh, Sohl-Dickstein, and Bengio 2017; Kingma
and Dhariwal 2018; Chen et al. 2018; Grathwohl et al. 2019;
Papamakarios et al. 2021).
The standard normalizing-flow formulation, however, is
designed around a tractable base distribution, most com-
monly an isotropic Gaussian. Maximum-likelihood training
evaluates the density of an encoded observation under this
base law together with the change-of-variables correction.
This construction is effective when the base distribution is
chosen for computational convenience, but it does not di-
rectly address settings in which the latent distribution is exter-
nally prescribed and accessible only through samples. Such
sample-only priors can arise from simulators, collections of
trajectories, empirical latent libraries, molecular samplers,
physical state distributions, or black-box generative models.
In these cases, the structure of the prior carries information:
it defines the coordinate law in which observations should be
represented, rather than merely supplying unstructured noise
for generation.
Let PX denote the data distribution and let PZ denote a
prescribed prior distribution. We assume access to indepen-
dent samples from both distributions, but do not assume that
the density of PZ can be evaluated. Our goal is to learn an
invertible map Fθ with inverse Gθ = F −1
θ
such that
(Fθ)#PX = PZ,
(Gθ)#PZ = PX .
(1)
Thus, encoded observations should follow the prescribed
latent law, while prior samples should decode into the data
distribution. Although the two equalities are equivalent for
an exact invertible map at the population level, enforcing
both during stochastic optimization provides direct training
signals in both directions.
Recent work has expanded invertible generative modeling
beyond conventional maximum-likelihood training. Sample-
based objectives, including sliced-Wasserstein discrepancies,
energy and proper-scoring-rule losses, and score matching,
show that normalizing flows can be trained without rely-
ing exclusively on tractable likelihoods (Coeurdoux, Dobi-
geon, and Chainais 2022; Chao et al. 2023). However, these
approaches typically retain an analytically specified base
distribution or focus on modeling a single target law. Fit-
ting an auxiliary density model to samples from the desired
prior offers one alternative (Golling et al. 2023), but intro-
duces an additional estimation stage whose errors can affect
the learned transport. Path-based approaches such as Flow
Matching instead learn dynamics along a chosen probability
path between the endpoints (Lipman et al. 2023), while drift-
ing methods construct distributional dynamics from discrep-
ancies or gradient flows (Gretton et al. 2026). Although these
1
arXiv:2611.26187v1  [cs.LG]  19 Nov 2026
methods can operate with samples from both distributions,
they require an interpolation, coupling, or drift construction
beyond the endpoint laws themselves. Flow Matching, in
particular, learns the endpoint laws only indirectly through
coupled samples; with the same network, solver, and training
budget, its endpoint error is 2.5–3.7 times that of PCF in our
controlled benchmark.
Our starting point is LeJEPA, which introduces Sketched
Isotropic Gaussian Regularization to match learned repre-
sentations to an isotropic Gaussian through projected empir-
ical characteristic functions (Balestriero and LeCun 2025).
This construction combines random one-dimensional pro-
jections with characteristic-function comparisons, provid-
ing a scalable sample-based mechanism for controlling a
high-dimensional distribution. We extend this mechanism
from representation regularization toward a fixed Gaus-
sian law to invertible generative modeling between general
sample-defined endpoint distributions. The proposed objec-
tive matches encoded data to independent prior samples and
decoded prior samples to independent data samples, requir-
ing neither prior-density evaluation, adversarial training, nor
source–target pairings. We study both an unregularized for-
mulation, which enforces the endpoint distributions, and a
transport-regularized formulation, which additionally favors
lower-cost invertible maps.
The approach is motivated by the fact that character-
istic functions uniquely characterize probability distribu-
tions and by the Cramér–Wold principle, which reduces
multivariate distribution matching to comparisons of one-
dimensional projections (Cramér and Wold 1936; Epps and
Pulley 1983). Random directions and a multiscale frequency
grid yield a differentiable minibatch objective based on
bounded Fourier features (Ansari, Scarlett, and Soh 2020;
Knop et al. 2020). We state endpoint identifiability for the
idealized all-direction, all-frequency discrepancy and evalu-
ate its practical finite-grid surrogate against alternative end-
point, path-based, and likelihood-based objectives.
Our main contributions are:
• We formulate prescribed sample-only prior learning as
bidirectional endpoint matching with a single invertible
map.
• We introduce PCF, a density-free two-sample objective
that extends projected characteristic-function regulariza-
tion to arbitrary endpoint distributions, with optional
transport-cost regularization.
• We establish endpoint identifiability for the idealized
discrepancy and compare its finite-grid surrogate with
endpoint-, path-, and likelihood-based alternatives.
Related Work
Likelihood-based and likelihood-free invertible models.
Normalizing flows learn tractable invertible transforma-
tions between a reference law and a data distribution, with
maximum-likelihood training enabled by the change-of-
variables formula (Dinh, Sohl-Dickstein, and Bengio 2017;
Kingma and Dhariwal 2018; Chen et al. 2018; Grathwohl
et al. 2019). Their invertibility has also been exploited for
unpaired domain translation through shared latent represen-
tations and cycle consistency induced by invertibility (Grover
et al. 2020). Subsequent work has reduced dependence on
likelihood through sliced-Wasserstein matching (Coeurdoux,
Dobigeon, and Chainais 2022), energy and proper-scoring-
rule objectives and score matching (Chao et al. 2023). An-
other strategy fits an auxiliary density model before learning
the transformation (Golling et al. 2023). These approaches
broaden the training objectives for invertible models, but gen-
erally retain an analytically specified reference distribution
or rely on an auxiliary density model.
Path-based
and
sample-to-sample
transport.
Continuous-time generative modeling has also devel-
oped toward simulation-free path learning. Flow Matching
trains vector fields along prescribed conditional probability
paths (Lipman et al. 2023), while minibatch and optimal-
transport couplings can produce straighter or lower-cost
trajectories (Pooladian et al. 2023). Symmetric MMD
objectives combine bidirectional endpoint matching with
transport regularization to learn invertible maps directly
from samples (Xiong, Ding, and Zhang 2025). Related
developments extend flow-based training to constrained and
function-valued domains (Xie et al. 2024; Kerrigan, Miglior-
ini, and Smyth 2024), conditional distribution transfer (Wahl
et al. 2025), and flow-map distillation (Sabour, Fidler, and
Kreis 2025). Drifting methods provide another sample-based
perspective by evolving particles through distributional
velocity fields (Deng et al. 2026), with recent analyses
connecting these dynamics to Wasserstein gradient flows
associated with kernel, Sinkhorn, and sliced-Wasserstein
discrepancies (Gretton et al. 2026). In contrast, our objective
directly matches the two endpoint laws without introducing
a probability path or coupling.
Characteristic-function distribution matching.
A com-
plementary line of work characterizes distributions through
one-dimensional projections and characteristic functions.
The Cramér–Wold principle and empirical characteristic-
function tests provide the classical foundations (Cramér and
Wold 1936; Epps and Pulley 1983). These ideas have been
used for latent distribution matching in autoencoders (Knop
et al. 2020), implicit generative modeling through weighted
characteristic-function distances (Ansari, Scarlett, and Soh
2020), and joint distribution learning (An and Jeon 2023; An,
Hong, and Jeon 2023). More recently, LeJEPA introduced
a scalable projected characteristic-function regularizer for
matching high-dimensional representations to an isotropic
Gaussian (Balestriero and LeCun 2025), with subsequent
work relating this construction to sliced kernel discrepan-
cies and simplified statistical variants (Zimmermann et al.
2025; Akbar 2026). Our method extends this characteristic-
function mechanism to two-sample matching between arbi-
trary endpoint distributions within a single invertible map.

Reward misalignment as an opportunity for materials
discovery
Ryotaro Okabe1,+,*, Shoki Kishida2,+,*, Abhijatmedhi Chotrattanapituk3, Dominic
Bollettieri4, Takuya Isogawa5, Yongqiang Cheng6, Mingda Li5,‡,*, and Masaki Adachi7,‡,*
1Department of Chemistry, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA 02139, USA
2Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138,
USA
3Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge,
MA 02139, USA
4Department of Physics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA 02139, USA
5Department of Nuclear Science and Engineering, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA 02139,
USA
6Neutron Scattering Division, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, TN 37831, USA
7Lattice Lab, Toyota Motor Corporation, Tokyo, 103-0022, Japan
+equal contribution.
‡equal contribution.
*Corresponding authors: rokabe@mit.edu, skishida@g.harvard.edu, mingda@mit.edu,
masaki adachi@mail.toyota.co.jp
ABSTRACT
Reward misalignment is usually regarded as a failure of artificial intelligence. In materials discovery with generative AI models,
however, disagreement between predefined rewards and expert judgment may reveal materials that the rewards overlook. We
investigate this possibility using electronic flat bands as a prime example. Experts mostly agree with a numerical bandwidth
score, but their disagreements are systematic and cannot be explained by an estimated 5% rate of mistaken labels. We learn
the experts’ preferences from pairwise comparisons and use them to guide a crystal diffusion model. The learned preferences
and numerical score agree on the flattest bands but diverge elsewhere. For example, the preferences favor KCo2As2 and CoGa,
reported compounds with partially flat bands that the score would discard. The framework also extends to synthesizability and
phonon properties. Our findings suggest that reward misalignment can expose opportunities for materials discovery beyond
what fixed rewards are designed to find.
Introduction
Artificial intelligence is taking on a growing share of materials discovery1–3. Generative models for crystals propose compounds
that have not been seen before4–8. They can be steered toward a prescribed symmetry or structural motif9,10 or toward a
computed property11,12, and such steering has already produced candidate superconductors13,14. Autonomous laboratories
and AI agents now carry out parts of the research loop itself15,16. Yet, despite these advances, AI-driven discovery remains
fundamentally constrained by how its objectives are defined. When materials are generated using predefined numerical rewards,
the search inevitably favors what those rewards are designed to recognize, potentially overlooking scientifically valuable
candidates that fall outside their definitions.
Defining an appropriate reward is particularly challenging in scientific discovery, where the significance of a material is
not always known in advance. Researchers often recognize promising features through their accumulated experience and
physical intuition, even when these judgments cannot be expressed as simple numerical criteria17,18. Whether a compound can
be synthesized is judged from experience, and stand-ins such as the distance from the convex hull capture only part of that
judgment19,20. Features of an electronic structure, such as a flat band, a Dirac cone or a van Hove singularity, are recognized as
patterns in a band diagram, and there is no accepted score for them. In machine learning, alignment means making a system
pursue what people actually intend, and misalignment is a gap between the objective that a system optimizes and that intent21.
In materials discovery, the objective is often a reward written by researchers themselves, such as a score for flat bands, while
their intent shows in the judgments they make. Misalignment here is therefore a gap between what researchers can write down
and what they actually prefer. A reward can favor candidates that experts would not choose and pass over candidates that
arXiv:2611.26186v1  [cond-mat.mtrl-sci]  19 Nov 2026
they would. In conventional AI applications, reward misalignment is generally regarded as a problem to be corrected, as it
can lead systems to pursue unintended outcomes22,23. Scientific discovery, however, suggests another possibility. What if
the disagreement between expert judgment and numerical rewards could itself reveal scientific opportunities that predefined
objectives fail to capture? Rather than merely correcting the discrepancy, identifying and exploring it may provide a route
toward unexpected materials discovery.
Here, we investigate this possibility using the discovery of electronic flat-band materials as a representative case. A flat band
near the Fermi level enhances the role of electron interactions, which makes flat-band materials platforms for unconventional
superconductivity, magnetism and other correlated phenomena24. Flatness is therefore a useful indicator for identifying
potentially interesting electronic structures, although it does not by itself establish their physical properties. Several numerical
descriptors have been proposed to quantify flat bands25,26, incorporating features such as bandwidth, proximity to the Fermi
level, and the extent of flatness in momentum space. However, these descriptors necessarily impose predefined criteria on
what constitutes a desirable flat band. We examine whether such criteria adequately capture expert judgment by comparing a
hand-designed bandwidth score with pairwise evaluations collected from researchers in materials science and condensed-matter
physics. The researchers choose between two structures rather than scoring each, because people judge more reliably by
comparison27,28. Such pairwise choices have been used to learn the intuition of medicinal chemists about molecules29.
We find that the disagreement between human experts and the numerical bandwidth score is systematic rather than random.
In blinded comparisons of electronic band structures, the majority of experts agrees with the score on most pairs, but their
disagreements exhibit substantial consistency across individuals (Fig. 1). Although human evaluations inevitably contain
mistakes, we statistically estimate that only about 5% of training labels are reversed30,31, insufficient to explain the observed
discrepancy. These results suggest that expert judgments contain a shared criterion that is not fully represented by the predefined
bandwidth score. We call this systematic difference between what a predefined reward favors and what experts prefer a
misalignment.
To explore the materials space associated with this misalignment, we employ a preference-learning approach to guide the
crystal generator. This approach learns the human latent reward, the unobserved criterion behind the experts’ choices, from
their pairwise comparisons (Fig. 2a). Given a preference label indicating that crystal A is preferred over crystal B, guidance
increases the generation probability of A while decreasing that of B (Fig. 2b). By learning from these pairwise preferences,
the guided generator becomes aligned with human experts’ judgments, producing crystals that better reflect their preferences.
To make the fit robust to mistaken labels, we combine direct distributional optimization32 with a robust Hölder score30 and
an explicit model of reversed labels31, which discounts the labels the fit cannot explain and estimates their fraction. In blind
evaluations, the guided generator produces structures preferred over those of the base model.
Crucially, the learned preferences reveal scientifically promising regions of materials space that the numerical score
overlooks. The human latent reward and the bandwidth score largely agree on structures with clearly flat bands, but their
rankings diverge for other candidates. Many structures that the latent reward ranks highly are ones that the numerical score
does not recognize as flat. A key source of this discrepancy is the rigid threshold imposed by the bandwidth score, which
requires a band to remain sufficiently close to the Fermi level over at least half of the sampled momentum path. In contrast, the
latent reward also favors structures exhibiting locally flat band segments, which may warrant further investigation even when
they fail the conventional criterion. Remarkably, these overlooked structures include previously reported materials such as
KCo2As233,34 and CoGa35, whose electronic structures show a flat band near the Fermi level and a pseudogap, respectively. We
also identify new candidate crystals and examine their electronic structures using first-principles calculations. These findings
illustrate how exploring the discrepancy between human preferences and numerical rewards can reveal materials candidates
that conventional reward-driven screening would discard.
The preference-based framework is also applicable beyond electronic flat bands. We demonstrate its generality using
synthesizability preferences derived from experimental records and phonon-related preferences derived from computed
descriptors. For synthesizability, a latent reward fitted to the experimental record identifies synthesized structures more often
than the distance from the convex hull does. In both cases, pairwise comparisons provide a practical means of learning
criteria for materials evaluation and guiding generation. More broadly, our findings suggest a different perspective on reward
misalignment in AI-driven scientific discovery. The disagreement between human judgment and numerical rewards is not
merely a limitation to overcome; it can also serve as a source of scientific opportunity, revealing promising directions that
predefined objectives were not designed to explore.
Results
Experts disagree with the bandwidth score in the same direction
The first question is whether the experts disagree with the bandwidth score at all, and if so, whether they disagree in the same
direction. If each expert’s choice were the score’s choice plus a random error, the score could replace the experts. To tell
random error from systematic disagreement, ten experts judged the same 200 pairs of band structures (Fig. 2a), so that their

The remaining disagreement is not simply random error. If each expert erred independently around the score, any two

Thermodynamically Consistent Neural Networks for a Universal
Fluid Gibbs Free Energy Equation of State
Xurui Li,∗Zhiguo Gan,∗Jiaming Zhang,∗and Diannan Lu†
Department of Chemical Engineering, Tsinghua University,
Beijing 100084, People’s Republic of China
Hongxi Zeng
School of Engineering, The University of Edinburgh,
King’s Buildings, Edinburgh EH9 3DW, United Kingdom
(Dated: November 20, 2026)
1
arXiv:2611.26183v1  [cs.LG]  19 Nov 2026
Abstract
Over the past three centuries, many thermodynamics researchers have worked to develop fluid
equations of state with both high accuracy and broad applicability, proposing various theoretical
frameworks and models. Building on these efforts, this study uses Gibbs free energy as the starting
point and introduces thermodynamically consistent neural networks to construct a fluid equation
of state based on Gibbs free energy (GEoS). This approach establishes a novel machine learning
framework that provides a unified representation of fluid states. GEoS performs well on the vapor-
and liquid-phase density test sets, with average absolute relative deviations (AARDs) of 5.25%
and 3.96%, respectively. It outperforms conventional volume-translated cubic equations of state
and existing machine learning models, demonstrating its effectiveness. Further analysis using the
UMAP dimensionality reduction method shows that most molecules in the test set belong to
extrapolation systems, confirming the strong generalization ability of the model. Finally, the test
results show that the PC-SAFT equation fitted using GEoS maintains high predictive accuracy,
providing a reliable basis for its practical application in industry.
I.
INTRODUCTION
An Equation of State (EoS) relates state variables to describe thermodynamic properties
under various conditions [1–4]. Fluid EoS forms the basis for calculating various fundamen-
tal physical properties [5, 6]. In the process industry, EoS is essential to determine states of
matter and phase behavior to guide process design. For example, core thermodynamic calcu-
lations are closely linked to EoS in fields such as petroleum and petrochemical technologies
[7, 8], supercritical fluid technologies [9–11], and CCUS technologies [5, 12–14].
Over past three centuries, researchers have proposed numerous EoS for pure fluids[5].
The most classic is cubic EoS[6, 15], which remains a workhorse in many petroleum industry
applications[8]. In 1873, van der Waals proposed the first equation to describe gas and liquid
phases in a unified form[3]. It serves as the foundation for cubic EoS[15], followed by mod-
els such as the Redlich-Kwong equation[16], Soave-Redlich-Kwong equation[17], and Peng-
Robinson equation[18]. However, these equations cannot accurately predict liquid density
∗These authors contributed equally to this work.
† Contact author: ludiannan@tsinghua.edu.cn
2
and near-critical behavior. To address this, researchers introduce various modifications[6],
such as new α-function methods[19, 20] and volume translation[21–23]. Despite these cor-
rections, cubic EoS still struggle to accurately describe the behavior of polar fluids and
high-pressure liquids.
Since the cubic equation era, fluid EoS research has shifted from directly constructing
p-V -T relations to Helmholtz energy frameworks that derive EoS via partial derivatives, now
the dominant approach. High-accuracy models built on this framework include the empir-
ical Helmholtz energy equation[24], SAFT[25–27] and its derivatives such as CPA[28] and
PC-SAFT[29]. These are widely applied: REFPROP integrates the empirical Helmholtz
energy EoS[30] as the highest accuracy benchmark in industry and science, and the inter-
national water‑steam standard IAPWS-IF97[31] follows the same paradigm. However, the
parameters of these EoS are usually obtained by fitting the experimental data[32, 33]. When
experimental data are unavailable, although group-contribution estimates[34] can be used,
this alternative method has limitations in accuracy and applicability [33].
With the rapid development of machine learning (ML), neural networks provide a promis-
ing approach to advancing fluid equations of state (EoS), enabling the rapid development of
highly accurate models[35]. In this area, some studies focus on energy-based EoS modeling.
Chaparro et al. employ ML to predict the EoS of Mie model fluids[36, 37], demonstrating the
feasibility of energy-based EoS modeling with ML. However, model fluids behave differently
from real fluids, so these models cannot be directly applied to predicting the properties of
real fluids. Other studies focus on predicting EoS parameters. Felton et al. propose ML-
SAFT, a model that predicts PC-SAFT parameters using ECFP4 fingerprints[38]. Winter
et al. propose SPT-PC-SAFT, which uses a Transformer architecture to extract molecular
features from SMILES strings and predict PC-SAFT parameters[33]. However, ECFP4 fin-
gerprints mainly describe two-dimensional molecular structures and may not fully represent
molecular conformations. In contrast, feature extraction from SMILES using Transformers
is a highly black-box process. Both limitations reduce confidence in the extrapolation ability
of these models.
Unlike existing studies that directly predict EoS parameters or residual Helmholtz free
energy, this study adopts the Thermodynamically Consistent Neural Networks framework
proposed in our previous work [39].
Molecular descriptors and the corresponding state
variables are used as inputs to construct a predictive model for the residual Gibbs free

condition and the non-negativity of the compressibility factor, are incorporated into the model.
(c) Prediction: The model predicts the logarithm of the fugacity coeﬀicient at a given temperature
and pressure, from which other thermodynamic properties, such as the compressibility factor, are
calculated via automatic differentiation.

obtained through automatic differentiation. FIG. 1 illustrates the workflow of this study.
II.
METHOD
A.
Database
The fugacity coeﬀicient database is calculated by CoolProp[40], which is an open-source
database of fluid properties, formulated based on the most accurate formulations in open
literature. From the 124 fluids available in CoolProp, we select 104 substances that also
appear in the DIPPR database, excluding predefined mixtures and rare gases. In total, 10
atoms are considered: C, H, D, O, N, S, Si, F, Cl, and I. Three substances are reserved
for leave-one-out testing to facilitate parameter tuning and ablation experiments. For more
details, please refer to Section 1 of the Supporting Information.
The region-based sampling results are shown in FIG. 2. 2000 points are uniformly sam-
pled by shifting the saturation line along the Tr direction, and another 2000 points along the
logarithmic pr (ln pr) direction. In the supercritical region, 2500 points are uniformly sam-
pled over the (Tr, ln pr) space. Due to the discontinuous derivative of the fugacity coeﬀicient

each region. Specifically, due to the unique behaviors in these two regions, half of the sam-
pled points are used as a validation set during training to serve as supervisory signals for
model saving. For more details, please refer to Section 1.2 of the Supporting Information.
B.
Feature Engineering
The molecular features of GEoS follow our previous strategy [39, 41]. RDKit [42] and
Mordred [43] calculate 2D molecular descriptors, while PubChemFP [44] serves as the 2D
structural fingerprint. To supplement 3D structural information, Gaussian [45] performs
conformational optimization at the B3LYP/6-31G* level, yielding 25 quantum chemical
descriptors. Previous studies demonstrate that models supplemented with quantum chemical
descriptors can effectively differentiate isomers [39, 41].
On this basis, with the critical molar density ρc(kmol/m3) as the prediction target, the
5
Boruta algorithm [46] is applied for feature selection in the entire DIPPR dataset, and
features with a median importance rank not greater than two are selected as target features.
The feasibility of the Boruta selection scheme has been verified in our previous studies
[39, 41]. The purpose of performing selection on the entire DIPPR dataset is to make the
feature space associated with our feature set more extensive because there are only 101
molecules available for training in Coolprop, and the feature set obtained by selection on it
is not representative enough.
For more details on feature engineering design, please refer to Section 2 of the Supporting
Information.

III.
RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS
A.
Overall performance in the test set
We collect a large number of density data from the ThermoData Engine (TDE) and
construct an independent test set to evaluate the generalization performance of the model.
The test set contains 74,078 liquid-phase density data points for 399 substances and 9,665
gas-phase density data points for 82 substances, none of which are included in model training.
10

NariQ: Sub-3-Bit Quantization for Long-Horizon
Agentic Tasks
Doyeob (Toby) Kim
Nari Labs
toby@narilabs.com
Abstract
Long-horizon agentic tasks require a model to call tools over many steps at contexts
of 100K tokens or more, yet many low-bit quantization methods are calibrated
on short web text and judged on perplexity. This mismatch is costly: existing
quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B at or below 3 bits per weight match BF16 on shorter
tasks like AIME, yet in published results solve at most 72% as many tasks as
BF16 on DeepSWE, a long-horizon agentic benchmark. We propose NariQ, a
trellis-coded post-training quantization method that calibrates on tokens generated
by the BF16 model in agent sessions. On Qwen3.8-27B, NariQ at 3.0 and 2.5
bits per weight stays level with BF16 on two long-horizon agentic benchmarks,
DeepSWE and Terminal Bench, as well as on AIME and RealWorldQA. Our
checkpoint at 2.0 bits per weight trails this performance. To our knowledge,
these are the first quantizations at or below 3 bits per weight shown to match
their full-precision version on long-horizon agentic tasks. We release the files as
Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF, with inference available through our llama.cpp fork
at https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp.
1
Introduction
Language models are increasingly used as agents working on long-horizon tasks. For example, a
single task in DeepSWE [8], a popular software engineering benchmark, takes an agent on average
about 150 tool calls and 50 minutes, with a median context of 92K tokens.
Near 4 bits per weight, quantization already preserves such agentic performance. NVIDIA’s NVFP4
version of Qwen3.8-27B [16] stays within 1.6 points of BF16 on Terminal Bench [13] and solves at
least as many DeepSWE tasks as BF16 [9].
Below 4 bits, existing quantized models still do well on short tasks, but not on long-horizon ones. For
example, the 3-bit GSQ-RCO quantization of Qwen3.8-27B [10] stays within a point of BF16 on
AIME (96.9% against 97.7%). Yet in Unsloth’s reported results it fully solves only 63% as many
DeepSWE tasks as BF16 (Table 1).
We therefore ask whether we can quantize a model to 3 bits per weight or fewer without losing its
long-horizon agent capability. The answer decides whether capable agents can run on consumer
GPUs, where the weights must fit into 8–32 GB.
A better weight format alone is unlikely to close this gap. Random rotations make weights close to
Gaussian [1, 21], and on Gaussians, trellis codes are already within about 10% of the rate-distortion
bound at 2 bits (mean squared error 0.069 against 0.063) [22]. We instead ask which tokens a
quantized agent must get right. Many low-bit methods are calibrated on short chunks of web text [5]
and judged on perplexity and short benchmarks, which say little about agents. They weight every
calibration token equally, whereas an agent’s quality depends on the tokens it writes.
Preprint.
arXiv:2611.26157v1  [cs.LG]  19 Nov 2026
We introduce NariQ, a post-training quantization recipe for long-horizon agentic use at 2.0, 2.5 and
3.0 bits per weight. NariQ keeps the standard trellis code and changes which tokens the loss counts,
which modules get which widths, and what data the scales are tuned on. It sets each module’s width
from an estimate of that module’s own loss, which stays informative for trellis codes. It codes the
output layer in bands by how likely the model is to predict each token, keeping every band at 2 bits or
more to protect rare tokens.
We evaluate agentic work, math, visual understanding and multilingual tasks. NariQ at 3.0 and
2.5 bpw is level with BF16 within noise on all benchmarks we ran; at 2.0 bpw, it trails BF16.
2
Method
A file at B bpw uses B bits per text-model parameter, including codes, scales, labels, embeddings
and the output layer. To build a file ˆθ whose next-token distribution stays close to BF16’s, we (1)
quantize modules at several integer widths, (2) estimate their loss from gradients, (3) allocate widths
within the budget, and (4) tune the scales.
We trellis-quantize each rotated matrix [22], using input- and output-side statistics to compensate
rounding error as in YAQA [23]. We retain input-only rounding unless two-sided rounding lowers
held-out curvature-weighted error by at least 5%; almost every module uses both sides. NariQ adds
four changes; Figure 1 shows their development sequence at 3.0 bpw.
First, the end-to-end loss counts only model-written tokens. Agent traces contain long tool outputs
and file contents that can dominate an all-token loss. For a calibration trace x (Section 3.1), let M
index the tokens generated by BF16. Our objective is

Second, widths are allocated by each module’s own loss term. Since the KL is minimized at BF16,
we use a second-order expansion around its weights and neglect interactions between modules’ errors,
so the total loss is a sum of per-module terms. Take one module and flatten its weights into a vector:
W at BF16 and Wk = W + Ek at width k. With H the module’s Hessian block at BF16, its loss
term at width k is ℓk = 1

G ≈HEc. RCO [7] scores a move to another width k̸ = c by the first-order change

and the 2-, 4- and 5-bit errors is 0.035, 0.009 and 0.004. We therefore neglect this term. The score is

the loss at the destination width.
NariQ instead uses the score to estimate the current loss: averaging 1

an estimate of ℓc. The gradient estimates ℓc only at the current width. To predict the other widths,
we assume a module’s loss scales with the code’s error: with rk the trellis code’s measured mean
squared error at width k, which falls about 4× per added bit, we predict ℓk ≈ℓc rk/rc. For example,
a module’s loss at 2 bits is predicted as about 3.9 times its loss at 3 bits.
Scaling a noisy gradient estimate to a distant width amplifies its noise. We combine estimates from
several width assignments, rescaling to a common width and weighting by inverse variance. We use
the mean plus two standard errors and apply a small positive floor.

Figure 1: Development sequence at 3.0 bpw, ending at an earlier checkpoint. Trellis coding has
3.2× lower agent KL than GPTQ+GSQ, with the scalar search’s probabilities re-rounded under
trellis costs. Subsequent changes reduce KL a further 2.7×. The model-token step also adds the
two-standard-error margin, so it does not isolate masking alone. Dashed: GSQ-RCO IQ3_XXS.
Choosing one width per module makes this a multiple-choice knapsack problem. We use dynamic
programming over a discretized budget, favoring the fullest feasible allocation. An exact-cost check
enforces the storage limit, but global optimality is not guaranteed. The loss estimate fails at 1 bit: at
2.0 bpw, moving the 12 modules the allocator had put at 1 bit up to 2 bits lowered KL by 7.2% for
only 0.021 bpw, far more than predicted. Every linear layer therefore stays at 2 bits or more.
Third, the output layer gets more bits for likely tokens. Only about 13% of its 248,320 tokens appear
as generated tokens in our calibration traces, although every row contributes to the softmax. For a
token with BF16 probability p, the KL curvature with respect to its logit is p(1 −p), which is close
to p for all but the most likely tokens. We therefore rank rows by their mean predicted probability,
as a proxy for sensitivity, and sort them into 16 bands of about 15,500 rows. We code each band at
its own width, as a separate module in the allocation. Rare tokens still need some precision: in our
tests, bands at 1 bit lowered KL on most traces but raised it on traces that use rare tokens, such as
multilingual text, so every band keeps at least 2 bits. At 3.0 bpw the bands lower the mean per-trial
KL by 12.1%. At 2.0 bpw the input embedding is also banded. It has no predicted probability, so its
rows are ranked by how often each token appears in the input, and unlike output bands, its rare-token
bands may use 1 bit.
Fourth, scale tuning uses general data as well as coding traces. With codes and widths fixed, we
tune every coded matrix’s scales and every norm weight to minimize L on coding agent traces and
BF16 replies to general prompts (math, science, chat, code and long documents), weighted 70:30.
An earlier 2.0 bpw file tuned on coding traces alone scored 77.3% on AIME against BF16’s 97.7%;
adding the general data raised it to 86.0%.
Format. We release the files as NariQ GGUFs [6]. The format rotates every matrix with randomized
Hadamard blocks [21] of power-of-two size. In attention and DeltaNet layers, one side of most
matrices is first shuffled by a seeded permutation. Because every block has power-of-two size, the
format needs no Hadamard sizes tied to a particular model. The codebook is computed from the
trellis state, as in EXL3 [24], so kernels decode the codes inside the matrix multiply.
3
Evaluating Low-Bit Files on Agentic Tasks
3.1
Data and Benchmarks
Calibration and development traces. Agent sessions of the BF16 model on open-source software
tasks, split by repository into calibration, development and reserve sets, with every repository shared
with DeepSWE removed.

Offline KL sets. KL from BF16 at model-written tokens on held-out agent traces (agent KL), on a
reserve set never used for selection, and on general and math replies (Appendix A).
DeepSWE v1.1 [8], at task-repository commit 0b9fabb. A software engineering benchmark of 113
tasks from 91 repositories in five languages. Claude Code drives the model, which SGLang [31]
serves. The agent runs with thinking on at maximum effort, up to 65,536 output tokens per request
and a limit of 3 hours per task. Each task gets one attempt; agent failures count as zero, and no task is
rerun. We report the DeepSWE score, the mean fraction of a task’s new tests that pass, the number of
tasks solved, where every new and existing test passes, and paired differences with standard errors.
Terminal Bench 2.1 [20]. Command-line tasks, each with its own tests and time limit. We run the 82
tasks Unsloth reports on, with 3 attempts each, the same agent and settings as DeepSWE, and each
task’s own time limit and internet access. We report the mean test reward over all attempts; a trial left
without a grade counts as zero.
AIME 2025+2026 [12], RealWorldQA [27] and MGSM [17]. Math, visual understanding and
multilingual tasks, to measure what a file keeps outside coding. Thinking is on at the chat template’s
default effort, with up to 131,072 output tokens for AIME and 32,768 for the others; a reply cut at
the limit counts as wrong. We sample 8 replies per AIME problem (avg@8), 3 per RealWorldQA
question and 1 per MGSM question, as in simple-evals [15].
Settings shared by every benchmark. Every file, BF16 included, runs with the same settings: a
262,144-token context window, the model card’s thinking-mode sampling (temperature 1.0, top-p
0.95, top-k 20), and no retries.
3.2
Baselines
Agent benchmarks (Table 1). We run BF16 and our files in our harness. For other quantized files we
use the DeepSWE and Terminal Bench 2.1 results Unsloth publishes for this model [25]: its Dynamic
V3.1 GGUFs, GSQ-RCO’s GGUFs [10] and the EXL3 files [24]. Unsloth uses mini-swe-agent [19]
and at least three passes per DeepSWE task [26]; we use Claude Code and one attempt. Table 1
reports each file relative to its own harness’s BF16, but this normalization does not remove harness
differences. Unsloth’s solved counts are its reported rates times 113, read from its chart to about
±0.5 tasks.

4
Results
4.1
Agent benchmarks
At 3.0 and 2.5 bpw, our files are level with BF16 on DeepSWE (Table 1). They solve 47 and 46 tasks
against BF16’s 44, and their DeepSWE scores are 84.9% and 84.5% against BF16’s 83.0% (paired by
task, +1.9 and +1.5 points, s.e. 3.2 and 3.6). At 2.0 bpw, our file solves 33 tasks and scores 75.7%,
7.3 points under BF16 (s.e. 3.3). In Unsloth’s reported results, every file at or below 3.0 bpw solves at
most 72% as many tasks as its BF16.
On Terminal Bench 2.1, our 3.0 and 2.5 bpw files score 102% and 96% of our BF16, within noise
of it (paired by task, +1.2 and −2.4 points, s.e. 3.5 and 3.2), and our 2.0 bpw file scores 84%, 10.2
points under (s.e. 3.5). The reported files at or below 3.0 bpw score 64–90% of Unsloth’s BF16.
4.2
Beyond coding
General ability holds (Table 2): on AIME, RealWorldQA and MGSM, our 3.0 bpw file is within a
point of BF16 and our 2.5 bpw file within 2.2 points. At 2.0 bpw, the largest drop is on AIME, 11.7
points.
4.3
Size and speed
NariQ’s text-only GGUFs, including embeddings and output layers, occupy 10.1, 8.4 and 6.8 GB
at 3.0, 2.5 and 2.0 bpw. Vision adds a shared 0.9 GB BF16 projector; the original 55.6 GB BF16
checkpoint includes vision and MTP. At these three budgets, our llama.cpp fork on one RTX PRO
6000 generates 89, 99 and 112 tokens/s at a 4K-token context, and 71, 77 and 85 at 64K, for a single
session.
5
Related Works
Codes and rounding. Low-bit formats include scalar and grouped codes [5, 11], and vector and
trellis codes [4, 21, 22], often applied after random rotations [1, 21]. EXL3 [24] ships the trellis
family for local inference. GPTQ [5] and LDLQ [1] round with the input Hessian, and YAQA [23]
adds the output side. We use QTIP’s bitshift trellis with a computed codebook.
Bit allocation and recovery. Mixed-precision allocation by sensitivity is established [29], and
search methods such as EvoPress [18] and RCO [7] optimize widths against the end-to-end loss;
GSQ-RCO [10] publishes files of this model built that way. Variable bit-width quantization [14]
learns widths per group, down to about 1 bit on the output layer. Fine-tuning scales and other
continuous parameters after quantization is common [2, 22]. Our allocator differs in reading the
end-to-end gradient as each module’s own loss term, which remains informative for codes whose
errors at different widths are uncorrelated.
Generated calibration data. FAQ [28] regenerates calibration data with a larger model from the
same family. OnQ [30] recovers low-bit reasoning through distillation on the quantized student’s
own trajectories. NariQ instead uses fixed BF16-generated tool-use traces, restricts its loss to
model-written positions, and allocates bits against that objective. We evaluate the resulting files on
long-horizon agentic tasks.
5
6
Limitations and Future Work
While our 3.0 and 2.5 bpw files are level with BF16 on all benchmarks we ran, evaluations on more
models, more agent harnesses and more agentic benchmarks remain future work. At 2.0 bpw, our file
trails BF16 by 7.3 points on DeepSWE and 11.7 on AIME, and we hypothesize that training beyond
scales and norms can recover it.
The multi-token prediction module is not yet quantized, and our llama.cpp fork is tuned for one GPU
generation (SM120); other GPUs run it slower, and GPUs older than Ampere fall back to the CPU.
We also plan to quantize the KV cache and activations, so long contexts fit on 16 GB consumer GPUs,
and extend the study to more models and more budgets at or below 3 bits.
7
Conclusion
NariQ calibrates and allocates bits around model-written tokens in agent sessions. On Qwen3.8-27B,
its 3.0 and 2.5 bpw files are level with BF16 on long-horizon agentic benchmarks. We release
the files as Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF, with inference available through our llama.cpp fork at
https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp.

AI tools assisted with writing, literature search, implementation, and research
analysis.

LOSS-GUIDED TSETLIN MACHINES:
MAKING THE
LEARNING OBJECTIVE EXPLICIT
Mayur Shende1
Runar Helin1
Ole-Christoffer Granmo1
Vladimir I. Zadorozhny2
1University of Agder, Norway
2University of Pittsburgh, USA
ABSTRACT
The Tsetlin Machine (TM) has no explicit notion of a loss function. Its learning
signal is fixed to an implicit, margin-based update rule (MBUR), with no way to
choose an objective function suited to a specific task. This paper introduces Loss-
Guided TM, which replaces MBUR with an explicit and swappable loss func-
tion. In our proposed method, clause feedback and weight updates are driven by
the loss, while keeping the Tsetlin Automaton and clause logic unchanged. The
approach incorporates cross entropy (CE), symmetric cross entropy (SCE), and
asymmetric loss (ASL). We evaluate Loss-Guided TM across six datasets that
span multiclass, multilabel, and binary classification tasks. With a suitable loss,
Loss-Guided TM matches or improves accuracy and F1 over MBUR on five of the
six datasets. The gains are greatest for the imbalanced multilabel datasets, where
ASL improves macro F1 by up to 9 percentage points. With CE, Loss-Guided
TM is also significantly better calibrated than MBUR on all six datasets, reduc-
ing calibration error by a factor of 3 to 11. A qualitative inspection shows that
the clause-based global interpretability, examined at the per-class level on image
and text data, is preserved when using the Loss-Guided mechanism. These results
show that our explicit TM learning objective allows direct targeting of uncertainty
calibration, data imbalance, and task structure, opening the TM to the broader
literature on loss functions.
1
INTRODUCTION
The Tsetlin Machine (TM) is a logic-based alternative to neural networks, applied across various
domains, such as image classification (Granmo et al., 2019; Grønningsæter et al., 2024), text cate-
gorization and natural language understanding (Berge et al., 2019; Saha et al., 2022; 2023; Bhattarai
et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2026), regression (Darshana Abeyrathna et al., 2019), contextual bandits
(Seraj et al., 2022), and board-game winner prediction (Giri et al., 2022). Its predictions are disjunc-
tions of conjunctive clauses over binarized input literals, directly readable as propositional logic.
Together with a novel learning strategy (finding common denominators and reasoning by elimina-
tion), TMs become easier to interpret than neural networks (Yadav et al., 2022; Shende et al., 2025;
Tarasyuk et al., 2026). Further work by Kuruge et al. (2025) and Helin et al. (2025) quantifies the
uncertainty of TM predictions. TM learning has also been related to that of the perceptron (Sharma
et al., 2022) and extended with regularization (Anjum & Zhan, 2024). The bit-level structure of the
TM makes it efficient to run, with reported reductions in computation cost and memory footprint
over comparable neural architectures (Kundu et al., 2026). This combination of competitive accu-
racy, interpretability, and efficiency positions the TM as a practical, transparent alternative to deep
learning (Lei et al., 2020).
A loss function defines what a model is actually being trained to do. Different loss functions can
produce different learned behavior even from the same architecture and the same data (Wasserman,
2004). Cross entropy, the standard choice for classification, corresponds to the model’s output repre-
senting a categorical or Bernoulli distribution over the labels, while mean squared error corresponds
to a Gaussian distribution (Goodfellow et al., 2016). More broadly, loss functions in the literature
are designed around the structure of a specific problem. This includes, among many others (Wang
et al., 2022), losses built for extreme class imbalance (Lin et al., 2020), for maximizing the margin
between classes (Cortes & Vapnik, 1995), for region overlap in segmentation (Milletari et al., 2016),
for matching entire distributions rather than individual predictions (Arjovsky et al., 2017), and for
1
arXiv:2611.26114v1  [cs.LG]  19 Nov 2026
Preprint
balancing reconstruction accuracy against a regularized latent representation (Kingma & Welling,
2014).
However, TMs do not have an explicit loss function as a neural network does. Instead, a TM uses
a heuristic update probability (Eq. 2), which is the normalized absolute error between the model’s
vote sum and the voting threshold (T). This update mechanism, here termed margin-based update
rule (MBUR), is hardwired directly into the TM’s learning algorithm, with no principled bridge to
the concept of loss functions. The TM therefore cannot optimize its performance using any of the
well-established objective functions, tailored to the various learning tasks. This paper introduces
a Loss-Guided learning mechanism for the TM that replaces MBUR’s heuristic update probability
with an explicit loss function, while retaining the Tsetlin Automaton based logical rule learning. We
evaluate this mechanism using three different loss functions, cross entropy (CE), symmetric cross
entropy (SCE), and asymmetric loss (ASL), assessing both predictive performance and interpretabil-
ity against MBUR across six datasets.
2
BACKGROUND
TM is a machine learning model built from finite-state learning automata and propositional
logic (Granmo, 2018). The Tsetlin Automaton (TA) is the model’s basic learning unit, a finite-state
machine that learns to select one of two actions, include or exclude, based on reward and penalty
signals from its environment. Each input feature is binarized and paired with its negation, forming
the set of literals. Each literal is assigned a TA, which decides whether to include or exclude the
literal. Thus, a single propositional logic clause is defined by a dedicated team of TAs that operate
on the literal set. In brief, the clause computes the conjunction ck = V
f∈Lk f of the literals its TAs
choose to include, where Lk is the subset of literals included by clause k’s automata. A clause is
active, ck = 1, when every literal in Lk is true for the current input, and inactive, ck = 0, otherwise.
The TM is initialized with the hyperparameters C clauses, threshold T, specificity s, and negative-
class sampling rate q. Here, we are considering the weighted coalesced variant of the TM (Glimsdal
& Granmo, 2021). Thus, each of the C clauses is shared among the classes. Each clause has a
weight per class, wik for clause k and class i, whose sign gives the clause’s polarity for that class.
Weights are initialized uniformly at random from {−1, 1} and move in discrete ±1 steps during
training (Abeyrathna et al., 2021). The class sum (vi) is the total vote of the model towards class i
and is calculated as:

EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN
4.1
DATASETS
MNIST (LeCun et al., 1998) is a standard image classification benchmark, containing 60,000 train-
ing and 10,000 test grayscale images across 10 digit classes. FashionMNIST (Xiao et al., 2017) is
similar to MNIST, with the same train/test split sizes across 10 clothing-item classes. CelebA (Liu
et al., 2015) is a multilabel face-attribute classification dataset, containing 162,770 training and
19,867 test images, each labeled with 40 binary facial attributes. This is a highly imbalanced dataset
and contains 9.03 labels per sample on average. For this dataset, images are resized to 64 × 64 RGB
and random horizontal flipping is applied during training. Since the TM needs binarized inputs, we
use 8-level thermometer encoding (Buckman et al., 2018) on the pixel values, except for MNIST,
which is thresholded using a static pixel intensity of 75.
IMDB is a binary movie review sentiment classification task, containing 25,000 training and 25,000
test examples. The text is preprocessed by removing stopwords and encoding words into binary bag-
of-words (unigram and bigram) features. We then select the top 12,000 features using a chi-squared
test. AG News (Zhang et al., 2015) is a multiclass text classification task, containing 120,000 train-
ing and 7,600 test examples across 4 news-topic classes. We follow preprocessing similar to IMDB,
with an additional lemmatization step, using only unigram features, and selecting the top 2,000
features. GoEmotions (Demszky et al., 2020) is a multilabel emotion classification task, contain-
ing 43,400 training and 5,400 test examples across 28 emotion labels. This is a highly imbalanced
dataset, averaging 1.18 labels per sample. Text is tokenized with a tweet-aware tokenizer that pre-
serves case, collapses repeated characters, and properly handles emojis and unicode characters. We
then remove stopwords, lemmatize, replace URLs with a placeholder, and encode the top 10,000
features selected from unigram and bigram bag-of-words.
4

4.2
IMPLEMENTATION AND EVALUATION DETAILS
MBUR and Loss-Guided TM are compared under matched capacity, meaning the clauses and speci-
ficity s hyperparameters are kept the same across the two models. All the models are trained for
100 epochs and use coalesced clauses. We did not conduct an extensive hyperparameter grid search
to optimize each condition. Instead, hyperparameters for MBUR were selected through initial trials
based on prior literature and understanding of T and q. For Loss-Guided TM, a similar approach
was used to select the learning rate η and feedback rate λ. Table 1 lists the selected hyperparameters
used for each experiment.
We use three different loss functions across datasets to demonstrate the use of different losses accord-
ing to the dataset. Cross entropy (CE) is the standard classification loss, measuring the divergence
between the predicted and true class distributions. Symmetric cross entropy (SCE) (Wang et al.,
2019) adds a reverse cross entropy term that stays bounded even when the model is confidently
wrong, improving robustness to label noise. Asymmetric loss (ASL) (Ridnik et al., 2021) applies
separate down-weighting factors to positive and negative predictions along with a hard threshold on
the gradient for confident negatives. This is designed to counteract the positive-negative imbalance
inherent to multilabel classification. For brevity, we refer to the Loss-Guided TM trained with CE,
SCE, or ASL simply by the name of the loss.

Stefan Martin, Jakob Schattenfroh, Patrick Schuenke, Felix Frederik Zimmermann,
Ingolf Sack, Christoph Kolbitsch, Andreas Kofler
Abstract— Objective: Magnetic Resonance Elastography
(MRE) is a non-invasive imaging technique for mapping
biomechanical properties of in vivo tissue, including shear
wave speed (SWS), but involves intrinsically slow data
acquisition and an ill-posed wave inversion. Instead of
relying on handcrafted image priors, we propose a data-
driven approach jointly combining image reconstruction
and MRE inversion for robust SWS estimation from un-
dersampled k-space data. Methods: Our physics-informed
reconstruction framework comprises two blocks: a model-
based neural network (NN)-regularized reconstruction mod-
ule and a phase-gradient inversion (k-MDEV) calculating
SWS from the reconstructed images. Concatenating both
blocks yields an end-to-end trainable method to estimate
SWS directly from measured k-space data. We evalu-
ated the method on retrospectively highly undersampled
brain MRE data and compared it to a total variation (TV)
minimization-based approach. We assessed the impact of
end-to-end training (qualitative images and SWS maps as
targets) versus pre-training (qualitative images as targets)
and applied the method also to in vivo data. Results: Our
approach significantly reduces NRMSE by 30% compared
to TV. End-to-end training improves SWS estimation over
separate image reconstruction and SWS calculation. Con-
clusion: Accurate SWS quantification is possible at accel-
eration factors up to 19. Our method significantly outper-
forms TV, highlighting the need for data-driven regulariza-
tion in this challenging MR problem. Further, our approach
successfully generalizes to in vivo data. Significance: We
present the first end-to-end trainable MRE reconstruction
method for estimating SWS maps directly from k-space.
NN-based reconstruction can enable rapid stiffness map-
ping for dynamic studies, functional imaging, and real-time
clinical feedback.
Index Terms— Magnetic Resonance Elastography, End-
to-End Learning, Physics-Informed Deep Learning
