I. INTRODUCTION
M
AGNETIC Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a versatile and
powerful imaging technique that allows the acquisition
of high-resolution qualitative images of the internal anatomy
of the human body. In quantitative MRI (qMRI), various quan-
titative parameters with specific biophysical correspondences
can then be estimated from the image data. MR Elastography
(MRE) [1]–[3] is a qMRI technique that provides detailed
maps of biomechanical properties, enabling a non-invasive
assessment of tissue stiffness. Externally induced mechanical
waves result in tissue displacements, which are encoded as
proportional phase shifts in the MR signal by motion encoding
gradients (MEG) that are incorporated into specially designed
MRI sequences. These phase shifts are tracked over time,
enabling the calculation of shear wave speed (SWS) [4], which
generally involves three steps: acquisition of k-space data,
reconstruction of complex-valued MR images from the data,
and estimation of quantitative SWS maps from these images
with an inversion method.
The brain is a fascinating target for MRE, particularly
for detecting and monitoring neurological disorders that are
associated with localized changes in tissue stiffness, such
as Alzheimer’s disease [5]. Conventional MRE techniques
typically require multiple time-resolved acquisitions, resulting
in extended acquisition protocols with prolonged scan times
and vibration exposure. These factors can increase patient
discomfort, reduce clinical efficiency, and limit temporal reso-
lution, making it difficult to investigate dynamic physiological
processes that require fast, continuous measurements. Real-
time MRE addresses these limitations by enabling high frame-
rate stiffness mapping [6]. This approach improves patient
comfort, reduces motion-related artifacts, and enables the
monitoring of dynamic changes in brain tissue properties
– such as those occurring during the Valsalva maneuver
[7] or cardiac-cycle-related brain pulsations, as demonstrated
in ultrasound elastography [8]. Recent studies have shown
the feasibility and clinical value of rapid MRE in various
applications, including subsecond mapping of liver stiffness
[9], evaluation of the response in skeletal muscle to loading
at frame rates of ∼6 Hz [6], and functional brain MRE [10].
Real-time stiffness mapping can be achieved by reducing
scan time through undersampled data acquisition. In this
work, we utilize a motion-robust single-shot spiral readout for
MRE data acquisition, enabling the capture of all required
2
IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERING, VOL. XX, NO. XX, 2026
data in a single shot per timestep and MEG. However, data
undersampling introduces challenges into MRI reconstruction,
yielding an ill-posed inverse problem necessitating the use
of regularization techniques to stabilize the reconstruction.
Importantly, the subsequent generation of MRE maps from
wave images is itself inherently ill-posed due to noise and
unknown boundary conditions.
Undersampled MRE images have been reconstructed using
established non-learning approaches, which are typically ap-
plied prior to elastography inversion. These include parallel
imaging and compressed sensing with sparsity priors, such
as MRE-specific phase or displacement regularization [11], as

HOW NETWORK TOPOLOGY AND DATA HETEROGENEITY SHAPE
DECENTRALIZED LEARNING:
A SPECTRAL ANALYSIS
A PREPRINT
Luigi Palmieri, Lorenzo Valerio, Chiara Boldrini, Andrea Passarella, Marco Conti
IIT institute of the National Research Council, Pisa
János Kertész
Central European University, Vienna
ABSTRACT
Network topology influences decentralized federated learning through information mixing and
the relative contribution of individual nodes. While existing analyses primarily focus on spectral
mixing properties, they often assume doubly stochastic aggregation, overlooking topology-dependent
influence under irregular communication networks. We develop a spectral framework that separates
two complementary mechanisms: the dominant eigenmode determines the consensus trajectory
and node influence, while non-dominant eigenmodes govern the propagation and attenuation of
disagreement. Under uniform neighborhood averaging, we show that the stationary influence is
proportional to node degree plus one and derive a bound relating model disagreement to spectral
mixing and gradient heterogeneity. We then investigate how these mechanisms interact with the data
distribution across nodes. Experiments across regular and heterogeneous network topologies reveal
nearly identical learning dynamics under IID data, while network size and connectivity affect how
unevenly distributed information is learned under non-IID data. For non-IID settings, we characterize
how the distribution of data across nodes shapes the relative contribution of local information to
consensus dynamics.
Keywords Decentralized federated learning · network topology · spectral graph analysis · data heterogeneity · stationary
distribution
1
Introduction
Federated learning (FL) enables multiple devices or organizations to collaboratively train machine learning models
without sharing their local data. While traditional FL architectures rely on a central server to coordinate training and
aggregate model updates [15], decentralized federated learning (DFL) removes this dependency by allowing nodes to
exchange model parameters directly with their neighbors [9,12]. This approach is particularly relevant in environments
where centralized coordination is impractical or undesirable, such as peer-to-peer networks, edge computing systems,
and distributed sensing infrastructures. However, decentralization also introduces new challenges, as the learning
process becomes dependent on the communication network connecting the participating nodes.
Understanding how network topology affects decentralized learning has therefore attracted considerable attention.
Existing theoretical analyses have investigated how the spectral properties of the communication matrix influence
information mixing, model disagreement, and convergence rates [9, 12, 18]. In particular, the spectral gap has
traditionally been used to characterize how quickly differences between local models are attenuated, although more
recent analyses have shown that the complete eigenvalue spectrum can provide a more accurate characterization of
topology-dependent convergence [23]. Several studies have also identified conditions under which the impact of
topology becomes limited [19,21], while others have shown that heterogeneous data distributions can substantially
alter its influence on learning [6,10]. Nevertheless, many of these analyses assume doubly stochastic mixing matrices,
arXiv:2611.26104v1  [cs.LG]  19 Nov 2026
Topology and Data Heterogeneity in Decentralized Learning
A PREPRINT
which assign equal influence to all nodes in the consensus process. This assumption simplifies the analysis but does not
necessarily reflect decentralized averaging over irregular communication networks.
Indeed, consider a decentralized system in which each node averages the models received from its neighbors, including
its own, assigning equal weight to each contribution. Although the communication graph may be undirected, the
resulting mixing matrix is generally not doubly stochastic: nodes with different degrees normalize their incoming
contributions differently. Consequently, the consensus component of the learning dynamics does not necessarily
correspond to a uniform average of the local models and updates. Instead, individual nodes contribute according to a
topology-dependent stationary distribution. Recent work has investigated the theoretical properties of row-stochastic
aggregation and its implications for decentralized optimization [13, 14]. However, the consequences of these non-
uniform stationary weights for the contribution of heterogeneous information located at different nodes remain less
explicitly characterized. This raises a question that convergence-oriented analyses do not fully address: beyond
determining how quickly information propagates, how does network topology determine which information has greater
influence on the learning process?
The answer becomes particularly relevant when data are heterogeneously distributed. In practical decentralized systems,
different nodes may observe different populations, environments, or classes, and some information may be available
only at a small subset of nodes. Under these conditions, the influence of local information depends not only on its
statistical properties but also on the position of the nodes holding it within the communication network. Previous
empirical work has shown that information available at highly connected nodes can propagate more effectively than
information located at peripheral nodes, leading to substantial differences in learning performance [20]. At the same
time, heterogeneous local gradients can continuously introduce differences between models, whose propagation and
attenuation depend on the spectral properties of the network [10,24]. Understanding decentralized learning therefore
requires considering both the influence assigned to individual nodes and the dynamics of disagreement among them.
In this paper, we investigate how network topology and data distribution jointly determine the influence of local
information in decentralized learning. While existing spectral analyses primarily characterize convergence and
information mixing, they provide less insight into how information held by different nodes contributes to the learning
process. We address this question by combining the spectral decomposition of DecAvg dynamics, i.e., the fully
decentralized version of FedAvg aggregation function [22], with a class-wise characterization of local gradients. This
allows us to distinguish the effects of network mixing from those of topology-dependent node influence, and to quantify
how the placement of heterogeneous information shapes the consensus trajectory. In particular, our analysis provides
a theoretical explanation for the hub amplification and peripheral dilution effects previously observed empirically,
identifying the conditions under which network structure can favor or suppress localized information.
The main contributions of this work are as follows:
• Topology-dependent information influence. We characterize how stationary influence weights interact with
heterogeneous local data distributions, deriving a class-contribution ratio that quantifies how node position and
data placement jointly determine the relative contribution of localized information to the consensus trajectory.
• Spectral analysis of learning dynamics. Building on established spectral properties of reversible mixing
matrices, we decompose DecAvg dynamics into consensus and disagreement components, characterizing how
stationary node influence, spectral mixing, and gradient heterogeneity jointly shape learning dynamics.
• Experimental evaluation. Through experiments on regular and heterogeneous network topologies, we
investigate the predicted effects of topology and data placement, showing limited topology dependence under
IID data and differences in the learning of localized information under non-IID data.
Our findings highlight that the impact of network topology on decentralized learning cannot be characterized solely
through connectivity or spectral mixing rates. The stationary distribution introduces an additional mechanism through
which topology influences learning, particularly when data are not uniformly distributed across nodes. This perspective
is especially relevant in decentralized deployments where communication patterns are constrained by the underlying
infrastructure and cannot necessarily be optimized or redesigned.
The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 introduces the system
model and DecAvg algorithm, while Section 4 derives its matrix representation. Section 5 develops the spectral
decomposition and characterizes consensus and disagreement dynamics. Section 6 investigates the interplay between
topology and data distribution, and Section 7 presents the experimental evaluation. Section 8 concludes the paper.

2
Related work
The relationship between network topology and decentralized learning has been investigated from several perspectives,
including spectral convergence analysis, data heterogeneity, aggregation protocols, and information propagation over
complex networks. We review these research directions below, focusing on their treatment of topology-dependent
learning dynamics and node influence.
2.1
Spectral Analysis of Decentralized Learning
Early analyses of decentralized stochastic gradient descent (D-SGD) established the importance of spectral connectivity
for convergence and model disagreement [12,17,18]. Subsequent work extended these results to generalization and
stability [25] and identified conditions under which the influence of network topology diminishes asymptotically [21].
Koloskova et al. [9] provide a unified convergence analysis of decentralized SGD variants, showing how spectral
connectivity, communication frequency, and gradient variability jointly affect learning performance. More recently,
3
Topology and Data Heterogeneity in Decentralized Learning
A PREPRINT
Takezawa et al. [23] demonstrate that convergence bounds based solely on the spectral gap can be overly pessimistic,
deriving a refined characterization involving the complete eigenvalue spectrum. These works primarily investigate
convergence properties under communication assumptions that yield uniform stationary node influence, rather than the
effects of topology-dependent weighting on heterogeneous local information.
2.2
Network Topology and Data Heterogeneity
The interaction between topology and data distribution has received considerable attention. Neglia et al. [19] investigate
conditions under which learning performance becomes largely independent of network connectivity, while Yuan et
al. [24] analyze how removing heterogeneity-induced effects changes the topology dependence of decentralized SGD
convergence. Other approaches explicitly incorporate data heterogeneity into communication. Dandi et al. [6] propose
adaptive mixing strategies that account for differences between local data distributions, while Le Bars et al. [10]
introduce neighborhood heterogeneity, a quantity that captures the interaction between communication topology and
local objectives. They use this characterization to derive convergence bounds and guide topology selection under
heterogeneous data. Huang et al. [7] provide a complementary framework based on sample-induced topology, jointly
modeling communication and stochastic optimization. While these studies establish that topology and data heterogeneity
cannot be considered independently, their primary focus is on convergence analysis or adapting communication to
mitigate heterogeneity, rather than characterizing how fixed network structures weight information held by different
nodes.
2.3
Non-Doubly-Stochastic Aggregation
Several approaches address decentralized learning with non-doubly-stochastic communication matrices. Push-sum
protocols [8] compensate for unequal aggregation weights through auxiliary normalization variables, enabling average
consensus over asymmetric networks. This principle has been extended to distributed optimization through subgradient-
push [16] and to stochastic decentralized learning through Stochastic Gradient Push [1]. More recent studies analyze
row-stochastic communication directly. Liang et al. [13] derive convergence guarantees and develop gradient-tracking
methods for row-stochastic networks. Particularly relevant to our work, Liu et al. [14] develop a stationary-weighted
Hilbert-space analysis of row-stochastic aggregation, establishing convergence bounds and identifying conditions
under which it can outperform doubly stochastic alternatives. Our analysis builds on these established properties
of row-stochastic aggregation but addresses a different question: how do the stationary weights induced by a fixed
communication topology interact with heterogeneous data placement? Rather than developing new convergence
guarantees or correcting non-uniform influence, we characterize how topology-dependent weights affect the contribution
of class-specific information to the consensus trajectory.
2.4
Network Structure and Information Propagation
Beyond convergence analysis, the structural position of nodes can influence how information propagates during
decentralized learning. Palmieri et al. [20] empirically investigate the interaction between network topology and data
placement, showing that information held by highly connected nodes can spread more effectively, while information
located at peripheral nodes may be diluted during aggregation. Their analysis considers several structural properties,
including degree and betweenness centrality, clustering, and community structure.The present work extends this
empirical investigation by providing an analytical characterization of the underlying mechanisms. In particular, we
connect the stationary influence induced by network topology to class-specific gradient contributions, deriving an
explicit relationship between node connectivity, local class proportions, and the relative contribution of localized
information to the consensus trajectory. A related but distinct direction is investigated by Badie-Modiri et al. [2], who
study the effects of network topology on decentralized learning with heterogeneous model initialization. In contrast, we
assume homogeneous initialization and focus on the interaction between network topology and heterogeneous data
distributions.

REVEALING PATHWAY INTERACTIONS IN
NETWORK COMPUTATIONS WITH
COMPLETE PATH CONTRIBUTION
Shenghua Liu∗,†
Department of Physics
Stanford University
Youssef Faragalla∗
Neurosciences Interdepartmental Program
Stanford University
Surya Ganguli
Department of Applied Physics
Stanford University
Stephen A. Baccus†
Department of Neurobiology
Stanford University
ABSTRACT
Networks pass signals through many layers of interconnected units, so explaining
what they compute means tracing how information travels from input to output
and how pathways interact. Most existing approaches analyze only pairwise inter-
actions between components such as units, layers or attention heads. Even when
these measurements are combined post hoc into a circuit, they do not capture
higher-order interactions along full causal chains (paths) from input to output,
and so cannot address how exponentially many paths interact to construct net-
work computation. This leaves a large set of mechanistic questions unanswerable,
for example whether inhibitory pathways veto excitatory ones, and how the two
combine to yield network decisions. To address this gap, we introduce Complete
Path Contribution, a method to decompose the network output into mathemati-
cally complete contributions of individual paths to study path-level interactions
directly and at scale. Partial summation then induces definitions of contributions
for any circuit at any granularity level, with completeness guaranteed at every
level. We further present an efficient algorithm that identifies the k strongest paths
without examining all of them, with runtime empirically linear in k rather than
exponential in depth. By applying Path Contribution to benchmark image clas-
sification networks, we quantify excitatory-inhibitory interactions and show how
they collectively construct network decisions at a level of detail previously un-
measurable. Furthermore, in an interpretable model of the mouse retina, it reveals
how dynamic receptive fields emerge from excitatory-inhibitory interaction motifs
among pathways between different cell types in response to time-varying natural
stimuli. Overall, Path Contribution reveals how a network’s causal pathways in-
teract at scale to transform input to output.
1
UNDERSTANDING NETWORK COMPUTATIONS: FROM NEURONS TO
CIRCUITS
Understanding neural network computations matters for advancing neuroscience and AI (Kriegesko-
rte, 2015; Richards et al., 2019), for model distillation (Hinton et al., 2015), and for AI safety
(Bereska & Gavves, 2024). Artificial and biological networks both compute in a distributed manner,
transforming the input through many stages of nonlinear operations (DiCarlo et al., 2012; LeCun
et al., 2015), often through the combined effect of excitatory (positively contributing) and inhibitory
(negatively contributing) units and pathways (Isaacson & Scanziani, 2011; Maheswaranathan et al.,
∗These authors contributed equally to this work.
†Correspondence to: sliu24@stanford.edu or baccus@stanford.edu.
1
arXiv:2611.26101v1  [cs.LG]  19 Nov 2026
Preprint
2023). Understanding a network therefore requires understanding not only its individual units, but
also how they coordinate in interacting pathways to transform input to output.
Parallel pathways carrying distinct signals are central to the visual system (Nassi & Callaway, 2009).
In primates, the parvocellular pathway is higher resolution, slower, chromatically sensitive, and less
adaptive to contrast, whereas the magnocellular pathway is lower resolution, faster, chromatically
insensitive, and more adaptive (Derrington & Lennie, 1984; Kaplan & Shapley, 1986; Solomon
et al., 2004). In cortex, the ventral stream is associated with object discrimination and the dorsal
stream with estimating object position and trajectory (Ungerleider & Mishkin, 1982; Goodale &
Milner, 1992).
Interactions between excitation and inhibition have long been known to underlie visual computa-
tion. Edge enhancement in the retina arises not from edge-specific excitation, but because inhibition
through parallel pathways cancels excitation in uniform regions away from edges (Ratliff & Hartline,
1959; Kuffler, 1953; Barlow, 1953). Similarly, object motion sensitivity, which flags moving objects
while rejecting background eye movements, arises because all retinal motion generates excitation,
but inhibition vetoes it wherever motion is coincident across the visual field ( ¨Olveczky et al., 2003;
Baccus et al., 2008). That this computation arises only two synapses after edge enhancement, yet
was discovered decades later, shows how challenging it is to connect interacting pathways to com-
putation. As features are computed through serial layers, canceling paths become difficult to find
because their net effect is zero. Identifying such mechanisms requires measuring the contributions
of individual pathways, including those that cancel, rather than only the net effects of units.
Excitation-inhibition interactions also underlie computations in artificial networks. In InceptionV1,
a car detector is excited by wheel features below and window features above, and inhibited by the
same features in the opposite positions; selectivity arises from subtracting a parallel pathway rather
than from excitation alone (Olah et al., 2020). In GPT-2 small, some attention heads copy the
correct name to the output while others suppress the token the model is about to predict, apparently
calibrating its confidence (Wang et al., 2022). Such cancellation can hide components from analysis.
In language models, ablating one head often triggers compensation by others, so a component’s net
effect can be near zero while its direct contribution is large (McGrath et al., 2023). Excitation and
inhibition are therefore properties of paths, not units.
1.1
TWO ORTHOGONAL AXES OF EXPLANATION
A full explanation of network computation is composed of two orthogonal axes. The parallel (or
disjunctive) axis typically involves first specifying a cut of the model’s computational graph (such
as neurons or weights in a layer). Then, the explanation offers an interpretable account of “what is
happening at this stage of the network”, such as features represented or causally important neurons.
Next, the second axis extends this explanation across depth, which is the serial (or conjunctive) di-
rection of explanation. Traditionally, one applies the method to many layers separately and observes
the evolution of the features or causal information contained, and sometimes pairwise interactions
between adjacent layers, but this does not constitute a full explanation because it does not answer
how representations or actions compose across many layers of the network to drive the output. This
higher-order composition happens in a combinatorial number of ways growing exponentially with
depth, which makes it an intractable problem so far.
1.2
THE LANDSCAPE OF INTERPRETABILITY TOOLS
The first stage of explanation is understanding how a single unit (neuron or component) computes.
A canonical framework from neuroscience characterizes a unit by how the input drives it, its recep-
tive field (RF), and how it drives the output, its projective field (PF) (Lehky & Sejnowski, 1988).
RF methods include spike-triggered averaging (De Boer & Kuyper, 1968), instantaneous receptive
fields (IRFs) (Maheswaranathan et al., 2023), most exciting inputs (Walker et al., 2019), and sparse
autoencoders (Bricken et al., 2023). PF methods include gradient-based attribution (Simonyan et al.,
2014; Ancona et al., 2018).
Other methods measure a unit’s total causal effect on the output, such as the raw gradient (Si-
monyan et al., 2014), SmoothGrad (Smilkov et al., 2017), and Integrated Gradients (Sundararajan
et al., 2017) for inputs, and LRP (Bach et al., 2015), DeepLIFT (Shrikumar et al., 2017), and Deep
2
Preprint
SHAP (Lundberg & Lee, 2017) for hidden neurons. Causal interventions (Vig et al., 2020; Geiger
et al., 2021) instead compare the original network with a modified one, so they do not explain a
unit’s PF in the unaltered network. None of these methods show how the RF and PF compose. A
related line of work does express a unit’s contribution as a composition of its RF and PF, including
activation times gradient (Shrikumar et al., 2017), neuron conductance (Dhamdhere et al., 2018;
Shrikumar et al., 2018), its application to retinal models (Tanaka et al., 2019; Maheswaranathan
et al., 2023), and contribution decomposition (CODEC) (Melander et al., 2026), which further ana-
lyzes population motifs of contributions within a layer.
However, fully explaining a neuron’s RF requires more than relating its input to its activation. We
must examine the network in between, since the transformation arises from many interacting parallel
pathways. Likewise, explaining its PF requires analyzing how the pathways from the neuron to the
output interact. A satisfactory method must therefore quantify each pathway’s role in a neuron’s
computation, with guarantees that pathway-level scores fully account for the neuron’s effect, and
that neuron-level effects in turn aggregate to fully account for the network output.
Existing circuit-level interpretability methods do not offer a satisfactory solution to this problem.
One line of related work here is circuit discovery (Conmy et al., 2023; Syed et al., 2024; Marks
et al., 2024; Ameisen et al., 2025) and model pruning (Hatefi et al., 2024; 2026). These methods
often identify the most important units first via causal interventions (Meng et al., 2022) or attribu-
tion (Kram´ar et al., 2024), and then compose them into a sparse circuit. These circuits may be more
interpretable than the full model, and in some cases tailored to semantic interpretation (Geiger et al.,
2021), but they do not quantify the contributions of individual paths. A small literature directly
quantifies the importance of paths (Lu et al., 2020; 2021; Du et al., 2023; Goldowsky-Dill et al.,
2023; Wang et al., 2022), but these works do not advance a notion of hierarchical completeness for
the paths of a neuron and, in turn, the neurons of a network.
1.3
A UNIFIED FRAMEWORK FOR ANALYZING NETWORK COMPUTATIONS AT THE UNIT AND
CIRCUIT LEVELS AT SCALE

a straight line path in input space. (B) A neuron’s contribution is a composition of its receptive
and projective fields. The RF and PF both involve many parallel pathways, and they compose

To address this gap, we introduce a principled and unified framework, Complete Path Contribution,
to quantify the causal contribution of each neuron, component, subnetwork (circuit), and full input-
output pathway and analyze them at scale (Figure 1). Our main contributions are as follows:
One algorithm for neurons, components, subnetworks, and paths.
Unlike previous methods
that first find important components in each layer and then compose them into a circuit post hoc, we
propose a single algorithm that directly measures the contribution of each path, which naturally in-
duces the contribution of any subnetwork as a sum over its paths. In particular, the contribution of an
input pixel and a hidden neuron recover Integrated Gradients and neuron conductance (Dhamdhere
et al., 2018) respectively, and the contribution of a convolutional channel recovers CODEC (Me-
lander et al., 2026).
3
Preprint
Hierarchical completeness.
Under our framework, a coarse component’s contribution is guaran-
teed to be an exact sum of the contributions of its finer components (e.g., paths through a neuron,
neurons in a convolutional channel), and the sum over any cut of the model’s computational graph
is guaranteed to equal the output difference with respect to a baseline. See Appendix A for the full
definition of subnetwork contributions and the proof of hierarchical completeness.
An efficient algorithm for finding the k strongest paths.
A full explanation of network compu-
tations involves characterizing a number of paths that is exponential in the number of layers. We
tackle this intractable problem by devising an efficient algorithm to identify the k strongest paths
without exhaustive enumeration. Instead, the runtime is empirically linear in the number of paths
requested. Overall, this work enables a unified view of component-based and circuit-based expla-
nations of network computation, and makes an initial effort towards a full explanation of network
computations at the path level via an efficient top-k algorithm.
2

2.1
THE CONTRIBUTION OF A PATH
The Path Contribution framework starts with defining the contribution of a single path. Consider a
feedforward neural network f with input x, baseline x′, and scalar output y = f(x). Let the input
be layer 0 and the output be layer L. Let A be the activations of the network, with Al

2.2
TOP-k ALGORITHM
The main challenge of fully explaining network computations rests in the intractability of the compo-
sitional interactions between components across layers: explaining what happens at every layer of a
network does not answer how they interact across layers. At the level of paths, our framework turns
this challenge into a single parallel aggregation of an exponential number of paths. Even though
characterizing that exponential set remains prohibitive in general, we devise an efficient algorithm
to identify the k paths with the highest absolute contribution without exhaustive enumeration.
Without integration and for a single stimulus, the path contribution is purely a product of the Jaco-
bians along the path. Taking the logarithm of the absolute value of the contribution, the problem
of finding the top-k paths reduces to finding the k longest paths in a directed acyclic graph (DAG),
which can be solved in time polynomial in both k and the network size (Tziavelis et al., 2025). Lu
et al. (2021) remarked that an algorithm with such worst case guarantees is impossible due to the
summation over the integration steps and inputs, but an algorithm that is efficient in practice is still
possible. We present such an algorithm that, within the range we tested, scales up to a 12-layer MLP
with 128 neurons per layer (784 × 12812 ≈1028 paths) in reasonable time on an M3 Pro MacBook
Pro.
The algorithm is a best-first branch and bound search, analogous to the A* algorithm, which uses a
heuristic bound to find an optimal path without exhaustively searching the graph. The intuition is
as follows. Let a prefix (i0, . . . , il) denote the set of all its completions. We now organize the path
set as a tree, each node being a prefix. The root is empty, which stands for all paths, and the leaves
are individual paths. For every node we compute an upper bound on |Cp| over all its completions.
We keep a priority queue ordered by bound, and always expand the most promising node. When a
node is expanded into complete paths, each is pushed with its exact |Cp| in place of a bound. When
a complete path is at the top of the queue, it is guaranteed to be stronger than any path not yet seen,
since its exact contribution outranks every bound still in the queue. The first k paths to be popped
from the queue are the top-k paths. A complete description of the algorithm and its pseudocode is
given in Appendix D.
3
NEURONS AND PATHS: A TOY INTERPRETABILITY CASE STUDY
In Figure 2, we consider a toy model that approximates a continuous exclusive-or (XOR) function
and examine what conclusions we would draw from a neuron-based vs. path-based approach re-
garding its computation. With activation analysis, we would be able to characterize the RFs of c
and d separately, examining which inputs excite them. Because their RFs are of opposite sign, one
may conclude that their RFs differ by an inhibitory connection, but nonetheless cannot deduce that
such a connection causally connects the two. Analyzing neuron contributions additionally allows
for causal conclusions. Because the activation and contribution of c are of opposite sign, the net
causal effect of c on d is negative whenever c is active, which yields a causal statement that c in-
hibits d as its projective field. However, this analysis misses interactions at the pathway level. In the
input region indicated by the green boxes, an inhibitory direct effect from a to d is canceled by an
excitatory effect along the path mediated by c. Analysis of a’s contribution would conclude that it
is not causally important at that input, even though it is active. This misses the E-I interaction in a’s
PF that results in a net zero effect. Therefore, a full explanation of network computation necessitates
path-level explanations.
The toy model also illuminates how Path Contribution relates to causal interventions. Path patch-
ing (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2023) simulates the output change if a specific path’s effect was re-
placed by that from a counterfactual input, here the zero baseline. In the framework of Shapley
values (Rozemberczki et al., 2022), a full characterization of a path’s causal effect among k to-
tal paths involves measuring its patching effect in 2k−1 coalitions (whether each remaining path is
patched or not; we will call these contexts), the mean of this score distribution being the Shapley
value. Path Contribution is a causal measure based on accumulating gradients (which are inherently
causal) instead of patching, but it coincides with path patching on linear networks. Furthermore, in
this nonlinear toy model, Path Contribution coincides with the Shapley values, while path patching
from the full model doesn’t, motivating Path Contribution as a useful representative statistic of the
full causal score distribution that enjoys the completeness property. See Appendix G for details.

From Sessions to Serving: Integrating LLM-Based Embeddings
into Retrieval for Production Content Recommendation
Zhixiong Hu
Autodesk
San Francisco, CA, USA
Meng Li
Autodesk
San Francisco, CA, USA
Maggie Zhang
Autodesk
San Francisco, CA, USA
Deborshi Goswami
Autodesk
San Francisco, CA, USA
David Bailey
Autodesk
San Francisco, CA, USA
James Bradley
Autodesk
San Francisco, CA, USA
Abstract
Personalized content recommendation on large marketplace web-
sites must reconcile heterogeneous candidate content (e.g., cus-
tomer stories, product pages, industry pages, and learning content)
with sparse, fast-changing user behavior, placing increasing de-
mands on the retrieval stage to represent user interest well, not
just the downstream ranking stage. We present LSER (LLM Ses-
sion Embedding Retrieval), a production content recommendation
system for autodesk.com that derives session- and history-level em-
beddings from a pretrained large language model (LLM) and adds
them as auxiliary user-side features in the retrieval-stage user tower
alongside existing learned sequence encoders. To keep user-side em-
beddings fresh under real-time behavior, we build a nearline serving
path that asynchronously refreshes sequential and LLM-derived
user vectors for our main content recommendation server. We
validate the incremental value of the LLM features through an ab-
lation study across our full multi-content-type catalog. Our results
indicate that integrating LLM-derived embeddings as additional
retrieval signals, together with production-grade nearline serving,
is technically feasible and can improve model performances.
CCS Concepts
• Information systems →Recommender systems; Retrieval
models and search; • Computing methodologies →Machine learn-
ing.
Keywords
Session Embeddings, Large Language Models, Retrieval-Augmented
Recommendation, Production Recommender Systems, Nearline
Serving
1
Introduction
Personalized content recommendation on large marketplace web-
sites such as autodesk.com must contend with highly heteroge-
neous candidate pools (customer stories, product pages, industry
pages, and learning content), sparse and bursty real-time behav-
ioral signals, and the need to reconcile short-term session intent
with long-term user context (e.g., product usage history). Classi-
cal two-stage retrieval-and-ranking pipelines address scale by first
retrieving a high-recall candidate set and then ranking it with a
learned model [6], but the quality of both stages is bottlenecked by
how well the retrieval stage represents a user’s evolving interests,
not just the ranking stage.
Recent work has shown that embeddings derived from large lan-
guage models (LLMs) carry rich semantic signal that complements
traditional ID-based collaborative representations in sequential and
session-based recommendation. Boz et al. [2] demonstrate several
ways of injecting LLM-derived item embeddings into sequential
recommenders, including aggregating them into a session-level em-
bedding for direct similarity-based retrieval. Liu et al. [9] use frozen
LLM semantic embeddings together with retrieval-augmented self-
distillation to address long-tail user and item coverage in sequential
recommendation, and Cui et al. [3] similarly use LLM-derived se-
mantic embeddings to retrieve informative contrastive pairs for
sequence encoder training. Kim et al. [8] instead let an LLM directly
consume the user/item embeddings of a pretrained collaborative
filtering model, avoiding the extensive fine-tuning that LLM-based
recommenders typically require. On the industrial side, LEARN [7]
freezes a pretrained LLM as an item encoder and aligns it to a twin-
tower recommendation objective at industrial scale on a short-video
platform, while TreeBridge [11] bridges the semantic/behavioral
gap between LLM embeddings and collaborative signals at Shopee
with an online-offline hybrid serving paradigm, reporting a mea-
surable lift in gross merchandise volume after deployment.
Beyond embedding-level integration, a parallel line of industrial
work has pushed retrieval and ranking architectures themselves
toward greater scale and expressiveness. Zhang et al. [18] establish
a scaling law for large-scale recommendation models analogous
to those observed for LLMs, and Zhai et al. [17] reformulate rec-
ommendation as a generative sequential transduction task with
their HSTU architecture, scaling to trillions of parameters and
demonstrating a power-law relationship between model quality
and training compute, while OneRec [4] replaces the conventional
cascaded retrieve-then-rank pipeline with a single end-to-end gen-
erative model. PinRec [1] and GRank [14] likewise adopt generative
retrieval at industrial scale, the latter unifying target-aware candi-
date generation with lightweight ranking to avoid the maintenance
cost of structured indices. Complementary to generative retrieval,
Zhang et al. [19] show that jointly optimizing recall and seman-
tic relevance with a multi-head item-to-item retrieval architecture
meaningfully improves both engagement and content diversity,
Fan et al. [5] propose a multi-embedding retrieval framework that
represents a single user with multiple embeddings conditioned on
implicit and explicit interests, and Lyu et al. [10] show that incorpo-
rating an offline-computed, extremely long user history embedding
is highly incremental on top of existing attentive sequence models
deployed across multiple production surfaces. Together, these sys-
tems illustrate that the retrieval stage itself — not only ranking —
arXiv:2611.26096v1  [cs.IR]  19 Nov 2026
is an increasingly active area where richer user/session represen-
tations, including those derived from LLMs, are being deployed at
industrial scale.
These results collectively confirm that LLM-derived session
and user representations, and richer retrieval architectures more
broadly, can meaningfully improve production recommender sys-
tems [4, 5, 7, 10, 11, 17, 19]. However, each of these systems was
developed and tuned for a specific company’s data, content catalog,
and serving infrastructure, and the concrete design decisions (how
the session encoder is adapted and fine-tuned, how its output is
integrated into an existing retrieval stage, and how the resulting
embedding is served with production latency and freshness con-
straints) are necessarily specific to each deployment context. We see
real value in reporting a concrete, end-to-end account of how this
integration was carried out in our own setting, to add to the body
of practical, reproducible evidence available to the community.
In this paper, we present LSER, a system built around our own
multi-content-type recommendation setting on autodesk.com and
the constraints of our existing serving infrastructure. We adapt
a pretrained LLM to produce session- and history-level embed-
ding vectors, concatenate them into our retrieval-stage user tower
as additional features (while retaining learned in-tower sequence
encoders for production), and build a nearline serving path that
refreshes learned sequential and LLM-derived user vectors in time
for our main content recommendation server. We validate their
incremental value through an offline ablation across our full multi-
content-type catalog, and further observe encouraging improve-
ments in engagement and downstream conversion metrics in an
online A/B test across several production surfaces. Our main con-
tributions are:
(1) We design an LLM-based embedding path that produces aux-
iliary session and history vectors, adapt a pretrained LLM
with custom modifications and a fine-tuning strategy tai-
lored to our multi-content-type setting, and integrate these
vectors into the retrieval user tower without replacing exist-
ing sequence encoders.
(2) We deploy nearline refresh of user-side embeddings for pro-
duction serving and validate the system with offline and
online experiments.
2
Method
2.1
Retrieval Architecture
LSER performs retrieval with a two-tower architecture: a user tower
that encodes a user’s short- and long-term interests into a single
dense representation, and an item tower that encodes each candidate
piece of content into a representation of the same dimensionality.
Retrieval reduces to an approximate nearest-neighbor search be-
tween the user vector and the item vectors in the catalog, which
scales to our full multi-content-type candidate pool (customer sto-
ries, product pages, industry pages, and learning content) at produc-
tion latency. This retrieval stage produces a smaller candidate set
of Top-𝐾items, which is then passed to a downstream ranking step
(outside the scope of this paper) that applies additional, more fine-
grained scoring before final content is shown to the user. Figure 1
gives an overview of the full system, spanning both the nearline
serving pipeline and the two-tower retrieval model described in
this section.
2.1.1
Notation. Let 𝑢∈U denote a user and 𝑖∈I denote a candi-

APPROXIMATE ADJOINT MODELS FOR MEMORY AND
COMPUTE-EFFICIENT ONLINE LEARNING OF HYBRID MODELS
A PREPRINT
Emilio González-Zamora1,2 *,
Pierre Tandeo1,2,
Laurent Debreu3,
Said Ouala1,2
1 IMT Atlantique, Lab-STICC, UMR CNRS 6285, 29238, Brest, France
2 ODYSSEY Team-Project, INRIA IMT-Atlantique CNRS, Brest, France
3 Univ. Grenoble Alpes, Inria, CNRS, Grenoble INP, LJK, Grenoble, France
ABSTRACT
Differentiable programming enables online calibration of numerical models by minimizing errors
accumulated along simulated trajectories. This includes estimating physical parameters and training
neural sub-models in hybrid configurations. Gradients are typically computed using adjoint methods,
or backpropagation through time (BPTT), whose computational and memory costs grow with the
length of the training window. This limits the duration and resolution of hybrid-model training, a
major bottleneck for realistic geophysical applications. Approaches like truncated BPTT reduces
memory use by discarding sensitivities across truncation boundaries, introducing gradient bias and
neglecting long-range dependencies. We propose a class of gradient approximation methods that
preserve the adjoint recurrence over the full trajectory while approximating only the pullback operators
within it. Exact pullbacks are computed by automatic differentiation at sparse anchor states only.
Between anchors, sensitivities propagate either through the identity (Zero-order) or through a reused,
frozen pullback (Pullback Reuse). This approximation makes the parameter pullback constant within
each chunk, allowing the gradient sum to factorize so that a single evaluation per chunk replaces one
per time step. We evaluate both on three systems of increasing complexity, an incomplete Lorenz-63
model, a large-eddy closure for two-dimensional quasi-geostrophic turbulence, and bias correction
in a multilayer quasi-geostrophic ocean model. Peak memory falls by up to an order of magnitude
and runtime up to fourfold, with Pullback Reuse staying closest to the exact gradient direction. In all
three cases, approximate gradients support hybrid-model training at comparable accuracy, showing
that effective online learning does not require exact gradients.
Keywords Differentiable programming · Hybrid models · Online learning · Machine-Learning · Numerical simulation ·
Gradient approximation Optimization
1
Introduction
Numerical simulations of fluid flows require representing the interactions between processes that span a continuum
of scales. Direct Numerical Simulations (DNS) resolve them explicitly, on a grid fine enough to capture the smallest
dissipative scale, which is tractable only at moderate Reynolds numbers and in idealized configurations (Moin and
Mahesh, 1998; Pope, 2000; Sandham et al., 2017). For realistic flows, Computational Fluid Dynamics and its geophysical
counterparts instead seek the best fidelity attainable under a fixed computational budget. Common strategies rely on
decomposing the flow into a numerically resolved large-scale and an unresolved remainder whose effect on the resolved
scale is represented by a sub-model or closure. Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) and Large Eddy Simulations
(LES) are canonical examples (Leonard, 1975; Mason, 1994; Meneveau and Katz, 2000; Ghosal, 1999; Pope, 2000).
Physics-based sub-models derive this closure from first principles, as in eddy-viscosity assumptions where the unresolved
scales are treated as mainly diffusive (Smagorinsky, 1963; Germano et al., 1991; Spalart and Allmaras, 1992; Wilcox,
∗Corresponding author: emilio.gonzalez-zamora@imt-atlantique.fr
arXiv:2611.26095v1  [cs.LG]  19 Nov 2026
2008); similar heuristics are used for unresolved processes in the ocean and atmosphere (Christensen and Zanna, 2022).
Their continuous form permits theoretical validation and analysis of the well-posedness of the resulting equations, but
they remain a significant source of uncertainty. Their free parameters are difficult to tune, and assumptions they encode
do not always hold in the regimes where they are applied. Unresolved scales, for instance, do not only dissipate energy
but they redistribute it and feed it back to larger scales, which diffusive closures cannot represent (Piomelli et al., 1991;
Kitsios et al., 2013; Jansen and Held, 2014; Zanna et al., 2017).
The increasing availability of high-resolution simulations and observations, together with the progress in deep learning,
has motivated a growing interest in the use of machine learning and artificial intelligence for numerical modeling.
A first line of work replaces the numerical model entirely by a data-driven surrogate, either through reduced-order
models evolving a low-dimensional representation of the flow (Ouala et al., 2020, 2023a,b), or through neural emulators
trained to reproduce the dynamics of the full state (Pathak et al., 2022; Bi et al., 2023; Lam et al., 2023). A second
approach, known as hybrid modeling, retains the physical dynamical model and adds a learned component to account for
unresolved dynamics, correct systematic model biases, or replace uncertain closure schemes. This learned component
is typically a deep neural network (Rasp, 2020; Ouala et al., 2024; Frezat et al., 2022; Maddison, 2026).
Two strategies exist for training the learned component of a hybrid model. Offline or a priori learning, trains the
sub-model independently of the dynamical system, as a supervised regression problem against a reference response.
This approach remains widely adopted for its conceptual simplicity and low computational cost (Zanna and Bolton,
2021; Frezat et al., 2021).Because the sub-model never interacts with the physics during training, however, it is sensitive
to the distribution shift between the training data and the states encountered during inference, and offline-trained
parameterizations may show degraded long-term predictive skill, unphysical behavior, or numerical instabilities once
coupled to the dynamical model (Frezat et al., 2022; Maddison, 2026; Yan et al., 2025).
Online or a posteriori learning, addresses these limitations by embedding the sub-model within the dynamical system
during training. The coupled hybrid system is unrolled over several time steps, the loss is evaluated on the resulting
trajectory, and the gradients are propagated through both the dynamical model and the sub-model. This formulation
typically relies on differentiable programming where the numerical solver is written in a framework that supports
automatic differentiation, so that the sensitivity of the simulated trajectory to the sub-model parameters is available. The
sub-model therefore learns on the states the coupled system actually visits, and accounts for the temporal dependencies
between them by minimizing the error accumulated along the unrolled hybrid trajectory. Online learning has been
shown to improve forecast skill, promote long-term stability, and reduce the volume of training data required (Frezat
et al., 2022; List et al., 2022; Ouala et al., 2024).
Beyond idealized cases, current work aims to demonstrate online learning on realistic, large-scale problems, with recent
examples in atmosphere (Kochkov et al., 2024) and ocean (Meunier et al., 2025) modeling. However, training through
long simulated trajectories remains computationally expensive and thus the major bottleneck. Exact gradients requires
information from intermediate simulation steps to be available during the backward pass, and thus it requires storing
every intermediate states before traversing them backwards, making memory grow with both the trajectory length and
the dimension of the model state. For systems with many degrees of freedom, this can limit the duration of the training
window and the resolution at which the hybrid model can be trained. This constraint may help explain why some
previous studies have relied on relatively coarse resolutions and limited domains (Kochkov et al., 2024; Meunier et al.,
2025). Approaches such as checkpointing (Griewank and Walther, 2000; Stumm and Walther, 2010; Chen et al., 2016)
and truncated backpropagation through time (TBPTT) offer different ways to manage these costs, but involve trade-offs
between memory, computation, and gradient accuracy. We discuss these approaches in more detail in Section 4.
In this work, we target the computational cost of online learning. We introduce a class of Pullback Approximation
methods that reduce the cost of the backward pass while propagating sensitivities across the full trajectory. The paper is
organized as follows. Section 2 formalizes the hybrid modeling framework and the online learning problem. Section 3
introduces the proposed gradient approximation methods within a unified framework that also covers backpropagation
through time and its truncated variant, Truncated Backpropagation Through Time (TBPTT), which serves as our
biased-gradient baseline. Section 4 situates them with respect to other strategies for reducing the cost of exact gradients,
and to related work in numerical analysis and deep learning. Section 5 describes the case studies and reports the results,
evaluating methods in terms of both model accuracy and computational cost. Section 6 discusses the implications and
outlines directions for future work.
2
Problem statement
Let us consider a hybrid dynamical system governed by the following parameterized ordinary differential equation
(ODE):
˙ut = F(ut) + M(ut, θ)
(1)

where ut ∈Rd denotes the state of the system at time t. The right-hand side is composed of two contributions. The first
term, F, represents the physics-based dynamical model which is derived from first principles or established empirical
formulations. The second term, M, is a data-driven sub-model designed to account for imperfections or unmodeled
dynamics in F. This component is typically implemented as a neural network parameterized by a set of trainable
parameters θ ∈Ra.
In practice, the continuous-time system in Eq.(1) is discretized and evolved in time using a numerical time-integration
scheme. We therefore introduce a mapping f that represents the numerical integrator of the system (1). Given an initial
state u0 ∈Rd, and a parameter vector, the system evolves through the recursive application of f to generate a rollout

Phantom of the Masquerade: Graph Neural Network-Based Detection of
Masquerade Attacks in Controller Area Networks
Nehal Ameen∗, Member, IEEE, Pablo Moriano†, Senior Member, IEEE, Irfan Ahmed∗, Senior Member, IEEE
∗Department of Computer Science, Virginia Commonwealth University, Richmond, VA 23284, USA
†Computer Science and Mathematics Division, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, TN 37830, USA
∗{ameennm, iahmed3}@vcu.edu, †moriano@ornl.gov
Abstract—The lack of built-in security in controller area
networks (CANs) exposes modern vehicles and industrial systems
to masquerade attacks that can compromise safety and reliability.
These attacks inject malicious messages that mimic legitimate
communication patterns, making them difficult to detect using
existing intrusion detection systems (IDS). Prior graph-based
IDS approaches often rely on shallow embeddings that decouple
representation learning from classification, which may limit their
ability to fully exploit structural and signal-level information. In
this paper, we propose PhantoMasq, a graph neural network
(GNN)-based framework for detecting masquerade attacks in
CAN systems. PhantoMasq models CAN traffic as message
sequence graphs enriched with lightweight statistical features
derived from signal behavior, enabling joint learning of struc-
tural dependencies and temporal characteristics. The detection
task is formulated as a graph-level classification problem and
solved using graph convolutional networks (GCNs). We evaluate
PhantoMasq on the ROAD dataset under a protocol that prevents
overlapping windows from spanning training and test data.
Across five masquerade attack types, PhantoMasq achieves mean
AUC-ROC between 0.831 and 0.999, with performance depending
on the transmission rate of the targeted identifier and the
magnitude of the induced signal deviation. Against a state-of-
the-art graph-embedding baseline evaluated on the same sliding-
window configurations, PhantoMasq achieves higher AUC-ROC
on all five attack types, by 0.13 to 0.36, and is less sensitive to
window configuration. Window-processing latency ranges from
2.33 to 5.94 ms per window on CPU, corresponding to a
throughput of 168 to 429 windows per second. We make our
implementation and experimental artifacts available to support
reproducibility.
Index Terms—Controller area network (CAN), intrusion de-
tection system (IDS), graph neural network (GNN), masquerade
attacks.
I. INTRODUCTION
Modern vehicles are evolving into complex, connected
cyber-physical systems, deeply reliant on the controller area
network (CAN) protocol for real-time communication between
electronic control units (ECUs). CAN underpins critical sys-
tems across not only automotive platforms, but also industrial
automation and medical devices [1]. Its cost-effectiveness and
low wiring overhead have made CAN a foundational tech-
nology. However, despite its widespread adoption, CAN lacks
built-in security mechanisms, making it critically vulnerable
to cyberattacks. Similar threats affect embedded controllers
in other cyber-physical systems, such as programmable logic
controllers in industrial control systems, where attacks and
detection methods have both been studied [2], [3].
Over the past decade, a series of high-profile attacks have
demonstrated the real-world consequences of insecure CAN
deployments. In 2015, two researchers remotely gained phys-
ical control of a Jeep Cherokee, prompting Fiat Chrysler to
recall 1.4 million vehicles [4], [5]. Shortly after, researchers
demonstrated remote brake disablement in a Corvette via CAN
message injection [6]. Similar vulnerabilities were exposed
in a Tesla Model S [7] and in heavy commercial vehicles
[8]. More recently, CAN injection attacks have been used
in coordinated vehicle thefts, affecting not only passenger
vehicles but also critical fleets such as ambulances and buses
[9]. These incidents underscore the urgent need for robust
CAN security mechanisms.
Originally developed in 1983 by Robert Bosch GmbH [10],
[11], CAN was never designed with adversarial environments
in mind. Its lack of encryption compromises confidential-
ity, while integrity is not guaranteed because error-detection
mechanisms cannot distinguish malicious manipulation from
benign faults. Availability is also at risk due to arbitration rules
that allow high-priority nodes to dominate communication,
enabling denial-of-service attacks [12].
Among the most challenging threats are masquerade attacks,
in which adversaries inject syntactically valid CAN messages
that mimic legitimate traffic patterns [13]. These attacks
can trigger unintended acceleration, disable braking systems,
or manipulate steering, while evading traditional intrusion
detection systems (IDS) that rely on rule-based or shallow
learning techniques [14]. Their ability to preserve expected
communication frequencies makes them particularly difficult
to detect.
Several deep learning-based IDS frameworks have emerged,
including sequential models such as long short-term memory
(LSTM) and gated recurring unit (GRU) architectures [15],
[16], as well as graph-based approaches [17], [18]. However,
many approaches do not jointly model temporal dynamics
and graph structure within a unified and reproducible graph-
level framework, often treating messages independently or
relying on heavily engineered features [19], [20]. Moreover,
many studies rely on proprietary datasets or closed-source
implementations, hindering reproducibility and limiting real-
world applicability [21], [22].
In this paper, we propose PhantoMasq, a graph neural
network (GNN)–based framework for detecting masquerade
attacks in CAN systems. Our approach represents CAN traffic
as message sequence graphs (MSGs) that capture both commu-
nication structure and temporal behavior through lightweight
statistical features derived from CAN signals. This graph-
based representation enables learning from sequential relation-
arXiv:2611.26094v1  [cs.CR]  19 Nov 2026
2
ships among CAN message identifiers, allowing the model to
identify subtle deviations associated with masquerade attacks.
We formulate detection as a graph-level classification problem
and use graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to distinguish
between benign and malicious traffic.
We evaluate PhantoMasq on the publicly available Real
ORNL Automotive Dynamometer (ROAD) dataset [23], a
widely used benchmark in vehicular network security, under a
protocol that splits each capture temporally before windowing,
so that overlapping windows never span training and test data.
Across five masquerade attack types, PhantoMasq achieves
mean AUC-ROC between 0.831 and 0.999. Attacks that
induce large deviations on frequently transmitted identifiers
are detected almost perfectly, while performance is lower for
attacks that alter a single bit or target a sparsely transmitted
identifier. Compared with a state-of-the-art graph-embedding
baseline evaluated on the same sliding-window configurations,
PhantoMasq achieves higher AUC-ROC on all five attack
types, with a window-processing latency of 2.33–5.94 ms
per window on CPU. In addition, we make the PhantoMasq
implementation and experimental artifacts available to support
reproducibility [24]. The main contributions of this paper are
summarized as follows:
• We introduce a graph-based representation of CAN traffic
using message sequence graphs that capture both struc-
tural interactions and temporal behavior.
• We formulate masquerade attack detection as a graph-
level classification problem and apply GNNs to learn
representations of CAN communication patterns.
• We demonstrate that lightweight statistical features sup-
port efficient detection of masquerade attacks, and char-
acterize how detection difficulty depends on the transmis-
sion rate of the targeted identifier and the magnitude of
the induced signal deviation.
• We evaluate under a protocol that prevents leakage be-
tween overlapping windows, report AUC-PR alongside
AUC-ROC to account for class prevalence as low as
5.4%, and provide the implementation and experimental
artifacts to support reproducibility.
II. BACKGROUND
A. CAN Protocol
CAN is a widely adopted and robust communication pro-
tocol that facilitates the exchange of messages between ECUs
in automotive and industrial applications, as well as medical
devices [25]. The CAN bus protocol was initially developed
by Robert Bosch GmbH, and the CAN 2.0 specification
was released in 1991 [10], [11], revolutionizing automotive
communication technologies. CAN was further standardized
internationally in 2011 by ISO 11898-1:2011 [26]. That stan-
dardization specified the requirements for high-speed, light-
weight communication and data exchange among various
vehicle subsystems, without taking security into account.
CAN is a broadcast protocol that operates on a multi-master
serial bus standard, enabling all ECUs connected to the bus to
send and receive signals at high speeds, up to 1 Mbps, without
a central computer. CAN frames carry messages containing
sensor readings, control information, and other data exchanged
among ECUs. For example, ECUs such as the transmission
control module, engine control unit, and the anti-lock braking
system broadcast data frames that provide information about
the vehicle’s current state [20], [27].
CAN encompasses the first two layers of the Open Systems
Interconnection (OSI) model, namely the physical and data-
link layers [1]. A CAN frame comprises several fields, two
of which we focus on for our research. The first is the
identifier (ID) field that serves as the frame header. This unique
identifier represents the message priority, as it is responsible
for arbitration, the process of prioritizing frames when multiple
ECUs are transmitting signals simultaneously. Lower values
indicate higher priorities. Standard IDs consist of 11 bits, while
extended IDs consist of 29 bits. The second field we focus on
is the payload, or data, field. It contains the actual data carried
by the frame, such as sensor readings or control commands,
encapsulated in a data field ranging from 0 to 8 bytes. Each
unique piece of information carried in the message is a distinct
signal. CAN frames that have the same ID encode the same set
of signals with the same format and are typically transmitted
at a fixed frequency to relay updated signal values.
To extract these signals from CAN payloads, a CAN
database (DBC) file is used to decode the binary data into
interpretable signal values, providing time-series information
on the network’s activity [28]. This process produces a struc-
tured, time-series representation of CAN signals, which is
commonly used in data-driven intrusion detection systems to
analyze relationships between physical signals.
The attacks that CAN intrusion detection systems aim to
detect can be broadly classified into three categories [23]:
• Fabrication attacks: A rogue ECU injects malicious
messages into the network, without disrupting normal
traffic from other ECUs [29].
• Suspension attacks: A legitimate ECU gets disabled
or disconnected, causing it to stop sending or receiving
messages temporarily [30].
• Masquerade attacks: A legitimate ECU is first sup-
pressed by a weak attacker, after which a strong attacker
impersonates it by injecting spoofed frames at realistic
timing and signal patterns [12].
Masquerade attacks are particularly challenging to detect due
to their ability to mimic legitimate traffic patterns. These
structural and temporal characteristics of CAN traffic motivate
graph-based representations, which can capture interactions
between message identifiers and support learning-based intru-
sion detection.
B. GNNs
GNNs are neural networks designed to operate on graph-
structured data, where entities are represented as nodes and
relationships as edges. GNNs have been widely applied in
domains such as cybersecurity and network analysis [31].
GNNs learn representations of nodes or entire graphs by
iteratively aggregating information from neighboring nodes
through a message-passing mechanism, enabling the model
to capture structural dependencies and interactions within
3
the data. In particular, GNNs can be applied to graph-level
classification tasks, where the goal is to assign a label to an
entire graph based on its structure and node features [32].
Among GNN architectures, GCNs are a widely used class
of models that leverage node features and local graph con-
nectivity to learn effective representations for classification
tasks, while maintaining computational efficiency and strong
empirical performance [33], making them suitable for graph-
level intrusion detection in CAN networks.
III. THREAT MODEL AND PROBLEM DEFINITION
Masquerade attacks in CAN pose significant risks to system
safety and reliability. In this section, we formalize the system
assumptions, adversarial capabilities, and detection objectives
considered in this work.
A. System Model
We consider an in-vehicle network based on the CAN
protocol, where multiple ECUs communicate via broadcast
messages over a shared bus. Each CAN message is identified
by an ID and carries payload data corresponding to signal
transmissions between the ECUs.
We assume that CAN traffic is continuously monitored and
collected at a central observation point (e.g., gateway ECU
or logging module), without modifying the underlying CAN
protocol. The monitoring system observes sequences of CAN
messages and processes them over fixed-length segments of
consecutive CAN frames, which are later implemented as
sliding windows in our methodology.
Within each segment, CAN messages are transformed into
a graph representation that captures message interactions over
time. Node attributes are derived from lightweight statistical
features computed from decoded CAN payloads. The detection
system operates passively and does not interfere with the
normal operation of the CAN bus.
B. Adversary Model
We consider a capable adversary with access to the CAN
bus, either physically or remotely through a compromised
ECU. The adversary can inject malicious CAN messages to
manipulate vehicle behavior.
We focus specifically on masquerade attacks, which are
among the most sophisticated and stealthy attack types in
CAN. These attacks combine elements of fabrication and
suspension. A weak attacker learns the transmission frequency
of messages sent from a targeted ECU and suppresses its
legitimate transmissions, while a strong attacker injects mali-
cious messages at the expected frequency using the same ID.
By preserving expected timing patterns and identifiers, these
attacks can evade detection methods that rely primarily on
these characteristics.
The adversary is assumed to have knowledge of:
• valid message identifiers,
• typical message transmission frequencies,
• general communication patterns on the CAN bus.
However, we assume that the adversary does not have com-
plete control over all ECUs simultaneously and cannot per-
fectly replicate the joint statistical and structural dependencies
present in legitimate CAN traffic over time. We do not assume
access to cryptographic protections either, as CAN lacks built-
in authentication mechanisms.
This threat model aligns with commonly studied CAN
intrusion scenarios and reflects realistic attacker capabilities
in vehicular networks [34].
C. Detection Objective
Given a sequence of CAN messages segmented into fixed-
length segments of consecutive CAN frames, the objective is
to classify each segment as benign or malicious (masquerade
attack) behavior.
For each segment, the detection system constructs a graph
representation and performs graph-level classification to label
it as benign or malicious.
The detection model should satisfy the following goals:
• Accuracy: achieve high detection performance across
diverse masquerade attack scenarios.
• Robustness: maintain detection performance across mas-
querade attack types and sliding-window configurations.
• Efficiency: operate with low latency to support near real-
time deployment.
IV. RELATED WORK
We discuss prior work closely related to GNN-based CAN
IDS in Section IV-A, followed by other graph-based CAN IDS
approaches in Section IV-B.
A. Closely Related Work
Recent research on IDS for CAN bus networks has increas-
ingly turned to GNN-based approaches to capture the complex
dependencies among messages exchanged between ECUs.
Zhang et al. [35] generated directed attributed graphs based
on CAN message streams over fixed intervals. Message con-
tents were encoded as node attributes, while the frequency of
ID pairs was captured as edge attributes. They proposed a two-
stage classifier combining one-class anomaly detection with
multi-class attack classification, and incorporated federated
learning to preserve data privacy. Their system detects multiple
attack types within 3 milliseconds.
Yang et al. [17] introduced CAN-ASTGCN, which detects
anomalies by modeling correlations among CAN bus sensors.
Their approach combines an attention-based spatio-temporal
GCN with a Sensor Parameter Adaptive Learning module,
achieving 97.68% accuracy across multiple attack scenarios.
He et al. [21] proposed the A&D-GNN, which constructs
directed attributed graphs using both arbitration and payload
fields to capture richer context, achieving 99.92% accuracy
on impersonation attacks in the OTIDS dataset. El-Dawy et
al. [22] developed a GAT-based IDS where nodes represent
IDs and edges encode message sequences, achieving real-time
detection with latency around 7 ms and up to 100% accuracy,
while analyzing the trade-off between graph size and runtime.
4
Wang et al. [36] introduced a dynamic semi-supervised
IDS that constructs temporal graphs and applies a Tempo-
ral Graph Attention Network (TGAT) with a TimeMemory
module. Their method leverages unlabeled data and supervised
contrastive learning, achieving very high F1-scores on the Car-
Hacking dataset.
Gao et al. [37] modeled CAN data as dynamic multivariate
signal graphs using graph transformers. Signals were treated as
nodes and dependencies as edges, with node features obtained
through reverse engineering of CAN payloads. Their method
was evaluated on the Car-Hacking and CAN-Injection datasets.
Du et al. [18] proposed UGL, a hybrid GCN and LSTM
model designed for UAVCAN systems. Their approach empha-
sizes graph construction and feature engineering, incorporating
message cycle, Hamming distance, and entropy, achieving up
to 100% detection accuracy for flooding attacks.
Hasan et al. [38] introduced CAN-GraphiT, a transformer-
based IDS that jointly models temporal and graph features
using self-attention. Their method achieves up to 98.66%
accuracy for masquerade attacks and maintains low inference
latency (0.1 ms), outperforming several deep learning base-
lines.
Jiang et al. [39] proposed an unsupervised graph contrastive
learning framework combined with adaptive hierarchical clus-
tering. While promising, their method achieved an AUC of
75% on the ROAD dataset.
Table I summarizes these GNN-based CAN intrusion detec-
tion approaches in terms of problem setting, model architec-
ture, datasets, evaluation metrics, and code/data availability.
Contrast with our work: Prior GNN-based approaches often
rely on complex temporal encoders, attention mechanisms, or
specialized graph constructions. In contrast, our work adopts
a simpler formulation by casting masquerade detection as a
graph-level classification problem and using a GCN to learn
representations directly from annotated MSGs. By combining
structural information with lightweight statistical features, our
approach achieves mean AUC-ROC scores ranging from 0.831
to 0.999 across five ROAD masquerade attack types, using
a relatively simple GCN architecture. Our work specifically
targets masquerade attacks, evaluates computational efficiency,
and releases the implementation and experimental artifacts to
support reproducibility.
B. Other Related Work
While GNN-based IDSs have be
