RL Can Only Reinforce What It Sees Succeed
Ruben Sanchez-Corcuera
Unai Zulaika
Aritz Bilbao-Jayo
Miguel Fernandez-de-Retana
University of Deusto
{ruben.sanchez, unai.zulaika, aritz.bilbao, m.fernandezderetana}@deusto.es
Abstract
When a familiar rule stops working, an agent has to weigh what pre-training taught it against what
it now observes. We ask how outcome-reward reinforcement learning (RL) changes this balance, in
a puzzle world where both sides are known: small language models trained from scratch on games
played by a Bayesian player, so that the prior and the right answer are exact. Base models hedge as
their corpus did, and RL turns that hedging into decisions, in whichever direction the reward favours.
But RL can only reinforce what it sees succeed. When the right action is rare, each run either learns
it everywhere or not at all, and which runs take off is predicted before training by one count: the
expected number of groups of attempts in which the action wins. About 35 such groups give even
odds. The count holds for new and repeated problems and for groups of 4 to 256 attempts, and across
learning rates, optimizers, GRPO variants and model sizes from 1.3M to 85M parameters, which move
the threshold but not what is counted.
1. Introduction
Imagine an agent that has learned, from thousands of games, that a key opens a locked chest. It turns the
key and nothing happens. Should it try again? Keys sometimes jam or go in the wrong way, so a single
failure says little. After three failures in a row, though, it becomes more likely that something has really
changed, that the key or the lock is broken, and that some other tool now does the job. A good agent
weighs what it learned before, its prior, against what it has just seen, the evidence, and switches when
the evidence wins.
Language-model agents face this conflict all the time. A coding agent calls a library function the way it
saw it in pre-training, and the call fails: was it a typo, a flaky test, or a new version of the library that
changed the interface (Liu et al., 2024)? A web agent clicks where a button used to be and nothing happens:
the page may still be loading, or it may have been redesigned. An assistant with long-term memory acts
on what it stored about a user, but the user has moved or changed their mind, and the memory itself is
now wrong (Chen et al., 2026b; Hu et al., 2026). In each case a single failure is ambiguous, and the agent
must decide how much evidence it takes to stop trusting what it knows. More and more of these agents
are shaped by reinforcement learning (RL) with outcome rewards (Lambert et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025).
So we ask a simple question: how does this post-training change who wins? Two answers sound equally
plausible. RL could make the agent more stubborn, because the familiar action is the one that usually
earns the reward. Or it could make the agent more responsive, because switching at the right moment
also earns the reward.
The question is hard to answer with pre-trained language models alone. We do not know how strong their
prior is, and when the evidence is noisy we do not know what the right answer would be. Most studies
of knowledge conflicts give a model one question and one contradicting document (Longpre et al., 2021;
Xu et al., 2024). Recent work lets the model act (Xu et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b), but it neither controls
the strength of the prior nor compares the same model before and after RL.
We therefore build a world in which both sides of the conflict are known. Puzzle rules are data, and
we train small GPT models from scratch on 9 million games played by a Bayesian player. This lets us set
exactly how often each rule is seen and how often it changes, and it tells us, at every point of a game, what
1
arXiv:2611.26084v1  [cs.LG]  19 Nov 2026
an ideal agent would do. We then post-train the models with outcome-reward RL and measure exactly
how their willingness to switch changes. The story that emerges has three steps.
RL turns hedging into decisions. Before RL, a model hedges the way its training data did: after each
failure it switches about as often as the Bayesian player would. RL replaces this hedging with decisions.
The agent switches when switching is the better bet and holds on when it is not, and it moves toward the
optimal policy in both directions.
But only if the right action is already tried. RL can only reward an action that the agent takes. When
we make switching rare in the training corpus, RL does not discover it, and it makes switching rarer still.
Near this boundary, each RL run is all or nothing: it either learns to switch for every rule at once, or it
learns nothing.
Whether a run takes off can be predicted by counting. RL learns from groups of attempts at the same
problem, and a group can teach the new action only if one of its attempts uses it and wins. Before training,
the base model tells us how many such groups a run can expect. That one number predicts which runs
take off: about 35 expected successful groups give even odds (Figure 1). It does not matter whether the
groups come from new problems or repeated ones, or how many attempts each group holds. The learning
rate, the optimizer and the size of the model change how many groups are needed, but not what has to
be counted. The count also changes what “rare” means: a switch that RL never learned with our budget
was learned with four to eight times more, as often as the count predicted.
Who wins, then, is not decided by RL itself. Whether post-training makes an agent stubborn depends on
how often the right action succeeds under the base model, and on how much experience RL gets to see it
succeed.
In summary, we make four contributions:
• A world where the prior is known. A puzzle environment and small language models trained
from scratch on games played by a Bayesian player, in which the strength of the prior, the evidence
and the optimal decision are all exact, together with an exact measure of how a model weighs them
before and after RL.
• RL makes agents decisive, not stubborn. Base models hedge like their corpus, and outcome-
reward RL moves their decisions toward the optimal policy in both directions: it switches more
where switching pays and less where it does not.
• When the right action is rare, each run is all or nothing. RL sharpens the prior when the
switch is rare, and near this boundary a run either learns the switch for every rule or for none.
• A count that predicts take-off before training. The expected number of groups in which the
new action wins, computed from the base model, predicts which of 400 runs take off, for new and
repeated problems and for groups of 4 to 256 attempts. Across twelve changes of recipe (910 runs),
the recipe moves the threshold but not what is counted.
We will release our code and data as open source.
2. A world where we know the prior
A game with an ambiguous failure. Our agent plays short text puzzles. It stands in a room whose exit
is blocked by one to three obstacles, such as a locked chest. Next to each obstacle lie two candidate tools,
for example a key and a hammer. The agent can take a tool, use a tool on an obstacle, and leave once
every obstacle is gone; the game lists the valid actions at each step and pays a reward of 1 if the agent
leaves within the step limit. There are 9 rules we test and 30 filler rules, and each one pairs an obstacle
with its default tool (D): the key opens the chest, the torch melts the ice wall.
In the normal world the default tool works 80 % of the time, and the other candidate does nothing. In a
changed world, as when a lock breaks in the real world, the default never works, and the other candidate,
the alternative (A), removes the obstacle. Every failure produces the same observation, “nothing”, so a

A model that hedges like the ideal believer has 𝑠(𝑘) ≈𝜋(𝑘). A model that decides has 𝑠(𝑘) near 0 below
the threshold and near 1 above it (Figure 2c). Everything we report is a comparison of 𝑠(𝑘) with 𝜋(𝑘).
Models that learn only from games we wrote. To know the prior, we write the whole pre-training

ideal believer. On each corpus we train a small GPT from scratch (Radford et al., 2019; Karpathy, 2022),

Because we write the corpus, we can turn three knobs that are hidden in a real pre-trained model. Exposure
sets how often a rule appears. Reliability sets how often the rule changes, through 𝜈. And rarity sets how

failed four times, too late to matter. The player is drawn per game and plays every obstacle in it, filler
rules included, so the general habit of switching early is as rare in the corpus as the switch on the test
rules. The smaller 𝜌, the less often the corpus shows the hammer at the moment it should be used: from
once in 23 decisions after two failures down to once in 23,000. Every measurement is exact: we score each
valid action by its probability under the model instead of sampling, and we compare each model after RL
with its own base model on the same decision points.
Outcome-reward RL, and why groups matter. We post-train with GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), without a
KL penalty and without dividing the advantage by the group’s spread (Liu et al., 2025). Each problem is one
obstacle in a world drawn from the same distribution as pre-training. The model plays N attempts at the
problem; each attempt’s advantage is its reward minus the mean reward of its group, and one gradient
step follows each batch. A step limit of four to seven moves makes the decision after a few failures a
last chance, where the reward-maximizing choice is exactly to switch when 𝜋(𝑘) passes 𝜏. Unless stated
otherwise, a run takes 200 steps of 512 attempts.
One property of this algorithm drives the rest of the paper. If every attempt in a group fails, or every
attempt succeeds, all advantages are zero and the group teaches nothing. A group pushes the model
toward the hammer only when at least one attempt actually switches and wins.
When a run takes off. We say that RL has taught a rule when the model’s switch probability for that
rule, after two or after three failures, rises by more than 0.05 above the base model, beyond the noise of
the measurement. A run takes off when it learns more than half of the nine rules. This is rarely a close
call: as Section 3 shows, a run almost always learns all nine rules or none.
3. RL turns hedging into decisions, if it sees the switch
Base models hedge like their corpus. We start with the models before any RL. When a base model
has seen the key fail twice, how does it split its bet between the key and the hammer? Almost exactly as
the ideal believer would (Figure 3a). For a rule that changes 5 % of the time, the model puts 22 % on the
hammer after one failure and 56 % after two; the Bayesian posterior says 21 % and 57 %. For a rule that
changes 30 % of the time, the whole curve sits higher, again on top of the posterior. Across all conditions,
a well-exposed model is off by less than two percentage points on average.
The model learns more than a single habit per rule. It tracks how reliable each rule is: rules that change
more often get a higher switch probability after the same evidence, and with high exposure the model
reproduces 95 % of the gap that the posterior predicts between a reliable and an unreliable rule. It also
tracks how much evidence it has seen, since its switch probability climbs with every failure. How often
a rule was seen matters less, and in a surprising direction: rules seen in only 900 games produce a flatter
curve, one that moves less with each failure. A model that has seen a rule rarely hedges more, not less.
RL makes the agent decisive, not stubborn. What should outcome-reward RL do to such a model?
One might expect it to strengthen the prior. Most of the time the key works, so most rewarded games are
games in which the agent used the key; RL should push the agent toward the familiar action and make
it slower to switch. It does the opposite. In all six combinations of objective and group size we tried, the
decisions where prior and evidence conflict moved toward the better choice, not toward the familiar one.
Figure 3b shows the pattern. After one failure of a reliable rule, the base model put 22 % on the hammer;
after RL it puts 10 %, because one failure is not yet enough reason to switch. After two failures, when
switching has become the better bet, it puts 77 % instead of 56 %. For an unreliable rule the change runs
the other way: after a single failure, the share on the hammer rises from 67 % to 84 %. Every condition
moves toward the best decision, whichever side that is.
RL does not make the model a better Bayesian. Its bets now depart from the ideal belief, in both directions,
because the reward does not pay for calibrated beliefs; it pays for good choices. And the choices are good:
on held-out problems, RL closes 74 % to 95 % of the gap in reward between the base model and the optimal
policy. Rules that were rarely seen in pre-training catch up as well.

often RL tried the hammer at a given decision barely predicts whether that decision improves; whether
its run takes off does.

Learning to Compare Neural Representations from
Parameterized Computation Graphs
Ya-Wei Eileen Lin1, Daniel Herbst1, and Stefanie Jegelka1,2
1Technical University of Munich; School of CIT, MCML, MDSI
2MIT; Department of EECS, CSAIL
Abstract
Comparing internal representations across trained models is important for identifying corresponding layers and
selecting components for model reuse. Yet, direct comparisons at inference require evaluating candidate models
on known reference inputs and collecting their internal activations. In this paper, we study whether internal
representation similarity measured across independently trained models can instead be learned to predict in unseen
models from their parameterized computations. We introduce a framework that applies a graph metanetwork for
mapping each internal site to an embedding derived from its upstream computations while accounting for hidden-
coordinate permutation and internal attention-basis transformations. We analyze the structural properties of our
estimators and derive conditional guarantees for layer retrieval and stitching candidate selection. Empirically, we find
that the learned predictors support relation estimation and low-regret layer retrieval. They also select useful stitching
connections while not being trained on stitching outcomes. This opens up a new way to study representation
similarity directly from trained neural networks: representational relations learned across a collection of trained
models can generalize to new computations, and that the predicted relations can guide candidate selection before
direct measurement or adapter fitting for functional evaluations.

its upstream computation. PARIS-Ind encodes each site independently and compares reusable embeddings using
relation-specific distance heads. PARIS-Joint allows the two site graphs to interact before predicting their relation.
Both are trained with internal representation similarity and rank candidate sites in unseen models without collecting
new base-model activations. Our metanetworks can guide the selection of sites and be used for adapter fitting.
2025b, Kriegeskorte et al., 2008, Diedrichsen and Kriegeskorte, 2017]. These methods emphasize different aspects of
representational similarity, including response geometry, neighborhood structure, and predictive behavior [Morcos
et al., 2018, Williams et al., 2021, Davari et al., 2023, Barannikov et al., 2022]. For instance, CKA [Kornblith et al.,
2019] compares response geometry through the alignment of centered kernel matrices, CKNNA [Huh et al., 2024]
focuses on local structure by restricting kernel alignment to shared nearest neighbors, and readout-based methods
compare representations through the disagreement of fitted predictors under a specified prediction protocol [Alain
and Bengio, 2016, Harvey et al., 2024]. Direct evaluation of these activation-based relations relies on responses to
shared reference inputs. Responses from multiple sites can be collected during the same model traversal, and the
responses or suitable comparison descriptors can be cached across comparisons. For previously unmeasured models,
however, the corresponding responses still need to be acquired. We investigate a different use of these measurements:
as supervision for learning how parameterized computations relate to the representations they produce. This leads to
our central question:
Can we learn to predict representation similarity scores in unseen models across different sites using only their
architecture and trained weights?
In this paper, we demonstrate that this is indeed possible. We study this question as a metanetwork learning task
[Unterthiner et al., 2020, Schürholt et al., 2021, Zhou et al., 2023b,a, Navon et al., 2023]: given two internal sites from
different trained models, we aim to predict how their representations are related. To do so, we need to know both
which sites we are comparing and which relation we want to predict. The weights of the layer immediately before
a site may miss earlier computations that shape its representation. In contrast, a single description of the whole
model cannot distinguish between sites without additional information. As such, we represent each site using the
computations that lead to it and train the metanetwork to learn relations measured from activations. This allows us
to study how well trained computations can predict different properties of representations, including their geometry
[Kriegeskorte et al., 2008, Raghu et al., 2017], neighborhood structure [Gwilliam and Shrivastava, 2022], and predictive
behavior [Alain and Bengio, 2016, Ding et al., 2021]. However, model parameters do not always make these relations
easy to recognize. Parameter symmetries [Hecht-Nielsen, 1990, Godfrey et al., 2022, Zhao et al., 2026] pose one
source of challenge for this learning problem (see Fig. 1). Even when tensor shapes match, relabelings of hidden units
can yield different parameter configurations that produce the same network function [Sussmann, 1992, Chen et al.,
1993, Ainsworth et al., 2023]. Distances computed directly in parameter space can conflate differences in learned
computation with differences in coordinate choice [Phuong and Lampert, 2020, Vlačić and Bölcskei, 2021, Stock and
2
Gribonval, 2023, Bona-Pellissier et al., 2023, Simsek et al., 2021]. Representational correspondence can also extend
beyond these parameter symmetries. For example, orthogonally rotating features preserves their inner-product
geometry while changing the individual feature values [Kornblith et al., 2019]. Different upstream computations may
produce similar representation geometry without being connected by these transformations. The learning problem is
thus both to recognize equivalent parameterizations and to characterize which differences in trained computations
matter for representational correspondence.
To this end, we introduce Parameter-based Analysis for Relational Inference of Sites (PARIS), a framework for learn-
ing internal representation relations from the computations that produce them (see Fig. 2). We build on graph
metanetworks that encode network parameters with their connectivity [Lim et al., 2024b, Kofinas et al., 2024]. To
accommodate variation in architecture, we represent each site’s upstream computation as a graph encoding its
architecture, trained parameters, and inference state. To account for permutation symmetries (e.g., hidden-coordinate
permutation and head permutation), the encoding maps relabelings of hidden units and channels to graph relabelings
while preserving parameter correspondences across successive layers. For attention, we encode the composed query-
key and value-output operators, which are invariant to the changes of basis within their internal spaces. To learn
representational correspondences beyond those induced by parameter symmetries, we train the graph metanetwork
using representation similarity between sites across independently trained models. At search time, it predicts these
relations for unseen models from their site graphs, without requiring new base-model forward passes.
We consider two variants that differ in when information from the two sites is combined. (i) PARIS-Ind maps each site
graph to a fixed embedding and compares embeddings using relation-specific distance heads. These embeddings can
be computed once and reused across comparisons. (ii) PARIS-Joint uses cross-attention between the two site graphs
before predicting their relation, allowing intermediate features of each site to interact with the other. Comparing
the two variants tests whether such interactions improve relation prediction beyond what can be achieved with site
embeddings.
Our contributions are fourfold: (i) we formulate and study the prediction of representation similarity between
internal representations in independently trained deep networks, using their parameterized upstream computations
as inputs, (ii) we develop a graph-metanetwork framework for this task and compare reusable site embeddings with
joint processing of site pairs, (iii) we analyze the structural properties of both estimators and derive conditional
bounds connecting prediction error to retrieval regret and stitching-candidate selection, and (iv) we evaluate how
well our models predict comparison scores, retrieve layers, and select stitching candidates across model populations
of varying widths and depths, showing that training on the representation similarity on parameterized computations
can support candidate selection without using stitching outcomes as supervision.
2
Related work
Our work connects the comparison of internal representations across models with learning from neural network
artifacts. We discuss the two topics here; App. A discusses extended related work.
Comparing and matching neural representations. Comparisons across independently trained networks have
been used to study recurring features and shared representational structure [Li et al., 2015, Gurnee et al., 2024, Huh
et al., 2024]. Activation-based approaches compare shared subspaces using SVCCA and PWCCA [Raghu et al., 2017,
Morcos et al., 2018], response geometry using CKA [Kornblith et al., 2019], or regularized linear prediction using GULP
[Boix-Adsera et al., 2022]. Model stitching evaluates compatibility by connecting parts of trained networks [Bansal
et al., 2021, Csiszárik et al., 2021], while component reassembly methods select fragments from model collections
[Yang et al., 2022]. Direct evaluation of activation-based relations depends on responses to reference inputs. In this
paper, PARIS addresses the complementary problem of predicting these relations from the parameterized computations
that produce the representations.
Learning from neural network parameters. Metanetworks learn from trained networks to predict model
properties, construct representations of their weights, or produce parameter updates. DWSNets and neural functional
networks account for hidden-unit permutation symmetries [Navon et al., 2023, Zhou et al., 2023a], while graph-based
metanetworks encode parameters with connectivity across diverse architectures [Lim et al., 2024a, Kofinas et al.,
2024]. Related work learns parameter alignment [Navon et al., 2024] and predicts functional similarity from synaptic
connectivity in simulated spiking networks [Haber and Schneidman, 2022]. Building on this perspective, our work
3
draws on graph-based methods for processing trained networks. We use these methods to study a different prediction
problem: learning activation-derived relations between internal sites from their parameterized upstream computations,
and used for retrieval and stitching candidate selection.
3
Parameter-based Analysis for Relational Inference of Sites
Our goal is to predict representation similarity between internal sites from architecture and trained weights alone
without evaluating the compared models on probe inputs at inference. Motivated by the geometry and symmetries of
weight space, we represent each site by a graph of its upstream computation, and train a metanetwork to recover
similarity scores computed from reference responses.

model. Model m contains a set of internal representation sites Sm. We write u = (m, s), with s ∈Sm, for an internal
representation site in model m, where a representation site is a tensor-valued location in the forward computation, e.g.,
the output of a residual block or the class-token activation after a Transformer block. We write Cu for the architecture
and trained parameters of the computation upstream of u, which allows us to distinguish two sites with identical

Understanding MoE Decisions Beyond Gradients
Zhen Xu
University of Chicago
Zitao Zhang
eBay
Kevin Zhao
eBay
Xuefeng Liu
University of Florida
Abstract
Understanding a language model’s decision
requires knowing how its internal computa-
tions affect its preference between answers.
Gradient-based methods estimate this influence
by predicting the effect of changing those com-
putations. In mixture-of-experts (MoE) models,
replacing one expert can change which experts
later layers select. Those switches can alter the
answer scores in ways that derivatives do not
capture. We introduce a predictor that uses the
model’s own expert outputs and selection rules
to estimate these extra effects, then adds them
to a second-order prediction. Across questions
from three benchmarks, our method reduces
the error in predicting answer-score changes by
60% on Qwen3.6 and 47% on Gemma4, rela-
tive to a multistep baseline using gradients and
second derivatives.
1
Introduction
Knowing a language model’s answer does not tell
us which computations shaped it. One way to inves-
tigate is to change part of the model and measure
how its preference between answers changes. Such
interventions provide evidence about the role of
internal computations (Meng et al., 2022; Wang
et al., 2022; Conmy et al., 2023). Gradient-based
attribution predicts intervention effects and helps
select which ones to examine (Syed et al., 2024;
Kramár et al., 2024). If a large effect receives
a small predicted score, an analysis may skip a
test that would have revealed something important
about the model’s behavior.
Mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models
make this prediction difficult in a particular way.
Each routed layer selects a few expert networks for
the current token (Shazeer et al., 2017). Replacing
one selected expert changes the input to later lay-
ers, which may then select different experts. The
final effect depends on both how expert outputs
change and which experts the model uses after-
ward. Even when router scores change smoothly,
swapping two different expert functions can make
the answer score jump. Local derivatives need not
capture that jump.
For a question with candidates A and B, this
gives a concrete test: predict how replacing an
expert shifts their score gap, including the conse-
quences of any later expert switches.
Second-order estimates and additional gradient
samples can describe a smooth response more accu-
rately (Zhang and Wang, 2026). Their intermediate
samples can even use different experts, yet sum-
ming the derivatives can still miss the effect of
crossing from one expert set to another. Prior work
shows that fixing expert choices can reduce a gap
between integrated-gradient attributions and the
measured response (Nguyen, 2026). We address
the prediction problem with those choices free to
change.
Our approach keeps the information supplied by
derivatives and adds an estimate of the effect of
later expert choices. We build this estimate from
the model’s own expert outputs and selection rules,
without fitting to measured intervention outcomes.
Across Qwen3.6, Gemma4, and three question col-

six model–dataset comparisons (Table 1). The gain
also changes which interventions an analysis finds:
on Qwen, it recovers 79.2% of the true top five
expert combinations, compared with 63.3% for the
five-step second-order baseline (Table 2). In ac-
tual model runs, keeping later expert choices fixed
makes the baseline nearly exact while retaining
over 90% of the mean intervention magnitude.

Why extra derivatives are not enough.
A

the extra response from expert switching (Appen-

Computation.

evaluating HVP1 for each intervention currently
cost more than direct edited forward passes in our
cached-suffix implementation (Appendix J). Re-
ducing this cost is an important next step toward
practical use.
5
Conclusion
The effect of replacing an expert depends on both
its output and the experts the model selects af-
terward.
Estimating those later choices makes
intervention predictions more accurate and helps
identify influential expert combinations. This pro-
vides better evidence about which changes affect
a model’s preference between answers. For MoE
models, understanding expert influence benefits
from tracking changes in the computation itself
alongside the information supplied by gradients.
4
Limitations
Our experiments cover two MoE models, three
multiple-choice question subsets, and expert re-
placements at three selected layers of the final
prompt position. We predict changes in a fixed
next-token logit contrast, rather than answer cor-
rectness or generated behavior. The structural re-
sponse also relies on clean-input expert outputs and
local derivatives, which may be less accurate for
large interventions.
The method requires white-box access and per-
intervention curvature computation. In our cur-
rent implementation, it is more expensive than di-
rectly executing the tested interventions. Finally,
the main results use FP32, while earlier BF16 mea-
surements show smaller gains. Generalization to
lower-precision settings requires further study.

Iterative Scarcity-Guided Exploration: Bootstrapping
Generative Auto-bidding from Narrow Support
Qingmao Yao1, Guangzheng Hu2, Yusen Huo4∗, Zhilin Zhang4∗
Chuan Yu2, Jian Xu2, Xu Chu1†, Bo Zheng2†, Xiaotie Deng1,3†
1Center on Frontiers of Computing Studies, School of Computer Science, Peking University
2Alimama Tech, Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba
3Department of Computer Science, City University of Hong Kong
4Independent Researcher
qmyao25@stu.pku.edu.cn, huguangzheng.hgz@taobao.com, huoyusen1@126.com
421525432@qq.com, {yuchuan.yc,xiyu.xj}@taobao.com
bozheng@alibaba-inc.com, {chu_xu,xiaotie}@pku.edu.cn
Abstract
Auto-bidding is a core algorithmic component in online advertising auctions. In
practical cold-start settings, iterative training is commonly used to compensate
for low-quality, narrowly supported historical data. Unfortunately, in iterative
training, representative diffusion-based AI-Generated Bidding (AIGB) methods
fail to sustain extrapolation beyond the narrow data support and stagnate at a
suboptimal level. In this paper, we theoretically attribute this stagnation to Signal-
to-Noise Ratio (SNR) collapse: the weak radial return signal is overwhelmed
by a curvature-induced penalty. To break this stagnation, we propose Iterative
Scarcity-Guided Exploration (ISGE), which introduces a guidance handoff: as
the return signal collapses, scarcity subsequently takes over as an exploratory
signal to elevate the SNR above a critical threshold. Specifically, ISGE iteratively
alternates between a Judger that assigns scarcity scores to trajectories and an
Explorer that performs guided generation of high-scarcity and high-return trajec-
tories, thereby bootstrapping from the narrow support with such self-generated
trajectories. Extensive experiments on the industrial AuctionNet benchmark demon-
strate that ISGE, starting from cold-start datasets, effectively surpasses the perfor-
mance of the Full-Dataset baseline within three iterations. Code is available at
https://github.com/alimama-tech/ISGE.
1
Introduction
Auto-bidding in online advertising is a complex sequential decision-making problem [1–3]. Recently,
diffusion-based AIGB methods have emerged as a powerful paradigm by formulating bidding as
trajectory generation via conditional diffusion planners [4–6]. However, these models heavily rely
on broad-coverage expert data. In practical cold-start settings for new advertisers or emerging
business sectors, historical data is often generated by conservative strategies, yielding a narrow,
low-quality distribution. Bootstrapping beyond this poor initialization requires iterative training,
yet existing diffusion planners lack efficient mechanisms to explore high-return out-of-distribution
(OOD) trajectories. This raises a central question:
Can diffusion-based AIGB methods perform efficient exploration to bootstrap a near-optimal policy
solely from low-quality, narrowly supported data in just a few iterations?

†Corresponding authors

Figure 1: Iterative Experiments on Trajectory Optimization Task (left) and AuctionNet Benchmarks
(middle, right). Vanilla Self-Training (orange) inevitably stagnates well below the optimal level
during iterative training. We term this self-locking. In contrast, our proposed ISGE (blue) successfully
breaks self-locking and consistently reaches or surpasses the Full-Data Oracle (red dashed line) within
just three iterations. Full results in Section 3.1 and Section 5.
Investigating this, we observe that vanilla self-training (naively iterating diffusion planners) suffers
from a bottleneck we term self-locking. As illustrated in Figure 1, despite initial extrapolation
capabilities, performance inevitably stagnates well below the optimum. We theoretically attribute
this to an inherent Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) collapse at the boundary of the training support. As
generated trajectories reach this suboptimal frontier, the return signal becomes sparse and misaligned,
failing to overcome the high-dimensional curvature penalty and trapping the planner.
To break self-locking, we propose Iterative Scarcity-Guided Exploration (ISGE). ISGE relies on
the core insight of a guidance handoff, utilizing scarcity (quantified via denoising autoencoder [7]
reconstruction error) as a robust auxiliary signal. Geometrically, scarcity acts as an outward manifold
repulsion field [8]. During reverse denoising, ISGE executes a guidance handoff: at early steps, return
guidance navigates the known landscape to push trajectories to the suboptimal boundary. When the
return signal inevitably collapses, scarcity subsequently takes over. This provides a stable outward
impulse that reliably pushes the trajectory deeper into unexplored OOD space, explicitly preventing
regression into the low-quality interior. By leveraging the local continuity of the return landscape,
this handoff forms a highly effective exploration heuristic.
Practically, ISGE alternates between a Judger scoring trajectory scarcity and an Explorer using
dual-condition guidance to generate high-return, high-scarcity “gift samples”. Extensive experiments
on the industrial AuctionNet [9] benchmark demonstrate that ISGE effectively bridges the data
quality gap, surpassing the Full-Dataset baseline within just three iterations from narrowly supported
cold-start data. To summarize, our main contributions are threefold:
1. We theoretically attribute return-guided self-locking to SNR collapse at the suboptimal boundary,
and establish a guidance handoff mechanism where scarcity subsequently takes over to elevate
the SNR and break the bottleneck.
2. We propose ISGE, an iterative framework that leverages return and scarcity guidance to generate
“gift samples” beyond the training support.
3. We demonstrate that ISGE bootstraps near-optimal policies from cold-start datasets, surpassing
the Full-Dataset baseline on the industrial AuctionNet benchmark within three iterations.
2
Preliminaries
Generative Auto-Bidding
Auto-bidding is a sequential decision problem with long horizons,
sparse rewards, and non-Markovian dynamics. Following standard settings (details in Appendix A),
an agent allocates a global budget to maximize total return while satisfying strict KPI constraints over
T steps. Diffusion-based AIGB [4] formulates this as conditional trajectory generation p(τ|y(τ)),
where τ = (s0, . . . , sT ) is the state trajectory and y(τ) is the target return (KPI constraints are
typically absorbed into the return via reward shaping). This conditional distribution acts as the policy,
implicitly determining a sequence of actions via an inverse dynamics model at = ϕ(st, st+1). The
planner effectively satisfies bidding objectives by generating state trajectories τ consistent with the
specified condition y.
2
Conditional Diffusion Models and Classifier-Free Guidance
Conditional diffusion models
transform decision-making to conditional trajectory generation. Letting x0 = τ denote the clean
trajectory, the forward process gradually corrupts it into pure noise xT ∼N(0, I). The reverse
process learns to iteratively denoise xt by predicting the added noise ϵθ(xt, y, t), conditioned
on both the guidance signal y (e.g., target return) and the timestep t. Classifier-Free Guidance
(CFG) [10, 11] avoids training an explicit classifier, making it lightweight for decision-making.
CFG jointly trains a conditional model ϵθ(xt, y, t) and an unconditional counterpart ϵθ(xt, ∅, t) via
random condition dropout. During sampling, the perturbed noise is given by: ˆϵ = ϵθ(xt, ∅, t) + w ·
(ϵθ(xt, y, t) −ϵθ(xt, ∅, t)), where w is the guidance scale.
3
Motivation and Theoretical Analysis
In this section, we first introduce a motivating example that empirically reveals the self-locking
bottleneck. We then establish a geometric optimization framework to demonstrate how an inherent
SNR collapse causes self-locking, and how scarcity breaks self-locking via guidance handoff.
3.1
Motivating Example: Self-Locking in Trajectory Optimization
Generative auto-bidding can be viewed as a high-dimensional trajectory optimization problem.
However, in real-world auction environments, the optimal bidding strategy is unknown and the
return landscape is highly complex, strictly limiting rigorous theoretical analysis. To isolate the
underlying optimization dynamics, we construct a tractable high-dimensional (D = 768) trajectory
optimization task: R(x) = e−β∥x−x∗∥2 (β > 0), where the global optimum x∗lies strictly outside
the narrow training support. As illustrated in Figure 1 (left), Vanilla Self-Training exhibits a distinct
dual-phase dynamic. While it initially extrapolates beyond the cold-start initialization, performance
abruptly stagnates at a suboptimal boundary by Iteration 2. Crucially, a Full-Data Oracle with an
identical architecture readily approaches the optimum, demonstrating that this stagnation is not a
model capacity limitation but a data bottleneck. We term this ubiquitous failure mode self-locking,
motivating our systematic theoretical analysis.
3.2
How Does the Diffusion Planner Optimize Trajectories?
To uncover the origins of self-locking, we cast the CFG-guided reverse denoising process as formal
trajectory optimization. By leveraging the score-matching property, CFG effectively injects an
implicit likelihood gradient ∇xt log p(y|xt) into the standard diffusion update. This reformulates the
sampling step into a biased Langevin dynamic (see Appendix B.1 for detailed derivations):

To break this self-locking, the diffusion planner requires a guidance handoff: a transition from the
collapsed return signal to a robust auxiliary signal that persists in the OOD vacuum. Crucially, since
the training data is confined to a suboptimal region, advancing toward the OOD optimum inherently
requires a stable outward impulse moving beyond the known data manifold. We identify scarcity as
the ideal geometric signal to execute this handoff.

Discussion.
Our theoretical framework relies on two primary abstractions. (i) We adopt a tractable
spherical return landscape. Intuitively, any smooth optimum admits a quadratic expansion; this
spherical abstraction establishes a conservative lower bound for analyzing general smooth landscapes

Complete-SVD: A Functional Norm Approach to Low-Rank LLM 
Compression
Alper Kalle†,*
Theo Rudkiewicz‡,*
Mohamed-Oumar Ouerfelli†
Mohamed Tamaazousti†
{alper.kalle,mohamed-oumar.ouerfelli,mohamed.tamaazousti}@cea.fr
theo.rudkiewicz@inria.fr
Abstract
Post-training low-rank compression of neural net­
works must not only approximate the original 
weights but also preserve the model’s input-
output behavior. Recent output-aware methods 
measure the compression error beyond the com­
pressed layer, at the model output, weighting 
logit changes by the observed next token or by 
the model’s predicted probabilities. We propose 
Complete-SVD, a method for large language 
models that minimizes the 𝐿2 distance between 
the logits of the original and compressed models, 
weighting all logit changes equally. Linearizing 
the network around the original weights, to­
gether with a Kronecker-factored approximation, 
reduces this objective to a weighted SVD with 
a closed-form solution. Its output-side factor is 
intractable to compute; we estimate it without bias 
from random probes, at a cost of K backward 
passes per sequence, independent of vocabulary 
size and sequence length. At matched settings 
with uniform ranks and WikiText-2 calibration, 
Complete-SVD achieves the lowest C4 and PTB 
perplexity in every setting, and at ratio 0.7 under 
LEMS rank allocation. Replacing the 𝐿2 distance 
by the Kullback–Leibler divergence (KL-SVD), 
with the same estimation framework, lowers cal­
ibration perplexity in most settings and raises 
downstream accuracy, but raises cross-corpus 
perplexity. Complete-SVD also improves IFEval 
instruction-following accuracy over the strongest 
prior output-aware methods throughout.
1   Introduction and Related Work
Large language models have driven rapid progress 
across reasoning and generation tasks (Kaplan et 
al., 2020), but their growing parameter counts 
make inference prohibitively expensive. Model

compression reduces this cost through quantiza­
tion (Frantar et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024; Xiao 
et al., 2023), pruning (Frantar and Alistarh, 2023; 
Ma et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2024), knowledge 
distillation (Hinton et al., 2015), or low-rank fac­
torization, which replaces each weight matrix by 
the product of two smaller matrices. Low-rank 
factorization retains dense operations that run ef­
ficiently on standard hardware. Post-training low-
rank methods differ in their per-layer objective, 
i.e., the criterion minimized by the low-rank ap­
proximation of each layer; rank allocation, storage 
schemes (Wang et al., 2025b), and cross-layer 
basis sharing (Wang et al., 2025a) are complemen­
tary to it. This work concerns the objective, that is, 
which change in the model the approximation of a 
layer should penalize.

the weight matrix of a linear layer and ̂ 𝑊 its

closest to 𝑊 in Frobenius norm, which treats 
all weight directions equally, and replacing the 
weights of an LLM by these approximations 
severely degrades its performance. Activation-
aware methods instead minimize the error on 
the layer outputs, ‖𝑋(𝑊−̂ 𝑊)‖

al., 2025c) solves this problem in closed form by

networks up to the compressed layer. This norm 
involves only the upstream network, i.e., the pre­

objective for a linear layer. The error at the layer 
output is not, however, the error of the model: it 
propagates through the downstream network, i.e., 
the following layers, which amplifies it along some 
directions and attenuates it along others, and, in a 
causal transformer, carries it to the predictions at 
all subsequent positions.
Error at the model output. Output-aware 
methods measure the error at the model output. 
Each compares the outputs of the original and 
compressed models through a discrepancy, whose 
local quadratic approximation weights a change 
of the layer output by its effect on the logits and 
by the importance that the discrepancy assigns to 
each logit change (Figure 1, panel b). A first family 
preserves the training loss through the empirical 
Fisher matrix, built from loss gradients at the ob­
served next token. FWSVD (Hsu et al., 2022) uses 
a diagonal approximation, GFWSVD (Chekalina 
et al., 2026) a Kronecker factorization fitted from 
a limited number of sequence-level gradients, and 
KFAC-SVD (Thoma et al., 2026) Kronecker fac­
tors estimated from token-level statistics, which 
alleviate the rank deficiency of GFWSVD. For 
each token, the empirical Fisher only penalizes the 
change in the log-probability of the observed next 
token, a single direction among all possible logit 
changes (Kunstner et al., 2019). A second family 
preserves the predictive distribution through the 
Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence, whose local 
quadratic approximation is governed by the true 
Fisher information (Amari, 1998). IO-SVD (Ab­
basi et al., 2026) compresses LLMs with this 
objective. IO-SVD approximates the true Fisher 
matrix through two reductions: it retains only the 
effect of a perturbation at a given position on the 
2
prediction at that same position, and it restricts the 
predictive distribution to its most probable tokens, 
renormalized. Both reductions are deterministic, 
so the resulting bias does not vanish as the calibra­
tion set grows (Appendix D.5.1).
Complete-SVD. Our objective is the 𝐿2 func­
tional distance between the original and com­
pressed networks, i.e., the mean squared Euclidean 
distance between their logits over the data distri­
bution. Every logit change is thus penalized with 
equal weight, whereas the Fisher objectives weight 
each logit change by the observed next token or by 
the probabilities that the model predicts on the cal­
ibration contexts (Figure 1, panel b). We find that 
the uniform weighting better preserves perplexity 
on corpora other than the calibration one (Figure 1, 
panel c). A Kronecker-factored approximation (K-
FAC) (Martens and Grosse, 2015; Eschenhagen et 
al., 2023) of the objective reduces the objective 
to a weighted SVD with a closed-form solution. 
Its two weights are the input covariance Σinput 
of activation-aware methods and the Gram matrix 
Σgrad of the logit Jacobians, which measures how 
strongly each direction of the layer output affects 
the logits.
Tractable estimation. The choice of objective 
also determines the cost of the output-side weight. 
The empirical Fisher is inexpensive because it 
involves only the loss, a single scalar whose gra­
dient takes one backward pass per sequence. The 
KL and 𝐿2 objectives involve every logit at every 
position, and computing Σgrad exactly takes one 
backward pass per vocabulary entry and per posi­
tion, tens of millions per sequence for Llama 2-7B. 
The linearity of the LM head absorbs the vocabu­
lary exactly, without any estimation, into the 𝐷×
𝐷 Gram matrix of the LM-head weights, with 𝐷 
the hidden dimension: the number of backward 
passes per output position drops from 𝑉 to 𝐷, 
a factor of about 31 for Llama 3-8B (𝑉≈128k, 
𝐷= 4096), and the resulting expression of Σgrad 
is still exact. Random probes with random signs 
on the output positions then yield an unbiased 
estimator of Σgrad costing 𝐾 backward passes per 
sequence, independently of the vocabulary size 
and the sequence length. With probes drawn from 
the predictive distribution, the same construction 
gives an unbiased estimator of the true Fisher, 
which yields KL-SVD, the KL objective of IO-
SVD without its reductions (see Appendix D.5.1 
for details). Comparing KL-SVD with Complete-
SVD then separates the choice of objective from 
the approximation used to compute it.
Our contributions are the following.
• Complete functional norm. We extend the 
functional-norm objective of Kalle et al. 
(2025) from the upstream network to the 
full model, and reduce it to a closed-form 
weighted SVD that penalizes all logit changes 
equally (Section 2.2).
• An unbiased estimator of Σgrad whose 
cost is 𝐾 backward passes per sequence, 
independently of the vocabulary size and 
the sequence length, validated against the 
exact matrix at reduced scale (Section 2.3). 
Drawing the probes from the predictive dis­
tribution, the same construction yields an 
unbiased estimator of the true Fisher matrix 
𝐹𝑠 at the same cost. Substituting it for Σgrad 
gives KL-SVD, the KL objective of IO-SVD 
without its reductions, which we show to be 
deterministic deviations from 𝐹𝑠 that persist 
for any calibration budget (Appendix D.5). 
KL-SVD shares every other component with 
Complete-SVD and therefore isolates the 
effect of the objective from that of its estima­
tion.
• Empirical evaluation. On Mistral-7B, Llama 
3-8B and Qwen3-8B calibrated on Wiki­
Text-2 with uniform ranks, Complete-SVD 
achieves the lowest C4 and PTB perplexity 
among all compared methods at both tested 
compression ratios (0.9 and 0.7). On Llama 
3-8B at ratio 0.9, it reduces PTB perplexity 
from 30.9 with IO-SVD, the strongest prior 
baseline, to 23.0. Without fine-tuning and 
combined with GPTQ, Complete-SVD com­
presses Llama 2-7B from 13.5 GB to 1.9 GB 
at a WikiText-2 perplexity of 16.7 (Section 3).

SlotFlow-GB: A Neural Framework for Trans-Dimensional Inference
of Overlapping Galactic Binaries
Niklas Houba,1, ∗Giovanni Giarda,1 and Davide Piras1, 2
1Institute for Particle Physics and Astrophysics, ETH Z¨urich, 8093 Z¨urich, Switzerland
2ETHZ Space Center, ETH Z¨urich, 8006 Z¨urich, Switzerland
The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will observe the millihertz gravitational-wave sky,
including millions of long-lived Galactic binaries (GBs), tens of thousands of which are expected
to be individually resolvable throughout the mission’s lifetime. Extracting these sources requires
jointly determining their number and physical parameters from strongly overlapping signals, posing
a computationally demanding trans-dimensional inference problem.
We introduce SlotFlow-GB,
a neural framework that constructs a learned approximation to the trans-dimensional posterior,
producing a probability distribution over source multiplicity and parameter densities for individual
binaries in a single evaluation, without requiring their number to be specified in advance.
We
demonstrate this framework using year-long LISA simulations containing up to ten binaries within
a 2 µHz frequency interval, focusing on a high-SNR regime in which source overlap, rather than
individual-source detectability, is the primary challenge. The inferred source count differs from the
true count by at most one in 94% of cases, while the model identifies individual binaries even when
their signals overlap strongly in frequency. A complete evaluation, including parameter sampling,
takes just 41 ms per band on one NVIDIA GH200 GPU, or 530 ms on eight laptop CPU threads. We
further demonstrate that these distributions can be used to initialize subsequent likelihood-based
inference, connecting fast amortized predictions with joint parameter estimation.
I.
INTRODUCTION
The millihertz gravitational-wave sky contains a large
population of Galactic binaries (GBs), tens of thousands
of which are expected to be individually resolvable by
the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) mis-
sion [1, 2]. Their signals are present simultaneously in
the data, and those from nearby frequencies can overlap
strongly. Recovering GB signals in a crowded band re-
quires solving two coupled problems: determining how
many binaries are present, and inferring the physical
parameters of each one.
Because the number of un-
known parameters changes with the number of super-
posed GB signals, the inference task is intrinsically trans-
dimensional.
Early studies showed that overlapping GBs could be
recovered using blocked annealed sampling with a vari-
able number of sources [3] and reversible-jump Markov
chain Monte Carlo [4, 5].
These methods were sub-
sequently developed into trans-dimensional global fits
that jointly infer multiple source populations and instru-
mental noise.
For instance, variable GB counts have
been treated with reversible-jump sampling [6–8], while
product-space model selection has also been suggested for
this problem [9, 10]. Other approaches construct the cat-
alog iteratively through repeated search and threshold-
ing [11]. Such analyses have been demonstrated on LISA
Data Challenge simulated datasets [12], including GPU-
accelerated implementations for large-scale inference [8].
∗nhouba@phys.ethz.ch
Neural posterior estimation [13–15] offers a different
strategy.
Instead of analyzing sources by exploring
the likelihood, a neural estimator is trained on simu-
lations to map the data directly to probability distri-
butions over candidate sources and their parameters.
This approach has become effective for current ground-
based gravitational-wave observations, where compact-
binary mergers can generally be treated as isolated
events [16, 17]. The DINGO package, for example, pro-
duces posterior samples for detected signals from ground-
based detectors in seconds [18, 19].
Space-borne gravitational-wave detectors such as LISA
present a different regime. The data is expected to be
signal dominated [2, 20], so parameter estimation can-
not generally be separated from determining how many
sources are present.
Neural posterior estimators have
been developed for individual sources in LISA [21] and,
more recently, for pairs of overlapping GBs [22]. These
models retain a fixed-dimensional inference target and
therefore take the number of sources as given.
Inference over a variable number of components has
been investigated in several settings within machine
learning.
Variational methods can represent variable-
dimensional distributions [23]; trans-dimensional flow-
matching posterior estimation can target astronomical
time series [24]; and our earlier SlotFlow work combined
slot-based representations with conditional normalizing
flows for sinusoidal and Gaussian mixtures [25].
However, extending these ideas to GBs in LISA is sub-
stantially demanding: each source has eight physical pa-
rameters, and distinguishing signals that overlap strongly
in frequency requires exploiting LISA’s time- and sky-
dependent response [26, 27].
arXiv:2611.26057v1  [astro-ph.IM]  19 Nov 2026
2
We introduce SlotFlow-GB, a neural framework for
end-to-end trans-dimensional inference that represents
an unknown population of Galactic binaries through a
distribution over source multiplicity and parameter den-
sities for individual sources.
It combines a fixed pool
of competing source slots [28], with no predefined as-
signment to individual binaries; a permutation-invariant
training loss that uses one-to-one matching to associate
predicted slots with injected sources [29]; and condi-
tional normalizing flows [30] that represent an eight-
dimensional parameter density for each candidate. These
densities retain correlations between individual source
parameters, but not between different sources.
We use this architecture to address four questions:
• Can one learned model estimate source counts and
parameter distributions for an unknown number of
overlapping GBs?
• Which information in the LISA response allows bi-
naries that strongly overlap in frequency to be dis-
tinguished?
• What is lost when the joint posterior is approxi-
mated by the marginal parameter densities of each
source?
• Can the candidate sources identified by SlotFlow-
GB provide useful initial conditions for subsequent
likelihood-based inference?
The paper is organized as follows. Section II defines
the inference problem and simulated data. Section III
introduces the SlotFlow-GB architecture and its proba-
bilistic representation of the sources. Section IV presents
several results, ranging from the evaluation of source
recovery, source counting, and source parameter uncer-
tainty to a demonstration of how SlotFlow-GB can guide
likelihood-based inference.
Section V summarizes our
conclusions and outlook.
II.
PROBLEM SETUP
The goal of inference is to determine, from the super-
position of all the GBs in a band, both how many are
present and the physical parameters of each. For a band
containing K binaries, we write the observation as

Exchanging the
labels of two binaries leaves the data unchanged, so

therefore recover the same sources regardless of how they
are assigned to its output slots. The natural inference
target is thus an unordered set of sources whose number
is unknown, which is the object SlotFlow-GB is designed
to approximate.
A.
Simulation domain
We simulate Tobs = 360 days of LISA observations in
the second-generation time-delay interferometry (TDI)
channels A, E, and T [31, 32], adopting the equal-arm
limit in which their instrumental noise is uncorrelated.
Each observation contains K GBs, with K drawn uni-
formly from {0, . . . , 10}. Including observations without
sources allows the network to learn when no binary is
present. The binary reference frequencies f0,i are con-
fined to a 2 µHz region near 3 mHz. We refer to one real-
ization of the source population and instrumental noise
as a scene.
The source frequencies are drawn uniformly within
±1 µHz of a common center frequency. For each scene,
this center is drawn uniformly within ±2 µHz of 3 mHz.
The network is not given the true center frequency. In-
stead, it receives an approximate center fc, obtained by
adding an independent uniform offset within ±30 nHz
to the true center.
This mimics the uncertainty of a
preceding frequency-localization step, which we do not
explicitly model. In contrast to a fixed band segmenta-
tion, however, the analyzed frequency window is not cen-
tered on fc. Instead, fc guides a search for the strongest
spectral peak, around which the window is then centered
(Sec. III A).
The remaining source parameters are drawn indepen-
dently.
The gravitational-wave amplitude A is sam-
pled log-uniformly over [10−22, 10−20], and the frequency
derivative
˙f
log-uniformly over [10−17, 10−15] Hz s−1.
Sky positions are isotropic, with ecliptic longitude λ uni-
form on [0, 2π] and sin β uniform on [−1, 1]. We draw
cos ι uniformly on [−1, 1], polarization angle ψ uniformly
on [0, π], and initial phase ϕ0 uniformly on [0, 2π]. These
distributions define the source priors used for training
and for the evaluation sets of Sec. II B, except where the
latter deliberately fix individual parameters in order to
isolate a specific effect.
3
The amplitude range is chosen to produce a deliber-
ately loud population rather than to reproduce the astro-
physical GB population. This allows us to study source
overlap and confusion in a regime where individual-
source detectability is generally not the dominant lim-
itation.
We generate the GB waveforms with jaxgb [33], as-
suming circular binaries with constant frequency drift,
and compute the LISA response using equal-armlength
orbits from lisaorbits [34]. The source frequencies oc-
cupy a 2 µHz interval in each scene, but the waveforms
are retained over a 128 µHz band centered on 3 mHz,
which comfortably contains the full signal response. We
add stationary Gaussian instrumental noise, generated
independently in the Fourier domain for each TDI chan-
nel using the one-sided SciRDv1 power spectral den-
sities implemented in lisatools [35, 36].
The noise
is simulated across the 1 mHz to 5 mHz range, and we
do not include an unresolved Galactic foreground. For
the full 360-day observation, the frequency-bin width is
δfbin = 1/Tobs = 32.15 nHz.
We simulate 2 × 106 scenes and train on the first 98%
of them, holding out the remainder as a validation split
(Sec. II B). Figure 1 illustrates one such simulated scene
containing seven overlapping GBs.
Their different re-
sponses in the A and E channels provide information
that helps distinguish sources with nearby frequencies.
B.
Evaluation sets
We evaluate SlotFlow-GB on three sets of simulated
scenes, summarized in Table I. All use the waveform and
noise model of Sec. II A and differ in how the source
parameters are sampled.
The population set measures
source counting and parameter recovery across the train-
ing distribution. The two-source set examines how fre-
quency separation, angular separation, and amplitude
contrast affect the recovery of overlapping binaries. The
multiplicity grid tests how recovery changes as the num-
ber of sources increases at approximately fixed frequency
spacing.
The population set is drawn from the held-out valida-
tion split of the training distribution.
This split com-
prises the final 2% of the 2 × 106 simulated scenes and
is disjoint from the training data.
We evaluate 20 480
scenes spanning the full range of source counts from zero
to ten.
The two-source set contains scenes with exactly two
GBs.
We characterize each pair by its frequency sep-
aration ∆f = |f0,1 −f0,2|, angular separation ∆Ω=
arccos(ˆn1·ˆn2), and amplitude ratio RA = Afaint/Aloud ≤
1, where ˆni denotes the unit vector toward binary i,
Afaint (Aloud) is the amplitude of the fainter (louder)
source, and smaller values of RA correspond to larger
differences in source amplitude.
We first consider a broadly sampled two-source set in
which ∆f and RA are drawn independently from log-
uniform distributions and ∆Ωfrom an isotropic angu-
lar distribution, rather than obtaining their joint distri-
bution from the training prior. The frequency separa-
tion extends to 4 µHz, beyond the maximum separation
of 2 µHz allowed by the training distribution. We then
consider controlled configurations with prescribed values
of ∆f, ∆Ω, and RA: a grid spanning all three quanti-
ties and three sets of one-dimensional cuts in which one
quantity is varied while the others are held fixed. These
experiments allow us to examine the effects of frequency
separation, sky separation, and relative source strength
separately.
The multiplicity grid test set increases the number of
sources while keeping their characteristic frequency spac-
ing approximately fixed. We consider K ∈{2, 3, 5, 10},
placing the source frequencies on a grid with nominal
spacing 200 nHz and a ±5% jitter to avoid exactly peri-
odic separations. The median minimum nearest-neighbor
separation decreases only from 200 nHz at K = 2 to
187 nHz at K = 10. This construction allows us to study
the effect of increasing source crowding without system-
atically reducing the characteristic separation between
neighboring binaries.
We quote the optimal SNR of an individual binary,

fined in Appendix B with instrumental noise only. Other
binaries in the scene and the unresolved Galactic fore-
ground are not included as additional noise in this defini-
tion. In the broadly sampled two-source set, the median
single-source SNR is 515, with the central 90% spanning
approximately 49–5400. The evaluated population also
includes sources with SNRs as low as ρ ≈30.
III.
METHODS
SlotFlow-GB maps a LISA observation directly to an
unordered set of candidate binaries and their parameter
densities in a single network evaluation, without perform-
ing a separate likelihood-based search. A fixed pool of
candidate source slots represents the set, with each slot
either describing one binary or remaining empty. Each
slot predicts an existence probability and conditions a
shared normalizing flow for the eight physical parameters
of its candidate source. These predictions provide both a
distribution over the number of binaries and parameter
densities for the individual sources. Figure 2 summarizes
the six stages of the method.
A.
Data representation and competing source slots
The input consists of the year-long TDI A, E, and

ABSTRACT
Comparison-based optimization uses ordinal feedback to minimize an objective
without observing numerical values. Sign-based methods estimate a local gradient
direction from symmetric perturbation pairs, retaining only the within-pair com-
parison signs. With complete batch rankings, these methods discard cross-pair
orders from the same endpoint evaluations. We study fixed-center recovery when
the nonlinear component is an unknown differentiable even nuisance, taking equal
values at opposite query points as in quadratic objectives. Combining reversed
cross-pair comparisons cancels shared nuisance offsets and yields constraints on
relative gradient projections without estimating a Hessian. An algorithm-agnostic
geometric framework characterizes candidate gradient directions consistent with
the batch ranking. We measure the nuisance by its relative shell variation τa, the
range of the nuisance on a radius-a sphere divided by a∥g∥, where g̸ = 0 is the
gradient in d dimensions. When τa ≤cε/

with Θ(d/ε) for sign-only recovery on the same class. This whole-cell guarantee
requires no variation bound as input to the decoder and matches a lower bound up
to logarithmic factors. Conversely, over well-conditioned positive-definite quadrat-
ics with no common bound on curvature relative to the gradient scale, complete
rankings offer no asymptotic minimax evaluation advantage over signs, even across
multiple feedback rounds. On two ridge-regression tasks under joint evaluation
and feedback-round caps, Reverse attains lower terminal relative optimization gaps
than Mirror and unit-normalized ranking-based zeroth-order stochastic gradient
descent (ZO-RankSGD) in separate cohorts. These experiments do not establish an
additional optimization benefit from Full over Reverse.

INTRODUCTION
In many black-box optimization and preference-learning problems, direct access to numerical ob-
jective values is unavailable, and the optimizer observes only ordinal comparisons (Cai et al., 2022;
Zhang & Ying, 2025; Ren et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). When candidate points are evaluated in a
batch, a ranking oracle returns their ordering in one feedback round (Tang et al., 2024; Saha et al.,
2024), separating query evaluations from round synchronizations.
Comparison-based baselines (Lobanov et al., 2024; Saha et al., 2025) query antipodal pairs ±xi
around the current iterate and keep only within-pair signs, discarding cross-pair orders from the
same batch. Sequential adaptive comparison methods achieve optimal Θ(d log(1/ε)) complexity
given supplied smoothness and gradient-norm bounds (Tao et al., 2026), at the price of multi-round
feedback. This raises a central question: when do batch rankings outperform within-pair signs?
At the current iterate, we study f(x) = F(θc + x) with f(x) = b + g⊤x + E(x). Here b = F(θc),
g = ∇F(θc)̸ = 0, and u = g/ ∥g∥is the unit gradient direction. The unknown component is
differentiable and even: E(−x) = E(x) and E(0) = 0. Every quadratic satisfies this decomposition
identically without knowing the Hessian, and general smooth objectives fit it via the calibrated

Opposite cross-pair orderings cancel this shared offset difference. Mirror keeps within-pair signs,
Reverse adds two-pair offset-cancelling orders, and Full enforces the complete batch ranking with
shared pair offsets (Figure 1). Small relative shell variation enables nearly optimal one-round whole-

This paper makes three contributions.
• We characterize Mirror, Reverse, and Full as nested consistency sets, explaining how shared-offset
cancellation extracts additional directional information from a fixed ranking (Section 2).
• We prove a nearly optimal conditional one-round recovery bound and a separate endpoint–round
barrier for unbounded relative curvature, identifying both the opportunity and the limit of ranking
information (Theorems 2 and 3).
• We evaluate information, point estimation, optimization, and computation separately, including
evidence of Full’s extra constraints and the absence of an established ridge-optimization benefit
beyond Reverse (Sections 4 and 6).

Reference-Free Humanoid Skateboarding via Termination-Shaped
Reinforcement Learning
Ganeshvar Soenessardien, Michael Przystupa and Kevin Sebastian Luck
Abstract— Humanoid locomotion research has advanced
rapidly on walking and running, but object-mediated locomotion,
in which a robot must coordinate its body with a passive
external object, remains difficult. One challenging task is
skateboarding, which requires simultaneous interaction with
the ground and a passive but movable platform to achieve
forward motion. Current methods for tackling skateboarding
with humanoid robots either require human demonstrations
or utilise analytic steering models that require system iden-
tification. In this paper, we introduce a deep reinforcement
learning framework that does not rely on prior data such as
demonstrations and enables robots such as the K1 humanoid
to learn to skateboard using model-free learning. The method
combines task rewards with exploit-blocking terminations. We
introduce a number of constraints restricting behaviours such
as losing the planted board foot, standing with both feet
on the board, excessive twisting, separation from the board,
and unstable board motion. Their changing prevalence during
training produces an implicit progression from stance control
towards sustained robot–board locomotion. Experiments are
performed on a simulated K1 humanoid robot in Mujoco. The
results demonstrate the feasibility of reference-free humanoid-
object locomotion with modest hardware constraints while
identifying limitations in movement style, statistical precision,
reproducibility and eventual hardware transfer.
I. INTRODUCTION
Humanoid robots can now walk, balance, recover from
pushes and traverse rough terrain using learned controllers
trained in massively parallel simulators [1]–[4]. Almost all
of these skills involve direct contact between the robot’s feet
and a static support surface. However, a large and practically
important class of behaviours is more difficult to master:
locomotion tasks in which a robot has to interact with a
passive object, that is neither actuated nor rigidly attached
to the body, to achieve movement. Pushing a cart, riding
a scooter, balancing on a mobility aid, or skateboarding all
share this structure. The object stores momentum, introduces
its own contact dynamics and can fail in ways the robot does
not always directly control [5]–[9].
Skateboarding is a particularly demanding instance of
object-mediated locomotion and therefore a useful bench-
mark for embodied artificial intelligence. To locomote with a
skateboard, a humanoid must keep one foot on a small, freely
rolling deck, and use the other foot to generate propulsion
against the ground while regulating the contacts among
three coupled bodies (robot, board and ground). Misplaced

contacts can induce foot slip, unwanted board rotation, incor-
rect foot-board contact patterns, failed phase transitions, or
degeneration into merely pushing the board rather than riding
it. Success therefore requires contact rich whole-body con-
trol, robot-object coordination and stable locomotion through
an under-actuated external system simultaneously [9]–[12].
This paper investigates applying reinforcement learning to
humanoid locomotion on a skateboard-like platform without
the use of task-specific priors used by recent humanoid
skateboarding systems. HUSKY, for example, achieves ag-
ile real-world humanoid skateboarding by combining Ad-
versarial Motion Priors (AMP) [13] from human pushing
demonstrations with a physics-guided lean-to-steer model
and trajectory-guided phase transitions, and validates the
resulting controller on real hardware [9]. Such reference data
and engineering are powerful when available, but they also
make the method depend on human demonstrations, physical
modelling and task-specific integration which are often not
available or hard to obtain. Furthermore, such data may be
hard to utilize due to the existence of the correspondence
problem between robot and human embodiment [14], [15].
This paper focuses on the harder and complementary case
of reference-free learning [16]. The controller receives no
motion-capture trajectory, no target joint-posture sequence,
and no explicit posture-tracking reward that tells it what
skating should look like. The skateboarding behaviour must
be selected and emerge by learning from the task reward,
the reset geometry and the early termination conditions. The
question is whether recognisable humanoid-board locomo-
tion can emerge from this minimal supervision alone and
what behaviour appears when no human motion prior is
present to shape its style.
Contribution:
The objective is to design, train, and eval-
arXiv:2611.26054v1  [cs.RO]  19 Nov 2026
uate a reference free reinforcement-learning controller that
enables a Booster K1 humanoid to propel a passive four-
wheel roller board forward while remaining upright, keeping
one foot on the board and using the other to push on the
ground. Three research questions structure the work:
RQ1 Feasibility and extent. To what extent can a Booster K1
humanoid learn recognisable skateboard propulsion without
any reference motion or explicit posture-tracking reward, and
what is the character of the resulting behaviour?
RQ2 Mechanism. Which reward and termination design
choices are necessary to prevent trivial exploit solutions and
steer the policy toward skating-like mechanics?
RQ3 Consistency and cost. How consistent is the learned
behaviour across independent seeds when trained under a
constrained hardware budget, and what does that budget
permit and preclude?
II. RELATED WORK
A. Humanoid and Legged Locomotion
The current generation of learned legged controllers is
enabled by GPU-accelerated simulators that run thousands
of environments in parallel, including Isaac Gym [17] and
MuJoCo-based frameworks such as mjlab, which is used in
this paper [18], [19]. Rudin et al. [20] learned quadruped
walking in minutes with massively parallel PPO, and learned
humanoid walking controllers have since been transferred to
real hardware [1], [21]. These works establish the simulation-
and-PPO recipe adopted here, but target locomotion over
static terrain; this paper adds a passive, freely rolling object
into the support chain.
B. Reference-Based and Reference-Free Motion Learning
A common strategy for natural looking physics-based mo-
tion is to supervise the policy with human or animal motion
data. DeepMimic tracks reference clips using an imitation
reward [22], while Adversarial Motion Priors (AMP) replace
explicit trajectory tracking with a learned discriminator that
rewards motions matching the statistics of a reference dataset
[13]. These methods are powerful because they inject a
strong prior over what motion should look like. The comple-
mentary line, to which this paper belongs, removes that prior:
Heess et al. showed that rich locomotion behaviours can
emerge from task reward and environment design alone [23].
This reference-free setting is often harder because the reward
can be underspecified and may admit many qualitatively
different solutions [16]. In particular, without a reference it is
difficult to converge to smooth motion that does not exploit
simulator artefacts. Characterising the solution that emerges
for humanoid skateboarding is a central aim here.
C. Robots on Dynamic Platforms and Skateboarding
Skating and rolling-platform locomotion have a long his-
tory in model-based robotics. Classical work analyses the
skateboard as a human-controlled non-holonomic system
[24], [25], while humanoid skating has been controlled
using model-based real-time balance and foot-force control
[11]. More recently, learning-based and optimisation-based
methods have been applied to legged robots on dynamic plat-
forms: quadrupeds have been taught to skateboard through
optimisation-based control [26] and to mount a skateboard
with reverse-curriculum learning [27]; hybrid automata learn-
ing has been applied to legged skateboarding [12] and
roller-skate-style swizzle gaits have been synthesised for a
humanoid [28].
The most direct point of comparison is HUSKY, a physics-
aware whole-body controller that enables a Unitree G1
humanoid to perform agile, humanlike skateboarding with
pushing, lean-to-steer turning and phase transitions, validated
in both simulation and the real world. The HUSKY system
is an instructive contrasting system to the work presented in
this paper. HUSKY achieves a natural stroke by learning an
AMP style reward from human pushing demonstrations [13],
derives steering from an explicit board-tilt/truck-steering
kinematic model, plans trajectories to bridge phases, and
performs sim-to-real identification of the physical board [9].
This paper instead removes the motion prior entirely, restricts
the task to a single push phase, replaces analytic steering
and trajectory planning with a termination-shaped feasibility
set, and stays in simulation on consumer hardware. The
reference-free result here is therefore best read as a lower
bound on what minimal supervision can achieve and provides
an empirical explanation on the value motion priors provide
for producing natural, agile skating.
III. PROBLEM STATEMENT
We investigate the problem of learning how to locomote
forward using a passively moved mobile platform (i.e.,
skateboarding) with reinforcement learning. We model the
problem as a contextual Markov Decision Process (cMDP)
(S, A, C, p(c), p(s0), p(st+1|st, at), r(st, at, c), γ) [29], [30].
The physical state is represented by 44 generalized positions
and 42 generalized velocities, hence S ⊂R86. Our context

A. Robot, Board, and World
The task is implemented in mjlab [19] using MuJoCo

is the Booster K1 humanoid [32]. The environment is a
flat 4 m × 4 m plane containing an unactuated four-wheel

overall, with an 18 mm deck thickness and a mass of 4.22 kg)
[33], which the robot can influence only through foot contact.
Episodes are capped at 1,000 control steps (20 s at a 50 Hz
policy rate over 200 Hz physics).

IV. METHODS
We solve the previously described MDP using proximal
policy optimisation (PPO) [34] setup with two task specific
components: a reward stack that favours conservative skating
over standing still or kicking the board (Section IV-D)
and early terminations whose changing dominance during
training induces an implicit curriculum (Section IV-E).
A. Observation Design
The actor receives an 89 dimensional observation ot
concatenated with the three-dimensional command c, giving
a 92 dimensional input. Table I lists its components and
corruptions. The critic receives 102 inputs: noise-free obser-

C. PPO Training Setup
The actor and critic are neural networks with hidden
dimensions (512, 256, 128), ELU activations, and input nor-
malisation. The actor parameterises a diagonal Gaussian
policy with an observation-dependent mean and a learned,
observation-independent log standard deviation for each of
the 22 action dimensions, initialised to 0 (standard deviation

deterministic estimate of the value. PPO uses 24 rollout steps
per environment, 5 learning epochs, 8 minibatches, discount
γ = 0.99, GAE λ = 0.95, entropy coefficient 0.005, clip
parameter ϵ = 0.2, clipped value loss with coefficient 1.0,
maximum gradient norm 1.0 and an adaptive learning rate
initialised at 10−3 with a target KL divergence of 0.01. Each
run uses 6,144 parallel environments. The actor is initialised

E. Termination-Shaped Curriculum
Unlike the standard fall and time-limit terminations, the
task-specific terminations below restrict which robot–board
interactions remain feasible. Such terminations act as hard
constraints; constrained RL formalises them explicitly [37]–
[39], and CaT [40] likewise enforces locomotion constraints
through terminations. We use plain terminations without a
constraint formalism and leave such a formulation to future
work. The principal curriculum driver is board_foot_-
displaced. At reset, the initial board-frame position of
the on-board foot is recorded and the episode terminates

The remaining terminations remove specific failure modes
