Fixing the Twin, Not the Detector: Sim-to-Real
Roadside LiDAR Detection from Digital-Twin Data
KuanLin Chen1,2,*  Feng-jui Kuo2
1Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Chung Yuan Christian University, Taoyuan, Taiwan
2Tacitt, Karma Laboratories, Inc., Baltimore, MD, USA
s11224246@cycu.edu.tw, raykuo@karmalabs.ai
*Corresponding author
Accepted for publication in the IEEE BigData 2026 Cup proceedings (UCF UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge). © 2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted.
Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses, in any current or future media, including reprinting/republishing this material for advertising or promotional purposes, creating
new collective works, for resale or redistribution to servers or lists, or reuse of any copyrighted component of this work in other works.
Abstract—Roadside LiDAR detectors are expensive to train on
real labels, and digital twins promise to replace these labels, but a
detector trained on a twin meets a different sensor, different ob­‐
jects and different annotation conventions on the real site. We de­‐
scribe the pipeline that placed first in the LUMPI track of the
UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge (IEEE BigData 2026
Cup, 0.5541 combined score) and fifth on its V2X-Real track
(0.8102). Every detector is a CenterPoint model trained only on
synthetic data, on a single 8 GB laptop GPU. Most of the gain
came from correcting differences between the twin and the real
site rather than from the detector. We align the twin’s coordi­‐
nates, point density and box convention with the test sensor, gen­‐
erate the pedestrians and riders that the twins lack, plus street
clutter as unlabeled negatives, and rebuild twin objects at real
size and real point density. A non-learned resampling to the per-
cell point density of unlabeled real frames lifts LUMPI realism
from 0.589 to 0.947, against 0.949 between real frames. Label-free
post-processing then exploits what a fixed roadside sensor guar­‐
antees: static structures recur in every frame, and real objects
have characteristic point statistics. Reporting the validation and
test gain of each component side by side, we find that corrections
of systematic sim-to-real differences transfer to the test set, typi­‐
cally keeping a quarter to three quarters of their validation gain,
while choices that fit the few objects of a validation set do not.
Index Terms—LiDAR, 3D object detection, sim-to-real, digital
twin, synthetic data, roadside perception, domain gap
I. Introduction
Roadside LiDAR sensors watch intersections from a fixed
pose and feed traffic monitoring and cooperative driving.
Training their 3D detectors needs labeled frames from each
site, which are slow and costly to collect. Digital twins of the
sites, rendered in a driving simulator, could supply unlimited
labeled data, but a detector trained on a twin meets a different
sensor pattern, different objects and different annotation con­‐
ventions on the real site.
The UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge [1] tests this
setting directly. Detectors may be trained only on synthetic
data and are scored on real frames of two intersections:
LUMPI in Hannover [2] and V2X-Real in Los Angeles [3].
Each submission holds 50 synthetic frames, scored for realism
against hidden real frames, and detections on 50 released real
test frames, scored by 3D mean average precision (mAP). The
organizers provide UrbanTwin digital twins of both sites [4]–
[6].
We ask three questions:
RQ1. Which differences between a digital twin and the real
site limit a detector trained only on the twin, and how much
of this gap can be closed by correcting the synthetic data,
with real data used only for statistics and validation?
(Sections IV and VII)
RQ2. What can label-free post-processing gain from the
fixed pose of a roadside sensor, and where does it stop?
(Sections VI and VII)
RQ3. When real frames may be used only for validation,
which validation gains carry over to the test set? (Sections
VII and IX)
We found that most of the achievable gain lies in the twin it­‐
self. Four differences between twin and test data decided the
score: the twins contain no walking pedestrians; twin frames
carry about 220,000 points while test frames are cropped to
50,000; twin objects are smaller and sparser than real objects,
and their boxes are tighter than real annotations; and the
LUMPI twin is offset from the real sensor frame. Correcting
these at the source, in the training and realism data, moved the
score more than any change to the detector or its post-
processing.
Our contributions answer these questions:
1. Source-level correction of the twin, guided only by
statistics of real labels and unlabeled real frames: twin
frames are aligned with the test sensor in coordinates,
density and box convention; objects are rebuilt at real
median size and real point density, extending size
normalization [7] to point density; and the pedestrians,
riders and street clutter that the twins lack are synthesized
procedurally, the clutter as unlabeled negatives.
2. A realism generator without any learned model: exact per-
cell density matching to unlabeled real frames lifts the
LUMPI realism score from 0.589 to 0.947, against 0.949
between real frames, and is the largest gain of our pipeline
(+0.14 combined).

3. Label-free post-processing that exploits a fixed sensor:
priors for structures that recur in every frame, point-feature
rules for real objects, and point-fitted box geometry.
4. A validation protocol on non-forbidden real frames, with
candidates and thresholds fixed before evaluation in the
final selection rounds, and an ablation that compares
validation and test gains. Corrections of systematic sim-to-
real differences typically kept a quarter to three quarters of
their validation gain on test, and the final LUMPI round,
validated on in-window frames recorded in the same
sessions as the test frames, kept about 85%. Choices fitted
to the few objects of a validation set lost on test.
The pipeline (Fig. 1) placed first in the LUMPI track
(0.5541 combined score) and fifth on V2X-Real (0.8102), with
every model trained on a single 8 GB laptop GPU. Section IX
distills six take-aways for training detectors on digital twins.
II. Related work
LiDAR simulation. Driving simulators such as CARLA [8]
render labeled LiDAR scans of virtual scenes, and the
UrbanTwin datasets [4], [5] use it to reproduce the LUMPI
and V2X-Real intersections. LiDARsim [9] narrows the gap
by building assets from real scans and learning the sensor’s
dropout, and domain randomization [10] trains on wide syn­‐
thetic variation so that the real data looks like one more varia­‐
tion. The challenge allows neither real scans in training nor a
learned real sensor model, so we correct the synthetic data
with a few statistics of real data instead.
Cross-domain 3D detection. Wang et al. [7] showed that
the gap between driving datasets is dominated by object size,
and that rescaling source objects to the target’s mean size re­‐
covers much of it. Self-training on unlabeled target frames, as
in ST3D [11], is the other main family, but it puts real frames
into training and is excluded here. Our real-size rebuilding of
twin objects applies the insight of [7] to a sim-to-real setting
and extends it to point density.
Roadside detection. Fixed infrastructure sensors appear in
LUMPI [2], V2X-Real [3] and DAIR-V2X [12]. We build on
the voxel detectors of OpenPCDet [13]: CenterPoint [14] as
the base model, ground-truth sampling from SECOND [15],
one Voxel R-CNN [16] member, and weighted box fusion [17]
to combine members. A fixed pose makes the background re­‐
peat in every frame, which our site priors exploit.
Point-cloud realism. The challenge scores the synthetic
frames with the Chamfer distance (CD) and earth mover’s dis­‐
tance (EMD) [18], the Fréchet point-cloud distance (FPD) [19]
and maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) [20] between pooled
synthetic and real points. These compare coarse 3D occu­‐
pancy, not individual objects, which is why per-cell density
matching is effective.
Earlier solutions. At an earlier edition of this challenge,
held with the DriveX workshop at ECCV 2026, Luo et al.
[21], [22] aligned the synthetic scan density with the test data,
combined transformer- and pillar-based detectors through
class-aware fusion, and built the realism frames by matching
the radial point density. We match the density per 3D cell in­‐
stead, which reaches the real-versus-real ceiling, and also cor­‐
rect object size, object density and the missing classes at the
source.
III. Challenge, data and metrics
Each track has its own synthetic training data, real test
frames and scored classes (Table I). The 50 test frames of a
track are real, unlabeled LiDAR frames; predictions are scored
by 3D mAP, the mean over classes of the average precision
(AP), at an intersection-over-union (IoU) of 0.5 for every
class, with the 40-point interpolated AP [23] used by the
KITTI benchmark [24] and without difficulty filtering. The 50
submitted synthetic frames are compared with 50 hidden real
frames after pooling and subsampling to 10,000 points, using
the four realism metrics of Section II, each normalized to [0,
1]. The combined score is 0.6 × min(1, mAP / 0.7) + 0.4 × the
mean normalized realism. The challenge had a development
and a final phase with separate leaderboards, both scored on
the same 50 test frames.
Three rules shaped the design. Detectors may be trained or
fine-tuned only on synthetic data. The 100 frames listed as for­‐
bidden, which include the test frames, may not be used for
training, validation, tuning or inspection of ground truth. The
remaining public real data may be used for validation, model
selection and box-size statistics, unlabeled real point clouds
may be used to calibrate the synthetic data, and every use of
real data must be disclosed (Section VIII).
The UrbanTwin data provide 9,000 synthetic frames per
track (UT-LUMPI [25] and UT-V2X-Real-IC [26]) with
seven-parameter boxes (center, size, heading). The four differ­‐
ences named in Section I look as follows. The twins contain
no walking pedestrians, and UT-LUMPI has no Person labels
at all. Twin frames carry about 220,000 points, while test
frames are cropped to 50,000. Twin objects are smaller and
sparser than real ones, and twin boxes are tighter than the real
annotation convention (a real Bicycle box includes its rider).
The LUMPI twin is offset from the real sensor frame by
(−1.25, 0.25, 0.04) m.

IV. Synthetic training and realism data
A. Training frames
Each twin frame is translated into the real sensor frame,
cropped to the evaluation range and randomly subsampled to
50,000 points, so the detector only ever sees the test density.
Labels are mapped to the track’s classes, and boxes with fewer
than 5 points are dropped. Because twin boxes are smaller
than the real annotation convention, the LUMPI Bicycle, Mo­‐
torcycle, Van and Bus training boxes are rescaled toward the
size statistics of non-forbidden real labels; predicted Car boxes
are set to the real median size at inference (Section VI).
B. Procedural pedestrians, riders and clutter
Neither twin contains walking pedestrians, so we synthesize
them inside the data loader. A person is sampled on capsule
and ellipsoid primitives (height 1.6 to 1.9 m, with a walking
stride), kept only on the side facing the nearest sensors, and
thinned to a point count drawn from a log-normal model of
points versus distance, calibrated to real pedestrian point
counts (LUMPI: median 70 points at 10 m). People are placed
on open ground and receive a Person box; a crowd variant
places groups of 2 to 5 people with mutual occlusion. On the
labeled V2X-Real validation frames, two thirds of the confi­‐
dent pedestrian boxes sat on unlabeled low clusters (bollards,
bins, sign posts, shrubs, parked bikes) that the twins lack, so
we add eight kinds of procedural street clutter as unlabeled
background with the same point model. For V2X-Real, where
riders count as pedestrians, one member was further fine-tuned
with procedural riders (a bicycle, scooter or motorcycle carry­‐
ing a seated person), boxed at the median size of real rider la­‐
bels.
C. Scene augmentations
Three augmentations target the remaining differences: ran­‐
dom point dropout (keep ratio U[0.4, 1] or U[0.3, 1]) for dis­‐
tant vehicles with fewer than 20 points; a whole-scene z shift
after ground-truth sampling (U(−0.2, 0.8) m on V2X-Real,
U(−0.6, 0.2) m on LUMPI), because the real ground does not
lie at the synthetic height; and box occlusion, which drops the
points in an azimuth window covering 20 to 60% of a box or
thins them with range.
D. Real-size, real-density objects
Twin objects are both too small and too sparse (Table II). At
50,000 points the twin’s cars extend 3.4 × 1.4 m and reach 1.2
m above the ground, against 4.0 × 1.8 m and 1.5 m for real
Car labels, and real objects of every class carry about twice
the points at the same range. On V2X-Real the gap is largest
for trucks. For the final members we therefore rebuilt the
training frames from the raw twin frames. Object points and
boxes are scaled per axis about the box bottom center to the
real median size, unless the enlarged footprint would touch an­‐
other box (3% of the LUMPI cars); before the frame is cut to
50,000 points, the points of every labeled object are kept with
2.3 times the keep probability of the other points. Fine-tuning
on these frames raised raw single-member Car AP on the in-
window LUMPI frames (M4w, Section VII-A) from 0.557,
0.562 and 0.570 to 0.623, 0.629 and 0.636, and Bicycle AP
from 0.044 and 0.035 to 0.074 and 0.082. On V2X-Real, the
first of the two truck members rebuilt this way raised second-
half truck AP by 0.064, the largest single gain of the final
V2X-Real rounds (Section VII-E); the same recipe did not
help vehicles, whose twin and real sizes differ less. Thinning
the test frames toward the twin’s density instead only lost ac­‐
curacy.
E. Realism frames
The realism metrics pool the 50 synthetic frames, so coarse
3D occupancy matters, not individual objects. Raw twin
frames score 0.589 on LUMPI because the twin places its
points differently from the real sensors. Each submitted frame
is built by per-cell density matching: the evaluation range is
divided into 1 m × 1 m columns with 25 height layers, and the
target count of a cell is the point budget times the real density
of that cell, measured on unlabeled non-forbidden calibration
frames. Twin points fill a cell where enough exist, and the re­‐
mainder is drawn uniformly inside it; about 29% of the sub­‐
mitted points are twin points. On held-out check frames this
gives realism 0.947 on LUMPI, against a real-versus-real ceil­‐
ing of 0.949, and 0.951 on V2X-Real; on the leaderboard
EMD fell from 2.9 to 1.10 and FPD from 75 to 0.53. Calibrat­‐
ing on the in-window frames of the final LUMPI round (Sec­‐
tion VII-D) lowered EMD further to 1.04 and FPD to 0.29.
V. Detector and ensembles
Model. Every member is a CenterPoint detector [14] from
OpenPCDet [13]: mean voxel features, a sparse residual 3D
backbone (voxels 0.1 × 0.1 × 0.25 m, stride 8; stride 4 for the
V2X-Real pedestrian members), a bird’s-eye-view (BEV)
backbone and one center head per class group; one V2X-Real
vehicle member adds a Voxel R-CNN second stage [16]. Input
is xyz only, because the test frames carry no intensity. Base
models train for 20 to 30 epochs with Adam [27] and a one-
cycle schedule [28] (peak learning rate 0.002, batch 4) on one
laptop GPU (RTX 5060, 8 GB). Most later members are 8-
epoch fine-tunes of their parent that add exactly one synthetic
ingredient of Section IV, so each member’s contribution can
be attributed. A member and its fine-tunes form a lineage, and
a package is one complete submission: members, fusion, post-
processing and synthetic frames.
Per-class ensembles. Members are fused per class by
weighted box fusion (WBF) [17]: boxes are clustered greedily
by BEV IoU (0.4; 0.6 for V2X-Real vehicles and, in the final
package, V2X-Real trucks), and each cluster becomes one box
with the score-weighted center and size, the heading of its top-
scoring box, and a score equal to the summed member scores
divided by the number of runs. A box found by one member
only is thus down-weighted, and a weak member dilutes every
cluster it misses: removing the oldest V2X-Real vehicle mem­‐
bers added 0.0035 vehicle AP on test. Each class comes from
its own member set, so a change to one class’s members
reaches another class only through the cross-class copies and
rider boxes of Section VI.
Test-time augmentation (TTA). On V2X-Real every mem­‐
ber runs with flips (none, x, y, xy), which raised validation
mAP from 0.434 to 0.461; on LUMPI flips gained on valida­‐
tion and lost on test. Rotating the scene about the sensor axis
by ±5° (V2X-Real also ±10°) and rotating the boxes back
transferred on both tracks, with combined test gains of
+0.0042 for V2X-Real pedestrians (measured together with a
change of the vehicle fusion threshold), +0.0039 for V2X-Real
trucks, +0.0022 for LUMPI Person and +0.0039 for LUMPI
Car and Truck. A rotation changes how points fall into voxels,
which adds diversity that flips do not.
Member sets. In the final LUMPI package, Person comes
from six z-shift members of the crowd and clutter lineage,
each run at 0° and ±5°. Car comes from two real-size members
(Section IV-D) at 0° and ±5°, plus the Car boxes of a third
real-size member of the Person lineage. Bicycle comes from
the same two real-size members; Truck, Bus and Motorcycle
come from two base models, Truck and Bus with rotations.
Van comes from a base model trained on the twin as released,
the best Van source on validation. On V2X-Real, vehicle and
truck come from the dropout members and their z-shift and
occlusion fine-tunes, and pedestrian from the stride-4 mem­‐

each set on in-window frames and added the two real-size

The Delayed Societal Cost of Unfairness
Giovani de Almeida Valdrighi
giovani.valdrighi@ic.unicamp.br
Instituto de Computação
Universidade Estadual de Campinas
Campinas, Brazil
Isabel Valera†
ivalera@cs.uni-saarland.de
Department of Computer Science
Saarland University
Saarbrücken, Germany
Marcos Medeiros Raimundo†
mraimundo@ic.unicamp.br
Instituto de Computação
Universidade Estadual de Campinas
Campinas, Brazil
Abstract
Fair machine learning typically evaluates the societal costs of a decision policy—the loss in-
curred by the decision-maker (DM) and the unfair distribution of costs among demographic
groups of decision-subjects (DS)—on static data, where reducing one often comes at the ex-
pense of the other. Yet decisions change the populations on which they act, and prior work
has shown that fairness interventions designed on static data may fail to benefit, or even
harm, the disadvantaged group over time. We investigate a complementary question: When
can a policy that is Pareto-optimal on pre-deployment data be outperformed by a fairer policy
once each is evaluated on the population it induces, reducing costs for one stakeholder with-
out increasing them for the other? In a setting where qualification scores evolve in response
to binary decisions and their outcomes, we show that under Rawlsian fairness, which never
lowers any group’s acceptance rate, placing sufficiently high weight on fairness reduces soci-
etal costs whenever accepting disadvantaged DS at the DM’s break-even point leaves them
in a state less costly to the DM than rejecting them. Under egalitarian fairness, which
may lower the advantaged group’s acceptance rate, this additionally requires the reduction
in DM loss on the disadvantaged group to outweigh the increase on the advantaged group.
Under both fairness notions, however, when DM loss is accuracy-based, improvements in the
post-deployment population may arise from declining DS qualification, revealing that gains
for the DM do not necessarily translate into better outcomes for DS. Our results show that
policy-induced population dynamics can overturn apparent performance–fairness trade-offs,
allowing fairer policies to reduce the delayed societal costs of decision-making.
†Equal advising.
1
arXiv:2611.26030v1  [cs.LG]  19 Nov 2026
1
Introduction
Algorithmic decision-making in consequential applications such as lending, hiring, and school admission
imposes societal costs: decisions cost not only the decision-maker (DM) but also the decision-subjects (DS),
and these costs can be unevenly distributed across demographic groups. This motivates a multi-objective
perspective in which, alongside DM loss, we introduce the (un)fairness of decisions as a secondary objective,
reflecting DS interests (Gupta et al., 2026). Since no single policy usually minimizes both objectives, we draw
our attention to Pareto-optimal ones, where one objective cannot be improved without worsening the other.
Such policies reveal the attainable trade-offs, i.e., how much DM loss increases to reach a given fairness
level (Wei & Niethammer, 2022; Menon & Williamson, 2018), and allow stakeholders to discuss which policy
to deploy. However, optimality is only defined on the static data on which policies are evaluated.
Decisions reshape the population they act on; e.g., a hired employee gains experience that strengthens future
application. Prior work has shown that, because of these effects, policies that are fair on static data may
fail to remain fair, or may even harm DS, over time (Liu et al., 2018; D’Amour et al., 2020). Methods that
account for decision effects require how it influences DS (Rateike et al., 2024; Wen et al., 2021), which can be
highly complex, or learning by exploration (Yin et al., 2023; Kilbertus et al., 2020), which can raise ethical
concerns in certain applications, e.g., a bail decision based on a coin flip (Kilbertus et al., 2020). Thus,
commonly, researchers still assess trade-offs between performance and fairness on a historical, static dataset,
even though each policy later faces societal costs from the population it shapes.
Throughout this paper, we use lending as a motivating example (Fig. 1). We consider DS from two demo-
graphic groups that apply for a loan, and a DM aims to accept applicants with a high chance of repayment.
Because qualification can be unevenly distributed across groups, optimizing only the DM loss yields poli-
cies that serve one group poorly.
The DM collects policies θ(λ) with different trade-offs by optimizing
(1−λ) performance+λ fairness for different fairness weights λ, and stakeholders agree on one policy from
these options. Once deployed, decisions affect DS; for example, a loan can enable professional training and a
raise, or become burdensome debt. When applicants return, the same policy faces this updated population.
Hence, its DM loss and fairness depend not only on its decisions but also on how it shapes the population
it interacts with.
In this context, we ask whether the trade-off agreed on before deployment on a static dataset persists
after it: can a fairer policy θ(µ), with µ > λ, dominate θ(λ) after deployment, i.e., be at least as good on
both objectives and strictly better on one when each policy is evaluated on the population it induces? We
formalize this question within performative prediction (Perdomo et al., 2020) and restrict the comparison to
Pareto-optimal policies on the static data, since these are the ones stakeholders choose before deployment.
Dominance means that a higher fairness weight would have been better for both stakeholders. We first show
that dominance occurs when the gains from the fairer policy from reshaping the population offset its static
suboptimality in DM loss while maintaining its fairness advantage. We then specialize this condition to
lending dynamics adapted from Liu et al. (2018), covering accuracy and selective DM costs, DS costs that
recover demographic parity (Dwork et al., 2012) and equality of opportunity (Hardt et al., 2016), and two
different theories of justice, Rawlsian (Rawls, 1971) and egalitarian (Arneson, 1999). The summary of our
findings is:
1. Under Rawlsian fairness, a higher fairness weight never lowers a group’s acceptance rate nor worsens
post-deployment fairness, so dominance depends only on the DM loss. If accepting disadvantaged
DS at the DM’s break-even point leaves them in a state cheaper for the DM than rejecting them,
every weight below some λ† > 0 is dominated (Theorem 5.2).
2. Under egalitarian fairness, which can lower the advantaged group’s acceptance rate, dominance
additionally requires the DM gain on the disadvantaged group to outweigh its loss on the advantaged
group.
3. When DM loss is based on the accuracy metric (i.e., defined by false positive/negative costs), post-
deployment gains can come from lowering DS qualification, so a DM gain does not imply DS are
better off.
2
Figure 1: Illustration of the decision-making process in which stakeholders (DM and DS) assess the optimal
trade-offs between performance and fairness, agree on a policy θ(λ), and deploy it.
Once deployed, the
policy supports decisions that will reshape the population it acts on. Over time, policies incur costs from
the updated distribution and may fail to remain optimal compared to other pre-deployment Pareto-optimal
solutions.
4. On FICO data, small fairness weights are dominated under selective costs, and the minimal weight
that produces a dominant solution grows as repayments raise scores more relative to how much
defaults lower them.
2
Related Work
2.1
Performance and Fairness Trade-offs
In this work, we focus on group fairness, one of the most common fairness principles in machine learning,
which measures unfairness by how unevenly costs are distributed across demographic groups (Mehrabi et al.,
2021). In this setting, how “unfairness” is measured can also differ; e.g., egalitarian fairness (Arneson, 1999)
aims to equalize costs across groups while Rawlsian fairness (Rawls, 1971) instead minimizes the loss of the
worst-off group. A large body of work has been produced in learning fair predictors, using, for example,
constrained optimization, representation learning, and post-processing (Mehrabi et al., 2021; Zafar et al.,
2017; Zemel et al., 2013; Hardt et al., 2016). A key distinction lies between constrained and multi-objective
perspectives. While in constrained fairness (e.g., (Zafar et al., 2017; Cruz et al., 2023)), the goal is to obtain
a classifier that minimizes DM loss with an upper limit on unfairness, multi-objective instead describes
the set of attainable trade-offs, quantifying how much DM loss increases for each fairness level (Menon &
Williamson, 2018; Wei & Niethammer, 2022; Gupta et al., 2026).
Prior work has debated whether this trade-off is inevitable. Some works argue that this occurs when qual-
ifications differ across groups (Menon & Williamson, 2018; Zhao & Gordon, 2022), while others argue that
this results from biased labels against the disadvantaged group (Wick et al., 2019; Dutta et al., 2020). In
this work, we argue that conflict between DM loss and fairness can also stem from evaluating policies under
a static distribution, while such trade-offs might not persist once deployed.
2.2
Fairness in Dynamic Settings
Research on long-term fairness studies fair decision-making when decisions reshape the population they
act on; for a complete survey, see Gohar et al. (2025). A central finding is that imposing fairness at each
round may fail to ensure fairness over the full period, or even harm the disadvantaged group (Liu et al.,
2018; D’Amour et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020; Mishler & Dalmasso, 2022; Zhang et al., 2019). When DM
knows the dynamics between decisions and DS distribution, or when random exploration is possible during
learning, prior work has proposed reinforcement learning algorithms to learn long-term fair policies (Yin
et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2022; Rateike et al., 2024; Wen et al., 2021; Raab et al., 2024). One interesting
perspective is how such dynamics interact with common fair results (Somerstep et al., 2024; Jung et al.,
2020). For example, Somerstep et al. (2024) showed that the decision effects can break the incompatibility
among common fairness metrics (Chouldechova, 2017; Kleinberg et al., 2017).
3
In this work, we use the Performative Prediction (Perdomo et al., 2020) modeling approach, in which each
parametrized model induces a specific distribution observed only after deployment. Prior work has already
connected performative prediction to long-term fairness. Hu & Zhang (2022) used it to learn a policy that
controls for both short- and long-term fairness, while Jin et al. (2026) proposed smooth losses that allow
repeated retraining to reduce unfairness. To the best of our knowledge, however, no work has addressed the
relationship between dynamics and the performance-fairness trade-off.
3
Background: Performance and Fairness Multi-Objective Optimization
Following Gupta et al. (2026), we frame decision-making as a multi-objective optimization problem in which
the decision-maker (DM) balances its institutional loss against the collective burdens experienced by decision-
subjects (DS).
Modeling and Notation
DS are represented by variables (X, Y, G), where X ∈X ⊆R is a scalar
score (e.g., an uncalibrated credit score), Y ∈Y := {0, 1} is an outcome label (e.g., loan payment), and
G ∈G := {0, 1} indicates membership in a salient demographic group (e.g., defined by gender). We denote
by ρg := P(G = g) > 0 the proportion of group g, by D the marginal distribution of X, and the probability of
a positive label given score x and group g by α(x, g) := P(Y = 1 | X = x, G = g), which we call qualification.
We also write 1{·} for the indicator function. Although simplified, this formulation permits us to isolate the
trade-off between performance and fairness (Liu et al., 2018; Gupta et al., 2026; Wilms & Heitz, 2026).
